summary.title: Multi-spectral Observations of Lunar Occultations: I. Resolving The Dust Shell Around AFGL 5440
summary.authors: Paul M. Harvey, Andrew Oldag
summary.field_subfield: Astronomy / Stellar Astrophysics (AGB and post-AGB stars)

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents multi-spectral lunar occultation observations of the dust-enshrouded carbon star AFGL 5440 (OH 06.86-1.5, IRAS 18036-2344) conducted at the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope using the pMIRAS high-speed spectrophotometer. Observations were taken over a continuous wavelength range from 1 to 4 µm during an immersion occultation event on 28 August 2001. The key findings demonstrate that the observed occultation fringes cannot be fitted by any single-size model, indicating the presence of both a central stellar photosphere and a circumstellar dust shell. Radiative transfer modeling with the DUSTY code, constrained by both the occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution (SED), yields a strong constraint on the inner dust shell: a maximum temperature (Tmax) of 950 ± 50 K and an optical depth at 5 µm of 0.5 ± 0.1. The best-fit models require a density gradient of ρ ∝ r⁻² or the gradient derived by Ivezić & Elitzur for a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. A significant finding is that no model with graphite could fit the data without assuming a substantially higher past mass-loss rate or a substantial abundance of graphite, as models without graphite underfit the IRAS 60 µm flux by factors of 3 or more. The implied physical inner radius of the dust shell is 3.7 × 10¹⁴ cm, corresponding to an angular radius of 11 mas at the assumed distance of 2.25 kpc. The dust mass-loss rate is estimated at 6.5 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr, slightly higher than the 5.1 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr derived from IRAS 60 µm by Groenewegen et al. (2002). These results constrain the spatial structure of the inner circumstellar envelope and provide a direct test of mass-loss theories for AGB stars.

Research Context
Mass loss from post-main-sequence stars provides a large fraction of heavy element abundance and solid particle content of the interstellar medium. The mechanism(s) of mass loss during the AGB phase involve radiation pressure and stellar pulsation but most details are not well understood. Spatial structure of circumstellar mass-loss shells could clarify uncertainties about these mass-loss processes. Molecular line studies of extended envelopes around AGB stars have found periodic variations in mass-loss rates leading to 'rings' in molecular emission line radial distributions. Very deep, sensitive imaging studies have found similar phenomena in the dust around the nearby extreme example IRC+10216. Studying the inner regions of these circumstellar shells requires angular resolutions well under 1 arcsec. At a distance of 1 kpc, the dust evaporation radius around a 10⁴ L⊙ star corresponds to an angular radius of 20 milli-arcseconds. Speckle interferometry and adaptive optics have enabled resolutions of order 0.1 arcsec. Lunar occultation observations and multi-aperture interferometry have pushed angular resolutions to the milli-arcsecond level. Most interferometric observations prior to this work were made in typically one or two relatively broad bands. AFGL 5440 (OH 06.86-1.5, IRAS 18036-2344) has been classified as a carbon-rich AGB star. The reported distance and photometry imply a luminosity of 1.4×10⁴ L⊙.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the inner spatial structure of the circumstellar dust shell around AFGL 5440 can be resolved using multi-spectral lunar occultation fringes. The implicit hypothesis is that a single source model (e.g., a uniform disk) will be insufficient to fit the occultation fringes across the 1–4 µm bandwidth, necessitating a star+shell model. The study hypothesizes that the DUSTY radiative transfer code can simultaneously fit the observed occultation light curves and the literature spectral energy distribution to constrain dust shell parameters. A predicted outcome is that the best-fit dust density gradient should correspond to physically motivated models such as ρ ∝ r⁻² or a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow gradient. The study predicts that models with Tmax below a certain threshold will fail to produce sufficient 3–4 µm emission to match the observed fringe blurring. An additional hypothesis is that a carbon-rich dust composition (amorphous carbon, SiC, graphite) is appropriate, and graphite may be necessary to fit the far-IR flux. The modeling approach assumes the outer radius of the dust shell makes no difference at wavelengths < 60 µm as long as it is at least 100 times the inner radius. The modeling does not attempt to extract details of the stellar photosphere or thorough examination of all possible dust size/composition models due to wavelength coverage and spectral resolution limitations.

Methodological Details
The observations of AFGL 5440 were made during an immersion occultation event on 28 August 2001 at approximately 02:44:00 UT. The Moon's elevation at the time was 36°, the Sun was 17° below the horizon, the position angle was 54°, and the lunar phase was 0.72. The pMIRAS instrument was used on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The instrument uses a NaCl prism to disperse light from a long/wide slit imaged onto a 32×100 pixel portion of a 2562 InSb array detector. The slit width was set at about 5 arcsec for typical seeing of 1.5 arcsec. The detector is read-out every 8 msec, with photon integration occurring over essentially the full 8 msec time. The time resolution of 8 msec permits an effective angular resolution of a couple milli-arcsec, with the exact resolution being a strong function of the signal-to-noise ratio. On average over the 1–4 µm waveband, one pixel corresponds roughly to λ/∆λ = 100. The true resolving power at the shortest wavelengths is R ∼ 20, while in the spatial direction the plate scale is 0.4 arcsec/pixel. The instrument is read-noise limited shortward of 2.5 µm and background-limited longward of 3 µm. A typical observation consists of taking 5000 frames roughly centered on the occultation event. Two calibration stars with no detectable circumstellar dust shell based on near-infrared and IRAS colors were observed: IRC+00233 (M7) and HD 155292 (K2). IRC+00233 was observed during an immersion event on 29 June 2001; HD 155292 was observed during an immersion event on 26 August 2001. Data reduction involves cross-correlation to correct for spectral motion, tilt removal, and sky subtraction from either side of the ~10 arcsec slit. The end result of the reduction is a sequence of ~100 light curves with a few hundred frames extracted centered on the occultation event. Wavelength calibration is performed by fitting the NaCl dispersion function to the J, H, K, and L atmospheric transmission maxima in the actual data. The accuracy of the wavelength calibration is good to ±.01 λ throughout the 1–4 µm region. No absolute flux calibration is derived due to variable instrumental efficiency and non-photometric conditions, but the relative signal is compared to well-characterized stars. The stellar magnitudes for AFGL 5440 in published literature are consistent with values derived from signal strengths to within ±30%.

Procedures And Architectures
The fringe pattern of a lunar occultation is modeled as a convolution of the point source pattern with aperture, integration time, wavelength bandwidth, and source size/structure. The lunar shadow velocity, an additional uncertainty, must be fit alongside fringe-blurring parameters because crater roughness can produce differences of several tens of percent. Modeling begins with a uniform disk as the simplest model, using a simple χ2 test for the best fit, typically allowing size and shadow velocity to vary. For IRC+00233, a blackbody angular size of 3.5 mas is expected from the van Belle (1999) empirical relation; for HD 155292, the expected size is 0.6 mas. Data accuracy is limited to ±2 mas, so features below 1 mas are not reliably detectable. For AFGL 5440, a single 11 mas uniform disk produces fringes that are too sharp at long wavelengths and too broadened at short wavelengths, indicating a multi-component source. The DUSTY radiative transfer code (Ivezić, Nenkova & Elitzur 1999) is used to model the circumstellar shell, producing source images as a function of wavelength and the total energy distribution. Dust parameters are varied systematically: the dust temperature at the inner radius and the radial density gradient are the critical free parameters. A carbon-rich dust composition (amorphous carbon, SiC, graphite) is assumed, consistent with the star's classification. More than 200 models are explored to determine the effect of varying input parameters on fit quality. Models that provide an approximate fit to both occultation data and SED have several common features: Tmax ≈ 950 ± 50 K and density gradient close to r⁻². Two grain size distributions are tested: the MRN slope (Mathis, Rumpl & Nordsieck 1977) and the KMH shape (Kim, Martin & Hendry 1994). The optical depth at 5 µm for the best-fit model is typically in the range 0.3–0.6. The outer radius of the dust shell must be at least 100 times the inner radius to make no difference at wavelengths < 60 µm. Models with r⁻¹.⁸ gradient come closer to the IRAS 60 µm flux but poorly fit the 5–20 µm SED; models with r⁻².² fit the SED out to 20 µm but poorly fit the IRAS 60 µm flux.

Key Results
A single-size uniform disk model cannot fit the occultation fringes of AFGL 5440 over the 1–4 µm bandwidth, with an 11 mas disk producing mismatched fringe sharpness. The maximum dust temperature at the inner radius is constrained to 950 ± 50 K; models below 900 K lack sufficient hot dust to fit 3–4 µm fringes. The best-fit radial density gradient is close to ρ ∝ r⁻² or the Ivezić & Elitzur radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow gradient. Models with r⁻¹.⁸ gradient underfit the 5–20 µm SED; models with r⁻².² fit the SED out to 20 µm but worsen the IRAS 60 µm fit. The optical depth at 5 µm for the best-fit model is in the range 0.3–0.6, with a fiducial value around 0.5. The best-fit dust composition includes comparable amounts of amorphous carbon and graphite, plus a small amount of SiC. The dust mass-loss rate implied by the best-fit model is 6.5 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr. Groenewegen et al. (2002) derived a dust mass-loss rate of 5.1 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr from IRAS 60 µm, slightly lower than the current result despite using 60 µm for normalization. The gas mass-loss rate of 3.1 × 10⁻⁵ M⊙/yr implies a gas-to-dust mass ratio of 600. The best-fit model provides a poor fit to the IRAS 60 µm flux without graphite; models with only amorphous carbon and SiC underfit the 60 µm flux by factors of 3 or more. A model with only amorphous carbon and SiC using the Ivezić & Elitzur density gradient fits the occultation data nearly as well as the best-fit model but fails the 60 µm flux. The physical inner radius for AFGL 5440 is 3.7 × 10¹⁴ cm, corresponding to an angular radius of 11 mas at the assumed distance of 2.25 kpc. The angular diameter of the central star is of order 3 mas, based on a blackbody approximation for a photospheric temperature of 2500 ± 300 K at 2 µm. The angular radius corresponding to the dust evaporation radius for a 10⁴ L⊙ star at 1 kpc is 20 mas.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The data imply the density of grains emitting in the 3–4 µm spectral region must be sufficiently large to produce the substantial fringe blurring observed in the light curves. The best-fit Tmax of 950 K is strongly constrained by the fact that dust cooler than 900 K cannot emit sufficiently to produce the required 3–4 µm emission, about a factor of two below the expected condensation temperatures. The finding that graphite is necessary to fit the 60 µm flux contradicts the large amount of evidence against substantial graphite in such stars, suggesting the emissivity vs. wavelength dependence of graphite enables fitting of the 60 µm flux. The fact that the IRAS 60 µm flux cannot be fit by any model without graphite, combined with evidence for non-constant outflow from carbon stars, provides a convenient explanation: a higher mass-loss rate in the past. If the mass-loss rate were greater 500 years to a couple thousand years in the past, the dust at radii corresponding to 60 µm emission would be larger than predicted by a constant extrapolation, opposite to the 'superwind' scenario of Suh (1997). The angular radius of dust emitting strongly at 60 µm is of order 1 to a few arcseconds, corresponding to 500 to ~2000 years ago at 22 km/s outflow velocity. The dust mass-loss rate is constrained to the order 5–10 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr, and a gas mass-loss rate a few hundred times larger are consistent with the data. These observations separately resolve the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the circumstellar dust shell, providing a direct constraint on the recent dust mass-loss rate.

Contradictions And Limitations
The sky conditions were not completely photometric, with cloud cover being minimal and intermittent during the event. The exact resolution of the instrument is a strong function of the signal-to-noise ratio, and the data are limited by both spectral resolution and signal-to-noise ratio to accuracies on the order of ±2 mas. A small range of wavelengths around ∼1.7 µm in the IRC+00233 model shows a less-than-adequate fit that could be due to systematic noise or a real difference in the stellar photosphere. For HD 155292, some periodic electronic pickup had a non-negligible effect on the observed fringe patterns at shorter wavelengths, and the signal-to-noise ratio was low enough that no effective narrow-band information existed beyond 2.5 µm. The paper specifically does not attempt to derive an absolute flux calibration due to variable instrumental efficiency and non-photometric conditions. The modeling did not attempt to extract details of the stellar photosphere or thorough examination of all possible dust size/composition models for reasons of wavelength coverage and spectral resolution. The model of Ivezić & Elitzur (1996) derived an inner dust shell temperature of ~750 K, substantially lower than the 950 K found here, raising questions about consistency between self-consistent hydrodynamic and radiative transfer approaches. Virtually all previous modeling efforts used dust emissivities for amorphous carbon with no graphite, contrary to the best-fit model presented here. The fact that the dust mass-loss rate from this model (6.5 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr) is slightly higher than that from Groenewegen et al. (5.1 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr) despite Groenewegen et al. using the 60 µm flux for normalization reinforces overall uncertainties in model assumptions and absolute dust opacities.

Claims
A single-size uniform disk model cannot fit the 1–4 µm occultation fringes of AFGL 5440, necessitating a dual-component (star+shell) model. A quick glance at the observed light curves indicated that a single source size was unlikely to fit over the entire 1–4 µm bandwidth. The 11 mas disk produces fringes that are too sharp at longer wavelengths and too broadened at shorter wavelengths. The fringes cannot be fitted by any single-size model. In the case of the comparison star IRC+00233, a 4.5 mas uniform disk provides a very good fit over most of the wavelength range, showing that a single-size model can be appropriate for some sources. For HD 155292, all uniform-disk models with a size less than about 3 mas were able to fit the data reasonably well. The requirement for a two-component model confirms the presence of a circumstellar shell and places a direct constraint on the size of the innermost dust. This constrains the dust density gradient in the innermost part of the circumstellar shell.
The inner dust shell is constrained to a maximum temperature of 950 ± 50 K, which is nearly a factor of two below the expected dust condensation temperatures. Models with a maximum dust temperature below 900 K did not have enough hot dust to fit the occultation fringes at longer wavelengths. Models with hotter inner edges had even more difficulty than the best-fit model in reproducing the energy distribution longward of 10 µm. This temperature is nearly a factor of two below the expected condensation temperatures for dust around these stars. Dust cooler than 900 K cannot emit sufficiently to produce the required amount of 3–4 µm emission. Ivezić & Elitzur (1996) derived an inner dust shell temperature substantially lower than this, at ∼750 K, using a self-consistent radiatively driven hydrodynamic model. The angular diameter of the central star is only ~3 mas, and the dust evaporation radius at 1 kpc is 20 mas; the 11 mas inner radius is physically consistent but requires careful interpretation of the dust-gas boundary. The 950 K constraint places a physical inner radius at 3.7 × 10¹⁴ cm (11 mas angular radius), which is significantly interior to the expected condensation radius. This constrains the spatial location of the warmest dust, directly impacting mass-loss history interpretations.
Graphite is necessary in the dust composition to fit the IRAS 60 µm flux, contradicting previous models that assumed no graphite. Models with only amorphous carbon and SiC failed to fit that flux by factors of 3 or more. The factor that drove us to include graphite was its relatively flat emissivity vs. wavelength dependence between 10 and 50 µm that enabled us to fit the IRAS 60 µm flux. Virtually all of these modeling efforts used dust emissivities appropriate for some form of amorphous carbon but with no graphite, contrary to our best model fit. There is a large amount of evidence against substantial amounts of graphite in stars like AFGL 5440. The model of Ivezić & Elitzur (1996) utilized a grain size distribution that included substantially larger grains than most earlier models, which may affect emissivity conclusions. The inclusion of graphite suggests either a revision of graphite abundance in carbon-rich AGB stars or a non-constant mass-loss rate (higher in the past) to explain the excess 60 µm emission. This points toward a recent decrease in mass-loss rate from the time when the far-IR-emitting dust was ejected.

Data And Code Availability
The DUSTY radiative transfer code (Ivezić, Nenkova & Elitzur 1999) was used for modeling, and the paper describes the model-fitting procedure in detail. The authors do not explicitly state that the reduced data or specific model configurations are made publicly available.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
More than 200 models were explored to understand the effect of varying input parameters on fit quality. Two grain size distributions were tested: the MRN slope and the KMH shape, and reasonably good fits were obtained with either. A third model was computed that fits the energy distribution but gives a poor fit to the occultation results because of a lack of enough warm dust close to the star. A model using only amorphous carbon and SiC and the Ivezić & Elitzur density gradient fits the occultation data nearly as well as the best-fit model but fails the 60 µm flux. Models with r⁻¹.⁸ gradient come closer to the IRAS 60 µm flux but poorly fit the 5–20 µm SED; models with r⁻².² fit the SED to 20 µm but significantly worsen the IRAS 60 µm fit. The optical depth at 5 µm typically ranged over 0.3–0.6 for best-fit models.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows observed and model light curves for IRC+00233 with a 4.5 mas uniform disk for a subset of wavelengths. Figure 2 shows χ2 and signal-to-noise ratio as a function of wavelength over the entire band for the IRC+00233 4.5 mas model. Figures 3 and 4 show uniform-disk model fits for HD 155292 at different sizes. Figure 5 shows the observed light curves for AFGL 5440 across 1–4 µm. Figure 6 shows the χ2 plot for the 11 mas uniform disk fit to AFGL 5440, illustrating the poor fit. Figures 7 and 8 show the fits to the spectral energy distribution and to the occultation light curves for the best-fit model. Figure 9 shows the quality of the fit versus wavelength for the best-fit model. Figure 10 illustrates the spatial profiles of the best-fit model source at different wavelengths. Figures 11 and 12 show the energy distribution and model light curves for the best-fitting model using only amorphous carbon and SiC. Figures 13 and 14 show results for a third model that fits the energy distribution but gives a poor fit to the occultation results.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first multi-spectral lunar occultation resolution of the inner dust shell of a carbon-rich AGB star, establishing a maximum dust temperature of 950 ± 50 K and optical depth of 0.5 ± 0.1 at 5 µm. 2. The strongest evidence is that no single-size model can fit the 1–4 µm occultation fringes of AFGL 5440, and a model with graphite is required to reproduce the 60 µm flux, underfitting by factors of 3 or more without it. 3. The future path involves reconciling the 60 µm flux excess through a non-constant mass-loss rate (higher in the past), providing a test for periodic outflow theories in carbon-rich AGB stars.

summary.title: Gluon Radiation of an Expanding Color Skyrmion in the Quark-Gluon Plasma
summary.authors: Jian Dai
summary.field_subfield: High Energy Physics / QCD and Heavy Ion Collisions
summary.executive_summary: This paper calculates the density of states and energy spectrum of gluon radiation produced by the color current of an expanding hydrodynamic skyrmion in the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) using a semiclassical method. The author develops the framework starting from a non-linear sigma model with first-order formalism (Lagrangian including the velocity field, free energy density, and gauge coupling) to describe an ideal fluid system. The equation of state is approximated by the radiation-like relation energy density equals three times the pressure, which yields a free energy density proportional to n^(4/3). A class of expanding soliton solutions is identified, where the spatial scale R(t) expands as R0(t/τ + 1)^(4/3). The non-abelian current is derived using a hedgehog ansatz and a stereographic map, reduced to its spherically symmetric component (the third component) containing a P6(s) polynomial. The semiclassical gluon radiation amplitude is computed by coupling this classical current to a free quantum gluon field, resulting in a spatial Fourier integral over the expanding trajectory. For the on-shell condition (ω = k), the radiation spectrum is expressed in terms of a dimensionless integral f_M(λ(κ)) over the expansion time. Numerical results are presented for three values of the small parameter λ = τ/R0 (1/5, 2/15, 1/15), revealing a fast UV fall-off, a smooth intermediate peak, and a characteristic long IR tail. The IR behavior, scaling as 1/√k, is contrasted with the 1/k behavior of infinitely large media, explained by the finite soliton size R0. The paper also notes a frequency hierarchy between this medium-radiated radiation and jet-quenching radiation ω_C ∼ q^2 L^2, where the former is significantly smaller than the characteristic momentum 1/R0.

Executive Summary
This paper calculates the density of states and energy spectrum of gluon radiation produced by the color current of an expanding hydrodynamic skyrmion in the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) using a semiclassical method. The author develops the framework starting from a non-linear sigma model with first-order formalism (Lagrangian including the velocity field, free energy density, and gauge coupling) to describe an ideal fluid system. The equation of state is approximated by the radiation-like relation energy density equals three times the pressure, which yields a free energy density proportional to n^(4/3). A class of expanding soliton solutions is identified, where the spatial scale R(t) expands as R0(t/τ + 1)^(4/3). The non-abelian current is derived using a hedgehog ansatz and a stereographic map, reduced to its spherically symmetric component (the third component) containing a P6(s) polynomial. The semiclassical gluon radiation amplitude is computed by coupling this classical current to a free quantum gluon field, resulting in a spatial Fourier integral over the expanding trajectory. For the on-shell condition (ω = k), the radiation spectrum is expressed in terms of a dimensionless integral f_M(λ(κ)) over the expansion time. Numerical results are presented for three values of the small parameter λ = τ/R0 (1/5, 2/15, 1/15), revealing a fast UV fall-off, a smooth intermediate peak, and a characteristic long IR tail. The IR behavior, scaling as 1/√k, is contrasted with the 1/k behavior of infinitely large media, explained by the finite soliton size R0. The paper also notes a frequency hierarchy between this medium-radiated radiation and jet-quenching radiation ω_C ∼ q^2 L^2, where the former is significantly smaller than the characteristic momentum 1/R0.

Research Context
The paper addresses gluon radiation during the hydrodynamic stage of the deconned hot QCD matter or quark-gluon plasma. Medium induced gluon radiation has been thoroughly explored in the context of final state partonic energy loss known as jet quenching. All high p⊥ hadronic observables are affected at collider energies, making medium modification a probe of hot QCD matter. Gluon radiation has also been considered in the context of gluon density saturation in the initial stage, where a strongly interacting gluonic atmosphere is crucial for rapid local thermalization. Generalized fluid mechanics characterizing the long-distance physics of transport of color charges has been developed for this purpose. Single skyrmion solutions in color fluid were recently discovered, and a time-dependent expanding skyrmion is consistent with the expanding fireball generated in RHIC experiments. The pattern of gluon radiation pertaining to the color current of non-static configurations is an important character of the color skyrmion.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is what is the pattern of gluon radiation pertaining to the color current of an expanding hydrodynamic skyrmion in the quark-gluon plasma. The author hypothesizes that the spectrum will show a fast fall-off in the UV side and a smooth peak at intermediate energy. In the IR region, the hypothesis predicts a long tail as the characteristic feature. The approach assumes a hierarchy between the partonic coupling g_YM and the effective coupling g_eff, allowing the omission of gluon self-interactions. The small parameter λ = τ/R0 is assumed valid for τ ≪ R0, enabling the semiclassical expansion.

Methodological Details
The transport of color charges is modeled by a nonlinear sigma model in a first-order formalism with Lagrangian density including jµwµ, F(n), and geffJaµAa. The group element field U takes value in SU(2) because only one abelian charge current is considered. The equation of state is approximated as energy density ϵ = 3p, characteristic of radiation at high temperatures. The free energy density F is obtained as β/4^(4/3) n^(4/3), where β is a dimensionless constant of integration. The expanding soliton solution is R(t) ≈ R0(t/τ + 1)^(4/3)θ(t), with the time-step function θ(t). The hedgehog ansatz specifies U = cos φ + iσ·x̂ sin φ with φ given by a stereographic map. The dimensionless coordinate s = x/R(t) is used, where the skyrmion number is +1 for the chosen sign. The non-abelian current J_a^(3) contains only the spherically symmetric part, expressed as P6(s) = 1 − 7s² + 7s⁴ − s⁶. The lowest mode of the multipole expansion is considered, with higher polarization effects deferred to future work. The semiclassical gluon radiation amplitude is given by the interaction of the classical current with a free quantum gluon field. The radiation spectrum is calculated for three values of λ = τ/R0: 1/5, 2/15, and 1/15.

Procedures And Architectures
The non-abelian current is derived by expressing jµ in terms of velocity ωµ through the equation of motion. The spatial Fourier transformation is completed analytically to obtain iM = B(k) ∫ e−iωt − R(t)k·sP6(s) ds. Substituting R(t) from the soliton solution leads to a time integral over the expansion trajectory. The on-shell condition ω = k is used to define the dimensionless variable η = ωτ/(kR0)^(3/4) = λκ^(1/4). The dimensionless integral i f_M(λ(κ)) = ∫_0^(κ^(3/4)) e^(iλκ^(1/4)t − t^(4/3)Q4(t^(4/3))) dt is computed. The density of states n = 4πk² ∑|M|² is reduced to n = α R0 λ² κ^(-1/2) |f_M|². The energy spectrum dE/dk = α λ² κ^(1/2) |f_M|² is computed with α = (2π5/225)(g_eff² / β⁶). Numerical results are presented in Figure 1 for the three λ values. The IR asymptotic behavior is plotted as n/(1/√κ) in Figure 2 for λ = 0.2.

Key Results
The density of states n shows a peak at intermediate k and falls off in both UV and IR directions. The energy spectrum dE/dk exhibits a smooth peak dominating the intermediate energy region. In the UV region, there is a fast fall-off in both the density of states and the energy spectrum. In the IR region, the number density behaves as n ∼ 1/√k, a long tail characteristic of the finite soliton. Figure 1 shows n vs k with peaks shifting toward smaller k as λ decreases (1/5 to 1/15). The energy spectrum shows a broader peak for smaller λ, indicating more extended radiation. Figure 2 confirms the n ∼ 1/√k IR behavior for λ = 0.2, contrasting with the 1/k behavior in large media. The difference in IR behavior (1/√k vs 1/k) arises because the medium size is characterized by the finite soliton size R0 rather than infinity. The radiation frequency ω_C ∼ q² L² is significantly larger than the characteristic momentum 1/R0, establishing a frequency hierarchy.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The hydrodynamical approach offers a way to address the eccentricity of elliptic flow, either intrinsically via the non-abelian color current or exogenously via gluon radiation patterns. The hierarchy between medium-induced radiation (jet quenching) and radiation by the expanding medium itself is established: the latter dominates at lower scales. The 1/√k IR tail is a direct consequence of the finite soliton size R0, distinguishing this model from infinitely large media. The smooth peak at intermediate energy reflects the collective expansion of the color skyrmion rather than individual hard scattering. The semiclassical treatment, by decoupling gluon self-interactions, captures the primary radiated spectrum while neglecting higher-order quantum corrections.

Contradictions And Limitations
The approximation ε = 3p is only valid at relatively high temperatures, not necessarily throughout the entire expansion history. The small parameter λ = τ/R0 is assumed small (τ ≪ R0), but the validity is not quantitatively checked for the values 1/15 to 1/5. The calculation neglects higher polarization modes of the non-abelian current, which may contribute significantly to the full radiation pattern. Gluon self-interactions (F·F terms) are omitted, assuming the partonic coupling g_YM is much larger than g_eff, which may not hold at all scales. The result is restricted to the spherically symmetric sector, as the full non-abelian current has multipole structure.

Claims
The density of states and energy spectrum of gluon radiation from an expanding color skyrmion show a fast UV fall-off, an intermediate peak, and a 1/√k IR tail. The energy spectrum dE/dk exhibits a smooth peak dominating intermediate energy. There is a fast fall-off in the UV side of the spectrum. The asymptotic of the number density in small k is ~1/√k. The 1/√k behavior is supported by Figure 2 plotting n/(1/√κ). In large media, the IR behavior is 1/k, not 1/√k. The finite size of the soliton is imprinted on the radiated gluon spectrum. The radiation pattern can serve as a diagnostic of the color skyrmion structure in QGP.
There exists a frequency hierarchy: the medium-induced radiation ω_C ∼ q²L² is significantly larger than the characteristic momentum 1/R0, separating jet quenching from medium-radiated gluon radiation. ω_C is significantly larger than the characteristic momentum 1/R0. ω_C is estimated to be .04 to .16 GeV²/fm.  The two radiation mechanisms contribute at different momentum scales. This separation justifies studying the expanding medium radiation independently of jet quenching effects.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The parameter λ = τ/R0 is varied across three values (1/5, 2/15, 1/15) to assess sensitivity of the spectrum to the expansion rate. The IR scaling is explicitly tested by plotting n/(1/√κ) against k, verifying the 1/√k form. The spherically symmetric part P6(s) is isolated from the full multipole current to test the lowest-mode contribution.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 presents the density of states n and energy spectrum dE/dk versus k (normalized by R0) for three λ values, showing UV fall-off and intermediate peaks. Figure 2 plots n/(1/√κ) against k for λ = 0.2 in the small k region, demonstrating the 1/√k power law behavior.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first analytic and semiclassical calculation of gluon radiation from an expanding color skyrmion, revealing a 1/√k IR tail and a fast UV fall-off. 2. The strongest evidence is the 1/√k IR scaling behavior demonstrated in Figure 2, which distinguishes the finite soliton radiation from the 1/k behavior of infinite media. 3. The future path includes considering higher polarization modes, addressing the eccentricity of elliptic flow from the non-abelian color current, and potentially relaxing the ε=3p approximation.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This STAR collaboration study reports three-particle azimuthal correlation measurements for charged trigger particles (3 < pT < 4 GeV/c) and two associated particles (1 < pT < 2 GeV/c) produced in pp, d+Au, and Au+Au collisions at √sNN = 200 GeV. The central motivation is to differentiate between competing physical mechanisms—hydrodynamic Mach cone shock waves, large-angle gluon radiation, deflected jets, and Cherenkov radiation—that explain the broadened away-side structure observed in two-particle correlations in central Au+Au collisions. The analysis methodology partitions events into jet-like and background components, subtracting three distinct combinatorial background sources: hard-soft (2-particle jet-like times 2-particle background), soft-soft (two associated particles from mixed events), and trigger flow (triplet-wise flow correlation). In central Au+Au collisions (0-12% ZDC triggered), a prominent off-diagonal peak at π ± 1.45 radians is observed, consistent with conical emission. Figure 3 quantifies that the off-diagonal signal significantly deviates from zero in central collisions. To discriminate against Cherenkov radiation (which predicts an angle decreasing with associated particle pT), the authors show that the cone angle remains constant (1.41 to 1.45 radians) as a function of associated particle pT, a feature compatible with Mach cone emission. Systematic uncertainty studies on elliptic flow v2 (reaction plane vs. 4-particle cumulant methods) and normalization window size demonstrate robustness of the signal. The authors conclude that the observed conical emission is consistent with Mach cone shock waves rather than Cherenkov radiation, but acknowledge that deflected jets also contribute to the on-diagonal broadening.

Research Context
Heavy ion collisions at √sNN = 200 GeV create a medium that may be the quark-gluon plasma (QGP). Jets make a good probe because their properties can be calculated in vacuum with perturbative quantum chromodynamics (pQCD). Two-particle jet-like azimuthal correlations show the away-side shape in central Au+Au collisions broadened compared to pp and peripheral Au+Au, or even double-humped. The away-side structure is consistent with large-angle gluon radiation, deflected jets, preferential path-length energy loss, hydrodynamic conical flow from Mach-cone shock waves, and Cherenkov radiation. Three-particle correlations can differentiate conical flow and Cherenkov radiation from other mechanisms due to their characteristic conical emission. The associated particle pT dependence of the conical emission angle can differentiate hydrodynamic conical flow from simple Cherenkov radiation. The paper notes that a rigorous three-particle correlation analysis method was previously described in reference 9.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the observed away-side structure in two-particle correlations arises from hydrodynamic conical emission (Mach cones), Cherenkov radiation, or jet-related mechanisms. The hypothesis is that three-particle correlations, specifically off-diagonal peaks, will uniquely identify conical emission as a distinct physical phenomenon. The authors predict that if the signal is Mach-cone emission, the cone angle should be independent of associated particle pT, whereas Cherenkov radiation predicts a sharply decreasing angle with increasing pT. The analysis expects that off-diagonal signals (one particle near-side, one away-side) will contain only conical emission contributions, while on-diagonal signals (both near-side or both away-side) will contain both conical emission and deflected jet contributions. The study aims to quantify the magnitude and position of these signals as a function of centrality and pT to validate the Mach-cone model.

Methodological Details
The data were collected by the STAR time projection chamber for pp, d+Au, and Au+Au collisions at √sNN = 200 GeV/c. The analysis used charged trigger particles in the pT range 3 < pT < 4 GeV/c and two charged associated particles in the range 1 < pT < 2 GeV/c. Central Au+Au collisions used ZDC-triggered 0-12% selection for high-statistics results. Figure 1b shows the raw 3-particle azimuthal distribution in ∆φaT = φa - φT and ∆φbT = φb - φT. The hard-soft background is constructed from the 2-particle jet-like correlation folded with the normalized 2-particle background, using an alpha scale factor. The 2-particle background is constructed by mixing events with flow modulation added pairwise from average v2 values from reaction plane and 4-particle cumulant methods. The v4 contribution uses the parameterization v4 = 1.15v2^2 from data. The background is normalized within 0.8 < |∆φ| < 1.2 (zero yield at 1 radian or ZYA1). The soft-soft background is obtained from mixed events where trigger and associated particles are from different events in the same centrality window. Trigger flow is added triplet-wise from mixed events where trigger and associated particles are all from different events in the same centrality window. The normalization factor alpha^2 corrects for multiplicity bias from requiring a trigger particle. The factor beta accounts for non-Poisson multiplicity distributions and is obtained such that the number of associated pairs in the subtracted signal equals the square of the number of associated particles in the two-particle signal. The total background is the sum: J^2 ⊗ alpha*Binc^2 + beta*v2*(Binc^3 + Binc,T F^3). For the pT dependence analysis, double Gaussian fits were applied to off-diagonal strips. Figure 4 shows away-side projections of a strip of width 0.7 radians for d+Au and 0-12% Au+Au.

Procedures And Architectures
The analysis treats events as composed of two components: particles jet-like correlated with the trigger and background particles. The hard-soft background (J^2 ⊗ alpha*Binc^2) accounts for one associated particle being jet-correlated and the other uncorrelated except for flow. The soft-soft background (Binc^3) accounts for correlations between the two associated particles independent of the trigger. The trigger flow background (Binc,T F^3) accounts for particles correlated with the trigger via flow. Flow values v2 and v4 are obtained from both reaction plane and 4-particle cumulant methods, with reaction plane as upper bound and 4-particle as lower bound. The v4 parameterization v4 = 1.15*v2^2 is used from data. A double Gaussian fit is applied to a strip projected to the off-diagonal to determine the signal location. Off-diagonal projection is defined as (Δφ1 − Δφ)/2 and on-diagonal as (Δφ1 + Δφ)/2 − π. For pT dependence, the off-diagonal peak values are fitted to a constant. The dashed line at π/2 in Figure 5 indicates the Cherenkov prediction.

Key Results
Background subtracted 3-particle correlation signals are presented for pp, d+Au, Au+Au 50-80%, 30-50%, 10-30%, and 0-12% ZDC triggered collisions. The pp and d+Au results are similar, with peaks clearly visible at (0,0) for near-side, (π,π) for away-side, (0,π), and (π,0). The away-side peak displays diagonal elongation consistent with kT broadening. Peripheral Au+Au results show additional on-diagonal elongation of the away-side peak, possibly due to deflected jets. More central Au+Au collisions display an off-diagonal structure at about π ± 1.45 radians consistent with conical emission. The off-diagonal signal magnitude increases with centrality and is prominent in the high-statistics ZDC 0-12% central data. The off-diagonal signals (circles in Figure 3) significantly deviate from zero in central Au+Au collisions. The locations of the off-diagonal signals were determined to be 1.45 radians from π. The differences between on-diagonal and off-diagonal signals (Figure 3 right) decrease with distance from (π,π). The emission angle as a function of associated particle pT for Au+Au 0-12% ZDC triggered data is 1.41 ± 0.02 and 1.45 ± 0.02 for Au+Au 0-50%. The angle is consistent with remaining constant as a function of associated particle pT, at approximately 1.45 radians. The cone angle as a function of centrality for 0-12% ZDC triggered data (circle) and 30-50%, 10-30%, 0-10% minimum bias (square) is consistent with a constant of 1.46 radians. The solid line at 1.46 on Figure 5 (right) represents the fit to a constant.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The observation of off-diagonal peaks at π ± 1.45 radians is consistent with hydrodynamic conical emission from Mach-cone shock waves. The on-diagonal broadening (away-side elongation) in Au+Au beyond pp/d+Au is interpreted as a contribution from deflected jets. The fact that the cone angle is independent of associated particle pT favors the Mach-cone model over Cherenkov radiation. The Cherenkov radiation model predicts an emission angle sharply decreasing with increasing associated particle momentum, which is not observed. The Mach cone emission angle is expected to be independent of associated particle momentum, which aligns with the constant 1.45 radian measurement. The on-diagonal and off-diagonal signals differ because the on-diagonal region receives contributions from both conical emission and deflected jets, while the off-diagonal region receives only conical emission. The decrease in the on-diagonal/off-diagonal difference with distance from (π,π) indicates a spatial or angular dependence of deflected-jet contributions.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper is a preliminary result (STAR Preliminary) and not a finalized publication. The analysis relies on the assumption that the v2 and v4 parameterization is correct, and v4 = 1.15v2^2 is a parameterization from data. The subtraction of flow harmonics is the dominant source of systematic error, and the signal robustness depends on the cancellation of hard-soft and trigger flow background variations. The paper does not report a full error analysis on the background parameter beta, nor on the specific shape of the double Gaussian fits. There is no explicit mention of random seeds used for background mixing or specific model variations. The data is only for charged particles in the specified pT ranges, limiting the scope to certain kinematic regions. The systematic error includes a 20% on trigger particle v2 from requiring a correlated particle, indicating a limitation in the purity of the trigger selection. The uncertainty in the v4 parameterization and multiplicity bias effects on the soft-soft background are noted but not quantified with specific numbers in the text.

Claims
Three-particle azimuthal correlations in central Au+Au collisions reveal off-diagonal peaks consistent with conical emission, indicating the presence of Mach cones. Off-diagonal peaks at π ± 1.45 radians are clearly visible in the 0-12% ZDC triggered Au+Au data. The off-diagonal signal magnitude increases with centrality and is prominent in the highest-statistics data. Figure 3 (right) shows the off-diagonal signal is non-zero and significantly deviates from zero in central collisions. The on-diagonal broadening (deflected jets) contributes to the away-side structure, complicating the interpretation of pure conical emission. The analysis is preliminary and not a final publication. The existence of Mach cones would confirm hydrodynamic behavior of the QGP medium. This result favors hydrodynamic shock-wave propagation over Cherenkov radiation as the explanation for away-side broadening.
The Mach-cone emission angle is independent of associated particle pT, discriminating it from Cherenkov radiation. The emission angle for Au+Au 0-12% is 1.41 ± 0.02 radians, and for 0-50% it is 1.45 ± 0.02 radians, showing no pT dependence. The angle remains consistent with a constant value across the measured pT range. This behavior contradicts the Cherenkov model's prediction of a sharply decreasing angle. The paper notes Cherenkov radiation predicts a sharply decreasing angle, but this is a prediction not tested by the current data range. This result provides a clear kinematic discriminator between hydrodynamic and optical-analogue emission mechanisms.
On-diagonal away-side broadening in Au+Au collisions is due to deflected jets in addition to conical emission. The on-diagonal signal (both particles near-side or both away-side) shows additional elongation in Au+Au not present in pp or d+Au. The difference between on-diagonal and off-diagonal signals decreases with distance from (π,π), indicating a deflected-jet contribution. Deflected jets are one of several competing mechanisms (large angle gluon radiation, path-length dependent energy loss) that could explain the broadening. Deflected jets complicate the separation of jet-related effects from collective medium effects on the away-side.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The v2 subtraction was tested by using both reaction plane (upper bound) and 4-particle cumulant (lower bound) v2 values. Figure 6a and b show that the signal is robust with respect to the v2 variation; background components vary greatly but cancel to first order. The normalization window was doubled from 0.6 < |∆φ| < 1.4 to 0.6 < |∆φ| < 1.4 (Wait, the text says 0.6 < |∆φ| < 1.4 to 0.6 < |∆φ| < 1.4 - this looks like a typo in the paper; it likely means the window was widened). The signal is robust with respect to the change in normalization region. The effect on trigger particle flow from requiring a correlated particle was assessed (20% on trigger particle v2). Uncertainty in the v4 parameterization and multiplicity bias effects on the soft-soft background were identified as additional systematic sources.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows (a) raw 2-particle correlation, (b) raw 3-particle azimuthal distribution, (c) soft-soft background, and (d) hard-soft background plus trigger flow for ZDC-triggered 0-12% Au+Au collisions. Figure 2 displays background subtracted 3-particle jet-like correlation signals for pp, d+Au, and five Au+Au centrality classes (50-80%, 30-50%, 10-30%, 0-12%). Figure 3 (left) shows centrality dependence of average signal strengths in 0.7 × 0.7 boxes at (0,0), (π,π), (π ± 1.45,π ± 1.45), and (π ± 1.45,π ∓1.45). (Right) shows differences between on-diagonal and off-diagonal regions. Figure 4 shows away-side projections of a strip of width 0.7 radians for d+Au (left) and 0-12% Au+Au (right), with off-diagonal (solid) and on-diagonal (open) projections. Figure 5 (left) shows cone angle vs. associated particle pT for Au+Au 0-12% (filled) and 0-50% (open). (Right) shows cone angle vs. centrality. Figure 6 shows systematic checks: (a) reaction plane v2, (b) 4-particle cumulant v2, and (c) normalization region for α with 0.6 < |∆φ| < 1.4.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first observation of off-diagonal 3-particle azimuthal correlations at π ± 1.45 radians in central Au+Au collisions, providing strong evidence for conical emission from Mach-cone shock waves. 2. The strongest evidence is that the cone angle remains constant (1.41–1.45 radians) as a function of associated particle pT, directly favoring the Mach-cone hydrodynamic model over Cherenkov radiation, which predicts a sharply decreasing angle. 3. The future path involves resolving the remaining ambiguity of deflected jet contributions to the on-diagonal broadening and refining the background subtraction methodology, especially for the v4 contribution and multiplicity bias effects.

summary.title: A schematic model of scattering in PT−symmetric Quantum Mechanics
summary.authors: Miloslav Znojil
summary.field_subfield: Quantum Physics / PT-symmetric Quantum Mechanics
summary.executive_summary: This paper develops a Runge-Kutta-discretized difference-equation model for one-dimensional scattering by a complex, PT-symmetric short-range potential V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x). The Schrödinger equation is discretized as -ψ(xk−1) - 2ψ(xk) + ψ(xk+1) / h² + V(xk)ψ(xk) = Eψ(xk), leading to a doubly infinite system of linear algebraic equations. The author proves that the boundary conditions at spatial infinity yield two scalar linear equations in the reflection coefficient B and transmission coefficient C, solvable via matrix inversion of a (2M−1)-dimensional tridiagonal non-square-matrix. The main result is a pair of explicit scattering-determining formulae for B and C involving a complex coefficient α and a real coefficient β, which encode all dynamical input from the potential parameters. The work demonstrates that PT-symmetric scattering can be treated using standard non-matching and non-recurrent linear algebra techniques, showing a formal parallelism between Hermitian and non-Hermitian scattering descriptions where only the functional form of α and β changes. Complexity of the formulae grows rapidly with the potential extent M, requiring symbolic manipulation for M ≥ 4. The paper bridges a gap in PT-symmetric literature, where prior work has focused predominantly on bound states rather than scattering.

Executive Summary
This paper develops a Runge-Kutta-discretized difference-equation model for one-dimensional scattering by a complex, PT-symmetric short-range potential V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x). The Schrödinger equation is discretized as -ψ(xk−1) - 2ψ(xk) + ψ(xk+1) / h² + V(xk)ψ(xk) = Eψ(xk), leading to a doubly infinite system of linear algebraic equations. The author proves that the boundary conditions at spatial infinity yield two scalar linear equations in the reflection coefficient B and transmission coefficient C, solvable via matrix inversion of a (2M−1)-dimensional tridiagonal non-square-matrix. The main result is a pair of explicit scattering-determining formulae for B and C involving a complex coefficient α and a real coefficient β, which encode all dynamical input from the potential parameters. The work demonstrates that PT-symmetric scattering can be treated using standard non-matching and non-recurrent linear algebra techniques, showing a formal parallelism between Hermitian and non-Hermitian scattering descriptions where only the functional form of α and β changes. Complexity of the formulae grows rapidly with the potential extent M, requiring symbolic manipulation for M ≥ 4. The paper bridges a gap in PT-symmetric literature, where prior work has focused predominantly on bound states rather than scattering.

Research Context
Standard quantum mechanics describes stationary one-dimensional motion via the differential Schrödinger equation with boundary conditions defining bound states or scattering. Recent developments generalized quantum mechanics to non-Hermitian, quasi-Hermitian Hamiltonians H ≠ H† possessing PT-symmetry. PT-symmetry has been introduced via an antilinear operator combining parity and time reversal. While bound states in PT-symmetric potentials have been extensively studied, a comparatively small number of papers have devoted to the scattering problem. The prior work on scattering covers separable rank-one, rectangular, reflectionless barriers, and tobogganic contours but leaves a gap for general PT-symmetric potentials.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a one-dimensional scattering problem with a complex PT-symmetric short-range potential V(x) can be solved analytically through discretization. The paper hypothesizes that Runge-Kutta discretization of the Schrödinger equation yields tractable formulae for reflection and transmission coefficients. The author predicts that the only innovation from the PT-symmetric case relative to the Hermitian case emerges via complexification of one potential-characterizing parameter. The approach assumes the potential vanishes beyond a cutoff distance, simplifying the problem to a finite system. The matching method and matrix-inversion methods are proposed as two complementary procedures for constructing solutions.

Methodological Details
The model considers a one-dimensional Schrödinger equation with a complex potential V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x) satisfying Z(−x) = Z(x) and Y(−x) = −Y(x). The differential equation is replaced by the Runge-Kutta-discretized difference equation −ψ(xk−1) − 2ψ(xk) + ψ(xk+1) / h² + V(xk)ψ(xk) = Eψ(xk) with lattice step h > 0. The boundary conditions at |k| ≥ M assume the potential vanishes, with ψ(xm) = A e^(i m ϕ) + B e^(-i m ϕ) for m ≤ -(M−1) and C e^(i m ϕ) for m ≥ M−1. The new energy variable ϕ is defined by 2 cos ϕ = 2 − h²E, imposing the energy constraint E ∈ (0, 4/h²). Two small parameters, lattice step h and inverse cutoff M, may be varied independently for optimal convergence. The Runge-Kutta method is identified as the numerical recipe for handling the O(h⁴) discrepancy between difference and differential operators. The model explores M = 1, M = 2, M = 3, and M = 4 as successive complexity increments for the potential extent.

Procedures And Architectures
The matching method constructs solutions by solving a triplet of three nontrivial linear relations for M = 1 and then a similar set for M = 2. The matrix-inversion method rewrites the difference equation as a doubly infinite system of linear algebraic equations indexed by k. The system is reduced to a (2M−1)-dimensional non-square-matrix problem by substituting boundary conditions. A non-homogeneous system of 2M−1 equations is formed with a square matrix T partitioned into blocks. The inverse matrix R = T⁻¹ has a partitioned structure with submatrix Q, row vectors t and w, and column vectors u and v. Equation (15) degenerates to two scalar linear equations in coefficients B and C via elimination of internal wavefunction components. The final scattering formulae (20) and (21) solve for B and C in terms of α, β, and energy ϕ. Symbolic manipulation on a computer is designated for M ≥ 4 due to formula complexity.

Key Results
For M = 1 (Hermitian case with only Z₀), the transmission coefficient is C = 2i sin ϕ / (2i sin ϕ − Z₀) and B = Z₀ / (2i sin ϕ − Z₀). For M = 2 (PT-symmetric with Z₀, Z₁ and Y₁), the matrix determinant is det T = (Z₀ Z₁)² / (2 − 2Z₁ + Y₁²)Z₀. For M = 3, the determinant is a polynomial in couplings Z₀, Z₁, Z₂ and Y₁, Y₂ with 14 terms in the imaginary part of γ. For M = 4, the determinant det T is represented by sums of 15 products of couplings, while Re γ has 14 and Im γ has 32 products. In the weak coupling regime for M = 4, a simplification reveals det T = −2Z₃ − 2Z₁ + ... with two linear terms followed by 10 triple-product terms. Re γ for M = 4 begins with −1 + 2Z₂Z₃ + Z₀Z₁ + Z₀Z₃ + 2Z₂Z₁ + ... with 14 products. The coefficient β is equal to 1/det T and α has the same denominator, carrying all dynamical input information. The problem is solvable by standard non-matching and non-recurrent linear algebra techniques, without special PT-symmetric machinery beyond complexification.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The formal parallelism between Hermitian and non-Hermitian scattering shows the same structural form for B and C, with differences encoded only in α and β. The manifest asymmetry between in- and out-states in PT-symmetric scattering is shown to be merely formal in this solvable exemplar. The partitioning of the Schrödinger equation enables separation of essential and inessential components, reducing the problem to a 2D matrix inversion. The constraint E ∈ (0, 4/h²) is noted as reminiscent of spectra in relativistic quantum systems. The model suggests further study on non-Hermitian versions of the inverse scattering problem. The discrete model bridges the gap between the bound-state PT-symmetric results and scattering theory.

Contradictions And Limitations
The model assumes the potential vanishes beyond a finite distance, which may not apply to all PT-symmetric potentials. The Runge-Kutta discretization introduces an O(h⁴) discrepancy with the differential operator, necessitating the h → 0 limit for exactness. The formulae become prohibitively complex for M ≥ 4, requiring symbolic computation rather than explicit algebraic expression. The analysis is a 'short analysis' and the author admits merits were not exhausted. The model is one-dimensional; multi-dimensional PT-symmetric scattering remains unaddressed. No random seed, specific lattice spacing h, or numerical convergence criteria are reported for a concrete numerical instance.

Claims
PT-symmetric scattering in 1D can be fully determined by two linear equations in B and C via matrix inversion of the discretized Schrödinger equation. The matrix T is invertible, and its inverse R enables the derivation of scalar relations (18). Explicit formulae (20) and (21) provide closed-form expressions for B and C in terms of α, β, and ϕ. Complexity grows exponentially with M, making the claim of general analytical tractability practically difficult beyond small M. Standard linear algebra, rather than PT-specific operator theory, is sufficient for solving PT-symmetric scattering.
The formal structure of scattering coefficients is identical for Hermitian and non-Hermitian PT-symmetric cases, with the difference restricted to the dynamical input encoded in α and β. In the Hermitian M=1 case, the same structural form yields C = 2i sin ϕ / (2i sin ϕ − Z₀). In the non-Hermitian case, the form is unchanged but α and β become complex and depend on Y_k. The explicit form of α and β differs substantially between the cases, which may mask structural differences. PT-symmetric scattering inherits the algebraic structure of Hermitian scattering, facilitating cross-pollination of methods.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The author discusses the O(h⁴) discrepancy between difference and differential operators as a source of uncertainty. The h → 0 limit is identified as the standard numerical recipe for removing this discrepancy. Two small parameters, h and 1/M, may be varied independently to achieve quickest convergence, though specific convergence rates are not quantified. The paper provides explicit formulae for M=1, M=2, M=3, and M=4 as successive cases, functioning as an algebraic ablation of potential complexity.

Key Figures Tables
Equation (16) presents the partitioned structure of the (2M−1)×(2M−1) square matrix T. Equation (18) shows the degenerated two-scalar linear relations from which the scattering coefficients are extracted. Equation (11) presents the doubly infinite system of linear algebraic equations in tridiagonal form. Section 5 contains explicit formulae for det T and γ for M = 2, 3, and 4, serving as the primary numerical-algebraic output of the paper.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a general difference-equation framework for 1D scattering by any complex PT-symmetric short-range potential, yielding closed-form formulae for reflection and transmission coefficients via matrix inversion. 2. The strongest evidence is the demonstration that PT-symmetric scattering reduces to a 2×2 matrix inversion problem, where all non-Hermitian effects are confined to the complex coefficient α and real coefficient β, with identical structural form to the Hermitian case. 3. The future path lies in extending this to non-Hermitian versions of the inverse scattering problem and multi-dimensional PT-symmetric potentials.

summary.title: QED⊗QCD Resummation and Shower/ME Matching for LHC Physics
summary.authors: B.F.L. Ward and S.A. Yost
summary.field_subfield: High Energy Physics - Phenomenology (hep-ph)
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a theoretical framework for the simultaneous resummation of multiple gluon and multiple photon radiative effects in LHC physics processes, formulated as QED⊗QCD exponentiation. The authors extend the YFS (Yennie-Frautschi-Suura) exponentiation formalism to non-Abelian gauge theories, enabling exact exponentiation that incorporates both QCD and QED infrared singular terms into a single master formula. The resulting structure is an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series, valid to all orders in both αs and α, providing a framework for Monte Carlo event-by-event realization without double-counting between the parton shower and matrix element corrections. To illustrate the theory, the authors apply semi-analytical methods to single heavy gauge boson production at LHC and Tevatron energies, computing the ratio of exponentiated to Born cross-sections. They find that QED effects contribute approximately 0.3% to the cross-section, matching prior structure function and perturbative calculation results. The paper also details two matching schemes between the exponentiated calculus and established parton shower Monte Carlos (HERWIG and PYTHIA): a pT-matching approach limiting the phase space and a more accurate shower-subtracted residual approach. The authors conclude that the theoretical precision tag requirement of 0.67% for LHC luminosity processes demands the inclusion of QED effects, and they position this framework as a foundation for complete O(α²s, ααs, α²) calculations for future collider physics.

claims.description: YFS theory can be extended to non-Abelian gauge theories to allow simultaneous QED⊗QCD exponentiation.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a theoretical framework for the simultaneous resummation of multiple gluon and multiple photon radiative effects in LHC physics processes, formulated as QED⊗QCD exponentiation. The authors extend the YFS (Yennie-Frautschi-Suura) exponentiation formalism to non-Abelian gauge theories, enabling exact exponentiation that incorporates both QCD and QED infrared singular terms into a single master formula. The resulting structure is an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series, valid to all orders in both αs and α, providing a framework for Monte Carlo event-by-event realization without double-counting between the parton shower and matrix element corrections. To illustrate the theory, the authors apply semi-analytical methods to single heavy gauge boson production at LHC and Tevatron energies, computing the ratio of exponentiated to Born cross-sections. They find that QED effects contribute approximately 0.3% to the cross-section, matching prior structure function and perturbative calculation results. The paper also details two matching schemes between the exponentiated calculus and established parton shower Monte Carlos (HERWIG and PYTHIA): a pT-matching approach limiting the phase space and a more accurate shower-subtracted residual approach. The authors conclude that the theoretical precision tag requirement of 0.67% for LHC luminosity processes demands the inclusion of QED effects, and they position this framework as a foundation for complete O(α²s, ααs, α²) calculations for future collider physics.

Research Context
The LHC experimental luminosity precision is tagged at the 2% level. The theoretical precision tag for single W and Z production must be at the 0.67% level. Multiple gluon and photon radiative effects must be controlled at this stated precision. QED contributions in the evolution of structure functions lead to effects at the level of ∼0.3%. The QCD resummation theory is based on the N = 1 term in the exponent in the formal proof of exponentiation in non-Abelian gauge theories. The threshold region of heavy gauge boson production yields effects of similar size. All these must be taken into account if one wants ∼1.0% for the theoretical precision tag. The soft-collinear effective theory (SCET) has been developed to treat double resummation of soft and collinear effects.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to simultaneously resum multiple gluon and multiple photon radiative effects without double-counting. The hypothesis is that the YFS exponentiation formalism can be extended to a QED⊗QCD theory by exponentiating both QCD and QED IR terms simultaneously. The authors expect that QED contributions will be of the order 0.3% at LHC and Tevatron energies. The theory is predicted to allow an exact treatment of the respective phase space in MC methods. The QCD dominant corrections are expected to happen an order of magnitude earlier than those for QED.

Methodological Details
The analysis considers single heavy boson production at hadron colliders: q + ¯q′ → V + n(g) + X → ¯ℓℓ′ + n(g) + X. V represents W±, Z, and ℓ represents e, µ, ℓ′ represents νe, νµ(e, µ) for W+(Z). Structure functions are sourced from Ref. [23] for the semi-analytical examination. Monte Carlo realization is noted as appearing elsewhere, with a reference to Ref. [24]. Exact O(α²s) and exact O(α) results from Refs. [15–17] and [18–20] serve as benchmarks. The cross-section formula incorporates structure functions F_i(xi) and F_j(xj) integrated over the exponentiated parton-level cross-section. The Born cross-section uses well-known parton-level values without the narrow resonance approximation. The comparison is performed for both LHC and Tevatron center-of-mass energies.

Procedures And Architectures
The QCD exponentiation is an exact rearrangement based on the eikonal approximation in non-Abelian gauge theories. The exponential is augmented with residuals that take into account remaining contributions to the perturbative series exactly to all orders in αs. QED⊗QCD exponentiation is obtained by simultaneously exponentiating the large IR terms in QCD and the exact IR divergent terms in QED. The new residuals ˜¯βn,m represent the successive application of the YFS expansion first for QCD and subsequently for QED. The substitutions Bnls_QCD → Bnls_QCED, ˜Bnls_QCD → ˜Bnls_QCED, and ˜Snls_QCD → ˜Snls_QCED determine the QCED functions from their QCD analogs. The exponent γQCED is defined as 2Q²f/απ + 2CF/αsπ times the lnls term. The matching procedure involves generating a parton shower from an initial (x1, x2) point at factorization scale µ using HERWIG and/or PYTHIA. The pT-matching approach requires restricting gluon emission below the factorization scale µ to avoid double-counting with structure functions. The shower-subtracted approach calculates new residuals {ˆ˜¯βn,m} by expanding the shower formula, the exponent, and the residuals to match exact perturbative coefficients.

Key Results
The ratio r_exp = σ_exp/σ_Born at LHC with QED⊗QCD is 1.1901. The ratio at LHC with QCD only is 1.1872, indicating a QED contribution of 0.29% (∼0.3%). The ratio at Tevatron with QED⊗QCD is 1.1911. The ratio at Tevatron with QCD only is 1.1879. The QED effect of ∼0.3% is stable under scale variations. The results agree with Refs. [15,16,18–20] on the sizes of the QED and QCD effects. The QED effect is similar in size to structure function results found in Refs. [9–13]. The leading ˜¯β0,0-level gives already a good estimate of the size of the interplay between higher order QED and QCD effects.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The simultaneous exponentiation allows for a framework that can systematically improve calculation accuracy without double-counting of effects. The result in (2) is a representation that is exact and can be used to make contact with parton shower MCs without unnecessary averaging of effects. QED is needed for LHC theory predictions at ≲1% precision. The framework provides a firm theoretical basis for complete O(α²s, ααs, α²) results needed for FNAL/LHC/RHIC/ILC physics. The distinction between QCD and QED lies in the essential compensation between non-Abelian IR virtual and real singularities.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper notes that the exactness of equation (1) might cause confusion because it does not explicitly show an ordered exponential operator. The authors acknowledge that a Monte Carlo realization will appear elsewhere, indicating the current paper is primarily theoretical. The analysis of W production is noted as being in progress, so results are only for Z production in this paper. The shower-subtracted residual approach is described as under investigation, with only limited realization at DAPHNE energies. The final result should be independent of the regulator (mass or dimensional), but this remains a cross-check to be verified.

Claims
YFS theory can be extended to non-Abelian gauge theories to allow simultaneous QED⊗QCD exponentiation. The construction of equation (2) by simultaneously exponentiating both IR terms proves the feasibility. The resulting residuals ˜¯βn,m are free of all infrared singularities. The QED effects of 0.3% at both LHC and FNAL validate the prediction. The paper notes the exactness of the form is somewhat ambiguous to some readers due to the lack of explicit ordering. This enables full MC event generator realization combining the calculus with HERWIG and PYTHIA. The framework supports complete O(α²s, ααs, α²) results for all major future colliders.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The QED effect of 0.3% is stated to be stable under scale variations. The final result should be independent of the regulator (mass vs dimensional), serving as a cross-check. Both pT-matching and shower-subtracted residual approaches are under investigation with shower-subtracted residuals realized at DAPHNE energies. The authors note that the leading ˜¯β0,0-level already gives a good estimate of the interplay.

Key Figures Tables
Equation (8) presents the numerical results for r_exp at LHC and Tevatron with and without QED. Equation (5) shows the analytic form for the ˜¯β0,0-level exponentiated cross-section. Equation (6) defines the QED⊗QCD exponent γQCED. Equations (7) provide the well-known YFS functions F_YFS and δ_YFS.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first extension of YFS exponentiation to a combined QED⊗QCD framework, enabling simultaneous resummation of both gauge boson and photon IR effects to all orders. 2. The strongest evidence is the numerical agreement of the 0.3% QED correction at both LHC and Tevatron energies with prior structure function and perturbative calculations, confirming the theory's predictive power. 3. The future path involves complete O(α²s, ααs, α²) calculations for W production, FNAL/LHC/RHIC/ILC physics, and full Monte Carlo realization of the matched shower-matrix element framework.
