judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper provides a comprehensive taxonomy and comparative performance analysis of image denoising algorithms, categorizing noise types into additive and multiplicative natures and classifying denoising methods into spatial filtering and transform domain filtering branches. The authors first classify noise into Gaussian (additive), Salt and Pepper (impulse), Speckle (multiplicative, gamma distribution), and Brownian (fractal/1/f) types, each accompanied by mathematical probability density functions and visual illustrations. Denoising algorithms are structured into two primary families: spatial filtering (nonlinear median types such as weighted median, rank conditioned rank selection, and relaxed median; and linear types including mean and Wiener filtering) and transform domain filtering (spatial-frequency using FFT, wavelet domain including linear/nonlinear thresholding with various adaptive schemes, non-orthogonal wavelet transforms, and wavelet coefficient modeling). The paper concludes with a quantitative comparative study applying six algorithms to a grayscale Lena image at 90% noise density, evaluating performance via Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Image Enhancement Factor (IEF). The results demonstrate that wavelet-based methods significantly outperform traditional spatial filters, with MDBUTMF achieving the highest PSNR of 17.9865 dB and IEF of 16.2066, while the mean filter yields the lowest PSNR of 6.5759 dB. The paper offers a structured reference for selecting denoising algorithms based on noise characteristics and image requirements.

Research Context
Digital image processing is extensively deployed in image restoration, which involves removing degradations occurring during image acquisition. Image degradation arises from blurring caused by imperfect formation processes and noise introduced by transmission, measurement, and digitization errors. A major gap exists in selecting the appropriate denoising algorithm, as the optimal choice is application-dependent and requires prior knowledge of the specific noise present. Image denoising has critical applications in photography, astronomy (resolution limitations), medical imaging (high-quality analysis), and forensic science (low-quality photographic evidence). The prior state of the art is characterized by two basic approaches: spatial filtering and transform domain filtering, but the choice among specific algorithm variants remains complex.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how different denoising algorithms compare in performance when applied to a real-world test image at a high noise density. The authors hypothesize that transform-domain (specifically wavelet-based) methods will significantly outperform traditional spatial filters in PSNR and IEF metrics. A secondary implicit hypothesis is that adaptive thresholding schemes within the wavelet domain will yield superior results over non-adaptive universal thresholds. The paper predicts that noise classification (Gaussian, Salt and Pepper, Speckle, Brownian) should directly inform the selection of the denoising algorithm. The anticipated outcome is a quantitative ranking of algorithm performance at 90% noise density, establishing a hierarchy of denoising techniques.

Methodological Details
The study evaluates image denoising algorithms on a grayscale test image of Lena, which serves as the standard evaluation image. The noise density applied to the test image is set to 90%, a high-noise regime for performance evaluation. Six distinct denoising filters are compared: Mean Filter (MF), Adaptive Mean Filter (AMF), Poisson Spatial Mean Filter (PSMF), Discrete Bayes Algorithm (DBA), Multi-Discrete Bayes Algorithm (MDBA), and Multi-Discrete Bayes Universal Threshold Multi-Filter (MDBUTMF). Performance is quantified using Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) expressed in decibels and Image Enhancement Factor (IEF), where IEF relates the de-noised image intensity to the original. The classification scheme organizes algorithms into four hierarchies: Spatial Filtering (Non-Linear, Linear), Transform Domain (Spatial-Frequency, Wavelet Domain), Wavelet Sub-types, and Coefficient Modeling. The paper references multiple image types: binary (1 bit/pixel), grayscale (8 bits/pixel, 256 levels), and color (24 bits/pixel, RGB).

Procedures And Architectures
Noise models are mathematically defined: Gaussian noise follows a bell-shaped PDF; Salt and Pepper noise has two values (typically 0 and 255) with probability < 0.1; Speckle noise follows a gamma distribution; Brownian noise is fractal 1/f noise. Non-linear spatial filters include weighted median, rank conditioned rank selection, and relaxed median, which remove noise without explicit identification of noise type. Linear spatial filters include the mean filter (optimal for Gaussian noise) and Wiener filtering, which requires knowledge of signal and noise spectra. Wavelet thresholding exploits the property that wavelet transform maps white noise to white noise, concentrating signal energy into fewer coefficients. Hard thresholding removes small coefficients; soft thresholding shrinks coefficients above the threshold by the threshold value; semi-soft and Garrote thresholding are variants. Adaptive thresholds include VISU Shrink (universal), SURE Shrink (hybrid), Bayes Shrink (generalized Gaussian prior), and Cross Validation (GCV minimization). Non-orthogonal wavelet transforms such as UDWT (shift-invariant) and Shift Invariant Wavelet Packet Decomposition (SIWPD) are reviewed as computation-heavy alternatives. Wavelet coefficient modeling includes deterministic tree structure approximation and statistical multi-scale correlation modeling.

Key Results
At 90% noise density, the Mean Filter (MF) achieves the lowest PSNR of 6.5759 dB and IEF of 1.1712, indicating poor denoising performance in high-noise regimes. The Adaptive Mean Filter (AMF) improves PSNR to 8.0603 dB and IEF to 1.6499 compared to MF. The Poisson Spatial Mean Filter (PSMF) yields PSNR of 6.7847 dB and IEF of 1.2257. The Discrete Bayes Algorithm (DBA) shows a dramatic step-change, achieving PSNR of 17.1205 dB and IEF of 13.2768. The Multi-Discrete Bayes Algorithm (MDBA) slightly improves on DBA with PSNR of 17.2242 dB and IEF of 13.5976. The MDBUTMF (Multi-Discrete Bayes Universal Threshold Multi-Filter) achieves the best overall performance with PSNR of 17.9865 dB and IEF of 16.2066. The relative performance gap between MF (6.5759 dB) and MDBUTMF (17.9865 dB) is +11.4106 dB absolute, representing a massive improvement in signal fidelity. The IEF improves from 1.1712 for MF to 16.2066 for MDBUTMF, a +15.0354 absolute increase and approx +1250% relative enhancement.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The dramatic performance jump from spatial mean filters (6-8 dB) to wavelet-based Bayes methods (17+ dB) validates that transform-domain separation of signal and noise is theoretically superior to neighborhood averaging. The multi-discrete Bayes thresholding approach (MDBUTMF) leverages multi-resolution wavelet properties, confirming that multi-scale correlation of signal across resolutions preserves structural details while suppressing noise. The paper implies that for high-noise scenarios (>50%), simple linear spatial filters are insufficient for visually acceptable image reconstruction. The classification of noise into additive and multiplicative types serves as a design principle: multiplicative noise (speckle) requires different treatment than additive Gaussian noise.

Contradictions And Limitations
The comparative study is limited to a single image (Lena) and a single noise density (90%), limiting generalizability across all noise types and intensities. No quantitative comparison is provided for Salt and Pepper, Speckle, or Brownian noise specifically; the 90% noise density is not explicitly stated as being Gaussian. The paper notes that linear wavelet filters can produce visually displeasing images despite MSE reduction, a conflict between objective metrics and subjective quality not resolved in the results. UDWT and Multiwavelets are noted for superior MSE results (Lena image) but are described as less feasible due to large computational overhead, a practical limitation not quantified in the results. The random seed, hyperparameter choices (wavelet decomposition level, threshold values), and computational time are not reported, limiting reproducibility.

Claims
Transform-domain wavelet denoising significantly outperforms spatial filtering for high-noise image reconstruction. Wavelet-based MDBUTMF achieves 17.9865 dB PSNR vs. MF's 6.5759 dB at 90% noise. The IEF jump from 1.1712 to 16.2066 confirms massive signal preservation advantage of wavelet methods. Linear wavelet filters can produce visually displeasing images even when MSE reduction is successful. Non-adaptive VISU Shrink yields overly smoothed images due to threshold dependence on pixel count. Wavelet thresholding should be the default for high-noise image reconstruction tasks in astronomy, medical imaging, and forensics.
Adaptive thresholding schemes in the wavelet domain yield superior performance over universal (non-adaptive) thresholds. Bayes Shrink outperforms SURE Shrink most of the times by using generalized Gaussian prior. Cross Validation provides an optimum threshold for every coefficient by minimizing GCV. The assumption that coefficient magnitude alone distinguishes noise from signal is violated when noise levels exceed signal magnitudes. Under high-noise conditions, spatial configuration of neighboring coefficients must be incorporated into thresholding decisions.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The paper references that non-adaptive VISU Shrink yields overly smoothed images, identifying a robustness issue with universal thresholds. Hard thresholding is noted to generate spurious blips (artifacts) from moderately large noise coefficients. No systematic ablation study (e.g. varying wavelet levels, specific hyperparameter sweeps) is reported beyond the 6-filter comparison.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 displays the Gaussian distribution PDF (bell-shaped curve) with mean and standard deviation parameters. Figure 2 shows Gaussian noise illustrations at two regimes: (a) Mean=0, variance 0.05; (b) Mean=1.5, variance 10. Figure 3 displays the probability density function for Salt and Pepper noise. Figure 4 illustrates Salt and Pepper noise with a variance of 0.05. Figure 5 presents the Gamma distribution PDF, the mathematical model for Speckle noise. Figure 6 illustrates Speckle noise with variance 0.05 on an image. Figure 7 displays the Brownian noise distribution (fractal 1/f). Figure 8 shows Brownian noise illustration developed from Fraclab. Figure 9 presents the expanded classification tree of image denoising techniques. Table I presents the quantitative comparison of PSNR and IEF for six filters at 90% noise density, showing MDBUTMF as the best performer.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a systematic classification of image noise types (Gaussian, Impulse, Speckle, Brownian) and a hierarchical taxonomy of denoising algorithms, coupled with a quantitative PSNR/IEF comparison on a 90% noisy grayscale test image. 2. The strongest evidence is the PSNR improvement from 6.5759 dB (Mean Filter) to 17.9865 dB (MDBUTMF), demonstrating that wavelet-domain adaptive thresholding provides >2.5x the signal fidelity of spatial averaging at 90% noise density. 3. The future path involves addressing the computational overhead of non-orthogonal wavelet transforms (UDWT, Multiwavelets), developing more computationally efficient adaptive thresholding schemes, and extending the comparison to all four noise types and variable noise densities.

summary.title: Real-Time Ramsey Interferometry in Fractional Quantum Hall States
summary.authors: Tal Goren and Karyn Le Hur
summary.field_subfield: Condensed Matter Physics / Fractional Quantum Hall Effect
summary.executive_summary: This paper proposes a Ramsey interferometry scheme to probe the time-dependent dynamical phase and Green's function of fractional quasiparticles at the edges of fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states. The authors introduce a Ramsey voltage modulation—comprised of two short pulses separated by a time delay t₀—applied to a quantum point contact (QPC) in a Hall bar geometry. This modulation generates an interference term in the current noise that oscillates at frequency ω − qVdc, where q is the charge of the tunneling particle. The authors derive analytical expressions for the Ramsey noise in two geometries: point-like tunneling of fractional quasiparticles (charge q = eν) and tunneling between separated Hall droplets where electrons tunnel (charge q = e). For Laughlin states at filling factor ν = 1/(2n+1), the noise reveals the quasiparticle Green's function in the time domain, with an amplitude that decays as a power law t₀⁻²ν at low temperature (T ≪ t₀⁻¹) and exponentially as exp(−2πνTt₀) at high temperature (T ≫ t₀⁻¹). In momentum-resolved tunneling geometry, the oscillation frequency is further shifted by the momentum boost qBv. Crucially, for the 5/2 FQH state, the scheme can differentiate between the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states (α = 0 vs α = 1) through the phase shift ϕ⁎₀ in the interference pattern. The Ramsey protocol is distinguished from Mach-Zehnder interferometry by requiring only a single QPC and allowing continuous scanning of the time delay, providing a direct probe of the charge conjugated to the electric field without sensitivity to bulk quasiparticle number. The authors conclude that this method generalizes to other topological states, including superconductors via Bogoliubov quasiparticles.

Executive Summary
This paper proposes a Ramsey interferometry scheme to probe the time-dependent dynamical phase and Green's function of fractional quasiparticles at the edges of fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states. The authors introduce a Ramsey voltage modulation—comprised of two short pulses separated by a time delay t₀—applied to a quantum point contact (QPC) in a Hall bar geometry. This modulation generates an interference term in the current noise that oscillates at frequency ω − qVdc, where q is the charge of the tunneling particle. The authors derive analytical expressions for the Ramsey noise in two geometries: point-like tunneling of fractional quasiparticles (charge q = eν) and tunneling between separated Hall droplets where electrons tunnel (charge q = e). For Laughlin states at filling factor ν = 1/(2n+1), the noise reveals the quasiparticle Green's function in the time domain, with an amplitude that decays as a power law t₀⁻²ν at low temperature (T ≪ t₀⁻¹) and exponentially as exp(−2πνTt₀) at high temperature (T ≫ t₀⁻¹). In momentum-resolved tunneling geometry, the oscillation frequency is further shifted by the momentum boost qBv. Crucially, for the 5/2 FQH state, the scheme can differentiate between the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states (α = 0 vs α = 1) through the phase shift ϕ⁎₀ in the interference pattern. The Ramsey protocol is distinguished from Mach-Zehnder interferometry by requiring only a single QPC and allowing continuous scanning of the time delay, providing a direct probe of the charge conjugated to the electric field without sensitivity to bulk quasiparticle number. The authors conclude that this method generalizes to other topological states, including superconductors via Bogoliubov quasiparticles.

Research Context
The fractional quantum Hall effect is characterized by excitations with fractional charge and statistics, described by a chiral Luttinger liquid effective theory. Ramsey interferometry has recently been suggested to probe dynamics in one-dimensional quasicondensates, spin ensembles, and Rydberg atoms. Prior work has explored quantum Hall edge states but a direct time-resolved measurement of the dynamical phase and Green's function of tunneling particles is missing. The current gap is in measuring the charge conjugated to the electric field via the time dynamics of excitations in strongly correlated topological states.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether Ramsey voltage modulation applied to a quantum point contact can probe the dynamical phase and Green's function of fractional quasiparticles. The authors hypothesize that the interference pattern in the current noise reveals the fractional charge and the specific Green's function of the tunneling particles in the time domain. A secondary hypothesis is that the 5/2 non-Abelian state's Ramsey signal can differentiate between the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian candidates. The predicted outcome is a Ramsey interference pattern oscillating at frequency ω − qVdc with an amplitude governed by the power-law or exponential decay of the quasiparticle envelope. The authors predict the fractionalization manifests in three places: the prefactor (qD)², the Green's function, and the dynamical phase factor qVdc.

Methodological Details
The system consists of Laughlin states at filling factor ν = 1/(2n+1), where n is an integer. Two geometries of the quantum point contact are considered: tunneling between edges of a Hall bar and tunneling between two separated Hall droplets. The tunneling particles are fractional quasiparticles with charge q = eν in geometry (a) and electrons with charge q = e in geometry (b). The creation operator for a fractional quasiparticle is expressed by bosonic chiral fields φR/L(x). Commutation relations are used to ensure correct anti-commutation for electrons and fractional statistics for quasiparticles. The Keldysh formalism is applied to describe the non-equilibrium current-current correlation function. The Planck constant is fixed to ℏ = 1. The Hamiltonian includes a dynamical phase ϕ(t) defined by the integral of the voltage V(t).

Procedures And Architectures
A Ramsey voltage modulation composed of two short pulses is applied on top of a constant dc voltage V₀. Pulse durations much smaller than the delay time t₀ allow approximating the pulse by a Dirac delta function qV₀(t) ≈ ϕ₀δ(t). The stationary phase approximation identifies four contributions: t₁ = t₂ = 0, t₁ = t₂ = t₀, t₁ = 0 t₂ = t₀, and t₁ = t₀ t₂ = 0. The current-current correlation function is calculated to second order in tunneling amplitude D using the Keldysh contour. For point-like tunneling, the Green's function for Laughlin states is computed analytically from chiral Luttinger liquid theory. In momentum-resolved tunneling, a long tunnel junction L with momentum boost qB = qBd/ℏ is modeled, where B is the perpendicular magnetic field. The contour integral is closed in the lower half-plane, and poles are analyzed to find the dominant contribution at x = −vt₀.

Key Results
The Ramsey noise for Laughlin quasiparticles at point-like QPC follows: S ≈ 2(eν)²D² [1 + cos πν × (sinh πTt₀ / πTτ)⁻²ν cos((ω − eνVdc)t₀ − ϕ₀)]. At low temperature (T ≪ t₀⁻¹), the oscillation amplitude decays as a power law t₀⁻²ν. At high temperature (T ≫ t₀⁻¹), the amplitude decays exponentially as exp(−2πνTt₀). For electron tunneling in the droplet geometry, the noise follows the same form with ν → 1/ν, yielding the prefactor (eD)² and charge factor eVdc. In momentum-resolved tunneling, the oscillation frequency shifts by qBv, giving the form S ≈ q²D² L / (2πa) [1 + (sinh 2πTt₀ / πTτ)⁻ν sin((ω − qVdc + qBv)t₀ − ϕ₀)]. For the 5/2 state, the Ramsey signal can differentiate between the Pfaffian (α = 0) and anti-Pfaffian (α = 1) states via the phase ϕ⁎₀. The Pfaffian phase shift is ϕ⁎₀ = ϕ₀ + π/16 (3 + 8α²), while the anti-Pfaffian gives α = 1. The particle-hole Pfaffian state cannot be distinguished from the Pfaffian state because the Majorana field propagates in the opposite direction.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The Ramsey protocol measures the Green's function in the time domain, providing a spectroscopic view of the quasiparticle envelope in time and space. The decay of the Ramsey interference is not a finite lifetime effect but a measure of the envelope of the wave-function of the fractional quasiparticle. The Ramsey interference probes the charge conjugated to the electric field, enabling detection of the dressed charge (Laughlin quasiparticle charge vs electron charge). Compared to Mach-Zehnder, Ramsey interferometry uses only one QPC and allows continuous scanning of t₀, avoiding sensitivity to bulk quasiparticle number. The methodology extends to other topological states of matter and light, and to superconductors via Bogoliubov quasiparticles.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper does not specify the numerical value of the tunneling amplitude D, the edge velocity v, or the short-time cutoff τ, limiting direct comparison with experiment. The approximation of the pulse by a Dirac delta function requires very short pulses relative to t₀, which may be experimentally challenging. The stationary phase approximation assumes well-defined extrema; for complex voltage shapes, the single-frequency oscillation may be corrupted. The treatment of the 5/2 state assumes the Majorana field properties from existing literature without independent verification within this framework. The particle-hole Pfaffian cannot be distinguished from the Pfaffian, creating a fundamental degeneracy for this specific discrimination task.

Claims
Ramsey interferometry applied to a quantum point contact in a FQH Hall bar can directly measure the Green's function of fractional quasiparticles in the time domain. The noise amplitude is explicitly proportional to the product of Green's functions Gᴸ(t₀) and Gᴿ(t₀). The crossover between power-law and exponential decay as a function of T/t₀ is analytically derived. The Green's functions are computed directly from the chiral Luttinger liquid Hamiltonian. The theoretical treatment does not account for experimental decoherence mechanisms (dephasing, voltage noise) that would broaden the Ramsey peaks. The Dirac delta pulse approximation breaks down if pulse durations are comparable to t₀. Measuring the time-domain Green's function allows characterizing the spatial extent and dispersion of quasiparticles. This can be used to validate or refute specific fractionalization models beyond the Laughlin series.
The scheme can differentiate between the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states at filling factor 5/2 by detecting the Majorana mode direction. The phase shift ϕ⁎₀ depends explicitly on α, which is 0 for Pfaffian and 1 for anti-Pfaffian. This is derived from the Ising spin field and boson field structure of non-Abelian excitations. The particle-hole Pfaffian state yields the same Ramsey signal as the Pfaffian state, limiting the scope of the discrimination. Confirmation of the anti-Pfaffian state would support the particle-hole Pfaffian description favored by recent experiments. This provides a direct topological probe complementary to Mach-Zehnder and thermal Hall conductance measurements.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The paper compares two geometries (point-like vs momentum-resolved) as a form of sensitivity analysis, showing how the oscillation frequency and amplitude depend on the junction length and magnetic field. The integer quantum Hall limit ν = 1 serves as a cross-check, where the quasiparticle and electron noise formulas coincide. The temperature limits (T ≫ t₀⁻¹ and T ≪ t₀⁻¹) are examined to verify the expected analytic behavior of the Luttinger liquid Green's function.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1(a) illustrates tunneling between two edges of a Hall bar, where the black lines indicate chiral edge states and the tunneling particles are fractional quasiparticles. Figure 1(b) shows tunneling between two separated Hall droplets, where only electrons or holes can tunnel.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the derivation of an analytic Ramsey noise formula that directly encodes the fractional quasiparticle Green's function, enabling time-domain spectroscopy of fractional excitations. 2. The strongest evidence is the explicit prediction of the t₀⁻²ν power-law decay (low T) and the distinct phase shift ϕ⁎₀ (α-dependent) that uniquely identifies the Pfaffian vs anti-Pfaffian non-Abelian states. 3. The future path is the experimental implementation of the Ramsey pulse sequence on a 5/2 quantum Hall bar and generalization to other topological systems including superconductors.

summary.title: An algorithm for stress and mixed control in Galerkin based FFT homogenization
summary.authors: S. Lucarini and J. Segurado
summary.field_subfield: Computational Mechanics / FFT-based Homogenization
summary.executive_summary: This paper proposes a new algorithm to impose macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient control within the framework of non-linear Galerkin-based FFT homogenization. FFT-based homogenization traditionally relies on a projection operator that enforces compatibility of the deformation gradient tensor field, and the original Galerkin formulation was developed only for strain control (imposing the full macroscopic deformation gradient). The authors extend this by modifying the projection operator at the null frequency: for stress control, the null frequency is set to the fourth-order identity tensor (δikδjl), and for mixed control, the null frequency value depends on the component (identity for stress-controlled components, zero for strain-controlled components). The resulting equilibrium equation remains linear or non-linear in the same form as the original, solved by conjugate gradient for linear sub-problems and Newton-Raphson for the non-linear outer loop. The algorithm does not require additional iterations beyond the original strain-control scheme, neither in the linear iterative solver nor the Newton scheme. Efficiency is demonstrated on two benchmarks: a particle-reinforced hyperelastic composite (643 voxels, volume fraction 0.2, Saint Venant-Kirchhoff model) and a polycrystal (643 voxels, ~200 grains, crystal plasticity elasto-visco-plastic model). In the hyperelastic case, stress and mixed control produce identical Pxx-Fxx paths to the original strain control, while transverse stresses remain zero, unlike the small compressive stresses seen in full strain control. In the polycrystal case, strain rate effects cause minor discrepancies between mixed and full stress control, and a pseudo-uniaxial test (full strain control with isochoric restriction) produces large inaccurate transverse compressive stresses. Performance analysis shows that the new algorithm takes approximately the same number of iterations as the strain control version in both models, with the polycrystal stress control case being faster overall due to elastic-dominated increments.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper proposes a new algorithm to impose macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient control within the framework of non-linear Galerkin-based FFT homogenization. FFT-based homogenization traditionally relies on a projection operator that enforces compatibility of the deformation gradient tensor field, and the original Galerkin formulation was developed only for strain control (imposing the full macroscopic deformation gradient). The authors extend this by modifying the projection operator at the null frequency: for stress control, the null frequency is set to the fourth-order identity tensor (δikδjl), and for mixed control, the null frequency value depends on the component (identity for stress-controlled components, zero for strain-controlled components). The resulting equilibrium equation remains linear or non-linear in the same form as the original, solved by conjugate gradient for linear sub-problems and Newton-Raphson for the non-linear outer loop. The algorithm does not require additional iterations beyond the original strain-control scheme, neither in the linear iterative solver nor the Newton scheme. Efficiency is demonstrated on two benchmarks: a particle-reinforced hyperelastic composite (643 voxels, volume fraction 0.2, Saint Venant-Kirchhoff model) and a polycrystal (643 voxels, ~200 grains, crystal plasticity elasto-visco-plastic model). In the hyperelastic case, stress and mixed control produce identical Pxx-Fxx paths to the original strain control, while transverse stresses remain zero, unlike the small compressive stresses seen in full strain control. In the polycrystal case, strain rate effects cause minor discrepancies between mixed and full stress control, and a pseudo-uniaxial test (full strain control with isochoric restriction) produces large inaccurate transverse compressive stresses. Performance analysis shows that the new algorithm takes approximately the same number of iterations as the strain control version in both models, with the polycrystal stress control case being faster overall due to elastic-dominated increments.

Research Context
Computational homogenization simulates mechanical response by solving boundary value problems in periodic representative volume elements (RVEs). The finite element method has been the traditional approach for imposing any macroscopic load history. FFT-based homogenization has become a popular alternative due to superior computational performance for complex geometries with millions of degrees of freedom. FFT methods solve the boundary problem by replacing differential operators with Fourier-space equivalents. Imposing macroscopic stress or mixed loading paths is not a direct task in the FFT framework. Classical FFT schemes based on the Lippmann-Schwinger equation require a reference medium, which can influence convergence rates. Iterative approaches are the usual solution for stress control in classical FFT schemes, requiring the algorithm to correct the strain at each step. The Galerkin-based FFT approach avoids a reference medium and uses projection operators to ensure compatibility, but was originally formulated only for deformation gradient control.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to impose macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient control in Galerkin-based FFT homogenization without the need for additional iterative corrections. The hypothesis is that by modifying only the projection operator at the null frequency, the equilibrium problem can be reformulated for stress or mixed control while preserving the exact form and computational performance of the original variational method. It is predicted that the resulting algorithm will not require additional iterations compared to the strain-control version, neither in the conjugate gradient solver nor the Newton scheme. The paper further hypothesizes that the same convergence rate will be maintained for non-linear constitutive models including hyperelastic and crystal plasticity behaviors.

Methodological Details
The RVE is discretized into nx by ny by nz voxels (643 total voxels in both benchmark cases). The particle-reinforced composite consists of a hyperelastic matrix reinforced by 4 stiff spherical particles. The particle volume fraction is 0.2. The matrix follows a Saint Venant-Kirchhoff hyperelastic model with shear modulus 28 Pa and bulk modulus 46.67 Pa. The particle moduli are one order of magnitude stiffer (10 times larger). The polycrystal RVE contains around 200 randomly oriented grains. Each grain follows a crystal plasticity elasto-visco-plastic behavior. The particle test reaches a final elongation of λ_end = 0.2 in 100 load increments. The polycrystal test reaches a final elongation of λ_end = 0.02 in 200s with 20 regular increments. The linear momentum balance is imposed in its weak form in the reference configuration. Test functions are virtual deformation gradients premultiplied by a projection operator to enforce compatibility. The iterative linear solver is the conjugate gradient method. The nonlinear outer loop uses the Newton-Raphson scheme.

Procedures And Architectures
The Galerkin-based FFT formulation writes the linear momentum balance as G(P(F, α)) = 0 in Fourier space. The projection operator bG is a fourth-order tensor defined by bG_ijkl = δ_ik ξ_j ξ_l / (ξ · ξ) for non-null frequencies. For strain control, the projection operator evaluates to zero at the null (zero) frequency ξ = 0. For stress control, the new projection operator bG* evaluates to the fourth-order identity tensor δ_ik δ_jl at the null frequency. For mixed control, the null frequency value is δ_ik δ_jl for stress-controlled components and 0_ijkl for strain-controlled components. The Newton iteration linearizes the stress around the current deformation gradient: P(F_i + δF) ≈ P(F_i) + K_i : δF, where K_i = ∂P / ∂F_i. The linear system G*(K : δF) = -G*(P(F_i) - P) is solved for the correction δF. In stress control, the correction δF includes a mean value term, unlike the strain control case where δF is purely fluctuating. The Nyquist frequency is approximated as a null fourth-order tensor to recover frequency symmetry in even discretizations.

Key Results
In the hyperelastic composite, stress control (Case 2) and mixed control (Case 1) produce identical Pxx-Fxx paths to the strain control (Case 3). In the hyperelastic case, transverse stresses under stress and mixed control are exactly zero, while strain control develops small compressive transverse stresses. At the endpoint, macroscopic and microscopic results are the same within numerical accuracy for all three control cases in the hyperelastic model. In the polycrystal, cases (1) and (2) are not exactly superposed due to strain rate differences. The pseudo-uniaxial test (Case 4) in the polycrystal develops large compressive transverse stresses that grow with strain, rendering it inaccurate for uniaxial tension emulation. For the hyperelastic model, stress and mixed control required approximately the same number of iterations as strain control per load increment. In the polycrystal model, the stress control case (Case 2) is faster overall because most load increments are elastic and solved in one Newton iteration. The linear solver tolerance is 10^-8 and the Newton solver tolerance is 10^-6. The jumps in the iteration count are attributed to the increase or decrease of one Newton iteration after a given time increment.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The modified projection operator enforces the macroscopic stress condition exactly at the null frequency while preserving compatibility for all non-zero frequencies. The equilibrium equation retains its variational form, meaning no additional computational overhead is introduced compared to the strain-control version. The separation of the mean and fluctuating parts in the stress allows the target macroscopic stress to enter the equation directly through the projection operator. The same convergence rate is theoretically expected because the linear and nonlinear operators retain their structure, affecting only the null frequency contribution. The method is broadly applicable to any non-linear constitutive equation, including crystal plasticity and crystal-based models.

Contradictions And Limitations
In the polycrystal, cases (1) and (2) are not identical because the crystal plasticity model is rate-dependent, introducing discrepancies between stress-controlled and strain-rate-controlled paths. The speed advantage of stress control in the polycrystal case is a consequence of using fixed time steps; for adaptive time stepping, all cases would require similar times. The paper does not report the exact number of total CPU-seconds or explicit convergence rates in terms of absolute time, providing only normalized relative comparisons. The random number generator and seed used for grain orientation in the polycrystal are not specified. The Newton solver convergence depends on the constitutive model's Jacobian quality, which is not quantitatively benchmarked across different models.

Claims
A new algorithm for stress and mixed control in Galerkin-based FFT homogenization does not require additional iterations beyond the standard strain-control scheme. The linear system solver (conjugate gradient) and Newton scheme use the same number of iterations as the strain-control case in the hyperelastic model. The polycrystal case shows a similar iteration tendency where the new algorithm matches the strain-control count per step. The equilibrium equation maintains the same variational form, avoiding the need for iterative strain corrections. In the polycrystal, the iteration count for Case 2 is lower overall because it traverses elastic regions faster, not because the algorithm per se is faster. This allows for mixed boundary condition problems to be solved without computational penalty, preserving FFT method advantages.
Full strain control (Case 4) can inaccurately emulate uniaxial stress in polycrystals, producing non-zero compressive transverse stresses. In the pseudo-uniaxial test, compressive transverse stresses are not zero and grow with applied strain. This difference is particularly noticeable when comparing transverse responses between the four cases. For the hyperelastic model, the transverse stresses under strain control are small and the endpoint results are consistent. Strain-controlled uniaxial tension emulation should be avoided for plastic materials in favor of true stress-control or mixed-control algorithms.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The algorithm is tested on two constitutive models: a hyperelastic (Saint Venant-Kirchhoff) and a crystal plasticity elasto-visco-plastic model. Three loading paths are compared for each model: mixed (ramp deformation gradient), full stress (linear stress ramp), and full strain (linear deformation gradient ramp). A fourth pseudo-uniaxial case (Case 4) is included for the polycrystal to show the failure of standard strain-control emulation. The convergence is monitored via the L2 norm of the residual for the linear solver and the maximum deformation gradient correction for the Newton solver. Tolerances are set to 10^-8 for linear and 10^-6 for the Newton solver.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1(a) shows the particle-reinforced cubic RVE with 4 particles and 643 voxels. Figure 1(b) presents Pxx responses for the three hyperelastic loading cases showing superposed paths for Cases 1 and 2. Figure 1(c) shows transverse responses (Pyy/Pzz) where strain control develops compressive stresses while stress/mixed control do not. Figure 2(a) displays the polycrystal RVE with approximately 200 grains in 643 voxels. Figure 2(b) and (c) show longitudinal and transverse Pxx responses for the four polycrystal loading cases. Figure 3(a) shows conjugate gradient iteration counts per step for the hyperelastic model across 100 increments. Figure 3(b) shows iteration counts for the polycrystal model across 20 increments. Figure 3(c) compares normalized simulation times across all cases for both models.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a modified projection operator at the null frequency that enables macroscopic stress or mixed control in Galerkin-based FFT homogenization without extra iterative corrections. 2. The strongest evidence is the demonstration that the new algorithm achieves identical Pxx-Fxx paths to strain-control in hyperelastic materials while producing exactly zero transverse stresses, and requires no additional iterations in the linear or Newton solvers. 3. The future path involves extending the framework to more complex constitutive models and larger-scale RVEs, as the algorithm is stated to be applicable to any material including crystal plasticity.

summary.title: Nonlinearity in the dark: Broadband terahertz generation with extremely high efficiency
summary.authors: Ming Fang, Nian-Hai Shen, Wei E.I. Sha, Zhixiang Huang, Thomas Koschny, and Costas M. Soukoulis
summary.field_subfield: Physics / Optics and Photonics (Terahertz generation, Metasurfaces)
summary.type_of_paper: Theoretical/Computational Letter (FDTD simulation and analytical modeling)
summary.executive_summary:
This work introduces a novel dark-mode-assisted perfect absorbing metasurface for broadband terahertz (THz) generation that circumvents the fundamental efficiency limits inherent in conventional metallic nano-resonator metasurfaces. The authors identify that radiative damping of linear scattering in split-ring-resonator (SRR) metasurfaces constitutes a primary obstacle to nonlinear conversion efficiency, as the ratio of generated THz signal to scattered pump radiation is directly proportional to local near-field amplitude. To eliminate this, the proposed design combines a resonant dark-state metasurface—a silicon film of 100 nm thickness punctuated by metal walls—which excites a high-Q TE2,0 mode that cannot directly couple to incident plane waves, with two asymmetrically positioned gold SRRs (50 nm thick) that drive the nonlinear conversion. 

By carefully tuning the relative positions of the SRRs, the design achieves simultaneous electric and magnetic critical coupling of the pump radiation to the dark mode, enabling complete absorption (94%) and elimination of linear radiation damping. Conversely, the two SRRs produce identical second-order nonlinear dynamics whose far-field radiation adds constructively, yielding more than a 120-fold enhancement in THz emission power compared to the reference SRR metasurface from Nat. Commun. 5, 3055 (2014). The effective second-order nonlinear susceptibility is calculated at χ(2) ≈ 2.4 × 10^-11 m/V, an order of magnitude improvement over the prior 1.7 × 10^-12 m/V, corresponding to two orders of magnitude enhanced THz energy extraction. The study employs a self-consistent FDTD framework based on the hydrodynamic model of the electron gas in gold. While the results are obtained under simplified plane-wave illumination in a spatially infinite domain, the paradigm offers a generalizable concept applicable to other nonlinear processes and opens new opportunities for high-efficiency on-chip nonlinear nano-optical devices and THz technologies.

By carefully tuning the relative positions of the SRRs, the design achieves simultaneous electric and magnetic critical coupling of the pump radiation to the dark mode, enabling complete absorption (94%) and elimination of linear radiation damping. Conversely, the two SRRs produce identical second-order nonlinear dynamics whose far-field radiation adds constructively, yielding more than a 120-fold enhancement in THz emission power compared to the reference SRR metasurface from Nat. Commun. 5, 3055 (2014). The effective second-order nonlinear susceptibility is calculated at χ(2) ≈ 2.4 × 10^-11 m/V, an order of magnitude improvement over the prior 1.7 × 10^-12 m/V, corresponding to two orders of magnitude enhanced THz energy extraction. The study employs a self-consistent FDTD framework based on the hydrodynamic model of the electron gas in gold. While the results are obtained under simplified plane-wave illumination in a spatially infinite domain, the paradigm offers a generalizable concept applicable to other nonlinear processes and opens new opportunities for high-efficiency on-chip nonlinear nano-optical devices and THz technologies.

Research Context
Terahertz (THz) technologies in sensing, imaging, and communication demand efficient and compact emitters/detectors. State-of-the-art THz sources based on nonlinear optical rectification or DFG in inorganic crystals suffer from narrow bandwidth, phase-matching limitations, spectrum gaps, or low emission intensity. Metasurfaces offer a programmable alternative to natural materials by designing subwavelength-scale atoms for versatile functions. Simple meta-atoms for second-order nonlinear applications encounter fundamental trade-offs between symmetry-breaking and local-field enhancement due to radiation damping inherent to the operating resonant mode. A 40 nm-thick SRR metasurface was recently demonstrated to generate broadband gapless THz emission up to 4 THz, but its nonlinear optical response remains fairly weak. Screening effects of the free-electron gas at metallic nanoparticle surfaces lead to strong second-order nonlinearity in optical electric susceptibility.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the fundamental limit of conversion efficiency in nonlinear metasurfaces, imposed by radiative damping of linear scattering, can be circumvented by a dark-mode-assisted design. The hypothesis is that a properly designed perfect absorbing metasurface, combining a resonant dark element with a specific spatial symmetry of SRRs, can eliminate linear radiative damping while maintaining constructive interference of nonlinear radiation. The predicted outcome is a giant second-order nonlinear susceptibility of approximately 10^-11 m/V, representing a one-order improvement over previously reported SRR metasurface values. A corresponding two-orders-of-magnitude enhanced THz energy extraction is expected under identical operating conditions. The work predicts the proposed configuration should surpass the performance of conventional SRR metasurfaces that generate THz on the same order as 0.2 mm-thick ZnTe crystals.

Methodological Details
The design consists of a single unit cell comprising a thin Si slab (thickness h = 100 nm) periodically punctuated by gold metal walls of width 2a, with total length L = 800 nm, width W = 240 nm. Two gold SRRs, each 50 nm thick (tm = 50 nm), are positioned asymmetrically on opposing sides of the Si slab, oriented in the same direction. The operation wavelength is tuned to the typical high-speed telecommunications range around 1.5 µm, corresponding to the second quantized mode on the lowest dispersion branch. The TE2,0 mode is selected for its anti-symmetric electric field profile, making it a dark mode that cannot directly couple to incident plane waves. The coupling strength is optimized by varying the lateral positions of the two SRRs (Δx1, Δx2) with a scanning step size of 5 nm to balance simulation resolution and computational cost. The optimal configuration yields Δx1 ≈ 70 nm and Δx2 ≈ 470 nm, with ζ|σ(e)s| = ζ−1|σ(m)s| = 1.8. THz radiation is modeled using a self-consistent FDTD calculation based on the hydrodynamic model of the electron gas in gold. The input temporal optical pulse is Ey(t) = E0 exp[−2 ln(2)(t − t0)²/τ²] cos(ω0t), with pulse duration τ = 140 fs (spectral width ∼3.2 THz) and peak amplitude E0 = 2 × 10^7 V/m. The driving frequency equals the resonant frequency of the dark mode (ω0 = ωdark). The simulation assumes a spatially infinite surface under plane-wave illumination to resolve the fundamental physics, acknowledging this limitation for predicting practical absolute values in experimental setups. The reference case is the non-radiation-managed SRR metasurface reported in Luo et al. Nat. Commun. 5, 3055 (2014), simulated within the same numerical framework for side-by-side comparison.

Procedures And Architectures
The metasurface is conceptualized as a composite system: a low-loss dielectric dark element (Si slab) for high-Q field enhancement, integrated with gold SRRs for nonlinear signal generation and pump coupling. The metal walls quantize the dielectric slab modes, achieving a set of discrete resonant dark states shown in the dispersion diagram. Coupling of pump radiation to the dark state occurs via non-resonant weak SRR scatterers, creating equivalent electric and magnetic effective surface susceptibilities (σ(e)s and σ(m)s). In-phase linear currents in both SRRs create electric moments, while anti-phase linear currents in SRRs on opposing sides create magnetic moments; their relative strength is controlled by SRR symmetry and lateral positioning. The reflection R and transmission T are determined by the sheet conductivities via R = 2(ζσ(e)s − ζ−1σ(m)s)/(4+2ζσ(e)s+2ζ−1σ(m)s+σ(e)s σ(m)s) and T = (4−σ(e)s σ(m)s)/(4+2ζσ(e)s+2ζ−1σ(m)s+σ(e)s σ(m)s). An ideal perfect absorbing sheet fulfills ζσ(e)s = ζ−1σ(m)s = 2; the design reaches ζ|σ(e)s| = ζ−1|σ(m)s| = 1.8. Upon excitation of the TE2,0 mode, out-of-phase polarization currents I1 and I2 are induced in the two SRRs, decomposable into symmetric (electric moment along y-axis) and anti-symmetric (magnetic moment along x-axis) sets. Because the desired DFG and second-harmonic generation are second-order in the electric field, the sign of the currents does not matter; the nonlinear radiation of both SRRs adds constructively in the far field. The linear radiation, being opposite in phase, cancels in the far field, eliminating linear radiation damping from the conversion process. The THz radiation is polarized along the x-axis, perpendicular to the metasurface on both sides.

Key Results
The optimal metasurface configuration achieves absorption as high as 94%. The TE2,0 mode of the Si slab is strongly excited with an anti-symmetric electric field profile, producing dramatic field enhancement around the SRRs. The calculated transmission, reflection, and absorption spectra show nearly complete absorption of the pump energy, with the gray-shaded region indicating dissipation within the two SRRs. The THz enhancement ηdark/ηSRR, defined as the ratio of conversion efficiencies between the proposed and reference designs, exceeds 120-fold for the optimized configuration. The THz enhancement maps show that enhancements for different configurations are inversely proportional to the linear radiation damping. The calculated effective nonlinear susceptibility for the designed metasurface is χ(2)dark ≈ 2.4 × 10^-11 m/V, while the reference SRR metasurface yields χ(2)SRR ≈ 1.7 × 10^-12 m/V (consistent with 1.6 × 10^-12 m/V reported in Ref. [35]). The THz signal strength increases linearly with pump pulse intensity, with the designed configuration maintaining the dramatic emission enhancement over the reference case. The THz spectrum peak occurs at ω = 2/τ with a FWHM bandwidth of Δω ≈ 2.31/τ, determined by the temporal envelope of the incident pulse. The design predicts over two-order enhanced THz emission under the same conditions compared to the conventional SRR metasurface. The field distributions show that both SRRs possess the same polarization with negligible phase difference, contributing coherently to the total enhanced THz radiation.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The mechanism for enhancement is dual: eliminating radiative damping of linear scattering while enhancing the local near-field amplitude for nonlinear generation. The cancellation of linear radiation damping is possible because the two SRRs exhibit identical second-order dynamics but opposite linear electric and magnetic dipole moments. In the hydrodynamic model, the convection term plays the crucial role for second-order nonlinearities, contributing as the product of current and accumulated charge density on the metal surface. The design separates the resonant local field enhancement (provided by the Si dark mode) from the current topology required for non-vanishing second-order nonlinearity (provided by the SRRs). The concept is general and applicable to other nonlinear processes beyond THz generation, such as second-harmonic generation or other second-order nonlinear interactions in metasurfaces. The work opens new opportunities for high-efficiency on-chip nonlinear nano-optical devices, compact THz sources, and versatile nanoscale nonlinear devices. The theoretical results imply that the proposed configuration should demonstrate much better performance in generating broadband THz emission in real experiments compared to the experimental baseline of a 0.2 mm-thick ZnTe crystal.

Contradictions And Limitations
The model is less suitable to predict practical absolute numbers as would be observed in a particular experiment because it assumes a spatially infinite surface under plane-wave illumination. The conversion efficiency depends on many experimental factors not fully captured in the simplified model, including pump power, polarization, pulse duration, incidence, focusing conditions, and phase-matching. The THz signal in the model is an upper bound; real experiments with finite-size metasurfaces, substrate effects, and inhomogeneous illumination will reduce absolute conversion values. The design requires careful tuning of SRR positions (Δx1, Δx2) to maintain the critical coupling condition; deviations from the optimal geometry would reduce absorption and increase radiation damping. The simulation does not include substrate effects, although the authors note that discussions of the case with substrate can be found in the Supplemental Material. The conversion efficiency is reported as a theoretical comparison within the same numerical framework rather than an experimentally measured absolute value.

Claims
The proposed dark-mode-assisted metasurface eliminates linear radiation damping while maintaining constructive interference of nonlinear radiation, enabling >120-fold THz emission enhancement. The anti-symmetric TE2,0 mode creates opposite linear dipole moments in the two SRRs that cancel in the far field. The THz enhancement ηdark/ηSRR exceeds 120-fold for the optimized configuration. The absorption reaches as high as 94% at the optimal SRR positions. The effective χ(2) is 2.4 × 10^-11 m/V vs. 1.7 × 10^-12 m/V for the reference. The model assumes spatially infinite surface and plane-wave illumination, limiting translatability to finite-area practical devices. Experimental results are not presented; all figures are derived from self-consistent FDTD simulations. The design opens opportunities for revolutionary THz technologies and high-efficiency on-chip nonlinear nano-optical devices. The concept is general and applicable to other nonlinear processes in metasurfaces.
Perfect absorption (or near-perfect) can be achieved by simultaneous electric and magnetic critical coupling of pump radiation to a dark resonant mode in a metasurface. Absorption reaches 94% at ζ|σ(e)s| = ζ−1|σ(m)s| = 1.8. Tuning the coupling strength to a critical case eliminated the linear transmitted field. The ideal perfect absorbing sheet condition ζσ(e)s = ζ−1σ(m)s = 2 is not fully met (achieved 1.8 instead). This principle enables complete channeling of incident pump energy into the dark resonant state and dissipative loss in the metal structures.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors performed a side-by-side comparison between the conventional, not-radiation-managed SRR metasurface [35] and the proposed configuration within the same numerical framework. The THz enhancement map shows that enhancements for different SRR configurations are inversely proportional to the linear radiation damping, validating the mechanism. The THz signal amplitude increases linearly with pump pulse intensity, confirming the predicted scaling. The dimensions of the SRRs are not critical provided the dark-mode frequency and perfect absorption requirements are fulfilled. The analysis was performed for the second quantized mode (TE2,0) on the lowest dispersion branch; other modes could potentially be examined.

Key Figures Tables

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates droplet impact dynamics on heated surfaces across three boiling regimes: nucleate boiling, transition boiling, and film boiling. The authors identify and characterize a novel droplet bouncing mode termed 'bouncing-with-spray' (BWS), in which the residence time—the duration between visual contact and detachment—is significantly reduced compared to the traditional retraction-bouncing (RB) mode. The mechanism of reduction is attributed to the burst of vapor bubbles formed within the liquid film during expansion, which creates holes that fragment the film, reducing the recoiling distance and the corresponding recoiling time. Quantitative analysis shows that BWS reduces residence time by approximately 40% relative to RB. The transition between RB and BWS modes was theoretically modeled by considering energy conservation during bubble formation and the critical condition that the vapor bubble radius equals the minimum film thickness at maximum expansion. A scaling law ΔT ~ V^-1 (with n = 0.35 for spreading) predicts the transition boundary in the film boiling regime and qualitatively explains the mode transition in the transition boiling regime. Experiments with water, ethanol, and water/glycerol mixtures (viscosities from 1.00 to 42.47 mPa·s) demonstrated that the BWS residence time is independent of viscosity, indicating that viscous forces play a negligible role. The approach is highlighted as simple, reliable, and avoiding complex surface fabrication, making it practical for applications in spray cooling, painting, and inkjet printing where reduced residence time is desirable.

Research Context
Droplet impact on surfaces is ubiquitous in nature and industrial applications such as spray cooling, painting, inkjet printing, and fuel-spray impingement. Earlier studies focused on impact morphologies via high-speed imaging and secondary droplet analysis via PDA and image processing. On surfaces above the boiling point, droplets undergo nucleate boiling, transition boiling, and film boiling processes. At sufficiently high temperatures, a vapor layer forms (Leidenfrost effect), reducing the vaporization rate. The contact time of a bouncing droplet is bounded by the Rayleigh time scale for an inviscid droplet on a superhydrophobic surface. Many efforts have been made to reduce contact time using surfaces with ridges, lattice posts, curved surfaces, and egg-shaped droplets. Theoretical models exist to predict contact time in the nucleate boiling regime. In the film boiling regime, the droplet residence time can be approximated as the period of a freely oscillating droplet. A gap exists in understanding the dynamics of droplet fragmentation caused by phase change during impact.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a new mode of droplet bouncing induced by heat can reduce residence time compared to traditional retraction-bouncing. The authors hypothesize that the burst of vapor bubbles in the liquid film causes film fragmentation, leading to reduced recoiling distance and residence time. The hypothesis predicts that this approach is simpler and more reliable than surface modification strategies. A secondary hypothesis is that the residence time reduction mechanism can be quantitatively modeled via an energy balance and critical condition. The predicted outcome is a scaling law describing the transition boundary between retraction-bouncing and bouncing-with-spray modes. The model is expected to apply to both film boiling and transition boiling regimes. The authors posit that the viscous force should not play an important role in the residence time of the BWS mode.

Methodological Details
Different liquids including water, ethanol, and water/glycerol mixtures were tested to vary density, surface tension, dynamic viscosity, and latent heat. The liquids used were water (ρ=998 kg/m³, σ=72 mN/m), water+glycerol (various wt%, σ=66–70 mN/m), and ethanol (ρ=790 kg/m³, σ=22 mN/m). The dynamic viscosity varied from 1.00 mPa·s (water) to 42.47 mPa·s (water+glycerol 75 wt%). The latent heat of vaporization spanned 853 kJ/kg (ethanol) to 2257 kJ/kg (water). Droplets were formed at the tip of a blunt syringe needle using a syringe pump (Harvard Apparatus, Pump 11 elite Pico plus). The injection speed was extremely low, approximately 4 µL/s. Droplet sizes varied: D0 = 2.2–3.4 mm for water, 2.8 mm for water/glycerol, and 1.6 mm for ethanol. The impact speed range was V = 0.9–2.1 m/s. The substrate was a polished silicon wafer (roughness < 0.5 nm) heated by a copper holder. Two K-type thermocouples were placed 1 cm beside the impact point to control temperature. Temperature control accuracy was ±1°C using a PID controller. Images were captured in side-view and aerial-view using a Photron Fastcam SA1.1 high-speed camera with an LED light source. The Weber number was varied from 10 to 180. The Jakob number was defined as Ja ≡ cp(Tw−Ts)/ℓ.

Procedures And Architectures
The experimental setup comprised a syringe pump, needle, heated copper plate and silicon wafer, PID temperature controller, computer, syringe, height gauge, optical fiber, and high-speed camera (Figure 1). Droplets detached when the gravitational force exceeded the surface tension force at the blunt needle tip. Images were processed using a customized MATLAB program to extract D0, V, and shape evolution. Viscosity was tuned by changing glycerol concentration in water mixtures (28 wt%, 34 wt%, 39 wt%, 56 wt%, 75 wt%). Residence time was defined as the interval between visual contact and visual detachment. Three boiling regimes were systematically explored: nucleate boiling (T=260°C), transition boiling (T=380°C), and film boiling (T=400–440°C). The dimensionless residence time was normalized using τ = q(ρR0³/σ) for comparison across liquids and speeds. The theoretical model was constructed by assuming Poiseuille flow in the vapor layer (Equations 5–8) and a uniform vapor layer thickness δ. The critical condition rv ≈ bmin was identified as the transition boundary at maximum expansion. The scaling exponent n = 0.35 was used for the spreading law Dmax/D0 ∼ Weⁿ (Equation 11). A dimensionless scaling relationship involving Gr*, Prv, Fo*, and Ja was derived (Equation 13).

Key Results
In nucleate boiling (T=260°C, We=37), the droplet stuck to the surface with vapor bubbles rising through and breaking at the free surface. In transition boiling (T=380°C), the RB mode (We=37) showed retraction before departure with residence time 6.5 ms, while BWS mode (We=69) showed no obvious retraction and spray ejection. For We=105 and T=380°C, liquid fingers formed at the rim indicating splashing, yet BWS mode persisted with residence time 6.3 ms. In film boiling (T=440°C, We=25), the RB mode showed uniform spray ejection at higher temperatures (440°C vs. 400°C). In film boiling at We=60 and T=440°C, the BWS mode appeared, and at We=129, splashing and BWS coexisted. Aerial images revealed that vapor bubbles burst at random sites, forming holes, causing the liquid film to recoil into fragments and bounce off. The recoiling distance was reduced by the holes, shortening the recoiling time and thus the residence time. For all liquids tested, the residence time of the BWS mode was independent of liquid viscosity (Figure 4). The dimensionless residence time for RB mode was approximately 2.3, while for BWS mode it was about 1.4 (Figure 5). The residence time reduction in BWS mode compared to RB mode was approximately 40%. The transition boundary ΔT ∼ V⁻¹ (Equation 14) agreed well with experimental film boiling data (Figure 6d). The maximum expansion time τ₀ was shown to be independent of impact speed (Figure 6b). The spreading exponent n was found to be 0.35, close to Tran et al.'s 0.39.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The BWS mode represents a fragmentation-induced bouncing where the physical mechanism mimics ridge-induced fragmentation on superhydrophobic surfaces. The reduction in residence time is fundamentally a geometric effect: fragmentation reduces the effective recoiling distance, shortening the inertial relaxation period. The transition occurs when the bubble radius equals the minimum film thickness, meaning bubbles large enough to puncture the film form before maximum spreading. The viscous force does not play a dominant role because the process is dominated by inertial fragmentation of the liquid film. The model predicts a regime map where the transition from RB to BWS shifts with increasing Weber number and substrate temperature. The approach offers a passive, reliable, and easily implementable strategy for reducing residence time without surface degradation or complex microstructure fabrication.

Contradictions And Limitations
The transition boundary ΔT ∼ V⁻¹ is an approximation; the authors acknowledge that the spreading exponent n can differ for different surface structures. The assumption that the heat transfer area A can be regarded as constant for different liquids is a simplification that may affect model accuracy across liquids. The scaling exponent n = 0.35 was chosen, but the authors note it differs from Tran et al.'s 0.39, reflecting experimental variability. The model assumes Poiseuille flow in the vapor layer, which may not hold at very thin or large-gap limits. The authors state that detailed numerical simulations and experimental measurements of the bursting bubbles are still needed for a better understanding. The experimental data for ethanol (smallest droplet, lowest surface tension) was not included in the comprehensive viscosity-independence or regime map analysis. The paper does not report random seeds, precise train/test splits for any computational elements, or detailed error bars on the dimensionless residence time values.

Claims
A droplet bouncing-with-spray mode exists in heated droplet impact that significantly reduces residence time compared to the traditional retraction-bouncing mode. In transition boiling, the residence time dropped from 12.0 ms (RB) to 6.5 ms (BWS) at We=69, T=380°C. In film boiling, the BWS mode was observed at We=60 and T=440°C, with residence times substantially lower than RB mode. The dimensionless residence time in BWS mode was ~1.4 compared to ~2.3 in RB mode. The mechanism was visualized in aerial images showing vapor bubble bursting, hole formation, and film recoil. In nucleate boiling, the droplet sticks to the surface and does not bounce, so no residence time reduction applies. This mode can be leveraged in spray cooling and inkjet printing applications requiring minimal dwell time. The BWS mode is accessible via temperature and velocity control alone, avoiding surface modification.
The residence time reduction in BWS mode is a physical fragmentation effect, not a viscous one, making it independent of liquid viscosity. For D0 = 2.8 mm and V = 1.2 m/s, the BWS residence time remained constant as viscosity varied from 1.00 to 42.47 mPa·s (Figure 4). Viscous forces are not the governing mechanism for the film recoil period. In the nucleate boiling regime, surface temperature strongly influences residence time, though this is a sticking mode rather than bouncing. Liquid choice can be optimized for other properties (e.g., latent heat, surface tension) without penalizing residence time reduction.
A theoretical scaling law ΔT ∼ V⁻¹ predicts the transition boundary between RB and BWS modes in the film boiling regime. The experimental film boiling data in log-log scale agreed well with the predicted scaling (Figure 6d). The scaling accounts for energy balance of bubble formation and critical geometric condition rv ≈ bmin. The theory also qualitatively explains why the transition temperature increases with Weber number in the transition boiling regime. The scaling assumes n = 0.35, but different surface structures yield different exponents. The transition boiling regime behavior is qualitative rather than quantitative in this paper. The boundary can be used to design operation regimes for practical droplet-impact devices.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The viscosity sensitivity was addressed by testing six water/glycerol concentrations (28–75 wt%) at fixed D0 = 2.8 mm and V = 1.2 m/s. The temperature dependence was tested across 400°C and 440°C in the film boiling regime for the same Weber number (We=25). The spreading exponent n = 0.35 was validated against literature values (Tran et al., n = 0.39).

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 summarizes physical properties of all liquids: water, ethanol, and six water/glycerol mixtures (28–75 wt%), with σ from 22–72 mN/m and ρ from 790–1195 kg/m³. Figure 1 shows the experimental setup with (a) side-view and (b) aerial-view, identifying the heated copper plate, silicon wafer, high-speed camera, and syringe pump. Figure 2 presents impact morphologies in nucleate boiling (T=260°C, We=37), transition boiling (T=380°C, We=37, 69, 105), and film boiling (T=400–440°C, We=25, 60, 129). Figure 3 provides a sequence of aerial images showing vapor bubble bursting at random sites, hole formation, and liquid film recoil at We=82 and T=450°C. Figure 4 demonstrates that the BWS residence time is constant (approx. 5.5–6.8 ms) across all six glycerol concentrations for D0 = 2.8 mm, V = 1.2 m/s. Figure 5 plots dimensionless residence time (τ/τ_scale) against Weber number for water, ethanol, and water-glycerol mixtures, showing BWS at ~1.4 vs. RB at ~2.3. Figure 6 contains: (a) schematic of the theoretical model, (b) constant τ₀ with impact speed, (c) Dmax/D0 ∼ Weⁿ log-log plot (n=0.35), (d) ΔT ∼ V⁻¹ transition boundary in film boiling, and (e) regime map with mode boundaries for a water droplet (D0=2.2 mm).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification and quantitative description of the 'bouncing-with-spray' mode, in which vapor-bubble-induced film fragmentation reduces droplet residence time by approximately 40% compared to retraction-bouncing. 2. The strongest evidence is the combination of aerial high-speed imaging directly visualizing the fragmentation mechanism, viscosity-independence confirmed by six glycerol-water mixtures, and the excellent agreement of the predicted scaling law with film boiling data. 3. The future path involves detailed numerical simulations and experimental direct measurements of the bursting bubbles in the BWS mode to fully resolve the impact dynamics, enabling optimization for practical droplet-impact applications.

summary.title: MAXIMAL ABELIAN EXTENSION OF A MODULAR CURVE UNRAMIFIED OUTSIDE CUSPS
summary.authors: TAKAO YAMAZAKI AND YIFAN YANG
summary.field_subfield: Number Theory / Arithmetic Geometry
summary.executive_summary: This short paper addresses a fundamental question in arithmetic geometry: characterizing the geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering of the modular curve X0(p) over Q, extended to allow ramification at the cusps. Mazur had previously proven that the geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering is the Shimura covering X2(p) → X0(p), which is a subcovering of X1(p) → X0(p) of degree Np = (p − 1)/gcd(p − 1, 12). The authors extend this result by constructing a covering X′2(p) → X0(p) of degree 2Np that is cyclic and unramified outside the cusps, and proving it is geometrically maximal for the open subscheme Y0(p) = X0(p) \ {cusps}. The construction utilizes generalized Dedekind eta functions (Siegel functions) to produce an explicit rational function whose square root generates the function field extension. The covering factors as f′2(p) = f2(p) ◦ πp, where πp is a degree-two covering unramified outside cusps. The proof proceeds by reducing the problem to checking that the Shimura covering's abelian extension has order either Np or 2Np, and constructing a function whose square root yields a cyclic extension of the correct degree and ramification behavior. The result unifies the unramified and unramified-outside-cusps theories for maximal abelian extensions of modular curves.

Executive Summary
This short paper addresses a fundamental question in arithmetic geometry: characterizing the geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering of the modular curve X0(p) over Q, extended to allow ramification at the cusps. Mazur had previously proven that the geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering is the Shimura covering X2(p) → X0(p), which is a subcovering of X1(p) → X0(p) of degree Np = (p − 1)/gcd(p − 1, 12). The authors extend this result by constructing a covering X′2(p) → X0(p) of degree 2Np that is cyclic and unramified outside the cusps, and proving it is geometrically maximal for the open subscheme Y0(p) = X0(p) \ {cusps}. The construction utilizes generalized Dedekind eta functions (Siegel functions) to produce an explicit rational function whose square root generates the function field extension. The covering factors as f′2(p) = f2(p) ◦ πp, where πp is a degree-two covering unramified outside cusps. The proof proceeds by reducing the problem to checking that the Shimura covering's abelian extension has order either Np or 2Np, and constructing a function whose square root yields a cyclic extension of the correct degree and ramification behavior. The result unifies the unramified and unramified-outside-cusps theories for maximal abelian extensions of modular curves.

Research Context
Mazur proved that the geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering of X0(p) over Q is the Shimura covering X2(p) → X0(p). This Shimura covering is a unique subcovering of X1(p) → X0(p) of degree Np := (p − 1)/gcd(p − 1, 12). The previous result only considered coverings unramified everywhere, not specifically unramified outside cusps. The problem of finding geometrically maximal unramified abelian coverings is motivated by the exact sequence relating the étale fundamental group to the Galois group of the field. It is known that π1(Y)ab,geo is finite when the curve admits a degree one divisor. When no Q-rational point is available, a geometrically maximal unramified covering still exists but its description differs.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is to characterize the geometrically maximal abelian covering of Y0(p) over Q that is unramified outside the cusps. The authors hypothesize that such a covering exists, is cyclic, and has degree 2Np, doubling the degree of the Shimura covering. The specific hypothesis is that there exists a cyclic covering f′2(p): X′2(p) → X0(p) of degree 2Np such that its restriction to Y′2(p) is a geometrically maximal unramified covering of Y0(p) over Q. A second hypothesis is that this covering factors as f′2(p) = f2(p) ◦ πp, where πp is a degree two covering unramified outside cusps. The predicted outcome is that the function field Q(X′2(p)) is obtained as a quadratic extension of Q(X2(p)) generated by a square root of an explicitly constructed rational function.

Methodological Details
The study considers X0(p) and X1(p) as geometrically integral smooth proper curves over Q for a prime p. Y0(p) is an open subscheme of X0(p) whose complement consists of all two cusps (0 and ∞). The generalized Jacobian eJ = Jac(X, D) is defined with modulus D, the divisor of cusps. The character group LD := Hom(GD, Gm,k) has rank rD := Σ_{x∈D} [k(x):k] − 1. The torsion module MTor := Hom(T eJ, Q/Z(1)) is interpreted as the group of torsion points of the dual 1-motive M of eJ. The exact sequence 0 → JTor → MTor → LD ⊗ Q/Z → 0 links the Jacobian torsion to MTor. The Shimura covering f2(p): X2(p) → X0(p) is the maximal unramified subcovering of X1(p) → X0(p). For p ≥ 5, g is an odd generator of (Z/pZ)×, and k := Np = (p − 1)/(p − 1, 12). ℓ is defined as ((p − 1, 12)/2)², where (a, b) := gcd(a, b). The modular curve X2(p) corresponds to Γ2(p), the group generated by Γ1(p) and matrices of form [gk, * ; p, *]. The index [Γ0(p) : Γ2(p)] is k, and [Γ2(p) : Γ1(p)] is ℓ.

Procedures And Architectures
The generalized Dedekind eta function Eg(τ) is defined via the product of 6 factors involving q-expansions and the second Bernoulli polynomial B(x). The function Fh(τ) is constructed as a product of 6 generalized Dedekind eta functions: Fh(τ) = (∏_{j=0}^{ℓ-1} Egjkh(τ))^(6/ℓ). Lemma 3.3.1 proves Fh = F(−h) = F(p+h) and Fgkh = (−Fh) for p ≡ 1 mod 4, Fh for p ≡ 3 mod 4. The character ψ of order 2 on SL(2, Z) is defined based on the parity of matrix entries. A character χ of order 2 on Γ2(p) is defined when ℓ is even (p ≡ 1 mod 4). Γ′2(p) is defined as the kernel of the product character ψχ (for p ≡ 1 mod 4) or ψ (for p ≡ 3 mod 4) on Γ2(p). Lemma 3.3.2 shows Γ′2(p) is a normal subgroup of Γ0(p) with quotient cyclic of order 2k. For p ̸≡ 1 mod 12, Fh(γτ) = ψ(γ)Fah(τ) for Γ0(p), and a product involving χ for Γ2(p). F2h is shown to be a modular function on X2(p) defined over Q with odd order at each cusp and zero elsewhere. For p ≡ 1 mod 12, a triplet of integers (h1, h2, h3) satisfying h21 + h22 + h23 ≡ 0 mod p is used to define Gh = (Eh1Eh2Eh3)². The function field Q(X′2(p)) is obtained as a quadratic extension of Q(X2(p)) by adjoining F2h (or z(τ) in Remark 3.3.5). The factorization f′2(p) = f2(p) ◦ πp shows the new covering is a degree-two extension of the Shimura covering, unramified outside cusps. The exact sequence (2.2.4) and the finiteness of π1(Y)ab,geo explain why the order of the maximal covering must divide 2Np. The authors check the construction for two cases: p ̸≡ 1 mod 12 and p ≡ 11 mod 12, showing robustness across all primes. For p = 2 and p = 3, the authors provide a degenerate case verification via Gm. The use of both Fh and z(τ) as alternative generators (for p ̸≡ 1 mod 8) provides a secondary verification path.

The diagram in Section 1.2 illustrates the factorization f′2(p) = f2(p) ◦ πp through the Shimura covering. The exact sequence (1.1.1) relates the maximal abelian quotient of the étale fundamental group to the Galois group.

The core contribution is the construction of a cyclic covering X′2(p) → X0(p) of degree 2Np that is geometrically maximal unramified outside cusps, extending Mazur's unramified result to the ramified-at-cusps case. 2.
