judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper addresses the computational bottleneck in semantic segmentation for embedded deployment, specifically within the context of automated driving. While extensive research has focused on efficient, task-agnostic encoders, decoders remain computationally expensive and under-explored. The authors propose a novel, task-independent decoder architecture using a VGG10 (10-layer) classifier as a generic encoder. The core contribution is a multi-variant non-bottleneck layer featuring residual learning, cascade skip connections, and dual kernel types (1D and 3D) combined with fusion of multiple convolution kernels (3x3, 5x5, and 1x1). The architecture is evaluated on a private urban driving dataset (1280x384 resolution, 4 classes) under a restricted runtime budget. A systematic ablation study comparing eight decoder variants (D1–D8) and several non-bottleneck layer combinations demonstrates that the optimal configuration achieves a 10% improvement in mean IoU over the baseline. Specifically, the proposed decoder improves lane and curb class IoU by 12% and 18%, respectively, with a runtime overhead of less than 2 ms on custom automotive hardware. The work underscores that decoder design, rather than just encoder optimization, is a critical lever for real-time semantic segmentation on embedded platforms.

Research Context
Semantic segmentation provides complete semantic scene understanding where each pixel is assigned a class label. Industrial applications for automated driving face a computational bound because of limited resources on embedded platforms. Recent research has focused on designing efficient encoders that are mostly task agnostic. Unlike image classification and bounding box detection, decoders are computationally expensive for the semantic segmentation task. Existing methods use task-specific encoders (e.g., SegNet, UNet, DeepLab2) with heavy usage of dilated convolutions and information fusion. None of these methods use a task-independent lightweight encoder model as used in this work. The methods do not support multi-task learning practices where a single encoder provides shared features.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a task-independent, lightweight decoder design can improve semantic segmentation accuracy within a fixed runtime budget. The authors hypothesize that a novel non-bottleneck layer with cascaded skip connections and residual learning can overcome high gradient flow issues in shallower networks. They predict that the decoder can learn semantic features that the generic, non-semantic encoder fails to capture. They hypothesize that experimentation with various design choices within the decoder will yield performance improvements over the baseline. The authors expect that the best decoder configuration will show improvement particularly for under-represented classes (lanes and curb). A secondary hypothesis is that the decoder can be optimized with less than 2ms runtime overhead on automotive hardware.

Methodological Details
The study uses a dataset owned by the organization, consisting of urban scene images with dimension 1280x384. The dataset is divided into Training (3016), Validation (981), and Test (1002) sets. Semantic segmentation is performed on 4 critical classes: lanes, curb, road, and void (everything else). A single channel annotation was developed where each pixel has only one class label. The encoder is a VGG (Simonyan and Zisserman, 2014) style classifier of 10 layers trained on ImageNet. Convolution layers use a kernel size of 5x5 followed by Batch Normalization and ReLU activation. The last encoder layer produces 256 feature maps. Experiments were executed using the Keras framework on an NVIDIA Ti-tan X 12G GPU with 24 GB RAM. Optimization uses the Adam optimizer with weight decay of 0.9 and batch size of 4. Training starts with an initial learning rate of 0.0005 with polynomial decay over 350K iterations. No data augmentation technique was performed during training. Transfer learning from ImageNet pre-training was used due to the small dataset size and shallow model.

Procedures And Architectures
The architecture follows a standard encoder-decoder pair where the encoder extracts features and the decoder reconstructs the input space. For reconstruction, deconvolution layers are used instead of max-unpooling as used in SegNet. Feature maps are downsampled from 256 in the encoder to 4 in the decoder, concentrating on the 4 output classes. Intermediate feature maps are pulled from the second and third last convolution layers of the encoder. The proposed non-bottleneck layer contains both 1D and 3D kernels for multi-directional feature extraction. Features are fused from multiple convolution kernels of sizes 3x3, 5x5, and 1x1. The non-bottleneck layer has two variants: type-1 and type-2. The type-2 variant uses dilated convolution with kernel sizes 3x3 and 5x5, with dilation rate kept constant at 1. The optimal configuration uses non-bottleneck layers sequentially: (2N1)(2N1)(2N2)(2N2), meaning 2 type-1 after deconvolution 1 and 2, and 2 type-2 after deconvolution 3 and 4. No non-bottleneck layer is used after the fourth deconvolution. Batch size during training was varied between 4 and 8 for different variants. Dropout is not used in the model.

Key Results
The optimal decoder configuration achieves a mean IoU of 0.7441, which is a 10% improvement over the baseline configuration. For the lanes class, IoU improved from 0.4943 (D1) to 0.5304 (Optimal), representing a 12% improvement. For the curb class, IoU improved from 0.4296 (D1) to 0.4696 (Optimal), representing an 18% improvement. The road class maintains a high IoU of 0.9314 in the optimal configuration. The average class accuracy for the optimal configuration is 0.6534, a notable increase from the baseline. The runtime increase of the proposed network over a standard FCN decoder is less than 2ms on custom automotive hardware. The decoder D8, a simple configuration, achieves a mean IoU of 0.727, near the optimal performance. Without data augmentation or class weighting, non-bottleneck layers improved curb segmentation while causing slight deterioration for lanes. The encoder consumes most of the runtime as it is much wider than the decoder.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The non-bottleneck architecture with residual connections and multiple skip paths addresses the high gradient flow problem in shallower networks. The multiple convolution kernels (1D, 3D, 3x3, 5x5, 1x1) allow capturing semantic information from different receptive areas simultaneously. Cascaded skip connections distribute the incoming gradient among all paths during back-propagation, enabling training of deeper yet lightweight networks. The use of task-independent encoders implies that a single pre-trained model can serve multiple down-stream tasks (segmentation, detection, classification). The finding that decoder design choice matters independently of encoder choice demonstrates that the decoder represents a significant portion of the overall computation. Dilated convolution with dilation rate 1 was chosen over higher rates to balance receptive field expansion with embedded runtime constraints.

Contradictions And Limitations
The dataset is private (owned by the organization), preventing external replication of the exact results. No data augmentation or class weighting techniques were used, which may affect generalization. The encoder is described as  Aggregated residual transformation was found to show adverse effects for lightweight networks, limiting the applicability of standard residual strategies. The dilation rate was kept at 1; incremental dilation was not explored due to computational cost. The study is preliminary, and the authors acknowledge that further research is needed for a systematic family of meta-architectures. The 3016-image training set is described as very small, increasing the risk of overfitting.

Claims
The proposed non-bottleneck decoder architecture provides 10% mean IoU improvement over the baseline within an automotive runtime budget. The optimal configuration achieves a mean IoU of 0.7441 compared to the baseline's 0.7255. The runtime overhead is less than 2ms on custom automotive hardware. No data augmentation or class weighting was used, which may have artificially constrained the baseline performance. Decoder design is a critical architectural lever that can be optimized independently of encoder choice for embedded semantic segmentation.
The non-bottleneck layer with multi-kernel fusion specifically improves under-represented classes (lanes and curb) by 12% and 18% IoU respectively. Lane IoU improved from 0.4943 (D1) to 0.5304 (Optimal), a +3.7% absolute gain. Curb IoU improved from 0.4296 (D1) to 0.4696 (Optimal), a +4.0% absolute gain. Without class weighting, the improvement in lanes was described as  For imbalanced scene data, decoder architectural changes can act as a form of implicit class rebalancing.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Eight decoder variants (D1–D8) were tested to ablate kernel sizes, skip connections, and dilated convolutions. Batch size was varied from 4 to 8 to assess sensitivity (D2 vs D3, D5 vs D6). Non-bottleneck layer configurations were permuted in different sequences (e.g., 2N1 vs 2N2) to identify the optimal arrangement. The optimal configuration was identified through systematic optimization of non-bottleneck layer order.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the typical encoder-decoder architecture of the CNN-based semantic segmentation network. Figure 2 illustrates the design of non-bottleneck layers with 1D and 3D kernels. Figure 3 shows the specific encoder-decoder pair used, with VGG10 as encoder and the proposed optimal decoder. Figure 4 compares qualitative segmentation outputs of the proposed optimal decoder against a standard FCN decoder on two image examples. Table 1 presents quantitative results for all eight decoder variants and optimal configurations, showing average class accuracy and IoU.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a novel, task-independent decoder architecture using a cascaded non-bottleneck layer with multi-kernel fusion (1D, 3D, 3x3, 5x5, 1x1) and residual skip connections, achieving 10% mean IoU improvement. 2. The strongest evidence is the 18% IoU gain for the curb class and 12% for lanes, with only <2ms runtime overhead, demonstrating that decoder design—not just encoder optimization—is critical for embedded real-time segmentation. 3. The future path involves building a systematic family of meta-architectures with a fixed run-time budget and learning the optimal configuration using meta-learning techniques.

summary.title: Lusin characterisation of Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators
summary.authors: Tan Duc Do, Trong Ngoc Nguyen, and Truong Xuan Le
summary.field_subfield: Harmonic Analysis / Partial Differential Equations
summary.executive_summary: This paper establishes the Lusin area characterization of Hardy spaces H^p_L(Rd) associated with the Hermite operator L = -Δ + |x|^2 on Rd for d ∈ {3, 4, 5, ...} and p ∈ (0, 1]. The authors prove that the Hardy space defined via the maximal function of the Poisson semigroup is equivalent to the space defined via the Lusin area integral, i.e., H^p_L(Rd) = H^p_S(Rd) as quasi-normed spaces. A key novelty is the use of derivatives of the form ∂_j + x_j, which are specific to Hermite operators and were first suggested by Thangavelu. The proof strategy involves intermediate spaces HL,max and H^p_A defined via an operator A that is a discrete version of the Lusin integral, and an atomic decomposition involving (p, 2, M)-atoms. Additionally, the authors prove that the Riesz transforms R^L_j = (∂_j + x_j)L^{-1/2} are bounded on H^p_L(Rd) for all j ≥ 1. The results extend earlier work that covered only the p = 1 case to the full range p ∈ (0, 1]. Key preliminary estimates on heat and Poisson kernel decay, atom decompositions, and tent space techniques underpin the main arguments.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper establishes the Lusin area characterization of Hardy spaces H^p_L(Rd) associated with the Hermite operator L = -Δ + |x|^2 on Rd for d ∈ {3, 4, 5, ...} and p ∈ (0, 1]. The authors prove that the Hardy space defined via the maximal function of the Poisson semigroup is equivalent to the space defined via the Lusin area integral, i.e., H^p_L(Rd) = H^p_S(Rd) as quasi-normed spaces. A key novelty is the use of derivatives of the form ∂_j + x_j, which are specific to Hermite operators and were first suggested by Thangavelu. The proof strategy involves intermediate spaces HL,max and H^p_A defined via an operator A that is a discrete version of the Lusin integral, and an atomic decomposition involving (p, 2, M)-atoms. Additionally, the authors prove that the Riesz transforms R^L_j = (∂_j + x_j)L^{-1/2} are bounded on H^p_L(Rd) for all j ≥ 1. The results extend earlier work that covered only the p = 1 case to the full range p ∈ (0, 1]. Key preliminary estimates on heat and Poisson kernel decay, atom decompositions, and tent space techniques underpin the main arguments.

Research Context
Hermite operators play a significant role in the harmonic oscillator and have been studied extensively. Hardy spaces with rich structures are of fundamental interest in harmonic analysis. Similar Lusin area characterizations exist for classical Hardy spaces in the literature. The authors' approach uses derivatives ∂_j + x_j which are specific to Hermite operators. These derivatives were first suggested by Thangavelu in a prior work. The work is motivated by prior results that only covered the p = 1 case for Hermite Hardy spaces.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether H^p_L(Rd) can be characterized in terms of Lusin area integrals associated with the Hermite operator. The primary hypothesis (Theorem 1.1) is that H^p_L(Rd) equals H^p_S(Rd) as quasi-normed spaces for all d ≥ 3 and p ∈ (0, 1]. A secondary hypothesis (Theorem 1.2) is that the Riesz transforms R^L_j = (∂_j + x_j)L^{-1/2} are bounded on H^p_L(Rd) for all j ≥ 1. The expected outcome is an equivalence of quasi-norms, which would generalize the p = 1 result to the full range p ∈ (0, 1].

Methodological Details
The study considers the Hermite operator L = -Δ + |x|^2 on Rd for d ∈ {3, 4, 5, ...}. The index range is p ∈ (0, 1], corresponding to Hardy spaces. The space H^p_L(Rd) is defined as the completion of {f ∈ L^2 : MLf ∈ L^p} under the quasi-norm ||·||_H^p_L = ||ML ·||_L^p. The Poisson semigroup P_t = e^{-tL^{1/2}} is the contraction C0-semigroup associated with L. The Lusin integral Sf(x) involves the gradient ∇_L = (∂_t, ∂_1 + x_1, ..., ∂_d + x_d). Heat kernel estimates for gt and pt from Proposition 2.2 and 2.3 provide the foundational kernel bounds. An H^p_L-atom decomposition exists for p > d/(d+δ), enabling the use of atom-based arguments. The intermediate space H^p_{L,max} is defined via the sup over the cone {(t,y) : |x-y| < t}. The operator A is defined as a discrete Lusin-type operator and shown to be bounded on L^2. Tent space techniques and atomic decompositions in tent spaces are employed for the reverse inclusion.

Procedures And Architectures
The Lusin integral is defined as Sf(x) = ((∫_Γ(x) t^{1-d} |∇_L P_t f(y)|^2 dy dt)^1/2) with Γ(x) = {(y,t) : |x-y| < t}. The gradient ∇_L includes both ∂_t and the operators ∂_j + x_j, distinct from the classical gradient. Intermediate spaces H^p_{L,max} and H^p_A are constructed to facilitate the proof of the main equivalence. H^p_L ⊂ H^p_{L,max} is proven first using atom estimates and the Poisson kernel's decay. H^p_A ∩ L^2 = H^p_L is established via atomic characterizations and tent space arguments. The final equivalence H^p_L = H^p_S is proven through interpolation, Fubini-type estimates, and Lebesgue dominated convergence. The Riesz transform boundedness proof uses the L^2-boundedness of A and the previous equivalence. Density of L^2_c(Rd) in H^p_L(Rd) is used to extend results from L^2 to the full space.

Key Results
Theorem 1.1 establishes H^p_L(Rd) = H^p_S(Rd) as quasi-normed spaces for d ≥ 3, p ∈ (0, 1]. The equivalence holds with the same quasi-norms ||·||_H^p_L and ||·||_H^p_S. Theorem 1.2 proves that all Riesz transforms R^L_j = (∂_j + x_j)L^{-1/2} are bounded on H^p_L(Rd). Boundedness holds for all j ∈ {1, 2, 3, ...}, extending the classical Riesz transform theory to Hermite Hardy spaces. Proposition 3.1 proves H^p_L(Rd) ⊂ H^p_{L,max}(Rd) under the condition d/(d+δ) < p ≤ 1. Proposition 4.9 establishes H^p_A(Rd) ∩ L^2(Rd) = H^p_{L,at,M}(Rd) for M > d/2(1/p - 1/2). Proposition 4.11 concludes H^p_L(Rd) = H^p_A(Rd) ∩ L^2(Rd) by combining atomic and maximal characterizations. Lemma 6.1 shows L^2_c(Rd) is dense in both H^p_L(Rd) and H^p_{L+2}(Rd). Lemma 6.2 establishes H^p_L(Rd) = H^p_{L+2}(Rd), enabling the Riesz transform proof.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results generalize prior work that was restricted to p = 1 to the full range p ∈ (0, 1]. The specific gradient ∂_j + x_j reflects the structure of Hermite operators and distinguishes this work from classical Lusin characterizations. The equivalence between maximal and Lusin area characterizations suggests a robust theory of Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators. The atomic decomposition approach provides a concrete tool for estimating functions in these spaces. The boundedness of Riesz transforms is a standard expected result in Hardy space theory, now established for the Hermite setting.

Contradictions And Limitations
The result requires d ≥ 3, so the case d = 1, 2 is not covered in this paper. The atomic decomposition for H^p_L requires p > d/(d+δ), restricting the range of p for atom-based arguments. The paper references [Jiz12] whose results are for p = 1, so the generalization to p < 1 is a limitation of prior work the paper addresses. No specific quantitative constants are provided for the equivalence, only that a constant C exists. The Riesz transform boundedness is proven only for the operators ∂_j + x_j, not for other combinations.

Claims
The Hermite Hardy space H^p_L(Rd) is equivalent to the Lusin area space H^p_S(Rd) for p ∈ (0, 1]. The inclusion H^p_L ⊂ H^p_S follows from Propositions 3.1 and 5.4. The reverse inclusion uses Proposition 4.11 and the fact that H^p_A is contained in H^p_S. The result requires d ≥ 3, so for d = 1, 2 the claim is not established in this paper. Functions in H^p_L can be characterized by their Lusin area integral, a standard tool in harmonic analysis. The equivalence extends the classical theory to the Hermite operator setting.
The Riesz transforms R^L_j = (∂_j + x_j)L^{-1/2} are bounded on H^p_L(Rd). The boundedness is proven on H^p_L ∩ L^2 and extended by density. The proof uses the equivalence between H^p_L and H^p_{L+2} and the boundedness of the operator A. The boundedness is only stated for j ≥ 1, not for any arbitrary operator. This completes the standard toolkit for Riesz transforms in the context of Hermite Hardy spaces.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first Lusin area characterization of Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators for the full range p ∈ (0, 1], extending prior work that only covered p = 1. 2. The strongest evidence is the complete proof of equivalence H^p_L(Rd) = H^p_S(Rd) via intermediate spaces, atomic decompositions, and interpolation estimates, with the Riesz transforms also shown to be bounded. 3. The future path lies in extending these results to other operators, lower dimensions (d = 1, 2), or obtaining quantitative constants for the equivalence.

summary.title: Deep-Learning-based Millimeter-Wave Massive MIMO for Hybrid Precoding
summary.authors: Hongji Huang, Yiwei Song, Jie Yang, Guan Gui, Fumiyuki Adachi
summary.field_subfield: Telecommunications / mmWave Massive MIMO Precoding
summary.type_of_paper: Research paper presenting a novel framework with simulation validation
summary.executive_summary: This paper proposes a deep-learning-enabled millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive MIMO framework for effective hybrid precoding, addressing the fundamental limitations of conventional schemes: high computational complexity and failure to fully exploit spatial information. The authors regard the selection of hybrid precoders for obtaining an optimized decoder as a mapping relation within a deep neural network (DNN), treating the entire system as a black box. The DNN architecture, constructed as an autoencoder with multiple fully connected layers and a noise layer, is trained using an unsupervised learning approach via stochastic gradient descent with momentum. The learning policy employs geometric mean decomposition (GMD) to reformulate the complex channel matrix into a semi-unitary combiner and precoder structure. The loss function, defined as the Frobenius norm difference between the DNN-generated precoder and the GMD-based reference precoder, is minimized while enforcing phase-shifter and transmit power constraints. judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper proposes a deep-learning-enabled millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive MIMO framework for effective hybrid precoding, addressing the fundamental limitations of conventional schemes: high computational complexity and failure to fully exploit spatial information. The authors regard the selection of hybrid precoders for obtaining an optimized decoder as a mapping relation within a deep neural network (DNN), treating the entire system as a black box. The DNN architecture, constructed as an autoencoder with multiple fully connected layers and a noise layer, is trained using an unsupervised learning approach via stochastic gradient descent with momentum. The learning policy employs geometric mean decomposition (GMD) to reformulate the complex channel matrix into a semi-unitary combiner and precoder structure. The loss function, defined as the Frobenius norm difference between the DNN-generated precoder and the GMD-based reference precoder, is minimized while enforcing phase-shifter and transmit power constraints. Simulation results using the Saleh-Valenzuela channel model (P=3, 28 GHz) demonstrate that the DNN-based approach achieves lower bit error ratio (BER) and higher spectrum efficiency compared to conventional SVD-based hybrid precoding, fully digital SVD precoding, GMD-based methods, and spatially sparse precoding. A complexity analysis confirms the proposed method's advantage with O(L²NsN²t) complexity, significantly lower than previous methods. Robustness analysis via mean square error (MSE) versus iterations shows the DNN-based scheme converges at approximately 11 iterations, outperforming the analog precoding scheme which requires 22 iterations. The authors also find that lower learning rates enhance system performance at the cost of slower convergence, and batch size selection (10, 20, 50, 100) presents a trade-off between convergence stability and BER degradation.

Research Context
Wireless data traffic is predicted to increase over 10,000-fold by 2030, necessitating fifth-generation (5G) solutions. Millimeter-wave bands are attractive due to a ten-fold increase in carrier frequency and orders-of-magnitude enhancement in free-space pathloss. Massive MIMO is a potential technique for enhancing system throughput in mmWave communications. Hybrid precoding was proposed to reduce hardware complexity and energy consumption associated with mixed signal components. Successive interference cancellation-based and GMD-based hybrid precoding schemes exist but face limitations. Existing precoding schemes have high computational complexity and require complicated bit allocation strategies. The GMD-based scheme can avoid bit allocation issues but still faces challenges with non-convex constraints and structural exploitation. Conventional mathematical methods like SVD and GMD are too weak to exploit sparsity statistics of mmWave massive MIMO. Traditional low-complexity schemes are realized at the cost of degrading hybrid precoding performance. Deep learning has emerged as a technology for handling explosive data and addressing complicated nonlinear, non-convex problems. Previous deep-learning-based communication works cover beam selection, NOMA, and massive MIMO but a dedicated hybrid precoding framework is lacking.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to design a framework integrating deep learning into hybrid precoding to overcome complexity and performance limitations of conventional methods. The authors hypothesize that a DNN can capture structural information of the hybrid precoding scheme through the training stage. The hypothesis is that the DNN, regarded as an autoencoder, can map input data to optimized precoders while lowering computational complexity. The predicted outcome is that the DNN-based approach will minimize the bit error ratio (BER) and enhance spectrum efficiency compared to conventional schemes. The authors further predict the DNN-based strategy will achieve better hybrid precoding performance at substantially reduced computational complexity. The hypothesis extends to the conclusion that the DNN can approach each iteration of the hybrid precoding algorithm, effectively solving the non-convex optimization problem.

Methodological Details
The study considers a mmWave massive MIMO system with one BS having a uniform linear array of Nt antennas. The user has Nr received antennas, and the BS sends Ns independent data streams to the user. The BS and user are assumed to have Nt and Nr RF chains, respectively, satisfying Ns ≤ NRFt ≤ Nt and Nt ≤ NRFr ≤ Nr. The Saleh-Valenzuela channel model is employed for the channel matrix H ∈ CNt×Nr with P non-line-of-sight components. The BS has no information on all communication links (blind case). The channel model is parameterized with P = 3 non-line-of-sight components. The carrier frequency is set to 28 GHz. The antenna spacing is d, and the wave-length is λ, with the channel having low-rank characteristic. The network is trained for 45,000 iterations in the simulation. The learning rate is set at 0.001 for the robustness analysis. Keras is used to construct and process the DNN framework. The DNN input layer is a fully connected layer with 128 units for feature capture. The next two hidden layers for encoding consist of 400 and 256 units, respectively. A noise layer of 200 units is inserted to mix distortion. The decoding hidden layers consist of 128 and 64 units. The output layer employs a custom activation function to enforce power constraints.

Procedures And Architectures
The DNN is constructed as an autoencoder, regarded as a black box where activation functions optimize multiple layers and create mapping relations. The input layer uses ReLU activation for the input and hidden layers. The output layer uses a special activation function f(s) = min(max(s, 0), Ns) to enforce the transmit power constraint. The GMD method is adopted to decompose the channel matrix, reformulating the received signal as y = WQRH. The loss function is defined as the Frobenius norm of the difference between the DNN-generated precoder R1 and the GMD-based precoder RARD. An unsupervised learning training approach is used: RA and RD are initialized as empty, random sequences are generated, and the DNN is trained to extract structural statistics. After training, optimal RA and RD are obtained from the input signal vectors without requiring iterations during testing. The stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm with momentum is employed to process the loss function. The momentum parameter α and learning rate ε control the velocity update in the weight adjustment. The algorithm, detailed in Algorithm 1, includes initialization, sequence production, DNN construction, environment simulation, SGD training, and RA/RD updating. The error threshold is set to τ = 10⁻⁷ for the training termination condition. During training, the physical AoA θr_p and AoD θt_p are generated randomly to obtain the bias between R1 and RARD. The mean square error (MSE) = E||R1 - RARD||² is introduced to analyze precoding performance.

Key Results
In Fig. 2, the DNN-based scheme outperforms the SVD-based hybrid precoding, fully digital SVD-based precoding, fully GMD-based precoding, and the new GMD-based precoding scheme across the SNR range. The performance improvement is more apparent between the deep-learning-based strategy and conventional methods due to the DNN's excellent representation ability. The DNN-based scheme outperforms the fully GMD-based digital precoding scheme, implying that non-convex optimization in hybrid precoding can be solved with deep learning. In Fig. 3, the BER performance degrades with increasing batch size (10, 20, 50, 100) because larger batch sizes may induce slower convergence. Too small a batch size leads to unstable convergence, necessitating careful batch size selection for optimal performance. In Fig. 4, the hybrid precoding performance in the DNN-based method is optimized by adopting a lower learning rate. A larger learning rate causes a higher validation error, while a lower learning rate enhances system performance at the cost of slower convergence. In Fig. 5, spectrum efficiency improves as SNR increases in all schemes, and the proposed DNN-based scheme outperforms the spatially sparse precoding and fully digital GMD-based precoding. The performance gap between the DNN-based scheme and other approaches widens as SNR increases. In Fig. 6, both the proposed DNN-based scheme and the sparse precoding method converge at approximately 11 iterations. The analog precoding scheme requires approximately 22 iterations to converge, showing slower convergence. The MSE of the DNN-based scheme is superior to that of the analog precoding and sparse precoding schemes. The computational complexity of the DNN-based scheme is O(L²NsN²t). The SIC-based hybrid precoding scheme has complexity O(2NrNs(N²t(K + NsNr))). The spatially sparse precoding method has complexity O(2N³r(N⁴rNt + N²rL² + N²rN²tL)).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The DNN-based approach works because the DNN is capable of capturing structural information of the hybrid precoding scheme through the training stage. The excellent recognition and representation abilities of deep learning enable the spatial features of the mmWave massive MIMO system to be exploited. Regarding the entire system as a black box allows the DNN to capture useful features for hybrid precoding without explicit mathematical modeling of the channel statistics. The DNN can approach each iteration of the hybrid precoding algorithm, suggesting that the DNN implicitly learns the optimization trajectory. The superiority over fully GMD-based digital precoding implies the DNN-based hybrid scheme captures more spatial structure than is available with fixed low-dimensional digital decomposition alone. A promising future direction is applying deep learning to the channel feedback issue to alleviate codebook size and feedback overhead problems.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors note that the selection of the best learning rate remains an open issue as it involves a trade-off between performance and convergence speed. Larger batch sizes degrade BER performance due to slower convergence, creating a trade-off with convergence stability at small batch sizes. The training dataset consists of structural features and input data sequences, but the exact statistical distribution of the generated sequences is not fully specified beyond 'random'. The complexity analysis is asymptotic; concrete runtime on hardware is not reported. The paper does not report the exact GPU hardware or training time for the 45,000 iterations. The number of users K is not explicitly quantified in the simulation results, though it appears as a variable in the complexity expression. The simulation environment simulator and specific channel realizations are not described in detail beyond the SV model parameter P=3.

Claims
The DNN-based hybrid precoding scheme achieves superior BER and spectrum efficiency compared to all conventional hybrid and digital precoding baselines. The DNN-based method outperforms conventional schemes in BER as shown in Figure 2. Spectrum efficiency is highest for the DNN-based scheme in Figure 5. MSE is superior to analog and sparse precoding in convergence accuracy. With increasing batch size, the BER of the DNN-based scheme degrades. Lower learning rates enhance performance but induce slower convergence, not eliminating the trade-off. The DNN-based framework demonstrates that the non-convex optimization in hybrid precoding can be solved by deep learning. The framework is extensible to other communications tasks such as channel feedback optimization.
The DNN-based scheme significantly reduces computational complexity compared to SVD and GMD-based hybrid precoding. The complexity of the proposed method is O(L²NsN²t). The SIC-based scheme has O(2NrNs(N²t(K + NsNr))) complexity. The spatially sparse method has O(2N³r(N⁴rNt + N²rL² + N²rN²tL)) complexity. The DNN approaches convergence in about 11 iterations versus 22 for analog precoding. The complexity is reported as asymptotic, and practical execution time on hardware is not quantified. The reduced complexity makes the DNN-based scheme more feasible for real-time deployment in mmWave systems.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors investigate the effect of batch size (10, 20, 50, 100) on BER performance. Different learning rates are evaluated in Figure 4, showing a performance-convergence trade-off. The learning rate is set to 0.001 for the robustness/MSE versus iterations analysis. The error threshold τ = 10⁻⁷ serves as the convergence criterion. The MSE performance is tracked across iterations to compare convergence speed and quality against baselines.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the DNN architecture: an input layer (128 FC), two hidden layers (400, 256), a noise layer (200), two decoding hidden layers (128, 64), and an output layer with special activation. Figure 2 presents BER versus SNR for the proposed DNN-based scheme against SVD-based hybrid, fully digital SVD, fully GMD, and new GMD-based precoding. Figure 3 shows BER versus SNR for the proposed method with different batch sizes (10, 20, 50, 100). Figure 4 displays BER versus SNR with different learning rates. Figure 5 compares spectrum efficiency versus SNR across DNN-based, spatially sparse, and fully digital GMD-based schemes. Figure 6 plots MSE versus iterations for the DNN-based, analog precoding, and sparse precoding methods. Table I provides a quantitative comparison of computational complexity for the proposed DNN-based, SIC-based, and spatially sparse precoding schemes.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first DNN-based framework for hybrid precoding in mmWave massive MIMO, treating the precoder selection as a black-box mapping learned through GMD-based unsupervised training. 2. The strongest evidence is the combination of lower BER, higher spectrum efficiency, and faster convergence (11 vs 22 iterations) demonstrated in Figs. 2, 5, and 6 against all conventional baselines. 3. The future path involves applying deep learning to the channel feedback issue to alleviate codebook size and feedback overhead constraints in mmWave systems.

summary.authors: Mahammed Kamruzzaman, Abdullah Al Monsur, Shrabon Das, Enamul Hassan, Gene Louis Kim
summary.field_subfield: Natural Language Processing / AI Ethics
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces BanStereoSet, a 1,194-sentence fill-in-the-blank dataset specifically designed to measure stereotypical social biases in multilingual LLMs for the Bangla language. The authors addressed specific Bangla linguistic challenges, such as the absence of gendered pronouns, by inserting gender-specific phrases. They also corrected five types of StereoSet pitfalls identified by Blodgett et al. (2021). Evaluation was conducted across four multilingual LLMs (GPT-4o, Mistral-7B, llama3.1-70B, and Gemma2-27B) using three prompting templates, with results reported as stereotypical response rates averaged across all three templates. The comparative analysis between Bangla and English versions revealed no consistent, major difference in model bias across languages, though Mistral showed improved performance on caste bias in Bangla versus English. The authors conclude that culturally and linguistically adapted datasets are necessary for developing equitable language technologies in Bangladeshi contexts, and they acknowledge limitations regarding regional variations, binary gender representations, and explicit versus subtle bias capture.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces BanStereoSet, a 1,194-sentence fill-in-the-blank dataset specifically designed to measure stereotypical social biases in multilingual LLMs for the Bangla language. Recognizing that prior bias research was predominantly English-centric, the authors localized content from StereoSet, IndiBias, and the GenAssocBias dataset, covering nine bias categories: race, profession, gender, ageism, beauty, beauty in profession, region, caste, and religion. The dataset was constructed by translating English source sentences to Bangla using GPT-4 with few-shot learning, followed by manual review by four native Bangla-speaking annotators. The authors addressed specific Bangla linguistic challenges, such as the absence of gendered pronouns, by inserting gender-specific phrases. They also corrected five types of StereoSet pitfalls identified by Blodgett et al. (2021). Evaluation was conducted across four multilingual LLMs (GPT-4o, Mistral-7B, llama3.1-70B, and Gemma2-27B) using three prompting templates, with results reported as stereotypical response rates averaged across all three templates. The comparative analysis between Bangla and English versions revealed no consistent, major difference in model bias across languages, though Mistral showed improved performance on caste bias in Bangla versus English. The authors conclude that culturally and linguistically adapted datasets are necessary for developing equitable language technologies in Bangladeshi contexts, and they acknowledge limitations regarding regional variations, binary gender representations, and explicit versus subtle bias capture.

Research Context
Despite the global adoption of LLMs like GPT-4, Llama, and Gemini, many studies have revealed undesirable biases and stereotypes within these models. Prior datasets measuring these biases have been predominantly in English, with limited work in other languages such as French, Hindi, Italian, and Arabic. Bengali has 233.7 million native speakers worldwide, ranking fifth in the world, yet research on bias specific to the Bengali language remains sparse. Recent Bengali-specific studies have primarily addressed gender and religious biases, with no comprehensive dataset covering a broader spectrum of bias categories in the Bengali cultural context. Stereotypical biases extend beyond gender and religion to include race, profession, beauty, ageism, caste, and region, impacting individuals as significantly.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to comprehensively measure stereotypical social biases in multilingual LLMs specifically for the Bangla language. The authors hypothesize that a fill-in-the-blank dataset incorporating culturally and linguistically adapted content can capture biases prevalent within the Bangla-speaking community. The implicit hypothesis is that LLMs will exhibit varying degrees of bias across different models and categories, and that Bangla-specific linguistic features (like lack of gendered pronouns) necessitate unique adaptations. A comparative hypothesis is whether LLM bias differs significantly between Bangla and English versions of the same dataset. The authors predict that models will treat StereoSet-derived categories with higher bias due to extremely negative attributes, while GenAssocBias categories should trend toward balanced distribution.

Methodological Details
The BanStereoSet dataset consists of 1,194 sentences spanning 9 categories: race, profession, gender, ageism, beauty, beauty in profession, region, caste, and religion. Race: 241, Gender: 178, Religion: 56, Profession: 206, Ageism: 134, Beauty: 130, Beauty Profession: 126, Caste: 60, and Region: 63 examples comprise the dataset. Race, gender, religion, and profession data were derived from the StereoSet dataset. Beauty, beauty in profession, and ageism categories were derived from the GenAssocBias dataset (Kamruzzaman et al., 2024b). The caste bias category was adopted from the IndiBias dataset. Regional bias data was freshly curated using a human-LLM partnership across 17 major cities in Bangladesh. English sentences were translated into Bangla using GPT-4 with few-shot learning for enhanced accuracy. Four native Bangla-speaking annotators fluent in English reviewed each translation, and incorrect ones were modified. Gender-specific phrases (ekjon purush/ekjon mohila) were added to 76 sentences to address the absence of gendered pronouns in Bangla. English names (John, Judy) were replaced with Bengali names (Mehedi, Sumiya) in 12 sentences for cultural relevance. References to US cities (Boston) were replaced with Bangladeshi cities (Dhaka) in 6 sentences. Five StereoSet pitfalls were corrected manually, affecting 47, 9, 15, 58, and 35 sentences respectively. Sentences were retained only if at least three annotators reached a consensus. For caste data, 'sent-more' targeted caste provided stereotype options and 'sent-less' targeted caste provided anti-stereotype options from IndiBias.

Procedures And Architectures
Four multilingual LLMs were evaluated: GPT-4o, Mistral-7B, llama3.1-70B, and Gemma2-27B. Three prompting templates were used: a baseline template and two paraphrases. The baseline prompt instructed models to select the appropriate word from the options without considering order, providing only a single plain Bangla text answer without explanation. Results were averaged across all three prompting templates following Gupta et al. (2023). A comparative run was conducted using the four models on the English version of the dataset with modified sentences (pitfalls removed) and zero-shot learning. The region data used ChatGPT to generate sets of 10 stereotypical, 10 anti-stereotypical, and 10 unrelated attributes for each city, followed by annotator validation and sentence generation. Stereotypical engagement rates exclude unrelated engagements, which are included solely to assess model behavior unrelated to bias. For GenAssocBias categories, unrelated terms were used to examine neutral engagement.

Key Results
In Bangla, GPT-4o exhibited the highest average stereotypical response rate at 73.78%, while Mistral achieved the lowest at 55.41%. In Bangla, Gemma achieved the highest caste bias at 79.31%, and Mistral performed best on 7 of the 9 bias categories. In English, Mistral remained the least biased model on average, but Gemma became the most biased. For the religion category in Bangla, GPT-4o scored 55.55%, Mistral 59.52%, Llama 45.09%, and Gemma 53.70%. For the region category in Bangla, Mistral scored the best at 67.44%, followed by Llama at 78.72%, GPT-4o at 82.14%, and Gemma at 81.48%. In English, GPT-4o scored 81.12% on gender bias, Mistral 72.34%, Llama 82.74%, and Gemma 84.37%. All models show high levels of profession and region bias and relatively low levels of religion bias in both Bangla and English. Mistral can successfully handle caste bias in Bangla but not in English, suggesting culturally-dependent sensitivity. On average, GPT-4o and Gemma are more biased in Bangla sentences, while Mistral and Llama are more biased in English sentences. Overall, there is no consistent, major difference in model biases between Bangla and English.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
A fair model's stereotypical engagement should ideally be close to 50%, meaning it treats stereotype and anti-stereotype attributes uniformly. For StereoSet-derived categories, the desirable stereotypical response is lower than 50% to account for extremely negative attributes. The findings indicate significant biases across all tested models, reinforcing the necessity for culturally and linguistically adapted datasets. The model's improved performance on caste bias in Bangla but not English suggests a degree of cultural sensitivity that depends on the language of communication. The results underscore a stark gap between popular models in their ability to handle bias in less common languages compared to English.

Contradictions And Limitations
The dataset may not adequately represent regional variations in stereotypes throughout Bangladesh as biases vary between different areas. The focus on binary gender (man and woman) restricts the ability to address biases concerning non-binary or gender-nonconforming identities. Translation challenges from English to Bangla may lead to inaccuracies or cultural mismatches despite annotation efforts. The relatively small size of certain categories, such as region bias (63 examples), might limit comprehensiveness. Crucial categories such as sexual orientation, socioeconomic status, or disability were not included. The dataset predominantly captures explicit biases, which may neglect more subtle or underlying biases. Effectiveness of model evaluations could be compromised by the models' limited proficiency in Bangla, which might skew results.

Claims
BanStereoSet comprehensively captures stereotypical biases across 9 social categories in the Bangla language, filling a critical research gap. The dataset covers 9 categories: race, profession, gender, ageism, beauty, beauty in profession, region, caste, and religion. Each category has specific counts: Race 241, Gender 178, Religion 56, Profession 206, Ageism 134, Beauty 130, Beauty Profession 126, Caste 60, Region 63. Data was localized from StereoSet, IndiBias, and GenAssocBias, supplemented with freshly curated regional data. The dataset only captures explicit biases, neglecting more subtle or underlying biases. Crucial categories like sexual orientation, socioeconomic status, and disability were not included. The region category has only 63 examples, limiting its comprehensiveness. The dataset provides a foundation for developing more equitable language technologies in Bangladeshi contexts. It encourages extension of bias research beyond English and reflects diverse linguistic realities.
Multilingual LLMs exhibit significant stereotypical biases in Bangla, with a stark gap between model performances. GPT-4o achieved an average stereotypical response rate of 73.78% in Bangla. Gemma achieved the highest caste bias in Bangla at 79.31%. All models show high levels of profession and region bias. Mistral achieved the lowest average bias in Bangla at 55.41%, indicating some models perform comparably well. All models continue to show low levels of bias in religion in both Bangla and English. The findings underscore the importance of culturally nuanced datasets for training equitable AI systems. The gap between models highlights that simply extending an English-centric dataset is insufficient.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Results were averaged across three prompting templates to ensure robustness of bias estimates. A comparative English-language evaluation was performed to isolate language-specific effects from model-specific bias. Zero-shot learning was used for the English comparative run. Unrelated engagements were excluded from bias scores, and separate analysis was conducted for GenAssocBias neutral engagement. Five StereoSet pitfalls were manually identified and corrected based on Blodgett et al. (2021) criteria.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows an example completion task for race bias: 'The person from Afghanistan on the plane looked like a BLANK' with options businessman, terrorist, travel. Figure 2 illustrates translation adjustments: (a) gender-specific phrase addition, (b) name replacement (John to Mehedi), (c-f) StereoSet pitfall corrections. Figure 3 shows an example of caste bias data creation from IndiBias with stereotype, anti-stereotype, and unrelated options. Figure 2(g) presents an example sentence of regional bias: 'People in Dhaka are always relaxed/busy/funny' (Bangla version). Table 1 presents the main results: bias analysis across four models for 9 categories in both Bangla and English, reported as stereotypical response rates.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is BanStereoSet, a 1,194-sentence fill-in-the-blank dataset covering 9 social bias categories specifically for the Bangla language. 2. The strongest evidence is that all four LLMs exhibit significant stereotypical biases in Bangla, with GPT-4o averaging 73.78% and Mistral at 55.41%, while Mistral uniquely handles caste bias in Bangla but not English. 3. The future path involves developing culturally and linguistically adapted datasets to guide the creation of more equitable language technologies in Bangladeshi contexts.

summary.title: SYSTEMS OF HECKE EIGENVALUES ON SUBSCHEMES OF SHIMURA VARIETIES
summary.authors: STEFAN REPPEN
summary.field_subfield: Mathematics, Algebraic Geometry, Arithmetic Geometry (Shimura Varieties, Hecke Algebras)
summary.executive_summary: This paper establishes that the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in the coherent cohomology of automorphic line bundles on any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme of a mod p abelian type compact Shimura variety at hyperspecial level are identical to those appearing on the full Shimura variety. The central result, Theorem A, generalizes previous works (Serre-Tate, Goldring-Koskivirta, Terakado-Yu) that were restricted to smooth, zero-dimensional subschemes, by extending the theory to higher-dimensional and singular subschemes. The authors prove that for a compact abelian type Shimura variety at hyperspecial level, the sets of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in the direct sum of H0(SK, V(η)) over all L-dominant characters η are the same as those appearing on any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme YK. The proof construction involves a multi-step inductive process: intersecting the subscheme YK with the smallest length stratum it meets, and successively removing nonsingular points of the intersection to isolate a smooth, closed subscheme ZK that admits a nowhere-vanishing Hecke-equivariant section. This smooth subscheme ZK is then used as a bridge, applying a going-up argument via Hasse invariants and a going-down argument involving conormal exact sequences modified by the ideal sheaf filtration. The paper further extends these results to noncompact Shimura varieties and nonclosed subschemes, including Ekedahl-Oort strata, length strata, and central leaves, providing a comprehensive framework for comparing Hecke eigenvalues between subschemes and the total variety. Corollary 3.3.3 synthesizes these results for specific stratifications and central leaves.

The results extend to noncompact Shimura varieties, Ekedahl-Oort strata, length strata, and central leaves, provided the subscheme is closed or meets the basic locus.

top_influential_citations.Terakado-Yu [TY22] (Theorem 5.4): This paper extended the eigenvalue equality to central leaves in the basic Newton stratum, and the current work extends this from zero-dimensional central leaves to higher-dimensional cases.

top_influential_citations.Serre's letter to Tate [Ser96]: The original observation that eigenvalues on the modular curve match the supersingular locus, which serves as the historical prototype for all subsequent generalizations.

The proof construction involves a multi-step inductive process: intersecting the subscheme YK with the smallest length stratum it meets, and successively removing nonsingular points of the intersection to isolate a smooth, closed subscheme ZK that admits a nowhere-vanishing Hecke-equivariant section. Corollary 3.3.3 synthesizes these results for specific stratifications and central leaves.

Research Context
The mod p fiber of an abelian type Shimura variety at good reduction carries an action of the prime-to-p Hecke algebra. Several well-studied subschemes—including Ekedahl-Oort strata, length strata, Newton strata, and central leaves—are invariant under this Hecke action. Serre, in a famous letter to Tate, showed that the Hecke eigenvalues in the mod p modular curve cohomology match those in the supersingular locus. This result was generalized by Goldring-Koskivirta, proving eigenvalues match for the Kisin-Vasiu integral model and the unique zero-dimensional Ekedahl-Oort stratum. Terakado-Yu further extended this to any central leaf in the basic Newton stratum of a Hodge-type Shimura variety. Prior works restricted subschemes to smooth objects of dimension 0, leaving the higher-dimensional and singular cases unaddressed.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in coherent cohomology of automorphic line bundles on any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme are the same as those on the full Shimura variety. The hypothesis is that this equality holds for any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme YK of the special fiber SK, regardless of dimension or smoothness. The paper predicts that the equality will also extend to nonclosed subschemes, such as Ekedahl-Oort and length strata, and to central leaves. The authors hypothesize that for noncompact Shimura varieties or nonclosed subschemes, analogous results hold under additional conditions such as properness or meeting the basic locus. The proof is predicted to require a further going-down argument to bypass the absence of a nowhere-vanishing section on singular YK and the non-exactness of the conormal sequence.

Methodological Details
Let (G,X) be a Shimura datum of abelian type, and assume G is the cuspidal quotient Gc. Fix a prime p ≠ 2 over which G is unramified, and let Kp be a hyperspecial subgroup of G(Qp). Let K = KpKp be a sufficiently small open compact subgroup, and SK denote the special fiber of the Kisin-Vasiu integral canonical model. The stack of G-zips G-Zipμ is a smooth algebraic κ-stack of dimension 0, and for Hodge type, a smooth surjective morphism ζK: SK → G-Zipμ exists. An automorphic vector bundle on SK is defined as a bundle isomorphic to ζ*K V(r) for a representation r of the Levi subgroup. The Hodge line bundle ω is defined as det ΩSK, the determinant of the sheaf of differentials. The Ekedahl-Oort and length stratifications of SK are obtained via pullback of the stratification of G-Zipμ. Hasse invariants arise as sections of ω^r whose nonvanishing locus is exactly a given stratum, guaranteed by prior results in [GK19]. The Hecke action is defined via trace operators on push-pull of sheaves along finite étale transition maps. The G(Apf)-equivariance of subschemes is established through the universal property of reduced subschemes and finite étale properties of transition maps.

Procedures And Architectures
The construction begins by defining M(YK) as the direct sum of H0(YK, V(η)) over all L-dominant characters η of the Levi torus. For Theorem A, the authors identify the minimal length stratum SK,i0 intersected by YK and define an inductive sequence of subschemes Z(i)K. Each Z(i)K is formed by taking the reduced subscheme of (Z(i-1)K / Z(i-1),smK), leading to a decreasing chain of closed subschemes. Since YK is Noetherian, the sequence stabilizes at a smooth, closed subscheme ZK. A Hasse invariant Hai0 is restricted to ZK; its nonvanishing locus is proven to be ZK by checking that its zero locus lies outside YK. The going-down argument relates H0(ZK, V(η)) to H0(SK, V(η)) using a modified conormal exact sequence argument from [GK19], involving the ideal sheaf filtration. The going-up argument applies the same logic in reverse, using a nowhere-vanishing Hasse-invariant section of ω^r to relate eigenvalues between subschemes. The conormal sequence IK/I2 → ΩSK|ZK → ΩZK → 0 is proven equivariant, and for smooth ZK, the conormal term is locally free. Serre vanishing is applied to ensure H1 vanishes for sufficiently large ample twisting, making the restriction map on H0 surjective. The Hodge line bundle ω is replaced by any ample Hecke-equivariant line bundle in the proof, as noted in Remark 3.2.5.

Key Results
Theorem A: For a compact abelian type Shimura variety at hyperspecial level, the systems of Hecke eigenvalues in M(YK) are the same as in M(SK) for any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme YK. The result holds for noncompact Shimura varieties and nonclosed subschemes, such as Ekedahl-Oort strata and length strata, as stated in Corollary 3.3.3. For a central leaf C(x), if SK is proper and C(x) is closed in the Ekedahl-Oort stratum containing it, eigenvalues match M(SK). If YK meets the basic locus, the eigenvalue systems are the same even without properness. If YK = ζ*KY for a closed substack Y of G-Zipμ, then M(YK) ↭H M(SK). For a nonclosed subscheme YK ⊂ SK, the eigenvalue system of M(SK) is contained in M(YK), while the reverse holds if YK is closed in SΣK. The existence of Hasse invariants is crucial for the going-up argument but not needed for the going-down argument of the zero-dimensional case. The result generalizes the Serre-Tate, Goldring-Koskivirta, and Terakado-Yu results to higher-dimensional and singular subschemes.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The main theoretical implication is that Hecke eigenvalues on subschemes of Shimura varieties are determined by the geometry of the special fiber rather than the full variety. The proof mechanism—reducing to a smooth subscheme with a Hasse-invariant section—suggests a general strategy for comparing cohomology on equivariant subschemes. The role of Hasse invariants is highlighted as the critical bridge between zero-dimensional and higher-dimensional results. The equivariance of the Ekedahl-Oort and length stratifications via G-Zip is fundamental to the Hecke-theoretic structure. The result places Shimura varieties within a broader framework of Hecke-equivariant geometry where eigenvalues are preserved across strata.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper assumes the theory of toroidal compactifications of abelian type Shimura varieties has not yet been fully developed, limiting the noncompact treatment. The assumption G = Gc (cuspidal quotient) is a technical condition that could potentially be relaxed but is needed for the surjective morphism to G-Zip. For the noncompact case, an additional assumption is required that a G(Apf)-equivariant divisor exists such that ω^k(−D') is ample. The conormal sequence is neither exact nor consists of locally free sheaves for singular YK, necessitating the complex inductive reduction. The paper does not explicitly address the case where p=2, as it assumes p ≠ 2.

Claims
The systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in the coherent cohomology of automorphic line bundles on any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme of a compact abelian type Shimura variety at hyperspecial level are identical to those on the full variety. Theorem A proves M(YK) ↭H M(SK) for any closed YK. Corollary 3.2.7 shows M(YK) ↭H M(ZK) for any two closed equivariant subschemes. The proof uses Lemma 3.2.2 for the going-down and Lemma 3.2.4 for the going-up. Serre vanishing ensures the surjectivity of the restriction map for large twists. For nonclosed subschemes, the containment is one-way unless additional conditions are met. If YK is not closed in the compactification, the reverse containment may not hold. This implies that the eigenvalue systems are robust under taking closed equivariant subschemes. It allows computations of Hecke eigenvalues on smaller subschemes rather than the full variety.
The results extend to noncompact Shimura varieties, Ekedahl-Oort strata, length strata, and central leaves, provided the subscheme is closed or meets the basic locus. Theorem 3.3.2(d) handles closed substacks of G-Zip. Theorem 3.3.2(c) addresses subschemes meeting the basic locus. Corollary 3.3.3 confirms the result for Ekedahl-Oort and length strata. For central leaves, the Hasse invariant restricts to a section with C(x) as its nonvanishing locus. For a general nonclosed YK that does not meet the basic locus, the containment M(SK) ⇝H M(YK) may be strict. This connects the theory to the Newton stratification and other geometric decompositions of Shimura varieties. The existence of Hasse invariants for all strata is the unifying principle.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Remark 3.2.5 states that ω can be replaced by any ample, Hecke-equivariant line bundle in the proofs. The assumption G = Gc is noted as a technical condition that does not affect the main theorems' content. The going-down argument is modified from [GK19] by inserting the ideal sheaf filtration to handle non-locally-free conormal terms.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is proving that systems of Hecke eigenvalues on any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme of a compact abelian type Shimura variety at hyperspecial level are identical to those on the full variety, extending prior dimension-0 results to all dimensions. 2. The strongest evidence is the inductive construction of a smooth closed subscheme ZK from YK via length-stratum intersections and singularity removal, which admits a Hasse-invariant section serving as a bridge for both going-up and going-down arguments. 3. The future path involves developing the theory of toroidal compactifications for abelian type Shimura varieties and extending these results to non-hyperspecial levels and general p-adic integral models.

summary.title: Anomalous Hall effect from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling
summary.authors: Longju Yu, Hong Jian Zhao, Yurong Yang, Laurent Bellaiche, Yanming Ma
summary.field_subfield: Condensed Matter Physics / Spintronics and Topological Transport
summary.type_of_paper: Theoretical and computational (phenomenological theory + first-principles calculations)
summary.executive_summary: This paper establishes a phenomenological theory for the spontaneous and electric-field driven anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in crystalline magnets, specifically identifying nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling as the mechanism. By applying a group-theoretical symmetry analysis to the 122 magnetic point groups (MPGs), the authors show that both type-I and type-III MPGs host AHE components driven by uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric fields via nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. The Hall vector, defined as M = (σzy, σxz, σyx), transforms under MPG symmetry operations similarly to a magnetization vector, allowing for direct mapping. A key finding is that all electric-field driven AHE conductivities are reversible by reversing the magnetic order parameter (+L to -L), consistent with Onsager reciprocity. The theory identifies 90 MPGs (type-I and type-III) that support either spontaneous or electric-field driven AHE. To validate the theoretical predictions, first-principles calculations were performed on two representative compounds: Cr2O3 (¯3′m′ MPG, Néel temperature 307 K) and CoF2 (4′/mm′m MPG, Néel temperature 39 K). In Cr2O3, first-order responses to uni-axial fields yield σzy, σxz > 100 S/cm at 4 MV/cm, while a third-order response gives σyx < 20 S/cm via Ey. In CoF2, second-order responses dominate: bi-axial [Ex,Ez] and [Ey,Ez] yield σzy, σxz reaching 10 S/cm (total field 4 MV/cm), while uni-axial Ex or Ey yields σyx > 200 S/cm. The paper emphasizes that nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling offers an alternative avenue for probing magnetic orders in spintronic devices beyond linear mechanisms already exploited in the layer and electric Hall effects.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper establishes a phenomenological theory for the spontaneous and electric-field driven anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in crystalline magnets, specifically identifying nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling as the mechanism. By applying a group-theoretical symmetry analysis to the 122 magnetic point groups (MPGs), the authors show that both type-I and type-III MPGs host AHE components driven by uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric fields via nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. The Hall vector, defined as M = (σzy, σxz, σyx), transforms under MPG symmetry operations similarly to a magnetization vector, allowing for direct mapping. A key finding is that all electric-field driven AHE conductivities are reversible by reversing the magnetic order parameter (+L to -L), consistent with Onsager reciprocity. The theory identifies 90 MPGs (type-I and type-III) that support either spontaneous or electric-field driven AHE. To validate the theoretical predictions, first-principles calculations were performed on two representative compounds: Cr2O3 (¯3′m′ MPG, Néel temperature 307 K) and CoF2 (4′/mm′m MPG, Néel temperature 39 K). In Cr2O3, first-order responses to uni-axial fields yield σzy, σxz > 100 S/cm at 4 MV/cm, while a third-order response gives σyx < 20 S/cm via Ey. In CoF2, second-order responses dominate: bi-axial [Ex,Ez] and [Ey,Ez] yield σzy, σxz reaching 10 S/cm (total field 4 MV/cm), while uni-axial Ex or Ey yields σyx > 200 S/cm. The paper emphasizes that nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling offers an alternative avenue for probing magnetic orders in spintronic devices beyond linear mechanisms already exploited in the layer and electric Hall effects.

Research Context
The anomalous Hall effect (AHE) is a fundamental transport phenomenon where an applied voltage induces a transverse Hall current response, serving as a platform for exploring topology-related transport properties. AHE spontaneously occurs in ferromagnets or antiferromagnets with specific magnetic configurations, and even in antiferromagnets with weak or tiny magnetization. External fields capable of inducing magnetization should, in principle, induce AHE as well, making magnetoelectric coupling an interesting avenue. Recent studies demonstrate that gate voltage can induce AHE via linear magnetoelectric coupling, such as the layer Hall effect and electric Hall effect. However, an electric-field induced AHE arising from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling remains largely unexplored, representing a significant gap in the literature. The work addresses this gap by applying a group-theoretical approach to establish a phenomenological theory for spontaneous and electric-field driven AHE in crystalline materials.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is: what are the symmetry requirements and phenomenological expressions for spontaneous and electric-field driven AHE in crystalline magnets via nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling? The authors hypothesize that a wide spectrum of magnetic point groups will host AHE driven by uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric fields from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. A key prediction is that these electric-field driven anomalous Hall conductivities must be reversible by reversing the magnetic order parameter, governed by the Onsager reciprocity relation. The authors anticipate that Cr2O3 and CoF2, as representative materials belonging to the identified MPGs, will showcase the predicted AHE via first-principles calculations. The hypothesis is that the effective magnetic fields Bα_eff, expanded in powers of electric field, will govern the Bα-coupled AHE conductivities under various field configurations.

Methodological Details
The study uses a group-theoretical approach based on the 122 magnetic point groups categorized into three types: type-I (spatial operations only), type-II (time-reversal as independent operation), and type-III (time-reversal only in combination with spatial operations). Type-II MPGs are omitted because they host time-reversal symmetry T that forbids magnetization and electric field does not break T, so they cannot host electric-field induced AHE. A total of 90 type-I and type-III MPGs are identified as supporting spontaneous or electric-field driven AHE components, summarized in Table I. First-principles calculations are performed on two representative semiconductors: Cr2O3 with a Néel temperature of 307 K and CoF2 with a Néel temperature of 39 K. Both materials have no more than 10 ions per primitive cell, making the computational costs affordable. Cr2O3 belongs to the ¯3′m′ MPG, and CoF2 belongs to the 4′/mm′m MPG (P4′/mmm′ magnetic space group). The anomalous Hall conductivity σαβ is expressed through the Berry curvature formula involving the Levi-Civita symbol and Fermi-Dirac distribution. The Hall vector M = (σzy, σxz, σyx) is defined, establishing a correspondence between AHE conductivities and magnetization components.

Procedures And Architectures
The effective magnetic field Bα_eff is expanded in a power series of the electric field Eβ: Bα_eff = λα + Σ_β λαβEβ + Σ_βγ λαβγEβEγ + Σ_βγδ λαβγδEβEγEδ + ... The λ coefficients characterize spontaneous, first-order, second-order, and third-order magnetoelectric couplings, respectively. For each of the 90 MPGs, the symmetry operations are applied to (Mα, Eα) to derive the functional form of Bα_eff, detailed in Supplementary Tables 9, 10, and 11. For the ¯6m2.1 MPG, the explicit form is derived: Bx_eff = λxxxz(E²_x − E²_y)E_z + λxyzE_yE_z, B_y_eff = −2λxxxzE_xE_yE_z − λxyzE_xE_z, B_z_eff = λzxxxE_x(E²_x − 3E²_y). First-principles calculations compute the full Brillouin zone AHE conductivities σαβ as a function of chemical potential relative to the Fermi level. Electric field magnitudes of 4 MV/cm (or equivalent components totaling 4 MV/cm) are used to extract the linear, quadratic, and cubic responses in both Cr2O3 and CoF2. The calculations probe four AHE conductivity components in each material under different field configurations: Ex, Ey, [Ex,Ez], and [Ey,Ez] for Cr2O3; [Ex,Ez], [Ey,Ez], Ex, Ey for CoF2.

Key Results
The phenomenological theory identifies 90 magnetic point groups that host spontaneous or electric-field driven AHE, classified by uni-axial (red), bi-axial (bipartite), or tri-axial (tripartite) field drives. In Cr2O3 (¯3′m′ MPG), σzy driven by Ex and σxz driven by Ey are both larger than 100 S/cm at 4 MV/cm electric field via first-order response. The maximum value of σyx in Cr2O3 driven by Ey = 4 MV/cm via third-order response is less than 20 S/cm. In CoF2 (4′/mm′m MPG), σyx is driven by uni-axial E²_x or E²_y (second-order), while σzy and σxz come from bi-axial ExEz and EyEz responses, respectively. For CoF2, with total field 4 MV/cm (Ex=Ez=2√2 MV/cm or Ey=Ez=2√2 MV/cm), σzy and σxz reach 10 S/cm, while σyx from Ex=4 MV/cm or Ey=4 MV/cm exceeds 200 S/cm. Reversing the magnetic order parameter from +L to −L in both Cr2O3 and CoF2 reverses the sign of all electric-field induced AHE conductivities, confirming Equation (2). A quenching behavior occurs in 10 MPGs on the condition that bi-axial or tri-axial electric fields are along specific directions, where a conductivity component vanishes at specific field orientations. For the 4mm.1 MPG, σyx is induced by fourth-order magnetoelectric coupling E³_xE_y or E_xE³_y, but vanishes when |Ex| = |Ey| due to the (E²_x - E²_y) factor.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The Hall vector M transforms under MPG operations identically to the magnetization vector, implying that the AHE is fundamentally linked to the magnetic symmetry of the crystalline material. The Onsager reciprocity relation σαβ(+L) = σβα(-L) combined with the anti-symmetric σαβ = −σβα yields σαβ(+L) = −σαβ(−L), demonstrating that AHE sign reversal is a symmetry requirement. The work shows that AHE can be controlled and probed electrically without magnetic fields, opening a new route for data readout in non-volatile magnetic memory devices. The findings suggest that nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling is a broad and untapped resource for engineering exotic transport phenomena in magnetic semiconductors. The theoretical framework establishes a predictive pipeline: identify MPG → derive field-response → compute first-principles → select candidate materials.

Contradictions And Limitations
The quenching behavior in 10 MPGs for specific field orientations introduces a constraint on practical device design, as the AHE signal can be nullified at certain field ratios. The authors note that for the 4mm.1 MPG, they only show the E³_xE_y case in Table I and omit E_xE³_y to save space, though both contribute equally to σyx. The analysis is restricted to the intrinsic AHE mechanism; extrinsic mechanisms (skew scattering, side-jump) are not addressed. The first-principles calculations are limited to two candidate materials; a broader experimental validation across all identified MPGs is not provided. The paper does not report random seeds, specific k-point grids, or the exact functional used for DFT calculations in the main text.

Claims
Nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling can drive electric-field induced AHE in a broad range of magnetic point groups. 90 type-I and type-III MPGs were identified via group-theoretical analysis as hosting such AHE. The Hall vector M obeys the same symmetry rules as magnetization, making AHE theoretically predictable. Table I categorizes all 90 MPGs with specific field-drive color codes. Type-II MPGs do not host electric-field induced AHE because time-reversal cannot be broken by electric field. Quenching occurs in 10 MPGs for specific field directions, limiting the universality of the response. Practical device design must avoid quenched field configurations. The effect opens a new data readout channel in spintronics.
Electric-field induced AHE is fully reversible by reversing magnetic order, providing a signature for magnetic order identification. Onsager reciprocity combined with anti-symmetry of σαβ yields σαβ(+L) = −σαβ(−L). First-principles results for Cr2O3 (Figs. 2a,b,d) show induced conductivities with opposite signs for +L and −L. First-principles results for CoF2 (Figs. 2e,f,g,h) confirm the reversal of all computed AHE components upon order parameter flipping. The quenching in 10 MPGs shows that at specific field configurations, the signal is zero regardless of order parameter. Reversal of AHE can be used as an unambiguous probe of magnetic order (+L vs −L).
Cr2O3 and CoF2 are representative materials for electric-field induced AHE via nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. Cr2O3 shows σzy, σxz > 100 S/cm at 4 MV/cm through first-order response. CoF2 shows σyx > 200 S/cm at 4 MV/cm through second-order response. Both materials belong to the predicted MPGs (¯3′m′ and 4′/mm′m). Computational feasibility confirmed by no more than 10 ions per primitive cell. Only two materials are tested; this does not generalize to all 90 identified MPGs. Experimental verification of these specific conductivity values is not reported in the paper. These materials could serve as experimental testbeds for the proposed spintronic applications.

Data And Code Availability
The paper does not explicitly state whether the code or data used for first-principles calculations are available.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The resemblance between Figs. 2(a) and 2(b) for Cr2O3 is explained by the shared λxx coefficient in B_x_eff and B_y_eff for the ¯3′m′ MPG. The quenching behavior in 10 MPGs is systematically summarized in Supplementary Table 12. The quenching in 4mm.1 MPG is explicitly noted to occur only when |Ex| = |Ey|.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1(a) and (b) sketch the crystal and magnetic structures of Cr2O3 and CoF2 with magnetic moments shown by red arrows. Figure 2(a)-(d) depict AHE conductivities in Cr2O3 as a function of chemical potential driven by Ex, Ey, Ey, and Ez. Figure 2(e)-(h) show AHE conductivities in CoF2 driven by [Ex,Ez], [Ey,Ez], Ex, Ey. Table I lists the 90 type-I and type-III MPGs with AHE components coded by field drive type (uni-axial, bi-axial, tri-axial). Supplementary Table 9 shows explicit Bα_eff expressions for key MPGs like ¯6m2.1 and 4mm.1.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the group-theoretical mapping of the 122 magnetic point groups to AHE symmetries, establishing that nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling drives AHE in 90 MPGs. 2. The strongest evidence is the first-principles confirmation of both first-order (Cr2O3: >100 S/cm) and second-order (CoF2: >200 S/cm) electric-field driven AHE, with full sign reversal upon flipping magnetic order. 3. The future path lies in experimental verification of the predicted AHE in Cr2O3 and CoF2, and exploiting the nonlinear AHE for non-volatile memory data readout and magnetic order probing.

summary.title: Enabling Real-Time Conversations with Minimal Training Costs
summary.authors: Wang Xu, Shuo Wang, Weilin Zhao, Xu Han, Yukun Yan, Yudi Zhang, Zhe Tao, Zhiyuan Liu, Wanxiang Che
summary.field_subfield: Computer Science / Natural Language Processing - LLM Duplex Decoding
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces DUplex decOding (DUO), a channel-division-multiplexing decoding strategy that equips large language models with duplex capabilities—simultaneous input processing and output generation—with minimal training overhead. Conventional LLM-powered dialogue systems operate on a turn-based paradigm, precluding real-time interactive feedback, while existing duplex models (e.g., MiniCPM-Duplex) require substantial retraining due to time-division-multiplexing strategies that diverge from backbone model training. DUO addresses this by establishing parallel decoding channels: one autoregressively generating output while the other pre-fills key-value cache and predicts input tokens. Two state tokens (<1> for user query, <2> for no-query text) signal channel transitions. The model requires only 10K training samples (vs. 500K for MiniCPM-Duplex) and 400 training steps (vs. 10,000) on 8 A100 GPUs for 25 minutes (vs. 40 A100 GPUs for 36 hours). Human evaluation across 40 multi-turn dialogue sessions with three evaluators demonstrates that MiniCPM-Duo significantly outperforms MiniCPM-Duplex in responsiveness and human-likeness, while maintaining comparable factuality and faithfulness. Standard benchmark comparisons across CMMLU, MMLU, HumanEval, etc., show comparable general-capability retention with Minimal training. The method is implemented via KV-cache management and Flex-Attention, adding no forward passes beyond standard decoding. A case study illustrates adaptive behavior during user interruption and non-awakening scenarios. The authors conclude that DUO provides a low-cost path to real-time, fluid human-AI interaction without compromising general model performance.
