Conventional LLM-powered dialogue systems operate on a turn-based paradigm, precluding real-time interactive feedback, while existing duplex models (e.g., MiniCPM-Duplex) require substantial retraining due to time-division-multiplexing strategies that diverge from backbone model training. DUO addresses this by establishing parallel decoding channels: one autoregressively generating output while the other pre-fills key-value cache and predicts input tokens. Two state tokens (<1> for user query, <2> for no-query text) signal channel transitions. The model requires only 10K training samples (vs. 500K for MiniCPM-Duplex) and 400 training steps (vs. 10,000) on 8 A100 GPUs for 25 minutes (vs. 40 A100 GPUs for 36 hours). Human evaluation across 40 multi-turn dialogue sessions with three evaluators demonstrates that MiniCPM-Duo significantly outperforms MiniCPM-Duplex in responsiveness and human-likeness, while maintaining comparable factuality and faithfulness. Standard benchmark comparisons across CMMLU, MMLU, HumanEval, etc., show comparable general-capability retention with Minimal training. The method is implemented via KV-cache management and Flex-Attention, adding no forward passes beyond standard decoding. A case study illustrates adaptive behavior during user interruption and non-awakening scenarios. The authors conclude that DUO provides a low-cost path to real-time, fluid human-AI interaction without compromising general model performance.

Research Context
Conventional LLM-powered dialogue systems operate on a turn-based paradigm that precludes real-time interactive feedback. Human conversations involve simultaneous listening and thinking, which current systems lack. Prior duplex models like MiniCPM-Duplex use a time-division-multiplexing strategy that requires substantial computational resources for retraining. The designed procedure of existing duplex methods diverges substantially from the backbone model, making fine-tuning costly. MiniCPM-Duplex requires approximately 5,000K samples for training, posing a significant data and computation overhead.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how to equip LLMs with duplex capabilities—simultaneous input preprocessing and output generation—while minimizing additional training costs. The authors hypothesize that a channel-division-multiplexing decoding strategy, as opposed to time-division, will enable duplex interaction without substantial retraining. The model is expected to handle two specific interactive scenarios: non-awakening interaction (filtering non-query input) and interruption interaction (pausing generation to address a new query). The hypothesis predicts that state tokens can effectively signal whether a query should be addressed or ignored with minimal additional training. The authors predict that MiniCPM-Duo will significantly enhance naturalness and human-likeness of user-AI interactions over the baseline.

Methodological Details
The foundation model used is MiniCPM-2.4B, following Zhang et al. (2024). The DUO training dataset comprises 10K samples, significantly smaller than the 500K samples used for MiniCPM-Duplex. The DUO dataset was constructed from Duplex-UltraChat, adapted from a time-division format to a standard turn-based format. State tokens <1> and <2> were appended to indicate whether to respond to a query. Non-query text for non-awakening scenarios was generated using ChatGPT with optimized prompts. Human evaluation was conducted with three participants, each holding a Bachelor's degree. 40 multi-turn dialogue sessions were recorded through a voice-based interactive demo. Speech-to-text and text-to-speech conversions used Google's cloud ASR and TTS APIs.

Procedures And Architectures
DUO employs a channel-division-multiplexing decoding strategy with parallel decoding of queries and responses. The input channel pre-fills the key-value cache and predicts the next tokens cyclically. The output channel generates new tokens autoregressively in each processing cycle. Tokens generated by input and output channels do not attend to each other despite sharing prefix tokens. The attention mask is modified to prevent cross-channel attention while preserving language modeling in each channel. State token <1> denotes a user query; the output channel is suspended and the input channel transitions to output. State token <2> denotes no-query text; the model continues responding to the original query. DUO is implemented using Flex-Attention for non-standard attention mechanisms. The input channel predicted tokens α are set to 4. DUO does not increase the number of forward passes compared to standard decoding.

Key Results
MiniCPM-Duo was trained for 400 steps on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for about 25 minutes. In contrast, MiniCPM-Duplex required 10,000 steps on 40 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for 36 hours. The DUO learning rate was 1e-5 with a constant scheduler and a batch size of 112. In CMMLU, MiniCPM-Duo achieved 50.66 vs. MiniCPM-Duplex 48.53 and MiniCPM 51.30. In MMLU, MiniCPM-Duo scored 53.13 vs. MiniCPM-Duplex 53.76 and MiniCPM 53.45. In HumanEval, MiniCPM-Duo scored 51.83 vs. MiniCPM-Duplex 49.39 and MiniCPM 50.00. In HellaSwag, MiniCPM-Duo scored 59.78 vs. MiniCPM-Duplex 50.85 and MiniCPM 61.40. Figure 2 shows MiniCPM-Duo wins in responsiveness and human-likeness, with ties in factuality and faithfulness. MiniCPM-Duplex trained on the same 10K scale as DUO showed performance drop, indicating poor duplex capability when inadequately trained.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The channel-division-multiplexing approach preserves the model's original capabilities more than time-division-multiplexing. The data format remains largely unchanged, requiring only the addition of state tokens. DUO enables simultaneous autoregressive generation and input preprocessing without increased forward passes. The results imply that duplex capabilities can be retrofitted to LLMs via decoding modification rather than architectural retraining.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study primarily focused on language models, limiting generalizability to other domains. Multimodal testing was not performed; the authors aim to extend to multimodal in future research. The DUO approach is inherently designed for versatility but current experiments do not validate multimodal adaptation. MiniCPM-Duplex trained on the 10K dataset showed poor duplex capability, yet the paper doesn't quantify the extent of the failure.

Claims
DUO enables real-time duplex interaction with minimal training costs compared to time-division approaches. DUO requires only 400 steps on 8 A100 GPUs (25 mins) vs. 10,000 steps on 40 A100 GPUs (36 hours) for the baseline. The DUO dataset is 10K samples vs. 500K samples for MiniCPM-Duplex. DUO does not increase forward passes relative to standard decoding. MiniCPM-Duplex trained on the 10K dataset shows performance drop, indicating some training is still necessary for duplex functionality. Low-cost duplex decoding can be applied to various LLMs without extensive infrastructure.
MiniCPM-Duo outperforms MiniCPM-Duplex in responsiveness and human-likeness in human evaluation. Figure 2 explicitly shows MiniCPM-Duo wins in responsiveness and human-likeness. The case study in Figure 3 demonstrates adaptive behavior during user interruption and silence. MiniCPM-Duo does not outperform MiniCPM-Duplex on all metrics; factuality and faithfulness are marked as ties. In MMLU, MiniCPM-Duo (53.13) is lower than both MiniCPM-Duplex (53.76) and MiniCPM (53.45). Responsiveness is the primary benefit of channel-division-multiplexing over time-division.

Data And Code Availability
The authors refer to the repository for the decoding strategy implementation.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
MiniCPM-Duplex trained on the same 10K scale dataset as DUO was tested with identical hyperparameters. The results show performances drop, indicating inadequately trained MiniCPM-Duplex has poor duplex capability.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the channel-based parallel decoding architecture, showing the input/output channel split and the attention mask structure. Figure 2 presents the human evaluation comparison across five criteria: responsiveness, human-likeness, factuality, faithfulness, and overall satisfaction. Figure 3 is a case study showing user query, state token prediction, and adaptive generation during interruption. Table 1 reports benchmark performance on CMMLU, MMLU, BBH, HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, ARC-e, ARC-c, and HellaSwag.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is DUO, a channel-division-multiplexing decoding strategy enabling parallel input/output processing with only 10K training samples and 400 steps. 2. The strongest evidence is the human evaluation showing MiniCPM-Duo wins in responsiveness and human-likeness over MiniCPM-Duplex, confirmed by the case study. 3. The future path lies in extending DUO to multimodal settings where input tokens are encoder-extracted features from various modalities.

summary.title: Spontaneous scalarization of Bardeen black holes
summary.authors: Lina Zhang, Qiyuan Pan, Yun Soo Myung, De-Cheng Zou
summary.field_subfield: Gravitational Physics / General Relativity and Quantum Cosmology
summary.executive_summary: This paper investigates the spontaneous scalarization of Bardeen black holes within the framework of Einstein-nonlinear electrodynamics theory coupled with a scalar field. Bardeen black holes are regular, spherically symmetric black hole solutions free of singularities, initially proposed by Bardeen. The authors examine two scalar coupling forms: quadratic (f(φ) = 1 - αφ²) and exponential (f(φ) = e^-αφ²). The central finding is the existence of infinite (n = 0, 1, 2, ···) branches of scalarized charged black holes (SCBHs) with magnetic charge g, triggered by a tachyonic instability of the unscalarized Bardeen solution. Specifically, the n = 0 branch of SCBHs is found for coupling parameters α ≥ α_n=0(g), where α_n=0(g) is the threshold of tachyonic instability. For representative magnetic charge g = 0.2 and mass M = 0.5, the threshold is α_th(g) = 12.712. The n = 0 branch is shown to be stable against radial perturbations for both quadratic and exponential couplings, rendering it an end point of the Bardeen black hole and opening pathways for observational implications. Other branches (n ≠ 0) are conjectured to be unstable, following established results in Einstein-Maxwell-scalar theory. The work demonstrates that the stability of the n = 0 branch is independent of the magnetic charge g, and that the bifurcation point increases as the magnetic charge decreases, making scalarization harder to realize for smaller charges.

claims.description: Bardeen black holes undergo spontaneous scalarization, producing infinite branches of scalarized charged black holes.
The n = 0 branch of SCBHs is stable against radial perturbations for both quadratic and exponential scalar couplings.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates the spontaneous scalarization of Bardeen black holes within the framework of Einstein-nonlinear electrodynamics theory coupled with a scalar field. Bardeen black holes are regular, spherically symmetric black hole solutions free of singularities, initially proposed by Bardeen. The authors examine two scalar coupling forms: quadratic (f(φ) = 1 - αφ²) and exponential (f(φ) = e^-αφ²). The central finding is the existence of infinite (n = 0, 1, 2, ···) branches of scalarized charged black holes (SCBHs) with magnetic charge g, triggered by a tachyonic instability of the unscalarized Bardeen solution. Specifically, the n = 0 branch of SCBHs is found for coupling parameters α ≥ α_n=0(g), where α_n=0(g) is the threshold of tachyonic instability. For representative magnetic charge g = 0.2 and mass M = 0.5, the threshold is α_th(g) = 12.712. The n = 0 branch is shown to be stable against radial perturbations for both quadratic and exponential couplings, rendering it an end point of the Bardeen black hole and opening pathways for observational implications. Other branches (n ≠ 0) are conjectured to be unstable, following established results in Einstein-Maxwell-scalar theory. The work demonstrates that the stability of the n = 0 branch is independent of the magnetic charge g, and that the bifurcation point increases as the magnetic charge decreases, making scalarization harder to realize for smaller charges.

Research Context
Spontaneous scalarization is a dynamic process imparting scalar hair to black holes without changing weak-field predictions. This phenomenon is a strong gravity phase transition caused by tachyonic instability from nonminimal coupling. Bardeen proposed the first regular black hole solution which is spherically symmetric and free of singularities. In general relativity, singularity theorems suggest singularities are inevitable inside black holes. Regular black holes are of great interest for understanding fundamental issues including singularities and nonlinear electrodynamics. The physical source of Bardeen black holes was initially unclear, later attributed to nonlinear electromagnetic sources.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether Bardeen black holes undergo spontaneous scalarization under quadratic and exponential scalar couplings. The authors hypothesize that a tachyonic instability triggers the formation of scalarized charged black holes from the Bardeen background. It is predicted that the n = 0 branch of SCBHs exists for α ≥ α_n=0(g) and is stable against radial perturbations. The study aims to identify bifurcation points for infinite (n = 0, 1, 2, ···) branches and verify the stability of the fundamental branch. The authors also investigate if the n = 0 branch remains stable for both quadratic and exponential coupling forms.

Methodological Details
The theory is Einstein-nonlinear electrodynamics coupled with a scalar field with coupling function f(φ). The nonlinear function L(F) is defined with parameter s = |g|² / M, where g is magnetic charge and M is mass. The Bardeen black hole metric is f(r) = 1 - 2Mr² / (r² + g²)^(3/2) with a magnetic field F_θφ = g sin θ. Two coupling forms are used: quadratic f(φ) = 1 - αφ² and exponential f(φ) = e^-αφ². The tachyonic instability is assessed via the linearized Klein-Gordon equation for a perturbed scalar δφ. For the analysis, the s(l = 0)-mode is chosen as the only permissible mode for scalar perturbations. Three representative magnetic charges g = 0.175, 0.200, and 0.250 are used for the stability and bifurcation analysis. The mass is fixed at M = 0.5 for the numerical solutions and stability analysis.

Procedures And Architectures
The linearized scalar equation is rewritten in tortoise coordinates r* = ∫dr/f(r) to obtain a Schrödinger-type equation. The scalar potential V(r) is derived and the negative region near the horizon is observed as a signal of instability. The stability threshold α_th(g) is determined by numerically solving for a growing mode e^Ωt with ingoing-outgoing boundary conditions. For the SCBH numerical solution, a metric ansatz N(r) = 1 - 2m(r)/r, δ(r), and φ(r) ≠ 0 is assumed. Three coupled differential equations for {δ(r), m(r), φ(r)} are derived from the Einstein-scalar-nonlinear electrodynamics equations. Near-horizon approximations for m(r), δ(r), and φ(r) are determined and matched with asymptotic far-region solutions. The n = 0 branch of SCBHs is constructed numerically for α values just above the bifurcation point. Stability of the SCBH is analyzed by introducing radial perturbations and solving the corresponding Schrödinger equation for the scalar mode. The stability condition requires the frequency Ω to be negative for the decaying mode, indicating no growing modes.

Key Results
The tachyonic instability threshold α_th(g) is found to be α_th(0.175) = 17.338, α_th(0.200) = 12.712, and α_th(0.250) = 7.251. For g = 0.2, the first three bifurcation points (α_n) are identified as α_{n=0} ≈ 12.712, α_{n=1} ≈ 75.114, and α_{n=2} ≈ 190.590. The n = 0 branch of SCBHs is found for α = 13.048 (quadratic coupling) and α = 13.667 (exponential coupling) at g = 0.2. For the quadratic coupling, the SCBH horizon at ln r = -0.0683 is very close to the Bardeen horizon at ln r = -0.0671. The n = 0 branch is stable against l = 0 scalar perturbations for all three magnetic charges g = 0.175, 0.200, 0.250 for both coupling forms. The negative Ω values obtained in Fig. 6 confirm the stability of the n = 0 branch for both quadratic and exponential couplings. The bifurcation point α_{n=0}(g) decreases as g increases, meaning scalarization becomes harder for smaller magnetic charges. All non-zero branches (n ≠ 0) are expected to be unstable against radial perturbations.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The n = 0 branch of SCBHs is considered an end point of the Bardeen black hole, making observational implications possible. The infinite branches (n = 0, 1, 2, ···) of SCBHs arise because all are found by spontaneous scalarization from the same Bardeen background. The similarity of potentials between quadratic and exponential couplings suggests the scalarization mechanism is robust to the specific coupling form. The violation of the strong energy condition at the center of the Bardeen metric supports its status as a regular black hole. The result that stability is independent of g extends the scalarization theorem to a broader class of Bardeen black holes.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors note that a negative potential region in V(r) near the horizon does not always imply instability, but is used as a proxy since deriving the instability condition is challenging. The full analysis is limited to the l = 0 (s-mode) perturbation, neglecting all higher angular momentum modes. Stability of n ≠ 0 branches is conjectured based on references rather than explicitly proven in this work. The authors do not report a systematic study over a wide range of masses M; the analysis is performed at the fixed value M = 0.5. Random seeds, convergence thresholds, and specific numerical methods for the shooting/matching procedure are not detailed.

Claims
Bardeen black holes undergo spontaneous scalarization, producing infinite branches of scalarized charged black holes. The bifurcations at α ≈ 12.712, 75.114, and 190.590 correspond to the first three branches. The linearized scalar equation yields a discrete set of α_n(g) values for different n. The n = 0 branch is found for any α ≥ α_{n=0}(g) for both quadratic and exponential couplings. The authors admit that the negative potential region is only a conjecture for instability and not always true. This establishes Bardeen black holes as a new testing ground for scalarization phenomena. Observational signatures may arise from the scalar hair of the n = 0 branch.
The n = 0 branch of SCBHs is stable against radial perturbations for both quadratic and exponential scalar couplings. Numerical solution of the exponential Schrödinger equation yields negative Ω for all tested g. The potential V_SCBH exhibits a large positive region outside the horizon for exponential coupling, suggesting stability. Stability is shown to be independent of the magnetic charge g = 0.175, 0.200, 0.250. The potentials still contain small negative regions near the horizon, though these do not induce instability. The n = 0 branch is a physical end point of the Bardeen black hole solution. The stability makes the n = 0 branch a viable candidate for gravitational wave and electromagnetic observations.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The stability is tested across three different magnetic charges g = 0.175, 0.200, 0.250, showing independence from g. Two different coupling forms (quadratic and exponential) are compared, with similar potential structures and stability outcomes. The n ≠ 0 branches are noted as likely unstable based on analogous results in other scalar-matter theories.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the α-dependent potential V(r, α, g) and plots for three α values, identifying the negative region as an instability signal. Figure 2 shows the curves of Ω in e^Ωt vs α, determining the instability thresholds for g = 0.175, 0.200, 0.250. Figure 3 plots the first three static perturbed scalar solutions ϕ(z) with zero-node counts n = 0, 1, 2. Figure 4 displays SCBH solutions for both quadratic and exponential couplings, comparing metric functions δ(r), N(r), ϕ(r) with the Bardeen f(r). Figure 5 shows the scalar potentials V_SCBH for l = 0 perturbations around the n = 0 branch for quadratic and exponential couplings. Figure 6 shows the negative Ω as a function of α for three g values, with dotted curves starting from α_n=0 and red lines denoting unstable Bardeen black holes.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that Bardeen black holes undergo spontaneous scalarization with infinite branches, the n = 0 branch of which is stable for both quadratic and exponential couplings. 2. The strongest evidence is the numerical stability result (Ω < 0) across three magnetic charges for both coupling forms, confirming that the n = 0 branch is the physical end point. 3. The future path involves investigating observational signatures of the n = 0 branch, analyzing n ≠ 0 branches, and extending the analysis to varying mass M and higher angular momentum modes.

summary.title: Three-dimensional topological valley photonics
summary.authors: Wenhao Li, Qiaolu Chen, Ning Han, Xinrui Li, Fujia Chen, Junyao Wu, Yuang Pan, Yudong Ren, Hongsheng Chen, Haoran Xue, Yihao Yang
summary.field_subfield: Photonics / Topological Photonics
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces and experimentally demonstrates a three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics framework characterized by a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley-contrasting physics. The authors extend the 2D valley photonics paradigm—which relies on a single pair of valleys with scalar Chern numbers—to a 3D system featuring triple pairs of valleys at the corners of the 3D Brillouin zone, each characterized by a valley Chern vector (VCV). The 3D photonic crystal structure is a diamond-like lattice with lattice constant a = 20 mm, composed of perfect electric conductor (PEC) spheres (diameters D1 and D2) connected by rods of diameters B1 = 2.4 mm and B2 = 1.2 mm. Inversion symmetry breaking (∆D = |D1 − D2| ≠ 0) gaps out nodal lines to form a complete photonic bandgap. The authors experimentally verify the vectorial nature of the valley states by selectively exciting and observing chiral Bloch modes using a vectorial chiral source array, measuring outcoupling directions at 13.8 GHz. They further demonstrate robust, canalized valley surface states on all sample surfaces (100), (010), and (001), showing diffractionless propagation along the +y direction for the Wx− valley. A key theoretical finding is the right-hand-thumb rule, which intrinsically links the direction of the valley Chern vectors to the circulating direction of the valley surface states. The work reveals potential applications in 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging, extending the concept to higher frequencies including terahertz and optical ranges.

claims.description: The 3D VPC exhibits vectorial valley-contrasting physics characterized by triple pairs of valleys with valley Chern vectors.
Robust canalized valley surface states exist on all surfaces of the 3D VPC shape and obey the right-hand-thumb rule.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces and experimentally demonstrates a three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics framework characterized by a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley-contrasting physics. The authors extend the 2D valley photonics paradigm—which relies on a single pair of valleys with scalar Chern numbers—to a 3D system featuring triple pairs of valleys at the corners of the 3D Brillouin zone, each characterized by a valley Chern vector (VCV). The 3D photonic crystal structure is a diamond-like lattice with lattice constant a = 20 mm, composed of perfect electric conductor (PEC) spheres (diameters D1 and D2) connected by rods of diameters B1 = 2.4 mm and B2 = 1.2 mm. Inversion symmetry breaking (∆D = |D1 − D2| ≠ 0) gaps out nodal lines to form a complete photonic bandgap. The authors experimentally verify the vectorial nature of the valley states by selectively exciting and observing chiral Bloch modes using a vectorial chiral source array, measuring outcoupling directions at 13.8 GHz. They further demonstrate robust, canalized valley surface states on all sample surfaces (100), (010), and (001), showing diffractionless propagation along the +y direction for the Wx− valley. A key theoretical finding is the right-hand-thumb rule, which intrinsically links the direction of the valley Chern vectors to the circulating direction of the valley surface states. The work reveals potential applications in 3D waveguiding, directional radiation, and imaging, extending the concept to higher frequencies including terahertz and optical ranges.

Research Context
Previous valley photonics was limited to 2D systems, where photonic confinement along the third dimension was obtained nontopologically. In 2D, a single pair of valleys at the corners of the Brillouin zone was described by two-band massive Dirac models with opposite scalar Berry curvature. These 2D valley systems supported single-polarization valley states, suffered from out-of-plane losses, and could only manipulate light in planar geometries. Complete control of light flow required a complete photonic bandgap, which remained a significant challenge. Existing 3D topological photonic insulators could only support surface states on certain surfaces, not all surfaces simultaneously.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether valley photonics can be extended to 3D with a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley-contrasting physics. The authors hypothesize that a 3D model involving triple pairs of valleys at the corners of the 3D Brillouin zone would exhibit vectorial band geometric quantities. They predict that the valley Chern vectors and the circulating propagation direction of surface states are intrinsically governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. The study aims to demonstrate canalized valley surface states on all surfaces of a 3D sample, a capability not previously achieved by any 3D photonic topological insulator. A vectorial chiral source array would allow selective excitation of individual valley states, verifiable by measuring outcoupling directions.

Methodological Details
The system is a 3D photonic crystal with lattice constant a = 20 mm and lattice vectors a1 = (a/2, a/2, 0), a2 = (0, a/2, a/2), and a3 = (a/2, 0, a/2). The structure is a diamond-like lattice where carbon atoms and bonds are replaced by perfect electric conductor (PEC) spheres and rods. Each face-centered-cubic (fcc) cell contains two spheres with diameters D1 and D2, with nearest-neighbor rods B1 = 2.4 mm and next-nearest-neighbor rods B2 = 1.2 mm. The configuration with D1 = 6.4 mm and D2 = 3.6 mm (ΔD ≠ 0) breaks inversion symmetry to form the complete photonic bandgap. The k · p effective Hamiltonian near each valley uses Pauli matrices σx,y,z and mass term m = (ω1 − ω2)/2. The vectorial chiral source array consists of four sources at relative positions (0,0,0), (−a/2, −a/2, 0), (−a/2, 0, −a/2), and (0, −a/2, −a/2). For the (001) surface modification, a metallic plate covers the surface with hole interval a/2. Boundary condition parameters are set to h = 6.25 mm and D3 = 4 mm for the outmost metallic sphere. Surface state propagation experiments are measured at 13.8 GHz for selective excitation and at 14.6 GHz for canalization mapping.

Procedures And Architectures
The k · p method is used to derive the effective Hamiltonian near each valley: H = ± [vD q · σ + m σ_z]. The vectorial chiral source array imposes phase winding on x-y, y-z, and x-z planes with four sources of relative phase delays. For Wy−, source phases are (0, π/2, π, 3π/2) and for Wy+, (0, −π/2, −π, −3π/2), forming clockwise or counterclockwise phase winding. Selective excitation of valley states is verified by measuring outcoupling fields in the y-z plane. The valley Chern vector is calculated by integrating Berry curvature around each valley: C_v = (∫Ωq dS / 2π). The boundary condition for topological surface states requires θ_V = π/2, achieved by the metallic plate and specific h and D3 values. Surface transmission is measured across the bandgap, and Fourier-transformed spectrums are obtained along L4–Wx−–L1. Right-hand-thumb rule verification involves positioning the source at the (001) surface center and measuring field distributions on (001) and (010) surfaces.

Key Results
At ΔD = 0, the crystal hosts nodal lines along Wα±–X (α = x, y, z) with six valley momenta: (±π/a, 2π/a, 0), (0, ±π/a, 2π/a), and (2π/a, 0, ±π/a). At ΔD ≠ 0, the nodal line degeneracies are gapped out to form a complete photonic bandgap. Eigenstates at Wz± display typical vortex profiles with opposite chirality as required by time-reversal symmetry. Measured outcoupling directions at 13.8 GHz are −32.9° for clockwise (Wy−) and +32.9° for counterclockwise (Wy+), with 0° for the X state. The valley Chern vectors are calculated as (±1/2, 0, 0), (0, ±1/2, 0), and (0, 0, ±1/2) for Wx±, Wy±, and Wz± respectively. Surface transmission maintains high values within the complete photonic bandgap, while bulk transmission is substantially lower. A nearly-linear surface dispersion is observed in the bandgap around the Wx− valley. Surface states propagate diffractionlessly along the +y direction, corresponding to the Wx− valley, with a flat isofrequency contour. At the sharp bend, the Wx− surface state smoothly passes from (001) to (010) with high transmission, changing direction to −z. Fourier transform analysis confirms only surface states around Wx− are excited on both surfaces, revealing valley-locking.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The vectorial nature of 3D valley states goes beyond binary valley degree of freedom and scalar valley-contrasting physics of 2D. The right-hand-thumb rule is an intrinsic relation between VCVs and valley surface states, both determined by the bulk Hamiltonian. Channelization is an intrinsic property of the surface states due to the flat isofrequency contour, independent of wavevector vertical to propagation. The canalized surface states offer promising opportunities for imaging and lensing. The highly directional outcoupling from valley states provides a mechanism for creating narrow-beam antennae. The 3D valley photonics concept is readily extendable to higher frequencies, including terahertz and optical ranges, using all-dielectric diamond-like crystals.

Contradictions And Limitations
The experiments were demonstrated at lower microwave frequencies (13.8 and 14.6 GHz); the full frequency range capability is not experimentally verified. The paper does not report the exact random seeds or specific fabrication tolerances beyond the nominal h and D3 values. The outcoupling direction for X states (0°) coexists with valley states at the same frequency, potentially complicating selective excitation. The 3D photonic crystal uses PEC materials, and the extension to all-dielectric crystals is proposed but not experimentally demonstrated.

Claims
The 3D VPC exhibits vectorial valley-contrasting physics characterized by triple pairs of valleys with valley Chern vectors. The k · p Hamiltonian with three Pauli matrices describes the near-valley physics. Berry curvature at Wz± has nonzero component only in the kx-ky plane. Valley Chern vectors are computed as (±1/2, 0, 0), (0, ±1/2, 0), and (0, 0, ±1/2). The scalar components (e.g., 0) mean the vectorial nature is only present in specific directions. This enables control of angular momentum of light through orbital moments.
Robust canalized valley surface states exist on all surfaces of the 3D VPC shape and obey the right-hand-thumb rule. High surface transmission vs low bulk transmission confirms surface states. Measured field distribution shows propagation along +y without scattering at the bend. Fourier transform shows valley-locking to Wx− on both (001) and (010) surfaces. The VCV (−1/2, 0, 0) and clockwise circulation on y-z plane satisfy the right-hand-thumb rule. Only the Wx− valley was explicitly demonstrated in the bend experiment; other valley directions are less detailed. Enables 3D waveguiding and lensing without intervalley scattering.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Next-nearest-neighbor rods (B2 = 1.2 mm) were added to suppress high-order modes and ensure clean bandstructure. The metallic plate features perforations with hole interval a/2 for source/probe insertion. The boundary condition verification relies on specific h = 6.25 mm and D3 = 4 mm parameters.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1(a) shows the cubic cell with two sublattices, lattice vectors a1, a2, a3, and the diamond-like metallic mesh. Figure 1(b) displays the band structure for ΔD = 0 (D1 = D2 = 5 mm) and ΔD ≠ 0 (D1 = 6.4 mm, D2 = 3.6 mm). Figure 1(c) shows the 3D BZ of the fcc unit cell with six valley positions and nodal lines. Figure 1(d) displays simulated eigenstates with Poynting vector arrows and phase colors on the (001) surface. Figure 1(e) shows simulated Berry curvature components of the first band at Wz±. Figure 2(a) illustrates the vectorial chiral source array with four sources and phase winding. Figure 2(b) provides a momentum-space analysis showing outcoupling directions of Wy−, X, and Wy+. Figure 2(d) shows measured electric field distributions at −32.9°, 0°, and +32.9°. Figure 2(e) displays measured far-field radiation patterns at Wy−, X, and Wy+. Figure 3(a) shows the (001) surface covered by a metallic plate with parameters h and D3. Figure 3(e) shows normalized measured transmission with bulk bandgap shadowed. Figure 3(g) displays measured and simulated surface dispersion around Wx− valley. Figure 3(h) shows isofrequency contours at 14.6 GHz with the dashed square representing the first BZ. Figure 4(a) illustrates the right-hand-thumb rule with VCV directions and propagation loops. Figure 4(b) shows field distributions before (#1) and after (#2) the bend. Figure 4(d) displays measured isofrequency contours before and after bend at 14.6 GHz.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the development of 3D topological valley photonics with a complete photonic bandgap and triple-pair vectorial valleys, extending 2D valley photonics to three dimensions. 2. The strongest evidence is the experimental observation of canalized valley surface states on all surfaces, the selective excitation of individual valley states at 13.8 GHz with measured outcoupling at ±32.9°, and the confirmation of the right-hand-thumb rule. 3. The future path includes extending the 3D valley photonics concept to higher frequencies (terahertz and optical) using all-dielectric diamond-like 3D photonic crystals, with applications in 3D waveguiding, directional antennas, and imaging.

summary.title: From Words to Wheels: Automated Style-Customized Policy Generation for Autonomous Driving
summary.authors: Xu Han, Xianda Chen, Zhenghan Cai, Pinlong Cai, Meixin Zhu, Xiaowen Chu
summary.field_subfield: Autonomous Driving / Reinforcement Learning / Natural Language Processing
summary.executive_summary: Words2Wheels is a framework designed to automatically generate style-customized driving policies for autonomous vehicles based on natural language user commands. Current autonomous driving systems face limitations in delivering command-based driving styles, often relying on predefined styles requiring expert input or data-driven methods (IRL) that struggle with style matching in Robotaxi scenarios and cannot generalize to new commands. Words2Wheels addresses these by using a Style-Customized Reward Function—generated via Large Language Models (LLMs) with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)—to map natural language commands to driving policies without requiring prior driving data. The framework comprises three core components: (1) Automated Policy Customization, which uses an LLM to select or generate Style Rewards from a database, (2) a Driving Style Database storing Style Rewards (code), Style Policies (pre-trained networks), and statistical data, and (3) a Statistical Evaluation module that uses a reserved test dataset to compare policy statistics against natural driving behavior. The system is tested in a car-following scenario using the HighD dataset with a 4K drone-captured roadway. The authors categorized user commands into three levels of directness (Level I: Direct, Level II: Indirect with strong hints, Level III: Indirect with mild hints). In human-in-the-loop comparisons against the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM) with 10 licensed drivers across 1,000 events, Words2Wheels was preferred in 72% of cases, IDM in 9.2%, and they were tied in 18.8%. The framework demonstrated 97.5% accuracy in rational analysis, 95% in decision-making, 92.5% in retrieval, and 85% in generation across 40 commands. A fuzzy memory function was validated with high recall (all but one case). The system uses GPT-4o-2024-08-06 as the base LLM, PPO for RL training, and 15% of the HighD data reserved as a test set. The approach supports zero-shot generalization to new commands without user driving data, bridging the gap between natural language preferences and concrete driving behavior.

Current autonomous driving systems face limitations in delivering command-based driving styles, often relying on predefined styles requiring expert input or data-driven methods (IRL) that struggle with style matching in Robotaxi scenarios and cannot generalize to new commands. Words2Wheels addresses these by using a Style-Customized Reward Function—generated via Large Language Models (LLMs) with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)—to map natural language commands to driving policies without requiring prior driving data. The framework comprises three core components: (1) Automated Policy Customization, which uses an LLM to select or generate Style Rewards from a database, (2) a Driving Style Database storing Style Rewards (code), Style Policies (pre-trained networks), and statistical data, and (3) a Statistical Evaluation module that uses a reserved test dataset to compare policy statistics against natural driving behavior. The system is tested in a car-following scenario using the HighD dataset with a 4K drone-captured roadway. The authors categorized user commands into three levels of directness (Level I: Direct, Level II: Indirect with strong hints, Level III: Indirect with mild hints). In human-in-the-loop comparisons against the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM) with 10 licensed drivers across 1,000 events, Words2Wheels was preferred in 72% of cases, IDM in 9.2%, and they were tied in 18.8%. The framework demonstrated 97.5% accuracy in rational analysis, 95% in decision-making, 92.5% in retrieval, and 85% in generation across 40 commands. A fuzzy memory function was validated with high recall (all but one case). The system uses GPT-4o-2024-08-06 as the base LLM, PPO for RL training, and 15% of the HighD data reserved as a test set. The approach supports zero-shot generalization to new commands without user driving data, bridging the gap between natural language preferences and concrete driving behavior.

Research Context
The uniform driving style of current autonomous vehicles (AVs) is a key criticism of the user experience. For instance, 52.46% of AVs involved in crashes were rear-ended, a rate 1.6 times that of conventional vehicles, emphasizing the need for gentler braking. Early approaches to driving style relied heavily on classification or calibration of predefined styles or patterns. These manually designed styles depend heavily on expert input, making the process cumbersome and requiring frequent adjustments. Data-driven approaches using clustering and Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) derive policies from natural driving behavior. IRL-based methods require a small amount of driving behavior data to match a specific style, which is difficult to obtain in Robotaxi scenarios. The inability to prioritize driving style metrics according to user preferences restricts style matching effectiveness. These methods are limited to selecting from existing styles and cannot customize based on user needs, creating a generalization problem. Recent foundation model work for user instructions adjusts specific behaviors like speed and lane changes but falls short at the overall style level. Foundation model approaches often involve the model in most decision loops, raising reliability and efficiency concerns.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether driving policies can be automatically customized to align with natural language user commands without prior driving data. The authors hypothesize that a Style-Customized Reward Function can bridge user input and a Style-Customized Driving Policy as a policy index in Reinforcement Learning. The hypothesis is that LLM-powered reward design, combined with a Driving Style Database and RAG, enables efficient retrieval, adaptation, and generalization of driving styles. The Statistical Evaluation module is hypothesized to ensure alignment with user preferences by comparing policy statistics against natural driving benchmarks. The authors predict that Words2Wheels will outperform existing methods in accuracy, generalization, and adaptability compared to predefined and data-driven styles. The generalization hypothesis asserts that the LLM's zero-shot capabilities allow the system to handle new commands without user behavior data.

Methodological Details
The study focused on the car-following scenario, which constitutes a significant portion of driving behavior and reflects diverse styles. Experiments utilized the HighD dataset, collected by a 4K resolution camera mounted on a drone flying over a roadway. Data extraction and the kinematic model for car-following behavior were based on FollowNet. To ensure objectivity, 15% of the data was reserved as a test set for the Statistical Evaluation module. User commands were categorized into three levels based on directness: Level I (Direct), Level II (Indirect with strong hints), and Level III (Indirect with mild hints). The Driving Style Database was initially populated with 8 styles: some data-driven from clustering plus IRL, others human-designed from literature. For policy generation from reward functions, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) was used. RL training was run 5 times with different seeds, selecting the Style Policy with the highest reward. The base LLM was GPT-4o-2024-08-06 with temperature set to 0.3 for deterministic generation. The number of selected style rewards was set to k = 3, and the number of top statistical metrics was n = 2 in Statistical Evaluation. A reserved test dataset was used for statistical comparison, with spatio-temporal filtering enabling precise quantitative analyses. For the human-in-the-loop study, 10 volunteers with valid driving licenses were recruited.

Procedures And Architectures
The system uses RAG: the LLM selects the top k relevant style rewards from the Driving Style Database, which can be parallelized. The LLM consults the Statistical Evaluation module to determine if a selected Style Reward has a semantically similar matched command. If a similar command is found, Words2Wheels uses the fuzzy memory function; otherwise, the LLM generates m new reward functions based on the best-suited existing one. The LLM's generation goes beyond parameter adjustments to logic modifications or restructuring. Style Reward generation and policy training run simultaneously in the backend. The Statistical Evaluation module selects the top n metrics most relevant to the command and compares policy statistics to natural data on the test set. The evaluation uses a Chain-of-Thought approach, prompting the LLM to select metrics, choose a function, and output a JSON analysis. The Driving Style Database stores Style Rewards as programming code, Style Policies as pre-trained neural networks, and analytical data in JSON format. Elements can be embedded as high-dimensional vectors to improve LLM retrieval efficiency. The fuzzy memory function stores user commands alongside their corresponding driving styles to enable rapid recall. The car-following model benchmarked is the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM) with its standard calibration.

Key Results
In the human-preference study, 72% of tested events had participants judge Words2Wheels to be a better match to the user command than IDM. For the command 'I’m going to be late for the date,' Words2Wheels was preferred in 72% of events compared to 12.5% for IDM. For 'Safety first. I have plenty of time,' Words2Wheels was preferred in 79.5% of events vs. 3.5% for IDM. IDM was preferred in only 9.2% of total events across all commands. In the case study of 40 commands, Words2Wheels achieved 97.5% success in rational analysis, 95% in decision-making, 92.5% in retrieval, and 85% in generation. The aggressive style command showed higher speeds and greater acceleration, while the conservative style maintained larger gap and relative speed. The aggressive style had a larger time headway, and the normal style showed higher jerk, suggesting the LLM did not prioritize all metrics. In the generation experiment with no aligned styles provided, the 'I'm going to be late' input generated higher speed, acceleration, and jerk. The 'Safety first' input generated greater spacing, time headway, and relative speed. In the fuzzy memory test, all but one case involving 'It's snowing and visibility has decreased' were successfully recalled. The system handled Level I commands slightly more accurately than Level II and Level III, aligning with human expectations. In Case 26, the LLM intentionally selected the Style Reward with the highest jerk value as a counterexample.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The use of LLM as a 'policy index' through Style Rewards reduces the complexity from full command-to-policy mapping to reward-to-policy mapping. Zero-shot generation from reward templates proves that new driving behaviors can be synthesized without any actual driving data from the user. The Statistical Evaluation module transforms subjective user preference commands into objective statistical metrics, creating a verifiable style benchmark. The fuzzy memory function reduces RL training requirements by reusing previously trained policies for semantically similar commands. The framework supports continuous enrichment: each new generated Style Policy can replace inferior existing ones, expanding the style range over time.

Contradictions And Limitations
The aggressive style under Words2Wheels showed larger time headway, which is counter-intuitive given the command, attributed to the LLM not prioritizing all metrics. The normal style showed higher jerk, suggesting the multi-objective trade-off between speed and comfort was not perfectly balanced by the LLM. In Case 19, the LLM misinterpreted the command 'You are allowing a large gap with the vehicle in front.' When acceleration and jerk values were negative, the LLM's understanding conflicted with human intuition. One fuzzy memory recall failed for 'It's snowing and visibility has decreased.' The system was only tested in a car-following scenario; scalability to complex highway or urban navigation remains unproven. The human-in-the-loop study used only 10 volunteers; larger and more diverse user groups are needed for statistical significance.

Claims
Words2Wheels is the first framework to automatically customize style-aware driving policies from natural language user commands without prior driving data. The authors state this is the first framework to bridge the gap between user preferences and driving behavior through automated policy customization. The generation experiment showed the system could produce styles matching commands even when no matching styles existed in the database. The LLM made errors in a few isolated cases (Cases 19 and 26) and struggled with negative acceleration/jerk values. One fuzzy memory recall failed for snowy conditions. The approach eliminates the need for style-specific driving data, enabling immediate personalization for Robotaxi and commercial AV fleets. The framework is extensible to fuzzy memory and multi-scenario expansion.
The Statistical Evaluation module provides an objective, automated benchmark for style alignment using natural driving statistics. The module uses a reserved test dataset to prevent overfitting and provide benchmarks for policy evaluation. The evaluation compared policy statistics against statistics of natural driving behavior for objective assessment. The LLM failed to produce intuitive results in some cases, such as negative jerk values conflicting with human intuition. The aggressive style command produced a larger time headway, indicating the statistical alignment was imperfect. Automated evaluation removes human subjectivity from style verification, essential for safety-critical AV systems.

Data And Code Availability
Code and demo are available at https://yokhon.github.io/Words2Wheels/. Experimental records are available at https://bit.ly/4giYhB7.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
RL training was run 5 times with different seeds, and the highest reward policy was selected to mitigate instability. The generation experiment used only 4 initial styles (instead of 8) to demonstrate the system's ability to generate new styles when none matched. The 15% reserved test data was used exclusively for Statistical Evaluation to prevent overfitting during policy training. User commands were tested at three different directness levels to evaluate robustness across varying command formats. The fuzzy memory function was tested with 3 experimental sets and 5 similar inputs each, showing robust recall across various semantic perturbations.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the high-level workflow: User Command -> Style Reward -> Style Policy. Figure 2 illustrates the three modules: Automated Policy Customization, Driving Style Database, and Statistical Evaluation. Figure 3 presents a step-by-step example of automated Style Policy generation using RAG and LLM reasoning. Figure 4 shows a simplified example of the Statistical Evaluation module's comparison between policy and natural data. Figure 5 compares customized policies over style-aware metrics (speed, acceleration, jerk, headway) for aggressive, normal, and conservative commands. Figure 6 evaluates generated policies when no aligned styles were provided, showing the system's generative capability. Figure 7 displays the user interface for the human-in-the-loop comparison tool. Table I categorizes user commands into three linguistic levels with example commands. Table II presents human preferences on driving style alignment, showing 72% preference for Words2Wheels over IDM across 1,000 events. Table III summarizes case studies across 40 commands, with success rates for analysis (97.5%), decision-making (95%), retrieval (92.5%), and generation (85%). Table IV tests the fuzzy memory function with similar commands, showing successful recall in 5 out of 6 test cases.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is Words2Wheels, a framework that uses LLM-generated Style Rewards as a policy index to bridge natural language commands and driving policies without prior driving data. 2. The strongest evidence is the human-preference study showing 72% of participants preferred the Words2Wheels-generated style over the standard IDM model across 1,000 tested events. 3. The future path includes expanding to complex multi-vehicle scenarios beyond car-following, refining the Statistical Evaluation module, and incorporating a Feedback and Reflection module for closed-loop reward improvement.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a spectro-temporal investigation of the neutron star low-mass X-ray binary (NS-LMXB) GX 9+9, classified as an atoll source, using AstroSat's Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) and Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT). The observation, taken on July 25, 2020 (Obs. ID: A09_018T01_9000003774), detected the source in a disk-dominating soft state across 0.7–25.0 keV. The spectral analysis, conducted in three flux levels (FL1-450-570 counts/s, FL2-570-650, FL3-650-770 counts/s), employed the model 'const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb)' using XSPEC (v12.13.0c), yielding an average inner-disk radius of 16.57 ± 1.29 km and total unabsorbed fluxes ranging from 5.94 to 7.30 × 10⁻⁹ erg s⁻¹ cm⁻². The HID (Figure 1) confirmed the source in the banana state. Timing analysis using LAXPC's microsecond resolution revealed no QPOs but a broad-band noise feature centered at approximately 0.1 Hz. Energy-dependent temporal modeling via the Garg et al. propagative model with reduced χ² ~ 0.80 demonstrated that the variability originates from a variation in inner-disk temperature (δkTin ≈ 0.56 ± 0.10%) coupled with fractional scattering (δfs ≈ 81 ± 32%) and a positive phase lag of 0.11 ± 0.08, indicating a propagation of perturbations from the disk to the corona. The source shows signs of transitioning toward a softer state as kTe slightly decreases and Tin increases with flux. The results are largely consistent with prior work by Iaria et al. (2002) regarding flux and are relatively consistent with their R_in estimate despite different assumed inclination and distance.

Research Context
GX 9+9 is a neutron star low-mass X-ray binary atoll source identified during a Galactic center sounding rocket mission. Atoll sources trace a 'C'-pattern in the hardness-intensity diagram, exhibiting hard island and soft banana states. The source has a 4.2-hour X-ray and optical waveband modulation and its distance is assumed to be 5-10 kpc. Estimated mass and radius for the compact neutron star are 0.2–0.45 M☉ and 0.3–0.6 R☉, respectively. Previous spectral models include power law, blackbody plus Comptonization, disk with Comptonized blackbody, and double blackbody with broad iron line. A simultaneous X-ray and optical timing investigation using SAAO and RXTE was previously conducted. GX 9+9 is not a well-studied source, and more precise timing information from AstroSat over RXTE is expected due to larger effective area and wider energy coverage.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is to perform a spectro-temporal investigation of GX 9+9 to identify the radiative origin of its variability. The authors aim to estimate source characteristics such as inner-disk radius, flux, and inner-disk temperature. A key objective is to compare the constancy between spectral and temporal analysis and compare estimated values with previously reported results. The hypothesis is that the source is in a soft/banana state and that spectral parameters will vary predictably with X-ray flux. The study tests whether a propagative model (Garg et al. [29]) can explain the energy-dependent rms and phase lag variability. The predicted outcome is that a variation in the inner-disk temperature combined with fractional scattering will explain the broad-band noise variability.

Methodological Details
A single AstroSat archival observation (Obs. ID: A09_018T01_9000003774) from July 25, 2020, was used. LAXPC and SXT were used for spectral analysis, with only LAXPC 20 data used due to abnormal gains in counters 10 and 30. LAXPC operates over 3–80 keV, while SXT operates in the 0.3–8.0 keV range. Data were processed using LAXPC software version Oct. 13, 2022, for level-2 products. SXT level-1 data were processed through the AS1SXTLevel2-1.4b SXTpipeline. SXT count rate exceeded the 40 counts/sec pileup threshold; an annular zone (outer 13 arcmin, inner 2 arcmin) was used for extraction. A 2% model systematic error was incorporated for background uncertainty. A gain fit was applied to SXT data with a slope of 1 and offset free (usually 0.02–0.09). Spectral data were grouped using ftool ftgrouppha. The HID was constructed with a binning time of 32s. Three distinct flux levels were segregated: FL1-450–570 counts/s, FL2-570–650, FL3-650–770 counts/s. Spectral fitting was performed in XSPEC (v12.13.0c) with HEASOFT (6.31.1). Strict simultaneous data from LAXPC and SXT were used for joint spectral fitting. The best-fit spectral model was const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb) with LAXPC 20 as base, SXT constant free for cross-calibration. The optical depth was frozen at 9, and edge models were required at 2.4 keV. Parametric errors were at 90% confidence level. Timing analysis used LAXPC data due to microsecond-order timing resolution. The PDS was generated in the 3–20 keV energy range over 0.003 Hz to 1 Hz.

Procedures And Architectures
The spectral model initially tested bbodyrad as the seed photon source, which failed with reduced χ² > 2. The diskbb component was subsequently used for soft photon emission from the accretion disk. The thermal Comptonization model (ThComp), an improved version of nThComp, was used for the Comptonization component. The energy range for ThComp was extended with 1000 log bins using 'energies 0.01 500 1000 log'. The inner-disk radius R_in was calculated using Equation 1 with k = 1.7, disk-inclination 60°, and distance 10 kpc. Total unabsorbed flux was estimated using the XSPEC 'cflux' model in the 0.01–100 keV extended range. A multi-Lorentzian approach was applied to the PDS to check for variability in FL1, FL2, and FL3. Two Lorentzians were required to fit the PDS; no QPOs or prominent BBN features were detected. The centroid frequency ν₀ was ~0.04 Hz and the characteristic frequency ν_c was ~0.1 Hz from ν_c = √(ν₀²+HWHM). RMS and phase lag spectra were obtained using the LAXPC subroutine 'laxpc_find_freqlag'. The Garg et al. [29] propagative model was applied: truncated disk with hot corona, relating spectral parameters to physical parameters. The model was fit in both rms and phase lag spectra. The simple scenario tested was changing inner-disk temperature (kTin) and fractional scattering (fs) with a time-delay relative to fs. An additional test introduced the combination of heating rate and optical depth, but yielded insignificant χ² (>2).

Key Results
The source was in the banana state at the time of observation, confirmed by the HID form in Figure 1. Total unabsorbed flux in the 0.01–100 keV range measured 5.94 × 10⁻⁹, 6.51 × 10⁻⁹, and 7.30 × 10⁻⁹ erg s⁻¹ cm⁻² for FL1, FL2, and FL3 respectively. The maximum unabsorbed flux of 7.30 × 10⁻⁹ erg s⁻¹ cm⁻² is comparable to the 7.8 × 10⁻⁹ erg s⁻¹ cm⁻² reported by Iaria et al. in the 0.1–100 keV range. The average inner-disk radius (R_in) was estimated at 16.57 ± 1.29 km, which is relatively consistent with the previously reported 27 ± 4 km by Iaria et al. (who used inclination ~43° and 5 kpc). The reduced χ²/dof for spectral fits were 152.95/118 (FL1), 103.86/111 (FL2), 120.96/109 (FL3), and 130.33/117 (full flux). A BBN-like feature was detected in the PDS centered at approximately 0.1 Hz (left panel of Figure 3). The RMS at ~0.1 Hz increased with energy, while the phase lag showed a decreasing trend with energy (Figure 3, right). The Garg et al. propagative model yielded a reduced χ² of ~0.80, confirming it as the best-fit for temporal modeling. The best-fit temporal parameters showed δkTin = 0.56 ± 0.10%, δfs = 81 ± 32%, and phase lag = 0.11 ± 0.08. The variation in spectral parameters (decreasing kTe, increasing Tin) with flux suggests the source is transitioning toward a softer state. The source was not detected with any hint of QPOs or prominent BBN features across the three flux levels. The positive phase lag indicates perturbations propagated from the inner-disk temperature variation toward the coronal region (variation in seed photon fraction).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The source's position in the banana state with a disk-dominating spectrum implies high accretion rate, consistent with the C'-pattern of atoll sources. The reduction in kTe and increase in Tin across flux levels supports the interpretation of transitioning toward a softer spectral state. The positive phase lag in the energy-dependent temporal model implies that the variability origin is the inner-disk temperature, with perturbations propagating outward to the corona. The propagative model (Garg et al.) relates spectral parameters to physical parameters, enabling the radiative origin of broad-band noise variability to be linked to seed photon fraction and inner-disk temperature variations. The result suggests that the coronal region is a Comptonizing medium between the truncated disk inner radius and the ISCO.

Contradictions And Limitations
The spectral fit reduced χ²/dof values are notably high (ranging from ~1.3 to ~1.8), suggesting systematic uncertainties or incompleteness in the model. The phase lag trend could not be fully relied upon because the error bars were consistent within the data points. The data quality was characterized as poor, constraining the reliability of all derived parameters. GX 9+9 is not a well-studied source, and the single archival observation limits the statistical power of the analysis. The addition of heating rate and optical depth to the temporal model yielded insignificant χ² values (>2), meaning these parameters could not be independently constrained. The BBN-like feature is spread over a range of frequency, making the peak position less well-defined than narrow QPOs.

Claims
GX 9+9 was observed in a disk-dominating soft (banana) state during the AstroSat observation. The HID form (Figure 1) is consistent with the banana state pattern of atoll sources. The spectrum is dominated by the diskbb component with kTe around 4 keV and Tin around 2 keV. The source was detected in the soft state during the observation. The reduced χ²/dof for the spectral fit is relatively high, suggesting the model might not perfectly capture the physics. This confirms GX 9+9's behavior as a typical atoll source in its high-luminosity state.
The average inner-disk radius of GX 9+9 is approximately 16.57 ± 1.29 km. R_in was calculated from N_dbb using the prescribed relation with k=1.7 and inclination 60°. The result is comparable to the flux-resolved and full-flux R_in estimates. The value (16.57 ± 1.29 km) differs from Iaria et al.'s 27 ± 4 km, though the authors note this is due to different assumptions (inclination ~43° vs 60° and 5 kpc vs 10 kpc). A smaller R_in may imply a more compact emission region or a different geometric interpretation of the inner disk.
The broad-band noise variability originates from a variation in inner-disk temperature propagating to a change in fractional scattering in the corona. The Garg et al. propagative model with δkTin and δfs yielded reduced χ² ~ 0.80. The positive phase lag (0.11 ± 0.08) indicates perturbation propagation from disk to corona. RMS increases with energy while phase lag decreases with energy. The phase lag error bars were consistent within data points, limiting reliability. No QPOs were detected, and BBN features are broad, making the frequency-domain interpretation less precise than for narrow QPOs. This supports the physical picture of a truncated disk with an intervening Comptonizing corona in the NS-LMXB system.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Spectral fitting was performed in three flux levels independently (FL1, FL2, FL3) plus full flux, with results compared. A bbodyrad-only model was tested and rejected (reduced χ² > 2). An additional temporal model including heating rate and optical depth was tested but failed (χ² > 2). Edge models were required at 2.4 keV for a better spectral fit. The optical depth was frozen at 9 to constrain the model.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the Hardness-Intensity Diagram (HID) of the source using AstroSat data, with binning time of 32s and different colors for flux levels. Figure 2 displays the best-fit spectra of FL1, FL2, and FL3 from top to bottom in the 0.7–25 keV energy range. Figure 3 (left) shows the PDS fit with a broad-band noise feature, and Figure 3 (right) shows the energy-dependent temporal modeling of fractional rms and phase lag. Table 1 provides the best-fit spectral parameters for FL1, FL2, FL3, and full flux, alongside temporal modeling parameters.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first spectro-temporal analysis of GX 9+9 using AstroSat, identifying the radiative origin of its broad-band noise as a variation in inner-disk temperature propagating to the corona. 2. The strongest evidence is the reduced χ² of ~0.80 from the Garg et al. propagative model and the corresponding positive phase lag of 0.11 ± 0.08, which supports the perturbation propagation hypothesis. 3. The future path requires further mission observations of GX 9+9 due to poor data quality and its status as a poorly studied source to obtain a better understanding of the source.

summary.title: Dense-TSNet: Dense Connected Two-Stage Structure for Ultra-Lightweight Speech Enhancement
summary.authors: Zizhen Lin, Yuanle Li, Junyu Wang, Ruili Li
summary.field_subfield: Audio Signal Processing / Speech Enhancement
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces Dense-TSNet, an ultra-lightweight speech enhancement network designed for resource-constrained edge devices. The core contribution is the Dense Two-Stage (Dense-TS) architecture, which replaces the dilated convolutions in the classic Two-Stage (TS) architecture with densely connected Two-Stage modules. This structural change addresses the uneven loss landscape problem that typically hampers narrow lightweight models, ensuring smoother optimization and improved final performance in later training stages. Additionally, the authors propose the Multi-View Gaze Block (MVGB) to capture global, channel, and local feature perspectives entirely via CNNs, avoiding the deployment complexities of Transformers or Mamba. The model operates on the magnitude spectrum from an STFT decomposition, uses the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset for training, and achieves competitive performance with only 14K parameters—positioning it as one of the first speech enhancement models with approximately 10K parameters. A critical loss function analysis reveals that while incorporating Metric Loss (PESQ-based) can improve objective scores, it may introduce pseudohallucination artifacts and negative subjective impacts when over-weighted, leading the authors to rely primarily on Consistency Magnitude Loss. The model achieves a PESQ of 3.05, CSIG 4.51, CBAK 3.58, and COVL 3.86, outperforming both the classic TS baseline (PESQ 2.96) and several larger lightweight methods including TSTNN (0.92M parameters) and CCFNet-Lite (160K parameters).

claims.description: Dense-TSNet is among the first speech enhancement models with approximately 10K parameters, enabling deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.
The Dense-TS architecture outperforms the classic Two-Stage architecture at the same parameter scale due to a smoother loss landscape.
The Multi-View Gaze Block (MVGB) is essential for high-quality denoising; removing any of its three views significantly degrades performance.

The core contribution is the Dense Two-Stage (Dense-TS) architecture, which replaces the dilated convolutions in the classic Two-Stage (TS) architecture with densely connected Two-Stage modules. This structural change addresses the uneven loss landscape problem that typically hampers narrow lightweight models, ensuring smoother optimization and improved final performance in later training stages. Research Context
Speech enhancement aims to improve speech clarity in noisy environments for applications such as voice calls and automatic speech recognition. Recent advancements have concentrated on deep neural networks using the Two-Stage (TS) architecture to enhance feature extraction. However, the complexity and size of these models remain significant, limiting applicability in resource-constrained scenarios. Narrow lightweight models often encounter performance bottlenecks due to uneven loss landscapes. Advanced operators such as Transformers or Mamba may lack the practical adaptability and efficiency that CNNs offer in real-world deployments. Research on single-channel speech enhancement models with around 10k parameters is still limited. This gap underscores the need for innovative approaches to develop effective models at this scale.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how to design an ultra-lightweight speech enhancement model that maintains performance while operating at around 10k parameters for edge devices. The authors hypothesize that a Dense Two-Stage architecture, replacing dilated convolutions with densely connected TS modules, will provide a smoother loss landscape and more robust refinement in later training stages compared to the classic Two-Stage model. They hypothesize that incorporating global, channel, and local perspectives through a CNN-only multi-view block can enhance feature extraction without the deployment overhead of non-convolutional operators. A secondary hypothesis explores whether integrating learned evaluation metrics (Metric Loss) improves perceptual quality, or if it introduces artifacts at high weights.

Methodological Details
The study utilizes the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset, known for its high-fidelity utterances. Speech samples are segmented into two-second intervals for STFT processing. STFT parameters include an FFT size of 400, a window length of 400, and a hop length of 100. Training is conducted with a batch size of 2 using the AdamW optimizer. The training runs for up to 1,000,000 steps. The model inputs only the magnitude spectrum derived from the complex STFT spectrum. The Classic TS baseline uses a channel count of 64. Dense-TSNet is configured with 14K parameters (4-channel version) and 356M MACs. The classic TS for comparison uses 6 channels with 388M MACs.

Procedures And Architectures
The input signal is converted to the time-frequency domain via STFT, extracting magnitude and phase from the complex spectrum. The classic TS architecture consists of a densely connected encoder-decoder with dilated convolutions and serially connected Two-Stage modules. Dense-TS replaces dilated convolutions in the Dilated Dense Block with Two-Stage modules, resulting in a network composed entirely of densely connected TS modules. Features are mapped to high-dimensional space using 1×1 convolutions, and the dilated dense block is omitted in favor of direct dense connections. For each layer i, input channels Ci = dense channel × (i + 1), and output channels Cout = dense channel. The output of each TS-MVGB is a serial connection: TS-MVGBi(x) = freq-MVGB(time-MVGB(x)). Dense connections concatenate the previous skip layer with the adjusted current layer output. The final output is a weighted residual: 0.2 × skip(depth−1) + x. The Multi-View Gaze Block (MVGB) comprises a Large Kernel Extractor (LKE), Learnable-Sigmoid Gate (LSG), and Channel Attention (CA). LKE establishes a global perspective using large kernel depthwise convolutions for long-range low-frequency features. CA reallocates weights to channels for channel-wise feature importance. LSG establishes local spatial perspectives using depth-wise, point-wise convolutions, and Learnable-Sigmoid activation. Finally, L-Sigmoid activation and 1×1 convolution decode the magnitude mask, which is multiplied by the noisy magnitude.

Key Results
Dense-TSNet (14K, 356M MACs) achieves PESQ 3.05, CSIG 4.51, CBAK 3.58, and COVL 3.86 on VoiceBank+DEMAND. The classic TS baseline (14K, 388M MACs) achieves lower PESQ of 2.96, CSIG 4.45, CBAK 3.58, and COVL 3.78. Dense-TSNet outperforms TSTNN (0.92M, PESQ 2.96), PHASEN (20.9M, PESQ 2.99), and MANNER-S-5.3GF (0.90M, PESQ 3.06, though MANNER achieves slightly higher PESQ but Dense-TSNet beats it on all other metrics). Dense-TSNet achieves lower MACs (356M) than the classic TS (388M) with the same parameter count. Ablation w/o LKE (global view) drops PESQ to 2.79, CSIG to 4.31, CBAK to 3.47, and COVL to 3.61. Ablation w/o CA (channel view) drops PESQ to 2.86, CSIG to 4.38, CBAK to 3.53, and COVL to 3.69. Ablation w/o LSG (local view) drops PESQ to 2.97, CSIG to 4.46, CBAK to 3.57, and COVL to 3.79. Ablation w/o Consistency Loss drops PESQ to 2.96, CSIG to 4.45, CBAK to 3.58, and COVL to 3.79. With P = 200 (λ2/λ1), PESQ increases to 3.28, but at P = 400, PESQ drops to 3.04 and a pseudohallucination distortion is introduced. Only complex loss (without Metric Loss) achieves PESQ 2.60, significantly lower than the proposed method.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The Dense-TS architecture addresses the early convergence limitations and uneven loss landscapes of narrow lightweight models through denser information flow. The multi-view design acknowledges that different signal components require different spatial perspectives: global for low-frequency, channel-wise for relevance weighting, and local for high-frequency detail. The choice of loss function reveals a fundamental tension: maximizing objective perceptual scores via Metric Loss can degrade actual subjective perception through artifacts. Relying on consistency between STFT-space reconstruction and target clean speech is more robust for perceptual quality than direct complex-domain optimization in lightweight settings.

Contradictions And Limitations
At P = 400 (high Metric Loss weight), training fails and a pseudohallucination distortion is introduced at P = 200, affecting perceptual quality. The model is tested only on the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset; no cross-dataset evaluation or real-world deployment verification is provided. Random seeds, exact hyperparameter values beyond optimizer name and batch size, and specific training schedules are not reported. The 6-channel vs 4-channel comparison uses different structures (classic TS vs Dense-TS), making the direct parameter-count comparison slightly heterogeneous.

Claims
Dense-TSNet is among the first speech enhancement models with approximately 10K parameters, enabling deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. The model has only 14K parameters, which is described as approximately 10k in the contributions. Table I compares Dense-TSNet (14K) against TSTNN (0.92M), PHASEN (20.9M), and CCFNet-Lite (160K). The authors state this is the first to achieve a model with approximately 10k parameters. The actual parameter count is reported as 14K, not exactly 10K, creating a slight discrepancy in the narrative. Enables speech enhancement on smartphones and cameras where memory and compute are strictly limited.
The Dense-TS architecture outperforms the classic Two-Stage architecture at the same parameter scale due to a smoother loss landscape. Dense-TSNet (14K, PESQ 3.05) exceeds Classic TS (14K, PESQ 2.96). Figure 4 shows Dense-TS achieves better performance in later training stages despite slower early convergence. The improvement is attributed to the smoother loss landscape provided by dense connections in the narrower model. The classic Two-Stage structure converges faster in the early stages than Dense-TS. Denser connection topologies are more effective for low-parameter, narrow-channel architectures.
The Multi-View Gaze Block (MVGB) is essential for high-quality denoising; removing any of its three views significantly degrades performance. w/o LKE (global view) drops PESQ from 3.05 to 2.79 (-0.26). w/o CA (channel view) drops PESQ from 3.05 to 2.86 (-0.19). w/o LSG (local view) drops PESQ from 3.05 to 2.97 (-0.08). The impact of LSG is smaller than LKE or CA, suggesting different view contributions are not equal. A multi-view approach is necessary to capture the diverse information needed for high-quality speech enhancement.

Data And Code Availability
Source codes will be released after paper acceptance. Audio samples can be found at https://github.com/huaidanquede/Dense-TSNet.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Table II presents ablation experiments for the MVGB module design, illustrating effects of LKE, CA, and LSG. The Consistency Magnitude Loss was validated against Metric Loss, showing Metric Loss over-weighting (P=400) causes training failure. Only complex loss (PESQ 2.60) was tested as a baseline and underperformed significantly. No cross-validation, sensitivity to hyperparameter ranges, or robustness to different noise types is explicitly tested.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: The overall architecture of Classic Two-Stage and Dense-TS (ours). Figure 2: The internal details of the LKE, LSG and CA within the MVGB. Figure 3: Training criteria of the proposed Dense-TSNet showing the loss functions. Figure 4: Training curves of Dense-TS and Classic-TS showing PESQ and magnitude error. Figure 5: Training curves of Dense-TS and Classic-TS showing Metric Loss effects (P=200, P=400, LMagConsis. only). Table I: Performance comparison with other methods on VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset. Table II: Ablation Study Results on the VoiceBank + DEMAND Dataset. Table III: Study of Loss Function comparing Consistency Mag. with Metric Loss at various P values.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the Dense-TS architecture: a densely connected Two-Stage network that enables high-quality speech enhancement at only 14K parameters by solving the uneven loss landscape problem of narrow models. 2. The strongest evidence is the ablation study and loss analysis: removing any MVGB view degrades PESQ significantly, and Metric Loss over-weighting (P=400) causes training failure, validating the design choices. 3. The future path is to explore further methods for compressing model size while maintaining perceptual quality, potentially extending to broader datasets and real-world deployments.
