summary.title: Recurrent Interpolants for Probabilistic Time Series Prediction
summary.authors: Yu Chen, Marin Biloš, Sarthak Mittal, Wei Deng, Kashif Rasul, Anderson Schneider
summary.field_subfield: Machine Learning / Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
summary.type_of_paper: Research paper presenting a novel generative model for time series forecasting
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces Recurrent Interpolants, a novel framework that combines the computational efficiency of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with the high-quality probabilistic modeling of diffusion models (specifically stochastic interpolants) for multivariate time series forecasting. While autoregressive models like RNNs and Transformers are standard for time series, their probabilistic outputs are typically restricted to simple probability families, and generative diffusion-based models suffer from scalability issues because model size scales with both feature dimension and window length. The authors address this by: 1) extending the theory of stochastic interpolants to a general conditional generation framework with extra control features; and 2) employing a conditional stochastic interpolants (SI) module for sequential modeling, where a large context window is encoded by an RNN into a history prompt (condition), and the generative SI module performs conditional generation from the current time point to the future time point. The method is trained using tuples of (xt+1, xt, xt-P:t-1), learning the joint distribution p(xt+1, xt | xt-P:t-1) with both marginals equal. Key theoretical contributions include Theorem 1, proving that the interpolant defines a dynamic density satisfying a transport equation. Empirically, the method is evaluated on synthetic two-dimensional datasets (8gaussians, Circles, Moons, Rings, Swissroll) and four real-world datasets (Solar, Exchange, Traffic, Wiki). In the real-world multivariate forecasting task, the SI-based model achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on three out of four datasets, outperforming both pure RNN baselines (Vec-LSTM) and other generative baselines (DDPM, SGM, FM) in terms of CRPS-sum, NRMSE, and ND metrics. The authors demonstrate that carefully modeling the probability distribution is critical for large-dimension time series prediction, and that initiating prediction from the current rather than noise distribution markedly improves quality. The code is planned for public release in the camera-ready version.

Executive Summary
This paper introduces Recurrent Interpolants, a novel framework that combines the computational efficiency of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with the high-quality probabilistic modeling of diffusion models (specifically stochastic interpolants) for multivariate time series forecasting. While autoregressive models like RNNs and Transformers are standard for time series, their probabilistic outputs are typically restricted to simple probability families, and generative diffusion-based models suffer from scalability issues because model size scales with both feature dimension and window length. The authors address this by: 1) extending the theory of stochastic interpolants to a general conditional generation framework with extra control features; and 2) employing a conditional stochastic interpolants (SI) module for sequential modeling, where a large context window is encoded by an RNN into a history prompt (condition), and the generative SI module performs conditional generation from the current time point to the future time point. The method is trained using tuples of (xt+1, xt, xt-P:t-1), learning the joint distribution p(xt+1, xt | xt-P:t-1) with both marginals equal. Key theoretical contributions include Theorem 1, proving that the interpolant defines a dynamic density satisfying a transport equation. Empirically, the method is evaluated on synthetic two-dimensional datasets (8gaussians, Circles, Moons, Rings, Swissroll) and four real-world datasets (Solar, Exchange, Traffic, Wiki). In the real-world multivariate forecasting task, the SI-based model achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on three out of four datasets, outperforming both pure RNN baselines (Vec-LSTM) and other generative baselines (DDPM, SGM, FM) in terms of CRPS-sum, NRMSE, and ND metrics. The authors demonstrate that carefully modeling the probability distribution is critical for large-dimension time series prediction, and that initiating prediction from the current rather than noise distribution markedly improves quality. The code is planned for public release in the camera-ready version.

Research Context
Autoregression models such as RNNs and Transformers have become the de facto tools for multivariate time series forecasting in finance, biology, medicine, and geophysics. These models can provide prediction uncertainty through probabilistic forecasting by incorporating specific parametric probabilistic models into the output layer. However, the probabilistic output layer is confined within a simple probability family because the density needs to be parameterized by neural networks. Recent works employ generative modeling using diffusion or flow-based models, extending to stochastic differential equations for probabilistic imputation and forecasting. Compared to a recurrent model where model size is proportional only to the number of features, generative model predictors suffer from scalability issues because model size is related to both feature dimension and the size of the window. A more computationally-friendly framework is needed for large-scale generative model-based time series prediction problems. Generative modeling excels at modeling complicated high-dimension distributions, but most models require learning a mapping from noise distribution to data distribution. Time series data is typically continuous and neighboring time points exhibit strong correlations, indicating that the distribution of future time points is close to that of the current time point.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether combining the computational efficiency of RNNs with the probabilistic modeling quality of stochastic interpolants can overcome the scalability limitations of pure generative time series forecasting models. The authors hypothesize that initiating the prediction of a future time point's distribution with the current time point (rather than from noise) is more straightforward and yields better quality. The framework hypothesizes that longer temporal dependency can be encoded by a recurrent neural network while the embedded history is passed as guidance to the generative model. A key theoretical hypothesis is that the stochastic interpolant can be extended to arbitrary joint distributions with extra control features and still satisfy a transport equation. The predicted outcome is that the SI-based model will achieve competitive or superior performance on both synthetic and real-world multivariate forecasting tasks compared to DDPM, SGM, FM, and pure RNN baselines. The authors expect that carefully modeling the probability distribution is critical for large-dimension time series prediction, as implied by the superior performance of generative models over pure RNNs.

Methodological Details
The model is applied to multivariate time series forecasting where the prediction is formulated as the conditional probability p(xt+1 | xt−P:t). The context window xt−P:t has a length P denoting the context window size, and xt ∈ RD represents the multivariate time series at time t with D dimensions. The training dataset consists of 3-tuples (xt+1, xt, xt−P:t−1), where xt ∼ ρ0 and xt+1 ∼ ρ1 for all t, so the marginal distributions are equal ρ0 = ρ1. A recurrent neural network encodes the context xt−P:t−1 into a history prompt ht. The generative model learns the joint distribution p(xt+1, xt | xt−P:t−1) by training conditional velocity and score functions. In the inference phase, the RNN encodes xt−P:t−1 into ht, and SI transports xt to the target distribution with condition ht. For multiple-step prediction, the model recursively runs the step-by-step prediction. The real-world datasets include Solar, Exchange, Traffic, and Wiki, with preprocessing following Salinas et al. 2019. The synthetic datasets consist of eight two-dimensional datasets: 8gaussians, Circles, Moons, Rings, and Swissroll. To make a fair comparison, all models use the same neural networks, batch size, training epochs, and hyperparameters. Importance sampling using the Beta distribution is leveraged to stabilize training over the diffusion time s.

Procedures And Architectures
The architecture (Figure 2) consists of an RNN encoding the context into ht, followed by an SI diffusion block that takes xt and ht as input. The velocity function b(s, x, s, ξ) and score function s(s, x, s, ξ) are modeled by deep neural networks. The interpolant is defined as xs = α(s)x0 + β(s)x1 + γ(s)z, where α(s), β(s), and γ(s) are schedules with α(0)=1, α(1)=0, β(0)=0, β(1)=1, and γ(0)=γ(1)=0. In Table 1, SI scheduler combinations explored include: quad (γ(s) = √s(1−s)), sqrt (γ(s) = √(2s(1−s))), trig (γ(s) = sin(πs)²), and linear (γ(s) = s(1−s)). The training loss minimizes the mean squared error of velocity and score functions: Lb = E[1/2||ˆb(s, xs, i, hi)||^2 - (˙αx0 + ˙βx1 + ˙γzi)^T ˆb] and Ls = E[1/2||ˆs(s, xs, i)||^2 + γ⁻¹zi^T ˆs]. During inference (Algorithm 2), the SDE integral is run for s ∈ [0, 1] following d~xs = [b(s, ~xs, h) + ε(s)s(s, ~xs, h)]ds + √2ε(s)dw. The model uses the forward SDE for generation, where ε(s) ≥ 0 is the diffusion variance. The score function ∇log ρt(x) = −γ⁻¹(s)E[z|xt = x, ξ] is optimized using a simple quadratic objective function.

Key Results
On synthetic two-dimensional datasets, the Wasserstein distance between generated samples and true data is reported in Table 1. SI with sqrt, linear scheduler achieves a Wasserstein distance of 0.59 on 8gaussians and 0.37 on Swissroll, while SI with trig, linear achieves 0.52 on 8gaussians and 0.16 on Swissroll. In the multivariate forecasting task (Table 2), SI achieves a CRPS-sum of 0.391±0.017 on Solar, 0.359±0.06 on Exchange, 0.083±0.005 on Traffic, and 0.080±0.007 on Wiki. Compared to the pure RNN baseline (Vec-LSTM), SI significantly outperforms it on all four datasets, with the largest relative improvement on Wiki (0.080 vs 0.133). Compared to DDPM, SI achieves lower CRPS-sum on Solar (0.359 vs 0.359 tied), Exchange (0.359 vs 0.364), Traffic (0.083 vs 0.058 FM better), and Wiki (0.080 vs 0.084). On the Traffic dataset, the FM model achieves the best CRPS-sum of 0.058±0.014, while SI achieves 0.083±0.005. On the Wiki dataset, the FM model (0.108±0.026) fails to capture the data distribution, while SI achieves 0.080±0.007. NRMSE results (referenced in Appendix C) show SI outperforms or matches other models on three out of four datasets. Figure 4 demonstrates that SI on the Solar dataset can make precise predictions and capture uncertainty even when scale of different dimensions varies a lot.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Theorem 1 establishes that the stochastic interpolant extends to arbitrary joint distributions and satisfies a transport equation, providing a continuous-time interpretation. The framework demonstrates that the probability distribution of xt as simulated by the interpolant equation results in a dynamic density function. The authors argue that carefully modeling the probability distribution is critical for large-dimension time series prediction, as indicated by the superior performance of generative models over pure RNNs. The approach bridges the gap between recurrent modeling (temporal dependence) and generative diffusion (high-quality density estimation), offering a unified framework for conditional time series generation. The use of the current time point as the starting distribution for prediction, rather than noise, is justified by the temporal continuity of time series data.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors note that the flow matching model (FM) achieves better performance than SI on the Traffic dataset (0.058 vs 0.083). The FM model on Wiki data (0.108) cannot capture the data distribution, and the authors report that flow matching hyperparameter searches were unable to yield satisfying results. The model is evaluated only on four real-world datasets; broader generalization to different domains is not empirically tested. The paper acknowledges that loss values become larger when s is close to the ends, necessitating importance sampling to stabilize training. The authors state they will publish the code only for the camera-ready version, suggesting the code is not yet publicly available at the time of the preprint.

Claims
Recurrent Interpolants (SI) combined with RNNs outperform pure RNN models for multivariate probabilistic time series forecasting. SI achieves CRPS-sum of 0.080±0.007 on Wiki while Vec-LSTM achieves 0.133±0.002. SI achieves 0.391±0.017 on Solar, outperforming DDPM's 0.359±0.061 in terms of reliability. On Traffic data, FM achieves 0.058±0.014, which is better than SI's 0.083±0.005. Carefully modeling the probability distribution is critical for large-dimension time series prediction.
SI can be extended to a general conditional generation framework with extra control features, as proven in Theorem 1. Theorem 1 proves the stochastic interpolant satisfies the transport equation for arbitrary joint distributions. The model supports conditional generation with condition ξ injected into both velocity and score functions.  The framework can be applied to a wide range of conditional tasks including image inpainting, time series imputation, and text generation.
Initiating prediction from the current time point rather than from noise significantly improves the quality of generated samples and alleviates learning challenges. Starting from an initial distribution proximate to the terminal data distribution remarkably alleviates learning challenges. Time series data is continuous and neighboring time points exhibit strong correlations, justifying this approach.  The method reduces inference complexity and enhances the quality of generated samples in generative time series forecasting.

Data And Code Availability
The authors state: 'We will publish the code for the camera-ready version.' indicating code is not currently public.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors test out different gamma-interpolant functions: quad, sqrt, trig, and linear. Most combinations achieve good results, with SI (trig, linear) achieving Wasserstein distance 0.52 on 8gaussians and 0.16 on Swissroll. Importance sampling using the Beta distribution is used to stabilize training over diffusion time s. The models are compared under the same neural network architecture, batch size, and training epochs for fairness.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the schedules α(s), β(s), γ(s) for stochastic interpolants with Example trig: γ(s) = sin(πt)². Figure 2 illustrates the model diagram showing RNN encoding context into ht followed by SI diffusion block. Figure 3 displays generated samples for 8gaussians, Circles, Moons, Rings, and Swissroll from DDPM, FM, SGM, and SI models. Figure 4 shows forecast paths on Solar dataset with median prediction and 50th/90th confidence intervals on 6/137 variate dimensions. Figure 5 shows the Time-Grad model for conditional time series prediction architecture. Table 1 reports Wasserstein distances between generated samples and true data for synthetic datasets. Table 2 reports CRPS-sum metrics on four multivariate real-world forecasting datasets.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the Recurrent Interpolants framework, merging RNN's computational efficiency with diffusion models' probabilistic modeling quality through a conditional stochastic interpolant that operates from the current time point to the future, avoiding the noise-to-data bottleneck. 2. The strongest evidence is the empirical demonstration across four real-world multivariate datasets (Solar, Exchange, Traffic, Wiki) where SI outperforms pure RNN baselines (Vec-LSTM) and is competitive with DDPM, SGM, and FM, alongside the theoretical guarantee in Theorem 1 that the interpolant satisfies a transport equation. 3. The future path involves extending the framework to broader conditional tasks, refining the hyperparameter sensitivity (especially for FM), and leveraging the generalized conditional generation theory for inpainting and imputation tasks.

summary.title: The properties of highly concentrated aqueous CH3COOK/Na binary electrolyte and its use in sodium-ion batteries
summary.authors: Shahid Khalid; Nicolò Pianta; Simone Bonizzoni; Piercarlo Mustarelli; Riccardo Ruffo
summary.field_subfield: Energy Chemistry / Aqueous Electrolytes for Sodium-Ion Batteries
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental research paper with comprehensive physico-chemical characterization and proof-of-concept electrochemical testing
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a comprehensive characterization of the physicochemical and electrochemical properties of highly concentrated aqueous CH3COOK/CH3COONa binary electrolyte systems, targeting the water-in-salt electrolyte (WISE) regime for sodium-ion battery applications. Four electrolytes were prepared with a fixed 20 mol kg−1 CH3COOK content and varying CH3COONa concentrations (1, 2.5, 5, and 7 mol kg−1). Thermal analysis via DSC revealed that the glass transition temperature (Tg) shifts to higher temperatures with increasing salt concentration, consistent with a transition from salt-in-water to water-in-salt behavior, while the most concentrated system (7N20K) exhibits a low liquidus temperature (≈0 °C) preventing premature crystallization. Rheological characterization confirms the acetate salts as 'structure-making' agents with Arrhenius-type viscosity increase and Vogel-Tamman-Fulcher ionic conductivity behavior. The 7N20K electrolyte achieves a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm−1 at 25 °C and an electrochemical stability window extending to 3 V in ideal conditions. A proof-of-concept battery was demonstrated using carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 NASICON (CLTP) as a sodium anode in 7N20K: first cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g−1, average charge efficiency of 96% at low current, 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles, and a charge transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV. Comparison with 1 M NaAc shows significantly degraded performance in the diluted system (36 mAh g−1 anodic capacity, 40% efficiency), underscoring the superiority of the WISE approach. The study confirms that aqueous acetate binary electrolytes can bridge the performance gap with organic counterparts while offering inherent safety and lower cost.

The 7N20K electrolyte achieves a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm−1 at 25 °C and an electrochemical stability window extending to 3 V in ideal conditions. Comparison with 1 M NaAc shows significantly degraded performance in the diluted system (36 mAh g−1 anodic capacity, 40% efficiency), underscoring the superiority of the WISE approach. The study confirms that aqueous acetate binary electrolytes can bridge the performance gap with organic counterparts while offering inherent safety and lower cost.

Research Context
Conventional organic carbonate electrolytes for Li-ion batteries suffer from low flashpoints, high viscosities, and thermal instability of LiPF6 which degrades to HF in moisture. The thermodynamic electrochemical stability window of water is limited to 1.23 V, creating a major barrier for aqueous batteries. Previous attempts to extend the ESW in diluted aqueous systems only reach 1.5 V, still far from organic counterparts. Water-in-salt electrolytes (WISE) developed by Suo et al. using 21 mol kg−1 LiTFSI enable a 3 V voltage window due to reduced water activity. However, fluorinated salts like LiTFSI exhibit severe toxicity and are prohibitively expensive, limiting practical implementation. Cost-effective, highly soluble salts like LiCl, CH3COONa, and CH3COOK are proposed as viable alternatives for WISE formulations. NASICON compounds offer stable structures with large ionic channels, making them ideal electrodes for highly concentrated environments. Despite previous investigations of KAc-based binary systems, a systematic study of the physicochemical properties of KAc/NaAc binaries is lacking.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is: what are the thermal, rheological, transport, and electrochemical properties of CH3COOK/CH3COONa binary electrolytes at WISE concentrations? The hypothesis is that increasing the second salt (NaAc) in the 20 mol kg−1 KAc solution will shift the system toward water-in-salt behavior, enhancing the electrochemical stability window. It is predicted that a compromise between transport properties (conductivity) and electrochemical stability window will be achieved at a specific intermediate concentration. The authors hypothesize that the 7N20K composition (7 mol kg−1 NaAc with 20 mol kg−1 KAc) will be the optimal WISE candidate due to its predicted broad ESW and adequate conductivity. A further hypothesis is that the carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 NASICON electrode can reversibly insert Na+ ions in this electrolyte, demonstrating practical viability. The study predicts that the chloride- or acetate-containing aqueous electrolyte will improve ion diffusion within the NASICON structure compared to organic analogs.

Methodological Details
Four binary electrolytes were prepared by dissolving NaAc and KAc in high-quality Milli-Q water (σ = 6.7 μS cm−1) under sonication. The fixed concentration of KAc was 20 mol kg−1, while NaAc concentrations varied at 1, 2.5, 5, and 7 mol kg−1, designated as 1N20K, 2.5N20K, 5N20K, and 7N20K. A 1 M NaAc solution was prepared as a diluted comparison reference. The carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 NASICON (CLTP) was synthesized via a one-pot sol-gel route using 1.78 g NH4H2(PO4)3, 3.51 g Ti(OC4H9)4, 0.52 g CH3COOLi·2H2O, and 0.58 g C6H12O6. The precursor was calcined at 800 °C for 6 h under argon flux at 50 ml min−1 gas flow. Pristine LiTi2(PO4)3 (LTP) was synthesized by the same route without C6H12O6 for comparison. Phase purity was confirmed by X-ray diffraction in the R-3c space group (JCPDS: 35-0754). For electrochemical testing in aqueous media, NASICON electrodes were dip-coated onto carbon cloth current collectors with an active material load of ≈6 mg cm−2. Electrochemical stability was measured in flooded three-electrode cells using glassy carbon as working, Pt mesh as counter, and double junction SCE as reference. For organic electrolyte characterization, coin cells were assembled in an Ar glovebox ([O2] < 0.1 ppm, [H2O] < 0.1 ppm) with loads of ≈2.4, ≈2.7, and ≈1.7 mg cm−2 for Li, Na, and K cells, respectively. Impedance spectroscopy used a dip probe cell with two Pt foils and a cell factor of 1.04 cm−1. GCPL measurements used a current cycle protocol: 10 cycles at 0.1 C, 0.5 C, 1 C, 5 C, 10 C, and 0.1 C; 1 C corresponds to 136 mA g−1. EIS temperature measurements ranged from 20 °C to 70 °C using 1 kHz to 100 kHz frequency range with 50 mV amplitude under N2 flux. A threshold of 0.1 mA cm−2 on the glassy carbon electrode was used to define decomposition limits. The n value for mobile ions in the impedance model was evaluated to be 1.7, and the ion concentration was taken as 12930 mol m−3.

Procedures And Architectures
DSC thermal analysis covered -120 °C to 90 °C with a heating/cooling rate of 1 °C min−1 and a 5 min isotherm at -120 °C. Viscosity shear tests used a parallel plate 50 mm setup at shear rates 10–300 s−1 at temperatures of 10, 20, 30, and 40 °C. Conductivity measurements were performed in a climatic chamber under N2 flux from 5 °C to 70 °C with 1 Hz to 200 kHz frequency range and 25 mV amplitude. EIS for electrode kinetics was conducted in a Faraday cage to eliminate environmental interference. LSV for stability window was performed at a fixed voltage sweep; the anodic threshold was 0.1 mA cm−2 on glassy carbon. For sodium intercalation tests, the NASICON was partially sodiated, and during de-sodiation measurements were interrupted at the middle of the first plateau. EIS spectra were collected at 10 °C steps from 20 °C to 70 °C for activation energy determination. All electrolytes were degassed with N2 flux prior to conductivity measurements. The Walden plot analysis compared molar conductivity vs. fluidity (η−1) at different temperatures to assess ionicity. Kohlrausch's law was applied to the 7N20K data at 25 °C to extract the infinite dilution molar conductivity (Λ₀).

Key Results
DSC revealed glass transition temperatures (Tg) below −70 °C, cold crystallization exotherms below −20 °C, and melting endotherms around 0 °C. Increasing NaAc concentration shifted Tg to higher temperatures, confirming the water-in-salt transition. The 1N20K and 2.5N20K samples showed no cold crystallization or melting, remaining frozen in the glassy state. The 5N20K sample exhibited a cold crystallization at −28.06 °C and 7N20K at −33.70 °C. Ionic conductivity follows Vogel-Tamman-Fulcher (VTF) behavior for all compositions. Ionic conductivity decreases with increasing salt concentration as expected in high-concentration electrolytes. The 7N20K electrolyte achieves a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm−1 at 25 °C, comparable to organic electrolytes. Viscosity follows Arrhenius behavior in the tested temperature range and increases with concentration, indicating 'structure-making' behavior. The activation energy of viscosity (Ea(η)) increases with salt concentration, matching conductivity-derived activation energies. Walden plot analysis classifies all electrolytes as quasi-ideal, with the 7N20K solution following Kohlrausch's law at 25 °C. At 25 °C, the infinite dilution molar conductivity (Λ₀) for the 7N20K electrolyte is 52.90 Ω cm² mol−1. Cathodic stability improves with increasing NaAc concentration, confirming suppressed hydrogen evolution due to reduced water activity. The 7N20K electrolyte demonstrates a stability window up to 3 V in ideal (small surface area, flooded cell) conditions. Carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (CLTP) in 7N20K shows a first cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g−1 with an average charge efficiency of 96% at low current. At 60 cycles in 7N20K, the CLTP electrode retains 90% of its initial capacity. Charge transfer activation energy (Ea(CT)) at the CLTP/7N20K interface is 0.12 eV. Diffusion coefficient (D) of alkaline ions in CLTP at room temperature is approximately 10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹. In the diluted 1 M NaAc electrolyte, CLTP anodic capacity drops to 36 mAh g−1 and charge efficiency to 40%. At 1 C (136 mA g−1) in 7N20K, the CLTP provides an average anodic capacity of 68 mAh g−1 with 99.0% charge efficiency.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The Tg increase with concentration indicates growing intermolecular interactions and the transition from salt-in-water to water-in-salt regime. The persistence of considerable conductivity at high concentration suggests the formation of water-salt structures where available water molecules cannot effectively shell cations. The structure-making behavior of acetate salts confirms that cations and anions strongly hydrate, contributing to molecular ordering and reduced water activity. The quasi-ideal behavior on Walden plots implies that ions remain largely dissociated even at the highest concentration. The low liquidus temperature of the 7N20K electrolyte prevents premature cell failure from salt crystallization during long-term cycling. The preferential insertion of Na+ over K+ in the NASICON structure is attributed to the higher energy required to accommodate the larger K+ ion. The low activation energy of 0.12 eV for charge transfer proves very good kinetic properties of the NASICON/electrolyte interface. The aquatic electrolyte improves the diffusion of alkaline ions inside the electrode structure compared to organic electrolytes. The 7N20K electrolyte represents a practical compromise between transport performance and electrochemical stability for sodium-ion batteries.

Contradictions And Limitations
The ESW estimation (0.1 mA cm−2 threshold on glassy carbon) may overestimate decomposition limits due to the large electrolyte amount and quasi-ideal electrocatalytic electrode with small surface area. The EIS measurements were conducted on a partially sodiated electrode, which may not capture the full range of the intercalation process. The temperature range explored for viscosity and conductivity was limited by instrumental constraints, necessitating Arrhenius rather than the more complete VTF fitting for viscosity. A single composition (32 mol kg−1 KAc with 8 mol kg−1 NaAc) was reported in the literature, but the authors focused on the 20/7 binary, leaving the absolute optimum concentration potentially unexplored. The n = 1.7 value for mobile ions in the impedance model is a simplified parameter and may not perfectly represent the actual intercalation kinetics. The study does not report a random seed or specific training/split data as it is an experimental paper; however, the calibration of EIS parameters depends on specific cell geometry not fully detailed.

Claims
The 7N20K (7 mol kg−1 NaAc + 20 mol kg−1 KAc) electrolyte is the optimal WISE configuration for sodium-ion batteries among the concentrations tested. The 7N20K solution achieves 21.2 mS cm−1 conductivity at 25 °C, comparable to organic systems. The stability window extends up to 3 V in ideal conditions, suppressing hydrogen evolution. The liquidus temperature is low enough to prevent crystallization during cycling. A previous report investigated a different concentration (32 mol kg−1 KAc with 8 mol kg−1 NaAc), suggesting the absolute optimum might lie elsewhere. This composition could be the practical standard for aqueous sodium-ion battery electrolytes.
Aqueous acetate binary electrolytes enable practical sodium-ion battery operation with performance approaching organic electrolytes. CLTP in 7N20K shows 85 mAh g−1 first cycle anodic capacity and 90% retention after 60 cycles. Charge transfer activation energy is only 0.12 eV, indicating excellent kinetics. Comparison with 1 M NaAc shows a ~2.5× improvement in anodic capacity (85 vs 36 mAh g−1). The 85 mAh g−1 capacity is still significantly lower than typical organic electrolyte sodium-ion cell capacities, indicating performance gap remains. Aqueous systems offer a feasible path toward safe, low-cost sodium-ion batteries.

Data And Code Availability
Supporting information is available free of charge, including shear stress vs. shear rate curves, XRPD patterns, SEM images, thermal analysis for NASICONs, and additional electrochemical characterization in organic electrolytes.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A comparison was conducted between the WISE electrolyte (7N20K) and the diluted 1 M NaAc electrolyte to isolate the effect of concentration on electrode performance. The pristine LiTi2(PO4)3 (LTP) was synthesized without glucose to confirm the role of carbon coating in enhancing conductivity. EIS measurements were performed at multiple temperatures (20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70 °C) to derive activation energies via Arrhenius plots, validating the temperature dependence. The GCPL protocol used a standardized current cycling sequence (0.1 C to 10 C and back) to ensure consistent comparison across different electrolyte concentrations.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 presents DSC thermograms showing Tg, cold crystallization, and melting endotherms for all four electrolyte compositions. Table 2 reports quantitative values for molar conductivity, activation energies, ionic conductivity, TO, and Tg for all electrolytes. Figure 2 shows temperature dependence of ionic conductivity (2a) and concentration dependence (2b) with VTF behavior. Figure 3 displays Arrhenius plot of viscosity (3a) and temperature dependence of viscosity (3b) confirming Newtonian fluid behavior. Figure 4 presents Walden plots (molar conductivity vs. fluidity) at different temperatures, classifying electrolytes as quasi-ideal. Figure 4b shows the Kohlrausch plot for the 7N20K electrolyte, extracting Λ₀ = 52.90 Ω cm² mol−1. Figure 5 presents LSV profiles showing electrochemical stability windows versus SHE. Table 3 summarizes cathodic and anodic decomposition potentials for all samples. Figure 7 shows C-rate performance (charge-discharge profiles) of CLTP in 7N20K and 1 M NaAc. Figure 8 shows EIS spectra of partially sodiated CLTP, displaying the depressed semicircle and Warburg tail. Figure 9 presents the Arrhenius plot of charge transfer resistance, yielding Ea = 0.12 eV.

Three Takeaways
1. The 7N20K aqueous acetate binary electrolyte (20 mol kg−1 KAc + 7 mol kg−1 NaAc) achieves a stable 3 V electrochemical window and 21.2 mS cm−1 conductivity, making it a viable WISE candidate for sodium-ion batteries. 2. The strongest evidence is the proof-of-concept battery demonstration where CLTP in 7N20K retained 90% capacity after 60 cycles with a charge transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV, outperforming the diluted electrolyte by over 2.4× in anodic capacity. 3. The future path involves optimizing the specific KAc/NaAc concentration ratio (beyond 7 mol kg−1 NaAc) and testing with full-cell configurations to confirm practical energy density and cycling longevity in sodium-ion devices.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper describes the development of a high-throughput screening (HTS) implementation of the freeze-float selection platform, expanding on a previous proof-of-concept system. The primary goal was to increase throughput and accuracy by introducing automated droplet generation, controlled-rate cooling, and semi-automated detection. The authors replaced manual repeat-pipetting with a Biomek 3000 robotic liquid handling system capable of dispensing 30 μL droplets into a 96-deep-well plate, theoretically enabling up to ~3,800 droplets at once. Monodispersity was confirmed via image analysis with a polydispersity of 9.2% (SD 2.86×10⁻⁵ / mean 3.10×10⁻⁴ m), leading to an expected nucleation temperature dispersion of ≤±0.09 °C. The cooling system was upgraded from a commodity freezer to an Asymptote VIA Freeze TM Research controlled-rate freezer (capable of precision down to -0.5 °C/min), holding up to 48×1 mL cryovials with 40 droplets each, increasing throughput by 38-fold (1920 droplets vs. 50). Key results include a significant improvement in temperature uniformity: the cell-to-cell thermal gradient was reduced from p = 4.4×10⁻⁷ at constant temperature (-28 °C) to p = 0.31 with linear cooling (-0.25 °C/min). In the controlled-rate freezer, interwell freezing temperature dispersion was 36% lower (p = 0.83, SD 0.73 vs. p = 0.31, SD 1.6 in the 96-well plate). INA droplets froze at -7.1 ±0.59 °C while non-INA droplets froze at -12.3 °C. A notable limitation was that droplets were unstable during transfer between laboratories due to static-electricity-induced coalescence, despite precautions including wet filter paper and an Ion Pump. The paper concludes that the integrated system significantly improves upon the previous iteration in efficiency, uniformity, and accuracy, though transferability remains an issue.

Research Context
The previous proof-of-concept freeze-float system accommodated up to 50 × 1 μL droplets in a 1 cm² cuvette. Low thermal conductivity of silicone oil prevented scaling up the footprint without significant thermal lag. Parallel setups of more than 5–10 cuvettes resulted in non-uniform results, with differences of a few degrees between cuvettes. Polydispersity in droplet emulsions is detrimental because freezing temperature is proportional to the logarithm of diameter. Swanson and co-worker showed a 2.3 °C difference in mean freezing temperature between 1 mm and 0.1 mm diameter droplets. Interfacing microfluidic uniform droplets with microtiter well plates for HTS was noted as not trivial. From statistical calculations, more than 30 droplets are required to observe a reliable freezing temperature.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central objective was to expand the freeze-float system to higher throughput and accuracy through automated generation and uniform temperature cooling. The first hypothesis was that a robotic liquid handling system would replace manual pipetting while maintaining monodispersity for quantitative detection. The second hypothesis was that a controlled-rate freezer (Asymptote VIA) would reduce cell-to-cell thermal gradients compared to commodity freezer or static temperature. The authors predicted that increasing the assay footprint from 50 to 1920 droplets would increase throughput by 38-fold. The stochastic freezing behavior hypothesis states that nucleation is a random process accelerated by INA, requiring a spread of freezing temperatures. Linear cooling rate was hypothesized to be important for the stochastic model of heterogeneous nucleation measurement. The system aimed to add functional advantages including increased efficiency, increased accuracy due to larger sample size, and increased uniformity of temperature distribution.

Methodological Details
The 96-deep-well plate was tested as the initial platform compatible with the Biomek 3000 robotic system. The silicone oil buoyant layer contained 1% silicone surfactant with an HFE-7500 cushion layer. 30 μL droplets were dispensed into the silicone oil layer of the 96-deep-well plate using Biomek 3000. At a standard rate of 1 droplet per 2 seconds, 40 droplets were generated in 96 wells in ~15 minutes. Monodispersity was assessed using 60 droplets with fluorescein dye in a 12-well plate. The droplet diameters were measured using Matlab automated circle detection program Droplet_Dispersion.m. The standard deviation of droplet radii was 2.86×10⁻⁵ m against a mean radius of 3.10×10⁻⁴ m. Calculated polydispersity was 9.2%, indicating sufficiently uniform volume for quantitative detection. To eliminate coalescence, HFE-7500 was placed as a bottom cushion layer. Static electricity from Biomek 3000 was mitigated using Auto-set Ion Pump (#19500, Charles Water). Wet filter paper was placed below the plastic plate when moving the droplet system. The Biomek 3000 successfully prepared 30 droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax colored with yellow fluorescein dye.

Procedures And Architectures
The Biomek 3000 robotic liquid transfer system replaced manual repeat pipetting for parallel droplet generation. A simple modification to the Biomek program allowed changing parameters of droplet generation including number and size. For temperature uniformity, the 96-deep-well plate freezing was first tested in a commodity freezer at constant -28 °C. The Asymptote VIA Freeze TM Research controlled-rate freezer was employed for the 48-cryovial setup. Each cryovial contained 50 μL HFE-7500, 1 mL silicone oil with 1% surfactant, 20 aqueous droplets (1 mg/mL Snomax + fluorescein), and 20 INA-free droplets (Coomassie Brilliant Blue). A metal cooling plate and sample holder were used to achieve homogeneous cooling through the vial-to-vial. The Asymptote instrument provides constant rate cooling with high precision down to -0.5 °C/min. A custom-made glass lid enabled automated image recording by generic digital camera. Python script KStest.ipynb (Source Code S3) was used to compare freezing temperature distributions via Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Droplet_Dispersion.m (Source Code S1) was used for automated circle detection and diameter analysis.

Key Results
The 96-well system showed cell-to-cell thermal gradient with p = 4.4×10⁻⁷ at constant -28 °C in a generic freezer. With linear cooling of -0.25 °C/min, the thermal gradient decreased to p = 0.31, but freezing time range increased with means of 47.4 and 50.6 min. In the Asymptote freezer, INA droplets froze at -7.1 ±0.59 °C, while non-INA droplets did not freeze until -12.3 °C. In a commodity freezer at mean temperature -7.5 ±0.97 °C, the controlled-rate cooling showed better detection of INA. The 96-well deep plate showed interwell freezing time dispersion with p = 0.31 and standard deviation 1.6. The Asymptote freezer showed less well-to-well freezing temperature difference with p = 0.83 and standard deviation 0.73. Overall freezing temperature dispersion was 36% lower in the Asymptote freezer compared to the 96-deep-well system. The freeze-float validation with Biomek 3000 showed INA droplets with good agreement to the previous report. The polydispersity of 9.2% led to expected nucleation temperature dispersion no more than ±0.09 °C.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The improved cell-to-cell uniformity (p = 0.31 to p = 0.83) suggests that controlled-rate cooling more effectively overcomes silicone oil's low thermal conductivity. The stochastic model requires a larger sample size (>30 droplets) to extract a reliable freezing temperature from the inherent distribution of nucleation temperatures. The 38-fold throughput increase demonstrates that the freeze-float method is viable for large-scale screening of ice-nucleating entities. The 36% reduction in dispersion confirms that the instrument-specific metal holder and linear cooling stabilize the thermal environment across all vials.

Contradictions And Limitations
Droplet stability was insufficient when the system was transferred certain distances (e.g., from one laboratory to another). Static electricity caused by friction caused coalescing during transport, rendering it unsuccessful to combine with a droplet generation system. Linear cooling improved thermal gradient uniformity (p = 0.31) but significantly increased the range of freezing time, with mean differences of 3.2 min between cells. The paper mentions the 96-well system could theoretically generate up to ~3,800 droplets but notes the rate can be further accelerated by a multi-head dispenser, implying the ~3,800 figure is for single-head operation.

Claims
The Biomek 3000 enables automated parallel droplet generation in multi-well plates that replaces manual pipetting while maintaining droplet monodispersity. The Biomek 3000 successfully generated 40 uniform droplets in 96 wells in ~15 minutes at 1 droplet per 2 seconds. Polydispersity was measured at 9.2% (SD 2.86×10⁻⁵ / mean 3.10×10⁻⁴ m), supporting sufficient volume uniformity. Validation with 30 droplets of 1 mg/mL Snomax showed freezing behavior in good agreement with the previous report. Droplets were unstable during transport, with static electricity causing coalescence. Droplet generation can be automated but the system is not yet portable; additional stabilization measures or a different design are needed for transfer.
The Asymptote VIA controlled-rate freezer reduces cell-to-cell thermal gradient and interwell freezing temperature dispersion compared to constant-temperature or generic freezer cooling. Thermal gradient at constant -28 °C was p = 4.4×10⁻⁷, while with linear cooling it improved to p = 0.31. The interwell freezing temperature in the Asymptote freezer had p = 0.83 (SD 0.73) vs. p = 0.31 (SD 1.6) in the 96-well generic freezer. Overall freezing temperature dispersion was 36% lower in the Asymptote freezer. Linear cooling significantly increased the range of freezing time, with mean differences of 3.2 min (47.4 vs. 50.6 min) between cells. The tradeoff between uniformity and freezing time range suggests that while the Asymptote freezer is superior for temperature accuracy, it introduces a temporal spread that may affect kinetic analysis.

Data And Code Availability
Source code for droplet dispersion analysis is provided as Source Code S1 (Droplet_Dispersion.m). Python script for K-S test is provided as Source Code S3 (KStest.ipynb).

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The uniformity of the 96-well platform was tested under both constant temperature and linear cooling conditions. Monodispersity was validated on a separate 12-well plate with fluorescein-labeled droplets. The cooling setup was compared across commodity freezer, 96-well plate, and Asymptote freezer systems. Static electricity was addressed using both an active Ion Pump and passive wet filter paper.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 A-B shows the 96-deep-well plate compatible with Biomek 3000, Figure 1C fluorescein-labeled droplets, Figure 1D-E droplet diameter measurements, Figure 2 freeze-float validation in commodity freezer, Figure 3 cell-to-cell thermal gradient in 96-well, Figure 4 INA freezing in Asymptote freezer, Figure 5 freezing temperature distribution in 96-well plate, Figure 6 lower dispersion in Asymptote freezer.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the integration of a robotic liquid dispenser (Biomek 3000) and a controlled-rate freezer (Asymptote VIA) to achieve a 38-fold throughput increase in freeze-float ice nucleation screening while maintaining droplet monodispersity and improving temperature uniformity. 2. The strongest evidence is the reduction of cell-to-cell thermal gradient from p = 4.4×10⁻⁷ (constant temperature) to p = 0.83 (controlled-rate freezer), with 36% lower freezing temperature dispersion and INA droplets freezing at -7.1 ±0.59 °C versus non-INA at -12.3 °C. 3. The future path requires resolving the droplet stability issue during transfer (static-electricity-induced coalescence) and further optimizing the trade-off between temperature uniformity and freezing time spread introduced by linear cooling.

summary.title: Dimeric cyclobutane formation under continuous flow conditions using organophotoredox catalysed [2+2]-cycloaddition
summary.authors: Helena F Grantham; Marc C Kimber; M F C Grantham; Kimber
summary.field_subfield: Organic Chemistry / Photoredox Catalysis and Continuous Flow Synthesis
summary.executive_summary: This study develops a continuous flow protocol for the organophotoredox-catalyzed [2+2]-cycloaddition of electron-rich alkenes, specifically vinyl carbazoles and styrenes, to synthesize dimeric cyclobutanes. The authors merge homogenous small-molecule organophotoredox catalysis (pyrillium-based) with a commercial off-the-shelf continuous flow platform to address the limitations of traditional batch organophotoredox dimerization, which suffered from excessive reaction times, cryogenic temperature requirements, and relatively high catalyst loadings (3 mol%). The batch synthesis of 1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane (t-DCzCB) using 3 mol% of the organophotoredox catalyst yielded 82% with deoxygenated acetone and cryogenic temperatures. In contrast, the continuous flow synthesis of 1 achieved 79% isolated yield at 0.1 mol% catalyst loading on a 10 mmol scale, with significantly reduced reaction times and without cryogenic conditions. Optimization revealed a yield of 93% at 1 mol% catalyst loading and 79% at 2 mol% catalyst loading under the optimal flow rate conditions. The scope was extended to a series of bromo-substituted vinyl carbazoles, providing 65% yield for 3-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole, 71% for 3,6-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole, 65% for the 4-fluoroarylated vinyl carbazole, and 57% for the tetra-alkyl substituted cyclobutyl dimer. Additionally, the method was applied to electron-rich styrenes, producing the lignan magnosalin at 40% yield on a 10 mmol scale with 0.25 eq. anthracene electron relay. The study demonstrates that continuous flow conditions outperform batch conditions in both chemical yield and time efficiency for this transformation, with reaction completions attainable in under 1 hour under flow versus significantly longer periods in batch.

claims.description: The continuous flow protocol achieves t-DCzCB with reduced catalyst loading and no cryogenic temperatures compared to batch organophotoredox conditions.
The methodology extends to a new class of functional carbazole cyclobutanes with various substitution patterns.
The method provides a scalable synthesis of the natural product magnosalin via styrene dimerization in continuous flow.

Research Context
Electron-rich alkene dimerization provides a convenient synthetic route to valuable cyclobutane functional materials and natural products. Vinyl carbazole is a monomer for conductive polymers and a precursor for t-DCzCB, a host material for blue electrophosphorescence and PhOLEDs. Naturally occurring styrenes such as E-asarone are precursors of dimeric cyclobutyl natural products including the anti-inflammatory lignan magnosalin. The synthesis is accomplished via radical cation-induced [2+2]-cycloaddition where the alkene radical cation intermediate is generated by chemical oxidation or photochemical methods. Chemical oxidation using Fe(III) salts, Ce(IV) salts, and Helquats has achieved dimerization of vinyl carbazole to t-DCzCB. Photochemical dimerization was first reported in 1965 using organophotosensitizers, and later TiO2 photodimerization was achieved. Visible light photoredox catalysis with Ru- and Ir-complexes demonstrated effectiveness in synthesizing symmetrical and unsymmetrical cyclobutanes. Nicewicz and coworkers reported dimerization using a pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst, but reaction times were excessive, cryogenic conditions were required, and catalyst loadings of 3 mol% were high compared to 0.025% for metal-based systems. Continuous flow technology offers advantages in photoredox transformations by providing more efficient irradiation of starting substrates leading to higher conversions. A heterogeneous photoredox fixed-bed flow process using metal-free polymeric carbon nitrides was reported for magnosalin through E-aserone dimerization. The gap addressed is the lack of efficient continuous flow protocols for organophotoredox catalyzed dimerization of electron-rich alkenes.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether merging homogenous organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow technology can provide a convenient synthetic route to t-DCzCB and a new class of functional materials. The authors hypothesize that continuous flow will improve the dimerization reaction by providing more efficient irradiation, reducing reaction times, and eliminating the need for cryogenic temperatures compared to batch organophotoredox conditions. They predicted that a new class of functional materials possessing functionality would be accessible and that improved synthetic routes to styrene-based lignan natural products could be realized. They anticipated this would provide a convenient, environmentally beneficial methodology showcasing the advantages of continuous flow over conventional batch chemistry. A sub-hypothesis was that the catalyst loading could be reduced to levels approaching Ru-based systems (0.025 mol%) while maintaining synthetic utility. The study aimed to demonstrate that the methodology is robust, general, and scalable for both carbazole-based host materials and styrene-based natural products.

Methodological Details
The batch synthesis of t-DCzCB was achieved using 3 mol% of the organophotoredox catalyst 10 in deoxygenated acetone at cryogenic temperatures. The continuous flow synthesis optimization was conducted using a commercial off-the-shelf continuous flow platform. Optimization required calibration of substrates 2 and 1, with full details in the supporting information. The optimal continuous flow conditions for t-DCzCB were 0.5 mL/min flow rate (tau = 20 min), 2 mol% catalyst loading at 450 nm irradiation. Substrate expansion was centered on synthesizing brominated t-DCzCB substrates as potential building blocks for transition metal cross coupling. Vinyl carbazoles (12a-24a) were synthesized using the method of Obora and coworkers, providing moderate to good yields. The only exception was 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (15a), which yielded very low isolation. Continuous flow dimerizations for brominated substrates used a reduced concentration of 0.2 M in acetone due to solubility challenges. Batch conditions for 12a required 5 days for dimerization. Continuous flow for 12a at 0.2 mL/min (tau = 50 min) provided improved yield. Electron-rich styrenes were tested in continuous flow with anthracene or diethylaniline as electron relays. E-aserone dimerization was performed on a 10 mmol scale with anthracene as an electron relay. The continuous flow reaction was performed at 1.00 mmol of 2 at 0.4 M in acetone.

Procedures And Architectures
The organophotoredox catalyst employed is a pyrillium-based catalyst (catalyst 10), a homogenous small molecule. The catalyst loading was varied from 1 mol% to 4.5 mol% in optimization experiments. Irradiation wavelengths probed included 450 nm, 405 nm, and 420 nm. Flow rates varied from 0.1 mL/min (tau = 100 min) to 5 mL/min (tau = 2 mL/min context). HPLC analysis with p-terphenyl as an internal standard was used for quantitative tracking. NMR analysis (1H NMR) was used for detection of products and checking for reversibility. The palladium-mediated Suzuki cross coupling of 13b with 4-methoxybenzene boronic acid used conditions of Kumar and Tao for conversion to 25. Palladium-mediated borylation with bis(pinacolato)diboron was used for conversion to 26. Electron relays were added to the starting solution of the styrene before introduction into the continuous flow apparatus. For the styrene substrates, 0.25 eq. of anthracene was used as the electron relay. Vinylation of 3,6-di-tert-butylcarbazole gave 23a in quantitative yields before dimerization.

Key Results
Batch synthesis of t-DCzCB at 3 mol% catalyst loading in deoxygenated acetone at cryogenic temperatures provided 82% isolated yield. Optimal continuous flow synthesis of t-DCzCB (0.5 mL/min, 2 mol% cat, 450 nm) achieved 93% yield (Table 1, entry 1). At 4.5 mol% catalyst loading, yield modestly reduced to 90% (entry 2). At 1 mol% catalyst loading, yield was 93% (entry 3). Lowering flow rate to 2 mL/min with 2 mol% catalyst reduced yield to 79% (entry 4). Lowering flow rate to 2 mL/min with 1 mol% catalyst gave 82% yield (entry 5). Flow rate of 0.1 mL/min (tau = 100 min) reduced yield of 1 to 53% (entry 6). Significant carbazole formation was observed in entry 6, attributed to background oxidation by adventitious oxygen. Flow rate of 0.5 mL/min with 405 nm or 420 nm irradiation provided comparable yields to 450 nm (entries 7 and 8). Dimerization did not proceed in the absence of catalyst (entry 9) or irradiation (entry 10). On a 10 mmol scale of 2 using 0.1 mol% of 10 at 0.5 mL/min, t-DCzCB was obtained in 79% isolated yield (entry 11). For 3-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (12a), batch gave 48% isolated yield (5 days); continuous flow at 0.2 mL/min gave 64% yield. For 3,6-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole (16a), continuous flow provided 65% isolated yield. For 2-chloro-9-vinylcarbazole (18a), continuous flow gave 61% yield; 2-methoxy-9-vinylcarbazole (19a) gave 45% yield. Bis-vinylated 2-hydroxycarbazole (20a) gave cyclobutyl bis-enolether in 25% isolated yield. The 4-fluoroarylated vinyl carbazole (22a) gave 65% isolated yield of 22b. The tetra-alkyl substituted cyclobutyl dimer 23b was obtained in 57% yield. The 3,6-bisarylated cyclobutane 24b was obtained in 50% yield. Palladium Suzuki coupling of 13b gave 25 in 75% yield. Palladium borylation gave 26 in 36% yield. 4-methoxy styrene (27) in continuous flow gave 28 in 44% isolated yield. Styrene (29) with diethylaniline gave pellucidin A in 22% isolated yield. E-aserone (3) on 10 mmol scale with anthracene gave magnosalin (4) in 40% isolated yield. Generally, under continuous flow conditions, completion could be attained in under 1 hour, whereas batch required significantly more time.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The formation of carbazole in entry 6 was attributed to background oxidation of 2 by adventitious oxygen within the flow system, facilitated by extended residence time. The reduced yield at long residence times (tau = 100 min) suggests potential reversibility of the dimerization reaction in continuous flow. The advantage of continuous flow lies in more efficient irradiation of starting substrates, leading to higher conversions compared to batch. The results demonstrate that the organophotoredox/continuous flow combination can deliver both novel cyclobutane host materials with functionality and styrene-based natural products. The method enables the synthesis of cyclobutanes that would otherwise be limited by the 3- and 6-position functionalization restriction in electrophilic aromatic substitution. The 0.1 mol% catalyst loading in flow nears the efficiencies of Ru-based systems (0.025 mol%), positioning organophotoredox catalysis as a competitive metal-free alternative.

Contradictions And Limitations
1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (15a) proved a very challenging substrate with no cyclobutane product detected by 1H NMR under both batch and continuous flow. The solubility of all vinyl carbazole substrates in acetone at 0.4 M was challenging, necessitating reduction to 0.2 M for the expanded scope. For 2,7-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole (17a), the batch reaction slightly outperformed the continuous flow conditions, contrary to the general flow advantage. The isolated yield for the bis-vinylated product 20a in 25% was modest, indicating reduced chemoselectivity or conversion for this specific substrate. The 2-arylated cyclobutane 21b showed only 22% isolated yield, attributed to poor solubility of 21a in acetone. The 3,6-bisarylated cyclobutane 24b gave only a modest yield of 50%. The authors note that the 10 mmol scale is a demonstration of scalability but the specific flow channel diameter or reactor volume is not explicitly detailed in the text.

Claims
The continuous flow protocol achieves t-DCzCB with reduced catalyst loading and no cryogenic temperatures compared to batch organophotoredox conditions. Batch synthesis required deoxygenated acetone and cryogenic temperatures with 3 mol% catalyst. Flow synthesis at 0.1 mol% achieved 79% yield on 10 mmol scale without cryogenic conditions. Reaction completion under flow was attainable in under 1 hour. At the most extended residence time (tau = 100 min), yield dropped to 53%, and carbazole formed by background oxidation. 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole failed to produce any cyclobutane under either condition. The method provides a scalable, metal-free route to host materials for OLED technologies. Catalyst loadings of 0.1 mol% approach the performance of Ru-based systems (0.025 mol%).
The methodology extends to a new class of functional carbazole cyclobutanes with various substitution patterns. 3-bromo, 3,6-dibromo, 2-chloro, and 2-methoxy vinyl carbazoles were all dimerized with yields of 64%, 65%, 61%, and 45%. The 4-fluoroarylated substrate gave 65% yield, the tetra-alkyl dimer 57% yield, and the bisarylated dimer 50% yield. Bis-vinylated product provided two enol ether handles for post-modification or polymerization. 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole produced no cyclobutane product. 2,7-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole showed the batch reaction slightly outperforming continuous flow. The functionality allows for exploitation as novel functional materials beyond electrophilic aromatic substitution limits.
The method provides a scalable synthesis of the natural product magnosalin via styrene dimerization in continuous flow. E-aserone was dimerized on a 10 mmol scale to magnosalin in 40% isolated yield. No cryogenic temperatures were required and time periods were significantly shorter than batch. The yield of 40% is lower than the batch yield of 22%? No, wait—batch was lower. Actually, the text says 40% yield for flow. Let me re-read: 40% isolated yield in flow; batch was 22% with diethylaniline. No contradiction here. Demonstrates distinct advantages over traditional batch chemistry including scalability.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Flow rate was varied from 5 mL/min to 2 mL/min to 0.1 mL/min to probe potential reversibility, showing yield decrease from 93% to 53%. Irradiation wavelengths of 405 nm and 420 nm were tested alongside 450 nm, giving comparable yields. Dimerization was tested in the absence of catalyst and absence of irradiation to confirm requirements. Three flow rates were trialed for the brominated substrate 12a at 0.2 mL/min. The electron relay anthracene was tested at 0.25 eq. for the styrene dimerization.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 (Optimization study) shows flow rate, catalyst loading, wavelength, and isolated yield (%) for the VCZ to t-DCzCB dimerization with A (yield), B (conditions), C (10 mmol scale 0.1 mol% cat, 79%), D (blank). Scheme 1 shows cyclobutane dimers as functional materials and natural products. Scheme 2 illustrates the radical cation-induced [2+2]-cycloaddition mechanism and the two generation methods. Scheme 3 shows the merged organophotoredox and continuous flow protocol for t-DCzCB and lignans. Scheme 4 shows the batch vs flow comparison for VCZ dimerization with Table 1. Scheme 5 shows the synthesis of brominated t-DCzCB substrates and their dimerization in batch vs flow. Scheme 6 shows palladium-mediated post-modification of bromocyclobutanes to products 25 and 26. Scheme 7 shows the extension to electron-rich styrenes and E-aserone.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is merging homogenous organophotoredox catalysis with a commercial continuous flow platform to deliver cyclobutane host materials and natural products with reduced catalyst loadings and time. 2. The strongest evidence is the reduction of catalyst loading from 3 mol% in batch to 0.1 mol% in flow for t-DCzCB, while maintaining 79% yield on a 10 mmol scale without cryogenic temperatures. 3. The future path involves exploiting the functionality of the new cyclobutane class as photophysical host materials and continuing expansion into further natural product and material targets.

summary.title: A New Organocatalytic Desymmetrization Reaction Enables the Enantioselective Total Synthesis of Madangamine E
summary.authors: Shinya Shiomi; Benjamin D A Shennan; Ken Yamazaki; Ángel L Fuentes De Arriba; Dhananjayan Vasu; Trevor A Hamlin; Darren J Dixon
summary.field_subfield: Synthetic Organic Chemistry / Total Synthesis
summary.executive_summary: This paper reports the 30-step enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E, a complex marine natural product, enabled by a novel organocatalytic desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition. The key reaction converts a prochiral 4-aminocyclohexanone derivative bearing a tethered β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin into a bicyclic nitroalkane in near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity (99% ee, single diastereomer), concurrently establishing three stereogenic centers including a quaternary carbon. The reaction was developed using Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst 9f at 20 mol% loading in dichloromethane with benzoic acid co-catalyst. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations rationalized the enantioselectivity by identifying TS1 as the most energetically favorable transition structure (ΔΔG‡ = 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹ above the next lowest energy TS), corresponding to the experimental 99% ee. The total synthesis proceeded through a scalable route to the nitroolefin precursor, an oxidative lactamization, a two-step Z-selective olefination of a sterically hindered ketone, and ring-closing metathesis. The macrocyclic E ring was closed via Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation catalyst in PhMe at 110 °C with p-benzoquinone, yielding the diamide in 71% yield. The strategy demonstrates that a single early chirality-inducing step can set all stereochemical information in the madangamine ABC-ring system. The route was validated by X-ray diffraction confirming absolute configurations and by analytical data consistent with Chida and Sato's previous work.

claims.description: A novel, highly enantioselective organocatalytic desymmetrization reaction of β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefins constructs a chiral bicyclic core in near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity, establishing three stereogenic centers concurrently.
The 30-step enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E demonstrates the utility of organocatalytic desymmetrization as a key enabling strategy.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper reports the 30-step enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E, a complex marine natural product, enabled by a novel organocatalytic desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition. The key reaction converts a prochiral 4-aminocyclohexanone derivative bearing a tethered β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin into a bicyclic nitroalkane in near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity (99% ee, single diastereomer), concurrently establishing three stereogenic centers including a quaternary carbon. The reaction was developed using Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst 9f at 20 mol% loading in dichloromethane with benzoic acid co-catalyst. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations rationalized the enantioselectivity by identifying TS1 as the most energetically favorable transition structure (ΔΔG‡ = 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹ above the next lowest energy TS), corresponding to the experimental 99% ee. The total synthesis proceeded through a scalable route to the nitroolefin precursor, an oxidative lactamization, a two-step Z-selective olefination of a sterically hindered ketone, and ring-closing metathesis. The macrocyclic E ring was closed via Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation catalyst in PhMe at 110 °C with p-benzoquinone, yielding the diamide in 71% yield. The strategy demonstrates that a single early chirality-inducing step can set all stereochemical information in the madangamine ABC-ring system. The route was validated by X-ray diffraction confirming absolute configurations and by analytical data consistent with Chida and Sato's previous work.

Research Context
The madangamine family, isolated from Xestospongia genus sea sponges, possesses a complex pentacyclic fused-ring system with two nitrogen atoms. All family members share a common diazatricyclic ABC ring core and a macrocyclic E ring. Prior to this work, only two total syntheses of madangamine family members and one formal synthesis of madangamine A had been reported. Amat's 2014 synthesis used a stereoselective cyclocondensation of phenylglycinol to establish a bicyclic BC scaffold. Chida and Sato's 2017 synthesis of madangamines A, C, and E used an N-acyl-iminium cyclization of an octahydronaphthyridine. A gap remained: intramolecular desymmetrizing variants that concurrently establish a quaternary carbon center via nitroolefins were unreported. Natural products are forecast to play a prominent role in the future of medicinal chemistry.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question was whether a catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization of β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefins could access the madangamine AC bicyclic motif. The authors hypothesized that the AC bicyclic motif would be well-suited for construction from a desymmetrization reaction, providing a rigid scaffold for further elaboration. A secondary hypothesis was that intramolecular desymmetrization with nitroolefins, which establishes a quaternary carbon center, was synthetically viable and could be controlled enantioselectively. The predicted outcome was a reaction yielding a chiral bicyclic core in near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity, enabling the total synthesis of madangamine E in 30 steps.

Methodological Details
The key substrate was a 4-aminocyclohexanone derivative (6) bearing a tethered β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin. A range of chiral single enantiomer primary and secondary amine organocatalysts (9a-9k) including trans-cyclohexanediamine and proline-derived scaffolds were screened. The reaction was performed in dichloromethane at 20 mol% catalyst loading with benzoic acid as a co-catalyst. Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst 9f gave the bicyclic adduct 8 in 70% yield as a single diastereomer in 99% ee. A simplified bifunctional primary amine catalyst 9e gave 8 in 51% yield in 96% ee. The route to nitroolefin 17 required a new high-yielding scalable sequence starting from 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal. Selenoxide elimination for nitroolefin installation proceeded in 52% yield over 3 steps with E:Z = 3.8:1. The optimal solvent mixture for selenoxide elimination was Et2O:CH2Cl2 (2:1, 0.03£M). The bicyclic nitroalkane 18 was obtained from 17E in 95% yield and >99% ee on a >5g scale. The total synthesis was completed in 30 steps from simple achiral starting materials.

Procedures And Architectures
The reaction pathway begins with primary amine addition to the ketone forming hemiaminal Int1, followed by water elimination to imine Int2. Tautomerization of imine Int2 produces enamine Int3, the nucleophile for the Michael addition. The stereoselectivity-determining C-C bond forming intramolecular Michael addition proceeds through TS1, yielding iminium-nitronate Int4. The reaction is highly exergonic with ΔGrxn = -19.4 kcal mol⁻¹ and the step is irreversible. DFT calculations identified 16 possible transition structures for the Michael addition step. TS1 is the most energetically favorable by ΔΔG‡ = 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹ over the second-lowest structure, matching the experimental 99% ee. The bicyclic ketone 20 was protected as methyl enol ether 19 using p-toluenesulfonic acid in methanol. Nicolaou's IBX-NMO-mediated oxidation of ketone 20 gave enone 21 in moderate yield. Wittig homologation used (methoxymethyl)triphenylphosphonium chloride and NaHMDS as base with a saturated aqueous NH4Cl quench at 60 °C for 3 hours to improve yield from 26% to 86%. Oxidative lactamization was performed with AZADO, copper chloride, 2,2'-bipyridine, and DMAP under air to close ring B. RCM of 25 used Grubbs 1st generation catalyst in CH2Cl2 at 40 °C under high dilution to close ring D in 82% yield. Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation catalyst in PhMe at 110 °C with p-benzoquinone as co-catalyst closed the E ring in 71% yield. The final double amide reduction used excess LiAlH4 in Et2O to give synthetic madangamine E in 72% yield.

Key Results
Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst 9f afforded bicyclic adduct 8 in 70% yield, a single diastereomer in 99% ee, confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction. A simplified bifunctional catalyst 9e gave 8 in 51% yield in 96% ee, indicating a narrow catalyst structure allowance. In the model substrate 7, the intramolecular Michael addition is highly exergonic with ΔGrxn = -19.4 kcal mol⁻¹. TS1 is 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹ lower in energy than the next-lowest TS, corresponding to the experimental 99% ee, in excellent agreement with DFT. The new route to nitroolefin 17 provided multigram quantities of the desired β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin. Treatment of 17E with 20 mol% 9f gave bicyclic nitroalkane 18 in 95% yield, >99% ee, on >5g scale. The Wittig homologation yield improved from 26% to 86% upon adopting a rigorous NH4Cl quench at 60 °C for 3 hours. The RCM closure of the D ring afforded tetracyclic enone 26 in 82% yield. The Hoveyda-Grubbs RCM gave diamide 30 in 71% yield, with the spatial organization of alkenes noted as a critical factor. The final reduction gave synthetic madangamine E in 72% yield with analytical data consistent with prior reports.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The catalytic cycle is rationalized by a cooperative push/pull-type mechanism where TS1 is stabilized by multiple hydrogen bonding interactions with the thiourea, nitro group, and enamine moieties. The stereoselectivity is determined by the deprotonation preference: for nitroolefins, the enolate is deactivated relative to the nitronate (pKa difference), making the intramolecular mechanism favorable. The early introduction of chirality via desymmetrization sets all three stereogenic centers, including the quaternary carbon, in a single step. The results demonstrate that organocatalytic desymmetrization is an enabling strategy for rapidly generating stereochemical complexity in high-value natural products. The spatial arrangement of alkenes profoundly affects RCM outcome, suggesting that the orientation of terminal alkenes dictates cyclization success.

Contradictions And Limitations
Most tested catalysts (9a-9d, 9g-9k) failed to provide the desired product, yielding complex mixtures instead of the cyclized bicyclic adduct. The standard Wittig homologation under initial conditions gave only 26% yield, requiring modification of the quench procedure. Amat's Wittig reaction of an octenoate phosphonium salt failed despite extensive experimentation, attributed to differing bond geometries and increased deprotonation competition in ketone 3. The RCM attempt to form the macrocyclic E ring directly failed due to distant spatial arrangement of terminal alkenes, requiring a change in order of operations. The reaction to ketones 3 resisted almost all trialled conditions, with deprotonation consistently out-competing desired functionalization. The selenoxide elimination was highly solvent-dependent, and only Et2O:CH2Cl2 (2:1) gave sufficient efficiency.

Claims
A novel, highly enantioselective organocatalytic desymmetrization reaction of β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefins constructs a chiral bicyclic core in near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity, establishing three stereogenic centers concurrently. Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst 9f gave the bicyclic adduct 8 in 70% yield as a single diastereomer in 99% ee. TS1 is 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹ more stable than the next lowest TS, in excellent agreement with the experimental 99% ee. The bicyclic nitroalkane 18 was obtained in 95% yield and >99% ee on a >5g scale. Most tested catalysts yielded complex mixtures rather than the cyclized product. The simplified catalyst 9e gave only 51% yield in 96% ee, indicating a narrow catalyst scope. This reaction provides a new method for constructing stereogenic quaternary carbon centers from nitroolefins. The early introduction of chirality enables the rapid generation of structural complexity in natural product synthesis.
The 30-step enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E demonstrates the utility of organocatalytic desymmetrization as a key enabling strategy. The synthesis was completed in 30 steps from simple achiral starting materials. The final product matched analytical data of Chida and Sato and the isolation team. The route included scalable steps like the 17 g scale organozinc-copper Michael addition. The macrocyclic E ring RCM failed on the first attempt, requiring a change in the sequence of events. The ketone 3 functionalization required Ishihara's triorganozincates because Amat's Wittig failed. The strategy highlights the potential of organocatalysis for the synthesis of high-value saturated molecular scaffolds. Future macrocyclization campaigns should be guided by the spatial organization of reacting alkenes.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A catalyst screening of 11 primary and secondary amine catalysts showed only two (9f, 9e) gave the desired product, highlighting a narrow structure allowance. The model substrate 7 was validated by DFT calculations, with 16 transition structures searched and the mechanism confirmed to be push/pull-type. The selenoxide elimination efficiency was tested across solvent mixtures, identifying Et2O:CH2Cl2 (2:1, 0.033M) as optimal. The Wittig homologation was tested under standard conditions (26% yield) versus a rigorous quench (86% yield), validating the protocol modification. The RCM of ketone 3 was tested using Amat's Wittig conditions, then Ishihara's triorganozincate reagents, and finally the alternative route through intermediate 27.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the pentacyclic fused-ring system of the madangamine family with two nitrogen atoms. Figure 1B illustrates the structures of madangamine A, D, and E, highlighting differences in the D ring. Figure 1C shows the retrosynthetic strategy for madangamine E. Figure 2A depicts the previously reported desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition to unsaturated esters. Figure 2B presents the catalytic cycle of the new desymmetrization reaction of nitroolefins. Figure 2C shows the computed DFT reaction pathway including intermediates Int1-Int7 and transition structures. Figure 3 displays the computed transition structures for the key stereoselectivity-determining step. Figure 4A shows the restructured route to nitroolefin 17. Figure 4B shows the application of the desymmetrization reaction in the synthesis of madangamine E.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a new organocatalytic desymmetrization of β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefins that constructs a bicyclic core with 99% ee, concurrently setting three stereocenters including a quaternary carbon. 2. The strongest evidence is the near-perfect enantioselectivity (99% ee, single diastereomer) of the bicyclic adduct 8, supported by both experimental X-ray diffraction and DFT calculations confirming the most stable transition structure (ΔΔG‡ = 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹). 3. The future path lies in applying catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization to other complex saturated molecular scaffolds and refining macrocyclization strategies based on alkene spatial organization.
