summary.title: Tuning the Dielectric Response in a NC Material through Nanoparticle Morphology
summary.authors: Archita Adluri; Brett Henderson; Irina Paci
summary.field_subfield: Computational Materials Science / Dielectric Physics
summary.type_of_paper: Theoretical/Computational study using Density Functional Theory (Car-Parinello Molecular Dynamics)
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates how the morphology (size, shape, and orientation) of molecular-scale silver nanoparticle inclusions in a magnesium oxide (MgO) matrix affects the dielectric response of the nanocomposite material. Using the Modern Theory of Polarization and Car-Parinello Molecular Dynamics (CPMD) within the Quantum Espresso framework, the authors model dielectric permittivity enhancements ranging from 30% to 100% with inclusion sizes between 8 and 32 atoms. Three rod-like and five disk-like silver inclusions are analyzed relative to their alignment (parallel or perpendicular) with an externally applied electric field. Key findings reveal that asymmetric inclusions provide orientation-dependent dielectric enhancements exceeding simple volume-ratio predictions; for instance, multi-layer disks show over 70% enhancement in dielectric permittivity at similar loading to rod-like counterparts. The study identifies that interfacial effects near the nanoparticle-matrix boundary—manifested as localized polarization fields and Born effective charge variations—dominate the dielectric response. Born effective charge maps demonstrate that perpendicular alignment produces significant depolarization extending over large cell regions, while parallel alignment localizes enhancement at the interface poles. The authors note that at <30 atoms, the nanoparticle's quantum behavior (polarizable electron density without a formal band structure) differs from bulk metallic behavior. A significant caveat is the periodic boundary condition artifact (quantum of polarization) that requires post-processing corrections. The work demonstrates that nanoscale dielectric engineering can be tuned via particle geometry rather than just concentration, with implications for high-k gate dielectrics, super-capacitors, and quantum computing components.

claims.description: Nanoparticle morphology (size, shape, and orientation) independently and synergistically determines the dielectric response of an Ag/MgO nanocomposite beyond simple volume-ratio predictions.

top_influential_citations.Exact Citation String (Rank 1): [1] (Previously cited work by the same group using Modern Theory of Polarization for Ag 8/MgO NC)
top_influential_citations.Detailed justification sentence explaini: This is the foundational prior work from the same group that first applied the Modern Theory of Polarization to Ag 8/MgO nanocomposites, establishing the methodology and the finding of significant interfacial effects that this current paper extends.

Spaldin's work on the quantum of polarization effect provides the theoretical framework for interpreting and correcting the charge jumps that occur in periodic CPMD simulations when electrons polarize across unit cell boundaries.

The Quantum Espresso code package provides the actual CPMD implementation, the underlying DFT engine, and the Modern Theory of Polarization functionality used to perform all polarization calculations in the study.

Car-Parinello Molecular Dynamics is the core electronic structure method used throughout the paper for both structural relaxation and polarization calculations, enabling the explicit modeling of ionic and electronic degrees of freedom.

These standard pseudopotentials provide the basis set approximations for Mg, O, and Ag atoms that enable efficient CPMD calculations within the DFT framework, directly enabling the study's computational tractability.

Research Context
The demand for new high-k dielectric materials is driven by energy storage and processing power reaching limits of single-phase materials. Nanocomposite materials combining a standard dielectric matrix with high/mid-k or conducting inclusions offer tunable dielectric and mechanical properties. The research identifies a specific need for tunable dielectric constants in transistors, super-capacitors, and quantum computing. Traditional Si/SiO2 gate manufacturing has reached limits where significant current leakage and tunnelling dominate at few-nanometer sizes. Prior studies have shown that even point defects at the atomic scale cause noticeable changes in polarization potential. Molecular nanoparticles (up to 100 atoms) bridge the gap between single-atom dopants and traditional nanoparticles with metallic properties. Effective medium approximations are suitable for macroscale mixtures but do not provide insight into quantum response and local field effects. A previous study by the group used the modern theory of polarization for Ag 8/MgO and found significant interfacial effects. The current work extends that study to explore effects of distribution and shape of mNP inclusions on dielectric capacity. The study targets the regime where size, shape, and orientation greatly alter inclusion electron behavior and atomic-scale polarization.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how the nanoparticle size, shape, and orientation relative to the applied field affect the dielectric permittivity of an Ag/MgO nanocomposite. The study hypothesizes that nanoparticle morphology will modulate the local electrostatic fields at the inclusion-matrix interface, thereby tuning the overall dielectric constant. It is predicted that asymmetric inclusions (rods, disks) will provide orientation-dependent dielectric enhancement exceeding predictions from simple volume ratios. The hypothesis extends to the quantum of polarization effect, where periodic boundary conditions introduce artificial charge jumps requiring mathematical correction. The authors anticipate that disk-like inclusions, with more moving electrons and greater space to polarize, will show higher polarization than similarly sized rods. A further hypothesis is that 2D nanoparticles (421, 441) will show decreased polarization when aligned perpendicular to the field because inclusion electrons are not free to move in the z-direction.

Methodological Details
The matrix material is magnesium oxide (MgO), a high-k metal-oxide gate dielectric with bulk dielectric constant of 8-9.8 and bandgap of 7.8 eV. MgO was chosen due to its cubic crystal structure, isotropic polarization, and low number of polarizable d-electrons from a computational standpoint. The nanoparticle inclusions consist of silver atoms built on an ideal Ag fcc lattice. Three rod-like inclusions and five disk-like inclusions were modeled. The specific rod inclusions are labeled Rod224, Rod223, and Rod12.48 (notably the text mentions a 224 rod and a 223 rod in the results). The specific disk inclusions are disks 332, 432, 442, 421, and 441. The matrix extended 2 MgO layers beyond the edge of the inclusion in each direction to keep the cell from conducting into its periodic image. The %loading ratios of inclusions to matrix were kept between 3-5% to allow sufficient matrix to separate periodic images of the mNP. Models were built using the Avogadro software. The inclusion atoms were treated such that volume occupied by an inclusion atom is, on average, the same as the volume occupied by individual matrix ions. Electronic structure calculations used LDA functional and CPMD in the Quantum Espresso code versions 6.0 and 6.6. Mg atoms were described using Bachelet-Hamann-Schluter norm-conserving pseudopotentials. O and Ag atoms used Rappe-Rabe-Kaxiras-Joannopoulos ultra-soft pseudopotentials from MaterialsCloud. A wavefunction cutoff of 50-60 Ry and charge density cutoff of 560 Ry were used. Total energy convergence criteria was increased from 10-4 to 10-8; force threshold of 10-4 was used. Electron masses were 300 a.u. then increased to 450 after initial damped minimizations to accelerate convergence. Brillouin zone was sampled at the Gamma point. Periodic boundary conditions were applied. A static field of 0.001 a.u. was applied along the z-axis for polarization calculations. No thermostat was applied, and temperatures were not controlled, as temperature effects were negligible. Test runs with thermostats between 200 and 600 K showed temperature effects on geometry were negligible.

Procedures And Architectures
The CPMD method in Quantum Espresso follows two major stages: structural relaxation and polarization. Relaxation involved: 1. Initial electron minimization with Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization; 2. Damped dynamics steps to allow ions and electrons to minimize fully; 3. Lattice vector relaxation to remove stress from the cell due to the inclusion. Low-frequency polarization calculation uses the Modern Theory of Polarization in a static field of 0.001 a.u applied along the z-axis. The reference polarization is the cell without an applied field. Electronic and ionic polarization is calculated using damped dynamics (P epsilon damped), showing mainly ionic polarization. After fully relaxing the electronic structure in the field (P epsilon relax), electronic polarization describes electrons moving into the Ag-MgO interface. Dielectric constant εr = 1 + 4π(P epsilon damped - P epsilon relax) / epsilon field. The values are volume averages over a periodic cell and are not true dielectric constants as surface charge and edge effects are not taken into account. The CPMD procedure is implemented in steps (Figure 5) including structural relaxation, electronic structure calculation, damped polarization, electronic response, and fully-relaxed static polarization. Born effective charges were calculated by computing the difference in force experienced by each atom under zero-field and static polarization. Forces were normalized to the bulk matrix to highlight the effect of the NP. The quantum of polarization correction addresses cases where explicit particle-like electrons polarize into the neighboring image cell, shifting polarization by n x box length. Mathematical corrections for polarization jumps are shown in Figure 6 for post-processing. Electronic structure calculations were carried out in a zero field environment prior to polarization steps.

Key Results
Inclusion of silver atoms distorted the local structure up to approximately 3 Angstroms from the edge of the mNP. The previous work on a single spherical Ag 8 mNP showed an ≈30% increase in εr with ≈4% mNP volume ratio. Dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30-100% were observed with inclusion sizes varying from 8 to 32 atoms. Rod-like and disk-like inclusions further enhanced the dielectric response beyond the spherical case. Multi-layer disks (disks 332, 432, 442) exhibit more than 70% enhancement in εr over the matrix permittivity at similar volume loading. For Rod224, ε parallel results in a greater increase from bulk at 9.23 than the perpendicular value. Disk442 has twice the x,y dimensions of Rod223 yet has a polarization increase of more than twice in comparison. Disk-shaped mNPs (332, 432, 442) all showed higher polarization than similarly sized rods due to more moving electrons with greater space to move. 2D nanoparticles (421 and 441) show a decrease in polarization compared to the bulk in both directions because inclusion electrons cannot move in the z-direction. Born effective charge maps for Rod224 show enhancement of the polarization field in matrix regions adjacent to the NP poles in the direction of the applied field. A depolarization region (red/yellow in BEC plots) arises in the equatorial region where the effective ionic charge is less than in the absence of external field. Perpendicular polarization shows a much larger depolarization field around the nanoparticle that never decays to the normal bulk values. The Born effective charges resemble an induced field on the nanoparticle with moving electrons throughout the simulation creating areas of higher and lower force. Parallel orientation: the 'reach' of the induced field is further physically and also stronger. Perpendicular orientation: the BEC converges to +2,-2 values of matrix in a very short distance, meaning a smaller field and lower average dielectric constant.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The Born effective charges reflect the influence of NP polarization on the charge distribution in the matrix ions, providing effective maps of the local electrostatic field. The induced field is strongly localized to two layers of matrix ions at the interface, while the depolarization field extends over larger regions. The shape of the nanoparticle influences the shape and reach of the induced polarization: parallel orientation has a longer-reaching and stronger induced field. The dielectric enhancement in general is more complex than simple correlation to mNP length; disk-shaped mNPs with fewer atoms can match or exceed rod-like counterparts. The electronic polarization is driven by silver d-electron polarization coupling to the oxygen p-band. The Wannerization of Wannier functions was attempted but nanoparticles larger than 8 atoms failed to converge due to high delocalization. Induced fields in nanoscale composites provide a pathway to understand quantum materials behavior as materials become smaller and more precise. The perpendicular response in the matrix can sometimes dominate, leading to a calculated dielectric constant lower than for the pure matrix. The nature of the induced field depends on electron dynamics as the metal atom polarizes.

Contradictions And Limitations
The calculated values for εr are volume averages over a periodic cell and do not account for surface charge and edge effects inherent in real finite materials. The periodic boundary conditions introduce quantum of polarization effects where charge shifts by n x box length, requiring post-processing corrections. The LDA functional is known to underestimate bandgaps; however, the authors note that most density of states near the Fermi level arises from NP states, mitigating the error for these systems. Wannier function localization was attempted but failed for nanoparticles larger than 8 atoms due to high delocalization and movement of Wannier centers. Computational constraints limit the study to nanoparticles up to 32 atoms; the authors suspect a threshold at which exponential growth changes as the inclusion behaves more metallic. The paper notes that %loading is not the only important factor; aggregation and separation of inclusions are also very important for actual material performance. The study does not explicitly report the random seed used for CPMD, nor specific training/test splits (non-applicable here) but the reproducibility would depend on the seed and ensemble averaging.

Claims
Nanoparticle morphology (size, shape, and orientation) independently and synergistically determines the dielectric response of an Ag/MgO nanocomposite beyond simple volume-ratio predictions. Disk-shaped inclusions show more than 70% dielectric enhancement at similar volume loading to rod-like counterparts. Disk442 has twice the x,y dimensions of Rod223 yet has a polarization increase of more than twice. Rod-like inclusions of the same cross-section show polarization increasing with length due to more polarizable electrons. Parallel alignment maximizes the reach and strength of the induced field, while perpendicular alignment generates large depolarization. The dielectric enhancement is noted to be significantly more complex than a simple correlation to mNP length. 2D nanoparticles show a decrease in polarization compared to bulk, opposing the enhancement trend. Sometimes the perpendicular response in the matrix dominates, leading to a lower calculated dielectric constant than for pure matrix. Dielectric materials for high-k gates and super-capacitors can be engineered via nanoparticle geometry tuning. Molecular-scale NC materials provide a pathway to understand quantum polarization effects as devices miniaturize. Future designs must maintain close control on orientation and aggregation, as direction effects are critical.

Data And Code Availability
The study uses CPMD implemented in the Quantum Espresso code versions 6.0 and 6.6. Specific pseudopotentials from MaterialsCloud were used for O and Ag atoms. Models were built using Avogadro software. The exact repository or code availability statement is not explicitly provided in the text.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Test runs using thermostats between 200 and 600 K showed that temperature effects on geometry were negligible. The inclusion of an additional 2 MgO layers beyond the inclusion edge ensures that NP-induced distortion does not extend to neighboring cells. The study considers multiple inclusion types (rods, disks) and sizes to ensure the observation is not specific to one geometry. Wannier function localization was attempted as an alternative approach but failed for larger nanoparticles, demonstrating a sensitivity to nanoparticle size.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows an example nanocomposite with a Ag 12 inclusion embedded in the MgO matrix, illustrating local distortion. Figures 2 and 3 show the three rod-like and five disk-like inclusions modeled in the study. Figure 4 outlines the six steps of the electronic structure relaxation procedure. Figure 5 shows the polarization calculation steps using QuantumEspresso, continued from electronic structure calculation. Figure 6 shows the mathematical corrections for polarization jumps during post-processing due to the quantum of polarization effect. Figure 7 and others indicate that much of the density of states in the vicinity of the Fermi level arises from NP states. Figure 9 shows interpolated maps of Born effective charges for the NC with a 224 rodlike inclusion, with subpanels (a) parallel and (b) perpendicular polarization. Table 1 presents εr values for Ag/MgO NCs with rod-like and disk-like inclusions across various sizes and orientations.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first explicit modeling of how nanoparticle size, shape, and orientation jointly determine the dielectric response in a metal-oxide nanocomposite at the molecular scale using CPMD and the Modern Theory of Polarization. 2. The strongest evidence is the orientation-dependent dielectric enhancement of >70% for multi-layer disks at volume loadings comparable to rod-like inclusions, demonstrating that morphology is a critical tuning knob independent of concentration. 3. The future path is to extend the methodology to other high-k matrices (SiO2, HfO2), explore additional transition metal inclusions (Cu, Co, Fe), and model inclusion-inclusion interactions to build a complete picture of quantum polarization in nanocomposites.

summary.title: Low density interior in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets expels ions to the subsurface
summary.authors: Shahrazad M A Malek (Memorial University of Newfoundland); Ivan Saika-Voivod (Memorial University of Newfoundland); Styliani Consta (The University of Western Ontario)
summary.field_subfield: Computational Chemistry / Biophysical Chemistry; Molecular Dynamics of supercooled water nanodroplets and ion distribution
summary.executive_summary: This study provides direct computational evidence that supercooled aqueous nanodroplets develop a heterogeneous radial structure featuring a low-density core of tetrahedrally coordinated water surrounded by a higher-density, more disordered subsurface. The authors perform molecular dynamics simulations of single Na+ and multiple Na+ ions in water clusters ranging from N = 100 to N = 1100 water molecules at temperatures of 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K. The central finding is that at 200 K (supercooled conditions), the single Na+ ion is expelled from the droplet's center and resides in the subsurface region (within approximately 0.1 nm of the peak in Voronoi-based water density), whereas at 300 K, the radial ion distribution is nearly uniform. For multiple ions, the expulsion from the core is similarly observed at 200 K, with peaks appearing at specific radial distances (e.g., two peaks at 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm for N = 1100). The authors introduce a reference analytical model of 'electrostatic confinement' (EC), predicting that a single ion in a charged dielectric droplet is subject to a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass. The model successfully predicts the uniform distribution at room temperature but fails to capture the behavior at supercooling, where the heterogeneous water structure overrides the electrostatic confinement. The work highlights that the tetrahedral core at low temperature expels ions to the subsurface, a finding that has practical implications for native mass spectrometry, electrospray ionization, and understanding the preservation of macromolecular conformations in supercooled droplets. The smallest clusters (N = 100) do not form a tetrahedral core because the central water molecules are directly solvating the ion, and the droplet is subject to large shape fluctuations.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study provides direct computational evidence that supercooled aqueous nanodroplets develop a heterogeneous radial structure featuring a low-density core of tetrahedrally coordinated water surrounded by a higher-density, more disordered subsurface. The authors perform molecular dynamics simulations of single Na+ and multiple Na+ ions in water clusters ranging from N = 100 to N = 1100 water molecules at temperatures of 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K. The central finding is that at 200 K (supercooled conditions), the single Na+ ion is expelled from the droplet's center and resides in the subsurface region (within approximately 0.1 nm of the peak in Voronoi-based water density), whereas at 300 K, the radial ion distribution is nearly uniform. For multiple ions, the expulsion from the core is similarly observed at 200 K, with peaks appearing at specific radial distances (e.g., two peaks at 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm for N = 1100). The authors introduce a reference analytical model of 'electrostatic confinement' (EC), predicting that a single ion in a charged dielectric droplet is subject to a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass. The model successfully predicts the uniform distribution at room temperature but fails to capture the behavior at supercooling, where the heterogeneous water structure overrides the electrostatic confinement. The work highlights that the tetrahedral core at low temperature expels ions to the subsurface, a finding that has practical implications for native mass spectrometry, electrospray ionization, and understanding the preservation of macromolecular conformations in supercooled droplets. The smallest clusters (N = 100) do not form a tetrahedral core because the central water molecules are directly solvating the ion, and the droplet is subject to large shape fluctuations.

Research Context
The spatial distribution of ions in droplets determines chemical reactivity in atmospheric and man-made aerosols. Applications include spray-based ionization for native mass spectrometry and droplets as microreactors for chemical synthesis. Computational studies of supercooled clusters are limited because they are notoriously challenging to equilibrate. Prior studies by Voth et al. showed that below freezing, H3O+ and Na+ were excluded from the cluster interior in clusters of up to 100 H2O molecules. Previous atomistic simulations by the same group at 300–450 K found nearly uniform radial ion distribution in droplets of ~1000 H2O molecules. Anomalous, inverted radial density profiles have been observed in pure supercooled water clusters for N ≥ 200 molecules. A reference analytical model for the forces determining a single ion's location in a fluctuating droplet has been missing from the literature.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the low-density tetrahedral water core in supercooled nanodroplets differentiates the ion distribution from room temperature. The authors hypothesize that at supercooling, the single Na+ ion will be expelled from the core to the subsurface, unlike at room temperature. The hypothesis was not previously testable because small cluster sizes (≤100 water molecules) precluded the formation of the low-density core. The research question extends to multiple ions: whether they also show core expulsion at supercooling and how this relates to the solvent structure. The authors seek to characterize the relationship between ion location and the radial water structure using Voronoi density, tetrahedral order, and fifth-neighbor distance. The theoretical question is whether the electrostatic confinement effect, when modeled analytically, can capture both room-temperature and supercooled ion distributions.

Methodological Details
The study simulates Na+ ions in aqueous nanodroplets at three temperatures: 200 K (supercooled), 260 K (intermediate), and 300 K (room temperature). System sizes range from N = 100 to N = 1100 H2O molecules, corresponding to diameters of approximately 1.8 nm to 4.0 nm. Water molecules are modeled with the TIP4P/2005 transferable intermolecular potential model. The Na+ ion is modeled using OPLS-AA parameters with a charge of +1 e. Simulations are performed in GROMACS v4.6.1 using molecular dynamics. Each nanodroplet is placed in a periodic cubic box with a cutoff at L/2 to avoid interaction between the droplet and its periodic images. The canonical ensemble (NPT) is used, with the Nosé-Hoover thermostat (time constant 0.1 ps) and a 2 fs time step via the leap-frog algorithm. For single Na+ runs, the ion is placed at the surface for most simulations, and at the center for two runs each at N = 360 and N = 776 at 200 K. For multiple Na+ ion runs, all simulations begin with ions near the droplet center of mass. Equilibration is assessed by comparing radial ion density profiles from surface-started vs. center-started simulations; for N = 776, convergence is reached after 400 ns. For N = 1100, the equilibration time is assumed to be longer by a factor of approximately 2 based on the ratio of relaxation times. Water structure is characterized by: ρ(r) (number density), ρv(r) (Voronoi volume density), qT(r) (tetrahedral order parameter), and d5(r) (fifth nearest neighbor distance).

Procedures And Architectures
The analytical model expresses the energy of a charged dielectric droplet as the sum of electrostatic and surface energy. The ion's energy relative to the COM is given by a harmonic potential form: E = K(ε) * (r - r_COM)^2. The spring constant K(ε) is maximized at a relative dielectric constant of ε ≈ 2.73. The geometric Gibbs-Boltzmann distribution predicts an ion's expected radial variance proportional to kBT / K(ε). For a single charge Q = 1e and a 1000-water-molecule droplet, the geometric confinement limit is approximately r^2 ≤ 12 Å. High charges are modeled by creating charged cyclic peptide models (charge ≥ 3e) to illustrate the EC effect. The simulation box size is large enough to avoid interaction between the water droplet and periodic images, with a cutoff at L/2. The leap-frog algorithm integrates equations of motion with a 2 fs time step in a canonical ensemble. Voronoi volumes are computed for O sites, ignoring H sites, with the average density defined as mass/volume over sampled configurations. The tetrahedral order parameter is defined using three nearest neighbor oxygen atoms within r_cut = 0.35 nm. Radial averaging is performed over a shell width of Δr = 0.05 nm. For the multiple ion case, the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann (NPB) equation is solved for a rigid spherical geometry as a reference.

Key Results
At high temperature (300 K, 260 K for small droplets), ρ(r) shows a flat interior and sigmoidal decay, while ρv(r) monotonically decreases or remains flat. At low temperature (200 K), ρ(r) shows significant layering for all sizes, with a density increase as r approaches the subsurface. Voronoi density ρv(r) decays to near zero approximately 0.3 nm before the number density ρ(r) does, marking the subsurface location. At 300 K, the single Na+ radial distribution is approximately constant in the interior and consistent with the electrostatic confinement model. At 200 K, the peak of the Na+ ion distribution is located within 0.1 nm of the subsurface peak in ρv(r) for N ≥ 200. The ion is expelled to the highest-density subsurface region, where the dielectric constant is elevated due to increased density. At 200 K, five Na+ ions show a radial distribution peak at approximately the same location as the single ion case. For N = 1100 with eight Na+ ions at 200 K, two peaks are observed at 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm. The lower peak at 0.52 nm corresponds to one ion that can exchange with the outer peak. At 300 K, the multiple ion distributions are almost uniform with an incipient broad maximum in outer layers. For 776 H2O and five Na+ at 300 K, the ion distribution decays as 0.42 exp(-(1.14-x)/1.2) with λ_PB ≈ 1.2 nm. For 1100 H2O and eight Na+ at 300 K, the fit is 0.40 exp(-(1.37-x)/1.3) with λ_PB ≈ 1.3 nm. The theoretical NPB value for water (ε = 75) yields λ_PB ≈ 0.8, indicating shape fluctuations make the theoretical value qualitative. At 200 K, the tetrahedral order parameter qT(r) shows a significant decrease coinciding with the subsurface density peak. The distance to the fifth neighbor d5(r) also shows a more disordered structure near the subsurface density peak at 200 K. The smallest cluster N = 100 at 200 K does not form a tetrahedral core; the Na+ lies one or two layers from the surface. The Na+ peak at N = 100, 200 K coincides with a local minimum in ρ(r), suggesting layering plays a significant role in small droplets.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
A heterogeneous solvent structure in supercooled nanodroplets creates a differentiated ion distribution compared to room temperature. The tetrahedrally coordinated low-density core expels Na+ ions to the more disordered high-density subsurface. The electrostatic confinement model predicts a harmonic potential for an ion in a charged dielectric droplet, but this prediction fails at supercooling when the heterogeneous water structure overrides electrostatic effects. At room temperature, the low charge of Na+ (Q = 1e) means geometric confinement dominates over the electrostatic force toward the COM, resulting in a nearly uniform distribution. The effect is expected to be more pronounced for higher charges (e.g., cyclic peptides or DNA/RNA) and smaller droplet radii. The observation that the ion prefers the higher-density subsurface is consistent with the dielectric constant increasing with density at constant temperature and polarization. The results suggest that the solvent organization, rather than just electrostatic or geometric effects, controls ion location in supercooled droplets.

Contradictions And Limitations
For N = 100 at 200 K, the Na+ peak occurs at a local minimum in ρ(r) rather than the maximum of ρv(r), suggesting layering overrides density effects in very small droplets. The electrostatic confinement model cannot be verified at supercooling because the low-density core fundamentally alters the ion's effective environment. The NPB theory for multiple ions cannot explain the 200 K distributions because the core expulsion is due to solvent structure, not electrostatic equilibrium. Shape fluctuations in droplets up to a few thousand water molecules make the theoretical λ_PB value only qualitative, limiting precise quantitative comparisons. The study uses single Na+ and only up to 8 ions, so the behavior of many ions is not fully explored. The authors acknowledge that statistics are difficult to obtain for radial quantities below r = 0.2 nm, making results noisy in that regime. The tetrahedrality parameter qT(r) must be artificially cut off beyond 1.6 nm because the increase in the surface layer is not indicative of actual tetrahedral order. The simulation time of 10–100 ns at 300 K is needed for accurate diffusion sampling, but it is unclear if this is sufficient for supercooled systems where relaxation is slower.

Claims
Supercooled nanodroplets develop a tetrahedral low-density core that expels ions to the subsurface, a phenomenon absent at room temperature. At 200 K, the Na+ peak is within 0.1 nm of the subsurface Voronoi density peak for N ≥ 200. At 300 K, the Na+ distribution is approximately constant in the interior. qT(r) and d5(r) show reduced tetrahedrality exactly at the subsurface density peak at 200 K. Multiple ions also show core expulsion with peaks at 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm at 200 K. At N = 100 and 200 K, the ion peaks at a local ρ(r) minimum, not the Voronoi maximum, suggesting layering may dominate. The smallest cluster N = 100 does not form a tetrahedral core, with the Na+ residing one or two layers from the surface. The findings suggest that the solvent structure, not just electrostatic interactions, controls ion distribution in supercooled droplets. The core expulsion of ions may affect the formation of conical deformations required for ion emission in electrospray.
The electrostatic confinement model correctly predicts the uniform Na+ distribution at room temperature but fails to describe the supercooled behavior. The model's predictions are consistent with simulation findings for a single Na+ at room temperature. The geometric Gibbs-Boltzmann distribution predicts an ion variance compatible with the uniform 300 K observation. The model predicts a harmonic potential centered at the COM, but simulations show the ion peak shifts to the subsurface at 200 K. The authors admit the model can only be extended by including ion size and hydrophobic effects, which were not fully included here. The model serves as a reference against which simulation data can be compared, providing a theoretical baseline for ion-in-droplet physics. The failure at supercooling highlights the importance of explicit solvent structure in ion-liquid interactions.
Multiple ions are expelled from the droplet core at supercooling, and their distribution cannot be described by the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann theory. At 200 K, multiple ions show peaks at 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm, with the core (r < 0.5 nm) virtually depleted. The NPB solution for a rigid sphere predicts an exponential decay toward the center, but simulations show core expulsion. The two-peak structure at N = 1100 does not indicate a metastable state; the lower peak can exchange ions with the outer peak. The ion expulsion has implications for Rayleigh fission and ion evaporation mechanisms in mass spectrometry. A conical deformation required for ion emission might be hindered by the low-density tetrahedral core.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors run two independent simulations per system (ion at surface vs. ion at center) at 200 K to assess equilibration convergence. For N = 776 at 200 K, ion density profiles from both starting positions converged after 400 ns. The equilibration time for N = 1100 is assumed to be ~2× longer based on the relaxation time ratio τ1100 / τ776 ≈ 2. The multiple ion simulations are assumed to have shorter relaxation times, with single ion simulations providing upper bounds. The NPB theory is used as a reference model, and the authors interpret its λ_PB value only qualitatively due to droplet shape fluctuations. Multiple system sizes (N = 100, 360, 776, 1100) and multiple ion numbers (up to 8) were used to test the consistency of the trends.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 reports system parameters: N (100, 360, 776, 1100), mean droplet molecule count N_d, relaxation time τ, simulation time, and temperature. Figure 1 plots the spring constant K(ε) as a function of the relative dielectric constant for a 1000-water-molecule droplet with an ion, showing the maximum at ε ≈ 2.73. Figure 2 shows the radial distribution of a charged peptide (8e+) in a droplet (R = 3.8 nm), demonstrating geometric confinement of the center-of-mass distribution. Figure 3 displays ρ(r), ρv(r), and ρNa(r) at 200 K (black) and 300 K (red), with (e) showing the single ion distribution at high T and (f) showing core expulsion at low T. Figure 4 provides a detailed comparison for N = 776 at 200 K vs. 300 K: (a) pure water densities, (b) subsurface peak in ρv(r), (c) equilibration check, (d) five-ion distribution, (e) qT(r) profile, and (f) d5(r) profile. Figure 5 compares multiple ion radial distributions at T = 300 K (droplet 776 H2O) and T = 200 K (droplet 1100 H2O), showing the shift from uniform to core-depleted.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is direct computational evidence that supercooled nanodroplets form a tetrahedral, low-density interior that expels Na+ ions to the high-density subsurface, whereas the ion distribution is uniform at room temperature. 2. The strongest evidence comes from the convergence of the single Na+ peak with the Voronoi subsurface density peak at 200 K (within 0.1 nm) for N ≥ 200, and the structural confirmation via reduced qT(r) and d5(r) at the same location. 3. The future path includes investigating the effect of higher-charged ions (peptides, DNA/RNA) on electrostatic confinement, understanding Rayleigh fission and ion emission in supercooled droplets, and interpreting macromolecular conformation data from supercooled electrospray droplets.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study demonstrates the application of the subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach to a hybrid experimental-plus-theoretical dataset to identify physicochemical constraints (SG rules) that exclusively describe materials and reaction conditions with outstanding catalytic performance in the selective oxidation of propylene. By using high-throughput experimentation (HTE) to synthesize 120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus, and DFT-calculated free-atom properties as candidate descriptive parameters, the authors identified temperature, phosphorus content, and composition-weighted electronegativity as key parameters governing high yields of acrolein and acrylic acid. The SGD approach identifies a subgroup containing only 15 data points (1.2% of the dataset) with an average oxygenate yield of 24.15%, five times the global average. The SG rules were validated by designing and testing four- and five-component catalysts, where the rules correctly predicted exceptional performance: the best four-component catalyst reached 60.19% oxygenate yield and the best five-component catalyst achieved 59.60%, both approximately twice the training set maximum of 26.85%. The study demonstrates that local modeling via SGD can circumvent explicit modeling of full catalytic progressions and guide the design of more complex catalyst compositions. However, the temperature rule from the three-component dataset was not transferable to the more complex systems, highlighting that reaction mechanisms can vary across materials and conditions. The approach requires additional data covering unexplored portions of the materials space to extend the domain of the SG rules.

Research Context
Heterogeneous catalysis is governed by an intricate interplay of surface reaction networks and typically unknown dynamic restructuring of the catalyst under reaction conditions. Explicit atomistic modeling of the full catalytic progression by first-principles methods is impractical for describing heterogeneous catalysis. High-throughput experimentation (HTE) allows testing large amounts of materials, but utilizing the information to decide on the next promising materials is not straightforward. The number of possible materials is practically infinite while the number of good catalysts is very small, making the direct approach unlikely to identify the needed catalyst material. Detailed characterization of each material in large libraries is typically not feasible, hindering in-depth understanding of processes governing reactivity. Distinct catalytic mechanisms operate depending on materials and reaction conditions, leading to an unbalanced distribution between high- and low-performance scenarios. Global models trained to minimize expected average prediction error do not necessarily allow focused modeling of the most interesting materials and mechanisms. Alternative approaches for catalyst design are therefore required to identify rules associated with high performance rather than average performance.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach can identify key physicochemical descriptive parameters and constraints that exclusively describe materials and reaction conditions with outstanding catalytic performance. The study hypothesizes that rules on temperature, phosphorus content, and composition-weighted electronegativity can be derived to describe high oxygenate yields. The SGD approach is predicted to identify a quality function that selects subgroups with the most outstanding distributions of target values relative to the whole dataset. The authors predict that the identified SG rules will reflect specific underlying processes resulting in outstanding performance rather than average behavior. A secondary hypothesis is that candidate descriptive parameters calculated by first-principles methods eliminate the need for extensive experimental material characterization. The rules are expected to guide the design of more complex catalysts containing up to five elements in their composition. The study hypothesizes that the SG rules derived from three-component catalysts will generalize to four- and five-component systems with similar structural motifs.

Methodological Details
120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus were synthesized and tested in the catalytic oxidation of propylene. The catalysts are three-component compositions in different proportions, prepared on a SiO2 pseudo-liquid support that may have a disordered or possibly amorphous structure. At each catalyst composition, several reaction temperatures between 200ºC and 400ºC were examined. All reactions were carried out in tubular, fixed-bed reactors with a consistent reaction feed of Ar, H2O, N2, O2, and propylene at molar rates of 4.015, 4.015, 104.40, 20.08, and 1.57 mmol/h, respectively. The same mass of catalyst was used in all reactions, keeping contact time constant across experiments. For the HTE data, 1220 measurements were obtained across 120 compositions and multiple temperatures. The target variable for SGD is the yield of oxygenate products acrolein and acrylic acid, defined as the sum of molar flow rates of these species in the outlet divided by the molar flow rate of propylene in the feed. 11 descriptive parameters were used in the SGD analysis: T, I, J, K, L, M, L, N, L, O, L, PQR, S, T, S, U. Properties were calculated for isolated atoms using DFT-PBEsol and the FHI-aims code. For a given catalyst composition, per-element free-atom properties are converted into system-specific properties by taking the composition-weighted average. Oxygen content is not included in the material characterization because its proportion is unknown from the catalyst formulation. The coverage term M(X, gh) controls subgroup size to prevent selection of small SGs with little statistical significance. The quality function uses the cumulative Janson-Shannon divergence, a symmetrized version of the Kulback-Leibler divergence, to measure dissimilarity between SG and whole dataset distributions.

Procedures And Architectures
The SGD approach starts with generating a pool of propositions, which for continuous parameters are inequalities constraining their values. Selectors are formed by a number of propositions connected by the AND operator to select subgroups with outstanding target value distributions. The SGD search maximizes a quality function measuring how outstanding specific subselections of data points are compared to the whole dataset. The three-component catalysts are ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus on SiO2; composition is more crucial than crystallinity. DFT properties are calculated at the free-atom level and then composition-weighted, meaning properties do not need re-evaluation for each new material. Four-component materials were designed by fixing phosphorus content to 0.60 and ruthenium molar content to 0.05, and varying the V-element and its molar content. V-elements selected are those with octahedral coordination in phosphorus-containing materials and maximum atomic radius difference of 0.10 Å compared to tungsten (1.45 Å). V-elements considered: niobium (1.45 Å), tantalum (1.45 Å), chromium (1.40 Å), molybdenum (1.45 Å), tin (1.45 Å), antimony (1.45 Å), tellurium (1.40 Å), and lead. For the four-component analysis, J_{V} was set to 0.035 for Mo, Nb and 0.050 for Ta, Sb. Five-component materials fixed V as tellurium and varied V^{sub} as molybdenum, niobium, tantalum, and antimony. Cross-validation was performed by training with randomly selected 90% of data points or excluding low-yield measurements (<3%). The HTE and theory SGD approach is applied sequentially: first identify rules from three-component data, then use them to design and test more complex compositions.

Key Results
50% of the measured materials and conditions result in less than 2% oxygenates yield, and only 41 out of 1220 measurements have yields above 20%. The average oxygenates yield over the whole data set is 4.83%, with a maximum yield of 26.85%. The selected SG with the highest cumulative Janson-Shannon divergence (0.693) contains 15 data points, approximately 1.2% of the data set. All 15 data points in this SG have high yield of oxygenates, with an average yield of 24.15%, five times higher than the whole-dataset average. The SG is described by three rules: 280 ≤ T ≤ 300ºC, J_K > 0.55, and 3.910 ≤ V_Y < 4.002 eV. The temperature rule indicates highest yields are at intermediate temperatures within 200-400ºC. The phosphorus content rule shows relatively high phosphorus content is needed for outstanding performance. The electronegativity rule effectively limits the range of Ru contents, as Ru is needed for conversion but too much leads to combustion. The best four-component catalyst achieved 60.19% oxygenate yield at 400ºC with 0.35 molar fraction of tellurium as V-element, within the VY SG rule window. The best five-component catalyst achieved 59.60% oxygenate yield at 400ºC with tantalum as V^{sub} and a composition-averaged electronegativity of 3.947 eV, within the VY SG rule threshold. The four- and five-component outstanding catalysts achieve oxygenate yields up to twice as large as any observation in the training dataset (highest 26.85%). Four- and five-component SGD results on 746 data points identified an SG with 18 data points (ca. 2.4% of the dataset) and highest cumulative Janson-Shannon divergence of 0.355. The four-component SG rules are T ≥ 360ºC, L_{α+1} ≤ 1.001 Å, and V_H < -1.593 eV. The temperature rule from three-component data (280-300ºC) is not transferable to four-component data, where T ≥ 360ºC is required.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The SGD rules on key parameters rationalize a local reactivity pattern particularly associated with exceptional catalytic performance rather than average behavior. The identified rules are expected to describe outstanding materials whose performance is governed by the same processes governing reactivity of exceptional materials in training data. The temperature rule's non-transferability from three- to four-component systems suggests that reaction mechanisms may shift as catalyst complexity increases. The shift from VY and J_K descriptors in the three-component SG to L_{α+1} and V_H in the four-component SG highlights that different composition-dependent parameters are required for different complexity levels. The approach demonstrates that local modeling is suitable for searching exceptional materials whose structures and functions are hardly modeled explicitly by theory. The ability to predict yields in untested compositions by applying rules derived from a training set establishes a generalizable design principle. The findings imply that catalyst design can be guided by combining DFT-calculated descriptors with HTE data through local AI techniques, bypassing explicit mechanistic modeling.

Contradictions And Limitations
The temperature rule derived from three-component data (280-300ºC) is not transferable to four-component data (≥360ºC), limiting the generalizability of the rule across complexity levels. Different composition-dependent parameters (L_{α+1}, V_H vs. J_K, V_Y) are required to describe the SG at different catalyst complexities, complicating unified rule application. It is unclear if SG rules can identify exceptional materials for any arbitrary ruthenium content or V-elements with significantly different radii compared to tungsten. Different mechanisms may operate on materials with different structural motifs, meaning the SGD might need additional data points covering so-far unexplored portions of the materials space. The oxygen content is not known from the catalyst formulation nor measured for all materials, and is therefore excluded from the characterization. The three-component catalysts are prepared on a SiO2 pseudo-liquid support and might present a disordered, possibly amorphous structure, with atomic structures not known in detail. Similar catalytic performance was found for crystalline and disordered phases at the same composition, indicating composition is more crucial than crystallinity, but this limits structural insight. The cross-validation and sensitivity analyses in the ESI (not fully reported here) are necessary to confirm rule robustness beyond the described perturbations.

Claims
The SGD-HTE-theory approach can identify interpretable, chemically meaningful rules on physicochemical parameters that exclusively predict exceptional catalytic performance and guide the design of more complex catalysts. The selected SG with 0.693 Janson-Shannon divergence contains 15 high-performing data points (1.2%) with an average yield five times higher than the global average. The best four-component catalyst (60.19%) and five-component catalyst (59.60%) both fall within the VY SG rule window derived from the training data. The rules on temperature, phosphorus content, and electronegativity were consistently reproducible in cross-validation and when excluding low-performing points. The temperature rule is not transferable across complexity levels (300ºC for three-component vs. ≥360ºC for four-component). Different descriptor parameters are required for the SG at different complexities, limiting a single unified rule set. The approach enables design of catalysts with oxygenate yields up to twice that of any training observation. Catalyst design can proceed with free-atom DFT calculations instead of extensive experimental material characterization.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Similar SG rules are obtained when training is performed with randomly selected 90% of the data points. The ranges of variation for minimum and maximum thresholds are [3.882, 3.910 eV] and [3.989, 4.031], consistent with the thresholds shown in Fig. 2F. SG rules constraining the V_Y parameter to an intermediate range are always observed when only 90% of the data is used. The quality function uses a coverage term to prevent very small SGs with little statistical significance from being selected. The Janson-Shannon divergence term favors SGs presenting target values as unusual as possible, focusing on exceptional high-performing materials. Cross-validation details, including the specific approach and Jensen-Shanon divergence formulation, are available in the ESI. The four- and five-component SGD analysis used the same 11 candidate descriptive parameters as the three-component analysis for direct comparison.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A illustrates the SGD approach workflow: generation of propositions (inequalities), formation of selectors (AND-connected propositions), and selection of subgroups with outstanding target distributions. Figure 1B shows the three-component catalyst compositions in a ternary diagram; Figure 1C shows the reaction scheme with oxygenate and combustion products. Figure 2A and B show propylene conversion versus oxygenates selectivity profiles and the distribution of yield of oxygenates across 1220 measurements, respectively. Figure 2C-F display the three SG rules on temperature, phosphorus content, and composition-averaged electronegativity, with Figure 2F showing the electronegativity limits on the ternary diagram. Figure 3B shows the ternary diagram with overlaid SG rules on electronegativity, limiting the range of Ru contents. Figure 4A maps four-component compositions with V-elements; bold values with stars indicate materials satisfying the SG rule 3.910 ≤ V_Y < 4.002 eV. Figure 4C and D show experimental HTE data for five-component catalysts with tellurium as V-element. Figure 5A-B show the four- and five-component SGD results on 746 data points; Figure 5C-F show the new SG rules: T ≥ 360ºC, L_{α+1} ≤ 1.001 Å, and V_H < -1.593 eV.

Three Takeaways
1. The SGD approach identifies local, interpretable rules (temperature, phosphorus, electronegativity) that exclusively describe exceptional catalytic performance in a hybrid HTE-theory dataset. 2. The SG rules correctly predicted oxygenate yields up to twice the training set maximum (60.19% and 59.60%), demonstrating the approach's predictive power for untested compositions. 3. The non-transferability of the temperature rule and the change in descriptor parameters across complexity levels indicate that reaction mechanisms shift, requiring expanded data to generalize the rules to unexplored materials spaces.

summary.title: Mechanochemical synthesis of eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4
summary.authors: Roger Borges; Amanda Soares Giroto; Rodrigo Klaic; Fernando Wypych (Universidade Federal do Paraná); Caue Ribeiro
summary.field_subfield: Chemistry / Agricultural Materials Engineering - Mechanochemical Synthesis
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental Research / Dataset and Method Development Paper
summary.executive_summary: This study demonstrates a solvent-free, mechanochemical process for synthesizing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) using eggshell waste (calcite) and potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KH2PO4) as precursors. The approach is framed within a reverse logistics context, repurposing millions of tons of food industry biowaste into high-value soil conditioners. Mechanochemical activation—applying mechanical energy via friction and impact—promotes solid-phase ion migration and bond breaking without liquid or solid waste, ensuring no unwanted byproducts. XRD characterization confirms the formation of K3CaH(PO4)2 (PDF 22-1218) and CaKPO4 (PDF 33-1002) phases, which are absent in previous eggshell-based hydroxyapatite syntheses. Solubility kinetic analysis in 2% citric acid demonstrates that the resulting phosphates exhibit a slower release of potassium and phosphorus compared to the precursor KH2PO4, while calcium release is significantly faster than from raw CaCO3 eggshells, positioning the material as a 'smart release' fertilizer. Soil release essays in a controlled sandy soil (78 g/dish, 75% water saturation) further validate this behavior: P diffusion at 2h/600 rpm reached 45 mg/kg at 30 days (15% recovery), contrasted with 107 mg/kg (40% recovery) for pure KH2PO4, and 30.97 mg/kg for bioavailable Ca. In-situ hydroxyapatite formation (PDF 9-432) under soil conditions explains the long-term release behavior. The P radial diffusion profile was 34% faster than struvite but 22% slower than the precursor, confirming intermediate release kinetics. TGA/DSC and 31P NMR MAS analyses confirmed the phase transitions, including intermediate pyrophosphate formation at δ = -4.78 ppm. The study establishes a novel mechanochemical protocol for K-bearing calcium phosphates, offering an eco-friendly alternative to traditional hydroxyapatite syntheses that use phosphoric acid solutions.

Executive Summary
This study demonstrates a solvent-free, mechanochemical process for synthesizing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) using eggshell waste (calcite) and potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KH2PO4) as precursors. The approach is framed within a reverse logistics context, repurposing millions of tons of food industry biowaste into high-value soil conditioners. Solubility kinetic analysis in 2% citric acid demonstrates that the resulting phosphates exhibit a slower release of potassium and phosphorus compared to the precursor KH2PO4, while calcium release is significantly faster than from raw CaCO3 eggshells, positioning the material as a 'smart release' fertilizer. Soil release essays in a controlled sandy soil (78 g/dish, 75% water saturation) further validate this behavior: P diffusion at 2h/600 rpm reached 45 mg/kg at 30 days (15% recovery), contrasted with 107 mg/kg (40% recovery) for pure KH2PO4, and 30.97 mg/kg for bioavailable Ca. The P radial diffusion profile was 34% faster than struvite but 22% slower than the precursor, confirming intermediate release kinetics. TGA/DSC and 31P NMR MAS analyses confirmed the phase transitions, including intermediate pyrophosphate formation at δ = -4.78 ppm. The study establishes a novel mechanochemical protocol for K-bearing calcium phosphates, offering an eco-friendly alternative to traditional hydroxyapatite syntheses that use phosphoric acid solutions.

Research Context
Eggshells represent millions of tons of food industry waste disposed in landfills, producing odors due to microbial growth. Reverse logistics is an instrument of economic and social development for solid waste restitution. Prior mechanochemical eggshell syntheses used phosphoric acid solutions instead of powder phosphate salts. No mechanochemical process has been reported for the production of K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 from eggshell and KH2PO4. Conventional methods use solid-state mechanochemical activation to promote chemical reactions via friction and impact forces. Existing literature reports hydroxyapatite synthesis from different precursors, but not the specific K-containing phosphates studied here.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a solvent-free mechanochemical process can synthesize K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 from eggshell calcite and KH2PO4 for soil conditioning. It was hypothesized that the resulting phosphates would improve nutrient management by providing a delay in P and K bioavailability compared to KH2PO4. A secondary hypothesis was that the new phases would increase calcium bioavailability compared to raw CaCO3 eggshells. The authors predicted the formed materials would act as smart release fertilizers due to different solubility based on metal cation size and charge. The expected mechanism involves sufficient applied energy to break reagent bonds and promote solid-phase ion migration to form a new structure.

Methodological Details
Eggshells were collected by the authors at home, washed with water, and dried at room temperature. Eggshell diameter ranged between 1 and 10 mm before grinding. KH2PO4 PA was supplied by Vetec. Milling employed a Fritsch Pulverisette 7 high-energy ball mill with a 250 ml zirconia bowl and five 15 mm zirconia balls. The weight ratio of eggshell to KH2PO4 was 1:1 (w/w). Milling times: 15 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 6 h, 12 h, and 24 h at 600 rpm. Milling speeds: 100, 200, 400, and 600 rpm for 2 h. The mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. X-ray diffraction (XRD) was performed using a Shimadzu XRD 6000 diffractometer, Cu Kα, 3-40°, 2° min⁻¹, 30 kV, 40 mA. 31P NMR MAS used an Avance III HD / Bruker, 10KHz, HPDEC sequence, ADP reference. TGA used a Q500 analyzer, 25°C-600°C for precursor and 20-900°C for samples, synthetic air, 10°C min⁻¹. DSC used a TA Q100 Controller with refrigerated cooling system. Acid digestion (H2SO4/H2O2, 8:1 v/v, 24 h at 250°C) determined nutrient content via atomic absorption (K, Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods. Pellets were obtained at 5 bar pressure in a steel pelletizer. Citric acid solution for release assays was at 2 wt% concentration. Soil for diffusion: 8.6 cm Petri dishes, 78 g dry sieved 2.0 mm mesh soil, target density 1.2 g·cm⁻³. Soil P diffusion images analyzed with GNU Image Manipulation Program v. 2.6.11. Soil release containers contained 50 g sandy soil at 75% water saturation. Pellet weight standardized to 300 mg of P per kg of soil. Release periods: 3, 7, 15, and 30 days. P quantified by molybdenum blue colorimetric method; K and Ca by flame atomic absorption spectroscopy (PerkinElmer PinAAcle 900T).

Procedures And Architectures
The milling process was performed in a solvent-free environment using friction and impact forces. Samples were milled at specific time/speed combinations to evaluate acid-basic reactions between eggshell and KH2PO4. Characterization followed milling: XRD, 31P NMR MAS, TGA, and DSC. Nutrient content determined by acid digestion and atomic absorption/colorimetric methods. For citric acid release: single pellet immersed in 300 mL 2% citric acid in 600 mL beaker, closed with PVC film, 25°C, magnetic stirring. Aliquots of 1.2 mL collected from 15 min to 30 days for kinetic modeling. P diffusion: pre-treated paper marked P diffusion in moist soil, scanned, and analyzed for area quantification of high P-zone. Soil release: aerobic conditions in plastic containers; solid residues removed and characterized by XRD after each period. Post-release analysis: K extracted by HCl (0.05 Mol/L), Ca by KCl (1 Mol/L), P by Mehlich 1 method. To further understand structural changes, milled samples were calcined at 280°C, 420°C, and 710°C and re-characterized by XRD. Samples milled at 600 rpm were suspended in water, dried, and characterized by XRD to observe phase transitions.

Key Results
XRD confirmed K3CaH(PO4)2 (PDF 22-1218) and CaKPO4 (PDF 33-1002) formed at 2 h and 400 rpm and above. Below 2 h and 400 rpm, only reactant diffraction patterns were found, indicating no chemical reaction. KH2PO4 TGA showed residual mass of 89% (theoretical 87%) after polycondensation at 300°C. Eggshell TGA experimental residue was 56% (theoretical 59%), confirming CaCO3 composition. Milled samples showed three mass loss events centered at 280°C, 420°C, and 710°C. Samples milled at 600 rpm showed similar thermal decomposition, but water loss at 340°C reduced with milling time. 31P NMR MAS of KH2PO4 showed single signal at δ = 3.74 ppm; milled samples showed shifts to δ = 3.28 ppm, δ = 2.82 ppm, and δ = 0.74 ppm. A pyrophosphate signal at δ = -4.78 ppm was observed in the 2 h at 600 rpm sample, indicating phosphate dimerization. In citric acid, P and K release for milled samples was slower than KH2PO4, while Ca release was faster than raw eggshell. P and K fitted better to pseudo-second order model (R² and qe/experimental qe) compared to linear or intraparticle diffusion. In soil, P increased from 0 to 107 mg/kg after 3 days for KH2PO4 (40% total P), while 2 h/600 rpm reached only 25 mg/kg. At 30 days in soil, 2 h/600 rpm P release reached 45 mg/kg (15% of total P content recovered). P radial diffusion of 2 h/600 rpm reached 1.99 cm at day 2, compared to 2.62 cm for KH2PO4 and 0 cm for struvite. At 30 days, P radial diffusion was 34% faster than struvite and 22% slower than precursor. K release in soil reached around 100% for both materials by 30 days. Bioavailable Ca increased to 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days for 2 h/600 rpm in soil, but showed no increase for eggshell precursor. Hydroxyapatite phase (PDF 9-432) was identified from 3 until 30 days in soil under XRD. All milled samples showed phase transition to Hydroxyapatite when suspended in water and characterized by XRD.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The mechanochemical reaction produces K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 through non-stoichiometric decomposition: KH2PO4 + CaCO3 → CO2 + H2O + K3CaH(PO4)2 + CaKPO4. The slower P and K release in phosphates compared to KH2PO4 is attributed to the formation of K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 phases with stronger bonds. The faster Ca release compared to raw CaCO3 demonstrates the conversion of insoluble calcite into soluble phosphate phases. In soil, the intermediate P release behavior is explained by in-situ hydroxyapatite formation (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2), which acts as a long-term slow-release reservoir. The material functions as a smart release fertilizer, delaying P and K bioavailability while increasing Ca bioavailability, suitable for soil systems at pH ~ 5. The solvent-free, no-waste mechanochemical process aligns with reverse logistics and green chemistry principles.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors note the process mechanism is 'still quite complex to evaluate,' limiting mechanistic certainty. The eggshells are assumed to be mainly composed of CaCO3, but the exact purity and minor component fractions are not specified. No kinetic constants for calcium release in citric acid could be compared quantitatively with the precursor. The TGA of milled samples at 600 rpm showed an unclear phosphate phase at 2 h, requiring supplementary thermal treatment to confirm. Soil release in the sandy soil system may not fully replicate all field conditions (single-pellet, static container). The exact stoichiometry of the K3CaH(PO4)2 phase is described as non-stoichiometric, limiting precise quantitative comparison.

Claims
The mechanochemical process produces K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 phases that are absent in conventional eggshell-to-hydroxyapatite syntheses. XRD patterns confirmed K3CaH(PO4)2 (PDF 22-1218) and CaKPO4 (PDF 33-1002) at 2 h and 400 rpm. 31P NMR shifts to 3.28, 2.82, and 0.74 ppm are consistent with calcium phosphate compounds. The literature reports hydroxyapatite synthesis from eggshell using phosphoric acid, not the K-containing phosphates produced here. The 2 h at 600 rpm sample showed an unclear phosphate phase requiring calcination to match K3CaH(PO4)2. This represents a novel material class of K-bearing calcium phosphates suitable as soil conditioners.
The milled phosphate materials exhibit slower P and K release than KH2PO4 but faster Ca release than eggshell CaCO3, enabling multi-nutrient management. In soil, P release for 2 h/600 rpm was 25 mg/kg (15%) vs 107 mg/kg (40%) for KH2PO4 at 3 days. Bioavailable Ca in soil reached 30.97 mg/kg (8% recovery) for 2 h/600 rpm vs no increase for eggshell. P diffusion was 22% slower than precursor at 30 days. In citric acid, the K release for milled samples was 'rather different' in behavior compared to P release. The material acts as a smart-release fertilizer that synchronizes P/K delay with Ca accessibility.
In-situ hydroxyapatite formation in soil conditions mediates the long-term phosphorus and calcium release profile. Hydroxyapatite phase (PDF 9-432) was identified from 3 until 30 days in soil. All samples milled at 600 rpm showed transition to hydroxyapatite when suspended in water and characterized by XRD. The exact rate of hydroxyapatite formation and its contribution to specific P/Ca release cannot be quantitatively decoupled from the parent phosphate. This mechanism suggests the material is particularly effective as a long-term slow-release fertilizer under acidic conditions.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Milling parameters (time and speed) were systematically varied: 15 min-24 h at 600 rpm, and 100-600 rpm at 2 h. Three mass loss events in TGA/DSC were investigated by calcining at 280°C, 420°C, and 710°C to identify crystalline phases. The 600 rpm samples suspended in water were characterized by XRD to confirm hydroxyapatite transition, a separate validation of soil results. Solubility was modeled with pseudo-first order, pseudo-second order, and intraparticle diffusion to establish robustness of kinetic description.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows XRD patterns of milled eggshell/KH2PO4 at various times and speeds, confirming K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 formation. Figure 2 presents TGA curves of KH2PO4, eggshell, and milled samples showing mass loss events at 280°C, 420°C, and 710°C. Figure 3 shows XRD patterns of milled samples calcined at 280°C, 420°C, and 710°C to identify phase transitions. Figure 4 presents 31P NMR MAS spectra of KH2PO4 and milled samples showing characteristic phosphate shifts. Figure 5 shows phosphorus and potassium release kinetics in 2% citric acid solution. Figure 6 presents soil nutrient release kinetics in sandy soil over 30 days. Figure 7 shows XRD of solid residues from soil after 3-30 days identifying hydroxyapatite formation. Table 1 reports kinetic constants and correlations for P and K release fitted to pseudo-second order model.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a novel, solvent-free mechanochemical synthesis of K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 from eggshell calcite and KH2PO4, repurposing food waste into a multi-nutrient soil conditioner. 2. The strongest evidence is the demonstration that milled samples delay P and K release (45 mg/kg vs 107 mg/kg at 30 days) while enhancing Ca bioavailability (30.97 mg/kg vs no increase for eggshell), confirmed by XRD and kinetic modeling. 3. The future path involves the development of nanocomposites (e.g., hydroxyapatite dispersed in urea/starch) to tune P and Ca solubilization for faster release applications, as suggested by the authors' own prior work.
