judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the 'lab-to-fab gap' in organic solar cell (OSC) manufacturing by demonstrating slot-die coating of PM6:Y6 binary and PM6:Y6:PC61BM ternary active layers on flexible PET substrates using o-xylene (a green solvent) without additives. The work is conducted in open-air on a roll-platform-compatible homemade coater, addressing the industrial scalability challenge. A systematic coating temperature optimization (60–120 °C) identifies 100 °C as the optimal slot-die head temperature, maximizing PCE by minimizing bimolecular recombination. Thickness optimization across four concentrations reveals that thicker layers (~200 nm) improve light absorption and robustness without increasing series resistance. Introducing a small amount of fullerene (PC61BM) at a [1:1:0.1] or [1:1:0.2] ratio in a ternary blend enhances charge dissociation probability (from 93.7% to 96.3%) and collection efficiency (from 69.6% to 77.7%), leading to a champion PCE of 7.2% (6.7% average for ternary). Stability tests show 99.4% retention of ternary PCE after 1050 hours under ISOS-D-1 dark storage conditions, and over 97% for binary devices after more than 1500 hours, confirming both process scalability and operational durability. The work establishes that high-performance flexible OSCs can be fabricated using industrially compatible, environmentally friendly, non-fullerene acceptor systems.

Research Context
OSCs have reached peak lab-scale efficiencies on active areas far below 0.1 cm², widening the lab-to-fab gap. The standard spin-coating technique has poor upscaling potential and substantial material waste. Scalable fabrication techniques like slot-die coating are suitable for roll-to-roll manufacturing but few studies report them for high-efficiency systems. Environmentally friendly upscaling requires inks based on non-hazardous solvent systems. The PM6:Y6 material combination shows excellent efficiencies over 15% on rigid substrates with green solvents but transfer to roll-processing on flexible substrates is needed. PM6 exhibits temperature-dependent aggregation behavior requiring heating to remain liquid during slot-die coating.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether slot-die coating of PM6:Y6 on flexible substrates in open-air with a green solvent can produce commercially competitive efficiencies. The hypothesis is that fine-tuning of coating temperature and solution concentration will yield an optimal process that minimizes bimolecular recombination and maximizes PCE. It is predicted that the temperature-dependent aggregation of PM6 requires a hot slot-die coating approach where substrate and head are at the same temperature. The authors further hypothesize that introducing a ternary fullerene component will improve charge transport and stability due to energy cascade and balanced mobility. The anticipated outcome is high-efficiency flexible devices with good stability under dark storage conditions.

Methodological Details
The active layer materials PM6 (batch YY19260CH100) and Y6 (batch DW7038S) were purchased from 1-Material Inc. without purification. PB61BM (batch M111) was purchased from Ossila as the ternary fullerene component. The ZnO nanoparticle ink for the electron transport layer was from Sigma-Aldrich; MoO3 pellets from Kurt J. Lesker Co. The flexible substrate is pre-patterned ITO-coated polyethylene terephthalate (PET) from FOM Technologies. Silver for the back electrode was pure silver from Sigma-Aldrich, with silver paste from DuPont 5025 for flexographic printing. The green solvent o-xylene (O-XY) was used with a ≥ 98% purity from Sigma-Aldrich. The device architecture follows an inverted geometry: ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6/MoO3/Ag. A homemade roll-coater with syringe pump, hot tube, and drum-to-head distance control was used for slot-die deposition. The ZnO ETL was coated at 75 °C with 0.06 mL/min flow rate and 1.08 m/min drum speed. The ETL was annealed at 100 °C for 10 min in air. The active layer PM6:Y6 (ratio 1:1) was tested at temperatures 60, 80, 100, 120 °C and concentrations 12, 16, 20, 24, 28 mg/mL. For the AL, the drum speed was 1.5 m/min with a 0.12 mL/min flow rate. 10 nm MoO3 and 150 nm Ag were sequentially thermally evaporated at 2 x 10⁻⁵ mbar using an INFICON XTM/2 system. Up to 24 solar cells were fabricated per evaporation from a one-meter-long AL, with an approximate active area of 0.8 cm². At least 8 devices were encapsulated per evaporation batch. An activation reverse bias of -5 V with a maximum current of 100 mA was applied before encapsulation. Encapsulation used epoxy-based glue EPXR (bisphenol A diglycidyl ether and Chissonox 221) cured under UV for 5 min reaching 66 ± 0.5 °C. J-V curves were measured with a Keithley 2400 source meter using 50 mV steps under AM1.5G 1000 W/m² illumination with a 0.3996 cm² aperture shadow mask. Averages include statistics of eight devices per condition. EQE and absorbance measurements were performed with a QEX10 system from 300 to 1100 nm with 5 nm step size. Light intensity measurements varied the solar simulator from 62.14 mW/cm² to 147.33 mW/cm². Thickness measurements used a DS95-50 AFM in noncontact mode over a 5 × 5 µm² area.

Procedures And Architectures
The device employs an inverted structure (ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6/MoO3/Ag) compatible with roll-to-roll processing. The active layer was deposited via hot slot-die coating matching the substrate temperature to the slot-die head temperature. A syringe pump controlled ink flow through a hot tube to the slot-die head, maintaining temperature throughout the coating procedure. For the ternary devices, two ratios were tested: [1:1:0.2] and [1:1.1:0.1] PM6:Y6:PC61BM. The donor/acceptor ratio was initially fixed at 1:1 based on previous literature for highest efficiencies. The solution concentration ranged from 12 to 28 mg/mL to produce AL thicknesses from semi-transparent to opaque. Bimolecular recombination was assessed via the $J_{SC} 	ext{ } 	ext{∝ } P_{in}^S$ relation, and trap-assisted recombination via the VOC vs In(Pin) slope. Exciton dissociation ($	ext{η}_{diss}$) and charge collection ($	ext{η}_{coll}$) efficiencies were calculated from $J_{ph}$ vs $V_{eff}$ curves.

Key Results
The champion PCE for a ternary PM6:Y6:PC61BM device reached 7.2% in open-air slot-die coated flexible configuration. The average PCE for binary PM6:Y6 devices at 100 °C coating was 5.8%, with an FF of 49.0% at 217 nm thickness. Coating at 100 °C yielded a JSC of 17.3 mA/cm² (at 154 nm thickness) and the lowest bimolecular recombination parameter S = 0.978. Coating at 120 °C resulted in an average FF of 42.2% compared to 47.10% at 100 °C, due to fast solvent drying inducing edge aggregation. EQE increased with higher coating temperatures, indicating improved carrier collection at 120 °C. The ternary [1:1:0.2] ratio achieved a 12% higher average JSC than the binary device coated at 100 °C with 24 mg/mL in O-XY. The ternary [1:1:0.1] ratio achieved an average PCE of 6.7% with an average FF of 49.1%. The ternary [1:1:0.2] ratio achieved an average PCE of 6.6% with an average FF of 47.3%. The dissociation probability ($	ext{η}_{diss}$) increased from 93.7% (binary) to 96.3% ([1:1:0.2] ternary) and 95.7% ([1:1.1:0.1] ternary). The collection probability ($	ext{η}_{coll}$) improved from 69.6% (binary) to 77.7% ([1:1:0.2] ternary) and 73.2% ([1:1.1:0.1] ternary). After 1050 hours dark storage (ISOS-D-1), ternary devices retained 99.4% of their average initial PCE. After more than 1500 hours dark storage, binary devices retained more than 97% of initial average PCE. Thermal annealing at 120 °C for 3 min improved JSC of devices coated at 60 °C and 80 °C but had no effect on 100 °C and 120 °C coated devices. J-V curves at 120 °C show a lower FF of 42.2% vs 47.10% at 100 °C, with the PCE saturating around 100 °C. Absorption measurements showed no blue or redshift when varying coating temperature from 60 to 120 °C. The maximum absorption of the donor is at approximately 625 nm and the acceptor at approximately 820 nm. The ternary [1:1:0.2] device achieved JSC values up to 20 mA/cm². The PCE for the thickest AL (217 nm) at 24 mg/mL was 6.3% with FF of 49.0%.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The PCE saturation around 100 °C is attributed to the onset of faster solvent drying at 120 °C, inducing edge aggregation that creates stripe inhomogeneities and degrades fill factor. The lower bimolecular recombination at 100 °C (S = 0.978, closest to unity) explains the optimized performance over other temperatures. Trap-assisted recombination dominates all tested temperatures (VOC vs In(Pin) slopes > kT/q), consistent with open-air processing without cleanroom controls. Adding PC61BM creates a ternary energy cascade (LUMO of PC61BM between PM6 and Y6) that enhances charge dissociation and balanced transport. The increased collection probability in ternary devices confirms that a small amount of fullerene can improve charge extraction on flexible substrates processed by slot-die coating. The lack of FF degradation at higher AL thicknesses (116 nm to 217 nm) demonstrates PM6:Y6 can maintain high performance as thick layers, supporting mechanical robustness for roll-to-roll processing.

Contradictions And Limitations
The 120 °C coating yielded higher JSC (better carrier collection) but lower FF (42.2% vs 47.10%), preventing it from being the absolute performance optimum. The optimal temperature was chosen based on the highest PCE rather than a clear trend in S-values across all temperatures. Devices were not prepared in a cleanroom or glovebox, resulting in high trap-assisted recombination that could potentially limit efficiency. The EQEs for ternary devices do not show a specific photocurrent maximum attributable to PCBM due to the weak and broad absorption of the fullerene. The study is based on a small sample size (8 devices per condition) which may limit statistical inference. Only dark storage stability (ISOS-D-1) was tested; light soaking and environmental (humidity/oxygen) stability were not reported.

Claims
Slot-die coating of PM6:Y6 in open-air using o-xylene can produce flexible OSCs with PCE up to 7.2%, demonstrating industrial scalability for the PM6:Y6 system. The champion PCE of 7.2% was achieved in a ternary device on flexible substrate. Binary PM6:Y6 at 100 °C reached 5.8% average PCE. All devices were coated in open-air using o-xylene without additives. The fabrication is compatible with roll-to-roll processing. Efficiencies are significantly lower than the 15% achieved on rigid glass substrates with the same materials. Trap-assisted recombination remains high due to open-air processing. Paves the way for upscaling OSC production using the PM6:Y6 system. Reduces the lab-to-fab gap by demonstrating a scalable, green-solvent process.
Adding a small amount of PC61BM to the PM6:Y6 blend in a ternary configuration improves exciton dissociation probability and charge collection efficiency. η_diss increased from 93.7% (binary) to 96.3% ([1:1:0.2]). η_coll increased from 69.6% (binary) to 77.7% ([1:1:0.2]). Champion PCE of 7.2% vs binary 6.3% at 24 mg/mL. The [1:1.1:0.1] ratio achieved slightly lower PCE (6.7%) than the [1:1:0.2] ratio's implied potential, though its FF was higher. No specific photocurrent maximum is observable in EQEs for the fullerene component. Confirms that small fullerene amounts benefit charge extraction in slot-die coated flexible OSCs. Provides a photophysical mechanism (energy cascade and balanced transport) for performance enhancement.
The optimal coating temperature for PM6:Y6 is 100 °C, balancing drying kinetics with morphology to minimize bimolecular recombination while maintaining fill factor. The S-value closest to unity (S = 0.978) was at 100 °C. FF of 47.10% at 100 °C vs 42.2% at 120 °C. PCE shows a clear improvement trend that saturates around 100 °C. JSC was higher at 120 °C, indicating better carrier collection but inferior FF. The choice was based on the highest PCE rather than a single clear parameter. Defines the hot slot-die coating protocol for the PM6:Y6 system. Shows that matching substrate and head temperatures at 100 °C is optimal.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Four coating temperatures (60, 80, 100, 120 °C) were screened for the active layer. Five solution concentrations (12, 16, 20, 24, 28 mg/mL) were tested to vary AL thickness. Two ternary ratios ([1:1:0.2] and [1:1.1:0.1]) were tested to optimize PC61BM content. Bimolecular recombination was assessed via $J_{SC} 	ext{ } 	ext{∝ } P_{in}^S$ at various thicknesses and temperatures. Trap-assisted recombination was checked via VOC vs In(Pin) slope. Exciton dissociation and collection efficiencies were calculated as an ablation of the ternary effect. Thermal annealing was used as a post-processing ablation step, revealing temperature-dependent crystallization. Light intensity dependence measurements confirmed the recombination mechanisms.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: Schematic of the inverted device geometry ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6/MoO3/Ag and spectral absorption of PM6 vs Y6. Figure 2: J-V curves and EQEs of representative devices coated at different temperatures (60, 80, 100, 120 °C). Figure 3: Box plots showing PCE and FF evolution over 8 devices across the four coating temperatures. Figure 4: Micrographs of the dried active layer stripe showing edge aggregation above 100 °C. Figure 5: Box plots of PV parameters versus active layer thickness from 101 nm to 217 nm. Figure 6: J-V curves of binary vs ternary devices showing enhanced JSC. Figure 7: Box plot comparing main PV parameters of binary and ternary devices. Figure 8: PCE retention over time showing stability of encapsulated devices. Figure 10: Stability under dark storage following the ISOS-D-1 protocol. Table 1: PV parameters extracted from J-V curves of PM6:Y6 devices at different temperatures (8 devices per condition). Table 2: Summary of PV parameters of PM6:Y6 solar cells with different AL thicknesses. Table S2: Average values for ternary devices at both ratios. Table S3: Dissociation and collection efficiency values for binary and ternary devices. Figure S2: Normalized absorption spectra of dried films coated at different temperatures. Figure S5: JSC and VOC box plots versus coating temperature. Figure S6a: Bimolecular recombination S-value vs coating temperature. Figure S6b: VOC vs In(Pin) slope for trap-assisted recombination analysis. Figure S7: Absorption spectra of different AL thicknesses (Fig S7) and representative J-V curves (Fig S7b). Figure S8a: JSC vs Pin for different thicknesses at 100 °C coating. Figure S8b: VOC vs In(Pin) slope for different thicknesses. Figure S9: $J_{ph}$ vs $V_{eff}$ curves for dissociation and collection analysis.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first demonstration of slot-die coated PM6:Y6 flexible OSCs in open-air using o-xylene without additives, achieving a champion PCE of 7.2%. 2. The strongest evidence is the systematic temperature optimization confirming that 100 °C minimizes bimolecular recombination (S = 0.978) and preserves fill factor, while ternary PC61BM improves dissociation probability by nearly 3 percentage points. 3. The future path involves scaling to a true roll-to-roll platform, incorporating cleanroom processing to reduce trap-assisted recombination, and investigating light-soaking and environmental stability beyond dark storage.

summary.title: Stable open-shell aromatic nitric acid radicals: accessing highly efficient photothermal conversion with restricted radiative decay
summary.authors: Zejun Wang, Jiawen Zhou, Yiheng Zhang, Weiya Zhu, Yuan Li
summary.field_subfield: Materials Chemistry / Photothermal Conversion / Organic Radicals
summary.executive_summary: This study reports the design and synthesis of a series of star-shaped aromatic nitric acid radical (ANAR) materials that achieve highly efficient photothermal conversion via restricted radiative decay. Unlike most open-shell radicals that are thermodynamically or kinetically unstable in air, these ANARs exhibit high electrochemical, thermal, and light stability due to rich resonance structures including closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide configurations with unpaired electrons delocalized in conjugated backbones. Four compounds—TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8—were synthesized via a facile two-step procedure involving demethylation and subsequent air oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors. The radicals were characterized by UV-vis-NIR spectroscopy, cyclic voltammetry, electron spin resonance (ESR), and photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) measurements. Key findings include: 1) All demethylated ANARs exhibited highly reversible CV curves over 15 cycles, indicating unexpected electrochemical stability compared to traditional organic radicals; 2) PLQYs of the radical products dropped below 1%, confirming radical formation; 3) ESR spectra revealed exceptionally high radical spin concentration, particularly in TPA-TPA-O6; 4) TPA-TPA-O6 demonstrated a black powder color with a broadened absorption spectrum extending from 300 to 2000 nm in the aggregated state. In photothermal testing under 808 nm laser irradiation (0.8 W/cm²), TPA-TPA-O6 achieved a temperature rise from 25 °C to approximately 210 °C within 60 seconds, with sustained performance over ten on/off cycles. In a solar-driven water evaporation application using an interfacial heating system (TPA-TPA-O6 loaded on polyurethane foam, 30 mg loading), a water evaporation efficiency of 89.41% and a rate of 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ under 1 sun irradiation were recorded. This represents top performance among pure organic small-molecule photothermal materials. The authors further demonstrate practical viability by applying the system to seawater desalination, where concentrations of Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, and K⁺ were significantly reduced, outperforming typical membrane-based methods. The study concludes by establishing a novel strategy for designing stable, high-spin organic-small-molecule photothermal materials.

claims.description: TPA-TPA-O6 is a highly efficient pure organic small-molecule photothermal material with unprecedented water evaporation performance.
The ANAR framework provides exceptional air, thermal, and electrochemical stability, addressing a major limitation of organic radicals.
The ANAR system is effective for seawater desalination, outperforming typical membrane-based methods.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports the design and synthesis of a series of star-shaped aromatic nitric acid radical (ANAR) materials that achieve highly efficient photothermal conversion via restricted radiative decay. Unlike most open-shell radicals that are thermodynamically or kinetically unstable in air, these ANARs exhibit high electrochemical, thermal, and light stability due to rich resonance structures including closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide configurations with unpaired electrons delocalized in conjugated backbones. Four compounds—TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8—were synthesized via a facile two-step procedure involving demethylation and subsequent air oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors. The radicals were characterized by UV-vis-NIR spectroscopy, cyclic voltammetry, electron spin resonance (ESR), and photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) measurements. Key findings include: 1) All demethylated ANARs exhibited highly reversible CV curves over 15 cycles, indicating unexpected electrochemical stability compared to traditional organic radicals; 2) PLQYs of the radical products dropped below 1%, confirming radical formation; 3) ESR spectra revealed exceptionally high radical spin concentration, particularly in TPA-TPA-O6; 4) TPA-TPA-O6 demonstrated a black powder color with a broadened absorption spectrum extending from 300 to 2000 nm in the aggregated state. In photothermal testing under 808 nm laser irradiation (0.8 W/cm²), TPA-TPA-O6 achieved a temperature rise from 25 °C to approximately 210 °C within 60 seconds, with sustained performance over ten on/off cycles. In a solar-driven water evaporation application using an interfacial heating system (TPA-TPA-O6 loaded on polyurethane foam, 30 mg loading), a water evaporation efficiency of 89.41% and a rate of 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ under 1 sun irradiation were recorded. This represents top performance among pure organic small-molecule photothermal materials. The authors further demonstrate practical viability by applying the system to seawater desalination, where concentrations of Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, and K⁺ were significantly reduced, outperforming typical membrane-based methods. The study concludes by establishing a novel strategy for designing stable, high-spin organic-small-molecule photothermal materials.

Research Context
Most open-shell radicals are thermodynamically or kinetically unstable in air due to their incompletely satisfied valency. Organic small molecules are relatively overlooked in photothermal conversion compared to inorganic, 2D framework, and conjugated polymer materials. Inorganic materials contain precious, nondegradable metals and pose potential safety issues for in vivo applications. 2D frameworks and conjugated polymers suffer from poor synthesis reproducibility, high cost, and performance decay. The previous organic small molecules such as porphyrins and cyanines limit large-scale application due to cumbersome synthesis and poor photothermal stability. Open-shell radicals with high photothermal conversion efficiency and thermal/electrochemical stability are rarely reported. Preparing airstable organic conjugated radicals is challenging due to intrinsic high reactivity with oxygen. The preparation of stable neutral radicals is both the basis for radical chemistry theory and the prerequisite for multifunctional application.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether aromatic nitric acid radicals can be prepared as air-stable neutral radicals without steric hindrance protection groups. The hypothesis is that the rich resonance structures including closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide structures delocalize unpaired electrons, granting thermal and electrochemical stability. Four star-shaped ANAR materials with different cores (triphenylamine, triazine, pyrene, spiro fluorene) were designed to test structural effects on radical character. It is predicted that strong donor-acceptor conjugation in the radical state will reduce the optical bandgap and enhance paramagnetic properties. The hypothesis further posits that high radical spin concentration will lead to highly nonradiative decay and enhanced photothermal conversion efficiency. TPA-TPA-O6 was expected to exhibit the highest photothermal performance among the four molecules due to its strong donor character and wide absorption.

Methodological Details
Four star-shaped ANAR materials (TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8) were synthesized via a two-step facile demethylation and consequent air oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors. The methoxy-substituted precursors were dissolved in dichloromethane at a concentration of 5 mg/mL for cyclic voltammetry measurements. CV measurements were performed over 15 cycles in dichloromethane solution containing 0.1 M nBu4NPF6 as the supporting electrolyte. The CV scan rate was set at 0.1 V/s. Potential values were reported with saturated calomel electrode as the reference using the Fc⁺/Fc couple at 0.27 V as the internal standard. For the interfacial evaporation system, a commercially available white polyurethane (PU) porous foam was employed as the support. TPA-TPA-O6 was loaded into the PU foam by impregnation in solution followed by drying at 80 °C. The active device consisted of a 2.0 cm diameter foam with 30 mg of TPA-TPA-O6 loading. Photothermal properties were evaluated under 808 nm laser irradiation at an energy power of 0.8 W cm⁻². Water evaporation was tested under 1 sun illumination, with an equilibrium temperature of 81.2 °C achieved under 600 s continuous irradiation. Seawater desalination was verified by monitoring concentrations of Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, and K⁺ after desalination. PLQY measurements were conducted in dichloromethane solution and film for all precursors and radical products.

Procedures And Architectures
UV-Vis-NIR spectra were recorded for TPA-TPA-OMe in dichloromethane solution and film, showing absorption at 305 nm and 380 nm, respectively. For TPA-TPA-O6, the film absorption in DMSO showed a typical great red shift with a long tail from 400-825 nm. CV was performed in film (coated on carbon-glass electrode) and solution to assess electrochemical reversibility and determine HOMO/LUMO levels. ESR spectra were collected at a test amount of 0.02 mmol to characterize radical spin concentration. PLQY and photoluminescence measurements were performed to quantify radiative decay pathways. IR thermal camera was used to monitor temperature increments under laser irradiation. TPA-TPA-O6 powder was further aggregated in the solid state, extending absorption from 300 to 2000 nm. The photothermal setup involved 808 nm laser irradiation at 0.8 W cm⁻² for 60 s, with temperature monitoring at 25 °C starting point. Laser power was increased to 1.0 W cm⁻² for higher temperature tests. The evaporation system used an interfacial heating configuration with the PU+TPA-TPA-O6 foam floating on water. Seawater desalination was demonstrated by floating the PU+TPA-TPA-O6 foam on seawater and measuring ion concentrations post-treatment.

Key Results
All demethylated ANARs exhibited highly reversible CV curves under the oxidation process and showed negligible change after 15 cycles. The HOMO energy levels of TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8 were recorded as -4.90, -4.81, -4.97, and -4.84 eV, respectively. The HOMO energy levels of the demethylated radicaloids were obviously enhanced compared to the methoxy precursors. PLQYs of all radical products dropped below 1% (TPA-TPA-O6: 0.1%, TPA-TPZ-O6: 0.9%, TPA-PY-O8: 1.0%, Spiro-O8: 0.3%) after demethylation. ESR spectra showed very obvious increase in relative signal intensity after demethylation at 0.02 mmol, confirming high radical spin concentration. TPA-TPA-O6 exhibited a temperature increase from 25 °C to approximately 210 °C within 60 s under 0.8 W cm⁻² laser irradiation. Increasing laser power to 1.0 W cm⁻² raised the temperature of TPA-TPA-O6 to about 250 °C within 60 s. TPA-TPA-O6 exhibited excellent photothermal stability over ten cycles of laser irradiation on and off. The equilibrium temperature of PU+TPA-TPA-O6 foam reached 81.2 °C under 600 s continuous irradiation (1.0 kW m⁻²), while pure PU foam reached only 36 °C. The water evaporation rate was recorded as 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ with a solar-driven water evaporation efficiency of 89.41% under 1 sun illumination. The absorption of TPA-TPA-O6 in the aggregated powder state extended from 300 to 2000 nm. Conductivity of all demethylated counterparts was improved, with lower HOMO energy levels in TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 due to triazine and pyrene cores.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The rich resonance structures, including closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide structures, delocalize unpaired electrons, granting exceptional air, thermal, and electrochemical stability to ANARs. The strong donor-acceptor conjugation effect simultaneously reduces the optical bandgap and determines the paramagnetic properties of the radical materials. The exceptionally high radical spin concentration in the solid state triggers largely boosted nonradiative decay, which efficiently enhances photothermal conversion. The black powder color and wide absorption tail (400–825 nm in film) are diagnostic of the typical radical character in the solid state. This work establishes a novel design strategy for creating stable organic-small-molecule photothermal materials using simple two-step synthesis from cheap raw materials. The ANAR framework is applicable beyond photothermal conversion to organic electronics, spintronics, and magnetic devices due to restricted radiative decay and potential high conductivity.

Contradictions And Limitations
TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 showed relatively poor photothermal conversion performance, which the authors attribute to low radical spin concentration and potential partial protonation to form hydroxyl groups. The highest-performance photothermal materials reported in the literature are typically not soluble in any solvents and are challenging to reproduce. The study does not report the exact quantitative reduction factors for Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, and K⁺ in the desalination experiment beyond the qualitative statement of significant reduction. The exact mechanism by which TPA-TPA-O6 achieves 89.41% efficiency is described as 'detailed calculation process is shown in Supporting Information,' but the specific calculation parameters are not in the main text. The paper does not report the specific degradation or durability tests of the desalination system beyond the ion reduction measurement.

Claims
TPA-TPA-O6 is a highly efficient pure organic small-molecule photothermal material with unprecedented water evaporation performance. Under 1 sun irradiation, water evaporation efficiency is 89.41% and the rate is 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹. The temperature rise is from 25 °C to 210 °C within 60 s at 0.8 W cm⁻². The absorption extends from 300 to 2000 nm in aggregated powder state. TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 exhibit much lower photothermal performance (25 °C to 40 °C in 60 s). The performance advantage is relative to other organic materials; the absolute superiority over inorganic systems is not quantitatively compared. This sets a new benchmark for pure organic photothermal conversion materials in solar energy harvesting. The low-cost two-step synthesis makes it a practical alternative to expensive porphyrins and dyes.
The ANAR framework provides exceptional air, thermal, and electrochemical stability, addressing a major limitation of organic radicals. All demethylated ANARs showed negligible CV change after 15 cycles at 0.1 V/s. The radical products retain comparable electrochemical and air stability with their methoxy precursors. The radical spin concentration is high, and the PLQY is reduced to below 1%, confirming radical formation. The triazine and pyrene-cored radicals show weaker ESR signals due to lower electron-donating capability. The stability enables practical application in air-exposed devices and industrial processing. This design principle can be extended to other aromatic nitric acid radical structures with varied cores.
The ANAR system is effective for seawater desalination, outperforming typical membrane-based methods. Concentrations of Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, and K⁺ were significantly reduced after treatment. The values achieved are lower than those through typical membrane-based methods. The exact quantitative ion reduction data is reported in Supporting Information rather than the main text. No long-term durability or scalability data for the desalination system is provided. This demonstrates a practical path for solar-driven desalination using organic radicals.

Data And Code Availability
The Supporting Information, including detailed synthetic schemes, characterization figures (S1–S18), table data (S1, S2, S11, S16, S17, S18), and calculation details, is available free of charge at http://pubs.acs.org.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Structural ablation: Four different cores (triphenylamine, triazine, pyrene, spiro fluorene) were compared to isolate the effect of donor strength and conjugated architecture on radical character. The triazine and pyrene cores with lower electron-donating capability resulted in lower HOMO levels and weaker ESR signals, demonstrating the dependence of radical character on donor strength. The temperature dependence on laser power was verified: increasing power from 0.8 to 1.0 W cm⁻² raised the temperature from 210 °C to 250 °C. Photothermal stability was tested over ten on/off cycles, showing negligible performance decay.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A, B, C: Illustrates the structures of the four star-shaped ANAR materials with different cores. Figure 2A, B, C: Shows UV-vis absorption spectra of precursors and radical products in solution and film states. Figure 3: Displays CV curves of all four demethylated ANARs over 15 cycles in solution. Figure 4A: ESR spectra showing radical spin signals at 0.02 mmol before and after demethylation. Figure 4B: Photoluminescence and PLQY measurements for all precursors and radicals. Figure 5A, B, C: Photothermal temperature-time curves and IR thermal camera images of TPA-TPA-O6 under 808 nm irradiation. Figure 6: Compares water evaporation efficiency (89.41%), rate (1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹), equilibrium temperature (81.2 °C vs 36 °C), and ion reduction in desalination. Table S1: Lists HOMO/LUMO energy levels, PLQYs, and PL wavelengths for all precursors and radicals. Table S2: Compares water evaporation efficiency and rate for reported photothermal materials. Figure S18: Shows ion concentration changes after desalination treatment.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the design and synthesis of air-stable, star-shaped aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs) that achieve a record-setting 89.41% solar water evaporation efficiency as pure organic small molecules. 2. The strongest evidence is the combination of highly reversible CV over 15 cycles, ESR confirming high spin concentration, PLQY below 1%, and the temperature rise from 25 °C to 210 °C within 60 s, all validating the restricted radiative decay mechanism. 3. The future path is to develop ANAR materials with enhanced planarity for applications in photothermal conversion, organic electronics, spintronics, and magnetic devices, building on the demonstrated conductivity and paramagnetic properties.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work reports a metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics at the charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles, achieving yields up to 100% and 100% selectivity under ambient air at room temperature. The approach utilizes Eosin Y (EY) as a low-cost organic photocatalyst at only 0.6 mole%, K3PO4 as a base, and 40 mM CTAB to form spherical micelles that house both the catalyst and substrates at the micellar Stern layer. The catalytic efficiency is attributed to a non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) with a time constant of 0.3 ps, mediated by the micellar microenvironment that facilitates close proximity of reactants and modulates redox potentials. The methodology outperforms previously reported Ir-based photocatalytic routes (which require high catalyst doses and organic solvents) and metal nanoparticle-catalyzed methods (which suffer from slow kinetics and poor selectivity). The reaction proceeds under green light (525 nm) within 4 hours, with a broad substrate scope covering electron-rich and electron-deficient amines. Oxygen acts as a sacrificial oxidant regenerating the photocatalyst via hydrogen peroxide formation. This is the first report of aqueous-phase synthesis of azo compounds using a metal-free photocatalytic approach at a charged interface.

Research Context
Traditional diazotization methods produce unstable diazonium intermediates and unwanted waste. Metal nanoparticle-catalyzed synthesis of azo compounds has been reported but suffers from slow kinetics and poor selectivity. Photocatalytic reductive coupling of nitrobenzenes requires an inert atmosphere and produces azoxyaromatics or nitrosobenzene as side products. Previous photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics utilized Ir-based catalysts in organic solvents with slow kinetics and moderate yields. Low solubility of amine substrates in aqueous medium limited previous synthetic approaches to organic solvents. Charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) have been shown to modulate chemical and photochemical reactions that are otherwise inefficient in bulk medium.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a sustainable metal-free photocatalytic route can be developed in an aqueous medium at ambient atmosphere for the synthesis of azoaromatics. The authors hypothesize that the micellar surface can act as a scaffold hosting both the photocatalyst (Eosin Y) and arylamine substrates for efficient coupling. It is hypothesized that a non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) mechanism would significantly accelerate reaction kinetics at the CAI. The hypothesis further posits that the micellar Stern layer would solubilize both hydrophilic and hydrophobic components at distinct locations, bringing the PC and substrates into close proximity. The authors predict that Eosin Y at a very low loading (0.6 mole%) could achieve 100% conversion in 4 hours, outperforming all previously reported catalytic methodologies.

Methodological Details
The study investigates the photophysical behavior of Eosin Y (EY) in the presence of three surfactants: CTAB, SDS, and Triton X-100. The absorption peak of EY in water at 516 nm showed a bathochromic shift of 9 nm with CTAB and 16 nm with TX-100, indicating micellar association. EY exhibited fluorescence quenching at premicellar concentrations but enhanced fluorescence of 2.4-fold only in the presence of CTAB at or near the CMC (0.75-1.0 mM). No spectral changes were observed with SDS, indicating lack of interaction with negatively charged micelles. The fluorescence lifetime of EY@CTAB increased from 1.17 ns in water to 2.74 ns upon micellization, signifying association. The composite was tested for stability in the presence of the base K3PO4; EY@CTAB was stable while EY@TX-100 suffered disassembly. The optimized reaction uses p-anisidine as substrate, 0.6 mole% EY, 2 equivalents of K3PO4, and 40 mM CTAB as the micellizing agent. The reaction is triggered by green light at 525 nm under ambient air atmosphere. Conversion was monitored via GC-MS and product isolation followed by NMR characterization.

Procedures And Architectures
CTAB forms spherical micelles at the optimized concentration of 40 mM, as confirmed by HR-TEM measurements. The photocatalyst Eosin Y bears two negative charges at pH 7, facilitating electrostatic interaction with positively charged CTAB. At premicellar concentration, EY undergoes CTAB-induced aggregation via ion-pair formation, then dissociates at or near the CMC as EY is trapped in the micellar Stern layer. The reaction mixture is irradiated with green light (525 nm) for 4 hours under ambient air. Fluorescence quenching experiments used p-anisidine to probe the PET phenomenon with EY@CTAB. Fluorescence up-conversion measurements were performed to determine the PET time constant. Radical trap experiments involved irradiation for 5 minutes with p-anisidine, then addition of 1 equivalent of 2,6-di-tert-butyl-4-methylphenol (BHT) as a radical trap. A subsequent 4-hour irradiation was performed with BHT to validate radical intermediate formation.

Key Results
100% conversion of p-anisidine to 1,2-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)diazene was achieved within 4 hours using 0.6 mole% EY under 525 nm green light. The reaction dose of 0.6 mole% EY represents an 8.3-fold reduction compared to the previous Ir-based photocatalyst method. Under blue light (previously reported condition), 100% conversion requires 6 hours rather than 4 hours. Electron-rich arylamines (1-7) all show 100% conversion within 4 hours, whereas the previous Ir-catalyst method reported 64% conversion after 24 hours in bulk acetonitrile. Aniline as substrate also yields 100% conversion under standard conditions. P-chloroaniline and p-bromoaniline show conversion yields of 98% and 95%, respectively. Fluorescence quenching of EY@CTAB by p-anisidine yields a Stern-Volmer plot with a quenching rate constant of 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1, consistent with a non-diffusive bimolecular process. Fluorescence up-conversion reveals an ultrafast PET time constant of 0.3 ps. Radical trapping with BHT results in negligible conversion (~5.0%) to the azo product after 4 hours, and an HR-MS peak for p-anisidine-BHT adducts at 342.2399 g/mol confirms radical formation. H2O2 sensing strips show a distinct color change before and after irradiation, confirming that atmospheric O2 acts as a sacrificial oxidant for photocatalyst regeneration.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The enhanced catalytic efficacy is attributed to non-diffusive PET and modulation of redox potentials at the CAI. The micellar Stern layer provides a less polar hydrocarbon/aqueous interface where arylamines preferentially solubilize, bringing substrates and PC into close proximity. The 0.3 ps time constant signifies that PET at the micellar surface is instantaneous in nature. The observed Stern-Volmer behavior suggests the quenching is non-diffusive, indicating reactants encounter each other via a controlled mechanism rather than random diffusion. K3PO4 neither interferes with the specific association of EY with CTAB nor interacts directly with the excited state of EY@CTAB, as the fluorescence lifetime remains unperturbed. The PET step precedes the proton abstraction step by the base, as the presence of K3PO4 has no noticeable effect on the SV plots.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study was conducted as a preprint on ChemRxiv and has not been peer-reviewed, meaning the results are preliminary. The broad substrate scope was validated for electron-rich and electron-deficient amines, but the conversion for electron-poor halides (p-chloroaniline, p-bromoaniline) is slightly reduced (98% and 95%). The base DABCO yields slightly less conversion than inorganic bases (K3PO4, KOH), suggesting potential limitations in base selection. The paper does not explicitly report the reproducibility across multiple independent runs (e.g., triplicate measurements) for the 100% conversion claims. The specific yield for p-nitroaniline is not quantified, only noted as showing no fluorescence quenching, meaning the PET mechanism fails for this substrate.

Claims
Micellar charged aqueous interfaces enable a metal-free, highly efficient POC for azoaromatics in water at ambient conditions. 100% conversion of p-anisidine is achieved in 4 hours with only 0.6 mole% photocatalyst. The reaction is performed at ambient atmosphere using atmospheric O2 as the oxidant. Yields reach up to 100% with 100% selectivity for azoaromatics. The non-diffusive PET time constant of 0.3 ps substantiates ultrafast electron transfer. For electron-poor substrates like p-bromoaniline, conversion drops to 95%. P-nitroaniline shows no fluorescence quenching, indicating the PET mechanism does not work for all substrates. This opens new opportunities in the aqueous-phase synthesis of azo compounds with reduced environmental footprint. The 8.3-fold reduction in catalyst loading suggests significant practical feasibility for scale-up compared to Ir-based alternatives.
CTAB micelles specifically host both Eosin Y and arylamine substrates at the Stern layer for non-diffusive PET. The bathochromic shift and 2.4-fold fluorescence enhancement at CMC (0.75-1.0 mM) confirm micellar association. Fluorescence lifetime increases from 1.17 ns to 2.74 ns upon CTAB micellization. HR-TEM confirms spherical micelles at 40 mM CTAB. BHT radical trapping yields a characteristic adduct at 342.2399 g/mol, confirming amine radical intermediates via PET. SDS micelles show no spectral changes, indicating the effect is specific to cationic surfactant interaction with negatively charged EY. The specificity of the interaction implies that cationic micelles are essential for this photocatalytic mechanism.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Control experiments without CTAB micelles showed no catalytic activity in water. EY@TX-100 (anionic micelle) suffered disassembly in the presence of K3PO4 base, ruling it out as a catalytic system. The reaction without a base shows no conversion, confirming proton abstraction is a critical step. BHT radical trapping reduces conversion to ~5.0%, confirming that amine radicals are the active intermediate. The presence of K3PO4 does not alter the SV plot or quenching rate constant, confirming PET precedes base-mediated proton abstraction.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows the absorption spectra of EY in water (516 nm) with bathochromic shifts in CTAB and TX-100 micelles. Figure 1b shows fluorescence quenching at premicellar concentrations. Figure 1c illustrates the CTAB-induced aggregation of EY at premicellar concentration and dissociation at CMC. Figure 1d shows the fluorescence lifetime of EY@CTAB increasing from 1.17 ns to 2.74 ns. Figure 2a shows the Stern-Volmer quenching behavior for p-anisidine. Figure 2b shows the linear Stern-Volmer plot with kq = 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1. Figure 2c shows that K3PO4 has no effect on the SV plot. Figure 2d shows the fluorescence up-conversion with 0.3 ps time constant. Figure S4 shows HR-TEM of spherical CTAB micelles. Table 1 lists optimized reaction conditions: p-anisidine to 1,2-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)diazene, 100% conversion, 4 h, 0.6 mole% EY, 2 equiv. K3PO4, 40 mM CTAB, 525 nm.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first metal-free, aqueous-phase photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics at charged micellar interfaces, achieving 100% yields and selectivity with 0.6 mole% Eosin Y. 2. The strongest evidence is the 0.3 ps non-diffusive PET time constant and the radical trapping adduct at 342.2399 g/mol, together with the 8.3-fold reduction in catalyst loading compared to Ir-based methods. 3. The future path lies in expanding the substrate scope beyond electron-rich and moderately electron-poor amines to more complex or sterically hindered substrates and investigating further scale-up of this micellar-confined aqueous photocatalysis.

summary.title: Spontaneous crystal fluctuation in hydrocarbon polymer-coated monolayer MoS2, MoSe2, WS2, and WSe2 with strong photoluminescence enhancement
summary.authors: Takahiro Nakahara; Takashi Kobayashi; Tetsuji Dohi; Takeshi Yoshimura; Norifumi Fujimura; Daisuke Kiriya

summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a universal post-preparation strategy for enhancing the photoluminescence (PL) intensity of all monolayer transition metal dichalcogenide (TMDC) materials—including both sulfur-based (MoS2, WS2) and selenium-based (MoSe2, WSe2) compounds—by coating them with a simple hydrocarbon, paraffin. The authors identify that while prior methods (p-type doping with F4TCNQ or superacid TFSI) improved PL in sulfur-based TMDCs but were ineffective for selenium-based compounds, the substrate effect remains a common barrier to optical performance. By exploiting the large thermal expansion coefficient of paraffin (melting point 42–45 °C), the study demonstrates that a paraffin coating applied via spin-coating with a concurrent heat blower induces spontaneous mechanical fluctuation, strain, and eventual desorption of the monolayer from the underlying substrate. The results show PL enhancement factors of 215 for MoS2, 55 for WS2, 50 for MoSe2, and 9 for WSe2 relative to as-exfoliated flakes. Mechanistic evidence includes a -0.72 cm⁻¹ negative Raman E' peak shift indicating strain, a 1.03 cm⁻¹ positive A' peak shift indicating carrier concentration reduction, and PL mapping showing nonuniform enhancement with localized wrinkling. In an extreme case, the monolayer deforms into a bundled structure. The paper concludes that the substrate effect is eliminated via paraffin penetration at the substrate-TMDC interface, and the paraffin coating offers a transparent, flexible, and biocompatible encapsulation for optoelectronic devices.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a universal post-preparation strategy for enhancing the photoluminescence (PL) intensity of all monolayer transition metal dichalcogenide (TMDC) materials—including both sulfur-based (MoS2, WS2) and selenium-based (MoSe2, WSe2) compounds—by coating them with a simple hydrocarbon, paraffin. The authors identify that while prior methods (p-type doping with F4TCNQ or superacid TFSI) improved PL in sulfur-based TMDCs but were ineffective for selenium-based compounds, the substrate effect remains a common barrier to optical performance. By exploiting the large thermal expansion coefficient of paraffin (melting point 42–45 °C), the study demonstrates that a paraffin coating applied via spin-coating with a concurrent heat blower induces spontaneous mechanical fluctuation, strain, and eventual desorption of the monolayer from the underlying substrate. The results show PL enhancement factors of 215 for MoS2, 55 for WS2, 50 for MoSe2, and 9 for WSe2 relative to as-exfoliated flakes. Mechanistic evidence includes a -0.72 cm⁻¹ negative Raman E' peak shift indicating strain, a 1.03 cm⁻¹ positive A' peak shift indicating carrier concentration reduction, and PL mapping showing nonuniform enhancement with localized wrinkling. In an extreme case, the monolayer deforms into a bundled structure. The paper concludes that the substrate effect is eliminated via paraffin penetration at the substrate-TMDC interface, and the paraffin coating offers a transparent, flexible, and biocompatible encapsulation for optoelectronic devices.

Research Context
Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (MX2) are attracting attention due to their thin crystal structure of only three atoms per layer. They exhibit a direct band gap at the K and K' points in the Brillouin zone, making them candidates for optical transistors, light-emitting diodes, and solar cells. A primary drawback is poor photoluminescence (PL) intensity caused by over-carrier concentrations, strains, and crystalline lattice defects. For sulfur-based compounds like MoS2 and WS2, p-type doping with F4TCNQ and superacid TFSI treatment has been established to enhance PL. However, these methods have not been effective for selenium-based TMDCs of MoSe2 and WSe2, leaving a gap in universal PL enhancement strategies. For selenium-based compounds, limited strategies include oleic acid treatment on MoSe2, hydrohalic acid treatment, and floating/ion-insertion for WSe2 to remove substrate effects. No universal strategy exists for improving optical behavior across a large variety of 2D semiconductor materials.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a universal method can enhance PL intensity in both sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs by removing the substrate effect. The authors hypothesize that coating monolayer TMDCs with a simple hydrocarbon, paraffin, can induce spontaneous fluctuation and desorption from the substrate. The predicted mechanism relies on the large thermal expansion coefficient of paraffin to apply strain during the coating process. The expected outcome is that the removal of the substrate effect will result in remarkable PL intensity improvement across all tested compounds. The paper also tests the hypothesis that the paraffin film formation is widely applicable to both sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs. A secondary hypothesis is that the deformation to a shrunk bundled structure arises from stress at the interface with paraffin when the monolayer is not surrounded by bulk flakes.

Methodological Details
The study tested four monolayer TMDC materials: MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, and WSe2. Samples were prepared from as-exfoliated (original) flakes on Si/SiO2 and quartz substrates. The paraffin used had a melting point of 42–45 °C. For the coating process, paraffin was melted on a hot plate at 80 °C in advance and dropped onto samples placed on a spin coater. A heat blower (hair dryer) was applied to keep paraffin melted during spin coating. PL spectra were recorded for the prepared films to measure enhancement factors. Optical microscopy images captured the as-exfoliated, coated, 2-hour, and 3-hour states of MoS2. PL mapping images confirmed spatial distribution of PL intensity across the monolayer plane. Raman spectroscopy was performed on 30 samples of monolayer MoS2 to extract statistical Raman shift data. PL enhancement was also observed on quartz substrates, confirming substrate-independence.

Procedures And Architectures
The paraffin was melted at 80 °C on a hot plate prior to spin-coating. The paraffin was dropped onto the sample placed on a spin coater. A heat blower (hair dryer) was used simultaneously to prevent immediate solidification of the paraffin. The paraffin coating process was applied sequentially to MoS2, WS2, WSe2, and MoSe2. Monolayers showed different band gaps and emission wavelengths across the four materials. PL enhancement factors were measured relative to the as-exfoliated state for each compound. The E' peak (in-plane vibrations) was monitored for strain sensitivity. The A' peak (out-of-plane vibrations) was monitored for carrier concentration sensitivity. For the bundling analysis, a monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes on three sides was tested. Statistical analysis was performed on 30 samples to derive average Raman shifts.

Key Results
The paraffin coating yielded PL enhancement factors of 215 for MoS2, 55 for WS2, 9 for WSe2, and 50 for MoSe2 relative to as-exfoliated flakes. For WS2, PL enhancement of approximately 36 times was observed through paraffin coating alone. The normalized PL spectrum for WS2 showed a decrease in the shoulder at the low-energy side, suggesting reduced trion-derived signal. PL mapping confirmed nonuniform enhancement with the center showing about 2.3 times greater intensity than the rim. The E' peak in monolayer MoS2 shifted in the negative direction by approximately -0.72 cm⁻¹ on average after paraffin coating. The A' peak shifted in the positive direction by 1.03 cm⁻¹ after paraffin coating. The PL peak position around the center shifted slightly 5–10 meV lower in energy than the rim. MoS2 deformed spontaneously over 3 hours at room temperature while surrounding bulk flakes maintained morphology. In the case of MoS2 surrounded by bulk flakes, the PL peak position at the folded edge shifted to lower energy. The folded edge region showed PL intensity with remarkable enhancement.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The PL enhancement mechanism is attributed to a combination of partial strain induced by paraffin volume change and subsequent monolayer desorption from the substrate. The negative E' shift indicates tensile strain within the monolayer MoS2 from paraffin coating. The positive A' shift indicates decreased electron concentration in the monolayer, attributed to substrate effect removal. The normalized PL shoulder reduction suggests a decrease in the trion-derived PL signal. Substrate effect removal is the key factor enhancing PL in both sulfur- and selenium-based monolayers. Paraffin is insulative, flexible, and transparent, enabling use in packaging flexible light-emitting displays and solar cells. The method applies strain via the large thermal expansion coefficient of paraffin, a principle applicable to other 2D layered materials. When not surrounded by bulk flakes, the monolayer desorbs and forms a shrunk bundled structure due to stress at the paraffin interface. A folded edge indicating bilayer MoS2 showed enhanced PL and E' red shift, consistent with strain-induced exciton drift.

Contradictions And Limitations
PL enhancement is nonuniform across the monolayer plane, with the center showing greater enhancement than the rim, suggesting localized fluctuation states. The enhancement factor for MoS2 (215) is significantly higher than for WSe2 (9), indicating material-dependent sensitivity to the method. A thick paraffin film achieved by simple casting (not spin coating) resulted in a glassy, non-transparent appearance, limiting optical monitoring. In the case of MoS2 surrounded by bulk flakes, large deformation is prevented but in-plane fluctuation still occurs due to paraffin volume shrinkage. The interpretation linking E' and A' shifts solely to substrate effect removal is noted as especially applicable for sulfur-based TMDCs. The folding edge region contains bilayer MoS2, introducing a structural heterogeneity that complicates pure monolayer strain interpretation. The paper states the process happens spontaneously, but does not provide specific timing for the onset of deformation in all materials.

Claims
Coating monolayer TMDCs with paraffin provides a universal post-preparation method for enhancing PL intensity in both sulfur- and selenium-based compounds by removing the substrate effect. PL enhancement factors of 215 for MoS2, 55 for WS2, 9 for WSe2, and 50 for MoSe2 demonstrate broad applicability. Raman shifts (-0.72 cm⁻¹ E', +1.03 cm⁻¹ A') confirm concurrent strain and carrier concentration reduction. The method was demonstrated on both Si/SiO2 and quartz substrates, confirming substrate independence. Enhancement varies by factor of >20 from MoS2 (215) to WSe2 (9), indicating the effect is not uniformly potent. The folded edge region contains bilayer MoS2, introducing a structural variable in the PL enhancement observation. The strategy is applicable to other 2D layered materials due to the underlying thermal expansion principle. Paraffin's transparency and flexibility enable integration into flexible light-emitting displays and solar cells.
The mechanism of PL enhancement is spontaneous deformation and desorption of the monolayer from the substrate caused by paraffin penetration at the interface. Optical microscopy shows monolayer MoS2 deforming spontaneously over 3 hours at room temperature. The E' Raman peak red shift indicates in-plane strain, while the A' blue shift indicates reduced carrier concentration. PL mapping shows nonuniform intensity distribution consistent with localized fluctuation and wrinkling. Surrounding bulk flakes prevent large deformation, but in-plane fluctuation persists, suggesting the mechanism is not pure desorption. The folded edge region's PL enhancement is associated with bilayer formation, which may confound the desorption interpretation. The method can be viewed as a mechanical strain engineering tool for 2D materials. The engineering is particularly useful for generating transparent and flexible optoelectronic devices.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The effect was verified on both Si/SiO2 and quartz substrates, confirming substrate independence. A thick film achieved by simple casting (no spin coating) was not transparent, contrasting with the spin-coated transparent films. The monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes on three sides served as a control to isolate in-plane fluctuation from out-of-plane bundling. PL mapping images confirmed the enhancement was present in the whole plane, but was nonuniform. Raman data was collected from 30 samples of monolayer MoS2 to provide statistical robustness for the shift values.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows the spin-coating setup for paraffin application on the samples. Figure 1b shows PL spectra for monolayer WS2 after paraffin coating with 36-fold enhancement. Figures 1c and 1d show optical microscopy and PL mapping images of paraffin-coated WS2. Figure 2a shows band gaps and emission wavelengths of the four TMDC monolayers. Figure 2b shows factors of enhancement for each monolayer, with MoS2 reaching 215. Figures 3a-d show time-dependent optical microscopy of MoS2 deformation at 0, 2, and 3 hours. Figure 3e shows the PL spectra of the deformed MoS2 sample with peak upshift. Figure 4 shows Raman E' and A' peak positions for 30 MoS2 samples before and after coating. Table 2 provides the average Raman shifts: E' at -0.72 cm⁻¹ and A' at 1.03 cm⁻¹. Figure 5 shows a monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes, with PL mapping and peak position distribution in the plane. Figures 5c and 5d illustrate the plausible PL enhancement mechanism involving in-plane fluctuation and partial desorption.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a universal post-preparation method using paraffin coating to enhance PL intensity in all monolayer TMDCs (sulfur- and selenium-based) by factors of 9 to 215, removing the substrate effect through spontaneous fluctuation and desorption. 2. The strongest evidence includes Raman statistical analysis of 30 MoS2 samples showing concurrent strain (-0.72 cm⁻¹ E') and carrier reduction (+1.03 cm⁻¹ A'), along with PL mapping showing nonuniform in-plane enhancement and peak shifts. 3. The future path lies in applying this hydrocarbon-coating strategy as a general strain engineering tool for 2D materials and in integrating the transparent, flexible, and biocompatible paraffin into flexible optoelectronic devices and solar cell packaging.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work reports the direct continuous flow partial oxidation of methane (POM) to methanol and acetic acid at atmospheric pressure and mild temperatures using hydrogen peroxide as the oxidant over a modified silica-supported bimetallic Au-Fe catalyst (AuFeHS). The authors address the 'holy grail' problem of selective methane oxidation, where thermodynamics typically favor complete oxidation to CO2. Using a modified deposition precipitation method, the authors synthesized a hydrophobic silica support functionalized with Fe (0.46 wt %) and Au (0.23 wt %) via a NaOH-assisted route. Key characterization by ICP-OES, XRD, XPS, XANES, EXAFS, and in-situ IR confirmed the atomic dispersion of Fe, the formation of Fe3-δ+ low-valent species stabilized by Au, and the presence of hydrophobic functionalization. In batch conditions at 20 bar (CH4:CO = 15:5), the catalyst achieved 1666 mmol/g(Fe+Au) of methanol with 95% selectivity within 30 minutes, and 3403 µmol/gcat of acetic acid with co-feeding CO. In continuous flow at atmospheric pressure (80°C), the catalyst yielded 224 mmol/g(Fe+Au) of methanol over 4 hours, and 648 µmol/gcat of acetic acid when CO was co-fed. The authors attribute the performance to the synergy between Fe3-δ+ sites (activated by Au) and the hydrophobic support environment that prevents peroxide-induced site blocking and promotes methanol desorption. Isotope labeling with CD4 confirmed that products originate from methane, not support ligands. The work represents a significant advancement over prior batch and high-pressure flow reports, demonstrating that the methane-to-methanol challenge can be addressed at benign conditions.

Research Context
Methane is a major constituent of natural gas and waste feedstocks, posing a global warming risk while being difficult to store and transport without high compression (10-100 atm). The activation of non-polar methane with a tetrahedral CH4 structure requires harsh reaction conditions, forming a significant bottleneck. Partial oxidation of methane (POM) to methanol is hindered by thermodynamics, where activated C-H bonds readily undergo complete oxidation to CO2. Direct conversion of methane to methanol is considered a 'holy grail' problem in catalysis that still eludes the community. Molecular oxygen and H2O2 are the two preferred green oxidants, but yields for methanol and other oxygenates have been poor. Prior reports on high-pressure batch processes for POM to methanol suffer from low product yield and harsh reaction conditions. Wang and coworkers reported 129.7 mmol/gCu·h for methanol over oxo-dicopper on carbon nitride, while Hutchings reported 7.02 µmol oxygenates in 30 min. Single-atom catalysts have shown promise, such as FeN4/GN-2.7 yielding ~114 µmol C1 oxygenates in 10h, and ZSM-5-Cu yielding 4800 µmol/gcat within 30 min. Continuous flow reports are limited, with a high-pressure process by Hutchings yielding 0.081 molProduct/kg·catalyst·h at 20 bar.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether methane can be partially oxidized to methanol and acetic acid at atmospheric pressure and mild temperatures using H2O2 as oxidant. The hypothesis is that a bimetallic Au-Fe catalyst supported on hydrophobic silica can stabilize low-valent Fe3-δ+ species capable of activating both CH4 and H2O2. The authors further hypothesize that co-feeding CO will act as a C1 building block to extend the reaction pathway to acetic acid. It is predicted that the continuous flow process at atmospheric pressure will surpass high-pressure batch yields in methanol and acetic acid productivity. The hydrophobic support is hypothesized to prevent site blocking by moisture, reduce gold nanoparticle aggregation, and facilitate methanol desorption. The work tests whether the synergism between Au and Fe can be harnessed to tune Fe oxidation states for optimal methane activation.

Methodological Details
A modified deposition precipitation (DP) method was used to disperse atomic clusters of Fe onto hydrophobic silica support. The best-performing catalyst (AuFeHS) contained 0.46 wt% Fe and 0.23 wt% Au, confirmed by ICP-OES. Hydrophobicity of the silica was confirmed by contact angle analysis yielding an observed angle of 118°. C-H vibration from silica confirmed hydrophobic functionalization in the support. FeHS images from HRTEM showed no contrast difference characteristic of Fe particles, suggesting atomic dispersion. Au nanoparticles of 1.3-3.0 nm were observed in AuFeHS, with a particle size distribution of 1.4-2.8 nm. The specific surface area of the AuFeHS catalyst was 392 m²/g. Batch screening was performed at 10 bar CH4 pressure with Fe loading fixed at 0.5 wt% and Au loading varied. Initial batch conditions were 0°C and 10 bar CH4 pressure. CO-co-feeding batch experiments were conducted at 50°C, 20 bar total pressure (15 bar CH4:5 bar CO). Continuous flow experiments were carried out at atmospheric pressure up to 7 hours, with temperature optimization at 80°C. The oxidant was 15% (w/v) H2O2. Product quantification was achieved by gas chromatography (GC) and NMR with standard calibrations. Isotope labeling experiments with CD4 were conducted to confirm methane origin of products. Control experiments confirmed no product without CH4 flow, oxidant, or catalyst.

Procedures And Architectures
Fe and Au were deposited onto silica support via a NaOH-assisted deposition precipitation route, incorporating Na into the Si-O-Na framework. Fe K-edge and Au L3-edge XANES spectra were measured against standards (Fe2O3, Au foil) to determine oxidation states. EXAFS was performed over a fitting range of 0-4 Å to extract radial distribution functions at Fe K-edge and Au L3-edge. In-situ IR spectroscopy was used to probe CO adsorption on Au metal atoms; signals at 2105 cm⁻¹ (Au0-CO) and 2175 cm⁻¹ (Auδ+-CO) were detected. Solid-state 29Si NMR confirmed Q2, Q3, Q4, and T2, T3 states in HS, with Na incorporation decreasing Q3 and Q2 states. 23Na NMR showed peaks at 7.32 ppm and -1.59 ppm confirming the Si-O-Na framework. Pyridine-adsorbed FT-IR showed a band at 1449 cm⁻¹ assigned to Lewis acid sites and ~1640 cm⁻¹ for -OH deformation. Batch reaction: 10 bar CH4, 15% H2O2, 0°C, 30 min residence time. Batch acetic acid reaction: 50°C, 20 bar (15:5 CH4:CO), 1 h. Continuous flow: 80°C, atmospheric pressure, up to 7 h, with 15% H2O2. ICP-OES confirmed Fe at 0.46 wt% and Au at 0.23 wt% in the catalyst.

Key Results
In batch conditions at 10 bar CH4, 0°C, the Fe-HS catalyst gave 285 mmol/gFe with 82% methanol selectivity. The bimetallic AuFeHS catalyst achieved a methanol yield of 1666 mmol/g(Fe+Au) with 95% selectivity in 30 min. The Au-HS (monometallic) catalyst gave only 47.6 mmol/gAu of methanol, confirming synergistic effects. With CO co-feeding at 50°C and 20 bar, acetic acid was the main product with 3403 µmol/gcat yield within 1 h. In the co-fed system, methanol was a minor product with yield of 166 µmol/gcat. CO2 selectivity was 10% with CO co-feeding at 50°C, compared to 5-6% with only methane. In continuous flow at atmospheric pressure, the AuFeHS catalyst achieved a steady methanol yield of 224 mmol/g(Fe+Au) over 4 h. The continuous flow acetic acid yield was 648 µmol/gcat within 4 h with CO co-feeding. The continuous flow methane yield reached 422 µmol·h⁻¹·gcat⁻¹ (0.42 mol·h⁻¹·kgcat⁻¹). Temperature optimization in continuous flow identified 80°C as the best condition. XPS confirmed Fe3+ at 710.6 eV and low-valent Fe3-δ+ at 709.5 eV on AuFeHS, while FeHS showed only Fe3+ at 710.3 eV. XPS showed 85% Au0 and 15% Auδ+ species in AuFeHS, with cationization attributed to charge donation to Fe. EXAFS Fe K-edge first peak at ~1.5 Å (lower than Fe foil) confirmed non-elemental iron, with two neighboring O shells at 1.94 and 2.11 Å. Fe XANES LCF showed 72% Fe3O4 and 28% FeO contributions in AuFeHS. Au FeHS XANES showed an L3 edge slightly higher than Au foil due to charge transfer. AuFeHS EXAFS Fe edge first peak was ~1.5 Å; Au L3-edge first peak > 2 Å confirmed elemental Au. The FeHS catalyst produced only 111 mmol/g(Fe+Au) methanol vs 224 mmol/g(Fe+Au) for AuFeHS on the same support, confirming the support effect.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The synergy between Au and Fe is attributed to the stabilization of low-valent Fe3-δ+ species by Au, which activate both CH4 and H2O2. The Fe3-δ+ sites are identified as the active centers for hydrogen peroxide activation, providing the -OH moiety for CH3 formation. Au nanoparticles, as excellent CO oxidation catalysts, provide low-energy activation sites for CO adsorption, enabling facile CO insertion. Hydrophobicity of the silica support prevents site blocking by peroxide-derived species, reduces gold particle sintering, and facilitates methanol desorption. The acidic sites on the bimetallic catalyst facilitate C-H σ-complex formation for methane activation and aid in Feδ+ site regeneration. Tuning active Fe species through bimetallic modulation is proposed as a strategy for lower alkane to oxygenate conversion. The NaOH-mediated route incorporates Na into the silica matrix, creating Si-O-Na framework that may influence acidity and hydrophobicity.

Contradictions And Limitations
The role of Na and Lewis acid sites in the overall POM reaction is beyond the scope of this study and requires further exploration. The electron flood gun used during XPS data acquisition precluded charge correction, and BE values are reported as recorded. A small nanoparticle of Au (1.3-3.0 nm) formed even at low loadings due to high surface energy, which might influence active site density. The Na incorporation in silica by NaOH deposition is confirmed, but the exact mechanism of how Si-O-Na affects catalysis is not fully elucidated. While hydrophobic silica outperformed SBA-15 (111 vs 0.78 mmol/gcat for Au-Fe), the precise mechanism of Na's contribution remains unclear. The paper notes that tuning active Fe species through bimetallic modulation is a 'clever way' but doesn't quantify the exact contribution of each bimetallic ratio.

Claims
The AuFeHS catalyst achieves unprecedented methanol and acetic acid yields at atmospheric pressure and mild temperatures using H2O2. In continuous flow at 80°C and atmospheric pressure, AuFeHS yielded 224 mmol/g(Fe+Au) of methanol. The continuous flow acetic acid yield of 648 µmol/gcat at 80°C and atmospheric pressure surpassed prior reports. The 422 µmol·h⁻¹·gcat⁻¹ methane yield in continuous flow is significantly higher than prior H2O2-based reports (1.81 µmol·h⁻¹·gcat⁻¹) and (0.081 mol·kg⁻¹·h⁻¹). While higher than H2O2-based flow reports, the batch yield of 1666 mmol/g(Fe+Au) is at 10 bar and 0°C, not the claimed 'benign' atmospheric conditions. The batch CO-co-fed yield of 3403 µmol/gcat occurs at 20 bar and 50°C, not atmospheric pressure. This suggests that the holy grail of methane-to-methanol at atmospheric pressure may be practically achievable with bimetallic catalysts. Commercialization of methane-to-oxygenate technologies becomes more feasible without high-pressure infrastructure.
The hydrophobic silica support is essential for preventing site blocking and enabling high methanol selectivity. Au and Fe supported on SBA-15 (hydrophilic) gave only 111 mmol/g(Fe+Au) methanol compared to 224 mmol/g(Fe+Au) on HS. Fe-SBA-15 and Au-SBA-15 produced only 0.30 and 0.15 mmol/gcat respectively, confirming the support role. Contact angle of 118° confirmed hydrophobic functionalization of the support. Lower physisorbed water was observed over the hydrophobic catalyst compared to SBA-15. The exact mechanistic contribution of hydrophobicity versus other support modifications (NaOH, Na incorporation) is not fully decoupled. Catalyst design for methane oxidation must prioritize hydrophobic environments to maintain peroxide accessibility and prevent over-oxidation.

Data And Code Availability
Supporting Information includes synthesis procedures, characterization methods, product calculations, XAS calculations, and activity data figures/tables. The material is available free of charge via the internet at http://pubs.acs.org.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Bimetallic screening varied Au loading while fixing Fe at 0.5 wt%, identifying 0.2% Au and 0.5% Fe as optimal. A comparison with SBA-15 support (hydrophilic) served as a support-effect ablation, showing reduced performance (0.30 and 0.15 mmol/gcat). Isotope labeling experiments (CD4) ruled out background reactions from support ligands as the product source. Control experiments with nitrogen gas feed resulted in no product formation, confirming CH4-dependent activity. Temperature optimization in continuous flow identified 80°C as optimal across multiple data points. XPS confirmed that FeHS (no Au) showed no low-valent Fe3-δ+ and correspondingly poor catalysis.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows FeHS HRTEM images with no contrast difference characteristic of Fe particles, indicating atomic dispersion. Figure 1b and 1c show Au nanoparticles of 1.3-3.0 nm in AuFeHS. Figure 1d shows elemental mapping of Au nanoparticles finely dispersed over FeHS. Figure 2a presents XPS spectra showing Fe3+ at 710.6 eV and Fe3-δ+ at 709.5 eV on AuFeHS. Figure 2c shows Fe K-edge XANES spectra with linear combination fitting results. Figure 3a and 3b show batch activity data for different catalysts at 0°C and 10 bar. Figure 3c compares AuFeHS with Au and Fe on SBA-15. Figure 3d shows CO-co-fed batch reaction products. Figure 4a shows continuous flow steady-state methanol production over 7 hours. Figure 5 shows solid-state 29Si NMR spectra of HS with Q2-Q4 and T2-T3 states. Figure 15 shows in-situ IR CO adsorption spectra on Au and Fe-loaded silica. Figure 18, 19 show CD4 isotope labeling NMR spectra.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the synthesis and application of a bimetallic Au-Fe/hydrophobic-silica catalyst that achieves methanol production at atmospheric pressure and 80°C using H2O2, yielding 224 mmol/g(Fe+Au) in continuous flow. 2. The strongest evidence lies in the synergistic effect between Au and Fe: the Fe3-δ+ species (709.5 eV) observed on AuFeHS but absent on FeHS, combined with continuous flow performance significantly outperforming both monolytal catalysts and prior H2O2-based reports. 3. The future path involves tuning active Fe species through bimetallic modulation for conversion of lower alkanes to oxygenates, while further exploring the role of Na and Lewis acid sites in the overall POM reaction.

summary.title: A Workflow for Identifying Viable Crystal Structures with Partially Occupied Sites Applied to Solid Electrolyte: Cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12
summary.authors: Julian Holland; Tom Demeyere; Arihant Bhandari; Felix Hanke; Victor Milman; Chris-Kriton Skylaris
summary.field_subfield: Materials Science / Computational Condensed Matter - Solid Electrolytes
summary.executive_summary: Despite the technological importance of cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO) as a superionic solid electrolyte for Li-ion batteries, experimental and theoretical works have failed to establish a consensus ground-state Li occupancy. Computational studies have historically relied on single experimental starting points, introducing ambiguity about whether calculated properties represent the true ground state. This paper presents a comprehensive combinatorial workflow to generate, filter, and energetically order all possible Li configurations for a c-LLZO unit cell. The workflow begins by eliminating overlapping Li atoms based on a geometrically derived 1.7 Å cutoff, reducing the combinatorial space from 7.4 × 10^34 to a manageable set. Symmetry-equivalent structures are then eliminated using a Local Sensitive Hashing (LSH) approach, reducing the count to approximately 2 × 10^6 unique structures. Energetic ordering is performed using a combination of COMPASSIII forcefield pre-selection and 1,235 single-point DFT calculations (ONETEP, PBE functional, 830 eV cutoff), which are used to train a multiple linear regression model. The model achieves a correlation of 0.9996, enabling full ranking of the configuration space. Four structures (all 8:48 occupancy) within 0.026 eV of the lowest energy are identified, with 19 of the 20 lowest structures sharing the same 8:48 ratio. The average energy of all structures lies 1.47 eV above the ground state. The workflow demonstrates that a large portion of previously reported structures are infeasible due to Li-Li overlaps. The methodology is provided as a freely accessible database for reproducibility, and the authors note that the approach could extend to other partially occupied crystals. Limitations include the absence of entropic contributions and the assumption of ordering retention upon geometry relaxation, tested on a small subset of 20 structures.
