judge_context:
Executive Summary
Despite the technological importance of cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO) as a superionic solid electrolyte for Li-ion batteries, experimental and theoretical works have failed to establish a consensus ground-state Li occupancy. Computational studies have historically relied on single experimental starting points, introducing ambiguity about whether calculated properties represent the true ground state. This paper presents a comprehensive combinatorial workflow to generate, filter, and energetically order all possible Li configurations for a c-LLZO unit cell. The workflow begins by eliminating overlapping Li atoms based on a geometrically derived 1.7 Å cutoff, reducing the combinatorial space from 7.4 × 10^34 to a manageable set. Symmetry-equivalent structures are then eliminated using a Local Sensitive Hashing (LSH) approach, reducing the count to approximately 2 × 10^6 unique structures. Energetic ordering is performed using a combination of COMPASSIII forcefield pre-selection and 1,235 single-point DFT calculations (ONETEP, PBE functional, 830 eV cutoff), which are used to train a multiple linear regression model. The model achieves a correlation of 0.9996, enabling full ranking of the configuration space. Four structures (all 8:48 occupancy) within 0.026 eV of the lowest energy are identified, with 19 of the 20 lowest structures sharing the same 8:48 ratio. The average energy of all structures lies 1.47 eV above the ground state. The workflow demonstrates that a large portion of previously reported structures are infeasible due to Li-Li overlaps. The methodology is provided as a freely accessible database for reproducibility, and the authors note that the approach could extend to other partially occupied crystals. Limitations include the absence of entropic contributions and the assumption of ordering retention upon geometry relaxation, tested on a small subset of 20 structures.

Research Context
Experimental and theoretical works have been unable to uncover the ground state configuration of cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12. Computational studies rely on an initial low-energy structure as a reference point. There is no consensus of c-LLZO's Li occupancy in the existing literature. The range of predicted structures in the literature indicates disagreement about the ground state. Without knowing if structures are close to the ground state, thermodynamic properties may not be well described.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central goal is to produce all possible structures of a c-LLZO unit cell and order them energetically. The researchers aim to ascertain the presence of a significant energy difference in choice of structure. A secondary hypothesis is whether structural properties such as the 24d:96h ratio indicate a structure's energy. The authors hypothesize that a geometric constraint of 1.7 Å can eliminate unphysical structures and narrow the occupancy range.

Methodological Details
The system is cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 with Hermann-Mauguin space group Ia 3d. Li atoms partially occupy the 24d and 96h sites. The 48g site is excluded as it is not reported in most refinements. The total number of ways to populate 120 sites with 56 Li is approximately 7.4 × 10^34. A geometric constraint of 1.7 Å is imposed as the minimal Li-Li distance. This cutoff is less than 2 times the ionic radius of Li and smaller than the minimum distance in t-LLZO. The crystal structure framework is based on Buschmann et al. (ref 19). Symmetry reduction is performed using Local Sensitive Hashing (LSH). LSH reduces pairwise comparison from O(N^2) to O(N). The final configuration space is reduced to approximately 2 × 10^6 structures. Data is split into test and training sets with a 1:3 ratio.

Procedures And Architectures
Initial generation produces approximately 2.3 × 10^8 structures including symmetry-equivalent duplicates. The connectivity matrix is constructed as distances between each Li atom to every other Li atom. LSH performs fast approximate similarity searches on monoatomic sub-lattices. LSH is validated against the ASE symmetry equivalence check for 12:44 and 13:43 ratios. Only approximately 1% of structures are symmetrically unique. 200 energetically lowest structures are selected via COMPASSIII forcefield for the first DFT subset. A second subset consists of a random selection of approximately 1000 structures across the configuration space. A total of 1235 single-point DFT calculations are performed. DFT is performed with ONETEP using the PBE GGA functional and a kinetic energy cutoff of 830 eV. Pseudopotentials are CASTEP on-the-fly generated. Structures are represented by a frequency occurrence list of all possible Li-Li interactions. A multiple linear regression (MLR) model fits the DFT energies to the structural representation. A Li dimer in vacuum is computed via 30 single-point calculations to determine the 1.7 Å cutoff justification.

Key Results
The MLR model achieves a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. All structures fall within a range of 5.8 eV of the lowest energy structure. 19 out of the 20 lowest energy structures have a 24d:96h ratio of 8:48. The 19th lowest structure has a ratio of 9:47. The average energy for all structures is 1.47 eV higher than the ground state. Average energy for each ratio increases with increasing 24d occupancy. Four structures, all 8:48, are within 0.026 eV of the lowest energy structure. The four lowest energy structures have very similar atomic coordinates and the same 24d configuration. COMPASSIII ordered the 13:43 ratio with a correlation coefficient of 0.991. COMPASSIII predicts more pronounced energy separation by ratio than ONETEP. The geometry-optimised lowest structure is 0.58 eV lower than the single-point lowest structure. The transition from 9:47 to 10:46 via 96h-to-24d site change occurred only once.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The energetic preference to avoid 24d occupation suggests strong repulsion or destabilizing interactions at these sites. The 8:48 ratio emerges as the most energetically favourable occupancy, with very small energy differences (0.026 eV) between top candidates. Movement from original crystallographic sites correlates negatively with energy, indicating that relaxation from ideal sites stabilizes structures. The method demonstrates that many previously reported structures are unphysical due to Li-Li overlaps at the 1.7 Å criterion. The workflow can be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals.

Contradictions And Limitations
The energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions. The method assumes reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation, tested only on 20 structures. A large-scale energy prediction of geometry-optimised structures falls outside the scope of this work. COMPASSIII predicts a more pronounced energy separation by ratio than ONETEP, which was considered too large to surmount. The LSH method is limited to monoatomic sub-lattices with predefined positions. Symmetry inclusion in the MLR model made a negligible difference.

Claims
The 8:48 Li occupancy is the most energetically favourable 24d:96h ratio for c-LLZO. 19 of the top 20 lowest energy structures have an 8:48 ratio. The 19th lowest structure breaks the trend at 9:47. Four structures are within 0.026 eV of the lowest energy. The energy difference between the top four is smaller than thermal energy at 298 K (1 kT). Geometry optimisation changed the ratio of one structure from 9:47 to 10:46, slightly shifting the picture. This finding should guide experimentalists targeting the most stable c-LLZO ground state. The small energy gap suggests experimental conditions could sample multiple nearly-degenerate configurations.
A large proportion of literature-reported c-LLZO structures are unphysical due to Li-Li overlaps. The 1.7 Å criterion eliminates structures with nearest-neighbour Li-Li distances below the ionic diameter. The red region in Figure 1 indicates ratios that cannot exist without Li-Li interaction below the crystal ionic diameter. The authors state that a large proportion of reported structures may not be feasible or stable. The cutoff was chosen at 1.7 Å, but any value between 1.67 Å and 2.3 Å would be suitable. Some literature structures may rely on different interpretations of ionic radii. Future computational work should use the full generated database for accurate property predictions. Literature studies based on unphysical structures may yield misleading thermodynamic data.

Data And Code Availability
All structures generated in this work are provided in a freely accessible database to improve accuracy and reproducibility. The database includes all possible configurations of the c-LLZO unit cell within the 1.7 Å constraint. The symmetry-checking scripts are provided in the supporting information.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The LSH symmetry-checking method was validated against ASE for two smallest ratios and produced the same counts. The Li dimer calculation confirmed a large energy penalty for Li atoms approaching 1.7 Å. Including symmetry of the structure in the MLR model made a negligible difference to overall results. A geometry relaxation test on 20 structures showed that site changes did not correlate significantly with energy.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the Li occupancy constraints, with a red region indicating forbidden 24d:96h ratios. Figure 2b plots the 20 lowest energy structures ranked by energy with their ratios. Figure 3 illustrates the workflow to identify the 4 final structures from given occupancies. Table 1 lists the number of structures for each 24d:96h ratio for one unit cell. Table S1 lists all experimental papers reporting 24d and 96h site occupancies. Table S2 lists all theoretical studies reporting 24d:96h ratios and structure generation methods. Figure S3 compares COMPASSIII relative DFT energies to ONETEP relative DFT energies. Figure S4 shows the Li dimer energy versus inter-atomic distance with the 1.7 Å point marked.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a complete energetic ranking of all physically permissible c-LLZO configurations using LSH-accelerated combinatorial generation and MLR trained on DFT. 2. The strongest evidence is the high MLR correlation (0.9996) and the observation that 19 of 20 lowest energy structures share the 8:48 ratio, identifying a single most-likely ground-state configuration family. 3. The future path involves extending the workflow to other partially occupied ion conductors and generating geometry-optimised surfaces for the identified low-energy structures.

summary.title: Self-assembling materials mimicking dynamic bio-interfaces in cellular activities
summary.authors: Noriyuki Uchida (Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology); Takahiro Muraoka (Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology)

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This Feature Article highlights recent advances in bioinspired supramolecular materials designed to mimic dynamic bio-interfaces—the contact sites between and within cells where critical biological processes such as adhesion, signal transduction, and substance transportation occur. The authors present four major material families that emulate distinct bio-interfacial functions: (1) stiffness-controlled peptide hydrogels (A16G-based) that reconstruct artificial extracellular matrices for neuronal migration in injured neonatal neocortex; (2) JigSAP-based peptide nanofibers with jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic dimerization that efficiently incorporate and sustained-release VEGF for angiogenesis in stroke models; (3) redox-responsive peptide hydrogels (JigSAP-IMI/MII) that undergo stimuli-triggered gel-sol transitions for controlled cargo release; and (4) phospholipid nanosheets (bicelles) stabilized by metal-binding peptides (Chol-MBP) and a photo-responsive molecular machine (AzoMEx) for extended blood circulation and endocytosis-like viral encapsulation. Each material strategy demonstrates that supramolecular assembly principles, such as β-sheet hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic dimerization, and metal-coordination, can be leveraged to recapitulate native cellular mechanisms for regenerative medicine applications.

Research Context
The mammalian brain has a very limited capability for regeneration of lost neurons and regaining function after injury, making neuro-regenerative therapies critical. The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a complex network of proteins and biomolecules that mediates cell adhesion, migration, and differentiation via ligand-receptor interactions. Phospholipid bilayers constitute the major component of cellular and organelle membranes, facilitating endocytosis, exocytosis, and signal transduction. Despite the importance of these bio-interfaces, a molecular approach enabling endocytosis-like transport with synchronized membrane deformation and substance transport remains critically unexplored. Recent progress in supramolecular chemistry and nanotechnology has made it possible to construct and functionalize dynamic biomimetic interfaces for regenerative medicine.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can supramolecular self-assembling peptide fibers with tuned stiffness and protein conjugation mimic the intrinsic scaffold functions of the ECM to promote neuroblast migration in vivo? Can a jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic dimerization motif in a peptide sequence enable efficient incorporation and sustained release of full-length growth factors from nanofibres? Can redox-active methionine substitution in supramolecular peptide sequences provide kinetically controlled, stimulus-responsive gel-sol transitions for drug delivery? Can a metal-binding peptide surfactant stabilize phospholipid nanosheets (bicelles) against dilution-induced aggregation for extended blood circulation? Can a photoresponsive molecular machine embedded in a phospholipid vesicle induce outside-in membrane fission for efficient encapsulation of large viral particles? The authors hypothesize that bottom-up supramolecular construction of bio-interfaces is an effective approach to develop biomaterials applicable to regenerative medicine and drug delivery.

Methodological Details
The study focuses on self-assembling peptide fibers as versatile supramolecular scaffolds for biomaterials applications. Peptide amphiphiles with fatty acid chains form cylindrical micelles, while diphenylalanine serves as a supramolecular fiber backbone. RADA16 (Arg-Ala-Asp-Ala) peptides form supramolecular nanofibers in aqueous media through β-sheet-type hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interaction. RADA-based peptides are composed of naturally occurring amino acids, enabling their incorporation into proteins as tag sequences via an E. coli expression system. JigSAP (Ac-RIDARMRADIR-NH2) incorporates the AXXXA motif (glycophorin A) that generates a jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surface for dovetail packing. JigSAP was dispersed at 1 wt% in DMEM, with conformational change from helical/coil to β-sheet monitored over 100 hours by circular dichroism. DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets were formed at a ratio of 5:1 (DPPC/Chol-MBP) for a total content of 5.0 wt%. Chol-MBP (PHGGGPHGG) was designed as a surfactant with a Cu(II)-binding imidazole motif. AzoMEx contains a diazocine core that undergoes photoisomerization-triggered opening-closing motion by changing the distance between two cationic NMe3+ moieties. M13 phage virus was introduced at a concentration of 22.6 × 10^11 virions/mL for encapsulation experiments. Fluorescent Cy5-labeled vesicles and nanosheets were filtered through 200-nm pores before tail-vein administration to mice. Block polymer coating of GUVDOPC/AzoMEx-pAsp consisted of poly(aspartic acid) and poly(ethylene glycol). Inject volumes were 100 μL of GUVDOPC/AzoMex-pAsp encapsulating M13 phages for the time-course studies. Plaque assays were performed on homogenized organs after 15 minutes post-injection, with spleen and liver samples diluted 10-fold. The peptide concentration for redox-responsive experiments was 1.0 wt% in DMEM containing 4 mM HEPES at pH 7.4. Hydrogen peroxide added for stimulus response was 30% H2O2 aq. For the in vivo stroke model, 1.6 ng of VEGF (tagged or untagged) was used. For the in vivo virus delivery, 5.0 wt% total content of FL DPPC vesicles and FL DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets was injected. Neonatal neocortex was injured at low temperature before injection of the various hydrogel formulations.

Procedures And Architectures
MD simulations visualized the self-assembling morphology of A16G curved fibers and the conformational transition of JigSAP to β-sheet. A8G (alanine-to-glycine substitution at middle position) forms bundled nanofibers and more robust hydrogels than RADA16. A16G (terminal alanine-to-glycine) forms curved fibers, with lower stiffness and thixotropic properties. EGFP was covalently conjugated to JigSAP, 5V, and RADA16 at the C-terminus for incorporation efficiency assays. JigSAP hydrogel was characterized by CD spectroscopy, TEM imaging, rheological analysis, and fluorescence assays. JigSAP-IMI and JigSAP-MII single-point mutations were created by replacing Met with MetO to introduce redox-responsiveness. Chol-MBP binds two Cu2+ ions via imidazole coordination to stabilize DPPC nanosheets at the membrane edge. DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets were formed by adding 2.0 equivalents of Cu2+ ions to the nanosheet dispersion. In vivo blood circulation was monitored by confocal laser scanning microscopy of the mouse earlobe (IV-CLSM). GUVDOPC/AzoMEx ([DOPC] = 180 μM, [AzoMEx] = 20 μM) was subjected to light-triggered photoisomerization to induce outside-in fission. GUVDOPC/AzoMEx-pAsp was coated with a pAsp-PEG block polymer to minimize non-specific adsorption and extend circulation. Time-lapse imaging of neuroblasts on culture dishes coated with A16G or A16G/A16G-Ncad mixture quantified migration rates. The mouse model of ischaemic stroke was produced by distal middle cerebral artery occlusion.

Key Results
The A16G hydrogel showed lower stiffness than RADA16, enabling enhanced mobility and thixotropic properties suitable for injection. Migration rate of neuroblasts was significantly higher on A16G-Ncad hydrogel than on A16G alone in vitro. In vivo, Dcx+ neuroblasts were abundantly observed in the A16G/A16G-Ncad hydrogel mixture in the injured neocortex, while sparse in A16G alone or A16G/Ncad mixture. JigSAP hydrogel exhibits a remarkably high rigidity of 1.1 × 10^4 Pa. Rheological analysis showed that G' and G'' decrease monotonically with shear strain, indicating robust supramolecular nanofibres. EGFP-JigSAP incorporation efficiency was 93 mol%, while untagged EGFP incorporation was only 3 mol%. EGFP-5V incorporation was 66 mol% and EGFP-RADA16 was 55 mol%, both higher than untagged EGFP. 21 mol% of EGFP-JigSAP was released after 24-hour incubation at 37 °C, reaching 39 mol% after 168 hours. EGFP-5V and EGFP-RADA16 release stagnated after 48 hours, with only 5 mol% and 8 mol% released even after 168 hours. JigSAP-IMI and JigSAP-MII formed hydrogels under physiological conditions, while their oxidised forms (JigSAP-IMI-Ox and JigSAP-MII-Ox) remained dispersed in solution. DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets maintained structure at 0.2 wt% dilution with 2.0 equivalents Cu2+ addition, whereas the undiluted nanosheet aggregated into spherical clusters <100 nm. FL DPPC vesicles aggregated and clogged in blood vessels, while FL DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets were homogeneously dispersed. M13 phages encapsulated in GUVDOPC/AzoMEx-pAsp showed higher blood stability than bare M13 phageCy5 via IV-CLSM. After distribution, M13 phage infectivity was retained in all organs: spleen (25.6 ± 13.2 × 10^9 virions/mg), liver (18.3 ± 3.2 × 10^9), kidney (1.3 ± 0.6 × 10^9), heart (1.1 ± 0.5 × 10^9), lung (0.5 ± 0.3 × 10^9), and brain (0.2 ± 0.1 × 10^9) virions/mg. Number of laminin/EdU double-positive endothelial cells increased in the injured stroke area when VEGF-JigSAP and JigSAP peptides were injected.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The A16G-Ncad fibrous self-assembly mimics both the structure and dynamic function of intrinsic scaffold cells, providing a novel strategy for neuro-regenerative therapy. The dovetail packing of JigSAP fibres, driven by the AXXXA motif's conformational transition, explains the high incorporation efficiency and sustained protein release. The redox-responsive gel-sol transition allows precise kinetic control of cargo release to coincide with target biological events. The metal-binding peptide (Chol-MBP) at the nanosheet edge inhibits dissociation, explaining the transition from unstable bicelles to circulation-stable carriers. The photoresponsive AzoMEx molecular machine enables artificial endocytosis-like fission, providing a mechanism for large biomacromolecule encapsulation that mimics cellular endocytosis. These supramolecular approaches represent powerful ways to develop unprecedented regenerative medicines and drug delivery systems by mimicking bottom-up bio-interface construction.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper is a feature article summarizing recent studies rather than a single experimental investigation; some results are from independent reports cited rather than experiments conducted within this specific study. While A16G forms a more robust hydrogel than RADA16, it has lower stiffness, and the authors do not quantify the exact stiffness values for A16G vs RADA16. The A16G-Ncad and A16G/Ncad mixture showed sparse neuroblasts in vitro, indicating that the N-cadherin tag alone is insufficient without the peptide-conjugate scaffold. The JigSAP hydrogel stiffness of 1.1 × 10^4 Pa is described as remarkably high but the absolute value relative to native ECM is not quantified. The release of EGFP-5V and EGFP-RADA16 stagnates after 48 hours, limiting their utility for long-term delivery compared to JigSAP. The in vivo M13 phage distribution showed the lowest virion count in the brain (0.2 ± 0.1 × 10^9), suggesting limited central nervous system penetration. The paper does not report specific random seeds, replicate numbers, or detailed statistical power analyses for the in vivo experiments.

Claims
A16G-Ncad peptide-tagged hydrogels can mimic the structure and dynamic function of intrinsic scaffold cells to promote neuroblast migration into injured neonatal neocortex in vivo. Dcx+ neuroblasts were abundantly observed in A16G/A16G-Ncad hydrogels in the injured neocortex. Migration rates were significantly higher on A16G-Ncad than on A16G alone in vitro. Neuroblasts were seen sparsely in the A16G-only and A16G/Ncad mixture, indicating that the tag alone is insufficient. This provides a novel strategy for neuro-regenerative therapy by reconstructing functional scaffold structures.
JigSAP peptide nanofibers with jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surfaces achieve 93 mol% incorporation efficiency for tagged EGFP proteins and sustained release over 168 hours, promoting angiogenesis in stroke models. EGFP-JigSAP incorporation efficiency was 93 mol% compared to 3 mol% for untagged EGFP. 21 mol% of EGFP-JigSAP was released after 24 hours, increasing to 39 mol% after 168 hours. Laminin/EdU double-positive endothelial cells increased in the injured area with VEGF-JigSAP injection. EGFP-5V and EGFP-RADA16 release stagnated after 48 hours, showing only 5 and 8 mol% at 168 hours. JigSAP demonstrates wide applicability to controlled sustained release of various full-length growth factors.
Chol-MBP metal-binding peptides stabilize DPPC nanosheets against dilution-induced aggregation, enabling homogeneous blood circulation, while a photoresponsive molecular machine (AzoMEx) induces endocytosis-like membrane fission for viral encapsulation. DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets were homogeneously dispersed in blood vessels, while FL DPPC vesicles aggregated and clogged. AzoMEx induced outside-in fission of GUVDOPC, encapsulating 22.6 × 10^11 M13 phage virions/mL. Infectivity was retained in all organs after blood administration, with the highest count in the spleen (25.6 ± 13.2 × 10^9 virions/mg). Nanosheets without Cu2+ aggregated into spherical clusters of less than 100 nm upon dilution to 0.2 wt%. The self-assembling approach is advantageous for stabilizing bicelle morphology for prolonged circulation and whole-body delivery. The AzoMEx-GUV technology could be applied to in vivo phage display for selection of peptides binding to ligands in living bodies.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A16G vs. RADA16: Substitution of alanine with glycine at the middle position (A8G) enhances flexibility but forms more robust hydrogels than RADA16. A16G vs. A16G-Ncad: The N-cadherin tag alone (A16G/Ncad) failed to promote neuroblast migration, highlighting the importance of the peptide-conjugated scaffold. JigSAP vs. 5V/RADA16: Incorporation efficiencies (93 vs 66/55 mol%) and long-term release profiles confirm JigSAP's superior performance. Cu2+ stabilization: DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets aggregated at 0.2 wt% without Cu2+ (clusters <100 nm) but maintained structure with 2.0 equivalents Cu2+ ions. AzoMEx: The cationic property of AzoMEx (NMe3+ moieties) was required for interaction with anionic M13 phage virus.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: Schematic of dynamic bio-interfaces in cellular activities, illustrating bio-macromolecules and supramolecular assemblies at bio-interfaces. Figure 2: Comparison of A8G, RADA16, and A16G morphologies (TEM, MD simulations) and hydrogel appearance; (a) schematic, (c) TEM, (d) TEM curved fibers, (e) hydrogel appearance, (f) MD simulations. Figure 3: In vitro and in vivo neuroblast migration; (a) time-lapse imaging on A16G/A16G-Ncad hydrogels, (b) in vivo Dcx+ distribution in neonatal neocortex. Figure 4: JigSAP characterization: (a-b) MD simulation, (c) TEM nanofibers (3.2 nm width), (d) hydrogel appearance, (e) rigidity (1.1 × 10^4 Pa), (f) rheological strain thinning, (g) EGFP conjugation, (h-j) incorporation efficiencies, (k) protein release profile, (l) neuronal regeneration schematic, (m-v) in vivo stroke experiments. Figure 5: Redox-responsive JigSAP-IMI and JigSAP-MII hydrogels and their gel-sol transition under 30% H2O2. Figure 6: Phospholipid nanosheet stabilization: (a) Chol-MBP design, (b) Cu-coordination mechanism, (c) aggregation at 0.2 wt%, (d) Cu2+ stabilization, (e-g) IV-CLSM circulation profiles of vesicles and nanosheets. Figure 7: AzoMEx-induced endocytosis: (a-d) AzoMEx photoisomerization mechanism, (e-k) GUVDOPC/AzoMEx-pAsp for M13 phage encapsulation, (l-n) in vivo circulation comparison, (o-t) organ distribution and plaque assays.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the development of multiple bottom-up supramolecular material systems that mimic dynamic bio-interfaces—reconstructing the ECM for neuronal migration (A16G-Ncad), enabling sustained growth factor release (JigSAP), and stabilizing lipid membranes for extended circulation and viral encapsulation. 2. The strongest evidence is the in vivo demonstration of neuroblast migration in the injured neonatal neocortex using A16G-Ncad hydrogels, and the organ-wide retention of infectious M13 phages after blood administration of GUVDOPC/AzoMEx-pAsp. 3. The future path lies in applying these supramolecular strategies to in vivo phage display for peptide selection in living bodies, and broader development of biomimetic interfaces with dynamic nature for unprecedented regenerative medicine.

summary.title: GUIDEMOL: a Python graphical user interface for molecular descriptors based on RDKit
summary.authors: Joao Aires (NOVA School of Science and Technology)
summary.field_subfield: Chemoinformatics / Computational Chemistry
summary.executive_summary: GUIDEMOL is a Python-based graphical user interface (GUI) application developed by Joao Aires that leverages the RDKit chemistry library to process molecular structures and compute molecular descriptors. The application addresses a practical gap in chemoinformatics: while RDKit offers powerful descriptor calculation capabilities primarily accessible via programming, scientists and students with no programming skills lacked a streamlined, accessible tool for QSPR/QSAR workflows. GUIDEMEL implements a minimalist interface using the tkinter package, allowing users to select input SMILES/structure files and generate 3D models through MMFF94 optimization. Beyond standard RDKit descriptors (RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, SMR_VSA, and molecular weight), the tool also computes direct 3D representations: electrostatic potential (EP) grids and voxel-based atomic property grids, both of which have gained relevance for deep learning and convolutional neural network applications. For reproducibility, a command-line interface (CLI) is provided for grid calculations. The source code is released under the three-clause BSD license, facilitating both commercial and non-commercial extension. The work is positioned as a teaching and practical tool rather than an algorithmic innovation, bridging the gap between RDKit's low-level API and end-user accessibility.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
GUIDEMOL is a Python-based graphical user interface (GUI) application developed by Joao Aires that leverages the RDKit chemistry library to process molecular structures and compute molecular descriptors. The application addresses a practical gap in chemoinformatics: while RDKit offers powerful descriptor calculation capabilities primarily accessible via programming, scientists and students with no programming skills lacked a streamlined, accessible tool for QSPR/QSAR workflows. GUIDEMEL implements a minimalist interface using the tkinter package, allowing users to select input SMILES/structure files and generate 3D models through MMFF94 optimization. Beyond standard RDKit descriptors (RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, SMR_VSA, and molecular weight), the tool also computes direct 3D representations: electrostatic potential (EP) grids and voxel-based atomic property grids, both of which have gained relevance for deep learning and convolutional neural network applications. For reproducibility, a command-line interface (CLI) is provided for grid calculations. The source code is released under the three-clause BSD license, facilitating both commercial and non-commercial extension. The work is positioned as a teaching and practical tool rather than an algorithmic innovation, bridging the gap between RDKit's low-level API and end-user accessibility.

Research Context
Molecular descriptors are fundamental to QSPR/QSAR methodology used by scientists across chemistry, biology, and material science. Chemoinformatics is increasingly integrated into curricula of chemistry, biology, and material science degrees, creating a need for teaching software. While RDKit implements a wide range of chemoinformatics tools and molecular descriptors, it is primarily used in machine learning projects requiring programming knowledge. Prior GUI solutions exist, such as PaDEL and the CDK Descriptor Calculator, but RDKit-based graphical interfaces were limited. 3D grid representations encoding atoms as voxels or electrostatic potentials have gained attention for processing by deep learning neural networks. Electrostatic potentials from point charges have long been used in 3D-QSAR and molecular similarity assessment. There was a practical gap for non-programmers to access RDKit descriptor calculations without writing Python code.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central objective is to develop a minimalist Python GUI that provides easy access to RDKit molecular descriptor calculation tools for non-programmers. A secondary objective is to enable calculation of direct 3D grid representations (EP and voxel) accessible via both GUI and CLI. The application is hypothesized to serve as a teaching tool for chemists and a template for other chemoinformatics GUI development. The software is designed to handle input SMILES/structure files and output descriptor data in CSV format with molecule names and IDs. The tool is intended to be extensible, allowing users to add other descriptors or trigger additional procedures.

Methodological Details
The software is built as a Python application using the RDKit chemistry library for molecular processing. The graphical interface is implemented using the tkinter package, which is the standard Python interface to the Tcl/Tk GUI toolkit. The interface is controlled by the tkinter grid geometry manager, with widgets including buttons, checkbuttons, radiobuttons, entries, labels, and a scrollbar. Native look-and-feel dialog windows from tkinter.filedialog are used for file and directory selection. A log file is automatically created in the output directory to register successful processing and failures. The input format supports SMILES and structure files; when no name is provided, the SMILES is used as the molecule name in the output. The output is a CSV file where the last columns contain the molecule name and the molecule ID position. The source code is released under the three-clause Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) license. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/jairesdesousa/guidemol. The paper notes that the bibliography is not fully provided in the source text for top citation analysis.

Procedures And Architectures
3D molecular models are generated from input structures using the RDKit function MMFFOptimizeMolecule with mmffVariant='MMFF94' and maxIters=5000. Pre-generation options include removing metals via MetalDisconnector, keeping the largest fragment via LargestFragmentChooser(preferOrganic=True), and neutralizing via Uncharger. Hydrogen atoms are explicitly added using Chem.AddHs(). For grid calculations with missing H, AddHs(addCoords=True) is used. The GUI enables selection of 3D descriptors from RDKit's rdMolDescriptors module: RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, and SMR_VSA. Exact molecular weight can also be selected as a descriptor output. Electrostatic potential grids are generated using either Gasteiger or MMFF partial atomic charges via AllChem.ComputeGasteigerCharges() or GetMMFFPartialCharge(). EP is calculated at each cube c as the sum over atoms i of q_i times r_ic, where q_i is partial charge and r_ic is distance to cube center, excluding atoms within 1 Å of center and beyond a user-defined cutoff. Voxelisation uses a user-defined 3D grid based on one of four properties: atomic number, partial charge (Gasteiger or MMFF), molecular refractivity, or logP via Wildman-Crippen. Voxel value at cube c is calculated as the sum over atoms i of p_i times exp(-r_ic^2 / (2*σ^2)), excluding atoms beyond cutoff. A CLI is provided for grid calculation with arguments: -i (input), -o (output), -g (pot/vox), -p (property), -cx, -cy, -cz (center), -r (resolution), -w (cutoff), -sx, -sy, -sz (grid size). The CLI example command uses: guidemol.py -i input.sdf -g pot -p Gasteiger -cx 0 -cy 0 -cz 0 -r 0.5 -w 3 -sx 5 -sy 5 -sz 5 -o outfile.csv.

Key Results
The tool successfully implements all 7 specified 3D descriptors from the RDKit rdMolDescriptors module in the GUI. It was observed that for some molecules (e.g., COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br) and descriptors (GETAWAY, MORSE, WHIM), different values were obtained with the same RDKit version (2022.9.5) in different runs or operating systems. The EP grid formula excludes contributions from atoms within 1 Å of the cube center (contribution set equal to partial charge) and atoms beyond the user-defined cutoff. The voxelisation formula incorporates a σ parameter determining how fast an atom's contribution decreases with distance. The logP property in voxelisation is calculated via _CalcCrippenContribs() of the rdMolDescriptors module using the Wildman-Crippen approach. The CLI example demonstrates an EP grid with Gasteiger charges, 5 Å side size, 0.5 Å resolution, 3 Å cutoff, centered at (0,0,0). The software supports both SMILES input for structure generation and native structure file input for direct descriptor calculation. A log file registers both successful processing and failures, providing an audit trail for batch jobs.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The tool positions itself as a teaching aid for chemistry and biology curricula, enabling non-programmers to engage with QSPR/QSAR methods. By bridging RDKit's advanced capabilities with a minimalist Tkinter GUI, it democratizes access to 3D descriptor calculation for computational chemistry applications. The inclusion of EP and voxel grids acknowledges the shift toward deep learning-based molecular representation in contemporary chemoinformatics. The BSD license and open-source availability facilitate the creation of a template for other chemoinformatics GUI applications.

Contradictions And Limitations
The author explicitly notes that different values were obtained for GETAWAY, MORSE, and WHIM descriptors with the same RDKit version across different runs or operating systems, indicating non-deterministic behavior in RDKit's 3D descriptor calculation. A specific example of this inconsistency was identified with the structure generated for COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br. The tool's 3D grid calculation excludes atoms within 1 Å of the cube center (setting their contribution equal to the partial charge), which may introduce artifacts depending on the grid resolution. The number of descriptors implemented is limited to those natively available in RDKit's rdMolDescriptors module; user extension is possible but requires coding knowledge. The 3D structure generation relies on a fixed MMFF94 optimization (5000 iterations), which may not be optimal for all molecular classes. The paper does not report formal benchmarks, validation against experimental data, or comparison with other software (e.g., Mordred, PaDEL) in terms of accuracy or throughput.

Claims
GUIDEMOL provides a minimalist GUI that democratizes access to RDKit's advanced descriptor calculations for users without programming skills. The tkinter package was chosen because it is the standard Python interface to Tcl/Tk and bundled with Python. The application is designed as a minimalist interface for routine chemoinformatics tasks. Users can choose input and output files via native look-and-feel dialog windows. Extension of the tool to other descriptors or procedures still requires programming knowledge, undermining the 'no programming skills' claim for advanced use. Lowering the entry barrier to RDKit may accelerate adoption of QSPR/QSAR workflows in educational settings.
3D grid representations (EP and voxel) in GUIDEMOL enable processing of molecules by complex deep learning algorithms. These types of representations have recently gained attention for processing by complex artificial intelligence algorithms with larger data sets. EP grids have long been used in 3D-QSAR and molecular similarity assessment. Voxel representations have been used to train deep learning neural networks.  The CLI and GUI access to EP/voxel grids could serve as a preprocessing step for CNN-based QSAR models.

Data And Code Availability
The source code is available at https://github.com/jairesdesousa/guidemol under the three-clause BSD license. The license allows both commercial and non-commercial use.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The author identified an issue where different values were obtained for GETAWAY, MORSE, and WHIM descriptors with the same RDKit version (2022.9.5) in different runs or operating systems. The example case for this instability is COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br. There are no formal ablation studies or comparative benchmarking against other descriptor calculation software.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the GUIDEMOL interface with tkinter widgets (buttons, checkbuttons, radiobuttons, entries, labels, scrollbar) organized by the grid geometry manager.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a minimalist, open-source Python GUI (GUIDEMOL) that bridges RDKit's powerful descriptor API with non-programmers, including 3D EP and voxel grid representations for deep learning. 2. The strongest evidence is the practical implementation of all 7 RDKit 3D descriptors, the CLI for grid calculations, and the identification of non-deterministic behavior in RDKit's own 3D descriptor computation. 3. The future path lies in user extension of the tool for additional descriptors, as a template for other chemoinformatics GUI applications, and integration into educational QSPR/QSAR curricula.

summary.title: A Single-domain Protein Catenane of Dihydrofolate Reductase
summary.authors: Jing Fang (Peking University); Tianzuo Li (Peking University); Jiyeon Lee (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Dahye Lim (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Lianjie Xu (Peking University); Yajie Liu (Peking University); Jongcheol Seo (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Wen-Bin Zhang (Peking University)
summary.field_subfield: Protein Engineering; Synthetic Biology; Topological Proteins
summary.type_of_paper: Research Article / Dataset and Methods Report
summary.executive_summary: This paper reports the design and synthesis of the first single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR), a two-ring mechanically interlocked polypeptide structure derived from a single linear domain. The design strategy avoids exogenous entangling motifs by rewiring the connectivity between the secondary structure motifs of the wild-type DHFR fold, exploiting the fold's own spatial entanglement as the catenane template. Synthesis is achieved in vivo via a streamlined post-translational processing pathway using two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs that facilitate cyclization and ring closure without additional in vitro steps. The target molecule (P-2) contains few exogenous motifs and was thoroughly characterized by LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, ion mobility mass spectrometry, and CD spectroscopy. The cat-DHFR variant retains catalytic activity (approximately 5 U/mg, a 5-fold reduction relative to the linear control at 14 U/mg) despite extensive topological reconfiguration. Kinetic and binding studies reveal that reduced activity is primarily due to compromised substrate and cofactor affinity (K_D increased ~173-fold for DHF, ~14-fold for NADPH) rather than turnover limitation alone. Notably, cat-DHFR exhibits enhanced stability against chemical denaturation in 5% DMSO, retaining 87% activity compared to 74% for the linear control, attributed to conformational restriction from mechanical interlocking. judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper reports the design and synthesis of the first single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR), a two-ring mechanically interlocked polypeptide structure derived from a single linear domain. The design strategy avoids exogenous entangling motifs by rewiring the connectivity between the secondary structure motifs of the wild-type DHFR fold, exploiting the fold's own spatial entanglement as the catenane template. Synthesis is achieved in vivo via a streamlined post-translational processing pathway using two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs that facilitate cyclization and ring closure without additional in vitro steps. The target molecule (P-2) contains few exogenous motifs and was thoroughly characterized by LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, ion mobility mass spectrometry, and CD spectroscopy. The cat-DHFR variant retains catalytic activity (approximately 5 U/mg, a 5-fold reduction relative to the linear control at 14 U/mg) despite extensive topological reconfiguration. Kinetic and binding studies reveal that reduced activity is primarily due to compromised substrate and cofactor affinity (K_D increased ~173-fold for DHF, ~14-fold for NADPH) rather than turnover limitation alone. Notably, cat-DHFR exhibits enhanced stability against chemical denaturation in 5% DMSO, retaining 87% activity compared to 74% for the linear control, attributed to conformational restriction from mechanical interlocking. The study demonstrates that linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability, establishing an entirely new horizon in protein science. The authors note that crystallography was not achieved, and topology was confirmed indirectly, but the work provides a general method for single-domain topological protein design.

Research Context
Natural protein domains serve as modules for new function but their linear backbone limits topological diversity. Topological proteins have been recognized as a unique dimension for protein engineering. Artificial topological proteins synthesized to date usually contain multiple domains, complicating the study of topological effects. Ideally, a single-domain topological protein should exhibit the most profound impact of chemical topology and provide an unusual scaffold. Yet, it remains challenging to prepare single-domain topological proteins, even for the simplest catenane or Hopf link. Rewiring has been performed on the SpyTag-SpyCatcher complex, and mutually orthogonal split-intein ligation pairs were recently reported for heterocatenanes. The authors envision that the need for an exogenous entangling motif may be eliminated by exploiting spatial entangled relationships among secondary structures.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a single-domain protein can be converted into a catenane without collapsing the fold and while retaining catalytic function. The hypothesis is that by rewiring the connectivity between secondary structural motifs of DHFR, the native fold can serve as its own entangling template for catenane synthesis. The authors predict that the rewired protein will possess a catenane topology (GLN > 0) and retain significant enzymatic activity. The design criterion specifies that the active site and adjacent regions should be left intact to preserve enzymatic function. The hypothesis extends that the mechanical interlocking of two rings will provide conformational restriction leading to enhanced stability against denaturation.

Methodological Details
The protein used is dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) from Escherichia coli, a model enzyme catalyzing reduction of 7,8-dihydrofolate to 5,6,7,8-tetrahydrofolate. Molecular design was guided by the Gaussian linking number (GLN) matrix of wt-DHFR (PDB: 4KJJ) to identify optimal splitting positions. Cleavage at residues 88 and 89 (between α-helix-C and β-sheet-5) generated two intertwined segments with GLN +0.726. The final cat-DHFR design comprised residues 1-88 as one ring and 89-159 as the second ring, with a total GLN of +1.120. A linear control (l-DHFR) was designed with identical amino acid composition but bearing extra amino acids at the N- and C-termini. Ring I was circularly permutated to generate new termini between residues 23 and 24, with rewired loops designed at 16 residues to bridge split motifs. The gene cassette contained two DHFR segments, two mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs for ring closure, and a TEV protease recognition sequence in the first ring. Genes were synthesized and subcloned into pMCSG19 and pET21a vectors. Expression was carried out in E. coli BL21(DE3) competent cells at 16°C for 20 hours. Proteins were purified under native conditions by Ni-NTA affinity chromatography followed by size exclusion chromatography.

Procedures And Architectures
The retrosynthetic analysis showed that circular permutation of ring I was necessary to place cyclization motifs on the opposite side and avoid steric hindrance from bulky split-intein pairs. Two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-inteins (pairs 25, 26) were used for in vivo reconstitution and cyclization. The TEV protease recognition site was pre-programmed in the first ring to enable proof of topology by proteolytic digestion. For the design optimization, multiple sites for ring closure were tested, with the site between residues 23 and 24 identified as most efficient. Linker length effects were probed by testing L2 of ring II with different sequences and lengths, showing that the shortest linker yielded ~1/5 the yield of the longest. Catalytic activity was assayed by monitoring absorbance at 340 nm at 25°C with NADPH and DHF. Binding affinities were determined by isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) with NADPH, DHF, and THF. Chemical stability was tested by adding DMSO to a final concentration of 5%. Ion mobility spectrometry (IMS) and collision-induced dissociation (CID) were used for topological characterization.

Key Results
SDS-PAGE showed a single band at approximately 22 kDa for l-DHFR and a major band at less than 20 kDa for cat-DHFR. The SEC overlay showed cat-DHFR eluting as a much broader peak at a slightly larger retention volume than l-DHFR. Far-UV CD spectra of cat-DHFR showed substantially reduced intensities of both the positive peak at ~200 nm and the negative peak between 210 nm and 230 nm compared to l-DHFR. Near-UV CD spectrum of cat-DHFR exhibited a positive ellipticity at ~290 nm similar to the linear control. Proteolytic digestion with TEV protease converted cat-DHFR to a linear fragment and a cyclic fragment, confirmed by SDS-PAGE and LC-MS. Cat-DHFR had catalytic activity of ~5 U/mg, a 5-fold reduction relative to l-DHFR (~14 U/mg), significantly higher than the 15% activity of the split-reconstituted fragments. The Km of cat-DHFR is approximately 5-fold that of l-DHFR, and kcat is approximately 38% that of l-DHFR. The catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) of cat-DHFR is reduced by an order of magnitude relative to l-DHFR. The disassociation constants (KD) for cat-DHFR are ~173-fold larger for DHF and ~14-fold larger for NADPH relative to l-DHFR. The KD for the product THF is increased by ~3.6-fold for cat-DHFR relative to l-DHFR. Cat-DHFR retained 87% activity in 5% DMSO, compared to 74% for l-DHFR. When tested on the same side of DHFR, ring closure produced only ~33% catenane with considerable single-ring side products.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The GLN of +1.120 confirms that the design successfully achieves catenane topology through topological rewiring. The reduced CD signal intensities suggest a loosening of secondary structure due to circular permutation and concatenation, but the overall fold remains intact. The retained enzymatic activity indicates that the active site and adjacent regions were sufficiently preserved despite the topological change. The order-of-magnitude decrease in catalytic efficiency is primarily attributed to compromised substrate (DHF) and cofactor (NADPH) affinity, with the ~3.6-fold increase in THF KD indicating the product can also leave more easily. The enhanced thermal resilience (87% vs 74% activity in DMSO) supports the hypothesis that mechanical interlocking imposes conformational restriction that stabilizes the enzyme. The results suggest that linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability, representing an entirely new horizon in protein science.

Contradictions And Limitations
Crystallography of cat-DHFR was attempted but no crystals of sufficient quality were obtained. The authors note that the approach requires extensive optimization to achieve high-yield expression and efficient catenane formation. The CD spectra of cat-DHFR show reduced intensity compared to l-DHFR, suggesting minor local disturbance to the folded structure. The SEC profile of cat-DHFR is a broader peak, which may indicate dynamic structural behavior due to coupled ring movement. The topological confirmation relies on indirect methods (proteolysis, IMS-MS, CID) because crystallography was unavailable. The authors acknowledge they have not been able to obtain a crystal structure, leaving the exact tertiary organization at atomic resolution unresolved.

Claims
The authors claim that the single-domain protein catenane cat-DHFR retains significant catalytic activity relative to the linear control despite extensive topological and sequence rewiring. Cat-DHFR retains ~5 U/mg activity compared to ~14 U/mg for l-DHFR, significantly better than the 15% retained by the split-reconstituted fragments. The Km is only 5-fold increased and kcat is at 38%, indicating the turnover capacity is only moderately impaired. The catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) is reduced by an order of magnitude, and DHF affinity (KD) is decreased ~173-fold. The reduced activity may be restored to match or surpass the linear control by directed evolution.
Cat-DHFR exhibits enhanced chemical stability compared to its linear counterpart, supporting the hypothesis that mechanical interlocking provides conformational restriction. In 5% DMSO, cat-DHFR retained 87% activity versus 74% for l-DHFR. The GLN of +1.120 confirms the catenane topology that drives this stability.  This suggests that mechanical interlocking enhances thermal resilience of the enzyme.
The design strategy allows conversion of linear proteins into single-domain catenanes with minimal exogenous motifs. The target P-2 molecule contains few exogenous motifs and the entangling template is the native fold itself. The cat-DHFR has almost identical amino acid composition to the linear control. Extra amino acids from the TEV site, rewired loops, and split-inteins are still present. Linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts representing a new horizon.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Testing of ring-closure on the same side of DHFR yielded only ~33% catenane, supporting the necessity of circular permutation to place cyclization motifs on the opposite side. Testing the L2 linker length showed the shortest linker produced ~1/5 the yield of the longest, indicating a critical length threshold before the method becomes non-robust. The design was optimized using GLN matrices to identify the most intertwined split position (residues 88 and 89) before synthesizing synthetic strategy.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows the molecular design of cat-DHFR with ring boundaries at residues 1-88 and 89-159 and retrosynthetic analysis. Figure 1d shows the GLN matrix calculation identifying the splitting position. Figure 2a shows SDS-PAGE of purified cat-DHFR (~<20 kDa) and l-DHFR (~22 kDa). Figure 2b shows SEC overlay confirming cat-DHFR as a broader peak at larger retention volume. Figure 2c shows LC-MS confirming accurate molecular weights of cat-DHFR and l-DHFR. Figure 2d shows far-UV CD spectra comparing cat-DHFR and l-DHFR. Figure 4c shows kinetic curves of DHFR activity at 340 nm. Table 1 reports Km, kcat, catalytic efficiency, and KD values for DHF, NADPH, and THF. Figure S3 shows the effect of cyclization site on ring closure yield. Figure S4 shows the effect of L2 linker length on catenane yield.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the design and in vivo synthesis of the first single-domain protein catenane of DHFR, demonstrating that a protein's native fold can serve as its own entangling template through topological rewiring. 2. The strongest evidence is the combination of GLN +1.120 confirming catenane topology, LC-MS/SDS-PAGE/protease cleavage confirming purity and structure, and the retention of ~37% enzymatic activity (5 U/mg relative to 14 U/mg) with enhanced chemical stability (87% vs 74% in DMSO). 3. The future path involves directed evolution to restore full enzymatic activity, crystallography for atomic resolution structure, and the application of this general method to other single-domain proteins with enhanced stability and novel scaffolds.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces a robotic platform designed to automate sequential electrochemical rate data collection for CO2 electroreduction, addressing the heavy data requirements of cohesive kinetic analysis that preclude manual implementation. The authors demonstrate the system by measuring reaction kinetics at three immobilized metal tetrapyrrole catalysts—cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin (CoTPP), and iron phthalocyanine (FePc)—over a wide range of voltages, CO2 partial pressures, and bicarbonate concentrations. The system enables each of ten sequential electrolyses to have a different electrode, electrolyte, gas-phase composition, and applied voltage, with online gas chromatography product quantification. The data reveal that common linearization strategies (Tafel and reactant order analyses) are insufficient for these catalysts, as both CO2 and bicarbonate order dependences are non-linear and/or change with applied potential. The authors attribute these non-idealities to electrolyte (bicarbonate) poisoning, surface coverage effects, and potential-dependent mixed control between competitive catalytic pathways. The study finds that CoPc and CoTPP share similar bicarbonate-inhibition trends (attenuated at more reductive potentials), while FePc shows amplified inhibition at more reductive potentials. The authors argue that cohesive kinetic analysis, combined with automation, can resolve apparent contradictions in literature by probing the full reaction surface rather than limited operating ranges. The paper positions this robotic workflow as a scalable alternative to high-throughput screening for probing complex catalytic mechanisms.

Research Context
Traditional electrocatalysis kinetics analysis relies on linearization of rate equations, assuming variables like voltage and concentration factor separately. Linearization strategies yield incomplete results when coverage effects, mixed control, or side reactions are present. The 59 mV/dec voltage scaling means surface coverages can change drastically within a few hundred millivolts. Cohesive kinetic analysis, involving quantitative model fitting over wide reaction ranges, is more robust but requires much more data. Cohesive kinetic analysis is more common in thermocatalysis than electrocatalysis. Previous meta-analyses of Tafel data showed slopes do not prefer interpretable values like 60 or 120 mV/dec. Cohesive kinetic analysis has previously shown electrolyte adsorption and mixed control at CoPc. Automation in electrocatalysis has mostly targeted high-throughput screening rather than kinetic analysis. Microliter-scale scanning droplet cells cannot automate kinetic analysis for non-100% Faradaic efficiency reactions. A parallel configuration with online product quantification of individual cells would be expensive.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether common linearization-based kinetic analyses are sufficient to characterize the reaction mechanisms of CO2 reduction at immobilized metal tetrapyrroles. The authors hypothesize that non-ideal behaviors such as electrolyte poisoning, coverage effects, and mixed control will be prevalent across these catalysts. A secondary hypothesis is that bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences will change with applied potential, indicating voltage-dependent mechanistic shifts. The study predicts that CoPc and CoTPP will exhibit similar mechanistic signatures due to their related structures. FePc is predicted to show a different mechanism with a species later in the catalytic cycle as the most abundant reactive intermediate. The authors hypothesize that these complex behaviors can be explained by models invoking off-cycle poisoning or on-cycle intermediates rather than single-pathway mechanisms. The study aims to show that automation can standardize the workflow for cohesive kinetic analysis in electrocatalysis.

Methodological Details
CoPc was dissolved in DMF and drop-casted onto calcined Toray060 carbon paper at a loading of 5.98 x 10⁻¹¹ mol/cm². CoTPP was drop-casted in carbon-black-containing DMF at 5.11 x 10⁻¹⁰ mol/cm², and FePc at 8.04 x 10⁻¹⁰ mol/cm². Carbon black was added to the less active catalysts to increase loading while avoiding aggregation. All catalysts were tested at low loadings where aggregation was not expected to be an issue. Electrolytes were prepared from stock solutions of 0.5 mol/L Na₂CO₃ and 1 mol/L NaClO₄. Stock solutions were bubbled overnight with CO₂ and stored before use. Electrolyte solutions were mixed to achieve overall 1 mol/L ionic strength with desired bicarbonate concentrations. Electrolyzes were queued in batches of ten, with each run using the same electrolyte composition within a set. The leak-free Ag/AgCl reference electrode was calibrated daily against a saturated calomel electrode and swapped every 1-3 days. Data was stored in an SQL database and processed via Python to output average current, CO current, and H2 current to Excel. A carbon paper disk working electrode of 10 mm diameter was clamped between top and bottom cell pans. The counter electrode was a 0.25 mm diameter platinum wire. Gas flow was initiated through the gas in port, then voltage was applied and online product quantification via GC began. A gas chromatograph was connected to the gas out port for online CO and H₂ detection. Cell body cleaning involved pumping milliQ water through an empty cell pan pair for several cycles. The common reservoir configuration was used so the electrolyte could be freshly bubbled with CO₂. The study used a three-electrode, undivided compartment cell configuration.

Procedures And Architectures
The robotic system moves horizontally to sequentially perform electrochemistry on each of ten cell pan pairs. The cell body moves vertically to open and close onto any given cell pan. For each electrolysis, electrolyte is pumped through the electrolyte in port on the side of the cell body. Two configurations were available: individual vials per cell pan or a common reservoir; the common reservoir was used. The robot waits a few minutes after electrolyte flow before applying voltage and initiating online GC detection. Upon electrolysis completion, electrolyte is pumped to a waste container and the cell is opened. After each set of ten electrolyses, the cell body is rinsed at a wash station. Cell body cleaning uses milliQ water for several cycles to prevent cross-contamination. A python script accesses run conditions, calculates averages, and outputs to Excel. The system was first validated by reproducing literature CoPc data in a classic three-compartment cell setup. The cell design uses a 10 mm diameter circle of carbon paper exposed to electrolyte. A platinum counter electrode was chosen over carbon to preclude anode oxidation products. The cell is a one-compartment design, admitting crosstalk between working and counter electrodes. The robot enables queueing up to ten electrolyses per single lab effort.

Key Results
Across all three catalysts, bicarbonate order dependence showed non-linearity and potential-dependent changes. At CoPc and CoTPP, bicarbonate order is most negative at less reductive potentials and positive at more reductive potentials. For FePc, bicarbonate inhibition is stronger at more reductive potentials, contrary to simple adsorption expectations. CoPc shows nearly ideal first-order CO2 dependence at both tested potentials. CoTPP shows CO2 order slightly below one, decreasing at more reductive potentials, consistent with surface saturation. FePc CO2 order curves for the two potentials intersect, meaning voltage inhibits the reaction at low CO2 pressures. Reproducing CoPc data using the automated setup showed rates up to ten times lower than previous manual reports. Faradaic efficiencies toward CO for CoPc in the automated runs were typically under 30%. On average, only c.a. 60% of Faradaic efficiency was attributable to CO and H₂ formation. Hydrogen evolution efficiencies were typically around 30 to 60%. Previous kinetic trends for CoPc were preserved despite the tenfold rate difference. Newly collected CoPc data was well-correlated with previous manual data. The CoPc and CoTPP mechanism models (Figure 2D) quantitatively describe the kinetic behavior. The CO2 saturation model (Figure 3D) captures CoTPP behavior with increasing surface coverage of the intermediate. The mixed control model with an on-cycle poisoning species (Figure 3E) captures the intersecting CO2 order curves for FePc. No mechanism with explicit off-cycle poisoning (Figures 2D, 2E) alone could quantitatively fit all experimental data; qualitative capture only.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The bicarbonate trends at CoPc and CoTPP are explained by a model of bicarbonate poisoning with positive electrosorption valency. At more reductive potentials, the poisoning equilibrium shifts away from the poisoned species, decreasing inhibition. The bicarbonate-dependent pathway attains greater rate control at more reductive potentials, yielding apparent positive dependence. For FePc, the trend is explained by the most abundant reactive intermediate being a species prior to the unoccupied site. Alternatively, the FePc trend can be modeled as mixed control between two pathways where high coverage of a bicarbonate-dependent intermediate diverts flux. Surface saturation effects are the mechanism for the sub-first-order CO2 dependence at CoTPP. The intersecting CO2 order curves at FePc indicate voltage directs unproductive flux towards accumulation of a poisoning species. At higher CO2 pressures for FePc, the CO2-dependent step after the poisoning species becomes fast enough to make the pathway productive. The study suggests ostensibly opposing literature observations may be reconciled by kinetic measurements probing only a limited operating range. The convergence of automation and cohesive kinetic analysis provides a strategy for dissecting electrocatalytic reaction complexity. The mechanisms proposed only qualitatively capture trends; quantitative statistical goodness-of-fit was not achieved.

Contradictions And Limitations
The undivided cell design leads to oxygen crossover and parasitic oxygen reduction current, preventing full Faradaic efficiency closure. The CO2 was bubbled into the electrolyte rather than fed through the electrode, which can influence measured kinetics. Rates reproduced via the automated system were tenfold lower than manual literature reports, raising questions about accuracy. CO Faradaic efficiencies were under 30%, significantly lower than expected. The proposed mechanisms only qualitatively capture the trends and do not quantitatively fit all experimental data. The random seed for the SQL database and specific electrode geometry beyond 10 mm are not reported. The specific software version and Python dependencies for the data handling pipeline are not reported. The exact electrolyte composition (specific CO2 partial pressure) is not fully specified in the summary. The study does not report on long-term electrode degradation or catalyst stability. The authors note that flow configuration can have unexpected influence even in non-transport-limited regimes.

Claims
The robotic platform enables flexible, automated electrochemical rate data collection, reducing labor and enabling testing across wide reaction conditions. The system automates sequential testing of up to ten electrochemical cells with different electrodes, electrolytes, and gas compositions. Online GC product quantification of individual cells is enabled within the robotic workflow. The workflow enables queueing up to ten electrolyses per single lab effort. The cell body was rinsed only after the full set of ten electrolyses, which could risk cross-contamination. The manual cleaning of cell pans remains a non-automated step. This approach can standardize and accelerate cohesive kinetic analysis workflows in electrocatalysis. The system may eventually incorporate membrane separation and better flow configurations.
CoPc and CoTPP share a similar reaction mechanism characterized by voltage-dependent bicarbonate inhibition attenuated at more reductive potentials. Both catalysts show bicarbonate order most negative at less reductive potentials and positive at more reductive potentials. A model with positive electrosorption valency and mixed control quantitatively describes both. CoPc and CoTPP exhibit nearly first-order CO2 dependence at both potentials. CoPc shows almost perfect first-order CO2 dependence, while CoTPP is slightly below one, indicating some structural difference. The structurally related tetrapyrroles share fundamental kinetic pathways. These mechanisms have not been previously discussed for immobilized tetrapyrrole CO2RR.
FePc exhibits amplified bicarbonate inhibition at more reductive potentials, requiring a mechanism with an early reactive intermediate. Bicarbonate inhibition at FePc is stronger at more reductive potentials. The model requires the most abundant reactive intermediate to be a species prior to the unoccupied site. The CO2 order curves for FePc intersect, indicating voltage-dependent inhibition at low CO2 pressure. An alternative mixed-control model also explains the FePc trend without explicit poisoning species. The mechanism at FePc is fundamentally different from the Co tetrapyrroles. Voltage-dependent mechanistic shifts are a pervasive feature across the catalyst class.

Data And Code Availability
All experimental data are available in .xlsx format at the ChemRxiv repository. A PDF containing reagent information, detailed protocols, and supplemental discussion is also available. The preprint is available at https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv-2023-h0zh1.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The automated setup was validated by reproducing CoPc data and comparing it to previous manual literature results. The newly measured rates were up to ten times lower than previously reported manual results. The CO Faradaic efficiencies were typically under 30%, lower than expected. Despite the rate discrepancy, the kinetic trends and correlation with previous work were preserved. Non-ideal hallmarks such as curvature and potential-dependent changes were clearly evident in the automated data. The study acknowledges that the undivided cell and bubbling flow may influence kinetics even in non-transport-limited regimes.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the overall robot design with the cell body and ten cell pan pairs. Figure 1B shows the cell assembly analogous to a three-electrode undivided compartment cell with gas-out port. Figure 2A-C show bicarbonate order dependence for CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc at two potentials. Figure 2D-G illustrate conceptual models for bicarbonate poisoning and mixed control pathways. Figure 3A-C show CO2 order dependence for CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc. Figure 3D-E illustrate CO2 saturation and mixed control models. Figure S5 shows the incomplete Faradaic efficiency closure (c.a. 60%). Figure S7 shows the reproduced CoPc kinetic trends compared to literature. Figure S8 shows the correlation between newly measured and previously reported CoPc data. Figure S9 provides aggregated rates for all three catalysts. Figure S10 shows CO and H2 selectivities for all three catalysts. Figure S10A shows CO Faradaic efficiencies typically under 30%. Figure S10 shows HER FEs typically around 30 to 60%.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a robotic platform that automates sequential electrocatalytic rate data collection, enabling cohesive kinetic analysis over wide reaction conditions for CO2 reduction. 2. The strongest evidence is that across CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc, bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences are non-linear and potential-dependent, behaviors that cannot be captured by standard Tafel or reactant-order analyses. 3. The future path includes incorporating membrane separation in the undivided cell, alternative flow configurations, and software to automatically enumerate mechanisms and suggest the most informative experimental conditions.

summary.title: Visualization of π-hole in molecules by means of Kelvin probe force microscopy
summary.authors: B Mallada, M Ondráček, M Lamanec, A Gallardo, A Jiménez-Martín, B De La Torre, P Hobza, P Jelínek
summary.field_subfield: Surface Science / Chemical Physics / Scanning Probe Microscopy
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents the first direct experimental visualization of a π-hole—a π-electron-deficient cavity in a halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbon—on a single molecule using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). The authors demonstrate that the substitution of peripheral hydrogens in anthracene with chlorine and fluorine substituents (forming 9,10-dichlorooctafluoroanthracene, FCl-An) reverses the quadrupole moment from negative to positive, creating the π-hole. The KPFM imaging reveals a characteristic submolecular 'bow-tie' pattern in the local contact potential difference (LCPD) across the FCl-An molecule, which is absent in pristine anthracene (An). Theoretical DFT calculations and KPFM simulations in excellent agreement confirm the experimental findings. Furthermore, the study quantifies the physical consequence of the π-hole on molecule–substrate interaction: the π-hole increases the ionization potential, suppressing charge induction at the Au(111) interface, which elevates the adsorption height from 330 pm for An to 360 pm for FCl-An (+30 pm absolute increase). SAPT0 energy decomposition reveals that the induction energy (electrostatic stabilization) is larger for An than for FCl-An, consistent with the observed height difference. The study establishes KPFM as a viable tool for submolecular charge distribution mapping and provides a fundamental link between submolecular electrostatic features and macroscopic physicochemical properties such as adsorption height and surface interactions.
