judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents the first direct experimental visualization of a π-hole—a π-electron-deficient cavity in a halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbon—on a single molecule using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). The authors demonstrate that the substitution of peripheral hydrogens in anthracene with chlorine and fluorine substituents (forming 9,10-dichlorooctafluoroanthracene, FCl-An) reverses the quadrupole moment from negative to positive, creating the π-hole. The KPFM imaging reveals a characteristic submolecular 'bow-tie' pattern in the local contact potential difference (LCPD) across the FCl-An molecule, which is absent in pristine anthracene (An). Theoretical DFT calculations and KPFM simulations in excellent agreement confirm the experimental findings. Furthermore, the study quantifies the physical consequence of the π-hole on molecule–substrate interaction: the π-hole increases the ionization potential, suppressing charge induction at the Au(111) interface, which elevates the adsorption height from 330 pm for An to 360 pm for FCl-An (+30 pm absolute increase). SAPT0 energy decomposition reveals that the induction energy (electrostatic stabilization) is larger for An than for FCl-An, consistent with the observed height difference. The study establishes KPFM as a viable tool for submolecular charge distribution mapping and provides a fundamental link between submolecular electrostatic features and macroscopic physicochemical properties such as adsorption height and surface interactions.

Research Context
Non-covalent interactions, governed by dispersion and electrostatic forces, determine the nature of intermolecular bonds crucial for supramolecular assembly and protein stability. In polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, the electron-rich delocalized π-bond system creates a negative quadrupole moment, as the larger electronegativity of carbon draws density from peripheral hydrogen. Substituting hydrogens with more electronegative atoms like fluorine or chlorine reverses the π-bond electron population, making it electron-deficient and giving the molecule a positive quadrupole moment. A π-electron-deficient cavity in the central part of the molecule is termed a π-hole, which significantly affects intermolecular interactions such as DNA base stacking. The concept of the π-hole had been developed exclusively on a theoretical basis using quantum calculations prior to this work. Experimental evidence for the π-hole had previously only been proven indirectly through measured data that could only explain its presence. A direct experimental observation clearly proving the existence of the π-hole had been lacking until this study. Scanning probe microscopy with functionalized probes has recently enabled unprecedented spatial resolution of σ-holes on individual atoms. The KPFM method that resolved the σ-hole was proposed as an ideal tool for real-space observation of the π-hole system.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a π-hole can be directly visualized in real space on a single molecule using KPFM. The authors hypothesize that the KPFM method, which resolved the σ-hole, is also capable of resolving the submolecular π-hole charge distribution. A secondary question addresses how the π-hole affects the adsorption and bonding interaction between molecules and a metallic substrate. The predicted outcome is that the π-hole will manifest as a submolecular variation in the LCPD with a characteristic bow-tie pattern in the FCl-An molecule, absent in An. It is predicted that the π-hole will increase the ionization potential of FCl-An, suppressing charge induction at the Au(111) interface and increasing the adsorption height. The study expects that DFT-calculated electrostatic potential and KPFM simulations will reproduce the experimental submolecular LCPD variation.

Methodological Details
The study investigated two molecular species: 9,10-dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) and anthracene (An). Molecules were co-deposited on an atomically clean Au(111) surface via simultaneous sublimation from two Knudsen cells in UHV at room temperature. The Au(111) substrate was prepared by repeated cycles of Ar+ sputtering at 1 keV followed by annealing at approximately 800 K. STM topography was acquired in constant current mode, and nc-AFM used a qPlus sensor with resonant frequency of approximately 30 kHz and stiffness of approximately 1800 N/m. The nc-AFM used a CO-functionalized tip with an oscillation amplitude of 200 pm, operating in frequency modulation mode. Both nc-AFM and KPFM images were captured in constant height mode. KPFM LCPD maps were obtained from a 64x80 pixels rectangular grid of size 3 nm x 5 nm over the molecules. Each data point in the KPFM grid was acquired in approximately 3 seconds, with each parabola containing 600 points. The KPFM data was fitted with a parabolic expression of the form Δf(V) = a × (V - LCPD)² + Δf*, within a bias range of (-150, 400) mV. The KPFM measurement height was chosen close to the Δf minima to ensure absence of tip relaxation and enhance contrast. DFT calculations used the PBE functional with a lightweight setup: light basis, no k-grid, and 4 atomic layers for the Au(111) slab. The surface supercell was a 6×6 unit cell for isolated molecules and a √39×√39 cell for the supramolecular structure, stretched/compressed to match two unit cells. Van der Waals corrections used the Tkatchenko-Scheffler method with Hirshfeld partitioning. Cluster calculations for SAPT0 used a single molecule and a 38-atom gold layer with (111) orientation. The PP model for AFM/KPFM simulations assumed a dz²-like charge quadrupole of -0.2 e/Å² for the CO tip termination.

Procedures And Architectures
Co-deposition of An and FCl-An was performed for 15 s in UHV conditions on the Au(111) sample at room temperature. STM was used to observe large-scale ordered molecular islands with alternating species, and nc-AFM resolved individual molecules. The supramolecular assembly was identified as a rhombic periodic structure with one An and two FCl-An molecules per unit cell. KPFM measurements employed the same CO-functionalized tip used for nc-AFM to map LCPD variation with atomic resolution. DFT calculations for free-standing molecules used the hybrid PBE0 functional and tight basis set, while surface calculations used PBE with light basis. For molecules on the surface, all atoms except bottom-layer Au atoms were allowed to relax; free-standing molecules were forced to remain planar. KPFM simulations were performed using the PP model adapted to a CO-terminated tip with a lateral spring constant of 0.25 N/m. LCPD values were extracted as the bias at which the fitted parabola has a maximum. Specific-site force-distance spectroscopy was acquired above the central benzene unit of both An and FCl-An molecules. SAPT0 calculations were performed by PSI4 in cc-pVDZ (cc-pwCVDZ-PP for Au) basis set.

Key Results
STM and nc-AFM images confirmed a rhombic periodic supramolecular structure with one An and two FCl-An molecules in the unit cell. The arrangement was dictated by attractive interactions between negatively charged F atoms, chlorine sigma-hole, and positively charged H atoms. KPFM images of FCl-An revealed a characteristic submolecular bow-tie pattern in the central part, absent in An. Simulated KPFM images matched the experimental data, reproducing the submolecular LCPD variation and the bow-tie pattern. Specific-site force-distance spectroscopy showed a 30 pm difference between the Δf-z minima of An and FCl-An. The relative adsorption heights above bare Au(111) were determined to be 330 pm for An and 360 pm for FCl-An. The 30 pm height difference matched the DFT total energy calculations of 325 pm and 355 pm for An and FCl-An, respectively. More significant induced electron density was observed in the An/Au(111) interface compared to the FCl-An/Au(111) interface. SAPT0 decomposition showed induction energy (electrostatic stabilization) is larger for An than for FCl-An. In all cases, attractive interaction dominated over dispersion energy compared to electrostatic and induction terms. The presence of chlorine atoms did not influence the adsorption height, as both molecules showed similar height trends.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The bow-tie pattern in FCl-An KPFM images is associated with the heterogeneous charge distribution of the π-hole due to different electronegativities of F and Cl modulating the π-system locally. The π-hole increases the ionization potential of the molecule, which suppresses charge density induction at the molecule/metal interface. This suppressed induction weakens induced electrostatic interactions, resulting in a larger adsorption height for FCl-An compared to An. The SAPT0 results confirm that while dispersion is the dominant stabilizing force, the π-hole reduces the electrostatic contribution to binding. The study demonstrates that submolecular charge distributions, such as π-holes, have measurable macroscopic consequences on adsorption behavior. KPFM is established as a powerful tool for real-space imaging of internal molecular charge distributions, opening possibilities for studying π-hole systems and their influence on chemical properties.

Contradictions And Limitations
AFM images do not provide direct evidence of the π-hole because FCl-An molecules are imaged brighter than An due to a topographic effect rather than charge difference. At short tip-sample distances, tip relaxations can noticeably influence the KPFM signal and generate measurement artifacts, causing deviations from parabolic behavior. Far tip-sample distances do not exhibit intramolecular features in KPFM images, limiting the range of observable contrast. The DFT calculations use a lightweight PBE functional with no k-grid for surface calculations, which is a simplification for large supercells. SAPT0 calculations were performed on a cluster model, and while similar to slab model results, represent an approximation. The SAPT0 cluster model used only one layer of 38 gold atoms, which may not fully capture bulk-like electronic effects. The choice of KPFM acquisition height close to Δf minima is critical; the Δf* images (at compensated LCPD) do not show submolecular resolution for either molecule.

Claims
KPFM directly visualizes the π-hole on a single molecule for the first time, confirming the theoretical prediction. Experimental KPFM images of FCl-An show a submolecular bow-tie LCPD pattern absent in An. KPFM simulations using PP-AFM code reproduce the submolecular LCPD variation in excellent agreement with experiment. The LCPD variation matches the DFT-calculated electrostatic potential of a free-standing FCl-An molecule. AFM images alone do not show the π-hole due to topographic contrast differences. At compensated LCPD (Δf*), no submolecular resolution is observed in either molecule. Confirms a long-standing theoretical prediction through direct experimental imaging. Establishes KPFM as a validated technique for submolecular charge distribution mapping.
The π-hole increases the adsorption height of the molecule on Au(111) by approximately 30 pm due to suppressed charge induction. Δf-z spectroscopy shows 30 pm difference between An and FCl-An minima. Relative heights are 330 pm for An and 360 pm for FCl-An above bare Au(111). SAPT0 shows induction energy is larger for An than for FCl-An, consistent with smaller adsorption height. The difference in height is only ~30 pm (approx 9%), which is a relatively small absolute change. Cl atoms do not influence adsorption height independently, as the effect is attributed to the π-hole, not individual substituents. Demonstrates that submolecular electrostatic features directly modulate macroscopic adsorption properties. Provides a quantitative link between charge distribution and bonding energy decomposition.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The KPFM contrast was tested as a function of tip-sample distance: far distances show no intramolecular features, while decreasing distance enhances submolecular contrast. KPFM height was chosen at Δf minima to exclude tip relaxation artifacts, confirmed by Δf* images showing no submolecular resolution. The supramolecular assembly arrangement was validated against AFM, STM, and DFT: the 1 An + 2 FCl-An rhombic unit cell is unambiguously resolved. The effect of substituents was isolated: the presence of chlorine atoms alone does not influence adsorption height. The DFT results were checked with hybrid PBE0 functional and tight basis set, showing no substantial changes in geometry or charge distribution. DFT and SAPT0 adsorption energy results gave very similar values, validating the energy decomposition analysis.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the molecular structures of An and FCl-An with negative and positive quadrupole moments respectively. Figure 2a and 2b show STM and nc-AFM images of the molecular self-assembly on Au(111) revealing the rhombic unit cell. Figure 2c shows the atomic-scale nc-AFM image of the assembly. Figure 2d shows the proposed arrangement dictated by F-, chlorine sigma-hole, and H interactions. Figure 3a shows the DFT-calculated electrostatic potential of free-standing FCl-An. Figure 3b shows the experimental KPFM LCPD map of FCl-An with the bow-tie pattern. Figure 3c shows the simulated KPFM LCPD map matching the experiment. Figure 3d shows the simulated KPFM LCPD map of An, revealing no submolecular variation. Figure 4a shows Δf-z force spectroscopy over the central benzene unit of both molecules. Figure 4b and 4c show DFT-calculated induced electron densities at the molecule/metal interface. Figure 6 shows a series of constant-height AFM images showing submolecular contrast emergence on FCl-An. Table S2 presents SAPT0 energy decomposition results for all three molecules. Table S3 presents the SAPT0 energy decomposition for all three molecules in cluster vs slab models.

Three Takeaways
1. The study provides the first direct experimental visualization of a π-hole on a single molecule, resolving a long-standing theoretical prediction through KPFM imaging of submolecular LCPD variation. 2. The π-hole has a quantifiable physical effect: it increases the ionization potential of FCl-An, suppresses charge induction at the Au(111) interface, and raises the adsorption height from 330 pm (An) to 360 pm (FCl-An), with the 30 pm difference confirmed by both force spectroscopy and SAPT0 energy decomposition. 3. KPFM with CO-functionalized probes is established as a viable technique for mapping submolecular charge distributions in single molecules, with implications for understanding how internal electrostatic features modulate non-covalent interactions and surface bonding.

summary.authors: James M Stevenson; Garvit Agarwal; Leif D Jacobson

Bonding analysis reveals that P-F and Li-O bonds correlate with stable structures, while C-O and Li-F bonds correlate with instability. judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work presents the first ranking of candidate solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) structures in lithium-ion batteries using a machine-learning force field (MLFF) trained via multitask learning. The authors address the challenge that no existing simulation method is fully applicable to the complex redox-reactive, multi-phase chemistry of SEI formation, which involves conductors, insulators, and reaction kinetics. They develop a Quaternion Representation Neural Network (QRNN) trained on four levels of theory: GFN1-xTB, PBE-D3, wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD, and a SPICE-specific hybrid head. The data generation pipeline combines active learning with enhanced reaction sampling (AFIR and NEB) and a new OPLS4 molecular dynamics SEI Simulator that produces plausible SEI geometries from 7416 atoms (1 M EC/LiPF6). The model is validated against the best available surface reaction energy barriers from DFT, as experimental SEI benchmarks do not exist. The ranking procedure involves annealing initial geometries at 400 K/1000 atm, followed by 20 ps MD trajectories at 300 K/1 atm to compute mean potential energies. Bonding analysis reveals that P-F and Li-O bonds correlate with stable structures, while C-O and Li-F bonds correlate with instability. The authors conclude that multitask QRNN training captures SEI redox chemistry and propose future comparison across multiple electrolyte formulations to optimize SEI chemistry.

Research Context
SEIs are a vital but poorly-understood class of materials that combine organic and inorganic components. The fundamental challenge is that the anode must be unstable with respect to the cathode but stable with respect to the electrolyte. Key questions about whether SEIs are amorphous or crystalline and how Li+ moves through them remain unanswered, limiting battery development. No existing method is fully applicable to simulating SEI systems involving conductors, insulators, and redox reactions. Pure density functionals (DFT) work well for metallic systems but badly underestimate reaction barriers. Hybrid functionals like wB97X yield improved barriers but struggle with metals and have poor periodic scaling, leaving SEI simulation out of reach. MLFFs promise DFT-level accuracy with classical force field sampling speeds.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a multitask QRNN trained on diverse chemical systems can capture the complex redox chemistry of SEI formation and rank candidate structures by energy. The authors hypothesize that including a general organic chemistry dataset (SPICE) in the multitask training will improve the model's latent space without imposing a heavy cost on capacity. A secondary hypothesis is that the SEI Simulator method with OPLS4 MD and reaction templates can generate plausible SEI geometries that serve as meaningful starting points for energy ranking. The authors further hypothesize that the most stable structures can be distinguished by specific bonding motifs (e.g., P-F vs. C-O bonds) and that the energy ranking is directly comparable across sets with identical atom counts. The prediction is that the QRNN model will provide stable dynamics even under the extreme annealing conditions (400 K, 1000 atm) required for SEI geometry preparation.

Methodological Details
The reference level for non-periodic systems is wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD, and for periodic systems it is PBE-D3 in a plane wave basis. A random subset of non-periodic systems was also labeled with PBE-D3 to improve information exchange between multitask output heads. The data generation uses multiple rounds of active learning, incorporating enhanced reaction sampling via AFIR and NEB on the QRNN potential energy surface. A supplemental SPICE dataset including elements H, Li, C, O, F, and P was added to the multitask training for broader chemical applicability. The SEI Simulator produces initial geometries from 700 molecules of EC and 52 ions each of Li+ and PF6-, totaling 7416 atoms at 1 M concentration. Four sets of candidates were defined with 5, 12, 23, and 33 added Li+ ions per box, arising after 40 iterations of the SEI Simulator. Training used hidden layers of sizes 256, 224, and 192, a batch size of 64, and the Adamax optimizer with learning rate 2e-3. A validation set of 1% (selected uniformly at random) was used, along with an exponential moving average (alpha = 0.001, averaged every 10 batches) for the final model. The loss function is energy and atomic force MSE for each theory level, plus charge MSE, with consistent charge labels across all heads. Periodic DFT was performed using Quantum Espresso at 40 Ry energy cutoff, 3x3x3 k-point bulk mesh, 3x3x1 surface mesh, using PBE functional with D3 dispersion.

Procedures And Architectures
The architecture is a QRNN (Quaternion Representation Neural Network) with four output heads corresponding to GFN1-xTB, PBE-D3, wB97X-D3BJ, and a SPICE-wB97X head. Gfn1-xTB was selected as the most suitable charge label source, providing the best compromise between accuracy and convergence across isolated and periodic systems. The hidden layer width was doubled compared to prior QRNN work to accommodate the expanded chemical scope. Decoupled weight norms were applied with norms not included in the optimizer; final weight decay was 1e-3 per batch. Initial geometries for solid-liquid interfaces started from a BCC lithium lattice placed next to equilibrated liquid EC with 2 Å spacing. Non-equilibrium geometries were generated by adding Gaussian noise to Cartesian coordinates; steric clashes were induced by setting Van der Waals radius factor to 0.5. Cluster extraction for gas-phase DFT used a uniform distribution radius from 3.0 to 5.2 Å with a 1.2 Å buffer for hydrogen. Annealing was performed at 400 K and 1000 atm for 100 ps NPT MD per system; ranking used 20 ps MD trajectories at 300 K, 1 atm.

Key Results
Adding SPICE data resulted in no increase in PBE-head validation RMSE on battery datasets and only an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE. The QRNN models produced stable dynamics under the extreme 400 K / 1000 atm annealing conditions, which is typically not observed for MLFFs. Bonding analysis (Figure 4) shows P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable (lower energy) structures. C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable (higher energy) structures. The most stable SEI candidate is identified as the lowest-energy structure from the 33-added-Li subgroup predicted by the wB97X-D3BJ output head. The model is this work's most complex redox-reactive system simulated using an MLFF or any method of comparable accuracy.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The observation that SPICE data added only 8% hybrid-head RMSE suggests the MLFF latent space contains unused capacity for broader chemical applicability. The ability to produce stable dynamics under extreme annealing conditions validates the QRNN architecture's robustness beyond equilibrium configurations. The correlation of specific bond types with energy (Figure 4) provides the first quantitative descriptor of stability in SEI candidate structures. The multitask strategy demonstrates that training on disparate datasets (general organic chemistry, metal surfaces, and electrolytes) simultaneously improves model generalization.

Contradictions And Limitations
Experimental benchmarks (density, diffusivity, viscosity, elastic modulus) do not exist for any SEI composition, precluding direct experimental validation. The model was trained on only a single electrolyte formulation (1 M LiPF6 in EC); full power requires comparing multiple formulations. High weight decay (3e-3) reduced the height of reaction barriers relative to reference barriers, necessitating the lower 1e-3 final weight decay. The current model scope is small compared to what is required for full SEI description; the authors do not regard it as final. NEB sampling focused only on EC decomposition reactions on Li surfaces, not on LiO or Li2CO3 surfaces, limiting the scope of the reactive dataset.

Claims
Multitask QRNN training combined with active learning can model complex SEI redox chemistry for energy ranking. The QRNN produced stable dynamics under extreme annealing conditions (400 K, 1000 atm). Bonding correlations (Figure 4) distinguish stable from unstable structures. The model ranks structures by energy and identifies a best candidate. No experimental values exist to validate density, diffusivity, or mechanical properties. Only a single electrolyte formulation was used. Future comparison across multiple electrolyte formulations will enable optimization of SEI chemistry via diffusivity and mechanical properties. This work provides the first plausible ranking to guide future experimental SEI design.

Data And Code Availability
The SEI candidate structures (seed*.pdb) and energies (energies.csv), along with plotting scripts (*.py), are available at: https://figshare.com/s/e842ae88023902700e12.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A sensitivity analysis showed that weight decay of 3e-3 produced smoother energy surfaces for NEB but reduced barrier heights. A weight decay of 1e-3 was selected for the final model to preserve barrier heights. Adding SPICE data showed only an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE, confirming the multitask strategy did not overtax model capacity. The model was not trained on DFT-generated MD, AFIR, or NEB geometries to avoid data leakage (training on test set). Validation was performed using only 1% of the data, with no significant effect from early stopping.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 4 shows bond counts (P-F, Li-O, C-O, Li-F) versus total system energy for the 33-added-Li candidate set, using the wB97X-D3BJ model output. Table 1 (referenced) contains surface reaction energy barrier validation against the best available DFT calculations. Figure 1 (referenced) shows the initial 1 M LiPF6 in EC solution structure (7416 atoms).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first energy-ranked set of SEI candidate structures produced via a multitask QRNN MLFF trained on both periodicity and cluster datasets, demonstrating MLFF capability for complex redox systems. 2. The strongest evidence is the QRNN's ability to maintain stable dynamics under 400 K / 1000 atm annealing and the clear correlation of P-F/Li-O bonds with lower-energy structures in the ranking. 3. The future path involves applying multiple electrolyte formulations, alternative architectures (Nequip, MACE, CHGNet), and ablation studies to determine critical dataset subsets.

summary.title: Biological activity of Ajuga iva extracts against the African cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis
summary.authors: Leena Taha-Salaime; Galina Lebedev; Jackline Abo-Nassar; Sally Marzouk; Moshe Inbar; Murad Ghanim; Radi Aly
summary.field_subfield: Entomology / Natural Products Pharmacology / Biological Pest Control
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates whether crude extracts from Ajuga iva, containing phytoecdysteroids and clerodane diterpenes, can serve as a natural pesticide against the African cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis, a major pest of cotton, maize, and other crops. The authors demonstrate that the crude methanolic leaf extract at three concentrations (50, 100, and 250 µg/µl) significantly increases larval mortality, reduces larval weight gain (LWG), and suppresses relative growth rate (RGR) in both first and third instar larvae. Specifically, first instar mortality rose from 5% in controls to 25%, 65%, and 85% at the three tested concentrations. Third instar larvae treated with 250 µg/µl crude extract exhibited reduced LWG (F3.104 = 20.334, p < 0.001) and no larvae survived beyond 8 days. A fractionated mixture of three purified phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) at 250 µg/µl produced similar inhibitory effects on RGR (F2.20, 18 = 6.172, p = 0.001) and larval survival. Histological analysis using DAPI and phalloidin staining revealed that treated larvae had smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei and reduced actin filament organization in the gut epithelium, supporting the conclusion that the phytoecdysteroids interfere with developmental processes and gut integrity. The study also confirms that the inhibitory effects are dose-dependent and persist even when treatment order is reversed, suggesting a non-deterrent, metabolic mechanism of action. The authors conclude that Ajuga iva extracts could be a promising component in integrated pest management (IPM) programs, providing a low-toxicity alternative to conventional chemical pesticides.

The authors conclude that Ajuga iva extracts could be a promising component in integrated pest management (IPM) programs, providing a low-toxicity alternative to conventional chemical pesticides.

Research Context
The African cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis is one of the most serious pests of cotton, maize, rice, alfalfa, potato, tomato, ornamentals and orchard trees. Insect pests are mainly controlled by insecticides, which constitute a risk to human health and the environment. Phytoecdysteroids are plant-produced steroids that are analogs of the steroid hormones that control molting and metamorphosis in arthropods. Ecdysteroids are not toxic to mammals because their structure is quite different from mammalian steroids and they are not expected to bind to vertebrate steroid receptors. The genus Ajuga also contains bioactive compounds such as clerodane diterpenes and iridoid glycosides. Previous studies showed that Ajuga remota extracts containing 20-hydroxyecdysone and cyasterone inhibited ecdysis and caused larval death in Bombyx mori. A dose of 5 μg/ml pure extracted A. iva ecdysterone reduced fecundity, fertility, and survival of Oligonychus perseae, while commercial 20-hydroxyecdysone had lesser effects. However, S. littoralis was not deterred from feeding by 20-hydroxyecdysone at 50-70 mg/kg, indicating a gap in understanding this species' response.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The authors hypothesized that the crude extract of A. iva leaves, containing the three phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone), would be a promising pest-control agent by interfering with molting and antifeedant activities. The first research question was: Does A. iva crude leaf extract affect S. littoralis larvae? The second question: Do phytoecdysteroids isolated from the crude leaf extract and commercial standards have different effects on the larvae? The third question: Do phytoecdysteroids have a direct effect on the larvae's gut? The study predicted that the inhibitory effects would be dose-dependent and would manifest as reduced growth, increased mortality, and suppressed pupation.

Methodological Details
Young and mature leaves and stems of fresh Ajuga iva plants were collected after blooming in July-November. Plant material was oven-dried at 55°C for 3-4 days and homogenized to a fine powder. For the crude extract, 24 g of leaf and stem powder were soaked in 240 ml of 100% MeOH, homogenized at 2500 rpm for 1 h, centrifuged at 112 g for 10 min, and concentrated under vacuum. The final methanol solution was dried in a chemical vaporizer for 5 days. LC-TOF-MS was used to confirm the presence of phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes. TLC on silica gel GF-254 plates (0.25 mm; 20 × 20 cm) separated components into well-defined spots. Three concentrations of the crude leaf extract were prepared: 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl. For the 250 µg/µl concentration, 1.2 g dried extract powder was dissolved in 4.8 ml ddH2O and Tween 20 (0.5 mg/ml). First instar larvae for bioassays were sourced from Murad Ghanim's laboratory, reared on castor bean leaves. Ten first instar larvae were placed on one treated castor bean leaf per replicate. The first instar experiment consisted of 11 replicates with 10 larvae each. For third instar larvae, 1 or 10 larvae were fed on one treated leaf for 4 or 8 days at 25°C. The third instar experiment used 20 replicates (n=20). Pupation rate was evaluated for an additional 15 days following the 8-day feeding period. Larval weight gain (LWG) data were from 10 replicates with 10 larvae in each replicate. Guts were dissected in 1X PBS, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 30 min, washed in 0.1% Triton X-100 for 30 min, incubated in 0.1% phalloidin for 30 min. Nuclei were stained with DAPI in hybridization buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 0.9 M NaCl). Visualisation was performed under a Leica SP8 and Olympus IX 81 confocal laser scanning microscope. Statistical analyses were performed with IBM SPSS software v.20 for Windows.

Procedures And Architectures
Mature castor bean leaves were smeared with a paintbrush with aqueous A. iva crude leaf extract (1:10 methanol solution) and Tween 20 (1.5 mg). Leaves were dried in a chemical hood for 2 h before larval placement. Control leaves were smeared with double-distilled water (ddH2O) and Tween 20. Larvae were allowed to feed for 3 days in a climate-controlled room at 25°C. For third instars, four treatment groups were tested: (1) crude extract for 4 days then fresh leaf for 4 more; (2) crude extract for 4 days plus fractionated phytoecdysteroid mixture; (3) crude extract for 4 days then ddH2O control; (4) ddH2O control for 4 days then crude extract. Relative growth rate (RGR) was calculated as (ln W2 - ln W1) / (t2 - t1). RGR comparisons used mixed-model ANOVA: repeated measures ANOVA until day 4 and two-way ANOVA from day 4 to the end. Survival rates were analyzed using a Friedman test due to non-normal distribution of data. Pupation rate was evaluated by checking whether larvae formed pupae after 15 days. LWG comparisons were assessed using repeated measures ANOVA. All statistical significance was reported at p < 0.05. For gut staining, larvae fed on 250 µg/µl crude extract for 8 days were tested after 7 days of treatment. The purified phytoecdysteroid fraction (250 µg/µl) was tested as a separate treatment group.

Key Results
First instar S. littoralis larvae showed significant mortality of 25%, 65%, and 85% after feeding on the three concentrations of A. iva crude leaf extract (50, 100, and 250 µg/µl, respectively), compared to 5% in control. Third instar larvae fed on the three crude extract concentrations showed reduced LWG (F3.104 = 20.334, 17.246, and 13.007, respectively, p < 0.001) compared to controls. All concentrations of crude leaf extract significantly decreased larval RGR (p < 0.001) compared to normally developing larvae. With the highest concentration (250 µg/µl), RGR decreased by 0.05 g/g/day on day 6 and by 0.20 g/g/day on day 8 compared to control (F3.16, 18 = 12.641, p < 0.001). All concentrations of A. iva crude leaf extract significantly reduced third instar larval survival after 11 days (X2,3 = 6.221, p = 0.038). None of the treated larvae survived more than 8 days for the highest concentration of crude leaf extract and 10 days for the other concentrations. When larvae were first fed on control leaves for 4 days then on crude extract for an additional 4 days, RGR was affected after day 5 (F3.16, 18 = 7.310, p < 0.001). With no surviving larvae in the delayed treatment group (X2,3 = 9.282, p = 0.021). When the order was reversed (crude extract for 4 days then control for 4 days), RGR decreased significantly on days 2-4 (F3.16, 18 = 4.595, 3.608, 8.113; p = 0.034, 0.02, 0.001 for 50, 100, 250 µg/µl, respectively). Castor bean leaves treated with 250 µg/µl of the mixture of the three fractionated and purified phytoecdysteroids significantly reduced RGR (F2.20, 18 = 6.172, p = 0.001) compared to control. Few larvae survived on the leaves treated with the purified phytoecdysteroid fraction (X2,3 = 11.305, p = 0.04). Larvae fed on 250 µg/µl crude leaf extract or the phytoecdysteroid mixture had smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei with the nuclei moved to the edges of the cell and thinner than normal. Phalloidin staining showed that actin filaments were smaller and their amount reduced in guts dissected from treated larvae compared to control. Larvae fed 250 µg/µl crude leaf extract or its phytoecdysteroid fraction for 8 days were unable to complete development and pupate after 15 days. The dying larvae had short limbs, small heads, decreased weight, and only stomach and chest pupated (nonpupation); none completed development to adult moths. A commercial mixture of three standards (ecdysterone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) at 100 ppm each fed for 8 days showed no significant effect on S. littoralis larvae.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results suggest that phytoecdysteroids in A. iva may affect insects by interfering with developmental stages, especially during metamorphosis, consistent with previous findings that ecdysteroids cause ecdysial failure. The suppression of pupation in S. littoralis is attributed to the reduction in LWG; larvae did not reach the threshold weight for pupation and died because they could not complete their life cycle. Gut cell destruction, characterized by histolysis, apoptosis, destruction of microvilli, and vacuole formation, supports the notion that the effect on pupation is a consequence of disruptions in hormonal balance affecting internal ecdysone levels. The disappearance of microfilament structures in actin could be a consequence of phytoecdysteroid titers in the crude extract, as actin microfilaments have been associated with rounding and loss of adhesion in response to secondary metabolites. The findings indicate that A. iva extracts could serve as a green pest-control agent, reducing risks to human health and the environment by targeting specific insect developmental pathways.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors did not fractionate clerodanes from A. iva crude leaf extract due to the difficulty in calibrating fractionation protocols and the high cost of commercial clerodane standards. Commercial standards (ecdysterone, makisterone A, cyasterone) were only used at a maximum of 100 ppm, which is very low compared to the 250,000 ppm concentration in the crude leaf extract and phytoecdysteroid fraction treatments, limiting direct concentration-by-concentration comparison. S. littoralis was not deterred from feeding by 20-hydroxyecdysone at 50-70 mg/kg (Jones and Firn 1978), in contrast to what was expected for phytoecdysteroid activity. The study used only three concentrations of crude extract, and the effect of clerodanes was not assessed separately. Tanaka reported altered epidermal sensitivity at 300 ppm ecdysone, which is higher than the standard concentration used in this study, potentially confounding the interpretation of standard vs. extract effects. No long-term field trials or multigenetic studies were conducted to confirm the persistence of effects across generations.

Claims
Crude methanolic leaf extract of Ajuga iva significantly inhibits the growth, survival, and development of Spodoptera littoralis larvae. First instar mortality was 25%, 65%, 85% at 50, 100, 250 µg/µl, versus 5% control Third instar LWG was reduced with F-values above 13, p < 0.001 RGR decreased by 0.20 g/g/day on day 8 at highest concentration No treated third instar larvae survived beyond 8-10 days S. littoralis was not deterred from feeding by commercial ecdysterone at 50-70 mg/kg Commercial standards at 100 ppm showed no significant effect Ajuga iva crude extracts could be developed as a natural insecticide or IPM component The effects are dose-dependent and consistent across multiple larval instars
The three phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, cyasterone) in Ajuga iva are the primary drivers of the insecticidal activity. The fractionated mixture at 250 µg/µl significantly reduced RGR (F2.20, 18 = 6.172, p = 0.001) Few larvae survived on the purified fraction (X2,3 = 11.305, p = 0.04) TLC showed Rf values of the three isolated phytoecdysteroids similar to commercial standards Commercial standards at 100 ppm (very low) did not produce effects, but this doesn't disprove the 250,000 ppm fraction The phytoecdysteroids target developmental and gut integrity specifically in lepidopterans
Phytoecdysteroids cause gut histolysis and actin filament disruption, contributing to reduced growth and mortality. Guts showed smaller actin filaments and reduced their amount compared to control Nuclei were smaller, abnormally shaped, and moved to the edges of the cell Gut cells showed histolysis with clear signs of apoptosis The paper does not directly correlate gut damage to systemic hormonal disruption with causal evidence (it is inferred) Gut damage leads to reduced LWG and weight-dependent pupation failure

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study tested the treatment order (crude then control vs. control then crude), confirming the effect is not a transient exposure but persistent metabolic disruption The purified phytoecdysteroid mixture was tested separately from the crude extract to isolate the effect of these compounds Statistical robustness: used t-tests for first instar, mixed-model ANOVA (repeated and two-way) for RGR, Friedman test for survival, and repeated measures ANOVA for LWG The experiment included a control group (ddH2O and Tween 20) to isolate the effect of the extract

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows TLC comparison of the three isolated phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, cyasterone) with commercial standards Figure 2a presents first instar survival: 25, 65, 85% mortality at 50, 100, 250 µg/µl crude extract versus 5% in control Figure 2b shows third instar LWG with F-values 20.334, 17.246, 13.007 (p < 0.001) for the three crude extract concentrations Figure 3a illustrates RGR reduction over 8 days, with decreases of 0.05 and 0.20 g/g/day at 250 µg/µl (F3.16, 18 = 12.641, p < 0.001) Figure 3b shows third instar survival: 100% in control versus 0% in crude extract after 8 days (highest concentration) and 10 days (other concentrations) Figure 4 illustrates reversed treatment order: control for 4 days then crude for 4 days, showing RGR reduction starting after day 5 (F3.16, 18 = 7.310, p < 0.001) and no survivors (X2,3 = 9.282, p = 0.021) Figure 4c shows the reverse order: crude for 4 days then control for 4 days, with RGR decreasing on days 2-4 (F3.16, 18 = 4.595, 3.608, 8.113; p = 0.034, 0.02, 0.001) Figure 5a shows RGR reduction by 250 µg/µl phytoecdysteroid mixture (F2.20, 18 = 6.172, p = 0.001) Figure 5b shows survival on the purified phytoecdysteroid fraction (X2,3 = 11.305, p = 0.04) Figure 6 presents confocal images of gut cells with DAPI (nuclei) and phalloidin (actin) in control versus 250 µg/µl crude and purified phytoecdysteroid treatments Figure 7 shows pupation: larvae fed 250 µg/µl crude or fraction for 8 days were unable to pupate after 15 days, with incomplete pupae showing short limbs and small heads

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first demonstration that Ajuga iva crude leaf extract and its purified phytoecdysteroid fraction (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, cyasterone) significantly reduce Spodoptera littoralis growth, survival, and pupation through a dose-dependent, metabolic mechanism. 2. The strongest evidence is the reversal experiment, showing RGR reduction starting after day 5 (F3.16, 18 = 7.310, p < 0.001) even when control diet was given first, and zero survival by day 8, confirming the effect is not due to initial feeding but to the extract components. 3. The future path involves characterizing the clerodanes (which were not isolated due to protocol difficulties), confirming the full synergistic role of Ajuga iva compounds, and evaluating longer-term IPM applications including multigenetic and field-scale assessments.

summary.authors: Russell J Gray
summary.field_subfield: Bibliometrics / Scientometrics; Open Access Publishing in Natural Sciences
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the relationship between Article Processing Charges (APC), Impact Factor (IF), Eigen Factor (EF), citability, and publisher country within the ecosystem of Golden Open Access (GOA) natural science journals. The author collected metadata from 237 vetted open-access natural science journals, extracting APCs, IF, EF, citation counts, and publisher countries. Using R statistical software and Pearson correlation analysis, the study found significant positive linear trends: APC is positively correlated with IF (r = 0.391, p < .001), EF (r = 0.303, p < .001), and citability (r = 0.323, p < .001). Furthermore, journals published in developed countries exhibited systematically higher APC, IF, EF, and citability compared to those in developing countries. The author argues that these findings demonstrate a structural inequality: high-impact publication is effectively pay-walled, favoring well-funded Western institutions and researchers while disadvantaging those in developing countries or without institutional affiliations. The author contextualizes this within the broader debate on GOA sustainability, noting that high APCs do not guarantee research reliability (citing Brembs, 2018) and that funding assistance mechanisms (e.g., Research4Life) contain exclusionary criteria that penalize international collaborations. The paper concludes that the GOA model risks prioritizing publisher profit and institutional prestige over equitable global scientific recognition, potentially burying important research (e.g., on endangered species) due to financial barriers.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the relationship between Article Processing Charges (APC), Impact Factor (IF), Eigen Factor (EF), citability, and publisher country within the ecosystem of Golden Open Access (GOA) natural science journals. The author collected metadata from 237 vetted open-access natural science journals, extracting APCs, IF, EF, citation counts, and publisher countries. Using R statistical software and Pearson correlation analysis, the study found significant positive linear trends: APC is positively correlated with IF (r = 0.391, p < .001), EF (r = 0.303, p < .001), and citability (r = 0.323, p < .001). Furthermore, journals published in developed countries exhibited systematically higher APC, IF, EF, and citability compared to those in developing countries. The author argues that these findings demonstrate a structural inequality: high-impact publication is effectively pay-walled, favoring well-funded Western institutions and researchers while disadvantaging those in developing countries or without institutional affiliations. The author contextualizes this within the broader debate on GOA sustainability, noting that high APCs do not guarantee research reliability (citing Brembs, 2018) and that funding assistance mechanisms (e.g., Research4Life) contain exclusionary criteria that penalize international collaborations. The paper concludes that the GOA model risks prioritizing publisher profit and institutional prestige over equitable global scientific recognition, potentially burying important research (e.g., on endangered species) due to financial barriers.

Research Context
The rise of Black (Sci-Hub) and Green (ResearchGate) Open Access has largely nullified the previous paywall system's ability to generate capital for journals. Many high-impact journals have transitioned to mandatory Golden Open Access to maintain profitability through scientific publication. The cost associated with publishing in open-access journals creates a problematic system of perceived reliability and importance linked to price. Previous evidence (Ellers et al., 2017) showed researchers from developing countries pay full developed-nation prices for high-impact "Mega-Journals." The alternative for unfunded researchers is publishing in lower IF journals, predatory journals, or questionable articles that impact credibility by affiliation. High-impact journals provide career acceleration through increased exposure via citations, making price barriers more consequential for researchers without funding. Despite the genuine concept of open-access science, the costly limitations of the GOA framework create substantial barriers to equitable publication.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is to determine the links between publication costs (APC), impact factor (IF), eigen factor (EF), and citability for journals in the natural sciences. The study also examines whether the country of publisher introduces disparities in APC, IF, EF, and citability. The implied hypothesis is that APC is positively associated with all quality metrics (IF, EF, citability), creating an unequal publication landscape. A secondary hypothesis is that journals from developed countries will exhibit systematically higher metrics across all four variables compared to those in developing countries. The study predicted that with increasing publishing costs, the impact, importance, and overall citation counts would also increase. The authors predicted that this would reveal structural inequality where publishers from developed countries have an advantage over those in developing countries.

Methodological Details
Data was acquired from the Directory of Open Access Journals (Morrison, 2008), yielding initial records of journal name, APC, country of publisher, and currency (n = 14275). A subset of journals (n = 1047) with biological science topics was identified via keyword querying (ecology, conservation, agriculture, species, forest, etc.). To address disparities between natural and medical sciences, journals with an IF >40 were excluded from the analysis. Excluded journals were verified via keywords to confirm they related to oncology, medical, and engineering rather than natural sciences. The final analysis used a deeply vetted dataset of open-access, natural science journals comprising 237 entries. R statistical software was used for all analyses, utilizing the scholar package for IF generation, quantmod for currency conversion to USD, dplyr and reshape2 for data cleaning, and ggplot2 for visualization. All currencies were standardized to USD for consistent comparison across international publishers. Pearson's correlation coefficient, accessed through ggpubr functions, was used to analyze correlations between APC, IF, EF, and citability. The country of publisher was separately examined against cost, citability, IF, and EF to locate disparities.

Procedures And Architectures
The initial data frame of 14,275 journal records was filtered by keywords (ecology, conservation, agriculture, species, forest, etc.) to identify biological science journals. The subset of 1,047 biological journals was further filtered: any journal with an Impact Factor exceeding 40 was removed to eliminate medical and engineering outliers. The author manually vetted the remaining journals to ensure all 237 belonged to natural sciences before running final analyses. Impact Factors were generated using journal name strings via the scholar package. All APC values were normalized to USD using the quantmod package for standardization across international currencies. Data cleaning, selection, and transformation were performed using dplyr and reshape2. Pearson's correlation analysis was conducted to assess the strength and significance of linear relationships between APC and IF, EF, and citability. Country-level subgroup analysis was performed to compare metric distributions between developed and developing country publishers. Visualizations were created using ggplot2 for exploring trends.

Key Results
A linear trend was found between IF, EF, and citability in relation to APC, indicating higher costs correlate with higher perceived impact. Journal publishers from developed countries were found to be more likely to have higher APC, IF, EF, and citability than those in developing countries. The mean APC across the 237 analyzed open-access journals was $1,344.27 USD. The mean Impact Factor (IF) of the analyzed journals was 2.855. The mean Eigen Factor (EF) was 0.017. The mean total citation count (citability) was 5925.92. APC was significantly positively correlated with IF, with a Pearson correlation of r(237) = 0.391 (p < .001). There was a highly significant positive correlation between APC and EF, with r(237) = 0.303 (p < .001). There was a highly significant positive correlation between APC and citability, with r(237) = 0.323 (p < .001). All three correlation coefficients were statistically significant at the p < .001 level, confirming the linear trends.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The data demonstrates that with increasing publishing costs, the impact, importance, and overall citations in open-access natural science journals also increase. Higher APC in prestigious journals is not linked to the reliability of the research published within them, according to Brembs (2018). The Impact Factor of prestigious journals creates a false perception of reliability in the research they publish, a phenomenon identified by Brembs (2013). The GOA paradox suggests that the more manuscripts a journal publishes, the more capital it generates, giving rise to predatory journals and editorial complacency. GOA journals may prioritize publisher profit over scientific integrity while maintaining prestige as credible outlets, creating a dual-standard environment. Irregular distribution of resources creates a bubble where higher-ranking institutions have access to expensive, higher-impact journals while lower-ranking institutions are forced into less expensive or closed-access journals. The current GOA framework promotes the false ideology that prestige and costliness of journal publications are equivalent to reliable science. The findings suggest that important research (e.g., on tropical biodiversity) may be sidelined due to APC funding constraints and exclusionary assistance criteria.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study relies on metadata from a single source (DOAJ), and while 237 journals are a substantial sample, it represents a specific subset of natural science GOA journals. The study is descriptive and correlational; Pearson's correlation cannot establish causality between APC and impact metrics. The author notes that APC funding assistance (e.g., Research4Life) has caveats—naming a developed-country collaborator can void eligibility, creating an arbitrary exclusionary rule. The author's personal experience (rejection from funding while publishing on Sumatran elephant research) introduces a self-reported anecdotal element that supports the discussion but is not a systematic finding of the study. The exclusion of journals with IF >40, while necessary to isolate natural sciences from medical/engineering, may omit relevant high-impact cross-disciplinary journals. The paper does not report the full distribution of publishers by country (only the direction of inequality), limiting granular geographic insights. Random seeds, specific R script parameters, and confidence intervals for the mean estimates are not reported, limiting reproducibility.

Claims
GOA journal publication costs (APC) are positively and significantly correlated with perceived prestige metrics (IF, EF) and actual citation impact (citability), confirming that higher fees buy higher impact. APC was significantly positively correlated with IF (r = 0.391, p < .001). APC had a highly significant positive correlation with EF (r = 0.303, p < .001). APC had a highly significant positive correlation with citability (r = 0.323, p < .001). Publishers from developed countries had higher APC, IF, EF, and citability. Brembs (2018) explicitly argues that expensive APC in prestigious journals are not linked to the reliability of the research published in them. Brembs (2013) indicates the Impact Factor itself creates a false perception of reliability rather than reflecting actual scientific quality. Higher APC acts as a structural barrier, favoring well-funded institutions and creating a two-tier system of global research exposure. Researchers without institutional affiliation have increasingly narrow options, impacting the quality and visibility of independent scientific output.
The GOA funding assistance model (e.g., Research4Life) contains exclusionary criteria that penalize international collaborations and individual researchers from developed countries without institutional affiliation, regardless of the quality of their research. Naming an international collaborator from a developed country as an author on a manuscript voids eligibility for financial assistance. The author's personal experience confirmed rejection from funding despite having eligible developing-country co-authors and no access to >$1000 for fees. Options for individual researchers without institutional affiliation are increasingly narrow. The author acknowledges that many financial support options do exist for GOA journals, with the limitations being caveats to eligibility. Important research on critically endangered species (e.g., tropical biodiversity) may fly under the academic radar due to APC funding constraints. Authors may be forced to remove collaborators from manuscripts to gain access to publication funds, a practice the author argues should not exist.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The author manually checked excluded journals (IF >40) via keywords to confirm they were related to oncology, medical, and engineering rather than natural sciences. A subset of 1,047 journals was initially queried, and the final analysis used the 237-journal deeply vetted dataset, representing a multi-stage filtering process. Currency conversion to USD was applied via the quantmod package to standardize APC values for cross-country comparison.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 displays the relationship between publisher country and the four metrics (APC, IF, EF, citability), showing that developed countries have higher values across all four.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the empirical demonstration that APC, IF, EF, and citability are positively correlated in GOA natural science journals, with developed-country publishers capturing a disproportionate share of prestige and visibility. 2. The strongest evidence is the triple significant correlation (p < .001) across all four metrics, coupled with the descriptive finding that mean APC is $1,344.27 USD while mean IF is 2.855, with all positive correlations confirmed. 3. The future path calls for addressing structural inequalities in the GOA publishing model to create a more inclusive environment where important research is recognized regardless of country or institutional affiliation.

summary.title: Highly sensitive and full-genome interrogation of SARS-CoV-2 using multiplexed PCR enrichment followed by next-generation sequencing
summary.authors: Chenyu Li, David N Debruyne, Julia Spencer, Vidushi Kapoor, Lily Y Liu, Bo Zhou, Utsav Pandey, Moiz Bootwalla, Dejerianne Ostrow, Dennis T Maglinte, David Ruble, Alex Ryutov, Lishuang Shen, Lucie Lee, Rounak Feigelman, Grayson Burdon, Jeffrey Liu, Alejandra Oliva, Adam Borcherding, Hongdong Tan, Alexander E Urban, Xiaowu Gai, Jennifer Dien Bard, Guoying Liu, Zhitong Liu
summary.field_subfield: Genomics / Molecular Diagnostics / COVID-19 Surveillance
summary.type_of_paper: Methodological development with validation in clinical specimens
summary.executive_summary: This study describes the development and validation of a highly sensitive multiplex PCR-based detection assay for SARS-CoV-2, designed to overcome the sensitivity limitations of standard RT-PCR which has been reported to identify only 47-59% of positive cases. The method utilizes 343 pairs of specific primers (two overlapping pools of 172 pairs) to simultaneously amplify hundreds of genomic targets, achieving a theoretical limit of detection of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. The assay was validated using S and N gene plasmids spiked into human cDNA, demonstrating detection from 8,900 down to 2.8 copies with a wide dynamic range and uniform amplicon recovery. The multiplex PCR products were confirmed by electrophoresis and further amplified for Illumina MiSeq sequencing. Thirteen nasopharyngeal swab specimens (viral loads 8–675,885 copies/uL) were fully sequenced, achieving 95-99% genome coverage at 100X depth with sequencing depths as low as 50,000 reads. Mutations including the D614G variant were identified across all specimens, and intra-host heterogeneity was characterized. A parallel metagenomic multiplex PCR method using random hexamer-adapters was developed, achieving >96% SARS-CoV-2 genome coverage with ~0.6M total reads per library without host depletion, demonstrating potential for detecting novel or emerging pathogens with moderate sequencing depth.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study describes the development and validation of a highly sensitive multiplex PCR-based detection assay for SARS-CoV-2, designed to overcome the sensitivity limitations of standard RT-PCR which has been reported to identify only 47-59% of positive cases. The method utilizes 343 pairs of specific primers (two overlapping pools of 172 pairs) to simultaneously amplify hundreds of genomic targets, achieving a theoretical limit of detection of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. The assay was validated using S and N gene plasmids spiked into human cDNA, demonstrating detection from 8,900 down to 2.8 copies with a wide dynamic range and uniform amplicon recovery. The multiplex PCR products were confirmed by electrophoresis and further amplified for Illumina MiSeq sequencing. Thirteen nasopharyngeal swab specimens (viral loads 8–675,885 copies/uL) were fully sequenced, achieving 95-99% genome coverage at 100X depth with sequencing depths as low as 50,000 reads. Mutations including the D614G variant were identified across all specimens, and intra-host heterogeneity was characterized. A parallel metagenomic multiplex PCR method using random hexamer-adapters was developed, achieving >96% SARS-CoV-2 genome coverage with ~0.6M total reads per library without host depletion, demonstrating potential for detecting novel or emerging pathogens with moderate sequencing depth.

Research Context
RT-PCR is the gold standard but only identifies 47-59% of true positive cases. Low viral load, sampling timing, RNA degradation, and mutations span primer binding sites limit detection. Heat inactivation of clinical samples may further reduce downstream diagnostic efficiency. NGS of the full-length viral genome is essential for surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 evolution. The assay must distinguish SARS-CoV-2 from other respiratory pathogens including influenza, adenovirus, and MERS-CoV. Prior studies show standard RT-PCR targets Orf1ab, E and N genes with 4-8 copy LOD at 95% confidence.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can multiplex PCR targeting hundreds of regions simultaneously improve LOD compared to standard RT-PCR? The multiplex PCR strategy is hypothesized to detect nucleotide fragments from degraded viral genomes and tolerate genomic variations. A mathematical model was built to estimate the RT-PCR LOD under 99% efficiency and 100bp amplicon length. The hypothesis was that increasing the number of simultaneously amplified targets would raise the frequency of detection in the mathematical model. A second question asks whether a multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method can uncover mutational diversity with modest sequencing depth. The predicted outcome is a detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability when using both primer pools.

Methodological Details
The assay was designed with 343 pairs of specific primers in two pools. Each pool contained 172 pairs with an average amplicon length of 99bp. Amplicons spanned the entire genome with an average gap of 76±10bp. Validation used two plasmids containing the S and N genes of SARS-CoV-2. Plasmids were spiked into cDNA generated from human total RNA. Copy numbers were determined by droplet-based digital PCR (ddPCR) using a Bio-Rad QX200. The viral load of 13 specimens ranged from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/uL. Sequencing was performed on an Illumina MiSeq platform. A mathematical model used a 29,903bp genome and 100bp amplicon length. The metamagnomic assay used random hexamer-adapters for amplification. A metagenomic library was prepared from 4,500 copies of N and S gene plasmids in 10 ng human gDNA. Mutations were detected by two independently developed algorithms. Mutation cutoff was set at >60% allele frequency for empirically true mutations. Intra-host mutations were filtered with a 20% allele frequency threshold.

Procedures And Architectures
The workflow involved multiplex PCR followed by a secondary PCR for sample indexing and sequencing primer addition. PCR products were first analyzed by high-resolution electrophoresis to visualize target peaks. For the metagenomic method, Paragon Genomics' background removal reagent and reverse transcription reagents were used. The multiplex PCR was performed, and library peaks were assessed for defined size distribution. Sequencing was performed as paired-end reads with typical depths of 1,000 reads per amplicon. Sub-sampling of 5 genomes to 150,000 and 100,000 total reads was performed to test minimal depth. The mathematical model assumed 6% amplification efficiency for single-stranded cDNA. It was further assumed that 80% of targeted regions would be amplified successfully. The metagenomic method required no additional host depletion to remove human gDNA or rRNA. The two primer pools overlapped, with the second pool targeting the gaps of the first. The 28 amplicons from the S and N gene plasmids were simultaneously targeted in the 172-amplicon panel.

Key Results
The RT-PCR mathematical model predicted a LOD of 4.8 copies at 95% probability with 99% efficiency. The RT-PCR predicted detection probability for one copy was only 26%. The 172-primer pool estimated a LOD of 1.15 copies at 95% probability. Both pools together yielded a calculated LOD of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. Plasmid library peaks were obtained from 8,900 down to 2.8 copies. Quantification showed a dynamic range from 1 to about 1,000 plasmid copies. The yield saturated when the copy number reached 1,700. RT-PCR detected a single target on the S gene rapidly dropped at 2.85 copies. Experimental observation yielded a 56% probability to detect 1.1 copies, exceeding the 12% theoretical prediction. Approximately 96% of amplicons were recovered at 14 copies, 77% at 2.8 copies, and 37% at 0.6 copies. About 95% of the genome was covered at 100X for 8 copies of virus. 98-99% of the genomes were covered at 100X for 22 to 675,885 copies at 5,000 reads per amplicon. One genome with 5,000 viral copies had 96% coverage at 100X, lower than expected. At 150,000 total reads, 93% of the genome was covered at 100X. At 100,000 total reads, 86% of the genome was covered at 100X. At 50,000 total reads per library, at least 58% was covered at 100X. 16% of recovered bases (13% of reads) were within the N and S genes in the metagenomic sample. 80% of SARS-CoV-2 and 78% of mitochondrial targets were covered in the metagenomic assay. Only 0.08% of human chromosomal regions were amplified in the metagenomic method. Optimization improved SARS-CoV-2 genome recovery to 96% in the metagenomic method. 0% of sequencing reads from the 13 samples aligned to MERS-CoV, CoV 229E, CoV OC43, CoV NL63, or CoV HKU1. The D614G mutation was found in 11 of 13 specimens. Mutations with %AF ≤ 60% were considered intra-host heterogeneity.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Multiplex PCR is more sensitive than RT-PCR because it simultaneously targets and amplifies hundreds of genomic regions, increasing detection frequency. The multiplex strategy tolerates mutations and can detect degraded viral fragments by providing alternative targets. The observed 56% experimental detection of 1.1 copies suggests the true single-stranded cDNA amplification efficiency is higher than the assumed 6%. The 0% cross-reactivity with other coronaviruses demonstrates the panel's high specificity for SARS-CoV-2. The clustered mutations at 7 loci likely reflect community transmission or close geographic clustering of the specimens. Intra-host mutations at low copy numbers with low read depth may be false positives caused by PCR noise or sequencing artifacts. Increasing sequencing depth alone may not improve coverage beyond the 10-fold difference routinely observed with this technology. The metagenomic method's >96% coverage with only 0.6M reads exceeds the 50% recommended threshold for genome drafting. The preferential amplification of 'random' base regions and human exonic regions suggests a selection bias of the hexamer strategy.

Contradictions And Limitations
A 20% allele frequency cutoff might miss true intra-host mutations occurring below that threshold. Absence of UMIs in the multiplex PCR means intra-host mutations may be contaminated with PCR and sequencing noise. Low viral copy number inputs and low read depth per amplicon can reduce allele frequency and introduce false mutations. One 5,000-copy specimen showed only 96% coverage at 100X, which was lower than expected. Fluorometry or spectrophotometry alone cannot differentiate target amplicons from primer dimers. The metamagnomic method's coverage was obtained without host depletion, potentially limiting sensitivity in host-rich samples. The authors caution that copy number and sequencing depth should be cautiously considered when low %AF mutations are reported.

Claims
The multiplex PCR assay provides a higher sensitivity limit of detection than standard RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2. The mathematical model predicted a 0.29-copy LOD using both primer pools versus 4.8 copies for RT-PCR. Experimental detection of plasmid library peaks down to 2.8 copies was achieved. The 172-primer pool alone predicted a LOD of 1.15 copies. The observed experimental detection was limited to 2.8 copies, not the predicted 0.29 copies. RT-PCR continues to identify 47-59% of positive cases in practice. The method could potentially detect SARS-CoV-2 in samples previously called negative by RT-PCR. The assay's robustness makes it suitable for low viral load scenarios.
The metagenomic multiplex PCR method achieves near-full SARS-CoV-2 genome coverage with modest sequencing depth without host depletion. 96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome was recovered with ~0.6M reads per library. Only 0.6M total reads per library were required, well below standard metagenomic requirements. 80% of SARS-CoV-2 and 78% of mitochondrial targets were covered without host depletion. The 10-fold coverage difference suggests increasing sequencing depth may not further improve targeted region coverage. Only 0.08% of human chromosomal regions were amplified, reflecting partial bias. The method is potentially cost-effective for surveillance compared to standard metagenomics. It could identify novel or emerging isolates with moderate sequencing depth.
The panel is highly specific for SARS-CoV-2 and does not cross-react with other human coronaviruses. 0% of sequencing reads aligned to MERS-CoV, CoV 229E, CoV OC43, CoV NL63, or CoV HKU1. Primers were specifically designed for the SARS-CoV-2 genome to avoid cross amplification. The authors acknowledge that primers could potentially amplify other coronaviruses due to shared sequence similarities. The panel could be expanded to include simultaneous detection of other respiratory viruses. High specificity supports its use in diverse clinical and surveillance settings.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Sub-sampling analysis of 5 genomes to 150,000 and 100,000 reads confirmed minimal depth requirements for mutation detection. The mathematical model was tested against a single-copy plasmid input, revealing that the experimental 56% detection probability was significantly higher than the 12% theoretical prediction. Two independent algorithms were used for mutation calling, with only mutations detected by both reported. Mutation allele frequency cutoffs (20%, 60%) were selected and validated against synthetic controls. The metagenomic method was optimized to improve SARS-CoV-2 genome recovery to 96%. A coverage correlation with viral copy number was assessed across 13 specimens.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the RT-PCR mathematical model predicting 4.8 copies LOD at 95% probability. Figure 1B depicts the two overlapping pools of 172 multiplex PCR primer pairs covering the genome. Figure 1C shows the predicted LOD of 1.15 copies for the 172-amplicon panel. Figure 1D outlines the experimental workflow from multiplex PCR to secondary PCR and sequencing. Figure 2A shows electrophoresis library peaks from 8,900 down to 2.8 plasmid copies. Figure 2B shows the dynamic range of peak quantification from 1 to 1,000 plasmid copies. Figure 2C shows the experimental 56% detection probability for 1.1 copies versus theoretical predictions. Figure 2D shows recovered read depth and GC distribution for plasmid libraries. Figure 2E shows the fraction of amplicons recovered at different plasmid copy numbers. Figure 3A shows genome coverage versus viral copy number for the 13 specimens. Figure 3B shows genome coverage at 100X versus total reads per library. Figure 3C shows the uniformity of amplicons amplified and recovered. Figure 3D shows the log10 distance of each amplicon to the mean. Figure 3E shows the clustering of mutations at 7 loci and intra-host heterogeneity. Figure 4A shows the fraction of recovered bases in the metagenomic library. Figure 4B shows SARS-CoV-2 and mitochondrial target coverage in the metagenomic assay. Figure 4C shows base coverage of viral vs human targets. Figure 4D shows the preferential amplification of human exonic regions. Figure 4E shows long gaps in human chromosomes. Figure 4F shows shorter gaps in SARS-CoV-2 and mitochondrial regions. Figure 4G shows the optimized 96% SARS-CoV-2 genome recovery in the metagenomic assay.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a multiplex PCR assay with 343 specific primer pairs that achieves a theoretical LOD of 0.29 copies at 95% probability, significantly improving upon standard RT-PCR's ~4.8 copy LOD. 2. The strongest evidence is the demonstrated detection of the full SARS-CoV-2 genome from 8 to 675,885 copies/uL in 13 clinical specimens, with 95-99% coverage at 100X depth and 0% cross-reactivity with other coronaviruses. 3. The future path involves expanding the panel for simultaneous detection of other respiratory viruses (e.g., influenza) and applying the metagenomic multiplex PCR method for surveillance of novel or emerging pathogens with moderate sequencing depth (~0.6M reads).

summary.title: Translational accuracy of a tethered ribosome
summary.authors: Celine Fabret (CNRS); Olivier Namy (CNRS)
summary.field_subfield: Molecular Biology / Ribosome Dynamics / Translational Fidelity
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the translational accuracy of Ribo-T, a tethered ribosome in Escherichia coli where the 30S and 50S subunits are covalently linked via a hybrid rRNA construct. Previously reported as functional and sustaining cell growth with a 107-minute doubling time (vs. 35 min wild-type), Ribo-T exhibits a 50% reduced protein synthesis rate, attributed to slower biogenesis rather than impaired activity. The authors tested Ribo-T against three recoding signals: -1 and +1 frameshifting, stop codon readthrough, and internal translation initiation. Surprisingly, Ribo-T maintains wild-type levels of -1 frameshifting (13–14%) regardless of the SD sequence, indicating insensitivity to SD-ASD interactions during elongation. In contrast, +1 frameshifting is severely impaired (2% vs. 33% WT), and Ribo-T ribosomes use SD sequences for initiation and frameshifting significantly less efficiently than wild-type. Stop codon readthrough is moderately impaired (0.04–0.07% vs. 0.01–0.11% WT), suggesting a slight defect in stop codon recognition. The authors propose that tethering via helix 44 alters the geometric orientation of the anti-Shine-Dalgarno sequence, disrupting the conformational dynamics required for SD-mediated signals and proper termination factor binding. The study demonstrates that ribosomal subunit mobility is not strictly required for core translational functions but modulates fidelity at specific checkpoints.
