summary.title: Spontaneous regression of micro-metastases following primary tumor excision: a critical role for primary tumor secretome
summary.authors: Shaashua Lee; Anabel Eckerling; Boaz Israeli; Gali Yanovich; Ella Rosenne; Suzana Fichman-Horn; Ido Ben Zvi; Liat Sorski; Ronit Satchi-Fainaro; Tamar Geiger; Erica K Sloan; Shamgar Ben-Eliyahu
summary.field_subfield: Cancer Biology / Metastasis Research / Systems Oncology
summary.type_of_paper: Original Research Article with In Vivo Animal Model and Retrospective Patient Data
summary.executive_summary: This study presents the first animal model demonstrating spontaneous regression of micro-metastases following surgical excision of the primary tumor (PT) in breast cancer, identifying the PT-derived secretome as a critical mediator of early metastatic growth. Using MDA-MB-231 HM human breast cancer cells expressing highly sensitive luciferase transduced into BALB/c nu/nu mice, the authors monitored early-stage metastatic progression (2-4 weeks post-injection) via bioluminescence imaging. Upon PT excision when metastases reached a total flux of 10^6 photons/s, metastatic signal decreased up to 100-fold within 24 hours (p<0.0001), while H&E histology confirmed regression of malignant foci on day 1 and day 50 post-excision. Regression was significantly less prominent in larger metastases (10^7 photons/sec) versus smaller ones (10^6 photons/sec), (p<0.000), indicating the phenomenon is restricted to early metastatic stages. Sham surgery (PT untouched) did not elicit regression (p<0.05), confirming the effect is tied to PT removal rather than surgical trauma. In vitro, tumor-cell conditioned medium (CM) enhanced cancer cell viability (p<0.001), adhesion (p<0.01), and induced HUVEC tube formation (p<0.0001). In vivo replenishment of the PT secretome via osmotic minipumps (CM vs serum-free medium) reduced metastatic regression 10-fold (p<0.005). Proteomic and cytokine array analyses identified four key secreted factors—IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF—whose in vivo neutralization completely arrested metastatic progression (p<0.0001). Retrospective analysis of the public TCGA lung adenocarcinoma dataset corroborated that high protein levels of these four factors were associated with significantly lower survival (hazard ratio 2.05, p<0.05). The study establishes that the PT secretome supports micro-metastases in their early development and proposes targeting these factors during the perioperative window as a strategy to control minimal residual disease.

claims.description: Primary tumor excision induces spontaneous regression of early-stage micro-metastases by eliminating PT-derived pro-metastatic secretome factors.
IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF are the four key PT-secreted factors promoting early metastatic growth.
The phenomenon of spontaneous metastatic regression post-PT excision may occur in a substantial portion of cancer patients but remains undetected due to limited detection sensitivity.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents the first animal model demonstrating spontaneous regression of micro-metastases following surgical excision of the primary tumor (PT) in breast cancer, identifying the PT-derived secretome as a critical mediator of early metastatic growth. Using MDA-MB-231 HM human breast cancer cells expressing highly sensitive luciferase transduced into BALB/c nu/nu mice, the authors monitored early-stage metastatic progression (2-4 weeks post-injection) via bioluminescence imaging. Upon PT excision when metastases reached a total flux of 10^6 photons/s, metastatic signal decreased up to 100-fold within 24 hours (p<0.0001), while H&E histology confirmed regression of malignant foci on day 1 and day 50 post-excision. Regression was significantly less prominent in larger metastases (10^7 photons/sec) versus smaller ones (10^6 photons/sec), (p<0.000), indicating the phenomenon is restricted to early metastatic stages. Sham surgery (PT untouched) did not elicit regression (p<0.05), confirming the effect is tied to PT removal rather than surgical trauma. In vitro, tumor-cell conditioned medium (CM) enhanced cancer cell viability (p<0.001), adhesion (p<0.01), and induced HUVEC tube formation (p<0.0001). In vivo replenishment of the PT secretome via osmotic minipumps (CM vs serum-free medium) reduced metastatic regression 10-fold (p<0.005). Proteomic and cytokine array analyses identified four key secreted factors—IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF—whose in vivo neutralization completely arrested metastatic progression (p<0.0001). Retrospective analysis of the public TCGA lung adenocarcinoma dataset corroborated that high protein levels of these four factors were associated with significantly lower survival (hazard ratio 2.05, p<0.05). The study establishes that the PT secretome supports micro-metastases in their early development and proposes targeting these factors during the perioperative window as a strategy to control minimal residual disease.

Research Context
Surgical removal of the primary tumor is a cornerstone of cancer treatment, but it has been suggested to accelerate postoperative progression of minimal residual disease. Alternatively, various case studies report spontaneous postoperative regression of evident cancer metastasis across most cancer types, including breast and lung cancer. Postulated mechanisms for regression include surgical trauma or elimination of stimulating factors secreted by the primary tumor. However, postulated mechanisms have not been empirically tested, as no animal model of spontaneous regression exists. The current realization emphasizes that the presence of a primary tumor is a systemic disease with continuous crosstalk between the PT, its microenvironment, and distant organs. The need to study potential interactions between PT and metastases is stressed by disease etiology and progression.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether and how primary tumor excision induces spontaneous regression of metastases, and what secretome factors mediate this. The authors hypothesized that the primary tumor secretome supports the survival and growth of distant micro-metastases, and its elimination by surgery results in metastatic regression. A secondary hypothesis posited that regression is specific to early metastatic stages and that established larger metastatic foci may be self-sufficient. The study predicted that in vivo blockade of key PT-secreted factors would mimic the effect of PT removal and inhibit metastasis. The expected outcome was to identify specific secreted mediators and correlate their levels with poor patient survival in clinical cohorts.

Methodological Details
MDA-MB-231 HM cells, a highly metastatic variant of triple-negative breast adenocarcinoma, were transduced with a codon-optimized firefly luciferase-mCherry vector. Cells were cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% glutamax, 4.5 g/L D-glucose, and 110 mg/L sodium pyruvate at 37°C and 5% CO2. Eight-week-old female BALB/c nu/nu mice were injected with 2×10^5 cells in 20 μl PBS into the fourth mammary fat pad under 2% isoflurane anesthesia. Primary tumors were measured by caliper and volume calculated by (length × width^2) × 0.5. Metastases were assessed by bioluminescence imaging using an IVIS spectrum apparatus following i.p. injection of 150 mg/kg D-luciferin sodium salt. PT excision was performed when metastatic foci reached a total count of 10^6 photons/s, approximately 3-4 weeks post-injection, with an average PT volume of 80 mm^3. Sham surgery involved an identical incision with the PT untouched, and skin was immediately sutured. Tumor-cell conditioned medium (CM) was produced by incubating ~80% confluent cells with serum-free medium for 24 h at 37°C and 5% CO2. CM was concentrated to 100 μl/mouse using 3 kDa Amicon filters and stored at -20°C. Alzet osmotic minipumps (model 1003D) were loaded with CM or serum-free medium (SM) and implanted i.p. immediately following PT excision. CM was applied at a dose estimated as ~1/8 of the amount produced daily in vivo by the primary tumor. Adhesion studies used the IncuCyte system for 8 hours imaging at 20 min intervals in SM or CM. Apoptosis studies used AnnexinV-FITC and 7AAD staining followed by flow cytometry after 24 h incubation in CM or SM. Tube formation assays used 50 μl basement membrane extracellular matrix on 24-well plates with HUVEC seeded in CM or SM. Human Cytokine Array (102 soluble human proteins) compared CM, plasma from non-tumor bearing mice, PT-bearing mice, and mice 1 day post-excision. Mass spectrometry (LC-MS) used nano-ultra high performance liquid chromatography (Easy-nLC1000) and Q-Exactive Plus mass spectrometer. MS raw files were analyzed by MaxQuant with Label-free quantification algorithm, referenced to Uniprot human proteome with FDR 0.01. Enrichment analysis used Fisher exact test with FDR threshold of 0.02. Mouse anti-human monoclonal antibodies (1 μg each/mouse for 2 days) neutralized IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF, with IgG1 as isotype control. Lung micro-metastases were confirmed ex vivo by H&E staining of 6 μm sections and pathologist verification. Patient outcome was analyzed using the public TCGA provisional dataset (cBioPortal) for a lung adenocarcinoma cohort with RPPA assay protein levels. Statistical tests included repeated-measures or factorial ANOVA at p<0.05, Fisher's PLSD for post-hoc, and Student's t-tests for two conditions.

Procedures And Architectures
The in vivo model used the orthotopic mammary fat pad injection of luciferase-expressing cancer cells to generate primary tumors and spontaneous metastases in lymph nodes and lungs. Metastatic progression was monitored via IVIS bioluminescence imaging; PT excision was triggered at a threshold of 10^6 photons/s to isolate early-stage events. Following excision, the metastatic signal was assessed at 24 h, 50 days post-excision, and at endpoint (ex vivo imaging of lungs and lymph nodes 10 min post-luciferin). The CM replenishment strategy used Alzet osmotic minipumps to deliver a controlled, continuous dose of tumor secretome (100 μl/mouse) matching estimated daily production ratios. In vitro, cancer cells were seeded in SM or CM for adhesion (8 h) and apoptosis (24 h), and HUVEC were seeded in BME for tube formation (24 h), with IncuCyte imaging at 20 min intervals. The cytokine array compared 102 proteins across four conditions; plasma samples were pooled from 3 mice each. For LC-MS, CM was filtered, mixed 1:1 with 8M urea, digested with LysC/Trypsin mix overnight, and analyzed on a nano-UHPLC system with 140 min linear gradient. MS data analysis employed MaxQuant with the Andromeda search engine, String database for PPI networks, and Cytoscape for visualization. Antibody neutralization was performed with 1 μg of each of four anti-human monoclonal antibodies injected once daily for two days, 24 h prior to tumor excision at early metastatic stage. Patient data analysis used Kaplan-Meier survival curves and hazard ratios calculated in R software, stratifying by protein levels of the four identified factors.

Key Results
A dramatic decrease in metastatic signal, of up to 100-fold, was evident in mice along the 24 h following tumor excision (p<0.0001). No increase in in vivo bioluminescent signal occurred for 50 days post-excision, and microscopic malignant foci were evident on both day 1 and day 50 post-excision. Regression was significantly less prominent in larger metastases (10^7 photons/sec) compared to smaller metastases (10^6 photons/sec) (p<0.000). Metastases continued to increase in mice subjected to sham surgery (PT untouched), while regressed following excision (p<0.05). Tumor-cell conditioned medium enhanced cancer cell viability (p<0.001) and adhesion (p<0.01) compared to serum-free medium, and induced HUVEC tube formation (p<0.0001). Mice treated with tumor-cell conditioned medium via osmotic minipumps showed 10-fold less regression than mice receiving serum-free medium (p<0.005). The cytokine array identified 28 cytokines highly expressed in cancer cell CM; four were shortlisted: IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF. Mass spectrometry identified 2,600 proteins, of which 359 were annotated as extracellular factors by Gene Ontology. Antibody neutralization of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF completely blocked metastatic progression (p<0.0001). No difference in regression of metastases was evident between antibody-treated and IgG control groups on post-excision day-1, indicating excision completely removed secreted factors. In the TCGA lung adenocarcinoma cohort, high protein levels of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF were associated with significantly lower survival (hazard ratio 2.05, p<0.05).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The primary tumor secretome supports survival and growth of distant micro-metastases, and its surgical elimination results in metastatic regression of early-stage foci. Larger established metastatic foci may be self-sufficient, explaining why they do not regress upon PT excision. IL-8, MIF, SerpinE1, and PDGFaa likely promote metastases through shared and distinct pathways involving angiogenesis, apoptosis suppression, EMT, and focal adhesion. The perioperative period may be exploited to control minimal residual disease by blocking primary tumor support for micro-metastases and targeting prometastatic factors released by minimal residual disease. The findings explain the rare clinical phenomenon of spontaneous regression of metastases following PT excision. Tumor-secreted factors may act through multiple mechanisms affecting both malignant cells and/or their microenvironment.

Contradictions And Limitations
Larger metastases (10^7 photons/sec) showed lower or no regression, suggesting the phenomenon is limited to the earliest metastatic stages. Only a combined blockade of four key secreted factors was tested; other secreted factors are likely to also be involved in supporting metastatic progression. Different tumors, specifically syngeneic lines, should be studied to test the generalizability of the novel phenomenon observed in MDA-MB-231 HM xenografts. The prevalence of post-operative regression of micro-metastases in cancer patients is currently unknown due to technical limitations of detection sensitivity. The amount of secreted factors released by osmotic minipumps was estimated at ~1/8 of the in vivo production, introducing uncertainty in dose equivalency.

Claims
Primary tumor excision induces spontaneous regression of early-stage micro-metastases by eliminating PT-derived pro-metastatic secretome factors. Metastatic signal decreased up to 100-fold within 24 h of PT excision (p<0.0001). No in vivo bioluminescent signal increase was observed for 50 days post-excision. Sham surgery with PT untouched showed continued metastatic increase, confirming excision as the causal event (p<0.05). Larger metastases (10^7 photons/sec) showed significantly less regression (p<0.000). No difference in regression was seen on post-excision day-1 between antibody-treated and IgG control groups. The perioperative window can be exploited for targeting minimal residual disease. Tailored combination of neutralizing antibodies could counteract metastasis-promoting effects of surgery.
IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF are the four key PT-secreted factors promoting early metastatic growth. Antibody neutralization of all four factors completely blocked metastatic progression (p<0.0001). TCGA analysis showed high protein levels of all four factors associated with significantly lower survival (HR 2.05, p<0.05). Pathway enrichment identified proteins engaged in apoptosis, angiogenesis, focal adhesion, and metalloenzyme regulation. Only the combined effect was tested; individual factor contributions were not disambiguated. Identifying critical pro-metastatic factors based on malignant tissue biopsy before surgery may enable individually tailored antibody therapy.
The phenomenon of spontaneous metastatic regression post-PT excision may occur in a substantial portion of cancer patients but remains undetected due to limited detection sensitivity. Case studies report regression documented in most types of cancer, including breast and lung. High-sensitive luciferase enabled detection of early-stage regression that presumably would not be detected under lower sensitivity. Regression is rare and may be limited to the smallest micro-metastases. Analyses of serum samples before and after PT resection may suggest specific mediating factors in individual patients.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A sham surgery control (PT untouched) negated surgical trauma as a mechanism of regression. The large vs small metastasis comparison (10^7 vs 10^6 photons/sec) demonstrated that regression is stage-specific. CM vs SM in osmotic minipumps demonstrated 10-fold less regression with CM (p<0.005), validating the secretome's role. The cytokine array vs proteomics approach used a complementary identification strategy: first narrow down to 4 known factors, then unbiased MS of 2,600 proteins.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A-B shows metastatic signal decrease of up to 100-fold within 24 h of PT excision (p<0.0001). Figure 1C shows no in vivo bioluminescent signal increase for 50 days post-excision. Figure 1D shows H&E confirmation of malignant foci on day 1 and day 50 post-excision. Figure 1E demonstrates significantly less regression in larger metastases (10^7 photons/sec) versus smaller (10^6 photons/sec), p<0.000. Figure 1F shows metastases regressed after excision but continued to increase after sham surgery, p<0.05. Figure 2A-C show CM enhanced viability (p<0.001), adhesion (p<0.01), and tube formation (p<0.0001) of cancer cells and HUVEC. Figure 2D shows mice with CM via osmotic minipumps had 10-fold less regression than SM group, p<0.005. Figure 3A shows String database PPI networks identifying pathways involved in early metastasis. Figure 3B shows antibody neutralization completely blocked metastatic progression (p<0.0001). Figure 3C shows no difference in regression between antibody-treated and IgG groups on post-excision day-1. Figure 3D shows Kaplan-Meier survival curves with HR 2.05 for IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF, p<0.05. Table S1 lists 28 cytokines identified in CM, with factors excluded if present in non-tumor bearing or post-excision plasma.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first animal model demonstrating that primary tumor excision induces spontaneous regression of micro-metastases (100-fold decrease, p<0.0001) by eliminating the PT-derived secretome. 2. The strongest evidence is the identification of four key PT-secreted factors (IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, MIF) whose in vivo neutralization completely arrests metastatic progression (p<0.0001) and correlates with significantly lower survival in patients (HR 2.05, p<0.05). 3. The future path involves exploiting the perioperative window to control minimal residual disease by targeting PT-secreted prometastatic factors using tailored antibody combinations identified from malignant tissue biopsy.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study demonstrates, for the first time, the use of Attenuated Total Reflectance Fourier Transform Infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy as an independent modality to monitor the global molecular activation dynamics of murine macrophage RAW 264.7 cells upon stimulation with CpG DNA and lipopolysaccharide (LPS). The authors utilized the non-destructive, rapid ATR-FTIR method to capture comprehensive changes in nucleic acids, proteins, lipids, and other metabolites simultaneously from a single cell sample. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) identified the 1750-850 cm⁻¹ region as the primary source of variation (PC-1 variability at 83%, PC-2 at 11%), guiding detailed spectral interpretation. Key findings reveal: (1) Nucleic acid content shows significant increases from 10 minutes through 6 hours post-activation (p < 0.1), with RNA-specific peaks (915 cm⁻¹) indicating rapid RNA synthesis within 2 hours followed by DNA synthesis after 6 hours; (2) LPS induces a pro-inflammatory transcriptomic burst but represses DNA synthesis and elicits cell-cycle arrest, consistent with prior gene expression studies; (3) Total protein concentration increases rapidly from 10 minutes to 2 hours post-treatment (p < 0.001) and then declines, aligning with documented regulatory mechanisms involving cytokine networks and protein secretion; (4) Both activators trigger de novo lipogenesis, increasing fatty acids, triglycerides, and cholesterol from the first minutes. The study validates that the RNA-specific peak (915 cm⁻¹) can define macrophage activation within the first minutes of stimulation, filling a temporal gap in prior activation assays. The authors conclude that ATR-FTIR spectroscopy provides a broad-view alternative to complex 'omics' techniques, capturing metabolite changes not readily accessible by conventional methods.

Research Context
FTIR spectroscopy has emerged as a powerful non-destructive, rapid, and high-throughput biomedical tool capable of revealing all delicate alterations in macromolecule conformation and concentration. A single IR spectrum acts as a fingerprint for all metabolites of the cell system, where peak area provides quantitative concentration and absorption frequencies reveal chemical bond nature. ATR-FTIR overcomes water absorption limitations and requires no sample preparation, with a minimal amount of sample sufficient for high-quality spectra. Macrophages constitute the front line of the immune system, possessing high structural and functional plasticity in responding to challenges. CpG DNA in bacterial DNA triggers macrophage proliferation, pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and antigen-presenting cell activation. LPS, occupying approximately 75% of gram-negative bacterial external surface, stimulates monocytes and macrophages to release a wide variety of biological response mediators. Both CpG DNA and LPS recognition pathways share high homology, utilizing MyD88 and activating NF-kB and AP-1 transcription factors. While 'omics' techniques provide precise molecule-specific data, they require complex sample preparation steps that can alter chemical ratios and post-translational modifications. A broad view of relative nucleic acid, lipid, and protein amounts not readily accessible by other techniques is needed, which FTIR provides. It is currently unknown whether CpG ODN-mediated immune activation leads to detectable global molecular changes via FTIR spectroscopy.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question asks whether global molecular changes in murine macrophage RAW 264.7 cells upon CpG DNA and LPS activation are detectable by ATR-FTIR spectroscopy. The study hypothesizes that activation-induced changes in nucleic acid, protein, and lipid concentrations will manifest as distinct spectral peak alterations detectable by FTIR. The specific hypothesis is that CpG DNA and LPS will induce rapid, time-dependent changes in the macromolecular composition of macrophages that align with known immunological activation pathways. A secondary hypothesis is that PCA can identify the primary sources of spectral variation and guide detailed peak analysis. The authors predict that the RNA-specific peak (915 cm⁻¹) will serve as a sensitive early indicator of macrophage activation. The expected outcome is that early-stage changes will reflect RNA synthesis followed by DNA synthesis, and rapid protein increase followed by gradual decline. Both activators are expected to trigger de novo lipogenesis, increasing triglycerides, cholesterol, and fatty acids.

Methodological Details
Murine macrophage-like RAW 264.7 cells were cultured at 37°C with 5% CO₂ in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and 2 mM L-glutamine. Sub-culturing was performed in 1/10 ratio upon reaching acceptable confluency, generally every 2-3 days to maintain logarithmic growth. Cells were harvested, spun at 1000 rpm (208g) for 10 minutes, and resuspended at 2x10⁶ cells/mL. Three treatment groups were established: control with 0.9% PBS; CpG DNA stimulated with 1 µM K3 ODN (endotoxin-free); LPS stimulated with 0.5 µg/ml LPS. Four time points post-treatment were measured to evaluate kinetics: 10 min, 30 min, 2 hours, and 6 hours. Before measurement, samples were spun at 1000 rpm, washed with 15 mL sterile PBS, and media discarded to remove organic compounds. All infrared interferograms were collected using a Perkin-Elmer Spectrum One FTIR spectrometer with a Diamond-ZnSe ATR crystal. Cell samples of 1 µl were dried with mild N₂ flux for 5 minutes to allow cells to settle on the crystal. Air background was measured and subtracted automatically, and PBS spectra were recorded and subtracted manually. Cell spectra were recorded in the 4000-650 cm⁻¹ region at 25°C. Interferogram collection used a 128 scan number at 2 cm⁻¹ spectral resolution. Each group was scanned in three independent scans, with the average constituting a replicate; n=5 replicates were used for data analysis. Post-processing included 13-point Savitzky-Golay smoothing and baseline correction at 3800-2750-1800-900 cm⁻¹. PCA was performed on the 3000-650 cm⁻¹ region using Unscrambler 11.0 software. Peak assignment utilized center of weight measurements and literature comparison; side-peak band assignment used second derivative spectra. Conformational alteration studies used bandwidth measurements at 75% peak height. Normality was tested using Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests in GraphPad Prism 8.3.

Procedures And Architectures
The experimental design followed a comparative cross-sectional structure with three treatment groups (PBS, CpG, LPS) and four time points (10 min, 30 min, 2 h, 6 h). After treatment, samples were returned to the incubator until the corresponding time point, then removed, spun at 1000 rpm, and washed with 15 mL PBS to eliminate media interference. ATR-FTIR data were collected in the 4000-650 cm⁻¹ range using a Diamond-ZnSe crystal, with 128 scans at 2 cm⁻¹ resolution. PCA was applied as an unsupervised multivariate data analysis (MDA) method without initial information input to reduce dimensionality. PCA was conducted on the spectral data matrix obtained at 0.5 cm⁻¹ resolution. The 1750-850 cm⁻¹ region was identified via PCA Loadings Plots as containing numerous peaks with high variation among samples. Peak assignments were grounded in literature (Table A1) and confirmed by center of weight measurements. Quantitative concentration data were derived by integrating the area under the peaks. Second derivative spectra were used for side-peak band assignment to resolve overlapping features. Conformational studies utilized bandwidth measurements at 75% peak height to assess changes in molecular environment.

Key Results
PCA revealed PC-1 explained 83% of the variability, identifying the vast source of variation, while PC-2 explained 11%. The 1750-850 cm⁻¹ IR region showed numerous peaks with high variation among samples in the Loadings Plots. CpG DNA stimulation induced significant increases in nucleic acid content at the 1238 cm⁻¹ peak from 10 min until 6 hours post-treatment (p < 0.1*). The RNA-specific ribose vibration peak at 915 cm⁻¹ showed significant increase from the first minutes post-CpG stimulation (p < 0.001***). The RNA-specific peak increase was maintained until 2 hours after CpG stimulation (p < 0.1*). Total protein content (Amide I, 1639 cm⁻¹) in CpG-treated cells increased significantly from 10 minutes to 2 hours (p < 0.001***). LPS stimulation also caused a rapid initial protein increase, which was reduced starting from the 2-hour time point. CpG DNA-induced protein loss after 3 hours was attributed to suppression by cytokines (IL10, MYC, NFKBIA, SOCS1, SOCS3, IL1RN, FOS) and loss of induction. The ester C=O stretching peak near 1741 cm⁻¹ showed a very significant increase during activation, correlating to elevated triglycerides and cholesterol from the first minutes. LPS stimulation elevated triglycerides and cholesterol concentration after 10 minutes. A significant increase in the COO- symmetric stretching peak at 1400 cm⁻¹ indicated increased fatty acid concentration. LPS was shown in prior gene expression studies to induce as many as 263 genes and is a potent pro-inflammatory and anti-proliferative agent. LPS-induced activation state could be defined as early as 41 minutes in prior studies, supporting the 10-minute detection in the current study. The 915 cm⁻¹ RNA-specific peak allows definition of macrophage activation state at the very first minutes of activation. DNA synthesis was determined to start from 6 hours after CpG stimulation, whereas RNA synthesis dominated until 2 hours.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The temporal sequence of RNA synthesis (0–2 h) followed by DNA synthesis (after 6 h) aligns with known biological processes of macrophage activation and proliferation. LPS induces a broad transcriptomic response but represses DNA synthesis and elicits cell-cycle arrest, consistent with prior findings that LPS inhibits macrophage proliferation. The rapid protein increase (10 min–2 h) followed by decline aligns with coordinated regulation by pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines. De novo lipogenesis in macrophages is linked to de novo fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis pathways, sharing Acetoacetyl-CoA as a common metabolite. CpG-induced lipogenesis modulates secretory activity carried out by the Endoplasmic Reticulum and Golgi, a pathway also important in cancer cells. FTIR spectroscopy, by capturing the broad metabolite profile simultaneously, offers complementary information to targeted 'omics' approaches. The study establishes ATR-FTIR as an independent modality for monitoring macrophage activation dynamics, validating the method's utility for innate immune response studies.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors acknowledge that the absorbance of IR light by water molecules superimposes on aqueous cell system signals, though Fourier transformation and ATR mitigate this. Quantitative concentration data from peak area integration may be subject to spectral overlap and normalization challenges inherent to FTIR. The study uses 128 scans at 2 cm⁻¹ resolution and 0.5 cm⁻¹ resolution for PCA; trade-offs between signal-to-noise and spectral resolution are inherent. Statistical significance thresholds (p < 0.1 for some nucleic acid comparisons) are less stringent than typical α = 0.05, requiring interpretation with caution. The study uses murine RAW 264.7 cells in vitro; results may not fully generalize to human macrophages or in vivo settings. The exact random seed, train/test split, or specific computational hyperparameters for PCA are not reported. Demographic or biological variation across different cell passages is not specified, though sub-culturing is described. The study does not report absolute concentrations, only relative changes via peak area integration. Mechanisms for CpG DNA-induced protein loss remain unstudied and are identified as a need for future work. The authors note that 'omics' techniques are more precise but the FTIR approach captures broader metabolic changes not readily accessible.

Claims
ATR-FTIR spectroscopy can independently monitor global molecular changes in murine macrophages during CpG DNA and LPS activation. The study demonstrates for the first time FTIR as an independent modality to monitor activation dynamics. Four distinct macromolecular classes (nucleic acids, proteins, lipids) showed distinct, time-dependent activation signatures. PCA confirmed significant clustering of samples by treatment group, validating the spectral data. The RNA-specific peak (915 cm⁻¹) provided statistically significant differentiation (p < 0.001) within the first minutes. Statistical significance at p < 0.1 for some nucleic acid comparisons suggests moderate rather than definitive discrimination. Water absorption remains a fundamental limitation of IR spectroscopy for aqueous systems. ATR-FTIR could serve as a rapid screening tool for macrophage activation in pharmacological and immunological studies. The method could guide the design of synthetic CpG ODNs for therapeutic uses by revealing how different motifs affect metabolite profiles.
CpG DNA and LPS both trigger rapid protein synthesis and subsequent de novo lipogenesis in macrophages. Amide I peak showed significant increase from 10 min to 2 h post-CpG treatment (p < 0.001). Ester C=O peak near 1741 cm⁻¹ increased from the first minutes, indicating triglyceride and cholesterol accumulation. COO- stretching at 1400 cm⁻¹ increased, confirming de novo lipogenesis. LPS-induced protein increase is reduced starting from 2 hours, showing different temporal dynamics compared to CpG. LPS represses DNA synthesis, contrasting with the eventual DNA synthesis following CpG activation. These results support the role of lipid metabolism as a downstream metabolic consequence of innate immune activation. A shared metabolic fate between fatty acid and cholesterol pathways suggests a coordinated metabolic reprogramming.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Three independent scans were performed for each group, with the average constituting a replicate. n=5 replicates were used in all data analyses. PCA provided a loadings-plot-based validation of spectral peaks, serving as an unsupervised sensitivity check. Second derivative spectra were used specifically for side-peak band assignment to resolve ambiguous overlapping features. Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests confirmed normality of datasets, validating assumptions for statistical inference.

Key Figures Tables
Figure A1 presents a comprehensive spectrum and second derivative of resting control RAW 264.7 cells in the 4000-650 cm⁻¹ region. Table A1 shows peak assignments based on literature for the identified spectral features. Table A2 presents area integration measurements for all peaks of interest across all study groups. Table 1 summarizes the treatment conditions: control (PBS), CpG (1 µM K3 ODN), and LPS (0.5 µg/ml). Figure 1.A shows the PCA Scores Plot with samples clustered by treatment along PC directions. Figure 1.B and 1.C show the PCA Loadings Plots for the 1750-850 cm⁻¹ region. Figure 2.A shows the nucleic acid region (1238 cm⁻¹ and 1085 cm⁻¹) at 10 min post-treatment. Figure 2.B presents bar diagrams of peak integration values for nucleic acid peaks at different time points. Figure 2.C shows the RNA-specific ribose vibration peak at 915 cm⁻¹. Figure 3.A and 3.B show the amide I and amide II region (1639 cm⁻¹, 1540 cm⁻¹) for protein content. Figure 3.C presents amide I band integration data over time. Figure 4.D and 4.E show the ester C=O stretching near 1741 cm⁻¹ for triglycerides and cholesterol. Figure 4.B and 4.C show the COO- symmetric stretching peak at 1400 cm⁻¹ for fatty acids.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first demonstration of ATR-FTIR as an independent spectroscopic modality for monitoring global, simultaneous molecular changes in macromolecular composition (nucleic acids, proteins, lipids) during macrophage activation by CpG DNA and LPS. 2. The strongest evidence is the time-resolved activation signature: RNA-specific peaks at 915 cm⁻¹ differentiate activation within 10 minutes (p < 0.001), followed by protein increase (p < 0.001 at 2 h), with RNA synthesis dominant until 2 h and DNA synthesis appearing after 6 h. 3. The future path involves characterizing the specific mechanisms of CpG-induced protein loss after 3 hours, and extending the approach to human macrophages and in vivo studies, and optimizing therapeutic CpG ODN designs based on revealed metabolic profiles.

summary.title: The Foster method: Rapid and non-invasive detection of clinically significant American Foulbrood disease levels using eDNA sampling and a dual-target qPCR assay, with its potential for other hive pathogens
summary.authors: John F Mackay, Rebecca E Hewett, Noa T Smith, Tammy L Waters, John S Scandrett
summary.field_subfield: Veterinary Diagnostics / Apiculture Molecular Diagnostics
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces the Foster method, a novel non-invasive environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling approach coupled with a dual-target hydrolysis probe qPCR assay for rapid detection of clinically significant American Foulbrood (AFB) in honeybee colonies. AFB is caused by Paenibacillus larvae, a spore-forming bacterium whose spores persist for over 30 years and cause rapid colony decline. Traditional diagnosis relies on subjective visual inspection of brood cells, which is time-consuming, prone to error, and requires hive dismantling. Previous molecular methods relied on single-target 16S gene qPCR with insufficient specificity, or culture-based methods requiring up to a week for results. The Foster method uses sterile foam-tipped swabs applied to the colony entrance for 3-5 seconds, eliminating the need to dismantle the hive. DNA extraction from swabs is combined with a dual-target qPCR assay (targeting the multicopy 16S gene for sensitivity and the single-copy ftsZ gene for quantification) plus an internal control. Validation across three cohorts of quarantine apiaries in New Zealand (late 2018 to early 2020) demonstrated that entrance swabs reliably differentiate infected from non-infected hives. Key findings include: analytical sensitivity down to 4 copies per 10 µL, 94-96% amplification efficiency, and a quantitative threshold of 565,000 spores per 10 bees/swab indicating a 95% probability of clinical signs. Pooling of up to 12 swab eluates also permitted individual hive detection. The study concludes that entrance swabbing provides a fast, one-time sampling method that can be extended to other bee pathogens and incursion pests, offering a clinically relevant risk assessment for beekeeping operations.

AFB is caused by Paenibacillus larvae, a spore-forming bacterium whose spores persist for over 30 years and cause rapid colony decline. Traditional diagnosis relies on subjective visual inspection of brood cells, which is time-consuming, prone to error, and requires hive dismantling. Previous molecular methods relied on single-target 16S gene qPCR with insufficient specificity, or culture-based methods requiring up to a week for results. The Foster method uses sterile foam-tipped swabs applied to the colony entrance for 3-5 seconds, eliminating the need to dismantle the hive. DNA extraction from swabs is combined with a dual-target qPCR assay (targeting the multicopy 16S gene for sensitivity and the single-copy ftsZ gene for quantification) plus an internal control. Validation across three cohorts of quarantine apiaries in New Zealand (late 2018 to early 2020) demonstrated that entrance swabs reliably differentiate infected from non-infected hives. Pooling of up to 12 swab eluates also permitted individual hive detection. The study concludes that entrance swabbing provides a fast, one-time sampling method that can be extended to other bee pathogens and incursion pests, offering a clinically relevant risk assessment for beekeeping operations.

Research Context
AFB is caused by Paenibacillus larvae, whose hardy spores remain infectious for over 30 years and cause rapid colony decline. In New Zealand, the percentage of hives reported as infected increased from 0.21% in 2015 to 0.46% in 2021, driven by increased hive densities and less skilled beekeepers. Traditional diagnosis relies on visual inspection of thousands of brood cells per hive through a roping test, which is subjective and laborious. Existing molecular methods have largely used single-target 16S gene qPCR, which lacks specificity and has been subject to primer re-design. Culture-based confirmation can take up to a week and is considered a variable process. Previous eDNA studies required dismantling the hive twice and repeat visits to install collection sheets, limiting rapid sampling.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a single, non-invasive entrance swab combined with dual-target qPCR can detect clinically significant AFB levels without hive dismantling. A specific hypothesis was that the entrance swab would provide sufficient P. larvae DNA to differentiate infected from non-infected hives without requiring whole-baseboard sampling. The study further hypothesized that pooling multiple swab eluates would allow individual hive detection within a single extraction for operational efficiency. A key objective was to establish a quantitative spore threshold that predicts the probability of clinical AFB signs, enabling risk-based management. The authors posited that the dual-target approach would enhance both sensitivity (via 16S) and specificity/quantification (via ftsZ) compared to single-target assays.

Methodological Details
Five quarantine apiaries across four regions (East Coast, Wellington, Wairarapa, South Canterbury) provided sampling from late 2018 to early 2020. Three sample types were initially compared: nurse bees, whole-baseboard swabs, and hive-entrance swabs. Bees were collected from brood frames in 50 mL sterile containers and frozen to euthanize. Swabs were sterile foam-tipped (Puritan), moistened with sterile water, and applied for 3-5 seconds. Bees and swabs were sent to the laboratory at ambient temperature by overnight courier. Bee samples were frozen at -20°C; swab samples were stored at ambient temperature until DNA extraction. Each bee sample contained 10 bees for DNA extraction using the Bee Pathogen DNA/RNA Extraction Kit. DNA was extracted via column-based kit with beadbeating using 0.5 mm and 2.3 mm zirconia silica beads. Bees were homogenized in a Mini Beadbeater 16 for 3 minutes with 3 mL DXL lysis buffer. Incubation was at 65°C for 10 minutes with manual inversion every 3 minutes. For swabs, 800 µL DXL buffer was added and homogenised in the beadbeater for 3 minutes. A synthetic DNA standard (gBlock, IDT) of 153 bp was used for quantification. Standards were generated from 10^6 copies per µL down to 2 copies per µL. The diluent for standards was a pooled DNA sample from P. larvae-free bees. Statistical analysis used binary logistic regression in Minitab and ANOVA to correlate spore levels with clinical signs. Data points were imputed via regression for two clinical hives with skewed spore numbers.

Procedures And Architectures
The study used a commercially available multiplex qPCR assay for P. larvae from Hall et al. (2021). The assay employed hydrolysis probe ("TaqMan®") technology, allowing quantification of each target by selected fluorescent wavelengths. Two independent targets were amplified: the multicopy 16S gene and the single-copy ftsZ gene. An internal control was included in an additional detection channel to confirm suitable DNA quality. Copies were calculated using the equation: Copies = ng * Avogadro's constant * copies/mole * length of standard x 660 g/mole * 1x10^9 ng/g. Swab eluates were pooled in groups of eight and later twelve for pooled applications. For pooled samples, 60 µL of each swab eluate was added to a 2 mL beadbeating tube. Cq values were converted to spore levels using the formula: Spores per 10 bees = 10^(Cq ftsZ - 3.48) x 50. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Key Results
Synthetic DNA standards showed analytical sensitivity down to 4 copies per 10 µL per reaction for both targets. Amplification efficiency in the multiplex was 94% for ftsZ and 96% for 16S, with linearity (r = 0.998) over 7 orders of magnitude. The 16S target typically amplified 3-5 cycles earlier than the ftsZ target in positive bee, honey, and hive material samples. Bee DNA extraction yielded OD260/280 between 1.8 and 1.9, indicating high purity. 45 hives were sampled up to 6 times in the first cohort, with 8 confirmed clinical and 6 presumed AFB. In the second cohort of 23 hives, 4 showed clinical signs; most others had no or low P. larvae levels. In the pooling experiment, single hives with higher AFB levels were clearly detected within pools of twelve hive samples. Binary logistic regression and ANOVA (p = 0.00) confirmed a strong relationship between spore levels and clinical signs. A spore quantity of 565,000 or more revealed a 95% probability of clinical signs in the hive. P. larvae levels on entrance swabs were similar to whole-baseboard swabs (Table 4), validating non-invasive sampling.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The 16S multicopy nature drove higher sensitivity but copy number variability among isolates precluded its use for quantification. The single-copy ftsZ gene was selected for quantification to ensure accurate spore counting. The ability to sample through the entrance removed the need to dismantle the hive, improving operational feasibility. The method demonstrated that PCR can detect pre-clinical infections or symptoms missed by visual inspection, as shown by Hive 11. The results suggest that entrance swabs can extend to other bee pathogens, including Nosema ceranae and potential incursion pests. The Foster method is a fast, one-time sampling and quantification method that provides clinically significant risk assessment.

Contradictions And Limitations
In two hives (11 and 12 in Table 2), bees showed high P. larvae while hiveware showed low or undetectable levels, conflicting with general trends. Subsequent investigation revealed the hiveware was new (<2 weeks old) and colonies were newly established from an unknowingly infected parent. In these cases, spores had not had enough time to deposit on entrance surfaces, indicating the method may have a time-dependent sensitivity. Spore levels never increased during monitoring for many hives, and became undetectable in some low-spore cases, limiting longitudinal interpretation. The study acknowledges that further research is needed to assess the accumulation rate of spores on hive surfaces and refine clinical thresholds. The random seed, specific train/test splits, or demographic data for the hives are not reported, limiting reproducibility of specific statistical models.

Claims
The Foster method enables non-invasive, rapid detection of clinically significant AFB levels through entrance swabbing alone without hive dismantling. Entrance swab spore levels were similar to whole-baseboard swab levels in the first cohort. A threshold of 565,000 spores predicted clinical signs with 95% probability. The method eliminated the need for dismantling and repeat visits. Hives 11 and 12 showed high bee spore loads but undetectable hiveware levels due to new hiveware. Spore levels in some low-spore hives became undetectable during monitoring. The method could be adapted for biosecurity surveillance of unwanted hive pests like tracheal mites or small hive beetle. The same DNA sample can be used for testing other bee pathogens including Nosema ceranae.
Pooling of up to 12 swab eluates in a single extraction maintains the ability to detect individual hives with high AFB loads. Even in pools of twelve, single hives with higher AFB could be clearly detected. Remnant samples from positive pools were tested individually for confirmation. No specific false-negative rate for pools is reported in the text. Pooling reduces time and costs for large-scale testing of multiple hives.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study compared three sample types (bees, whole-baseboard, entrance) to validate the entrance-only approach. Internal control Cq's were monitored across serial dilutions of swab DNA to confirm suitable quality and absence of inhibitors. A synthetic DNA standard with 153 bp was used to generate a 7-order-of-magnitude calibration curve. The 16S target was shown to amplify 3-5 cycles earlier, but copy number variability prevented its use for quantification.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 shows progression of P. larvae levels in three colonies over monitoring points, converted to spores per 10 bee or swab. Table 2 compares nurse bee P. larvae levels to entrance swab levels across 23 hives in the second cohort. Table 3 presents pooling results for groups of eight and twelve swab eluates. Table 4 shows levels of P. larvae and internal control on whole-baseboard vs. entrance swabs in the first cohort. Supplementary Figure 4 presents the ANOVA and logistic regression outputs confirming the spore-clinical relationship. Supplementary S1 contains the Cq values from the synthetic DNA standards.

Three Takeaways
1. The Foster method provides a rapid, one-time, non-invasive entrance-swabbing protocol coupled with dual-target qPCR that differentiates clinically relevant AFB from background levels without hive dismantling. 2. A spore quantity of 565,000 or more per 10 bees/swab correlates with a 95% probability of clinical AFB, establishing a quantitative risk threshold for beekeepers. 3. The methodology is extensible to other bee pathogens (Nosema ceranae) and biosecurity surveillance for invasive pests, and pooling protocols facilitate high-throughput operational use.

summary.authors: Jaspreet Singh (Griffith University); Thomas Litfin (Griffith University); Jaswinder Singh; Kuldip Paliwal (Griffith University); Yaoqi Zhou (Griffith University)

summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces SPOT-Contact-Single, a protein contact-map prediction method that leverages unsupervised transformer language model features (ESM-1b attention maps) instead of evolution-based multiple sequence alignments (MSAs). On the independent SPOT-2018 set, the method showed 48.7% and 48.5% F1-score improvement over TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact, respectively, for proteins with Neff=1. judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces SPOT-Contact-Single, a protein contact-map prediction method that leverages unsupervised transformer language model features (ESM-1b attention maps) instead of evolution-based multiple sequence alignments (MSAs). The authors address a fundamental limitation in structural biology: most contact-map predictors depend on homologous sequence information which is unavailable for many proteins, and generating these profiles is computationally intensive. The proposed architecture uses an ensemble of six residual neural networks (Duta et al. version) with 12 blocks, trained on a large dataset of 34,691 proteins. Six model variants were explored combining one-hot amino acid encoding, SPOT-1D-Single outputs (SS3, SS8, ASA, HSE, torsion angles), and ESM-1b attention maps (last layer vs. all layers). The ensemble achieved a 15% F1-score improvement over the single-sequence baseline SSCpred on the independent CASP14-FM test set and significantly outperformed evolution-based predictors (TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact) on proteins without homologs (Neff=1). On the independent SPOT-2018 set, the method showed 48.7% and 48.5% F1-score improvement over TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact, respectively, for proteins with Neff=1. Computational efficiency was a key finding: SPOT-Contact-Single made predictions in 116 seconds on CPU for 15 proteins, 22 times faster than TrRosetta, highlighting its suitability for genomic-scale prediction. The authors argue that while unsupervised features currently lag behind co-mutation information for high-homology proteins, the ESM-1b-based approach provides a computationally feasible, accurate alternative for isolated proteins, with the limitation of a 1024 residue sequence length constraint inherent to the ESM-1b architecture.

Research Context
Deep learning and statistical inference methods have produced significant headway in protein secondary structure and contact-and distance-map prediction over the past two decades. A common trait among existing methods is the use of multiple sequence alignment (MSA) and other homology-based profile information. However many proteins have very few or no homologs to generate MSA and homology profiles, and performance drops significantly in these cases. SSCpred was recently published as a single-sequence-based method using one-hot encoding and predicted one-dimensional structural properties from SPIDER3-Single. SSCpred performs adequately for proteins with few homologs but relatively poorer for proteins with more effective homologs when compared to MSA-based techniques. There is a need for exploring other possible features beyond one-hot encoding to improve single-sequence-based methods. Unsupervised deep learning methods inspired by NLP language models were introduced to extract protein features trained on reference libraries. ESM-1b uses a Transformer-34 model trained on Uniref50 and outputs an embedding and attention maps.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether ESM-1b's attention map, when concatenated with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs, can improve contact-map prediction beyond what is achievable with single-sequence features alone. The authors hypothesized that unsupervised learning features concatenated with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs would outperform the single-sequence-based SSCpred and MSA-based predictors for proteins with low effective number of homologs. A second hypothesis was that an ensemble of models trained through different training approaches and feature combinations would add to the performance improvement. The method aims to provide a much faster and reasonably accurate alternative to evolution-based methods useful for large-scale prediction. The authors also predicted that direct contact-map prediction and distogram-based prediction strategies would differ in performance, requiring both in the final ensemble.

Methodological Details
The training data was curated from the ProteinNet benchmark dataset consisting of 50,914 proteins submitted to PDB before 2016 with crystal structures at resolution < 2.5Å. Proteins were clustered at a sequence identity cut-off of 95% according to MMseqs2 to maximize training data. To minimize overfitting, 100 proteins were set aside as validation, and any protein with hits at e-value < 0.1 against these was removed. This left 39,120 proteins for the final training set after homology removal. Removing proteins longer than 500 residues yielded final sets of 34,691 training proteins and 88 validation proteins. The independent test set SPOT-2018 comprised 669 proteins released between May 2018 and April 2020, after removing homologs to pre-2018 sequences at e-value < 0.1. A sub-set of 46 proteins with Neff=1 was extracted from SPOT-2018 to form the Neff1-2018 set for de-novo and non-homolog protein testing. The CASP14-FM test set included 15 free modelling targets released at CASP14, proteins without known structural templates in the PDB at time of release. Input features included one-hot amino acid encoding, SPOT-1D-Single outputs (SS3, SS8, ASA, HSE, torsion angles), and ESM-1b attention maps from all twenty heads of the last layer or every layer. Attention maps were symmetrized and applied average product corrections (APC) as described by Rao et al. (2020). One-dimensional features were converted to two-dimensional features using outer concatenation.

Procedures And Architectures
The architecture is a 12-block ResNet, the maximum depth trainable on the available GPU, using a recently published improved ResNet version by Duta et al. (2020). Convolutional layers used a channel size of 64 and kernel size of 3. Six models were trained with the same architectural specifications but different input feature combinations. The first three models predicted inter-residue contacts as a binary classification, while the last three predicted inter-residue distances as distance bins with probabilities added for 0-8 Å. Direct contact-map models used Binary Cross-Entropy loss, while distogram models used Cross-Entropy loss. Hyperparameters included the Adam optimizer with learning rate of 0.001, batch size of 1, and early stopping of 3 epochs. The ensemble was formed by taking the mean of individual model results across the six models. Contacts are defined by an inter-residue distance of ≤ 8.0 Å between Cβ atoms. Contacts were categorized into short (7-11), medium (12-23), and long (≥24) ranges. Performance was assessed using top L/10, L/5, L/2, and L/1 highest-ranked predictions in terms of precision.

Key Results
On the validation set, training on one-hot encoding alone yielded an F1-score of 0.15 and MCC of 0.14. Adding SPOT-1D-Single output to one-hot encoding improved F1-score by 22.90%. Attention maps from the last layer of ESM-1b gave F1=0.51, MCC=0.50, precision=0.56, and AUC of ROC=0.95. This represented a 242% improvement in F1-score over one-hot encoding alone and 178% over SPOT-1D-Single + one-hot encoding. Concatenating all features (one-hot + SPOT-1D + ESM-1b all-layers) showed a further 2.92% F1-score increase over attention maps alone. Direct contact-map prediction performed slightly better than distogram-based prediction, though the difference was small. The ensemble SPOT-Contact-Single showed a 4% F1-score improvement over the second-best individual model on the validation set. On proteins without homologs (Neff=1) in the SPOT-2018 set, SPOT-Contact-Single achieved F1=0.32, compared to ~0.22 for TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact. This represents a 48.7% improvement over TrRosetta and 48.5% over SPOT-Contact on Neff=1 proteins. On the independent CASP14-FM test set, SPOT-Contact-Single showed a 15% F1-score improvement over SSCpred. The most improvement over SSCpred was in long-range contacts precision with a ~100% improvement. On a specific Neff=1 protein (5YKZ_A), SPOT-Contact-Single achieved F1=0.215, while TrRosetta and ESM-1b achieved 0.235 and 0.252, and SPOT-Contact 0.388 respectively. On CPU, SPOT-Contact-Single predicted 15 proteins in 116 seconds, 22 times faster than TrRosetta. On GPU, TrRosetta took 1926 seconds, 42 times slower than SPOT-Contact-Single.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The use of unsupervised transformer attention maps provides a viable alternative to co-mutation information from MSA for proteins with few or no homologs. While MSA-based methods still outperform single-sequence methods for proteins with high Neff, SPOT-Contact-Single reduces the gap significantly. The ensemble approach with different input combinations and both direct and distogram prediction strategies provides robustness and additive improvement. The computational efficiency of the single-sequence approach makes it suitable for genomic-scale prediction where sequence profile generation is prohibitive. The 1024 residue limitation of ESM-1b restricts use to protein domains rather than full multi-domain proteins without further processing. Future improvements may come from adopting more advanced architectures such as Transformer or Performer for the final prediction stage.

Contradictions And Limitations
The method is not competitive with MSA-based predictors for proteins with high Neff, as co-mutation information is still more effective than unsupervised features. The 1024 residue limit of ESM-1b makes it impossible to directly predict contact maps for proteins longer than 1024 amino acids. The difference between direct and distogram-based prediction was small, suggesting neither strategy is definitively superior. The paper does not report the exact number of training and validation proteins after length filtering—it only states 34691 and 88. The specific random seeds and hardware used for training are not reported. The paper uses only a small independent test set of 15 proteins for some comparisons, which may limit statistical power.

Claims
SPOT-Contact-Single outperforms both single-sequence and evolution-profile-based contact-map predictors on proteins with few or no homologs. On Neff=1 proteins, SPOT-Contact-Single achieved F1=0.32 versus ~0.22 for TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact. This represents a 48.7% improvement over TrRosetta and 48.5% over SPOT-Contact on the SPOT-2018 set. On CASP14-FM, it showed a 15% F1-score improvement over SSCpred. SPOT-1D-Single is not yet as competitive as evolution-based methods for proteins with higher Neff. For the Neff1-2018 example protein (5YKZ_A), ESM-1b actually had a higher F1 (0.252) than SPOT-Contact-Single (0.215) in some instances. The method provides a reasonably accurate screening tool for protein contact-map prediction without requiring MSAs. Computational speed advantages make it suitable for genomic-scale prediction.
ESM-1b attention maps provide a substantial boost over one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single features alone. Attention maps from the last layer gave F1=0.51, a 242% improvement over one-hot encoding. Adding all-layers attention maps yielded further improvement in precision across all contact ranges. The incremental gain of adding all features together (2.92%) was relatively modest. Unsupervised transformer features capture biologically relevant spatial relationships not present in one-hot encodings.

Data And Code Availability
The TrRosetta, SPOT-Contact, and ESM-1b methods have stand-alone programs available on GitHub or official websites. The SPOT-Contact MSA generation pipeline is available via the SPARKS lab server. SSCpred was accessed via a web server because no stand-alone version was available. The authors do not explicitly state the availability of SPOT-Contact-Single code or pre-trained weights.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Feature importance was assessed by training ResNet12 on different combinations: one-hot only, one-hot + SPOT-1D, and attention maps. The direct versus distogram prediction strategy was tested and both were included in the final ensemble. The ensemble was tested on the validation set, showing 4% F1-score improvement over the second-best individual model across all matrices. Performance was also validated on the Neff1-2018 test set and CASP14-FM. The authors note that the 1024 amino acid limitation is not a barrier because proteins are usually made of domains with less than 1000 residues.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the ResNet12 architecture with convolutional layers of channel size 64 and kernel size 3. Table 1 lists the six trained models with different feature combinations and prediction targets. Table 2 presents feature importance: one-hot only (F1=0.15), attention maps from last layer (F1=0.51), and all-layers attention. Table 3 and Supplementary Table S3 show direct versus distogram contact-map prediction performance. Table 4 shows ensemble learning performance: individual models versus the SPOT-Contact-Single ensemble. Table 5 compares SPOT-Contact-Single, TrRosetta, and SPOT-Contact on proteins without homologous sequences (F1~0.32 vs. ~0.22). Table 6 compares SPOT-Contact-Single, SSCpred, and ESM-1b on the CASP14-FM dataset. Fig. 2 shows precision for top predictions at short, medium, and long ranges. Fig. 3 plots F1-score as a function of Neff values for different predictors. Fig. 4 presents native and predicted contact maps for example protein 5YKZ_A.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first single-sequence protein contact-map predictor that uses unsupervised transformer language model attention maps (ESM-1b) instead of evolution-based profiles, providing a computationally efficient alternative for proteins with few homologs. 2. The strongest evidence is the 48.7% and 48.5% F1-score improvement over TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact on proteins without homologs in the SPOT-2018 set, along with the 15% improvement over SSCpred on the independent CASP14-FM set. 3. The future path includes using more advanced architectures like Transformer or Performer to further improve single-sequence contact-map prediction beyond evolutionary features.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
EcoEvoApps is an open-source R package (ecoevoapps) and companion website (https://ecoevoapps.gitlab.io) providing 11 interactive Shiny apps that simulate fundamental ecology and evolutionary biology (EEB) models. The project addresses the barrier that mathematical model language is foreign to empirical researchers and that quantitative biology education often neglects theoretical model pedagogy, focusing instead on statistics or general programming. The apps, selected by surveying undergraduate ecology syllabi and commonly-used textbooks (Gotelli 2008; Begon and Townsend 2020), implement models such as Lotka-Volterra predator-prey dynamics with various extensions (logistic growth, type II functional response) and abiotic resource competition. The package includes R functions (prefix run_) to simulate model dynamics, plotting functions (prefix plot_) returning ggplot2 objects, and shiny_ functions to launch apps from the console, serving as a bridge from interactive visualization to programmatic implementation. The first release includes nine apps available in English, Spanish, Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. The authors evaluated the educational utility in a pilot with 51 students at UCLA in an upper-division Ecology course using Island Biogeography and Lotka-Volterra competition apps; 40/51 students (78%) rated the apps as moderately to very helpful (scores of 6 or 7 on a 1-7 scale). A second survey at the University of Missouri confirmed substantial gains in student confidence. The project is open-source, customizable, and aims to expand into evolutionary biology and population genetics models, with future plans to develop new lesson plans for EEB educators.

Research Context
Integrating theory with empirical observation is a fundamental driver of progress in the life sciences, including ecology and evolutionary biology. Research synthesizing data with mathematical models enables generalization across systems, promotes conceptual understanding, and disentangles complex interactions. Such integration has applications in biological forecasts and informing science-society policy interfaces. A major barrier is that mathematical model language is foreign to those with empirical backgrounds, leading to fewer citations of equation-heavy papers. Instructors of quantitative courses receive worse student evaluations than those de-emphasizing quantitative topics, yet calls for quantitative training focus primarily on statistics or programming. Relatively few advances have addressed the pedagogy of theoretical models specifically in EEB education. Growing evidence suggests interactive tools allowing users to explore model structure independently increase student interest and understanding of quantitative concepts.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether interactive Shiny apps can facilitate communication and learning of theoretical EEB models for both individual learners and in classroom settings. The hypothesis is that providing a platform for interactive simulations of EEB models can bridge the gap between theoretical and empirical researchers. Specifically, the authors posit that allowing users to independently explore model structure and outcomes through interactive interfaces will improve understanding of quantitative concepts. The package is designed to serve as a gateway, helping users become familiar with coding and implementing theoretical models through a sequence from interactive apps to command-line functions. The pilot classroom study hypothesizes that guided exploration of specific models using the apps will improve student understanding of both the model as a whole and specific constituent concepts. The authors further posit that the open-source R-based framework will make the tools more accessible and customizable than existing education resources.

Methodological Details
The paper describes the first release of EcoEvoApps, an R package and website providing a collection of interactive apps. Eleven interactive apps were selected by surveying syllabi for undergraduate ecology courses and commonly-used textbooks (Gotelli 2008; Begon and Townsend 2020). Nine of the apps are available in English, Spanish, Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. The apps are hosted on RStudio's shinyapps.io servers or can be launched locally from the R console. A pilot classroom evaluation surveyed 51 students in an upper-division Ecology course at UCLA. The UCLA course used Island Biogeography and Lotka-Volterra competition models for the lesson. A second survey was conducted with students in a General Ecology course at the University of Missouri. The classroom activity included ~15-minute video lectures followed by a worksheet guiding students through the app. The UCLA IRB approved the study as exempt (UCLA IRB #20-002179); the MU IRB also determined it exempt (Project #2031063, Review #276104).

Procedures And Architectures
Under the hood, the Shiny apps use functions in the ecoevoapps package to simulate and visualize model dynamics. Simulations are conducted by functions with the prefix run_, which take parameter values, initial population sizes, and time steps as input. The run_ functions return a dataframe of population sizes over the specified time series. Plotting functions with the prefix plot_ take the run_ output and return a ggplot2 object. The app structure includes model descriptions, parameter tables, and references to relevant literature. The package includes shiny_ functions to launch apps directly from the command line, and a vignette with customization instructions. Model-specific vignettes provide instructions for simulating dynamics directly through R, e.g., vignette("predator-prey-interactions"). The predator-prey app includes a tab for the classic Lotka-Volterra model plus extensions for logistic prey growth and/or type II functional response. The app is available online at https://ecoevoapps.shinyapps.io/predator_prey_dynamics/ or via shiny_predprey().

Key Results
In the UCLA classroom study, 40 out of 51 students (approximately 78%) reported the apps were moderately to very helpful for learning the models as a whole. These students responded with scores of 6 or 7 on a 1-7 scale regarding the apps' helpfulness for model understanding. Students reported better understanding of specific concepts such as "carrying capacity" and "coexistence" after using the Lotka-Volterra competition app. Tracking individual students' interest and confidence before and after the activity showed substantial gains in student confidence, especially among students with higher interest in related topics. The MU survey confirmed similar results to the UCLA study, supporting the generalizability of the finding. The paradox of enrichment can be demonstrated: low prey carrying capacity (K=200) produces dampened oscillations, while high (K=500) produces unstable oscillations that limit system persistence. In the Lotka-Volterra app, the hump in the prey isocline determines whether the equilibrium point yields stable or unstable dynamics. The package includes 11 functions with the prefix shiny_ for command-line deployment in addition to the model-specific functions.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The apps function as a bridge, lowering the barrier to entry for mathematical model understanding for empirical EEB researchers. Interactive simulation allows users to independently explore model structure and outcomes, fostering a deeper conceptual understanding that complements analytical solutions. The open-source R implementation ensures accessibility, customizability, and integration with the common R programming environment in EEB. The pilot data suggests that interactive apps can serve as a formal instruction tool, providing measurable gains in student confidence and conceptual understanding of specific model parameters. The approach supports a broader paradigm of integrating theoretical and empirical EEB approaches, facilitating communication between the two research communities.

Contradictions And Limitations
Simulation-based learning may not provide all the same insights as analytical solutions, as noted by the authors. The current release is limited to ecological models; evolutionary biology and population genetics models are deferred to future releases. The classroom evaluation is a pilot with 51 students at one institution (UCLA) and a second at another (MU), which is not a large-scale multi-institutional study. The package includes 11 apps in the first release, with nine in multiple languages; further apps and translations are planned. The paper does not report specific effect sizes for confidence gains beyond "substantial gains," nor does it provide confidence intervals or p-values for the student ratings. The specific content of the worksheet used in the classroom study is referenced as a supplement (S3), so the exact guided exploration steps are not described in the main text.

Claims
EcoEvoApps provides a freely available, open-source interactive platform for simulating and learning fundamental EEB models, reducing the barrier for empirical researchers to engage with mathematical theory. The package is entirely open-source and written in R, making it accessible to the EEB community. Eleven interactive apps are available, selected from standard ecology syllabi and textbooks. The apps include model descriptions, parameter definitions, and references to relevant literature. The package includes R functions for direct simulation and plotting, serving as a bridge to programmatic implementation. Simulation-based tools do not replicate all the insights provided by analytical solutions. The first release is constrained to ecological models, with evolutionary biology models yet to be included. Wider adoption of the package could reduce the gap between empirical and theoretical EEB communities. Open-source R implementation enables community contributions of new apps, translations, and teaching plans.
Interactive Shiny apps improve student understanding of ecological models and specific model concepts in upper-division classroom settings. 40/51 students rated the apps as moderately to very helpful for learning the models as a whole. Students reported better understanding of carrying capacity and coexistence after using the Lotka-Volterra competition app. Substantial gains in student confidence were observed, particularly among high-interest students. Similar results were replicated in a General Ecology course at the University of Missouri. The pilot has a modest sample size (N=51) and the exact statistical magnitude of confidence gains is not quantified with CIs or p-values. The apps were used in conjunction with video lectures and a worksheet, making the isolated effect of the apps difficult to disentangle. The authors plan to develop and evaluate new lesson plans for EEB educators. The apps may inform instructional design for teaching quantitative EEB topics.

Data And Code Availability
The ecoevoapps package is open-source and available via GitLab. The website https://ecoevoapps.gitlab.io provides documentation, app links, and source code. The Shiny apps are hosted on RStudio's shinyapps.io servers and are freely available online. The package includes vignettes with instructions for customization, deployment, and model-specific simulation.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A second survey at the University of Missouri (MU) confirmed similar results to the UCLA pilot, providing cross-institutional support. The package includes functions with the prefix run_ for direct simulation, allowing users to conduct analyses beyond what is presented in the apps. The three-tab structure of the predator-prey app (classic, logistic prey, type II functional response, both) allows for comparative exploration of model extensions. Individual students' interest and confidence were tracked before and after the activity to detect gains, with the strongest effect among high-interest students.

Ethical Considerations
The classroom surveys were reviewed by the UCLA Institutional Review Board (UCLA IRB #20-002179) and the MU Institutional Review Board (Project #2031063, Review #276104). Both reviews determined the studies to constitute "exempt" studies.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 lists all models and functions included in the ecoevoapps package, including 11 model-specific functions and 11 shiny_ deployment functions. Figure 1 displays the predator-prey dynamics app with tabs for classic, logistic, type II, and combined extensions. Figure 2 shows screenshots of the predator-prey app illustrating the paradox of enrichment: Panel A with K=200 (dampened oscillations) and Panel B with K=500 (unstable oscillations). Figure 3A displays student ratings of the apps' helpfulness for learning models as a whole. Figure 3B displays student ratings for specific model concepts. Figure S2.1 in the supplements tracks individual students' interest and confidence before and after the activity.

Three Takeaways
1. EcoEvoApps is an open-source R package providing 11 interactive Shiny apps for simulating fundamental EEB models, selected from standard ecology textbooks and syllabi, and available in five languages. 2. Pilot evaluations of 51 UCLA students and a complementary MU survey demonstrated that the apps are moderately to very helpful (40/51) for learning models as a whole and specific concepts like carrying capacity and coexistence, with substantial confidence gains. 3. The project is designed to grow collaboratively, with future plans to incorporate evolutionary biology and population genetics models, develop new lesson plans, and invite community contributions in app development, translation, and teaching plan creation.
