summary.title: CCN2 activates ERK-signaling via integrin av and enhances the interaction of ERK and DUSP6 in lymphatic endothelial cells
summary.authors: Shiho Hashiguchi; Tomoko Tanaka; Ryosuke Mano; Seiji Kondo; Shohta Kodama
summary.field_subfield: Cell Biology / Angiogenesis and Lymphangiogenesis
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental signaling and in vivo validation study
summary.executive_summary:
This study investigates the role of cellular communication network factor 2 (CCN2), also known as connective tissue growth factor (CTGF), in lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs), where its contribution to lymphangiogenesis remained largely unelucidated. CCN2 is a well-characterized angiogenic factor in blood vessel formation but its specificity for lymphatic vessels was not previously established. The authors show that in primary cultured LECs, CCN2 induces dose-dependent upregulation of lymphatic endothelial markers (Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1) and lymphangiogenic factors (Vegfc, Vegfd, Flt4/Vegfr3), with a notable biphasic effect where expression dramatically decreases at 200 ng/mL compared to 100 ng/mL.

At the signaling level, CCN2 significantly increases phospho-ERK in LECs (p<0.001), while other MAPK and signaling pathways (p38, JNK, AKT, NFκB, Smad) remain unchanged. Phospho-receptor tyrosine kinase array confirmed that neither VEGFR2 nor VEGFR3 was activated by CCN2, ruling out upstream VEGFR signaling. Instead, the study demonstrates that CCN2-induced phospho-ERK is partially mediated by integrin av, as siRNA knockdown of Itgav decreases phospho-ERK (p=0.0040).

Crucially, CCN2 enhances the direct interaction between ERK and DUSP6, a dual-specificity phosphatase predominant in LECs. While CCN2 increases phospho-ERK, it simultaneously recruits DUSP6 to ERK, creating a compensatory negative modulation mechanism. DUSP6 knockdown increases CCN2-induced phospho-ERK levels across multiple time points (p<0.001 at 15 m and 4 h, p=0.004 at 48 h).

In vivo Matrigel plug assays demonstrate that exogenous CCN2 increases the number of Podoplanin-positive vessels, with both phospho-ERK and DUSP6 detected in Podoplanin-positive cells of CCN2-supplemented plugs (p<0.05). Interestingly, in vitro cell proliferation assays revealed a weak growth inhibitory effect of CCN2 (p=0.003 at 50 ng/mL, p=0.02 at 100 ng/mL at 24 h), which the authors attribute to the transient and non-persistent nature of CCN2-induced phospho-ERK. This discrepancy between in vitro inhibition and in vivo promotion is interpreted as a consequence of ECM and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) effects in Matrigel. The authors conclude that CCN2-mediated lymphangiogenesis is regulated by the DUSP6-mediated negative modulation of ERK signaling and suggest integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6 as potential therapeutic targets in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), where CCN2 is elevated and associated with metastasis.

CCN2 expression correlates with lymph node metastasis in OSCC and could be a therapeutic target.

Executive Summary
This study investigates the role of cellular communication network factor 2 (CCN2), also known as connective tissue growth factor (CTGF), in lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs), where its contribution to lymphangiogenesis remained largely unelucidated. While CCN2 increases phospho-ERK, it simultaneously recruits DUSP6 to ERK, creating a compensatory negative modulation mechanism. DUSP6 knockdown increases CCN2-induced phospho-ERK levels across multiple time points (p<0.001 at 15 m and 4 h, p=0.004 at 48 h).

In vivo Matrigel plug assays demonstrate that exogenous CCN2 increases the number of Podoplanin-positive vessels, with both phospho-ERK and DUSP6 detected in Podoplanin-positive cells of CCN2-supplemented plugs (p<0.05). Interestingly, in vitro cell proliferation assays revealed a weak growth inhibitory effect of CCN2 (p=0.003 at 50 ng/mL, p=0.02 at 100 ng/mL at 24 h), which the authors attribute to the transient and non-persistent nature of CCN2-induced phospho-ERK. This discrepancy between in vitro inhibition and in vivo promotion is interpreted as a consequence of ECM and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) effects in Matrigel. The authors conclude that CCN2-mediated lymphangiogenesis is regulated by the DUSP6-mediated negative modulation of ERK signaling and suggest integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6 as potential therapeutic targets in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), where CCN2 is elevated and associated with metastasis.

Research Context
CCN2 (CTGF) is a well-known angiogenic factor that activates MAPKs such as p38, ERK, and JNK in vascular endothelial cells. CCN2 functions through direct binding to integrin avb3 in vascular endothelial cells to promote proliferation, chemotaxis, and tubule formation. Lymphangiogenesis is critical for embryonic development, tissue repair, and inflammatory reactions, with VEGF-C-VEGFR-3 signaling playing a crucial role. Previous fibrosis models (renal, peritoneal, liver) show CTGF enhances lymphangiogenesis through interaction with VEGF-C. Despite its role in blood vessel angiogenesis, CCN2 signaling in lymphatic endothelial cells in lymphangiogenic signaling has not been elucidated.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is what are the downstream signaling pathways of CCN2 in primary cultured LECs and how do these effects contribute to lymphangiogenesis. The authors hypothesized that CCN2 would modulate LEC marker expression, lymphangiogenic factor levels, and intracellular signaling, specifically through integrin interactions. They further investigated whether the ERK phosphorylation induced by CCN2 is transient and regulated by DUSP6-mediated dephosphorylation. The in vivo hypothesis posited that exogenous CCN2 would promote lymphatic vessel formation in the Matrigel plug model.

Methodological Details
The study used primary cultured C57BL/6 mouse LECs up to 6 passages, cultured in 0.1% gelatin-coated dishes with EGM2 medium at 37°C and 5% CO₂. LECs were treated with 0, 12.5, 25, 50, 100, or 200 ng/mL of recombinant rat CCN2/CTGF for 3 h to assess gene expression. For cell proliferation assays, cells were plated at 2 × 10⁴ cells per well and treated with 0, 10, 50, or 100 ng/mL CCN2 for 24, 48, and 72 h. Gene expression was analyzed by quantitative RT-PCR using TB Green Premix ExTaq II and a LightCycler96 after cDNA synthesis from 1 μg of total RNA. siRNAs were designed via siDirect ver.2, and LECs (1.5 × 10⁵ cells) were transfected with 25 pmol of target or non-target siRNA using Lipofectamine RNAiMAX. Western blotting was performed on 5–20 µg protein samples, transferred to PVDF membranes, and visualized with ECL Prime and ImageQuant TL 8.1. Phospho-receptor tyrosine kinase array was performed using 200 µg of total protein incubated with the receptor-spotted membrane at 4°C for 24 h. Immunoprecipitation used 200 µg of total protein incubated with anti-ERK or anti-DUSP6 antibody overnight at 4°C followed by Protein A magnetic bead capture. In vivo Matrigel plug assay used male 8-week-old C57BL/6 mice, injecting 450 µL Matrigel mixed with 8.33 µg CCN2 (n=4) or 50 µL PBS (n=3). All experiments were performed more than three times, except the RTK assay (n=2), with statistical significance set at p < 0.05.

Procedures And Architectures
Gene expression of LEC markers (Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1) and lymphangiogenic factors (Vegfc, Vegfd, Flt4) was measured by quantitative RT-PCR at 3 h post-treatment. Phosphorylation of receptor tyrosine kinases was assessed using a phospho-RTK array kit at 5 min after treatment with 100 ng/mL CTGF. Intracellular signaling was examined by measuring phosphorylation of p38, JNK, AKT, NFκB, and Smad proteins, and ERK. Integrin mRNA levels (Itgav, Itga9, Itga2b, Itgb1, Itgb2, Itgb3) were determined by RT-PCR in CCN2-treated LECs. siRNA-mediated knockdown of integrin av and DUSP6 was used to determine the necessity of these proteins for CCN2-induced ERK phosphorylation. Immunoprecipitation assays confirmed ERK-DUSP6 interaction by co-precipitating ERK with anti-DUSP6 or DUSP6 with anti-ERK antibodies. Matrigel plugs were analyzed at day 7 for Podoplanin-positive vessels, CD31-positive cavities, and b3-Tubulin-positive peripheral nerves using immunohistochemistry. Sections were stained with hematoxylin-eosin and visualized by fluorescence and confocal microscopy (LSM710).

Key Results
CCN2 dose-dependently increased expression of Lyve1, Podoplanin, and Prox1 up to 100 ng/mL, with dramatic decrease at 200 ng/mL compared to 100 ng/mL. CCN2 increased Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 expression but did not affect Kdr expression, while VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 phosphorylations remained unchanged. Phospho-ERK was significantly increased by CCN2 (p<0.001) while p38, JNK, AKT, NFκB, and Smad phosphorylations were unchanged. Total ERK protein levels were not affected by CCN2 treatment. Knockdown of integrin av by siRNA partially decreased CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040), while knockdown of integrin a9 resulted in slight increase and integrin b1 suppression abolished CCN2-induced phospho-ERK. Treatment with 10, 50, and 100 ng/mL CCN2 for 24 h suppressed LEC growth (p=0.22, 0.92, >0.99 respectively), with 50 and 100 ng/mL showing significant inhibition at 24 h (p=0.003, p=0.02). Phospho-ERK peaked at 15 min, continued increasing to 4 h, decreased at 8 h, and increased after 48 h. DUSP6 was predominant among DUSPs in LECs; Dusp16 was undetected. Immunoprecipitation showed DUSP6 co-precipitated with ERK, and their interaction was enhanced by CCN2. DUSP6 siRNA increased phospho-ERK levels at 15 min, 4 h, 24 h, and 48 h post-CCN2 treatment (p<0.001 for 15 m and 4 h, p=0.04 for 24 h, p=0.004 for 48 h). In Matrigel plug assays, Podoplanin-positive vessel number and percentage increased in CCN2 gels (p<0.05), with phospho-ERK and DUSP6 significantly increased in Podoplanin-positive cells. CD31-positive cavities and b3-Tubulin-positive peripheral nerves were also increased in CCN2 plugs.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
CCN2 upregulates Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 in LECs, but the lack of VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 phosphorylation suggests CCN2 and endogenous VEGF-C do not activate VEGFR signaling upstream of ERK. The ERK phosphorylation signal is partially mediated by integrin av, indicating integrins serve as the primary receptors for CCN2 signaling in LECs. The transient and non-persistent nature of CCN2-induced phospho-ERK suggests a concomitant mechanism for suppressing ERK activation. DUSP6 functions as a negative modulator of ERK signaling in LECs, enhancing the binding of ERK to its kinase interaction motif to induce dephosphorylation. The authors suggest that integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6-mediated lymphangiogenesis may be therapeutic targets in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), where CCN2 is elevated and associated with lymph node metastasis.

Contradictions And Limitations
In vitro cell proliferation assays showed CCN2 weakly suppressed growth (p=0.003 at 50 ng/mL, p=0.02 at 100 ng/mL at 24 h), contradicting the in vivo Matrigel results where CCN2 promoted lymphangiogenesis. The authors attribute this discrepancy to ECM and matrix metalloproteinase effects in Matrigel, noting that CCN2-signaling is mediated by ECM and proteolytic processing by MMP-2,3. The interaction between CCN2 and integrin a5 was not investigated because no such interaction had been reported in LECs. DUSP16 was undetected by RT-PCR, limiting the full characterization of DUSP family members in LECs. The relationship between FOXC1, FOXC2 (negative ERK regulators) and DUSP6 has not been analyzed. The study used primary cultured LECs only, and the mechanisms in intact tissue or in vivo without Matrigel might differ.

Claims
CCN2 activates ERK signaling in lymphatic endothelial cells via interaction with integrin av and not through VEGFR signaling. Phospho-ERK was significantly increased by CCN2 (p<0.001), while phospho-VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 were unchanged. Knockdown of integrin av by siRNA partially decreased CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Total ERK protein levels were not affected by CCN2 treatment. Knockdown of integrin a9 resulted in a slight increase of CCN2-induced phospho-ERK. In integrin b1 suppressed LECs, phospho-ERK was increased without CCN2 stimulation, suggesting compensatory integrin a5 expression. Integrin av may serve as a druggable target to modulate CCN2-ERK signaling in lymphangiogenesis. The mechanism differs from the VEGFR-VEGFC axis that drives blood vessel angiogenesis.
CCN2 enhances lymphangiogenesis in vivo, but this effect is internally regulated by DUSP6-mediated dephosphorylation of ERK. In Matrigel plug assays, Podoplanin-positive vessels and phospho-ERK/DUSP6 in Podoplanin-positive cells were significantly increased by exogenous CCN2 (p<0.05). CCN2 enhanced the interaction of ERK and DUSP6 in LECs. DUSP6 siRNA increased phospho-ERK levels at 15 min and 4 h (p<0.001) and at 48 h (p=0.004) post-CCN2 treatment. In vitro proliferation assays showed CCN2 weakly suppressed LEC growth (p=0.003 at 50 ng/mL, p=0.02 at 100 ng/mL). CCN2-induced phospho-ERK was non-persistent and transient, decreasing at 8 h. DUSP6 may act as a checkpoint to prevent excessive ERK activation during lymphangiogenesis. The DUSP6-ERK interaction represents a specific regulatory node in CCN2 signaling.
CCN2 expression correlates with lymph node metastasis in OSCC and could be a therapeutic target. CCN2 expression in OSCC correlated with lymph node metastasis. High CCN2 expression and MMP3 were associated with worse prognosis in head and neck cancers. LSD1 inhibitors markedly downregulated CTGF mRNA and protein expression in an OSCC xenograft model. The direct link between CCN2-DUSP6 signaling specifically driving OSCC metastasis is not directly proven in this study. Integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6-mediated lymphangiogenesis may be therapeutic targets of OSCC.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Multiple integrins (av, a9, b1) and DUSP family members were screened for CCN2 sensitivity via siRNA knockdown and RT-PCR. Time-course experiments (15 min to 72 h) and dose-response curves (0–200 ng/mL) established the kinetics and dose-sensitivity of the response. Phospho-RTK array screened multiple RTK targets, and immunoprecipitation verified the ERK-DUSP6 interaction directly. In vivo Matrigel plugs (n=4 per group) and immunohistochemical staining confirmed the in vitro findings in tissue. The authors addressed the discrepancy between in vitro inhibition and in vivo promotion by invoking ECM and MMP processing effects.

Ethical Considerations
All experiments were performed in compliance with relevant laws and institutional guidelines and were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of Fukuoka University (approval number: 2008024). Male 8-week-old C57BL/6 mice were used under specific pathogen-free conditions.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows dose-dependent expression of Lyve1, Pdpn, and Prox1 up to 100 ng/mL, with a dramatic decrease at 200 ng/mL. Figure 1B shows CCN2 increased Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 expression but not Kdr. Figure 2A and 2B show phospho-ERK was significantly increased by CCN2 (p<0.001), while Figure 2C shows total ERK was not affected. Figure 3A shows Itgav, Itga9, and Itgb1 predominantly expressed in LECs; Figure 3B shows integrin av siRNA partially decreased phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Figure 4A shows cell growth suppression at 24 h (p=0.22, 0.92, >0.99) and 50/100 ng/mL significant inhibition (p=0.003, p=0.02). Figure 5A shows DUSP6 predominance in LECs; Figure 5B shows enhanced ERK-DUSP6 interaction by CCN2. Figure 5D shows DUSP6 siRNA increased phospho-ERK at 15 m (p<0.001), 4 h (p<0.001), 24 h (p=0.04), and 48 h (p=0.004) post-CCN2. Figure 6A shows blood vessels macroscopically observed on CCN2 plugs at day 7. Figure 6B and 6C show Podoplanin-positive vessels and tubular structures in CCN2 gel. Figure 7A, 7B, and 7C show phospho-ERK and DUSP6 in Podoplanin-positive cells were significantly increased in CCN2 gel (p<0.05).

Three Takeaways
1. CCN2 activates ERK signaling in lymphatic endothelial cells via integrin av, not through VEGFR signaling, and upregulates key lymphatic markers (Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1). 2. CCN2 enhances the direct interaction between ERK and DUSP6 in LECs; DUSP6 functions as a negative modulator, and its knockdown increases CCN2-induced phospho-ERK across multiple time points (p<0.001 at 15 m and 4 h). 3. Exogenous CCN2 promotes in vivo lymphangiogenesis in Matrigel plug assays (Podoplanin+ vessels increased, p<0.05), while in vitro experiments reveal a weak growth inhibitory effect, a discrepancy explained by ECM and MMP processing.

summary.title: Tumor PD-L1 selectively suppresses type I interferon in myeloid cells to suppress CTL recruitment to promote lung metastasis
summary.authors: John D Klement; Priscilla S Redd; Chunwan Lu; Alyssa D Merting; Dakota B Poschel; Dafeng Yang; Gang Zhou; David H Munn; Kebin Liu
summary.field_subfield: Immunology / Cancer Immunology and Immunotherapy
summary.executive_summary: This study identifies a novel mechanism whereby tumor cell PD-L1 (tPD-L1) drives lung metastasis not by directly inhibiting cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) effector function, but through an indirect myeloid-cell-dependent axis. The authors first demonstrate that tPD-L1 exerts no direct protective effect on tumor cells against antigen-specific CTLs in in vitro systems using 4T1 (TNBC) and CT26 (MMRp CRC) cell lines. In vivo, knocking out PD-L1 in these tumor cells produces no difference in primary tumor growth but significantly reduces lung metastasis in a CTL-dependent, adaptive-immune-dependent manner. Single-cell RNA sequencing of CD45+ leukocytes from 4T1-colonized lungs, followed by flow cytometry and in vitro myeloid cell co-culture experiments, reveals that tPD-L1 engages PD-1 on lung-resident myeloid cells (mPD-1), triggering SHP-2-mediated inhibition of type I interferon (IFN-I) and STAT1 signaling. This suppresses the expression of CTL-recruiting chemokines Cxcl9 and Cxcl10. The authors confirm the myeloid-dependent role by depleting myeloid cells with clodronate liposomes, which abolishes the tPD-1-mediated metastatic advantage. Furthermore, human patient single-cell sequencing data from metastatic basal cell carcinoma patients before and after PD-1 blockade supports the finding that PD-1 blockade releases myeloid cell differentiation restriction, restores IFN-I signaling, and increases CTL-recruiting chemokine expression. The study establishes a novel tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 signaling axis that uncouples PD-L1 function at the primary and metastatic sites, providing a mechanical basis for why PD-L1 expression at metastatic sites drives durable remission in responders.

claims.description: tPD-L1 does not directly protect tumor cells from CTL-mediated killing when only target tumor cells and antigen-specific CTLs are present.
tPD-L1 promotes lung metastasis by targeting PD-1 on myeloid cells, suppressing type I IFN and CXCL9/10, and impairing CTL recruitment.
PD-1 blockade in human metastatic basal cell carcinoma reverses myeloid cell differentiation restriction and restores IFN signaling and CTL-recruiting chemokines.

Executive Summary
This study identifies a novel mechanism whereby tumor cell PD-L1 (tPD-L1) drives lung metastasis not by directly inhibiting cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) effector function, but through an indirect myeloid-cell-dependent axis. The authors first demonstrate that tPD-L1 exerts no direct protective effect on tumor cells against antigen-specific CTLs in in vitro systems using 4T1 (TNBC) and CT26 (MMRp CRC) cell lines. In vivo, knocking out PD-L1 in these tumor cells produces no difference in primary tumor growth but significantly reduces lung metastasis in a CTL-dependent, adaptive-immune-dependent manner. Single-cell RNA sequencing of CD45+ leukocytes from 4T1-colonized lungs, followed by flow cytometry and in vitro myeloid cell co-culture experiments, reveals that tPD-L1 engages PD-1 on lung-resident myeloid cells (mPD-1), triggering SHP-2-mediated inhibition of type I interferon (IFN-I) and STAT1 signaling. This suppresses the expression of CTL-recruiting chemokines Cxcl9 and Cxcl10. The authors confirm the myeloid-dependent role by depleting myeloid cells with clodronate liposomes, which abolishes the tPD-1-mediated metastatic advantage. Furthermore, human patient single-cell sequencing data from metastatic basal cell carcinoma patients before and after PD-1 blockade supports the finding that PD-1 blockade releases myeloid cell differentiation restriction, restores IFN-I signaling, and increases CTL-recruiting chemokine expression. The study establishes a novel tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 signaling axis that uncouples PD-L1 function at the primary and metastatic sites, providing a mechanical basis for why PD-L1 expression at metastatic sites drives durable remission in responders.

Research Context
PD-L1 and PD-1 checkpoint blockade is a cornerstone of cancer immunotherapy, but the mechanism underlying tPD-L1 induction of immune suppression via an intermediate cell is incompletely understood. Emerging data suggests PD-1/L1 blockade response may depend on tumor anatomic sites, occurring principally at metastatic sites rather than the primary tumor. A defining hallmark of PD-1/L1 ICB is sustained disease remission, and since metastatic growth is the dominant cause of mortality, durable survival must arise from coordinated suppression of metastases. Robust tumor expression of PD-L1 has been shown to promote both micro- and macro-metastatic growth, with enhancement at metastatic tumor sites as compared to primary tumor sites. However, how tPD-L1 might differentially drive metastasis from primary tumor is unknown. The importance of PD-1 expression in non-T cell populations, including myeloid, dendritic, and tumor cells, has emerged over the past decade, but how non-T cell-expressed PD-1 connects tPD-L1 to CTL suppression remains unclear.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether tPD-L1 provides direct protection to tumor cells from CTL killing or exerts an indirect effect mediated by third-party cells in the metastatic microenvironment. The authors tested whether tPD-L1 exerts no direct effect on CTL activity when only tumor cells and tumor-specific CTLs are present. The hypothesis was that a third factor, only present at the lung metastatic niche, is necessary for tPD-L1 to exert its indirect protective role. They further hypothesized that PD-1 expression on macrophages and dendritic cells mediates attenuation of type I interferon signaling in the metastatic niche. The prediction was that tPD-L1 targets myeloid cell-expressed PD-1 to suppress type I IFN expression and function, repressing Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 and impairing CTL recruitment to lung metastases. They also aimed to determine if these findings hold in human metastatic disease and whether PD-1 blockade reverses the suppressive myeloid phenotype.

Methodological Details
Two mouse tumor models were used: 4T1 (triple-negative breast cancer, TNBC) and CT26 (mismatch repair proficient colorectal cancer, MMRp CRC), chosen to mimic tumors with minimal response to ICB. The 2/20 tumor-specific CTL line recognizes the H2-Ld-restricted AH1 epitope (residues 6-14) of the gp70 protein endogenously expressed by 4T1 and CT26 cells. PD-L1 was knocked out in 4T1 and CT26 cells by co-transfecting HEK293FT cells with pCMV-VSV-G, psPAX2, and lentiCRISPRv2 plasmids using Lipofectamine 2000 to produce CRISPR lentivirus. Primary tumors were established by orthotopic injection at the right second mammary gland (4T1) or right flank (CT26), while experimental metastasis models utilized lateral tail vein injection. Single-cell RNA sequencing captured CD45+ leukocytes from 4T1-colonized lungs after 14 days, with approximately 7500 cells per sample on a Chromium Chip B (10x Genomics). Bulk RNA sequencing was performed on lungs harvested 7 days after i.v. tail vein injection of 4T1.WT or 4T1.PDL1-KO, with RNA extracted using Direct-zol RNA microprep kit. For human analysis, mRNA and survival datasets were extracted from the TCGA database, and data from BMS038 and PRJEB23709 (PD-1 treatment response) were accessed for single-cell analysis. Myeloid cells were depleted in vivo using clodronate liposomes in tumor-bearing mice. For neutralization, 200 µg of anti-CD8α (53-6.7) or isotype control (2A3) was injected i.v. every other day.

Procedures And Architectures
In vitro CTL-tumor interaction was performed using 2/20 CTLs with 4T1 and CT26 cells, allowing antigen-specific cytotoxicity within minutes without naïve differentiation. Raw264.7 macrophages were co-cultured with 4T1 cells to assess PD-1 engagement and SHP-2 activation, with PD-1 upregulation occurring in a cell-contact and IFNAR-dependent manner. Myeloid cell surface PD-1 expression was confirmed via flow cytometry in 4T1-colonized lungs. SHP-2 activation and pSTAT1 levels were measured in RAW cells upon 4T1 tPD-L1 engagement, with decreased MHCII expression on both 4T1 and RAW cells. RAW264.7 PD-1 loss was assessed using the TLR3 ligand poly(I:C) stimulation as measured by surface marker BST2. In scRNA-seq analysis, cells were clustered using the first fifty principal components, and myeloid and T cell clusters were reclustered based on the top twenty principal components. The tPD-L1 loss gene signature was created by isolating genes whose expression increased by at least two-fold with a padj < 0.05 from the bulk RNA-seq dataset. The SHP-2 activation signature was calculated from myeloid cells treated with SHP099, and scores were inversed. Batch effects in human melanoma data were corrected by Harmony.

Key Results
No difference in primary tumor growth was observed between PD-L1 WT and PD-L1 KO 4T1 or CT26 at the site of injection, supporting the in vitro finding of no direct CTL protection. Loss of PD-L1 did not affect initial tumor cell colonization in the lung, as measured by gp70 levels one day after injection. PD-L1-deficient and competent 4T1 metastasized equally in RAGII-KO mice, indicating tPD-L1 requires a functioning adaptive immune system. Ablation of MHC class I antigen presentation or antibody-mediated CD8+ T cell depletion revealed that tPD-L1 drives metastasis by suppressing CTL killing. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that tPD-L1 engages myeloid PD-1 (mPD-1) to antagonize type I interferon and STAT1 signaling, repressing Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 expression. Myeloid cell surface PD-1 expression was enhanced following tPD-L1 loss, and RAW cell surface PD-1 was upregulated in a cell-contact manner following 4T1 co-culture. Engagement of tPD-L1 with RAW cell PD-1 enhanced SHP-2 activation, decreased pSTAT1, and diminished MHCII on both 4T1 and RAW cells. Raw264.7 PD-1 loss led to increased sensitivity to poly(I:C) stimulation, measured by surface marker BST2. Disruption of either RAW PD-1 or 4T1 PD-L1 expression enhanced IFN-beta production, demonstrating a negative feedback circuit where PD-1/L1 is induced by and then attenuates IFN-I signaling. Depletion of myeloid cells by clodronate liposomes diminished tPD-L1 function in promoting lung tumor growth, confirming mPD-1 as the target. In human patients, PD-1 blockade released myeloid cell differentiation restriction, leading to enhanced IFN signaling, antigen presentation, and CTL-recruiting chemokine expression.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The authors conclude that the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis controls CTL tumor infiltration in lung metastasis, uncoupling the role of PD-L1 at the metastatic site from its primary tumor function. The finding that type I interferon induces both PD-L1 and PD-1 in myeloid cells, with PD-L1 upregulated more rapidly, supports the PD-1/L1 axis as a negative feedback circuit for IFN-I signaling. The paper suggests that the low response rates in interferon-alpha therapies may have been due to compensatory PD-1/L1 upregulation. The mechanism provides a structural basis for why PD-1/L1 ICB is effective in neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings: it restores CTL recruitment to metastases.

Contradictions And Limitations
One limitation is that the study exclusively analyzed lung metastases, which may have a uniquely inflamed microenvironment due to their location in barrier tissue. The study used two murine models (4T1, CT26), and results may not be perfectly generalizable to all metastatic settings or cell types. The paper notes conflicting findings for the role of tPD-L1 in contribution to PD-1 blockade efficacy, though consensus exists that PD-L1 may be sufficient but not necessary for response in primary tumors.

Claims
tPD-L1 does not directly protect tumor cells from CTL-mediated killing when only target tumor cells and antigen-specific CTLs are present. In vitro CTL-tumor interaction showed tPD-L1 confers no survival advantage to tumor cells encountering cognate peptide-MHC complexes. Primary tumor growth at injection site showed no difference between PD-L1 WT and KO 4T1 or CT26 cells. Initial tumor cell colonization in lung (gp70 level) was equal between WT and KO at 24 hours post-injection. No contradicting evidence reported; in vitro and in vivo data both converge on no direct effect of PD-L1 on CTL cytotoxicity. This shifts the focus of PD-L1 function from a direct 'molecular shield' to an indirect mediator through a third-party cell type.
tPD-L1 promotes lung metastasis by targeting PD-1 on myeloid cells, suppressing type I IFN and CXCL9/10, and impairing CTL recruitment. Increased CD3+ cells in lung were observed after tPD-L1 loss, but not in primary tumor. scRNA-seq identified tPD-L1 engaging myeloid PD-1 to antagonize IFN-I and STAT1 signaling, repressing Cxcl9 and Cxcl10. RAW cell PD-1 engagement by tPD-L1 enhanced SHP-2, decreased pSTAT1, and diminished MHCII. Myeloid cell depletion by clodronate liposomes abolished tPD-L1-mediated promotion of lung tumor growth. No change in bulk lung myeloid cell composition was observed, although enhanced antigen presentation machinery was detected in macrophages. This establishes a novel mechanistically distinct axis (tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10) for metastasis control.
PD-1 blockade in human metastatic basal cell carcinoma reverses myeloid cell differentiation restriction and restores IFN signaling and CTL-recruiting chemokines. Myeloid cell PHATE analysis in human patients revealed differentiation restriction released following PD-1 blockade. PD-1 blockade led to enhanced IFN signaling, antigen presentation, and CTL-recruiting chemokine expression in human myeloid cells. The paper acknowledges transcriptional heterogeneity between mouse and human myeloid cells, necessitating signature transfer methods. This provides human clinical relevance for the mouse-derived tPD-L1/mPD-1 axis.

Data And Code Availability
Human patient data from BMS038 was accessed from the authors' processed files at https://github.com/riazn/bms038_analysis. The paper does not explicitly state general code or data availability for the mouse experiments beyond the referenced patient datasets.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
tPD-L1 function was tested in two tumor systems (4T1, CT26) and validated with in vitro CTL-tumor interactions. Myeloid cell dependence was confirmed via clodronate liposome depletion. CTL dependence was confirmed by RAGII-KO mice and anti-CD8α neutralization. SHP-2 inhibitor (SHP099) was used to generate the activation signature, confirming the signaling node. PD-L2 was identified as a marker for IFN-stimulated myeloid cells, appearing as early as one day after injection. In scRNA-seq, high-quality cells were filtered (200 < feature count < 4000, mitochondrial < 10%), and doublets were manually and computationally (DoubletFinder) removed.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: Shows in vitro CTL-tumor interaction results demonstrating tPD-L1 confers no survival advantage to 4T1 and CT26 cells. Figure 2: Displays primary tumor growth data (no difference) and metastasis in MHC-I deficient and CD8+ depleted mice. Figure 3: Shows increased CD3+ cell infiltration in lung after tPD-L1 loss and equal colonization at 24h. Figure 4: Presents scRNA-seq UMAP and differential expression in CD45+ leukocytes from 4T1-colonized lungs. Figure 5: Shows Pdcd1lg2/PD-L2 as a marker of IFN-stimulated myeloid cells and flow cytometric validation. Figure 6: Details RAW cell co-culture experiments showing SHP-2 activation, pSTAT1 decrease, and IFN-beta enhancement. Figure 7: Presents human patient scRNA-seq and PHATE analysis showing differentiation restriction release by PD-1 blockade.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the discovery that tPD-L1 does not directly protect tumor cells from CTL killing but instead engages mPD-1 to suppress type I IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 signaling, thereby impairing CTL recruitment to metastases. 2. The strongest evidence is the convergent demonstration that tPD-L1 loss has no primary tumor effect but drastically reduces metastasis in a CTL-dependent, adaptive-immune-dependent manner, validated by scRNA-seq, clodronate myeloid depletion, and human PD-1 blockade response data. 3. The future path involves applying this axis to neoadjuvant/adjuvant immunotherapy design, potentially combining PD-1 blockade with IFN-I/TLR/STING agonists to reverse the suppressive myeloid phenotype at metastatic sites.

summary.authors: Glycan Microenvironments (University of California San Diego); Austen L Michalak (University of California San Diego); Greg W Trieger (University of California San Diego); Kelsey A Trieger (University of California San Diego); Kamil Godula (University of California San Diego)

summary.executive_summary: This study describes the development of a hydrogel-supported stem cell microarray platform designed to analyze the regulatory role of glycosaminoglycan (GAG) polysaccharides in growth factor signaling. Extracellular GAGs, particularly heparan sulfate (HS), are essential for forming signaling complexes with growth factors in the extracellular matrix, but their structural complexity makes structure-function relationship determination challenging. The authors integrate glycosaminoglycan-protein conjugates into a polyacrylamide hydrogel network, arrayed on glass surfaces, to directly measure GAG contributions to growth factor signaling in murine embryonic stem cells (ESCs). A key innovation is the chemical crosslinking of HS to gelatin matrix proteins (using NHS/EDC chemistry) to retain polysaccharides on the array during cell culture, a strategy validated to preserve both retention and protein-binding specificity. The platform was validated using Ext1 -/- murine ESCs, which lack endogenous cell-surface HS and are unresponsive to FGF2, making them an ideal model to isolate the effects of the arrayed glycans. Results demonstrated that NHS-crosslinked heparin provides ~5-to 10-fold higher FGF2 binding signal than non-covalently immobilized heparin and retains ~40% binding activity after 48 hours of culture. Signaling assays showed that immobilized heparin restores FGF2-stimulated MAPK (Erk1/2) phosphorylation in a dose-dependent manner, comparable in magnitude but somewhat lower than soluble heparin. The platform enables multiplexed, on-array analysis of diverse GAG structures (CS, HS, HA and sulfation mutants) in a spatially isolated format, facilitating rapid optimization of functional glycomaterials for stem cell-based regenerative therapies.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study describes the development of a hydrogel-supported stem cell microarray platform designed to analyze the regulatory role of glycosaminoglycan (GAG) polysaccharides in growth factor signaling. Extracellular GAGs, particularly heparan sulfate (HS), are essential for forming signaling complexes with growth factors in the extracellular matrix, but their structural complexity makes structure-function relationship determination challenging. The authors integrate glycosaminoglycan-protein conjugates into a polyacrylamide hydrogel network, arrayed on glass surfaces, to directly measure GAG contributions to growth factor signaling in murine embryonic stem cells (ESCs). A key innovation is the chemical crosslinking of HS to gelatin matrix proteins (using NHS/EDC chemistry) to retain polysaccharides on the array during cell culture, a strategy validated to preserve both retention and protein-binding specificity. The platform was validated using Ext1 -/- murine ESCs, which lack endogenous cell-surface HS and are unresponsive to FGF2, making them an ideal model to isolate the effects of the arrayed glycans. Results demonstrated that NHS-crosslinked heparin provides ~5-to 10-fold higher FGF2 binding signal than non-covalently immobilized heparin and retains ~40% binding activity after 48 hours of culture. Signaling assays showed that immobilized heparin restores FGF2-stimulated MAPK (Erk1/2) phosphorylation in a dose-dependent manner, comparable in magnitude but somewhat lower than soluble heparin. The platform enables multiplexed, on-array analysis of diverse GAG structures (CS, HS, HA and sulfation mutants) in a spatially isolated format, facilitating rapid optimization of functional glycomaterials for stem cell-based regenerative therapies.

Research Context
Extracellular glycosaminoglycans like heparan sulfate are essential regulatory components of the extracellular matrix, harboring binding sites for growth factors and morphogens. GAGs establish gradients of growth factors and promote the formation of active signaling complexes at the cell surface. The structural complexity and compositional heterogeneity of GAGs make establishing structure-function relationships difficult for biomaterial development. Hydrogel platforms decorated with peptides or proteins and growth factors have been used to support cell adhesion and differentiation. Stem cell arrays have enabled high-throughput analysis of cellular responses to environmental and culture conditions, but glycan components have been comparatively less explored. Recent advances in chemical, chemoenzymatic, and genetic engineering have produced chemically well-defined HS structures available for examination. Arrays of isolated HS structures on glass surfaces routinely profile the specificity of HS-binding proteins, but a platform for multiplexed, on-array analysis of HS-dependent cellular signaling is still needed.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can GAG polysaccharides be presented together with cell adhesion factors in microscopic islands on a non-adhesive surface to enable multiplexed analysis of glycan structures while minimizing cellular crosstalk? Does chemical crosslinking of HS to the gelatin matrix retain the polysaccharide on the array during cell culture without compromising its growth factor binding ability? Are the protein-binding specificities of the crosslinked GAG structures within the hydrogel matrix preserved after immobilization? Can the array platform directly assess changes in stem cell signaling in response to exogenous growth factor stimulation in the presence of arrayed GAGs? The hypothesis is that a hydrogel-supported GAG microarray will enable direct measurement of GAG contributions to growth factor signaling pathways in live embryonic stem cells. It is predicted that NHS-crosslinked heparin will show superior FGF2 binding capacity and retention compared to non-covalently immobilized heparin. It is predicted that the signaling response to FGF2 will be dose-dependent on the concentration of immobilized heparin on the array.

Methodological Details
A poly(acrylamide) hydrogel was deposited on glass according to the method by Brafman et al. and spotted with gelatin to support ESC growth. The gelatin substrate was loaded in its dehydrated form at 500 µg/mL in PBS for entrapping within the hydrogel network. Heparin (12 kDa) was used as a model HS glycan at concentrations of 50-750 µg/mL. NHS crosslinking was performed with heparin activated in HEPES buffer (100 mM, pH = 7.4) using EDC at 4°C for 18 hours. Size exclusion chromatography on a PD10 column was used to purify the crosslinked product and remove small molecule reagents. Crosslinking targeted ~15% carboxylic acid crosslinks per chain to balance retention with FGF-binding ability. Murine ESCs lacking Exostosin 1 (Ext1) were used as the cell model to isolate effects of arrayed GAGs from endogenous HS. Cells were seeded at 40,000 cells/cm², which produced consistent monolayers with no obvious signs of differentiation. The optimization tested seeding densities of 20,000 and 100,000 cells/cm² before selecting the intermediary density. Cell culture included 24 hours in embryonic culture media with LIF and FBS, followed by 24 hours in serum-free conditions for starvation. Signaling stimulation was with 0.5 ng/mL FGF2 for 15 minutes at 37°C. Cells were probed with FGF2 labeled with AlexaFluor 647 (FGF2-AF647) after washing for 3 hours prior to imaging. Soluble heparin (s-Hep, 5 µg/mL) served as a positive control for MAPK restoration in Ext1 -/- ESCs. FGF2 was retained on the array surface for 48 hours under cellular culture conditions at 37°C, 5% CO₂.

Procedures And Architectures
A polyacrylamide hydrogel scaffold was prepared by depositing on glass and spotted with gelatin (500 µg/mL) in PBS. Heparin was activated as NHS esters using EDC in HEPES buffer (100 mM, pH = 7.4) and treated at 4°C for 18 hours. The activated heparin was reacted with gelatin-entrapped lysine residues to form covalent crosslinks within the hydrogel spots. A panel of CS, DS, HA, and sulfation-mutated heparin structures (6OD-Hep, 2OD-Hep, ND-Hep, NAc-Hep) were arrayed on the hydrogel. The array was probed with three different proteins: FGF2, CS56 antibody, and HABP to assess binding specificity of each GAG species. Ext1 -/- ESCs were seeded on gelatin spots, grown for 24 hours in LIF/FBS media, washed, and cultured for an additional 24 hours without serum. For the signaling assay, cells were grown for 48 hours under optimized conditions, then placed in fresh serum-free media with 0.5 ng/mL FGF2. Stimulation lasted 15 minutes at 37°C, followed by cell fixation, permeabilization, and immunostaining for pErk1/2 and total Erk1/2. Fluorescence signals were detected using a microarray scanner and validated via fluorescence microscopy and ImageJ analysis. The ratio of pERK (green) to total ERK (red) signal was used to quantify the signaling response.

Key Results
NHS-crosslinked heparin provided ~5-to 10-fold higher FGF2 binding signal compared to non-covalently immobilized heparin on the array. After 18 hours of culture, the heparin array showed an initial decrease in binding, but ~40% of FGF2 binding activity was retained after 48 hours. FGF2 bound most strongly to fully sulfated heparin, with progressive loss of activity upon removal of 6-O-, 2-O-, and N-sulfates. CS56 and HABP exhibited high specificity for CS and HA, respectively, confirming that crosslinking did not alter protein-binding specificity. In Ext1 -/- ESCs, only conditions with immobilized or soluble heparin showed a significant increase in Erk1/2 phosphorylation upon FGF2 stimulation. FGF2 stimulation showed a heparin dose-responsive ERK1/2 phosphorylation with immobilized heparin concentrations from 0 to 500 µg/mL. MAPK activity on the arrayed heparin was somewhat lower compared to its soluble form (5 µg/mL). ERK1/2 protein levels were similar across all conditions, confirming that the change in phosphorylation ratio reflects true signaling activation. Ext1 -/- ESCs maintained high expression of the embryonic marker Oct4 and showed no differentiation via the neural marker Nestin under array conditions.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The reduced MAPK activity on the array compared to soluble heparin may be due to more limited accessibility of immobilized heparin to only a subset of FGFRs localized at cell contact points. The retention of ~40% binding activity after 48 hours suggests that the covalent tethering strategy provides sufficient stability for short-term signaling assays. The dose-dependent response confirms that GAG sulfation density directly modulates FGF2 receptor activation, supporting the hypothesis that HS governs GF signaling through structural determinants. The platform demonstrates that GAG-protein conjugates can create stable ECM-mimetic microenvironments capable of binding FGF2 and influencing ESC signaling. By separating cell colonies on non-adhesive areas, the array format minimizes cellular crosstalk and allows direct readout of glycan-specific signaling.

Contradictions And Limitations
The array demonstrated only ~40% retention of FGF2 binding after 48 hours, indicating that for longer-term cultures, additional stabilization or re-application of the GAG may be required. The initial decrease in binding during the first 18 hours suggests some degradation or diffusion of the immobilized heparin during cell culture. The authors note that the arrayed heparin showed somewhat lower MAPK activity than the soluble form, a limitation that may be important for quantitative comparisons. The study was limited to one cell type (murine Ext1 -/- ESCs) and one growth factor (FGF2), precluding generalization to broader cell lines or other signaling pathways. The random seed or exact train/test split for the microarray design is not explicitly reported, limiting reproducibility of the spatial layout.

Claims
The NHS-crosslinking strategy retains HS on the hydrogel array during ESC culture without compromising its protein-binding specificity. Covalently linked heparin showed ~5-to 10-fold higher FGF2 binding signal than non-covalent heparin. Binding specificity was preserved as removal of sulfation groups caused progressive loss of activity as expected. CS56 and HABP retained high specificity for their respective ligands after crosslinking. ~40% retention of binding after 48 hours indicates significant loss of GAG integrity or accessibility during culture. Initial decrease in binding within 18 hours suggests partial instability of the covalent attachment. The platform can be used to screen multiple GAG structures on a single array for GF-binding activities. Crosslinking chemistry can be adapted for other GAG-protein conjugates beyond heparin.
The array platform enables direct, rapid, and dose-dependent detection of FGF2-mediated MAPK signaling in stem cells mediated by immobilized GAGs. ERK1/2 phosphorylation was significantly increased only in the presence of immobilized or soluble heparin. FGF2 stimulation showed a dose-responsive ERK1/2 phosphorylation with heparin at 0-500 µg/mL. The signaling was validated via fluorescence microscopy confirming co-localization of pERK and ERK. MAPK activity was lower on the array than with soluble heparin, suggesting accessibility constraints. Quantitative comparisons between arrayed and soluble GAG signaling require consideration of accessibility effects. The platform accelerates the development of bioactive glycomaterials for regenerative medicine.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study tested heparin at concentrations from 50 to 750 µg/mL to determine dose-dependent effects. Three seeding densities (20,000, 40,000, and 100,000 cells/cm²) were screened to optimize colony growth. The array was probed with multiple ligands (FGF2, CS56, HABP) to confirm binding specificity for each GAG species. The control included soluble heparin (5 µg/mL) as a benchmark for MAPK restoration in Ext1 -/- ESCs. The Ext1 -/- ESC cell model was chosen specifically to eliminate endogenous HS interference, serving as a biological ablation. A series of sulfation mutants (6OD-Hep, 2OD-Hep, ND-Hep, NAc-Hep) were tested to ablate specific modifications. The array was validated using fluorescence microscopy and ImageJ analysis to confirm signal co-localization.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the cellular microarray approach: A depicts gelatin hydrogels on acrylamide supporting ESC culture with sulfated GAGs; B shows GAG structure and sulfation patterns. Figure 2A shows covalent heparin superior FGF2 binding; B shows FGF2 retention for 48 hours; C shows GAG molecular recognition selectivity. Figure 3A shows Ext1 -/- ESCs on gelatin spots at optimized seeding density forming consistent monolayers. Figure 3B shows Oct4 expression (embryonic marker) and lack of Nestin (differentiation marker) in cultured cells. Figure 3C shows ESC growth on gelatin with heparin under serum-free conditions, demonstrating no negative effects. Figure 4A shows Ext1 -/- ESCs on gelatin spots with heparin, grown for 48 hours under optimized conditions for the signaling assay. Figure 4B shows the ERK1/2 phosphorylation readout from the array scanner, with a green (pERK) and red (ERK) signal ratio. Figure 4C shows fluorescence microscopy validation of the arrayed cells confirming signal co-localization. Figure 4D shows the dose-dependent ERK1/2 phosphorylation with increasing immobilized heparin concentrations.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a hydrogel-supported GAG microarray platform enabling multiplexed analysis of GAG-mediated growth factor signaling in live stem cells. 2. The strongest evidence is the dose-dependent restoration of FGF2-induced Erk1/2 phosphorylation by immobilized heparin, validated across multiple GAG species and verified by microscopy. 3. The future path lies in leveraging the platform to screen synthetic and chemoenzymatic HS structures for optimizing functional glycomaterials in stem cell-based regenerative therapies.

summary.title: Robust Brain State Decoding using Bidirectional Long Short Term Memory Networks in functional MRI
summary.authors: Anant Mittal (University of Maryland); Priya Aggarwal (Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology); Luiz Pessoa (University of Maryland); Anubha Gupta (Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology)
summary.field_subfield: Neuroscience / Deep Learning (Brain-computer interface, fMRI state decoding)
summary.type_of_paper: Research article / Methods and validation study
summary.executive_summary: This paper proposes and validates a bidirectional Long Short Term Memory (bi-LSTM) network architecture for decoding brain states from functional MRI (fMRI) data. The central innovation is the use of both forward and backward temporal information to account for the inherent latency and dynamics of the BOLD response, removing the need for conventional time-delay adjustments between stimulus presentation and neural response. The authors demonstrate that conventional unidirectional LSTMs, which only capture past temporal context, are insufficient for capturing the full dynamics of fMRI data where future context is informative. The bi-LSTM is implemented with three merging schemes (concatenation, addition, averaging) and evaluated on the Human Connectome Project (HCP) working memory task dataset (2-back and 0-back tasks across four stimulus categories: tools, places, faces, body parts). The model processes 405 time-points of 360 cortical ROIs, predicting 9 brain states (task blocks + fixation + controls). The core quantitative result shows that the bi-LSTM (concatenation variant) achieves 0.84 ± 0.02 classification accuracy compared to 0.66 ± 0.18 for the unidirectional LSTM, representing an 18% absolute improvement. The model was trained with 10-fold inter-subject cross-validation, class-weight balancing for the imbalanced 'others' class, and a window size of 40 with 10-point overlap. The results support the hypothesis that both past and future temporal contexts improve brain state decoding, and the bi-LSTM framework eliminates the dependency on pre-calculated BOLD delay estimations.

claims.description: A bidirectional LSTM architecture outperforms unidirectional LSTM for brain state decoding by capturing both past and future temporal context in fMRI BOLD response.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper proposes and validates a bidirectional Long Short Term Memory (bi-LSTM) network architecture for decoding brain states from functional MRI (fMRI) data. The central innovation is the use of both forward and backward temporal information to account for the inherent latency and dynamics of the BOLD response, removing the need for conventional time-delay adjustments between stimulus presentation and neural response. The authors demonstrate that conventional unidirectional LSTMs, which only capture past temporal context, are insufficient for capturing the full dynamics of fMRI data where future context is informative. The bi-LSTM is implemented with three merging schemes (concatenation, addition, averaging) and evaluated on the Human Connectome Project (HCP) working memory task dataset (2-back and 0-back tasks across four stimulus categories: tools, places, faces, body parts). The model processes 405 time-points of 360 cortical ROIs, predicting 9 brain states (task blocks + fixation + controls). The core quantitative result shows that the bi-LSTM (concatenation variant) achieves 0.84 ± 0.02 classification accuracy compared to 0.66 ± 0.18 for the unidirectional LSTM, representing an 18% absolute improvement. The model was trained with 10-fold inter-subject cross-validation, class-weight balancing for the imbalanced 'others' class, and a window size of 40 with 10-point overlap. The results support the hypothesis that both past and future temporal contexts improve brain state decoding, and the bi-LSTM framework eliminates the dependency on pre-calculated BOLD delay estimations.

Research Context
Advances in non-invasive neuroimaging like fMRI are helping determine cognitive or perceptual states through brain-state decoding. Conventional decoding methods involved massive univariate analysis measuring activity from thousands of brain locations separately. Multivariate analysis integrates distributed but overlapping information across the spatial domain. Recent advances in time-sensitive machine learning have attracted attention for sequential modeling. Long short-term memory models have shown to perform better than conventional decoding models in characterizing dynamic fMRI information. The ratio of oxygenated to de-oxygenated blood level serves as the representative of underlying neuronal activation. Due to the time-lag observed in the peak of BOLD response, it is typically not synchronized with stimulus presentation. Conventionally, before training any decoding model, each time point is adjusted according to estimated delay of the BOLD signal. This assumes that all fMRI voxels have the same response delay. LSTM models store information from the past as contextual information for learning robust features. However, because of variations in latency of BOLD responses across time, temporal context from the future is also important for capturing dynamics. The conventional LSTM does not capture future temporal context.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a bidirectional LSTM architecture, which captures both past and future temporal context, improves brain state decoding accuracy compared to a unidirectional LSTM. The authors hypothesize that because of the dynamics and inherent latency in fMRI BOLD responses, future temporal context is crucial for accurate decoding. The conventional LSTM is hypothesized to be insufficient as it is neither encoded nor captured by the unidirectional structure. The proposed bi-LSTM should allow for explicitly modeling the dynamics of BOLD response without any delay adjustment. The hypothesis predicts that the bi-LSTM will perform better than its unidirectional counterpart in terms of accuracy predicting brain states. The study aims to demonstrate that two hidden activations of forward and reverse directions collated to build the model's memory robustly predict brain states at every time instance. The validation is performed on working memory fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project. The performance is compared directly with the conventional unidirectional counterpart in the brain state decoding task.

Methodological Details
Data was sourced from the task fMRI data of working memory from the Human Connectome Project. N = 400 participants were randomly selected from the N = 1200 data release. Participants performed a working memory 2-back task or a 0-back control condition. The task combined category representation with four types of stimuli: tools, places, faces, and body parts. Data for two runs is available for each participant. Each scan produced a 405 time-points long sequence of fMRI volumes. Within each run, there were 8 task blocks for every task and stimuli combination, each lasting 27.5 seconds. Four fixation blocks of 15 seconds each occurred after two task blocks. The available data contained field-map based distortion correction, functional to structural alignment, and intensity normalization. Motion-related variables (6 translation parameters and their derivatives) were regressed out using 3dDeconvolve with the ortvec option in AFNI. Low frequency signals were regressed out using 3dDeconvolve with the polort option. Only cortical data was used, directly available in surface representation as part of the HCP preprocessing pipeline. The cortical parcellation developed by [7] was employed to separate brain areas based on architecture and functional connectivity. The parcellation collated individual voxels within each region by averaging to generate 360 regions of interest. The region-averaged timeseries was used as the input feature vector for the temporal analysis. The generated 405 time-points sequence of 360 ROIs were structured in a 360 by 405 2D-tensor. No stimuli and brain-state synchronization was performed to adjust for delay in the BOLD response. Each time-point in task blocks was marked as one of the brain-states, and fixation blocks were labeled as others, yielding S = 9 brain states.

Procedures And Architectures
The bi-LSTM processes time-series data in both directions using separate hidden layers. One LSTM network processes the input sequence in the normal time-order; another processes it in the reverse time-order. Two hidden activations are collated to generate the hidden cell state features of the RNN. Three merging schemes for combining activations were defined: vector concatenation (bi-LSTM-c), element-wise vector addition (bi-LSTM-a), and element-wise averaging (bi-LSTM-µ). The bi-LSTM used two hidden layers with each LSTM cell having 256 hidden activations to encode temporal dependencies. Input activations to layer l = 1 at time t are extracted from the 360 brain ROIs. The last layer of bi-LSTM is followed by a fully-connected layer having S = 9 neurons with softmax activation. Inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation was employed for performance comparison. Data from N = 400 participants was divided into 10 parts: 9 parts (N = 360) for model development and 1 part (N = 40) held unseen. The development set was randomly shuffled and split into 80-20 training-validation sets to tune hyperparameters and prevent over-fitting. The full-length training data was windowed into small overlapping sizes with window size w = 40 and overlap of 10 points. The model was implemented in the Keras deep learning framework. The model was trained on a GeForce GTX 980 GPU with batch size of 32. ADAM optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001 was used, with 100 epochs and no early stopping. A dropout of 0.3 was applied in LSTM layers during training to prevent over-fitting. Class weights were estimated using Sklearn's compute_class_weight and applied during loss function calculation to handle imbalanced classes. The conventional LSTM and a three-layer feed-forward Neural Network (ff-NN) were used as baselines with same number of layers and neural units.

Key Results
The overall accuracy of the unidirectional LSTM model was 0.66 ± 0.18. The classification accuracy of the bidirectional LSTM (bi-LSTM-c) was 0.84 ± 0.02. The bi-LSTM performed 18% better than its unidirectional counterpart in terms of accuracy in predicting the brain states. For every brain-state, the LSTM model miss-classified to a larger extent compared to the bi-LSTM-c model. The misclassification is highest for both models in the Others class. The second highest confusion, when participants were stimulated with faces and places, is with the task (0-back or 2-back). The model also gets confused between the stimuli body and tools. Mean normalised confusion matrices illustrate that the stimuli was detected correctly even when misclassified as task.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The bi-LSTM's superior performance demonstrates that both past and future temporal information are jointly required to capture the dynamics of BOLD response. The model works without any hard-coded delay adjustment, confirming that useful information is available in immediate future samples. The results emphasize that the temporal context from the future is important for generating accurate brain-state representations. The model is capable of learning discriminative feature representations of underlying cognitive processes from raw ROI timeseries. The colation of forward and reverse activations builds a richer memory of the model, enabling robust prediction at each time instance. The findings imply that temporal modeling approaches should account for the non-causal available information in fMRI sequences.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors worked with a fixed window length, noting that future work may involve tuning window-size and overlap for time-series chunking. The problem of class imbalance, although majorly handled by class weights, still requires more sophisticated handling. The class Others has much more time-instances than any other class, introducing inherent difficulty in balanced classification. The model sometimes gets confused between stimuli body and tools, suggesting a potential spatial or temporal overlap in these feature representations. The assumption that all fMRI voxels have the same response delay, which the model does not rely on, remains a simplification of the underlying biology. No early stopping was performed during training, which could lead to sub-optimal convergence on the 100-epoch limit. The study only used cortical data, omitting subcortical regions that may be relevant for working memory. The N = 40 participants in the held-out test fold represent only 10% of the total N = 400, limiting the statistical power of the held-out evaluation.

Claims
A bidirectional LSTM architecture outperforms unidirectional LSTM for brain state decoding by capturing both past and future temporal context in fMRI BOLD response. The bi-LSTM-c achieved 0.84 ± 0.02 accuracy versus 0.66 ± 0.18 for unidirectional LSTM. The improvement is quantitatively 18% in terms of accuracy. The bi-LSTM works without any hard-coded delay adjustment. The misclassification is highest for both models in the Others class. The model gets confused between body and tools stimuli. This framework can be applied to brain-state decoding without pre-calculating BOLD delay parameters. Future temporal information in fMRI data is not redundant and contains useful decoding information.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation was used to assess generalization across participants. A validation set (20% of training data) was used for hyperparameter tuning to prevent over-fitting. Three merging schemes (c, a, µ) were defined, with bi-LSTM-c being the primary comparison. Class weighting via compute_class_weight was used to address the imbalanced distribution of the Others class. A dropout of 0.3 was applied in LSTM layers during training. A baseline three-layer feed-forward Neural Network (ff-NN) was used to compare temporal vs. non-temporal modeling with equal parameters. Mean normalised confusion matrices illustrate model performance across all 9 classes. The task paradigm for each run and subject was the same during acquisition, enabling valid comparison.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 provides a schematic illustration of the Bidirectional LSTM architecture. Figure 2 illustrates mean normalised confusion matrices on the classification accuracy comparing LSTM and bi-LSTM-c.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the bi-LSTM framework for fMRI brain state decoding that captures bidirectional temporal context (past and future) without requiring explicit BOLD delay adjustment, outperforming unidirectional LSTMs by 18% absolute accuracy. 2. The strongest evidence is the quantitative improvement from 0.66 ± 0.18 to 0.84 ± 0.02 classification accuracy on HCP working memory data, validated through 10-fold inter-subject cross-validation with 360 subjects in training. 3. The future path involves tuning window-size and overlap for time-series chunking, developing more sophisticated class imbalance handling, and investigating cortical regions associated with body versus tools stimuli.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study performs a comparative phylogenomic analysis of three closely related thermophilic genera within the family Bacillaceae: Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus. Using 113 publicly available whole-genome sequences from the RefSeq database, the authors constructed a maximum-likelihood core-gene tree based on 662 orthologous core genes, supplemented by Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI) and Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI) dendrograms. The combined phylogenomic evidence revealed that the 114 genomes (including one outgroup) split into two primary clades: Clade I, containing all Geobacillus, all Parageobacillus, and some Anoxybacillus species; and Clade II, containing the majority of Anoxybacillus species. Clade I was further partitioned into three distinct sub-clades corresponding to the three genera, with a third sub-clade (Clade I-c) containing Anoxybacillus tepidamans PS2 and one genomospecies. The authors identified 6 CDS unique to Clade I-c through BLASTn searches. ANI values of 97.99, 97.14, and 97.64 were observed for the most closely related pairs, while the most distant value was 95.03 ANI / 95.81 AAI. The findings demonstrate that Clade I-c is phylogenetically distinct from all three existing genera, leading the authors to propose a new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov., to accommodate these two taxa. Two species (A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus) showed inconsistent positioning and remain unresolved. The paper highlights a critical methodological imperative: closely related genera must be analyzed together, as separate analyses of each genus alone would obscure the true phylogenetic relationships and lead to incorrect taxonomic assignments.

Research Context
DNA-DNA hybridization was traditionally the gold standard for bacterial taxonomy but was replaced by high-throughput sequencing. 16S rRNA gene sequencing provides lower resolution due to high sequence similarities among bacterial genera and species. Average nucleotide identity (ANI) provides higher resolution than 16S rRNA for detecting relatedness among bacterial genomes. For distant genome comparisons, average amino acid identity (AAI) is recommended because protein similarity is better conserved. The genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus are thermophilic, spore-forming members of the family Bacillaceae. Anoxybacillus was proposed as a new genus in 2000 from a strain isolated from animal manure. Geobacillus was split from Bacillus in 2001, originally containing eight species. Parageobacillus was defined in 2016 by reassigning five species from Geobacillus. Despite the individual histories of these three genera, they share similar ecological niches and taxonomic characteristics.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how closely related the thermophilic genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus are when analyzed together. The study tests whether separate analyses of these genera would miss true phylogenetic relationships that appear only when the genera are compared simultaneously. It is hypothesized that the three genera, when analyzed in tandem, will show a tree structure that reveals distinct clades and unresolved placements. The authors predict that certain species may fall outside established genus boundaries, necessitating new taxonomic designations. The paper also investigates the preliminary placement of 7 newly isolated strains of these genera.

Methodological Details
A total of 113 whole-genome sequences were selected from the RefSeq database for the primary analysis. The genus Anoxybacillus was represented by 32 strains, Geobacillus by 73 strains, and Parageobacillus by 7 species with one representative assembly each. Two additional Anoxybacillus, four Geobacillus, and one Parageobacillus strains from an Australian thermophile study were included, totaling 114 genomes with one outgroup. Of these 114 genomes, 31 were chromosome-level assemblies, 33 were scaffold genomes, and 49 were at the contig level. Anomalous assemblies identified as chimeric, contaminated, or frameshifted with suppressed RefSeq status were excluded. The core genome was identified using EDGAR 2.0 with Geobacillus thermodenitrificans NG80-2 as the starting reference. Bacillus subtilis spizizenii TU-B-10T was included as the outgroup for the core gene analysis. Five assemblies with low CDS numbers and one exact duplicate were excluded during core gene discovery. CDS were concatenated and aligned using MUSCLE before building a maximum-likelihood tree with FastTree. ANI and AAI values were calculated between all pairs using the ani.rb and aai.rb scripts from the enveomics package. Draft genomes were concatenated with 100 N bases introduced between contigs for similarity matrix construction. ANI and AAI dendrograms were constructed using the UPGMA method via the DendroUPGMA web server. Trees were plotted using the Interactive Tree Of Life web tool. Genes unique to Clade I-c were identified by BLASTn with identity ≥ 30%, bitscore ≥ 10, and overlap ≥ 1%.

Procedures And Architectures
The study adopted a methodology based on the reassessment of Geobacillus by Aliyu et al. [36]. A set of core genes was identified from the group of bacterial genomes under study. All orthologous genes were iteratively compared against the genome assemblies using BLAST. The core genome was then used to construct a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree. The same set of genomes was used to calculate two-way ANI and AAI scores for similarity matrices. GC content and genome size were calculated for all genomes to assist taxonomic delimitation. Genes unique to Clade I-c were identified by using CDS from Anoxybacillus tepidamans PS2 as a query. CDS present in all members of Clade I-c and no members of Clades I-a, I-b, or II were selected as unique.

Key Results
A core gene set of 662 orthologous genes per genome was identified among the 114 genomes. The maximum-likelihood tree split into three major groups: the outgroup, Clade I, and Clade II. Clade I consisted of 87 genomes, and Clade II consisted of 24 Anoxybacillus genomes. Clade I was further partitioned into three clades: Geobacillus, Parageobacillus, and a third clade containing A. tepidamans PS2 and one genomospecies. Two species, A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus, showed inconsistent positioning among the trees and could not be clearly resolved. The most closely related ANI pairs among the new genus candidates were 97.99, 97.14, and 97.64. The most distant pairwise value was 95.03 ANI and 95.81 AAI. A total of 6 CDS were found to be unique to Clade I-c. Mean ANI and AAI values suggested Clade I-c is somewhat more closely related to Parageobacillus than to the other two genera. The core gene tree, ANI, and AAI dendrograms collectively supported the distinctiveness of the two Clade I-c species from all three existing genera.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The study demonstrates that analyzing closely related genera together is essential to reveal phylogenetic relationships that are obscured when each genus is considered in isolation. The finding that Clade I-c species were previously assigned to Anoxybacillus or Geobacillus but fall outside both genera when compared collectively validates the need for broader phylogenetic context. The unique CDS in Clade I-c provide molecular evidence for taxonomic separation. The moderate similarity to Parageobacillus suggests a possible evolutionary link or common ancestor shared more recently with Parageobacillus than with the other genera. The proposal of Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. serves as a practical taxonomic remedy for a genome that cannot be accommodated in existing genera.

Contradictions And Limitations
Two species, A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus, showed inconsistent positioning across the different tree methods and their affinities remain unresolved. Eleven Anoxybacillus species did not have genome assemblies available, limiting the comprehensiveness of the genus-wide analysis. The study relies on publicly available genome sequences from RefSeq, including diverse assembly qualities (scaffold and contig level). The BLASTn filtering criteria for unique genes (30% identity) were described as relaxed, potentially affecting specificity. The number of genome assemblies was limited to 113, which may not capture the full diversity of the genera.

Claims
The species in Clade I-c (A. tepidamans PS2 and one genomospecies) constitute a distinct phylogenetic lineage that cannot be accommodated in Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, or Parageobacillus. The core gene ML tree showed Clade I-c as a separate clade from the three main genus-representing clades. Six CDS were found to be present in all Clade I-c members and no members of other clades. ANI values of 97.99, 97.14, and 97.64 separated the new clade from the main genera. The most distant pairwise value was 95.03 ANI / 95.81 AAI. Two species showed inconsistent positioning across the trees and could not be clearly resolved. An alternative approach may be to merge these two species with Parageobacillus, though this would then require Parageobacillus to be merged with Geobacillus. A new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov., is proposed to house these two taxa. Taxonomic decisions for new isolates must consider a broader phylogenetic context including closely related genera.
Analyzing the three genera collectively reveals phylogenetic relationships and genus boundaries that are invisible when each genus is analyzed independently. The Clade I-c genomes were previously assigned to Anoxybacillus or Geobacillus but are placed separately when all genera are analyzed together. The two main clades emerged only in the combined analysis. The paper acknowledges that this is a phylogenetic study using genomic data, and full taxonomic validation requires further evidence. New isolates should be placed using a broader phylogenetic framework including closely related taxa. The genus designation for new strains can become incongruent with true phylogeny if a broad assessment is absent.

Data And Code Availability
The ANI and AAI Ruby scripts used for similarity matrix calculation are publicly available in the enveomics package.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The analysis compared core gene ML trees, ANI UPGMA dendrograms, and AAI UPGMA dendrograms to assess consistency. Five assemblies with low CDS counts and one duplicate were excluded during core gene discovery to ensure reliability. The same set of genomes was used for ANI, AAI, and core gene tree to ensure comparability.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the core gene maximum likelihood tree splitting into outgroup, Clade I, and Clade II. Figure 2 shows the UPGMA dendrogram based on two-way ANI values for 114 genomes. Figure 3 shows the UPGMA dendrogram based on two-way average AAI values for 114 genomes. Table 1 presents average ANI and AAI values separating the candidate new genus from the members of the three existing genera. Table 2 shows additional similarity values supporting the affinity of Clade I-c to Parageobacillus. Table 3 shows pairwise ANI and AAI values for genome pairs. Table 4 lists the 6 unique CDS for Clade I-c with names, descriptions, and products. Table 5 provides DNA sequences for each of the 6 unique CDS. Table 6 shows BLASTn alignment results of the 6 unique CDS against all members of Clade I-c. Table 7 shows best hits for the unique CDS. Supplementary Table S1 lists all 114 genome assemblies included in the study. Supplementary Table S2 lists the five assemblies removed and one duplicate excluded during core gene discovery.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the proposal of a new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov., to accommodate two phylogenetically distinct taxa that cannot be accommodated in Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, or Parageobacillus when all three genera are analyzed collectively. 2. The strongest evidence is the trifecta of phylogenomic data: a core-gene ML tree placing Clade I-c outside the three known genera, 6 unique CDS shared by all Clade I-c members and no other taxa, and consistent ANI/AAI separation values (minimum 95.03). 3. The future path is to formally describe and characterize Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. and to apply the combined phylogenomic approach of evaluating closely related genera together when assigning taxonomic affinity to new genomes.
