summary.title: The structural basis for regulation of the glutathione transporter Ycf1 by regulatory domain phosphorylation
summary.authors: Nitesh Kumar Khandelwal, Cinthia R Millan, Samantha I Zangari, Samantha Avila, Dewight Williams, Tarjani M Thaker, Thomas M Tomasiak
summary.field_subfield: Structural Biology / ABC Transporter Mechanism
summary.executive_summary: This study resolves two cryo-EM structures of endogenously phosphorylated Saccharomyces cerevisiae Ycf1 (a glutathione transporter of the ABCC ABC transporter subfamily) at 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolutions, capturing distinct inward-facing open conformations designated IFwide (NBDs further apart) and IFnarrow (NBDs closer). The key finding is the visualization of the intrinsically disordered R-domain (residues 901–935) in a previously unobserved ordered state, phosphorylated at S908, T911, and S914. The phosphorylated R-domain forms an extensive interaction interface with NBD1 and the lasso domain, stabilized by electrostatic interactions with guanidinium groups (R716 on NBD1, R206 on lasso) and three hydrophobic surfaces (sites 1–3). The R-domain helix (residues 920–929) aligns with CFTR cryo-EM models and evolutionary coupling analysis from 13,723 homologs. Biochemical assays demonstrate that R-domain phosphorylation is required for maximal ATPase activity, as dephosphorylation substantially reduces activity and increases proteolysis accessibility. The two structures differ only by a rigid-body movement of the R-domain/NBD1 complex (hinge angle change from 130º in IFwide to 137.5º in IFnarrow) and the occlusion of the NBD1 ATP site in IFnarrow, with the NBD2 active site remaining open. The authors propose a model where the R-domain acts as a regulatory 'clutch' that, upon phosphorylation, transitions from a disordered/unbound state to a bound/ordered architecture, stabilizing NBD1 to recruit other domains into the IFnarrow conformation suitable for transport. The study also identifies a putative inhibitory phosphosite at S251 in the lasso domain and links the Ycf1 F713 mutation (CFTR delF506 equivalent) to the R-domain interface. These findings provide the first structural resolution of an intact R-domain with NBDs in any state, offering a mechanistic basis for R-domain-mediated regulation of ABC transporters.

claims.description: Endogenous R-domain phosphorylation on Ycf1 organizes the intrinsically disordered region into a stable, structured interaction scaffold with NBD1 and the lasso domain.
The transition from IFwide to IFnarrow is driven by a rigid-body movement of the R-domain/NBD1 complex, not by large conformational rearrangements of the R-domain scaffold itself.
Phosphorylation of a conserved lasso domain site (S251) provides a mechanism for negative regulation by electrostatic repulsion of the R-domain phosphate network.

Executive Summary
This study resolves two cryo-EM structures of endogenously phosphorylated Saccharomyces cerevisiae Ycf1 (a glutathione transporter of the ABCC ABC transporter subfamily) at 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolutions, capturing distinct inward-facing open conformations designated IFwide (NBDs further apart) and IFnarrow (NBDs closer). The key finding is the visualization of the intrinsically disordered R-domain (residues 901–935) in a previously unobserved ordered state, phosphorylated at S908, T911, and S914. The phosphorylated R-domain forms an extensive interaction interface with NBD1 and the lasso domain, stabilized by electrostatic interactions with guanidinium groups (R716 on NBD1, R206 on lasso) and three hydrophobic surfaces (sites 1–3). The R-domain helix (residues 920–929) aligns with CFTR cryo-EM models and evolutionary coupling analysis from 13,723 homologs. Biochemical assays demonstrate that R-domain phosphorylation is required for maximal ATPase activity, as dephosphorylation substantially reduces activity and increases proteolysis accessibility. The two structures differ only by a rigid-body movement of the R-domain/NBD1 complex (hinge angle change from 130º in IFwide to 137.5º in IFnarrow) and the occlusion of the NBD1 ATP site in IFnarrow, with the NBD2 active site remaining open. The authors propose a model where the R-domain acts as a regulatory 'clutch' that, upon phosphorylation, transitions from a disordered/unbound state to a bound/ordered architecture, stabilizing NBD1 to recruit other domains into the IFnarrow conformation suitable for transport. The study also identifies a putative inhibitory phosphosite at S251 in the lasso domain and links the Ycf1 F713 mutation (CFTR delF506 equivalent) to the R-domain interface. These findings provide the first structural resolution of an intact R-domain with NBDs in any state, offering a mechanistic basis for R-domain-mediated regulation of ABC transporters.

Research Context
ABC transporters are essential for membrane-associated lipid homeostasis, ion transport, and detoxification of diverse molecules. Ycf1 transports glutathione to sequester heavy metals and oxidized glutathione into the vacuole, acting as a redox sink and bioremediation target. Approximately half of all human ABC transporters are phosphorylated, but the regulatory mechanism remains poorly understood. The R-domain is predicted to be unstructured based on low sequence conservation and circular dichroism experiments estimating as low as 5% helical content. Recent NMR and cryo-EM studies of human CFTR and Ycf1 have revealed R-domain density near NBD1, but without assigned sequence. To date, no structure of an intact R-domain with NBDs has been determined in any state, prohibiting insights into precise interacting regions. Competing models exist for the R-domain: it could be completely disordered, semi-ordered between NBD1 and NBD2, or have other arrangements.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how R-domain phosphorylation regulates ABCC transporter activity and conformational transitions. The authors hypothesized that the R-domain interaction with NBD1, TMDs, and the lasso motif is highly dynamic and phosphorylation-dependent. They predicted that phosphorylation induces a structural transition from a disordered to an ordered R-domain bound to NBD1. It was further hypothesized that these R-domain interactions are necessary for the structural rearrangements required for ATP hydrolysis. The authors anticipated that the R-domain would be in an ordered state in their structures due to endogeneous phosphorylation. They predicted that the R-domain/NBD1 complex would move as a rigid body between IFwide and IFnarrow states.

Methodological Details
The study used endogenously phosphorylated Saccharomyces cerevisiae Ycf1 expressed in the DSY-5 strain. Two forms were purified: wild-type (WT) and the NBD2 Walker B mutant E1435Q. Protein expression was achieved in SC-His media (0.67% yeast nitrogen base, 2% glucose, 0.08% AA dropout) with a 50 mL primary culture grown for 24 hours at 30°C. A secondary 750 mL culture was grown for an additional 24 hours before induction with YPG media (1% yeast extract, 1.5% peptone, 2% galactose). The E1435Q mutant was used because the WT dataset did not yield homogenous particles for cryo-EM. E1435Q resulted in a Vmax of 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg, substantially lower than WT, enabling trapping of inward-facing conformations. Two cryo-EM structures were determined to 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolution. Drift correction was performed using MotionCor2 with a pixel size of 1.031 Å/pixel. CTF estimation used CTFFIND4.1; particle picking used a reconstruction of WT Ycf1. Ab-initio 3D map generation and 3D classification/refinement were performed in RELION 3.0 and 3.1. An initial model was built using SWISS-MODEL with 6jb1 as template, followed by manual building in COOT. Evolutionary coupling analysis used 13,723 sequences from Uniref90 via JackHMMR and PLMC, with a cutoff of ≥0.99. ATPase assays used 6.45 µg of protein at 30°C, monitoring NADH absorbance at 340 nm every minute for 30–45 min. ATP was held constant at 1 mM during GSSG stimulation experiments. Phosphorylation was confirmed by in-gel phosphoprotein staining and LC-MS/MS analysis with Scaffold Q+S. Dephosphorylation was achieved by Lambda phosphatase treatment for 45 min at 4°C. Limited proteolysis by trypsin at 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, and 15 µg/mL was used to assess surface accessibility. Substrate binding cavity volume was calculated using the 3V server with a probe size of 2.5Å, excluding NBDs.

Procedures And Architectures
Ycf1 gene was codon-optimized and cloned into p423_GAL1 with N-terminal Flag and C-terminal decahistidine tags. Cells were resuspended in lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-Cl pH 8.0, 300 mM NaCl, cOmplete protease inhibitor) and purified. For cryo-EM, apo conditions were used; E1435Q dataset produced two inward-facing conformations. Model building used secondary structure restraints, evolutionary couplings, and iterative real-space refinement in Phenix. Modrefiner assigned secondary structure; Isolde optimized model-to-map fit; Molprobity optimized geometry. ATPase activity was measured using an enzyme-coupled assay with PK/LDH, NADH, MgCl2, and PEP. Nonlinear regression fit with the Michaelis-Menten equation was used in GraphPad Prism 9. For in-gel staining, equal quantities (5 µg) of untreated and Lambda PP treated Ycf1 were separated on 10% SDS-PAGE. For LC-MS/MS, 10 µg of WT or E1435Q results were analyzed; minimum of two peptides with 95% confidence were required. Trypsin incubation was at 30 min on ice with soybean trypsin inhibitor (1 µg/mL) added after reaction.

Key Results
Two inward-facing cryo-EM structures were resolved at 3.4Å and 4.0Å, capturing IFwide (NBDs further apart) and IFnarrow (NBDs closer) states. The E1435Q mutant exhibited a Vmax of 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg, enabling trapping of inward-facing conformations. The R-domain (residues 901–935) is ordered: residues 920–929 form a helix, while 901–919 and 930–935 lack secondary structure. Three phosphorylation sites—S908, T911, and S914—were assigned based on additional electron density at these residues. Mass spectrometry and phosphostaining confirmed phosphorylation at all three sites in both WT and E1435Q Ycf1. Phosphates form extensive contacts with guanidyl groups of R716 on NBD1 and R206 on the lasso domain. The R-domain encircles NBD1 and is stabilized by a basic groove, intracellular loop 4, and the lasso domain. The R-domain helix (920–929) aligns with CFTR cryo-EM models and evolutionary coupling from 13,723 homologs. Hydrophobic interactions at three sites (I621–L802–I902–I904; F917–I1123–L1120; L912–I915–I1154) stabilize the R-domain/NBD1 interface. The buried surface area is ~1530 Å² (IFnarrow) and ~1338 Å² (IFwide) along the R-domain; specifically ~523 Å² and ~480 Å² between NBD1 and R-domain. The hinge angle between residues G913, G918, and G932 shifts from 130º in IFwide to 137.5º in IFnarrow. In IFnarrow, the NBD1 ATP binding site is rotated to occlude, while the NBD2 active site remains open. Dephosphorylation causes a more complete trypsin digestion, indicating increased protease accessibility. ATPase activity is drastically reduced in dephosphorylated Ycf1, confirming phosphorylation as a driver of active architecture. ATPase assays confirmed oxidized glutathione (GSSG) stimulates ATPase activity in the µM concentration range. A putative inhibitory phosphosite S251 in the lasso domain is accessible and poised for electrostatic repulsion of R-domain phosphates.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The R-domain acts as a regulatory 'clutch' that engages the motor upon phosphorylation but does not perform work itself. The model proposes that the R-domain transitions from an unbound/disordered state between the NBDs to a bound/ordered state near NBD1 upon phosphorylation. Phosphorylation-driven R-domain association with NBD1 stabilizes the active conformation, explaining why loss of any single R-domain phosphate is robust. The extensive electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions explain why mutations distal from phosphorylation sites can still cause dysfunction. The Ycf1 F713 mutation, equivalent to CFTR delF506, is in NBD1 adjacent to R-domain phosphates, coordinated by cation-pi interactions with R765 and R1150. The binding site of lumacaftor is in the outer perimeter of NBD1 near the R-domain binding site, rationalizing clinical corrector action. The finding of a single defined binding site for the conserved R-domain provides a mechanistic basis for allosteric modulation in diverse transporters.

Contradictions And Limitations
The R-domain is mostly disordered in other ABCC cryo-EM structures, conflicting with the ordered state observed here. The E1435Q dataset alone yielded homogenous particles, with no suitable particles from WT, limiting comparison across mutants. NBD2 is described as the less ordered of the two NBDs with weaker cryo-EM density, and a third IFtransition state was insufficiently detailed for model building. The authors acknowledge that phosphates themselves may block protease accessibility to some sites, confounding the interpretation of dephosphorylation proteolysis patterns. The structures do not rule out an inhibitory role for the unphosphorylated state, but functional data do not fully distinguish between unbound/disordered vs. loosely associated states between NBDs. Cell viability data from S908 and T911 mutants are cited as consistent with ATPase data but cannot directly prove the R-domain's mechanism of action. The R-domain hinge movement is minor (7.5º), and the authors note that R-domain positioning in their structure differs from a previous Ycf1 structure. The substrate-binding cavity volume was calculated excluding NBDs, which may not fully capture the functional volume of the transport pore.

Claims
Endogenous R-domain phosphorylation on Ycf1 organizes the intrinsically disordered region into a stable, structured interaction scaffold with NBD1 and the lasso domain. The R-domain shows a helical segment (residues 920–929) and is stabilized by a basic groove on NBD1. Three phosphorylation sites (S908, T911, S914) form electrostatic contacts with R716 on NBD1 and R206 on the lasso domain. Three distinct hydrophobic sites bury 1530 Å² (IFnarrow) and 1338 Å² (IFwide) of surface area. Dephosphorylation increases protease accessibility and reduces ATPase activity. Other ABCC cryo-EM structures reveal a mostly disordered R-domain without assigned sequence. NMR experiments point to discrete helical fragments, but the extent of order is debated. The R-domain position in this structure differs from that in a previously published Ycf1 structure. This defines a mechanism for how unstructured regulatory domains control ABC transporter function through conformational coupling. The robustness of this scaffold explains why loss of any single R-domain phosphate does not abolish activity.
The transition from IFwide to IFnarrow is driven by a rigid-body movement of the R-domain/NBD1 complex, not by large conformational rearrangements of the R-domain scaffold itself. R-domain/NBD1 interactions stay constant between IFwide and IFnarrow, related only by rigid body movements. The hinge angle change is only 7.5º (130º to 137.5º). Major structural changes occur only at the ATP binding sites, with NBD1 occluded in IFnarrow and NBD2 open. A third IFtransition state was insufficiently detailed to enable model building, leaving the full pathway unresolved. NBD2 is described as the less ordered of the two NBDs, reducing confidence in the active site description. This supports a model where R-domain phosphorylation stabilizes NBD1 to recruit other domains into the transport-ready conformation. The mechanism is analogous to a transmission clutch that engages the motor without performing work independently.
Phosphorylation of a conserved lasso domain site (S251) provides a mechanism for negative regulation by electrostatic repulsion of the R-domain phosphate network. S251 is the lasso domain equivalent to S251 in the Ycf1 homolog MRP1. S251 is accessible to the surface and positioned to disrupt R-domain interactions via charge repulsion. The cluster of R-domain and lasso domains in the structure explains the inhibitory role of this site. Phosphorylation of S251 was not observed in the cryo-EM structure. This provides a plausible structural explanation for the negative impact of lasso domain phosphorylation on Ycf1 function.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The E1435Q Walker B mutant was validated by reduced ATPase activity (Vmax 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg) to enable inward-facing state trapping. ATPase activity was tested in at least three technical replicates with nonlinear regression fitting. Dephosphorylation was confirmed by both in-gel phosphoprotein staining and LC-MS/MS analysis. Proteolysis accessibility was assessed at six different trypsin concentrations (0.5–15 µg/mL). Evolutionary coupling analysis utilized 13,723 sequences with PLMC scoring and a ≥0.99 cutoff. Substrate-stimulated ATPase activity subtracted basal activity prior to curve fitting.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A–C shows the cryo-EM maps at 3.4Å and 4.0Å, with structural models of WT and E1435Q Ycf1 in IFwide and IFnarrow conformations. Figure 1D shows ATPase Vmax of E1435Q at 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg. Figure 1F shows GSSG-stimulated ATPase activity with EC50 and Vmax parameters in the µM concentration range. Figure 2A–D details R-domain stabilization by basic groove, IC4, and lasso domain contacts. Figure 2E shows additional electron density at S908, T911, and S914 indicating phosphorylation. Figure 2F shows phosphostaining and LC-MS/MS validation of R-domain phosphorylation in WT and E1435Q. Figure 2G shows trypsin digestion patterns of endogenously phosphorylated vs. dephosphorylated Ycf1. Figure 2H shows reduced ATPase activity in dephosphorylated Ycf1. Figure 2C quantifies hydrophobic buried surface areas: ~1530 Å² (IFnarrow) and ~1338 Å² (IFwide). Figure 3A–E shows the R-domain/NBD1/lasso scaffold along a single axis, including hydrophobic sites and the x-loop/GRD motif. Figure 4A–C shows R-domain/NBD1–lasso contacts conserved between states, with ATP site occlusion in IFnarrow. Figure 4B shows the hinge angle of G913, G918, G932 shifting from 130º to 137.5º. Figure 4D shows the inhibitory role of S251 phosphorylation via electrostatic repulsion in IFwide. Supplementary Table S1 lists R-domain residues and sequence conservation. Supplementary Table S2 details LC-MS/MS phosphosite assignments.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first cryo-EM structure of an intact, endogenously phosphorylated R-domain bound to NBD1 in an ABC transporter, revealing a previously unobserved ordered regulatory architecture. 2. The strongest evidence is the combination of cryo-EM structural data showing specific electrostatic and hydrophobic contacts at S908, T911, and S914 with biochemical data demonstrating that dephosphorylation abolishes ATPase activity. 3. The future path lies in applying this R-domain-stabilization model to other ABCC and ABC transporters, identifying allosteric modulation sites, and correlating R-domain structural features with clinically relevant mutations and pharmacophores.

summary.title: Influence of plant growth regulators and nitrogen sources on the production and development of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk Hormonal treatment and fertilization to plant development
summary.authors: Leone Campos Rocha, Fábio Andrade, Teixeira, Márcio Dos Santos Pedreira, Daniela Deitos Fries, Giovanna Evely Leite Costa, Ana Cláudia Maia Soares, Daniel Lucas Santos Dias, Abdias José De Figueiredo, Angel Amaral Seixas, Camile Carvalho Pacheco
summary.field_subfield: Agronomy / Forage Science (Pasture Management)
summary.executive_summary: This study investigated the combined effects of seed treatment with plant growth regulators (PGRs) and different nitrogen fertilization methods on the germination, dry matter yield, and physiological composition of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk, a forage grass. The research was conducted at the Forage and Pasture Research Center, UESB, Brazil, between June and September 2017. Experiment 1 utilized a 2 x 4 factorial design comparing two seed types (coated and conventional) with four PGR levels (0, 8, 16, 24 mL.kg⁻¹ of seed) composed of auxin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹), cytokinin (0.09 mg.L⁻¹), and gibberellin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹). Experiment 2 evaluated two seed treatment levels (0 and 24 mL.kg⁻¹) across four nitrogen fertilization regimes: no fertilization, soil fertilization (75 kg.ha⁻¹ N), foliar fertilization (3 L.ha⁻¹), and multiple (soil + foliar) fertilization. Key findings include: (1) PGR treatment produced a quadratic effect on germination, with 10.3 mL.kg⁻¹ being the optimal level; (2) coated seeds outperformed conventional seeds in germination and GSI; (3) a significant interaction between seed type and PGR level existed for leaf and pseudostem dry mass, with coated seeds requiring lower levels (8.85 and 9.57 mL.kg⁻¹) for maximum yield; (4) soil fertilization independently increased dry mass of all structures (leaf, stem, shoot, root) and root volume; (5) the combination of PGR and soil fertilization maximized leaf, stem, and shoot dry mass; (6) PGR + multiple fertilization significantly increased root dry mass, while no interaction was found for chlorophyll pigments. The study concludes that lower PGR levels in coated seeds and soil N-fertilization are optimal for pasture establishment, and the authors recommend a PGR-soil fertilization synergy for maximizing structural development.

claims.description: Seed treatment with PGRs combined with nitrogen fertilization enhances Brachiaria decumbens growth and yield.
Coated seeds outperform conventional seeds in germination and structural mass production at low PGR levels.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigated the combined effects of seed treatment with plant growth regulators (PGRs) and different nitrogen fertilization methods on the germination, dry matter yield, and physiological composition of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk, a forage grass. The research was conducted at the Forage and Pasture Research Center, UESB, Brazil, between June and September 2017. Experiment 1 utilized a 2 x 4 factorial design comparing two seed types (coated and conventional) with four PGR levels (0, 8, 16, 24 mL.kg⁻¹ of seed) composed of auxin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹), cytokinin (0.09 mg.L⁻¹), and gibberellin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹). Experiment 2 evaluated two seed treatment levels (0 and 24 mL.kg⁻¹) across four nitrogen fertilization regimes: no fertilization, soil fertilization (75 kg.ha⁻¹ N), foliar fertilization (3 L.ha⁻¹), and multiple (soil + foliar) fertilization. Key findings include: (1) PGR treatment produced a quadratic effect on germination, with 10.3 mL.kg⁻¹ being the optimal level; (2) coated seeds outperformed conventional seeds in germination and GSI; (3) a significant interaction between seed type and PGR level existed for leaf and pseudostem dry mass, with coated seeds requiring lower levels (8.85 and 9.57 mL.kg⁻¹) for maximum yield; (4) soil fertilization independently increased dry mass of all structures (leaf, stem, shoot, root) and root volume; (5) the combination of PGR and soil fertilization maximized leaf, stem, and shoot dry mass; (6) PGR + multiple fertilization significantly increased root dry mass, while no interaction was found for chlorophyll pigments. The study concludes that lower PGR levels in coated seeds and soil N-fertilization are optimal for pasture establishment, and the authors recommend a PGR-soil fertilization synergy for maximizing structural development.

Research Context
The shortening of the soil preparation and planting window due to adverse climatic factors reduces time for recovering degraded pastures. Greater seed efficiency in germination and speed of emergence is necessary for efficient pasture recovery. Plant growth regulators act on signaling networks activating genes for photosynthesis and carbohydrate/protein degradation. PGRs at high levels per area are uneconomical, with forage reductions occurring as application increases. Low gibberellin concentrations of 5-10 g.ha⁻¹ are sufficient to positively affect forage yield. PGRs can improve water use, increase mechanical impedance in dry soils, and act on genes linked to growth under stress. Nitrogen expands the plant lifecycle, increasing growth rates in the vegetative phase and post-defoliation recovery. Nitrogen is an indispensable constituent of amino acids, proteins, and nucleic acids, stimulating cell division and elongation. Applications of nitrogen to degraded pasture increase water use efficiency and stimulate plant growth. The authors note that despite PGR potential, careful assessment of synthesis and cross-evaluations among phytohormones is needed.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central objective was to evaluate the effect of seed treatment with PGRs and nitrogen fertilization methods on growth and development. The study measured germinative characteristics, dry matter yield, and physiological composition (chlorophylls/carotenoids). The hypothesis was that PGRs would increase germination, mass yields of plant structures in coated seeds, and overall organogenesis. It was predicted that soil N-fertilization would increase dry mass production of leaf, stem, shoot, root, and root volume. Photoassimilate rates were expected to increase with soil fertilization and use of PGRs. The authors hypothesized that exogenous hormonal compounds act on the organogenesis of plant tissues, increasing Brachiaria decumbens development. Soil N-fertilization was expected to maximize photosynthetic processes and growth rates, thereby increasing mass yields.

Methodological Details
Experiments were conducted at the State University of Southwestern Bahia (UESB), Itapetinga-BA, between June and September 2017. Experiments took place in a greenhouse, the Forage and Pasture Research Center, and the Laboratory of Anatomy and Ecological Plant Physiology (LAFIEP). Germination was carried out under hermetic storage using a Mangelsdorf germination chamber (MA-401) at a 12h photoperiod and constant 28ºC. Growth and development evaluations were performed in a greenhouse; each pot contained eight liters (or 12 kg) of dry soil. Soil was collected at 0-20 cm depth, disintegrated, and passed through a 4-mm sieve. Experiment 1 used a 2 x 4 factorial scheme in a completely randomized design (CRD), comparing two seed types with four PGR levels. Seed types were commercial coated and conventional Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. PGR levels were 0, 8, 16, and 24 mL.kg⁻¹ of seed. Seeds were immersed in PGR solution for approximately two hours, wrapped in moist filter paper, with 25 seeds per replicate and four replicates per treatment. The PGR was composed of auxin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹), cytokinin (0.09 mg.L⁻¹), and gibberellin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹). Initial growth assessments (30 DAS) used a seedling tray with 32 cells per replicate and two replicates per treatment on sterilized coconut residue. Experiment 2 used two seed treatments (0 and 24 mL.kg⁻¹ PGR) across four nitrogen fertilization methods with four plants per replicate and four replicates per treatment, totaling 32 experimental units. The four nitrogen fertilization methods were no fertilization, soil fertilization, foliar fertilization, and multiple (soil + foliar) fertilization. At 30 DAS, a standardization cut at an average residue height of 15 cm was performed. Data collection followed two periods of 28 days after the standardization cut. Soil N fertilization was 75 kg.ha⁻¹ and foliar N fertilization was 3 L.ha⁻¹. The foliar fertilizer contained N: 1.37%, P: 2.5%, O5: 15.0%, Mg: 1.0%, S: 1.5%, Zn: 3.0%, Mn: 2.0%, Cu: 0.3%, B: 0.2%, Mo: 0.1%, Co: 0.1%. The fertilization recommendations followed the 5th Approximation of the Soil Fertility Commission for the State of Minas Gerais. Daily counts of germinated seeds were carried out for 14 days. Whole-plant yield was determined, followed by desiccation of root, stem, and leaf for fresh and dry mass. Chlorophyll extraction used 200 mg of fresh mass of the third fully expanded leaf with 5 mL DMSO in aluminum foil for 72 hours. Pigment readings were taken at 665, 649, and 480 nm via absorption spectrophotometry.

Procedures And Architectures
The statistical analysis used the MIXED procedure of SAS (SAS Inst. Inc., Cary, NC) with significance declared at P ≤ 0.05. Seed, PGR, and interaction effects were analyzed as fixed effects for all measurements in Experiment 1. Single-degree-of-freedom contrast statements were constructed for PGR effects: linear and quadratic. The maximum point of the quadratic effect was estimated from a regression equation. PGR, Fertilization, and interaction were analyzed as fixed effects in Experiment 2. Tukey test was used for comparison of means with significance at P ≤ 0.05. Germination speed index (GSI) was calculated following reference [9]. Dry mass production followed the protocol of reference [10]. Pigment quantification followed the protocol of reference [12]. Values were adjusted to mg.g⁻¹ of fresh mass.

Key Results
The interaction between seed type and PGR levels was not significant for germination or GSI. A quadratic effect of PGR levels on germination was observed regardless of seed type. The regression equation estimated that 10.3 mL.kg⁻¹ PGR promotes greater germination. Coated seeds had higher germination percentages and GSI values than conventional seeds. For the number of leaves and tillers, the interaction between seed type and PGR level was not significant. Based on the estimated equation, 12.8 mL.kg⁻¹ PGR resulted in higher root dry mass production. A significant interaction between seed type and PGR level was found for leaf and pseudostem dry mass production. Coated seeds required lower PGR levels for maximum leaf and pseudostem dry mass: 8.85 and 9.57 mL.kg⁻¹, respectively. Conventional seeds required higher levels: 15.5 and 18.1 mL.kg⁻¹ for leaf and pseudostem dry mass. At the highest PGR levels (16.0 and 24.0 mL.kg⁻¹), leaf and pseudostem dry mass production did not differ between seed types. The interaction between PGR use and nitrogen fertilization was significant for leaf, stem, shoot, and root dry mass. Soil fertilization independently resulted in higher yields for all evaluated structures regardless of PGR. When combined, PGR and soil fertilization produced the greatest dry mass for stem, leaf, and shoot. PGR reduced leaf, stem, and shoot production when combined with multiple fertilization (soil + foliar), differing from the absence of PGR. The use of PGR increased root dry mass only when combined with multiple fertilization; no influence was observed for other fertilization types. No significant interaction between PGR and nitrogen fertilization was found for chlorophyll a, b, total chlorophylls, carotenoids, or chlorophyll a/b ratio. There was a significant effect of PGR on chlorophyll a, and fertilization methods influenced levels of chlorophyll a, b, and carotenoids.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Exogenous hormones change hormonal balance, with increased auxin, cytokinin, and gibberellin levels after 24h of imbibition. Increased gibberellin implies greater intracellular transport of metabolites, weakening structures covering the radicle to overcome mechanical barriers. The combined hormone regulator modifies gibberellin/abscisic acid relationships, reducing seed dormancy. Seed coating provides protection against mechanical damage and nutrients to the embryo, favoring radicle and seedling emergence. Auxin in the PGR composition increases rhizogenesis by stimulating stem cell multiplication in quiescent centers. Auxin transport is mediated by PIN proteins on plasma membranes, contributing to hormonal homeostasis. The auxin/cytokinin interaction regulates meristem maintenance; both may act separately or antagonistically during embryogenesis. Coated seeds were superior because they are pure seeds with higher embryo quality, whereas conventional seeds had reduced efficiency. Nitrogen supply combined with PGR cellular acceleration and hormonal synthesis explains the synergistic increase in dry mass. Higher chlorophyll a levels, responsible for the photochemical phase, favor ATP synthesis via photophosphorylation, providing more substrate for development. Foliar nitrogen may participate in cytokinin synthesis, promoting chlorophyll synthesis and delayed senescence.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper notes that the role of auxins and cytokinins in regulating photosynthetic processes remains inconclusive. Previous studies with only cytokinin and auxin formulations showed no significant responses, contrasting this study's triple-hormone approach. The interaction between PGR and multiple fertilization actually reduced leaf, stem, and shoot dry mass compared to no PGR, a counter-intuitive finding. Root dry mass was only influenced by PGR under multiple fertilization, not under soil or foliar-only regimes. The authors do not report the exact number of plants per treatment for Experiment 1, only noting 32 cells per replicate with two replicates. The specific genotype and pedigree of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk are not detailed beyond the cultivar name. The duration of the experiments (June to September 2017) covers only a specific season; multi-season replication is not reported. The random seed number and specific treatment assignment details are not provided, though CRD is specified.

Claims
Seed treatment with PGRs combined with nitrogen fertilization enhances Brachiaria decumbens growth and yield. PGR 10.3 mL.kg⁻¹ gave optimal germination: 10.3 mL.kg -1 Soil fertilization gave highest yields regardless of PGR: soil fertilization PGR + soil gave greatest combined stem/leaf/shoot mass: combined Chlorophyll a increased with PGR: significant effect PGR reduced mass when combined with multiple fertilization: reduced leaf PGR had no effect on root dry mass under soil or foliar fertilization: no influence Lower PGR levels in coated seeds are recommended: Lower levels Soil N-fertilization should be the primary nitrogen source: soil N-fertilization
Coated seeds outperform conventional seeds in germination and structural mass production at low PGR levels. Coated seeds had higher germination/GSI: coated seeds had higher Coated seeds required 8.85/9.57 mL.kg⁻¹ for max mass: 8.85 and 9.57 Conventional seeds required 15.5/18.1 mL.kg⁻¹: 15.5 and 18.1 At highest PGR levels (24 mL.kg⁻¹), no difference between seed types: did not differ Pure Live Seeds evaluation is suggested: Pure Live Seeds

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Two separate experiments were conducted: Exp 1 (2x4 factorial) and Exp 2 (2x4) with different focuses. A 15 cm standardization cut at 30 DAS provided a uniform starting point for growth comparisons. Two replicates for initial growth assessments and four replicates for the main experiment provided baseline stability. Sterilized coconut residue served as substrate for 30 DAS assessments to maintain constant humidity.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 provides the composition of the foliar fertilizer spray: N 1.37%, P 2.5%, O5 15.0% etc. Figure 1 shows the digital thermo-hygrometer recording greenhouse conditions. Table 2 presents germination percentages and GSI by seed type. Table 3 shows root dry mass by seed type and PGR level. Table 4 shows leaf and pseudostem dry mass by seed type and PGR level. Table 5 shows dry mass production by PGR and fertilization. Table 6 shows chlorophyll a, b, total, carotenoids and ratio by PGR and fertilization.

Three Takeaways
1. PGR treatment with 10.3 mL.kg⁻¹ and soil N-fertilization at 75 kg.ha⁻¹ are the optimal combination for Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk establishment. 2. Coated seeds combined with lower PGR levels (8.85–9.57 mL.kg⁻¹) produce superior structural mass compared to conventional seeds, whose efficiency drops at low doses. 3. The future path involves evaluating Pure Live Seeds (PLS) to improve PGR use efficiency and further investigating the auxins/cytokinin-photosynthesis nexus.

summary.title: Impact of Chronic Total Occlusion Lesion Length on Six-month Angiographic and 2-year Clinical Outcomes
summary.authors: Jihun Ahn; Byounggeol Choi; Yeon Choi; Jae Kyeong Byun; Ahmed Mashaly; Kareem Abdelshafi; Yoonjee Park; Young Jang; Woohyeun Kim; Eunjin Park; Jin Oh Na; Cheol Ung Choi; Eungju Kim; Chang Gyu Park; Hongseog Seo; Dongjoo Oh; Jinsu Byeon; Sangho Park; Hyeyon Yu; Seung-Woon W Rha
summary.field_subfield: Cardiology; Percutaneous Coronary Intervention; Chronic Total Occlusion
summary.executive_summary: This prospective single-center study investigated whether chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion length impacts six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes following successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stents (DES). A cohort of 235 consecutive CTO patients treated between November 2004 and October 2010 at Korea University Guro Hospital was divided into long CTO (≥30 mm; n=159) and short CTO (<30 mm; n=76) groups. Baseline clinical characteristics differed: prior PCI was more frequent in the long group, while bifurcation lesions were more common in the short group. In-hospital intimal dissection was significantly more frequent in long CTO lesions. At 6 months, angiographic outcomes (ISR, binary restenosis, late loss) were statistically similar between groups, though the short group vessel diameter was significantly smaller (3.11 ± 0.43 mm vs. 2.92 ± 0.42 mm; p < 0.05). Over 2 years, hard clinical endpoints (total death, cardiac death, MI, MACE) showed no significant difference between groups. However, the long CTO group experienced significantly higher repeat PCI (18.8% vs. 7.8%; p < 0.05) and target vessel revascularization (TVR) (16.3% vs. 6.5%; p < 0.05). Multivariate logistic regression identified long CTO as an independent predictor of repeat PCI (OR 4.26, CI 1.53-11.9, p=0.006; OR 4.23, CI 1.52-11.8 for TVR, p < 0.05). The authors conclude that while long CTO lesions increase revascularization risk, they do not translate into increased mortality or hard ischemic events, suggesting PCI with DES is similarly safe for both lesion lengths.

claims.description: Long CTO lesion length is an independent predictor of repeat PCI and TVR but does not increase hard clinical endpoints at two years.
Intimal dissection is more frequent in long CTO lesions, suggesting a more complex or aggressive procedural approach.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This prospective single-center study investigated whether chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion length impacts six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes following successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stents (DES). A cohort of 235 consecutive CTO patients treated between November 2004 and October 2010 at Korea University Guro Hospital was divided into long CTO (≥30 mm; n=159) and short CTO (<30 mm; n=76) groups. Baseline clinical characteristics differed: prior PCI was more frequent in the long group, while bifurcation lesions were more common in the short group. In-hospital intimal dissection was significantly more frequent in long CTO lesions. At 6 months, angiographic outcomes (ISR, binary restenosis, late loss) were statistically similar between groups, though the short group vessel diameter was significantly smaller (3.11 ± 0.43 mm vs. 2.92 ± 0.42 mm; p < 0.05). Over 2 years, hard clinical endpoints (total death, cardiac death, MI, MACE) showed no significant difference between groups. However, the long CTO group experienced significantly higher repeat PCI (18.8% vs. 7.8%; p < 0.05) and target vessel revascularization (TVR) (16.3% vs. 6.5%; p < 0.05). Multivariate logistic regression identified long CTO as an independent predictor of repeat PCI (OR 4.26, CI 1.53-11.9, p=0.006; OR 4.23, CI 1.52-11.8 for TVR, p < 0.05). The authors conclude that while long CTO lesions increase revascularization risk, they do not translate into increased mortality or hard ischemic events, suggesting PCI with DES is similarly safe for both lesion lengths.

Research Context
While DES reduced restenosis, long coronary lesions remain a worse prognostic factor after PCI. CTO procedural success rates remain lower than non-CTO patients, and long-term outcomes are affected by clinical risk factors and lesion characteristics. There were no definite answers regarding CTO PCI outcomes according to lesion length, especially in the DES era. The study aimed to investigate whether CTO lesion length significantly impacts six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether angiographic and clinical outcomes differ between long and short CTO lesions after successful DES-treated PCI. The study expected adverse clinical outcomes including MACE and angiographic adverse outcomes would be more frequent in the long CTO group. The rationale for the hypothesis included worse clinical risk factors (prior MI, prior PCI) in the long group and the more frequent use of first-generation stents (paclitaxel-eluting) in long versus newer DES in short lesions. The predicted outcome was that long CTO lesions would drive higher rates of revascularization events and angiographic failure.

Methodological Details
A total of 235 consecutive CTO patients underwent successful PCI with DES from November 2004 to October 2010 at Korea University Guro Hospital, Seoul. The study was prospective, with data collected prospectively from a single center registry. Patients were divided into the long CTO group (angiographic lesion length ≥30 mm; n=159) and the short CTO group (angiographic lesion length <30 mm; n=76). CTO was defined as complete coronary obstruction with TIMI flow grade 0 and estimated duration ≥3 months, with or without visible collateral flow. Only de novo lesions were included; in-stent restenosis (ISR) as a cause of CTO was excluded. Loading doses of clopidogrel (300-600 mg) and aspirin (200-300 mg) were administered before the index procedure. Maintenance dual antiplatelet therapy consisted of aspirin (100 mg) and clopidogrel (75 mg), with clopidogrel encouraged to continue at least for 1 year. Adjunctive cilostazol (200 mg post-loading, 100 mg twice a day for at least one month) was added at physician discretion. Procedural success was defined as final angiographic diameter stenosis <30% and TIMI grade ≥2. The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board and all patients provided informed consent. Prior PCI was more frequent in the long CTO group, while bifurcation lesions were more frequent in the short group. Vessel size was smaller in the short group (3.11 ± 0.43 mm) compared with the long group (2.92 ± 0.42 mm); p < 0.05.

Procedures And Architectures
PCI procedures were performed with current guidelines using standard techniques and available guidewires. A variety of atheroablative devices were not utilized; mostly simple pre-dilation with balloon was performed to accommodate the unexpanded stent. All PCI was performed using DES, with the DES type decided by the operator during the procedures. QCA parameters were measured before PCI, immediately after, and 6 months post-index procedure. The primary angiographic endpoint was the incidence of binary restenosis at 6-12 months. Secondary angiographic endpoints were ISR, mean diameter stenosis, minimal luminal diameter, and late loss at 6 months. Two-year follow-up data were collected by face-to-face interview, medical record review, and telephone contact. The primary clinical endpoint was MACE (death, recurrent MI, revascularization including PCI and CABG), divided into TLR-MACE and TVR-MACE. Q-wave MI was defined as new pathological Q-waves in at least two contiguous leads with or without elevated creatinine kinase-MB. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 20; a 2-sided p < 0.05 was considered significant. Logistic regression adjusted for sex, age, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, prior PCI, and bifurcation lesion.

Key Results
In-hospital complications were similar between groups, except significant intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group (Table 2). Total death (3.1% long vs. 5.2% short; p = 0.43) was not significantly different between groups. Cardiac death (1.2% vs. 2.6%; p = 0.45) and MI (1.8% vs. 2.6%; p = 0.71) showed no significant difference. Overall MACE (21.3% vs. 13.1%; p = 0.13) was not statistically different between groups. The incidence of repeat PCI was significantly higher in the long CTO group (18.8% vs. 7.8%; p < 0.05). Target vessel revascularization (TVR) was significantly higher in the long CTO group (16.3% vs. 6.5%; p < 0.05). In multivariate analysis, long CTO was an independent predictor for repeat PCI with OR 4.26, CI 1.53-11.9, p=0.006. For TVR, the multivariate analysis showed OR 4.23, CI 1.52-11.8, p < 0.05. Six-month angiographic data were available for 99 long CTO patients (62%) and 45 short CTO patients (59%). ISR was 33.3% vs. 26.6% (p = 0.42) and binary restenosis was 19.1% vs. 8.8% (p = 0.12). Late loss was 0.65 ± 0.82 mm vs. 0.46 ± 0.56 mm (p = 0.13). Despite the numerical trend toward higher binary restenosis in the long group (19.1% vs. 8.8%, p=0.118), the difference was not statistically significant.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The similarity in hard endpoints (death, MI, MACE) suggests that PCI in long CTO lesions with DES is as safe as in short lesions. The higher TVR in long CTO lesions did not translate into mortality, a phenomenon also observed in the j-Cypher Registry. The authors propose that less myocardial viability and previously developed collateral channels in long CTO lesions may lessen the harmful physiologic effect of restenosis. The numerical trend toward higher binary restenosis in long lesions (19.1% vs. 8.8%) suggests that with longer follow-up and larger sample size, the difference may become significant. The vessel size difference (3.11 mm short vs. 2.92 mm long) did not affect angiographic and clinical outcomes because both exceeded the small vessel diameter threshold.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study was a prospective single-center registry, not a randomized controlled trial, with baseline imbalances between groups. Follow-up coronary angiography was not routinely performed; it depended on ischemic symptoms or physician discretion, introducing potential confounders. The sample size was relatively small, limiting statistical power to detect differences in angiographic outcomes. The two-year follow-up period was not long enough to evaluate long-term safety and efficacy. Use of first-generation DES was more frequent in the long CTO group, while newer generation DES predominated in the short group, a potential confounding variable.

Claims
Long CTO lesion length is an independent predictor of repeat PCI and TVR but does not increase hard clinical endpoints at two years. Repeat PCI was 18.8% in long vs. 7.8% in short group (p < 0.05). TVR was 16.3% in long vs. 6.5% in short group (p < 0.05). Multivariate analysis confirmed long CTO as predictor for repeat PCI (OR 4.26, p=0.006). Hard endpoints (death, MI, MACE) showed no significant difference (p=0.43, 0.45, 0.71, 0.13 respectively). Angiographic outcomes were numerically higher in long CTO (19.1% vs. 8.8% binary restenosis) though not statistically significant (p=0.118). PCI with DES in long CTO lesions is as safe as in short lesions regarding mortality and major ischemic events. Clinicians should anticipate higher revascularization rates in long CTO patients despite successful DES implantation.
Intimal dissection is more frequent in long CTO lesions, suggesting a more complex or aggressive procedural approach. Significant intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group (Table 2). The authors interpret this as suggesting more complex and aggressive recanalization procedure. Overall in-hospital complications were similar between the two groups. Longer lesions require more intensive recanalization techniques, increasing procedural complication risk.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The logistic regression model adjusted for multiple confounders: sex, age, hypertension, DM, CKD, prior PCI, and bifurcation lesion. Two-sided p < 0.05 was used consistently across all analyses. Vessel size was controlled by using the small vessel diameter threshold (Table 1, 25-27 references).

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 demonstrates baseline clinical and angiographic characteristics of the 159 long and 76 short CTO patients. Table 2 summarizes procedural and in-hospital complications, showing higher intimal dissection in long CTO. Table 3 presents two-year clinical outcomes (death, MI, MACE) stratified by group. Table 4 shows predictors for repeat PCI and TVR from multivariate logistic regression. Table 5 presents six-month angiographic outcomes (ISR, binary restenosis, LL) for the available subcohorts.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: Long CTO lesion length (≥30 mm) significantly increases the risk of repeat PCI (OR 4.26) and TVR (OR 4.23) after successful DES-treated CTO PCI, but does not independently increase hard clinical endpoints at two years. 2. The strongest evidence: Two-year hard clinical endpoints (total death, cardiac death, MI, MACE) showed no statistically significant differences between long (n=159) and short (n=76) CTO groups (p-values 0.43, 0.45, 0.71, 0.13), despite the long group having significantly higher repeat PCI (18.8% vs. 7.8%; p<0.05) and TVR (16.3% vs. 6.5%; p<0.05) rates. 3. The future path: A larger, long-term prospective registry is necessary to determine if the numerical trend toward higher binary restenosis (19.1% vs. 8.8%) in long CTO matures into a statistically significant difference and to confirm long-term safety beyond two years.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports the design, synthesis, and biological evaluation of 25 tricyclic 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2-e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-one hybrids as putative α-glucosidase inhibitors for type II diabetes management. The authors synthesized 25 compounds via a multistep procedure starting from diphenoxy-Ncyanoimidocarbonate, proceeding through 1,2,4-triazole intermediates to fused pyrimidine derivatives with varying substitutions at positions 4 and beyond. The compounds were subjected to in vitro α-glucosidase inhibitory assays using the p-NPG substrate and yeast-derived enzyme. Results revealed that the inhibitory activity ranged between 30% and 63% for the entire series. Eight compounds exceeded 50% average inhibition; of these, compounds 6d and 6h exhibited IC50 values lower than the reference drug acarbose. Specifically, compound 6h demonstrated the highest potency with an IC50 of 104.07 μM (reported in abstract as mM, likely a typo for μM given the context of the IC50 table). Molecular docking studies using Autodock software and the α-glucosidase structure (PDB: 3W37) revealed that compound 6h formed a stable ligand-enzyme complex with the lowest binding energy (-10.56 kcal/mol) and extra hydrogen bonds directed by Trp329. Acarbose established 10 hydrogen bonds and two hydrophobic interactions with Phe601 and Trp329, while compound 6h formed three hydrogen bonds with Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469. The study concludes that the aminobridge substitution at position 4 of the pyrimidine ring is critical for inhibitory activity, providing a new scaffold for non-sugar-mimetic antidiabetic agents that may overcome the gastrointestinal side effects of carbasugars like acarbose.

Research Context
Postprandial hyperglycaemia control via α-glucosidase inhibitors delays carbohydrate hydrolysis and reduces glucose absorption. The number of diabetic people increased from 108 million in 1980 to 422 million by 2014, with prevalence rising from 4.7% to 8.5%. Current inhibitors like acarbose, miglitol, and voglibose face clinical limitations due to significant gastrointestinal side effects such as flatulence and diarrhoea. Most current inhibitors are sugar mimetics requiring tedious synthesis and exhibiting side effects from colonic bacteria digestion of complex carbohydrates. The valienamine moiety in acarbose mimics the oxocarbenium ion-like transition state that binds and inhibits α-glucosidase. Scaffolds such as pyridine, triazole, and pyrimidine have been incorporated into compounds displaying antiviral, anticancer, anti-inflammatory, and fungicidal activities. The authors sought to overcome side effects of sugar mimetic agents by modifying well-accepted medicinal chemistry scaffolds.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a series of 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2-e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-ones be designed and synthesized with potent α-glucosidase inhibitory activity? Does the substitution at the nitrogen at position 4 of the fused pyrido-triazolo-pyrimidine ring modulate the inhibitory activity? Is a non-sugar-mimetic scaffold capable of achieving IC50 values competitive with or superior to acarbose? Can molecular docking reveal the binding mode and explain the structure-activity relationship of the highest inhibitors? The authors hypothesized that the aminobridge substitution at position 4 would provide stronger inhibition compared to direct N-alkylation.

Methodological Details
Twenty-five tricyclic 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2-e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-ones hybrids were synthesized and evaluated. The synthesis began with 2-hydrazino-3-carboxylic pyridine (5.5 mmol) reacting with diphenoxy-Ncyanoimidocarbonate (5 mmol) in ethanol (20 mL). Triethylamine (20 mmol) was added dropwise over 10 minutes at room temperature. The reaction was heated at 80 °C for 1–2 hours under conc. HCl acidification. The N-alkylated pyrido[3,2-e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-ones (2a-l) were obtained in yields of 45–83%. Compound 3 was obtained as a yellow amorphous powder in 90% yield via treatment with phosphorous pentasulfide in absolute pyridine. Compounds 6a-d were obtained in 60–68% yields by treatment of compound 5 with aromatic amines in pyridine (molar ratio 1:5). Compound 6e was obtained in 63% yield from reaction of 5 with hydroxylamine HCl in 1:2.5 molar ratio in boiling pyridine. Compound 6i was obtained in 74% yield by replacing chlorine in 5 with isoniazid in boiling toluene. For the inhibitory assay, α-glucosidase enzyme type 1 from Baker's yeast (1 mg) was dissolved in 1000 µL of cold PBS at pH 6.5 to give 0.125 unit/mL. The p-NPG substrate was prepared at a 20-mM concentration in phosphate-buffered saline. Samples were prepared at 200 µg/mL in 100% DMSO, with two-fold serial dilutions down to 1.56 µg/mL in 96-well plates. Each test compound was treated with 100 µg/mL concentration, and the assay was repeated three times. The α-glucosidase enzyme (20 µL), PBS (40 µL), and water (20 µL) were added to each well, pre-incubated at 37 °C for 10 minutes. The reaction was incubated for 30 minutes at 37 °C, measuring absorbance at 0 and 30 minutes. Molecular docking used Autodock software with the α-glucosidase structure from PDB code 3W37. All synthesized derivatives formed a complex with the target enzyme, with a relative standard deviation of binding energy less than 2.34 kcal/mol.

Procedures And Architectures
The synthesis proceeded in seven steps (i–vii) as detailed in the scheme. Step i: The triazole intermediate B was formed by reaction of 1,2,4-triazole with N-cyanoimidocarbonate in triethylamine/ethanol overnight. Step ii: B was treated with conc. HCl initially at room temperature followed by heating to 80 °C. Step iii: N-alkylation of compound 1 with alkyl or heteroalkyl halides in DMF with K2CO3 gave 2a–l. Step iv: Phosphorous pentasulfide in absolute pyridine converted 2a–l to thiones 3. Step v: Benzyl bromide in DMF with K2CO3 gave compound 4. Step vi: POCl3 in boiling benzene converted 1 to imidoyl chloride 5, confirmed by disappearance of C=O band at 1703 cm⁻¹ in IR. Step vii: Nucleophilic displacement of the imidoyl chloride in 5 with aromatic amines, hydroxylamine, isoniazid, or hydrazine hydrate gave 6a–i. The hydrazone derivatives 6g and 6h were prepared by reacting 6f with aldehydes in refluxing ethanol for 3–5 hours. IR spectra of 2a–l displayed absorption at 1670–1688 cm⁻¹ (C=O), while compound 3 showed a weak band at 1272 cm⁻¹ (C=S). 1H-NMR spectra of 1–6 were characterized by two spin coupling systems: 2H triplet (H-3'/5'), 2H doublet (H-2'/6'), 1H triplet (H-4') at δ 7.50–7.25 ppm for the 2-phenoxy moiety, and three pyridine-ring protons (H-6, 7, 8) at δ 8.9–7.5 ppm. Molecular docking employed Autodock software with PDB file 3W37. Binding energies were calculated, and the lowest binding energy was found to be −10.56 kcal/mol for compound 6h.

Key Results
The inhibitory activity of all 25 tested compounds ranged between 30% and 63% average percent inhibition. Eight compounds (out of 25) exhibited more than 50% average percent inhibition and were further evaluated for IC50. Compounds 3, 6c, and 6d showed average percent inhibition of more than 60%. Compounds 2a, 2d, 6a, 6b, and 6h showed average percent inhibition of more than 50% but less than 60%. The average percent inhibitions of 2a and 2d were 50.36% and 57.48%, respectively. Compounds 6a–d and 6h all exhibited average percent inhibition of more than 50%. Compound 3 at 100 µg/mL exhibited 60.38% activity against α-glucosidase. The IC50 of compound 3 was 167.82 μM. The IC50 of compound 2a was 304.13 μM, and compound 2d was 173.83 μM. Compound 6h exhibited the highest inhibition with an IC50 of 104.07 μM (abstract states mM, likely a typo for μM). Compound 6d showed IC50 values lower than that of acarbose, as did compounds 6a, 6b, 6c, and 6h. Acarbose established 10 hydrogen bonds with Asp232, Ala234, Asn237, Asp357, Arg552, Asp568, and His626. Acarbose had two hydrophobic interactions between the deoxyglucosamine methyl group and Phe601 and Trp329. Compound 2a formed only one hydrogen bond between its triazole nitrogen and Arg552, yielding a free binding energy of −8.12 kcal/mol. Compound 6h formed three hydrogen bonds with Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469, yielding a free binding energy of −10.55 kcal/mol. Compound 6a had a binding energy of −9.76 kcal/mol, and compound 6b had −9.17 kcal/mol. Trp329 formed hydrophobic bonds with both 2a and 6h, analogous to acarbose.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The aminobridge substitution of the pyrimidine ring at position 4 is responsible for the strong inhibitory activity compared to direct N-alkylation. Derivatization at the nitrogen at position 4 (N-substitution) had no significant effect on inhibitory activity except for 2a and 2d. The maximal inhibitory activity of compound 6h is mainly attributable to its lowest binding energy and the stability of the ligand-α-glucosidase complex. Trp329 plays a significant role in directing the ligand in the binding site of the α-glucosidase enzyme. The number of established intermolecular hydrogen bonds and binding energies explain the potency differences among the inhibitors. The study provides a new structural insight for the development of novel α-glucosidase inhibitors that differ from commonly employed carbasugars. These compounds can eventually be transformed into new clinical drugs for the treatment of type II diabetes.

Contradictions And Limitations
The abstract states compound 6h has an IC50 of 104.07 mM, while the context of the paper and the IC50 values of the series suggest this is likely 104.07 μM, creating a potential units discrepancy. The paper does not report the IC50 value of acarbose for direct comparison, though it is used as a positive control. Only six promising compounds (more than 50% inhibition) were subjected to IC50 determination, limiting the full scope of the SAR. The molecular docking was performed using a single protein structure (3W37), which may not capture conformational flexibility of the enzyme in solution. The inhibitory assay was conducted in vitro using a recombinant enzyme, so in vivo potency is not established. No statistical analysis (e.g., t-tests, ANOVA) of the percent inhibition and binding energies is reported between compounds.

Claims
The aminobridge substitution at position 4 of the pyrimidine ring confers significantly greater α-glucosidase inhibitory activity than N-alkylation. Compounds 6a–d and 6h exhibited average percent inhibition of more than 50%, while only 2a and 2d among the N-alkylated series crossed this threshold. The IC50 of compound 6h (the highest inhibitor) was 104.07 μM, while the best N-alkylated compound 2d was 173.83 μM. Molecular docking showed compound 6h formed three hydrogen bonds with binding energy −10.55 kcal/mol, whereas compound 2a formed only one hydrogen bond with binding energy −8.12 kcal/mol. The N-alkylated compounds 2a (50.36%) and 2d (57.48%) still retained over 50% inhibition, demonstrating some baseline activity at the same position. The aminobridge linkage provides additional intermolecular interactions (hydrogen bonding) that direct the ligand and stabilize the complex. Design strategies for this scaffold should prioritize N-substituted aminobridge at position 4 over direct N-alkylation for maximal potency.
Compound 6h is the most potent α-glucosidase inhibitor in the series, outperforming the reference drug acarbose. Compound 6h exhibited an IC50 of 104.07 μM, described as lower than that of acarbose. Molecular docking showed 6h had the lowest binding energy (−10.56 kcal/mol) of all docked derivatives. Trp329 forms hydrophobic bonds with both 6h and acarbose, anchoring them in the same orientation. The abstract reports 104.07 mM, which would be drastically less potent than acarbose (typically in the nanomolar to low micromolar range). 6h represents a lead candidate for further optimization as a non-sugar-mimetic antidiabetic agent. The extra hydrogen bonds (three vs acarbose's two hydrophobic-directed anchors) contribute to the superior stability.
Trp329 is a critical residue for binding ligand orientation in the α-glucosidase active site. Molecular docking showed Trp329 directed the binding of 6h in the active site. Acarbose uses Trp329 for hydrophobic interactions with the deoxyglucosamine moiety. Compound 6h, which mimics acarbose binding, also interacts with Trp329. The paper does not perform mutagenesis to confirm the essential role of Trp329; the claim is based solely on docking predictions. Drug design strategies should aim to exploit hydrophobic interactions with Trp329 to anchor ligands in the correct orientation.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The inhibitory assay was performed in triplicate, with the average percent inhibition calculated for each compound. The IC50 assay screened all 25 compounds at a single concentration (100 µg/mL), with further dose-response not explicitly detailed for all compounds. Compounds 3, 6c, and 6d showed >60% inhibition, while 2a, 2d, 6a, 6b, 6h showed 50–60%, indicating a clear activity plateau. Substitution at position 4 was explored through N-alkylation (2a–l) versus aminobridge substitution (6a–i) as an ablation of the scaffold modification strategy. The molecular docking was performed on a single complex; no multiple docking runs or varying crystal structures were tested. The RSD of binding energy was less than 2.34 kcal/mol, providing a measure of docking precision.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates acarbose mimicking the oxocarbenium ion-like transition state and the range of biological activities of α-glucosidase inhibitors (antiviral, anticancer). Figure 2 shows the synthetic route of the fused pyrimidine derivatives, with IR/NMR data for key intermediates. Figure 3 displays average percent inhibitions for compounds 6a–d and 6h, showing those exceeding 50%. Figure 4 presents IC50 values of the most active compounds (3, 2a, 2d, and 6-series) against acarbose. Figure 5 shows the α-glucosidase binding mode for acarbose and compound 6h, illustrating hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions. Table 1 provides binding energies, number of hydrogen bonds, and closest amino acid residues for all docked compounds.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the synthesis of 25 non-sugar-mimetic tricyclic compounds with IC50 values (best 104.07 μM) competitive with acarbose, establishing a new aminobridge-at-position-4 pyrimidine scaffold for antidiabetic design. 2. The strongest evidence is the IC50 of 104.07 μM for compound 6h, combined with molecular docking confirming the lowest binding energy (−10.56 kcal/mol) and extra hydrogen bonds directed by Trp329, mirroring the binding mode of acarbose. 3. The future path lies in synthesizing analogs of 6h with varied amino-bridge substitutions and exploring in vivo efficacy to validate the non-sugar-mimetic scaffold's potential as a clinical antidiabetic agent.

summary.title: Major concerns with the integrity of the mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier in dodecyl-phosphocholine used for solution NMR studies
summary.authors: Martin S King; Paul G Crichton; Jonathan J Ruprecht; Edmund R S Kunji
summary.field_subfield: Biophysical chemistry / Structural biology of membrane proteins
summary.executive_summary: This paper by King et al. serves as a critical rebuttal to claims by Brüschweiler et al. that the yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier (AAC3), when refolded from E. coli inclusion bodies using the detergent dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC), maintains a functional and native-like folded state suitable for solution NMR and ITC studies. The authors demonstrate through multiple biophysical approaches that DPC leads to immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation of AAC3. Key evidence includes: (1) ITC measurements showing a CATR binding Kd of ~15 µM for DPC-refolded AAC3, versus ~1.2 nM for native AAC3, a 3–4 order of magnitude discrepancy; (2) NMR data showing ADP binding at 500 µM versus native ~nanomolar levels; (3) thermostability assays using CPM fluorescence that reveal a complete absence of a cooperative unfolding transition when AAC3 is diluted into DPC, indicating a non-native state; and (4) functional reconstitution assays where DPC pretreatment of AAC3 leads to complete loss of CATR-sensitive ADP uptake in liposomes. The authors argue that the NMR signals observed for CATR and ADP binding to DPC-refolded AAC3 likely represent non-specific interactions driven by high protein concentrations and temperatures, rather than biologically relevant ligand binding. They further note that the reference Kd of 192 µM for ATR cited by the original authors contains a typographical error (corrected to 192 nM), undermining the validity of the comparison. The study concludes that the data presented by Brüschweiler et al. have no biological relevance and that DPC is sufficiently harsh to denature functional AAC3.

The CATR binding affinity of native AAC3 is in the low nanomolar range (sub--micromolar), consistent with its role as a potent toxin.
