Executive Summary
This paper by King et al. serves as a critical rebuttal to claims by Brüschweiler et al. that the yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier (AAC3), when refolded from E. coli inclusion bodies using the detergent dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC), maintains a functional and native-like folded state suitable for solution NMR and ITC studies. The authors demonstrate through multiple biophysical approaches that DPC leads to immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation of AAC3. Key evidence includes: (1) ITC measurements showing a CATR binding Kd of ~15 µM for DPC-refolded AAC3, versus ~1.2 nM for native AAC3, a 3–4 order of magnitude discrepancy; (2) NMR data showing ADP binding at 500 µM versus native ~nanomolar levels; (3) thermostability assays using CPM fluorescence that reveal a complete absence of a cooperative unfolding transition when AAC3 is diluted into DPC, indicating a non-native state; and (4) functional reconstitution assays where DPC pretreatment of AAC3 leads to complete loss of CATR-sensitive ADP uptake in liposomes. The authors argue that the NMR signals observed for CATR and ADP binding to DPC-refolded AAC3 likely represent non-specific interactions driven by high protein concentrations and temperatures, rather than biologically relevant ligand binding. They further note that the reference Kd of 192 µM for ATR cited by the original authors contains a typographical error (corrected to 192 nM), undermining the validity of the comparison. The study concludes that the data presented by Brüschweiler et al. have no biological relevance and that DPC is sufficiently harsh to denature functional AAC3.

Research Context
The authors have studied the yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier AAC3 extensively, solving its structure by electron and X-ray crystallography. Previous work included studying AAC3 interactions with specific inhibitors atractyloside (ATR) and carboxyatractyloside (CATR) by single--molecule force spectroscopy. The authors are addressing claims that AAC3 can be refolded to homogeneity from E. coli inclusion bodies using dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC). The prior study claimed AAC3 is maintained in a folded and active state for the duration of ITC and NMR experiments. The authors contend that in their hands, DPC leads to immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation when isolated from the inner membrane. The functional state of native AAC3 in the membrane was previously shown by functional complementation.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether AAC3 refolded from inclusion bodies in DPC retains its native tertiary structure and functional activity. The authors hypothesize that DPC denatures AAC3, leading to inactivation and loss of specific ligand binding. They predict that ITC Kd values for CATR binding to DPC-refolded AAC3 will be orders of magnitude higher than native values. They further hypothesize that ADP binding NMR shifts will be non-specific, occurring at concentrations far above native affinity. They predict that thermostability assays will show no cooperative melting transition in DPC compared to native detergent conditions.

Methodological Details
Thermostability assays used the thiol--reactive fluorophore N--[4--(7--diethylamino--4--methyl--3--coumarinyl)phenyl] maleimide (CPM) to monitor unfolding. A 5 mg mL --1 stock of CPM dissolved in DMSO was diluted 50--fold into a buffer of 20 mM PIPES pH 7.0, 100 mM NaCl, 0.1% dodecyl--maltoside, and 0.1 mg mL --1 tetraoleoyl cardiolipin. For dodecyl--phosphocholine assays, the buffer contained 3 mM DPC instead of dodecyl--maltoside. Approximately 1.5 μg of purified protein was added into a final volume of 45 μL. Fluorescence was measured on a Qiagen Rotorgene Q using the HRM channel, with excitation at 440--480 nm and emission at 505--515 nm. Measurements were made in 1 °C intervals from 25 to 90 °C with a ramp rate of 5.6 °C/min. ITC used a NanoITC--LV isothermal titration calorimeter (TA Instruments) at 10 °C. CATR was prepared as a 500 μM stock in buffer, and was titrated into purified 25 μM AAC3 at 0.83 mg mL --1. Injections were 2 μL in an initial volume of 170 μL at 3--min intervals with a stirrer speed of 350 rpm. Reconstitution used L--α--phosphatidylcholine and tetraoleoyl cardiolipin mixed in 20:1 w/w ratio (10 mg total lipid) in chloroform. Lipids were solubilized with 55 μL 25% v/v pentaethylene glycol monodecyl detergent before adding 30 μg of purified AAC3. Detergent was stepwise removed using 4 × 30 mg and 4 × 60 mg of Bio--Beads SM--2 in 20--min intervals. ADP uptake assays used a Hamilton MicroLab Star robot with 100 μL proteoliposomes per well of a 96--well filter plate (pore size 0.45 μm). Radiolabeled ADP ([14C])--ADP at 2.2 GBq mmol --1 gave a final concentration of 1.5 µM ADP.

Procedures And Architectures
For protein purification, particulate material was removed by ultracentrifugation at 140,000 g for 45 min at 4 °C. The soluble fraction was loaded onto a Ni--Sepharose high performance column at 1 mL min --1 on an ÄKTAprime. The column was washed with 40 column volumes of buffer (20 mM PIPES pH 7.0, 150 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole, 0.1% dodecyl--maltoside, 0.1 mg mL --1 tetraoleoyl cardiolipin). The column was further washed with 20 column volumes of buffer B (100 mM NaCl). The column material was resuspended with 500 μL buffer B and transferred to a vial with 5 mM CaCl2 and 75 μL Factor Xa, incubated at 10 °C overnight. The following day, the cleaved protein was separated by filtration and centrifugation, snap--frozen, and stored in liquid nitrogen. For ITC, both CATR titrant and protein samples were degassed under vacuum at 10 °C for at least 20 min. Thermostability was monitored using a modified procedure using a rotary qPCR machine. CATR:AAC3 molar ratios were 0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, and 100 for the thermostability experiments.

Key Results
For ITC, CATR binding to DPC-refolded AAC3 gave a Kd of ~15 µM. Native AAC3 (in dodecyl-maltoside/tetraoleoyl cardiolipin) gave an average CATR Kd of 72 nM in the authors' ITC measurements. The native Kd of 72 nM is 200 to 2000--fold lower than those reported by Brüschweiler et al.. For functional complementation in mitochondria, ADP transport was half--maximally inhibited by 1.2 nM CATR. In the membrane, published Kd values for CATR binding are all in the low nanomolar range. The NMR Kd for CATR binding to refolded AAC3 was ~150 µM, while ADP binding NMR yielded 500 μM. The ADP NMR Kd of 500 μM is ~85--fold higher than published consensus values in membrane and ~25--fold higher than solubilized carrier. In thermostability, the dodecyl--maltoside preparation showed a typical protein melt curve consistent with thermal denaturation of a folded protein. Adding CATR at a molar ratio of one or above caused a marked shift in AAC3 stability to higher temperatures. In the DPC preparation, a high signal with no transition was observed, showing AAC3 is in a non--native state. In the DPC case, CATR addition had no effect, demonstrating no functional binding site. Dilution of AAC3 into DPC before reconstitution resulted in complete loss of CATR--sensitive ADP uptake in liposomes. The CATR Kd value of 192 µM cited by the original authors was a typographical error; the corrected value is 192 nM.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The authors argue that the low-affinity binding observed in DPC is inconsistent with CATR's role as a powerful toxin requiring low nanomolar affinity. They contend that the limited and predominantly dynamic chemical shift perturbations observed for CATR binding are inconsistent with tight binding. The chemical shift perturbations for ADP were located on the matrix side, far from the consensus binding site in the central cavity. The authors suggest that the observed chemical shift perturbations could represent non--specific interactions promoted by high protein concentrations and temperatures in NMR experiments. The structural explanation for unliganded AAC3 stability relies on lateral membrane pressure and counter pressure from the water--filled cavity, which is absent in detergent micelles. They posit that binding of CATR introduces polar and van der Waals interactions that cross--link transmembrane α--helices, explaining high affinity and improved detergent stability. The authors conclude that the data presented by Brüschweiler et al. have no biological relevance due to the denaturation of AAC3 in DPC.

Contradictions And Limitations
The original authors cited a CATR Kd of 192 µM (typographical error) for comparison, while the actual corrected value is 192 nM. The original authors' NMR data showed CATR binding to refolded AAC3, but King et al. argue the observed dynamics are inconsistent with tight binding. King et al. acknowledge their own ITC experiments were difficult, with only 2 out of 10 trials succeeding due to low enthalpy and unstable apo--state in detergent. The authors note that the crystal structure was solved with CATR present, but purified and crystallized in maltoside detergents without CATR for 5--7 days. The paper is a rebuttal; the primary data (ITC, CPM, liposome assays) are generated by the authors of this commentary rather than in the original paper they are critiquing.

Claims
AAC3 refolded in DPC is in a non-native, denatured state and lacks functional activity for transport or specific inhibitor binding. The CPM thermostability assay showed a high signal with no cooperative melting transition in DPC, unlike the dodecyl--maltoside control. CATR addition in DPC yielded no stability shift, indicating no functional binding site was available. DPC pretreatment of AAC3 before liposome reconstitution resulted in complete loss of CATR-sensitive ADP uptake. The original study claimed to maintain AAC3 in a folded and active state for the duration of experiments. A limited number of NMR chemical shift perturbations for CATR binding were still observed in DPC. Any biochemical, structural, or thermodynamic measurements derived from AAC3 in DPC are of no biological relevance. Future solution NMR and ITC studies of membrane carriers in DPC may yield artifactual data reflecting non--specific interactions rather than native behavior.
The CATR binding affinity of native AAC3 is in the low nanomolar range (sub--micromolar), consistent with its role as a potent toxin. The authors' ITC gave an average Kd of 72 nM for native AAC3 in dodecyl-maltoside. Functional complementation in mitochondria showed half--maximal ADP inhibition by 1.2 nM CATR. Published Kd values for CATR binding to AAC in membrane are all in the low nanomolar range. The original study reported a CATR Kd of ~15 µM in DPC, which is ~125--fold higher than the native value. The NMR Kd for CATR binding in DPC was ~150 µM, while ADP binding was 500 µM. A discrepancy of 3–4 orders of magnitude between native and DPC-refolded affinities is physically inconsistent with a preserved structure.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors performed a detergent comparison: AAC3 in dodecyl--maltoside showed a typical melt curve, while in DPC it showed no transition. A liposome reconstitution experiment compared DPC pretreatment (complete loss of uptake) versus native dodecyl--maltoside reconstitution (preserved uptake). The thermostability assay used different CATR:AAC3 molar ratios (0 to 100) to demonstrate the stability effect in the folded state but not the DPC state.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows the dose--response of 1.2 nM CATR half--maximally inhibiting ADP transport in functional complementation experiments. Figure 1b shows the ITC isotherm for native AAC3 in dodecyl-maltoside/tetraoleoyl cardiolipin giving a Kd of 72 nM. Figure 1c shows the CPM thermostability melt curve for native AAC3 in dodecyl--maltoside with and without CATR. Figure 1d shows the CPM profile for AAC3 in 3 mM DPC, displaying a high signal with no transition and no CATR effect. Supplementary Figure 1a illustrates the ring of transmembrane α--helices held by lateral pressure and counter pressure from the water--filled cavity. Supplementary Figure 1b shows the CATR-induced cross--linking of transmembrane α--helices and improved stability in detergents. Supplementary Figure 2 shows the ADP uptake assay in liposomes comparing DPC pretreatment versus dodecyl--maltoside pretreatment. Supplementary Table 1 lists 24 different binding studies for CATR and ATR and highlights the typographical error in the 192 µM reference. Supplementary Table 2 compares the NMR-determined ADP Kd of 500 μM to consensus values in membrane and solubilized carrier.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is demonstrating that AAC3 refolded from inclusion bodies in DPC is in a non--native, denatured state with no functional activity, rendering all subsequent biochemical and structural data biologically irrelevant. 2. The strongest evidence is the 3–4 order of magnitude discrepancy in CATR Kd (~15 µM in DPC vs. 1.2 nM in native) combined with the complete loss of cooperative unfolding in DPC thermostability assays. 3. The future path requires using milder, native-like detergents (e.g., dodecyl-maltoside) or lipid nanodiscs for studying AAC3, and the authors emphasize that DPC is too harsh for membrane carrier preservation.

summary.title: Inhibitor of sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase impairs paramyxovirus replication
summary.authors: Naveen Kumar; Sanjay Barua; Nitin Khandelwal; Kundan Kumar Chaubey; Ram Kumar; Krishan Dutt; Yogesh Chander; Thachamvally Riyesh; Vir Shoor Singh; Bhupendra Nath
summary.field_subfield: Virology / Host-pathogen interactions / Antiviral drug discovery
summary.executive_summary: This study demonstrates for the first time that the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) regulates paramyxovirus replication, specifically for Newcastle disease virus (NDV) and peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV). Virus infection was shown to induce SERCA2 expression, which thapsigargin treatment could block. Time-of-addition assays identified that the inhibitor impairs multiple pre-budding steps, and virus step-specific assays confirmed thapsigargin does not affect attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding directly. Viral entry assays demonstrated reduced titers upon SERCA inhibition, and immunofluorescence revealed defective subcellular localization of viral proteins—with 70% of thapsigargin-treated cells showing cytoplasmic foci rather than cell surface localization (compared to 10–30% in controls). judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study demonstrates for the first time that the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) regulates paramyxovirus replication, specifically for Newcastle disease virus (NDV) and peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV). Using Vero cells infected with both viruses, the authors showed that the SERCA-specific inhibitor thapsigargin (a non-competitive inhibitor extracted from Thapsia garganica) significantly reduced viral progeny at non-cytotoxic concentrations, while overexpression of SERCA2 in HeLa and goat kidney cells rescued this inhibitory effect. Virus infection was shown to induce SERCA2 expression, which thapsigargin treatment could block. Time-of-addition assays identified that the inhibitor impairs multiple pre-budding steps, and virus step-specific assays confirmed thapsigargin does not affect attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding directly. Viral entry assays demonstrated reduced titers upon SERCA inhibition, and immunofluorescence revealed defective subcellular localization of viral proteins—with 70% of thapsigargin-treated cells showing cytoplasmic foci rather than cell surface localization (compared to 10–30% in controls). Notably, NDV acquired a significant partial resistance after 70 passages in the presence of 0.25 µM thapsigargin (100-fold inhibition vs. 10,000-fold at passage zero), whereas PPRV did not. This study marks the first report of a virus acquiring resistance to a host-targeting inhibitor and identifies SERCA as a potential antiviral drug target.

Research Context
Viral pathogens with high mutation rates easily develop resistance to drugs targeting viral proteins. The rise in drug resistance has prompted a shift toward developing novel antiviral strategies. Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites highly dependent on host cellular factors for replication. Host factors can be proviral (facilitating replication) or antiviral (inhibiting replication). Proviral host factors serve as targets for novel antiviral therapeutics. Protein phosphorylation and dephosphorylation are ubiquitous regulatory mechanisms in signal transduction. Three families of P-type Ca2+-ATPases (PMCA, SERCA, SPCA) regulate intracellular calcium homeostasis. SERCA transports Ca2+ from cytosol to the endoplasmic reticulum and is involved in signal transduction, apoptosis, and transcription. There are three SERCA genes (ATP2A1-3) coding for ten SERCA proteins through alternative splicing. The role of Ca2+-ATPases in virus replication is only beginning to be appreciated. A recent study suggests that SPCA1 supports virus replication. The authors previously screened kinase and phosphate inhibitors for antiviral potential against influenza A. SERCA inhibitor was identified as a candidate blocking NDV and PPRV replication.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether SERCA regulates paramyxovirus replication and how. The authors hypothesize that SERCA functions as a proviral host factor supporting NDV and PPRV replication. The predicted outcome is that inhibition of SERCA will reduce viral progeny and overexpression will rescue this effect. A secondary hypothesis is that infection-induced SERCA expression contributes to the viral life cycle. The authors also test whether viruses can acquire resistance to a host-targeting inhibitor. The specific mechanisms are predicted to involve viral entry and subcellular protein localization. A third hypothesis is that resistance is unlikely due to the high genetic barrier of host-targeting agents. The predicted outcome of long-term passage is that viruses may bypass dependence on the cellular factor.

Methodological Details
Cell lines used include Vero (African green-monkey kidney), 293T (human embryonic kidney), HeLa, and goat kidney cells. Cells were grown in DMEM supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum and antibiotics. PPRV and NDV were available in-house and characterized previously. Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. Thapsigargin (non-competitive SERCA inhibitor, sesquiterpene lactone) was procured from Sigma. Cytotoxicity was analyzed by MTT assay. Vero/MDBK cells were infected at MOI=0.1 with 0.5 µM thapsigargin or DMSO vehicle. Progeny virus was quantified by plaque assay. Virucidal assays used virus suspensions of ~10^6 pfu incubated for 1.5 h at 37°C in ten-fold thapsigargin dilutions. Time-of-addition and virus step-specific assays (attachment, entry, RNA synthesis, budding) were conducted. HeLa/goat kidney cells were transfected with empty vector (pCR3) or SERCA2 plasmid (pCR3-SERCA2) via Lipofectamine 3000. Overexpression assay: MOI=1; NDV harvest at 24 hpi, PPRV at 96 hpi. Immunofluorescence: Vero cells at ~20% confluency, MOI=5 for 2 h; thapsigargin at 3 hpi (NDV) or 10 hpi (PPRV). Fixation: 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min; blocking: 1% BSA for 30 min. Primary antibodies (rabbit anti-NDV/PPRV or mouse SERCA2) for 30 min in 0.2% saponin. Secondary antibodies (FITC anti-rabbit or Rhodamine anti-mouse) for 30 min in 0.2% saponin. Nuclear counterstain with DAPI; examined by fluorescence microscopy. Resistance selection: sequential 70 passages in Vero cells with 0.25 µM thapsigargin or 0.05% DMSO. At each passage: confluent monolayers infected, washed 5 times with PBS, incubated 72–120 h until ≥75% CPE. Infection of passage viruses at MOI=0.01 for subsequent round. Resistance comparison: P70-thapsigargin vs. P0/P70-control at MOI=0.1 with 24 h harvest. Western blot: Vero cells infected with NDV at MOI=5 for 1 h; thapsigargin or vehicle at 16 hpi.

Procedures And Architectures
The experimental design follows a structured progression from cytotoxicity and virucidal testing to functional relevance and resistance analysis. Cytotoxicity was tested at concentrations from 0.00064 µM to 2 µM in Vero/MDBK cells. Concentrations >2 µM were toxic, while ≤2 µM showed no significant effect over 96 h. The non-cytotoxic concentration of 0.5 µM thapsigargin was chosen for all functional assays. In the time-of-addition assay, inhibitor was applied at different time points post-infection. For NDV (10 h cycle), the highest inhibition was 30 min before infection. Inhibition progressively decreased from 1 to 6 hpi for NDV. For PPRV (24 h cycle), highest inhibition was 30 min prior to infection. PPRV inhibition progressively decreased from 4 to 24 hpi. In the entry assay, preattached virus at 4°C entered at 37°C in the presence of thapsigargin. In the resistance selection, 70 sequential passages were performed with a high genetic barrier strategy. Western blot used GAPDH as a housekeeping control for normalization of SERCA2 expression. Immunofluorescence used a dual-antibody approach to visualize viral proteins and SERCA2 co-localization.

Key Results
Thapsigargin at 0.5 µM significantly inhibited NDV and PPRV replication in Vero cells (Figs 1c, 1d). Thapsigargin significantly inhibited BHV-1 but not BPXV replication, indicating specificity for paramyxoviruses and BHV-1. Thapsigargin showed no virucidal effect on any tested virus at 0.5 µM or 5 µM over 1.5 h (Fig 1g). Overexpression of SERCA2 in HeLa/goat kidney cells facilitated NDV/PPRV replication and rescued the thapsigargin inhibitory effect (Figs 2a, 2b). PPRV infection induced SERCA2 expression in Vero cells, peaking between 24–72 hpi and declining at 96 hpi (Fig 3a). Thapsigargin treatment blocked the virus-induced SERCA2 expression. Thapsigargin did not affect virus attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding (data not shown). Thapsigargin treatment reduced NDV (Fig 5a) and PPRV (Fig 5b) entry titers. Immunofluorescence showed 70% of thapsigargin-treated cells had cytoplasmic foci, versus 10–30% in DMSO controls (Figs 6c, 6d). NDV showed partial resistance at P35, with 100-fold inhibition compared to 10,000-fold at passage zero (Fig 7a). A completely resistant phenotype was not achieved even after 70 passages of NDV (Fig 7a, 7b). PPRV showed no significant resistance even at passage 70 (Fig 7c). Control-passaged viruses did not acquire thapsigargin resistance, confirming it is a specific event rather than a general phenomenon.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The rescue of thapsigargin inhibition by SERCA2 overexpression confirms SERCA is a specific host factor required for replication. Virus-induced SERCA2 upregulation suggests the virus actively exploits the host calcium pump. Defective protein localization (cytoplasmic foci) suggests SERCA is required for viral protein transport from cytoplasm to cell surface. The ability of NDV to acquire partial resistance to a host-targeting agent challenges the general belief that viruses cannot escape host-factor targeting. SERCA may serve as a novel antiviral drug target due to the host's low genetic variability. Multiple calcium transporters (SERCA, PMCA, SPCA) may coordinate to facilitate paramyxovirus replication. Possible resistance mechanisms include changes in host-factor requirement (e.g., using alternative entry factors) or enhanced binding affinity.

Contradictions And Limitations
A complete thapsigargin-resistant NDV phenotype could not be achieved even after 70 passages. Fluctuations in viral titers and fold inhibition were observed during resistance selection, possibly due to inconsistent harvest time and MOI across passages. Perfect co-localization of SERCA and viral proteins could not be observed by immunofluorescence. Co-immunoprecipitation assays to analyze SERCA-virus interaction were unsuccessful. No direct interaction between SERCA and viral proteins was determined in this study. Data for step-specific assays (attachment, RNA synthesis, budding) are not shown. The authors note the MOI and harvest time were not similar at each passage for resistance studies.

Claims
SERCA regulates paramyxovirus (NDV and PPRV) replication by mediating viral entry and protein localization. Thapsigargin at 0.5 µM significantly inhibited NDV and PPRV in Vero cells. Overexpression of SERCA2 rescued the inhibitory effect of thapsigargin. Virus-induced SERCA2 expression was enhanced during infection. 70% of thapsigargin-treated cells showed cytoplasmic protein foci versus 10-30% in controls. Thapsigargin reduced entry titers for both NDV and PPRV. No direct interaction between SERCA and viral proteins was detected. Perfect co-localization was not observed in immunofluorescence. Data for attachment, RNA synthesis, and budding assays are not shown. SERCA is a novel candidate for antiviral drug development. Host-targeting strategies with high genetic barriers are viable for antiviral design.
NDV can acquire partial resistance to a host-targeting inhibitor (thapsigargin) through sequential passage. NDV showed 100-fold inhibition at P35 vs 10,000-fold at P0. Control-passaged viruses did not acquire resistance, confirming specificity. Complete resistance was not achieved even after 70 passages. PPRV did not acquire any significant resistance at passage 70. The general assumption that viruses cannot escape host-targeting agents may be incorrect. Mechanisms of resistance (alternative host factor use or enhanced affinity) require further study.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Cytotoxicity was tested across a range of 0.00064 µM to 2 µM to establish non-toxic dosage. Virucidal assays at 0.5 µM and 5 µM ruled out direct virion inactivation as the source of antiviral effect. Vehicle control (0.05% DMSO) was used across all inhibition and resistance assays. Overexpression used both empty vector (pCR3) and SERCA2 plasmid (pCR3-SERCA2) controls. Resistance comparison used matched MOI (0.1) and harvest time (24 h) to control for assay variability.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a, 1b show MTT cytotoxicity data (concentration vs cell viability). Figure 1c, 1d, 1e, 1f show antiviral efficacy (thapsigargin vs controls) for NDV, PPRV, BHV-1, BPXV. Figure 1g shows virucidal activity (thapsigargin at 0.5 and 5 µM vs virions). Figure 2a, 2b show SERCA2 overexpression facilitating NDV/PPRV replication and rescuing thapsigargin inhibition. Figure 3a shows SERCA2 expression profile over time during PPRV infection (GAPDH as control). Figure 3b shows thapsigargin blocking virus-induced SERCA2 expression. Figure 4a, 4b show time-of-addition inhibition profiles for NDV and PPRV. Figure 5a, 5b show reduced entry titers with thapsigargin. Figure 6a, 6b show immunofluorescence images of viral protein localization. Figure 6c, 6d quantify defective protein localization (cytoplasmic foci) in thapsigargin-treated cells. Figure 7a shows NDV resistance profile over 70 passages in the presence of thapsigargin. Figure 7b compares P70-thapsigargin virus to P0 and P70-control viruses. Figure 7c shows PPRV sensitivity across passage levels.

Three Takeaways
1. SERCA is a proviral host factor that facilitates paramyxovirus (NDV, PPRV) replication by mediating viral entry and proper subcellular protein localization. 2. NDV can acquire partial resistance to a host-targeting inhibitor (thapsigargin) through sequential passage (P35 significant partial resistance), while PPRV does not. 3. SERCA represents a novel, high-genetic-barrier host-targeting antiviral drug target, but the mechanism of resistance and direct SERCA-viral interaction require further study.

summary.title: MicroRNA-196a is regulated by ER and is a prognostic biomarker in ER+ Breast Cancer
summary.authors: Michael J G Milevskiy, Udai Gujral, Carolina Del Lama Marques, Andrew Stone, Korinne Northwood, Lez J Burke, Julia M W Gee, Kenneth Nephew, Susan Clark, Melissa A Brown, Mjg Milevskiy
summary.field_subfield: Oncology / Epigenetics and MicroRNA Regulation in Breast Cancer
summary.executive_summary: This study characterizes the transcriptional regulation and clinical significance of MIR196A (microRNA-196a) in estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer. MIR196A is transcribed from two genomic loci (HOXC/MIR196A2 and HOXB/MIR196A1) and has been implicated as an oncogene in breast, lung, and cell cycle regulation. The authors demonstrate that MIR196A2 expression is dynamically regulated by estrogen, with nascent RNA production peaking 40 mins following oestradiol addition in MCF7 cells, a response absent at the MIR196A1 locus. Structural characterization revealed that MIR196A2 shares a promoter with HOXC10 (PP1) and is regulated by long-range interactions between the promoter and two distal enhancer elements: the previously identified HOTAIR distal enhancer (HDE) and a novel MIR196A2-Enhancer (mE), both tethered via ERα-mediated gene looping. ChIA-PET and 3C confirmed physical interactions between both enhancers and the MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter. DNA methylation analysis showed the CpG island upstream of MIR196A2 is unmethylated in normal HMEC but methylated in MCF10A and MCF7 cells, and completely methylated in oestrogen-deprived/fulvestrant-treated cells but not tamoxifen-resistant cells. Clinically, METABRIC data reveal MIR196A is overexpressed in breast tumours compared to adjacent tissue, and its high expression correlates with poor survival in ER+ disease but better outcome in triple-negative breast cancer. Specifically, in ER+ tumours, low MIR196A expression predicts >95% 10-year survival, while the high-expression group shows 61% 10-year survival. Paradoxically, in premenopausal women, high MIR196A associates with good outcome, whereas in postmenopausal women, it associates with poor outcome. Therapeutic resistance models showed MIR196A significantly increased in tamoxifen-resistant (TAMR) and paclitaxel/adriamycin-resistant MCF7 cells, while almost depleted in fulvestrant-resistant (FASR) cells. These changes correspond to altered ERα binding at MIR196A enhancer and promoter regions in non-responders and metastatic tumours. The study provides a novel stratification method for therapeutically resistant breast cancer and highlights the role of HOX gene de-repression in resistance.

Executive Summary

MIR196A is transcribed from two genomic loci (HOXC/MIR196A2 and HOXB/MIR196A1) and has been implicated as an oncogene in breast, lung, and cell cycle regulation. ChIA-PET and 3C confirmed physical interactions between both enhancers and the MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter. DNA methylation analysis showed the CpG island upstream of MIR196A2 is unmethylated in normal HMEC but methylated in MCF10A and MCF7 cells, and completely methylated in oestrogen-deprived/fulvestrant-treated cells but not tamoxifen-resistant cells. Clinically, METABRIC data reveal MIR196A is overexpressed in breast tumours compared to adjacent tissue, and its high expression correlates with poor survival in ER+ disease but better outcome in triple-negative breast cancer. Specifically, in ER+ tumours, low MIR196A expression predicts >95% 10-year survival, while the high-expression group shows 61% 10-year survival. Paradoxically, in premenopausal women, high MIR196A associates with good outcome, whereas in postmenopausal women, it associates with poor outcome. Therapeutic resistance models showed MIR196A significantly increased in tamoxifen-resistant (TAMR) and paclitaxel/adriamycin-resistant MCF7 cells, while almost depleted in fulvestrant-resistant (FASR) cells. These changes correspond to altered ERα binding at MIR196A enhancer and promoter regions in non-responders and metastatic tumours. The study provides a novel stratification method for therapeutically resistant breast cancer and highlights the role of HOX gene de-repression in resistance.

Research Context
MicroRNAs are short non-coding RNAs that post-transcriptionally regulate gene expression and are involved in all hallmarks of cancer. MIR196A is transcribed from two genomic locations, the HOXC (Chr12) and HOXB (Chr17) loci downstream of HOXC10 and upstream of HOXB9 respectively. While MIR196A is overexpressed in breast tumours and a SNP in MIR196A2 is associated with decreased breast cancer risk, little is known about the regulation of the genes encoding this miRNA. The transcriptional regulation of miRNAs is a complex multi-faceted biological process significantly altered in cancer, yet enhancer regulation of miRNAs remains in its infancy. Previous studies have shown MIR196A targets Annexin-1 to alter angiogenesis, increases lung cancer cell growth through HOXA5 targeting, and influences the cell cycle by targeting p27/Kip1.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is to characterise the expression landscape of MIR196A including factors regulating its expression and explore potential roles of regulatory elements and factors in breast cancer prognostication. The authors hypothesised that MIR196A2 is transcriptionally regulated by oestrogen and controlled by long-range transcriptional regulation mediated by ERα tethered gene looping. The study also hypothesised that a consorted effort of multiple enhancers is responsible for the overexpression of HOXC genes in cancer, possibly driven by extensive binding and activity of ERα. The study further hypothesised that there is a change in the regulation and expression of HOX genes through and following menopause, which in turn impacts their contribution to the development of certain breast cancer subtypes. The final hypothesis suggests that the pathway to resistance in ER+ tumours involves de-repression and over-activation of promoter and enhancer elements, allowing tumour cells to sustain a stem-cell like state through HOX gene expression.

Methodological Details
Cell lines used included MCF7, Tamoxifen-resistant (TAMR), Fulvestrant-resistant (FASR), and oestrogen-deprived (MCF7x) cells obtained from AstraZeneca, authenticated by STR profiling. Publicly available genomic datasets were utilised: MCF7 ChIP-Seq (GSE14664), GRO-Seq (GSE27463), ChIA-PET (GSE39495), Breast tumour ERα ChIP-Seq (GSE32222), and DNA methylation from The Cancer Genome Atlas. METABRIC breast tumour expression and clinical information were sourced from EGAS00000083, and RNA-Seq from paclitaxel/adriamycin resistant cells was sourced from GSE68815. Luciferase reporter assays used 500 ng of modified pGL3 reporter constructs, 20 ng of pRL-TK transfection control, and 0.5 μL of Lipofectamine 3000 in MCF7 cells. RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent, DNase I treated with the DNA-free kit, and miRNA analysis was performed using miScript RT II kit and SYBR Green PCR Kit. qRT-PCRs were performed on a Corbet Rotorgene-6000, with miRNA expression normalised to snoRNA RNU6b. Survival analysis was performed using Cox proportional hazard regression in MedCalc (version 12.7), Kaplan-Meier curves in GraphPad Prism, and ROC curves for optimal cutoffs. 3C was adapted from Vakoc 2005, Hagege 2007, and Tan-Wong 2008, with cells grown to 60-80% confluence and fixed with 1% formaldehyde.

Procedures And Architectures
ChIP-Seq for RNA polymerase II in MCF7 cells demonstrated that polymerase binding in the region surrounding HOXC10 and MIR196A is dependent on oestrogen and repressed with tamoxifen or fulvestrant. GRO-Seq measured nascent RNA production, revealing a dramatic increase in the MIR196A2 region peaking at 40 mins following oestradiol addition, validated by qRT-PCR and RNA-Seq. ChIA-PET identified two major interaction sites with MIR196A2 promoters: the HOTAIR distal enhancer (HDE) and a novel MIR196A2-Enhancer (mE). 3C-qPCR demonstrated that both HDE and mE physically interact with each of the two MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter regions. Cloning of enhancer fragments downstream of luciferase reporters demonstrated significant augmentation of transcription for both PP1 and PP2, with HDE being most active in MCF7 cells. DNA methylation analysis showed the upstream CpG island is mostly methylated in non-malignant MCF10A and cancerous MCF7 cells, whilst unmethylated in human mammary epithelial cells. METABRIC data were clustered using the Multiple Experiment Viewer (MeV) with Manhattan average-linkage hierarchical clustering of both rows and columns.

Key Results
MIR196A expression highly correlates with HOXC genes in breast cancer, particularly HOXC10, while in normal breast cells the association is limited and observed most strongly with HOXC11 and HOXC10. GRO-Seq clearly indicates a dramatic increase in RNA production peaking at 40 mins following oestradiol addition, and this increase is specific to MIR196A2 but not MIR196A1. ChIA-PET identified two major interacting sites with MIR196A2 promoters: the previously identified HDE and the novel mE enhancer. 3C-qPCR confirmed that both HDE and mE physically interact with each of the two MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter regions. Luciferase assays showed PP1 (HOXC10 promoter) has the most active promoter in MCF7 cells, with HDE appearing to be the most active enhancer. The upstream CpG island is mostly methylated in MCF10A and MCF7 but completely methylated in oestrogen-deprived and fulvestrant-treated cells, and not in tamoxifen-resistant cells. Four distinct MIR196A expression clusters were identified; clusters 1 and 3 correlate strongly with hormone receptors and cofactors, while clusters 2 and 4 associate with EGFR and HER2. MIR196A is over-expressed in breast tumours compared to normal adjacent tissue, and over-expression is associated with an increase in tumour stage. In ER+ breast tumours, women with low MIR196A expression had >95% survival at 10 years, while most women in the high-expression group died within 17 years, with 61% at 10 years. In premenopausal women, MIR196A is one of the few significant biomarkers for ER+ tumours; multivariate analysis confirms it is significant before menopause. In postmenopausal women, all tested biomarkers were significant, including MIR196A, however high expression is now associated with a poor outcome. MIR196A expression is significantly increased in tamoxifen-resistant MCF7 cells (TAMR) whilst it is almost depleted in fulvestrant-resistant (FASR) cells. MIR196A expression again increases in paclitaxel and adromycin resistant cell lines compared to the treatment-sensitive cell line. ERα ChIP-Seq from human patients showed increased ERα occupancy at both enhancer and promoter regions of MIR196A in non-responders and metastases.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The CpG island lies within a transcriptionally active region (per GRO-Seq), and its hypermethylation in a high-transcription region may severely impair expression, suggesting ERα binding accompanied by cofactors is needed to maintain active transcription. The strong correlation between all HOXC genes and MIR196A in tumours, in contrast to normal tissues, suggests a consorted effort of multiple distal enhancers, possibly driven by extensive ERα binding. The reversal of MIR196A's prognostic value from good outcome in premenopausal women to poor outcome in postmenopausal women suggests a change in the regulation and expression of HOX genes through and following menopause, impacting breast cancer subtype development. The pathway to therapy resistance in ER+ tumours may involve de-repression and over-activation of promoter and enhancer elements, consistent with enhancer disruption reverting cells to a non-terminally-differentiated stem-cell-like state. As HOX genes are essential in embryonic development, they would be a valuable asset for tumour cells to sustain a stem-cell-like state, potentially driving therapy resistance.

Contradictions And Limitations
In the luciferase reporter assay, PP3 did not increase luciferase expression despite the binding of ERα falling within PP3, which contradicts the GRO-Seq finding of increased nascent RNA production at the same region. The CpG island associated with reduced breast cancer risk was found to lie within the transcriptionally active region of HOXC10 and MIR196A2, which is inconsistent with the traditional view of CpG islands as repressed transcription regions. The prognostic significance of MIR196A flips between pre- and post-menopausal ER+ patients, but the mechanistic basis for this reversal remains speculative and requires future investigation. It is currently unclear how dual-encoded miRNAs are regulated, and many exist in the genome, leaving the specific contribution of the two MIR196A loci as an open question. The study notes that high resolution chromatin interaction analysis of the HOXC locus in breast cancer cells, such as 5C or NG Capture-C coupled with ERα ChIP-Seq and ChIA-PET, would be required to fully test the multiple enhancer hypothesis. The paper is a bioRxiv preprint (May 23, 2018) and has not been confirmed by peer review at the time of writing, and the sample sizes for the METABRIC and clinical cohorts are not specified.

Claims
MIR196A2 is transcriptionally regulated by oestrogen through ERα binding at distal enhancers and the promoter, with physical looping confirmed by ChIA-PET and 3C. GRO-Seq shows a dramatic increase in nascent RNA at MIR196A2 peaking at 40 mins after oestradiol addition. ChIA-PET identified HDE and mE as major interacting sites with MIR196A2 promoters. 3C-qPCR demonstrated physical interaction between both enhancers and the MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter. Luciferase assays showed HDE is the most active enhancer in MCF7 cells. PP3 did not increase luciferase expression in the reporter assay despite ERα binding peak falling within PP3. Oestrogen-targeted therapies could be used to modulate MIR196A expression in ER+ breast cancer. The regulatory architecture (dual enhancers, shared promoter) is a model for other long-range ERα-mediated gene regulation.
High MIR196A expression is a prognostic biomarker of poor survival in ER+ breast cancer, particularly in post-menopausal patients and those resistant to therapy. In ER+ tumours, high MIR196A expression associates with 61% 10-year survival versus >95% for low expression. In postmenopausal women, high expression is associated with a poor outcome. ERα ChIP-Seq from non-responders and metastases showed increased ERα occupancy at MIR196A enhancer and promoter regions. MIR196A expression is significantly increased in tamoxifen-resistant and chemotherapeutic-resistant cell lines. In premenopausal women, high MIR196A expression is associated with a good outcome, contradicting the postmenopausal prognostic. In triple-negative breast cancer, high MIR196A expression associates with a better outcome. MIR196A could serve as a stratification marker to identify patients at risk of rapid progression in ER+ disease. The miRNA may be a target for therapeutic intervention in resistant ER+ disease.
MIR196A is almost depleted in fulvestrant-resistant cells but increased in tamoxifen-resistant and chemotherapeutic-resistant cells, indicating selective regulation in endocrine resistance. MIR196A is significantly increased in TAMR cells whilst almost depleted in FASR cells. MIR196A increases in paclitaxel and adromycin resistant MCF7 cells compared to treatment-sensitive cells. These expression patterns match DNA methylation changes to the HOXC10/MIR196A2 promoters in these same cells.  Resistance mechanisms in anti-estrogen versus anti-tamoxifen therapy involve distinct epigenetic signatures at the MIR196A locus.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study used qRT-PCR, RNA-Seq, and GRO-Seq independently to validate the oestrogen-dependent transcriptional increase at MIR196A2. DNA methylation data were correlated with both gene expression and clinical outcomes to strengthen prognostic claims. The 3C assay included control libraries undigested and unligated to assess HindIII digestion and ligation efficiency. Survival analysis included both univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazard regressions to control for covariates. A previous study by Jiang et al was cited to corroborate that mature MIR196A responds positively to oestrogen stimulation via ERα binding at PP3.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows ChIP-Seq and histone methylation data identifying a shared promoter with HOXC10 and methylation at the CpG island. Figure 1B presents GRO-Seq data showing the peak of nascent RNA at 40 mins after oestradiol and ChIA-PET data showing ERα/FOXA1 binding at PP1 and PP3. Figure 1C and D show qRT-PCR and RNA-Seq validation of oestrogen-induced MIR196A2 expression. Figure 2A shows ChIA-PET identifying HDE and mE as major interacting sites with the MIR196A2 promoters. Figure 2B shows 3C-qPCR results demonstrating physical interaction of both enhancers with the promoter region. Figure 2C shows luciferase reporter results comparing PP1, PP2, HDE, and mE activity. Figure 3A-C show MIR196A expression by cluster, correlation with hormone receptors, and PAM50 intrinsic subtype distribution. Figure 4A-D show METABRIC data including tumour stage correlation and survival curves for ER+ and TNBC. Figure 5A shows Kaplan-Meier curves for ER+ survival stratified by MIR196A, with pre- and post-menopausal groups. Figure 5B-D show expression in TAMR, FASR, and drug-resistant cells, and associated DNA methylation changes. Figure 5E shows ERα ChIP-Seq from human patients showing increased occupancy in non-responders and metastases. Table 1 reports multivariate analysis showing MIR196A as a significant biomarker for ER+ tumours arising before menopause.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the comprehensive characterization of MIR196A as an oestrogen-regulated, dual-locus miRNA whose transcriptional landscape includes ERα-tethered enhancer-promoter looping (HDE and mE) and specific oestrogen-dependent nascent RNA production. 2. The strongest evidence is the multi-technique validation of the regulatory architecture: GRO-Seq demonstrating oestrogen-dependent nascent RNA production specific to MIR196A2 (peaking at 40 mins), ChIA-PET and 3C confirming physical interaction between two distal enhancers and the shared HOXC10/MIR196A2 promoter, and luciferase assays identifying HDE as the dominant enhancer. 3. The future path should aim to uncover the precise mechanism of the prognostic flip between pre- and post-menopausal ER+ patients, determine whether the enhancer-promoter de-repression model is universally applicable, and investigate if MIR196A is required for resistance alone or in concert with other HOXC genes.

summary.title: Lack of negative density-dependence regulation in a dominant oak tree from a neotropical highland forest
summary.authors: Irene Calderón-Sanou, Luis Diego Ríos, Alfredo Cascante-Marín, Gilbert Barrantes, Eric J Fuchs
summary.field_subfield: Ecology / Tropical Forest Population Dynamics
summary.type_of_paper: Empirical field study with spatial statistics and GLMM modeling
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates whether conspecific negative density-dependence (CNDD), a proposed mechanism for regulating species coexistence and diversity, operates on seedling establishment of Quercus costaricensis, a monodominant oak in the Talamanca highland forests of Costa Rica. The authors tested the effects of conspecific seedling density, distance to the nearest adult, Chusquea bamboo shoot density, and herbivory on annual seedling survival and recruitment between 2014 and 2017 at the Cerro de la Muerte Biological Station (3100–3350 m a.s.l.). Using a sample of 3538 seedlings across four 400 m² plots, the researchers applied spatial statistics (Ripley's K-function) and generalized linear mixed-effects models with binomial and quasi-Poisson distributions. The central finding was that no CNDD effect was detected on seedling survival or recruitment, contradicting Janzen-Connell predictions. Instead, seedling survival was strongest at intermediate distances from adults (negative quadratic relationship), and bamboo density significantly reduced survival. Herbivory was ubiquitous (>99% of seedlings showed damage), but decreased at higher seedling densities, supporting the predator satiation hypothesis. In 2015, 1578 new recruits were recorded with 22.9% mean herbivory damage, significantly lower than 43.75% in the 2014 cohort. The authors propose that the lack of CNDD regulation, combined with potential predator satiation and ectomycorrhizal transfer from adults to seedlings, explains the dominance of Q. costaricensis in highland forests. Local density is instead regulated by herbivory and interspecific competition with Chusquea bamboo, which reduced seedling survival via resource competition, shade, and potential allelopathy.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates whether conspecific negative density-dependence (CNDD), a proposed mechanism for regulating species coexistence and diversity, operates on seedling establishment of Quercus costaricensis, a monodominant oak in the Talamanca highland forests of Costa Rica. The authors tested the effects of conspecific seedling density, distance to the nearest adult, Chusquea bamboo shoot density, and herbivory on annual seedling survival and recruitment between 2014 and 2017 at the Cerro de la Muerte Biological Station (3100–3350 m a.s.l.). Using a sample of 3538 seedlings across four 400 m² plots, the researchers applied spatial statistics (Ripley's K-function) and generalized linear mixed-effects models with binomial and quasi-Poisson distributions. The central finding was that no CNDD effect was detected on seedling survival or recruitment, contradicting Janzen-Connell predictions. Instead, seedling survival was strongest at intermediate distances from adults (negative quadratic relationship), and bamboo density significantly reduced survival. Herbivory was ubiquitous (>99% of seedlings showed damage), but decreased at higher seedling densities, supporting the predator satiation hypothesis. In 2015, 1578 new recruits were recorded with 22.9% mean herbivory damage, significantly lower than 43.75% in the 2014 cohort. The authors propose that the lack of CNDD regulation, combined with potential predator satiation and ectomycorrhizal transfer from adults to seedlings, explains the dominance of Q. costaricensis in highland forests. Local density is instead regulated by herbivory and interspecific competition with Chusquea bamboo, which reduced seedling survival via resource competition, shade, and potential allelopathy.

Research Context
CNDD is proposed as a main mechanism regulating species coexistence by reducing seedling survival in high-density patches. Tropical montane forests above 2500 m a.s.l. are commonly dominated by a few tree species compared to lowland forests. Quercus costaricensis represents over 90% of the basal stem area in the Talamanca mountain range. While temperate oaks show CNDD susceptibility, ectomycorrhizal transfer from adults can have a positive effect. CNDD regulation varies across species; common species may be less affected due to physiological traits or genetic diversity. Previous studies identified several traits influencing seedling tolerance to high conspecific densities, including shade tolerance and soil pathogen diversity. The processes structuring low-diversity tropical forests are not yet fully understood.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The main objective was to test for CNDD regulation on survival and recruitment of Q. costaricensis seedlings in highland Costa Rica. Specifically the study tested the effects of conspecific seedling density, distance to nearest adult, herbivory, and Chusquea bamboo density. Given the pronounced dominance and large seedling density of Q. costaricensis, the authors expected to find weak or no CNDD regulation. The authors also expected a positive effect of nearby adults on seedling recruitment, contrary to standard Janzen-Connell predictions. Chusquea bamboo, growing in dense clumps in the understory, was included as an important factor potentially limiting seedling survival. The hypothesis is that the lack of intraspecific density regulation at the seedling stage explains the oak's dominance.

Methodological Details
The study was conducted at Cerro de la Muerte Biological Station at 09°33' N, 83°44' W, between 3100 and 3350 m a.s.l. Four 400 m² plots (20 x 20 m) were placed in old growth forests undisturbed for at least 30 years. Plots were subdivided into 64 quadrats of 2.5 x 2.5 m for seedling censuses. A total of 3538 seedlings were mapped and tagged between 2014 and 2017. For each seedling, height, distance to the nearest conspecific adult, and conspecific seedling density in a 1 m radius were measured. Leaf damage was estimated using the qualitative index of herbivory developed by Núñez-Farfán and Dirzo. Bamboo stem density varied naturally among plots from 0 to 14 stems per m². The 2014 censuses were conducted before acorns had fallen to avoid newly germinated seedlings. Germination success in controlled conditions was 91% after 7 days. The 2014 fruiting year was considered the only masting event; less than 15% of adults reproduced in 2016. R statistical language (Version 3.2.2) with the spatstat library was used for spatial analyses. The lme4 package in R was used for the GLMM recruitment analysis.

Procedures And Architectures
The annual probability of seedling survival was modeled using a GLMM with a binomial distribution, standardizing all fixed effects. Variables included initial height, intraspecific seedling density, distance to nearest adult, herbivory, and Chusquea density as fixed effects. Quadrat and census year were included as random effects in the survival model. A dummy variable for age distinguished 2014 census seedlings from 2015 recruits. A second-degree polynomial effect for distance to nearest adult conspecific was included in the model. Full models included all variables and all second-order interactions. Spatial distribution was analyzed using the univariate Ripley's K-function with L(t)=(K(t)/π)0.5 transformation. Seedling recruitment per quadrat was analyzed using a GLMM with a quasi-Poisson distribution for the 2015 data. Plots were included as a random effect to account for spatial autocorrelation of seedlings within a plot. All explanatory variables were standardized to facilitate comparisons between effects.

Key Results
In the 2014 census, 2031 seedlings were mapped and tagged, showing spatial aggregation at all scales. Over 99% of censused seedlings had leaf damage, with approximately 71% showing intermediate damage of 10–75%. Contrary to Janzen-Connell, herbivory decreased at higher seedling densities and increased away from adults. Annual seedling survival dropped from 73.2% in 2015 to 64.38% in 2016 and 63.8% in 2017. Seedling height had the strongest positive effect on survival, while bamboo density and herbivory reduced survival. A significant interaction between seedling and Chusquea densities: high seedling density increased survival at low bamboo densities (<2.4 stems/m²) and decreased it at higher densities. Seedling survival was highest at intermediate distances from adults, following a negative polynomial function. In 2015, 1578 new recruits were recorded with 22.9% mean leaf damage (±1.06). Herbivory in 2015 recruits (22.9%) was significantly lower than in 2014 seedlings (43.75%), t = 25.798, p < 0.0001. Seedling recruitment significantly increased with conspecific seedling density, but failed to correlate with adult density or Chusquea density. Only five new seedlings were recorded in 2017 across all four plots, limiting recruitment analysis to the 2014 masting event. New recruits were easily identified in 2015 because cotyledons were attached to most seedlings even after one year. Only about 1% (15 seedlings) of 2015 recruits had leaves not fully developed for herbivory recording.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The absence of CNDD regulation on seedling survival and recruitment suggests that predator satiation at high density may protect seedlings. The positive effect of seedling density on recruitment suggests seeds are more likely to germinate in areas where they escape seed predation and herbivory. The negative quadratic relationship between survival and distance to adults suggests ectomycorrhizal transfer from adults facilitates seedling survival at intermediate distances. The lack of CNDD in a monodominant species aligns with observations in other masting tropical trees (Dipterocarps, Dicymbe corymbosa). Abundant species with high tolerance to leaf damage or long-lived leaves may accumulate only minor damage, contributing to weak CNDD. The study supports the Fricke and Wright (2017) prediction that dominant tropical trees are expected to have weaker CNDD regulation. Inter-specific competition with Chusquea bamboo and herbivory are identified as the primary regulators of local oak seedling density, rather than CNDD.

Contradictions And Limitations
The number of adults reproducing in 2016 was very low (<15%), limiting the analysis of 2016/2017 recruitment. Only five new seedlings were recorded in 2017, precluding recruitment analysis after the 2014 masting for that year. The study focused only on one species (Q. costaricensis), so results may not generalize to other highland or lowland oaks. Environmental factors like acidic soils, low temperatures, and high solar irradiance were noted but beyond the scope of the study. The qualitative index of herbivory (IH) is subjective and not quantified with precise damage area or species identification. Acorns were not produced in 2015, leaving a gap in annual cohort monitoring. Seed size effects were mentioned but not explicitly tested in this study design.

Claims
Conspecific negative density-dependence does not regulate seedling survival or recruitment of Q. costaricensis in tropical highlands. Annual seedling survival showed no significant CNDD effect in the GLMM. Herbivory, the primary agent of CNDD, decreased at higher seedling densities. Seedling survival remained above 62% annually despite high seedling densities. Seedling recruitment significantly increased with conspecific seedling density, a positive rather than negative response. Bamboo density and herbivory did significantly reduce seedling survival, suggesting density-related mortality from other factors. A significant interaction showed high seedling density decreased survival when Chusquea density was high. The lack of CNDD regulation explains why Q. costaricensis can achieve monodominance in Costa Rican highland forests. The study contradicts Janzen-Connell predictions for this species and may reshape theories on tropical forest composition.
Herbivore satiation and adult ectomycorrhizal facilitation operate at high seedling densities to eliminate CNDD effects. Herbivory decreased at higher seedling densities, supporting the predator satiation hypothesis. Survival was highest at intermediate distances from adults, suggesting ECM transfer from adults to seedlings. Higher survival after the 2014 masting (73.2%) when seedling number increased supports the satiation mechanism. The exact mechanism of ECM transfer was not experimentally validated in this study. Herbivory was still ubiquitous, with over 99% of seedlings showing damage. Seedlings escaping predation through density-dependent satiation provides a pathway for dense aggregation. Adult-to-seedling symbiont transfer may be a key mechanism in maintaining monodominance in oak-dominated forests.
Interspecific competition with Chusquea bamboo is a primary regulator of oak seedling density in highland forests. Bamboo density significantly reduced seedling survival in the GLMM. Bamboo clumps dominate the herbaceous layer, reducing resource space for tree seedlings. Bamboo water intake is very high, reducing water availability during low precipitation months. Chusquea could modify soil nutrients and litter thickness, hindering seedling development. Bamboo density did not correlate with seedling recruitment per quadrat. Management of bamboo could alter oak seedling establishment dynamics. The dense bamboo layer may constrain the maximum density that oak seedlings can reach.

Data And Code Availability
The authors state the preprint was posted to bioRxiv on May 23, 2018. The DOI is indicated as 10.1101/329177, but no specific repository or open data link is explicitly cited. The analysis was performed in R using the spatstat and lme4 packages.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A full model including all variables and all second-order interactions was built for the survival GLMM. The authors retained models including all variables of interest, significant interactions, and significant polynomial terms. The recruitment analysis included only 2015 data to isolate the year immediately following the masting event. Spatial autocorrelation was addressed by including plots as a random effect in the recruitment GLMM. Herbivory was recorded as a qualitative index, and no specific damage-area or species-identification quantification was reported. Seedling height was log-transformed and standardized before entry into the model. Standardization of all explanatory variables was performed to facilitate comparison of effects.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the Index of Herbivory distribution, with over 99% of seedlings having leaf damage and approximately 71% showing intermediate damage (10–75%). Figure 2 displays the partial effects of variables on seedling survival, highlighting the positive effect of height and the negative effects of bamboo density and herbivory. Figure S1 shows the spatial distribution of seedlings, demonstrating aggregation at all scales. Table S1 reports the full model output for survival, indicating significant interactions and retaining models with significant polynomial terms. Table S2 presents herbivory values (IH) by seedling density and distance to adult, showing herbivory decreased at higher densities.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is demonstrating the absence of CNDD regulation on seedling survival and recruitment of Q. costaricensis, contradicting Janzen-Connell predictions for this dominant oak. 2. The strongest evidence is the combined finding that herbivory decreases at higher densities, seedling survival remains high (>62%), and seedling recruitment significantly increases with conspecific density. 3. The future path involves testing if predator satiation and ECM facilitation are universal across dominant tropical trees, and investigating environmental factors like soil acidity and temperature that may modulate CNDD strength.

summary.title: Toxicity of TiO2, SiO2, ZnO, CuO, Au and Ag engineered nanoparticles on hatching and early nauplii of Artemia sp
summary.authors: Ch Lakshmi N Murthy; Mohammed M Idris; Shashi Singh
summary.field_subfield: Ecotoxicology / Nanomaterial Toxicology
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental research article reporting acute toxicity assays
summary.executive_summary: This study evaluates the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles (Ag, Au, CuO, ZnO, TiO2, SiO2) and three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, AgNO3) on Artemia sp. using a dual-endpoint approach: a hatching rate assay and a standard Artemia larval toxicity test. Nanoparticle physicochemical properties (size, aggregation, dispersion) were characterized in both Milli Q water and 25% NaCl salt water using TEM and DLS. Six nanoparticles at concentrations of 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L were tested in a hatching assay (24 h), and five concentrations (0.01–100 mg/L) were tested in a standard ARC toxicity protocol (up to 48 h). Oxidative stress was assessed using DCFDA and DHE fluorescence staining. The hatching rate dropped from a control mean of 74% ± 5.5% to ~29% in the presence of Ag and CuO at 100 mg/L, with only 50% of hatched nauplii viable. In the larval toxicity test, AgNO3 caused 80% mortality within 24 h, and Ag nanoparticles had an LC50 of ~10.12 mg/L at 24 h. A strong inverse correlation (r = -0.7853) was found between hatching rate reduction and larval mortality, with no statistically significant difference in paired T-test comparing viability and hatching rate (P = 0.683). The toxicity order was established as Ag > CuO > ZnO > Au > TiO2 > SiO2. The study concludes that the hatching rate of Artemia cysts provides a valid, cost-effective alternative or complementary end point to standard lethality tests for nanoparticle hazard identification.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study evaluates the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles (Ag, Au, CuO, ZnO, TiO2, SiO2) and three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, AgNO3) on Artemia sp. using a dual-endpoint approach: a hatching rate assay and a standard Artemia larval toxicity test. Nanoparticle physicochemical properties (size, aggregation, dispersion) were characterized in both Milli Q water and 25% NaCl salt water using TEM and DLS. Six nanoparticles at concentrations of 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L were tested in a hatching assay (24 h), and five concentrations (0.01–100 mg/L) were tested in a standard ARC toxicity protocol (up to 48 h). Oxidative stress was assessed using DCFDA and DHE fluorescence staining. The hatching rate dropped from a control mean of 74% ± 5.5% to ~29% in the presence of Ag and CuO at 100 mg/L, with only 50% of hatched nauplii viable. In the larval toxicity test, AgNO3 caused 80% mortality within 24 h, and Ag nanoparticles had an LC50 of ~10.12 mg/L at 24 h. A strong inverse correlation (r = -0.7853) was found between hatching rate reduction and larval mortality, with no statistically significant difference in paired T-test comparing viability and hatching rate (P = 0.683). The toxicity order was established as Ag > CuO > ZnO > Au > TiO2 > SiO2. The study concludes that the hatching rate of Artemia cysts provides a valid, cost-effective alternative or complementary end point to standard lethality tests for nanoparticle hazard identification.

Research Context
Nanomaterials with expanding diversity and unique properties pose increasing risks to the environment and human health, yet there is a dearth of information on their impacts. Most methodologies used in hazard identification are derived from chemicals in general, which may not be suitable for nanoparticles behaving differently from bulk materials. Aquatic systems are the inevitable receptacles for environmentally released nanomaterials, and filter feeders like Artemia are exposed via ingestion. Few studies have reported nanomaterial toxicity using Artemia sp., and hatching of hydrated cysts has not been established as an end point except in one study. Artemia are a non-selective filter feeder available worldwide in highly saline waters, making them a robust and cost-effective model for toxicological assays.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the hatching rate of Artemia cysts can serve as a valid bioassay end point to estimate acute nanoparticle toxicity. The study hypothesizes that the hatching rate and larval mortality will show good inverse correlation in sensitivity to nanoparticles, implying a second bioassay can be developed. It was predicted that the early developmental stages of Artemia would be highly vulnerable to the test nanomaterials despite the species generally being considered insensitive. The experiment aims to quantify the comparative toxicity of four metal oxide nanoparticles (TiO2, SiO2, CuO, ZnO) and two metal nanoparticles (Ag, Au). The study also intends to compare nanoparticle toxicity with soluble salt forms to distinguish between ionic and nanoparticle-specific effects.

Methodological Details
The study tested six engineered nanoparticles (Ag, Au, CuO, ZnO, TiO2, SiO2) and three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, AgNO3). Nanoparticles were obtained from the NANOVALID consortium: Nanologica AB (SiO2), Colorobbia (Ag), INMETRO (Au), Intrinsiq Materials (CuO), and Nanogate (ZnO). TiO2 particles were synthesized in-house using an existing protocol. Nanoparticle suspensions were prepared at 2 mg/mL for SiO2, TiO2, CuO, and ZnO, and sonicated at ~30 W with 50% pulse for 10 minutes. Silver nanoparticles were supplied at 4% with PVP as a stabilizing agent, and gold nanoparticles in water at 0.006%. Artemia cysts were from the San Francisco Bay strain, used at 1.0 gram per 1 litre culture. Cysts were hydrated in distilled water for 45 minutes, bleached with 20% sodium hypochlorite for 15 minutes, washed 6 times, and hatched in 25% salt water (pH 8.0). Temperature was maintained at 28°C, the optimum for hatching, and the experiment was repeated six times per nanoparticle type. In the hatching test, two concentrations (100 mg/L and 10 mg/L) were used, and results were recorded after 24 hours. In the standard toxicity test, 10 nauplii were transferred to six-well plates, and five concentrations (100, 10, 1, 0.1, 0.01 mg/L) were added. Viability was recorded at intervals of 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, and 48 hours. LD50 was calculated using Graphpad software, and correlation was assessed using online software and Microsoft Excel.

Procedures And Architectures
Nanoparticle characterization used TEM with a JEOL 2010 at 100 kV and 20 µ aperture on formvar-coated copper grids at 50 µg/mL. DLS measurements used a Horiba Nanopartica SZ100 system with suspensions at 25 µg/mL in Milli Q and salt water. Each DLS suspension was analyzed thrice over three days and reported as mean ± SEM. For the hatching test, three aliquots of 100 µL were taken from each flask after thorough mixing and counted under a stereo-microscope. The hatching test included continuous aeration to keep particles in suspension and continuous light for 24 hours. Oxidative stress was detected by treating nauplii with 10 µM DCFDA (dichlorofluorescein diacetate), imaged on a Zeiss Axiovert imager. Validity criterion for hatching was low mortality in the control; for the toxicity test, mortality was below 10% within 24 hours. The correlation test was performed between hatching rate and larval mortality across both datasets.

Key Results
Brine shrimp showed a control hatching rate of 74% ± 5.5% with viability of about 97%. In the presence of Ag and CuO nanoparticles at 100 mg/L, the hatching rate dropped to about 29%, with only 50% of hatched nauplii motile and viable. At 10 mg/L Ag nanoparticles, the hatching rate remained lower but viability was good at 85%. Copper oxide showed a hatching rate with better viability around 64% at 100 mg/L. Gold and silicon nanoparticles at 100 mg/L showed hatching rates at approximately 50–60%, with post-hatching mortality not being very high. TiO2 at 100 mg/L gave a hatching rate of 41.50% with 67.8% viability; at 10 mg/L it was 54% with ~90% viability. ZnO nanoparticles showed a hatching rate of 60% but caused cysts to clump together. In the larval toxicity test, AgNO3 (ionic silver) caused 80% mortality within 24 hours. The LC50 of Ag nanoparticles was approximately 10.12 mg/L at 24 hours. Other nanoparticles were nontoxic initially but caused concentration-dependent mortality after 30 hours. A very good inverse correlation between hatching rate reduction and mortality was found with a correlation coefficient of -0.7853. A paired T-test showed no statistically significant difference in mean viability and hatching rate across concentrations (P = 0.683). The final toxicity order was determined as Ag > CuO > ZnO > Au > TiO2 > SiO2.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The high toxicity of Ag and CuO could be due to ionic forms; centrifugation-resuspension confirmed that nanoparticle forms still cause toxicity. Even though ionic silver precipitates in high salinity, it still affected hatching and larval viability, suggesting nanoparticle-specific or residual ionic effects. The strong inverse correlation (r = -0.7853) implies that the hatching rate assay is a valid, simpler screening tool for nanoparticle hazard identification. Continuous aeration kept particles suspended, and the 24-hour duration eliminates the need for laboratory maintenance of test species, making the assay suitable for high-throughput use. DCDFA staining showed ROS in still-trapped nauplii and the gut of dead nauplii, particularly for Ag and CuO, suggesting oxidative stress and/or gut clogging as mechanisms. The use of cysts in batch cuts down variability, and the strict protocol makes the assay adaptable for hazard identification of nanomaterials.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study does not report the exact concentration of the control groups or the standard deviation for all control hatch rates beyond the 74% ± 5.5% value. There is no mention of the statistical significance tests applied to individual nanoparticle differences, only the correlation and paired T-test. The sedimenting behavior of particles by 48 hours in the ARC test was noted but not quantitatively characterized in terms of deposition rates. The exact number of cysts or nauplii per replicate in the hatching test is not explicitly stated (only aliquots of 100 µL are mentioned). The study notes no gross morphological abnormalities in nauplii hatched in the presence of nanoparticles, yet death occurred, suggesting a functional or biochemical mechanism rather than gross structural damage. The random seed or specific statistical tests (e.g., ANOVA vs. T-test) for multiple comparisons are not detailed.

Claims
The Artemia cyst hatching rate is a valid bioassay for nanoparticle toxicity screening. A strong inverse correlation (r = -0.7853) was found between hatching rate and larval mortality. The paired T-test showed no statistically significant difference between hatching rate and viability means (P = 0.683). The hatching rate dropped from 74% ± 5.5% to ~29% for Ag and CuO at 100 mg/L, mirroring the highest larval toxicity. Only one prior study ([14]) has used hatching of hydrated cysts as an end point, and earlier studies on metals [15–17] show the need for caution. The assay could be adopted for high-throughput nanoparticle hazard identification prior to validating for in vivo studies. Eliminating the need for laboratory maintenance reduces cost and time for toxicity screening.
Ag nanoparticles and CuO nanoparticles are the most toxic among the tested nanomaterials. Ag nanoparticles produced the lowest hatching rate (~29%) and an LC50 of ~10.12 mg/L. AgNO3 (ionic silver) caused 80% mortality within 24 hours, and Ag nanoparticles ranked very high in the toxicity order. The final toxicity ranking placed Ag first and CuO second among all nanoparticles. ZnO nanoparticles showed 60% hatching rate, which is better than Ag/CuO but lower than Au/TiO2/SiO2. Silver-based nanomaterials require heightened regulatory scrutiny in marine and aquatic environments.
Physicochemical behavior of nanoparticles changes significantly in salt water compared to Milli Q water. Silver, TiO2, CuO, and ZnO showed higher DLS values in salt water, while Au and SiO2 had lesser values. Visible flocculation and sedimentation were observed for CuO and ZnO nanoparticles in salt water by the third day. Ag, TiO2, and SiO2 did not show much difference in dispersion in Milli Q over three days but showed aggregate sizes in salt water on the third day.  Toxicity assays for nanoparticles must account for salinity-dependent dispersion, aggregation, and flocculation behaviors.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The hatching experiment was repeated six times with calculation of average and SEM for each sample. The nanoparticle suspensions were measured up to 48 hours to assess stability over time (Figure S1). A comparison between nanoparticle forms and soluble salt forms (AgNO3, CuSO4, ZnSO4) was conducted to assess ionic contributions to toxicity. Centrifugation and resuspension of nanoparticle suspensions confirmed that the nanoparticles themselves, not just released ions, contributed to toxicity.

Three Takeaways
1. The hatching rate of Artemia cysts is a valid and complementary bioassay end point to standard larval lethality tests for nanoparticle toxicity, with a strong inverse correlation (r = -0.7853). 2. Ag nanoparticles (LC50 ≈ 10.12 mg/L at 24 h) and CuO nanoparticles are the most acutely toxic among the six engineered nanoparticles tested on Artemia sp. 3. The future path involves adopting this assay for high-throughput nanoparticle hazard identification, with a need to account for salinity-dependent aggregation and flocculation in aquatic environments.
